en: The Vinaya-ksudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
Within these forty fascicles of the *Vinayakṣudrakavastu*, there are eight general sections; the grand framework is fully encompassed by one verse for each major section.
Within each of these sections, there are further sub-sections, which together comprise eight verses in total.
Within each of the distinct sections there are ten verses; together they comprise eighty-nine verses. Including the summary verses contained within, they total approximately one thousand lines.
If one can read, recite, and memorize them, one will be able to fully master their meaning.
The summary verse for the Great Gate says:
Bricks and stones, as well as cow hair; the three robes and the senior monk (sthavira);
relics and the sinews of a fierce beast; Gupatā and the nun; with the exception of the stūpa.
The first section of the Separate Gate, summarized in a verse, says:
Brick, rubbing, clipping nails, and the bowl; The mirror, the male organ, and stepping on robes;
The water filter, raw beans, and the bead; Washing the feet, the lower garment, and how it should be tied.
The first section, the first subsection, is summarized in verse as follows:
Bricks, rubbing with stone, white earth; Cow bezoar, incense, and [medicines] beneficial for the eyes;
Beating pillars and various cords; Garlands and seals—one should know these.
At that time, the Bhagavān was staying in the High Pavilion Hall beside the Monkey Pond in the city of Vaiśālī.
Then, during the first part of the day, the group of six bhikṣus took up their robes and bowls, intending to enter the city of Vaiśālī to beg for alms in succession.

Not far from the city was the grove of the Licchavis, a place secluded and serene where flowers and fruits flourished in abundance. Streams meandered through it and beautiful birds sang in harmony, like the Nandana Grove of Śakra, Lord of Devas. Within it were various implements for dispelling fatigue, as well as extraordinary musical instruments and other articles such as incense and bathing supplies.
At that time, the group of six monks said to one another:

"Nanda and Upananda! We have recently heard that this grove is lovely and that the World-Honored One constantly praises it as being like the Heaven of the Thirty-three. Let us go and see what magnificent sights it contains."

After the group of six had deliberated, they entered the park together and saw various long and short wooden pestles, hammers of diverse thicknesses, and stones of various sizes; all of these were intended for lifting and play, to exercise the body, disperse congestion, dispel ailments, and aid in the digestion of food.
Furthermore, he saw extraordinary and marvelous instruments for music, such as *kōnglǒu*, *qín*, *sè*, and various drums.

There were also incense and items for bathing, including floating bricks (*fúzhuān*) and cleansing powder (*zǎodòu*). The fragrant *yúgān* (myrobalan) fruit originates from Guangzhou; it is suitable for washing the hair.
In the West, it is called the *āmalaka* fruit; when used to rub the body or applied to the hair, it can turn white hair black again.

When the Group of Six saw this, they said to one another, "These various articles of pleasure fully satisfy our longing for sorrow. Now that we have exerted ourselves with toil, shall we first engage in singing, dancing, or bathing?"
One person said, "It has been a long time since we have bathed; it would be well for us to wash first.
Having reached this agreement, they all entered the pool together and immediately took floating bricks to scrub their bodies.

These six bhikṣus were all highly skilled and proficient in every craft; when they bathed and rubbed their bodies with bricks, various sounds of the five musical instruments would emerge, just as those skilled musicians produce sound by blowing, plucking, striking, and clapping.

At that time, a great multitude of people passed by; suspecting that music was being performed, they all listened intently and said to one another, "The Lumbinī Garden is filled with song and dance; we should go there for a moment to behold it."
The assembly all said,
"So be it," and immediately they vied with one another to enter the garden.
When the crowd entered, the group of six monks immediately went out and asked,
"Venerable ones! Where are the musicians now?"
He replied: "You foolish people, with ears that hear sounds yet minds deluded by likes and dislikes, how could anyone who finds pleasure in worldly things produce such wondrous and marvelous sounds?"
He asked, "Noble One! Who was it that produced the sound you just heard?"
He replied, "O noble one!
What you have heard was the sound produced by us while scrubbing our bodies with bricks at the time of bathing."
He replied, "Noble ones!
Do you venerable śramaṇas also have the five desires that afflict the body and mind?"
He replied, "Fool! We do not trouble others;
we enjoy sensual pleasures while not neglecting the cultivation of the path—what fault is there in this?"
"How could you, who are my teacher, act with such derision? You ought to remain silent and not invite calamity.
Hearing this, he became afraid and walked on with his mouth shut. Upon entering the city of Vaiśālī, at every crossroads, people raised clamorous discussions, each mocking and disparaging the other.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:
"For bhikṣus to scrub their bodies with bricks while bathing leads to such faults.
Therefore, bhikṣus should not use bricks to scrub their bodies as part of the bathing process."
"If one rubs the body with it, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

Since the Buddha did not permit rubbing the body with bricks, at that time the feet of the bhikṣus became covered in dust and grime and grew cracked and chapped. When they entered for alms, people saw them and spoke thus:
"Noble ones!..."
"Your feet are cracked and covered with much dust and grime; why do you not wipe them clean and maintain such an unsightly appearance?
He replied, "O worthy one!"
"The World-Honored One does not permit it.
They said, "Your bodies, O virtuous ones, are defiled; how can you be pure?"
The bhikṣus remained silent.
Having received the food, they returned to their quarters and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Previously this was established as a prohibition, but now it is permitted according to circumstances. I now allow the bhikṣus to rub their feet with bricks, but not any other part of the body.
If one rubs any other part, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
At that time, when the group of six saw that bricks were not permitted, they used pumice stones instead.
The Buddha said, "This also constitutes an offense against the Dharma (dharmātikrama).

The setting was the same as before. At that time, during the first part of the day, the bhikṣus took up their robes and bowls and entered the city to beg for food. They saw various brahmins using three fingers to take up white earth or white ash, smearing it upon their foreheads in three lines; those who so begged obtained much that was excellent and fine.
Having seen this, the group of six monks said to one another, "This is an excellent expedient; we should do likewise.
Thereupon, on another day, they drew three lines upon their foreheads and entered the city to beg for alms. Those who did not have faith saw them and laughed, saying:
"I now prostrate myself.
The group of six replied, "You fools do not understand the proper forms of etiquette; who is it that you ought to prostrate to?"
"Who should we pay homage to?
Those people replied, "We know only this:
whenever we see an elderly brāhmaṇa, we say..."
"Kneel and prostrate.
If one sees a bhikṣu, one should say:
"I pay homage."
“If that is so, why do you not pay respectful homage when seeing my bhikṣus, but instead speak of kneeling and bowing? He replied,
“Noble One!...”
"I observed that there were three lines upon the faces of you venerable ones; thus, I took you to be Brahmins and not Bhikṣus. We were ignorant of this, so please grant us your forgiveness.
The group of six remained silent.
At that time, having heard this, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:
"If there are bhikṣus who draw three lines across their faces, such a fault will ensue."
"Therefore, monks, one who draws three lines incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"Monks, one should not draw three lines with white clay."
Regarding this, when a bhikṣu was ill and a physician prescribed white clay to be smeared on his body, the bhikṣu did not dare to do so. He reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The former was an initial prohibition; this is a subsequent allowance."
"If a physician prescribes an ointment to be applied to the body, one may follow the physician's instructions and apply it without committing an offense.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, during the first watch of the day, the group of six bhikṣus took up their robes and bowls and entered the city to beg for food. They saw various brahmins applying *gorocanā* (cow bezoar) to their foreheads; as a result, they obtained much delicious food from those who were begging.
Having seen this, they said to one another, "This is an excellent expedient; we ought to do it.

Thereupon, on another day, they entered the city for alms with bezoar applied to their foreheads. When those who lacked faith saw them with their foreheads thus marked, they laughed derisively and said:
"I now prostrate! I now prostrate!
All questions and answers were as described above.
"We saw that your faces were adorned with ox-gall yellow pigment and thought you were Brahmins, not bhikṣus.
We were ignorant; we pray you will grant us your forgiveness."
The group of six monks remained silent.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:
"If there are bhikṣus who adorn themselves by marking their foreheads with ox-gallstone (gorocanā), such a fault will arise."
"Therefore, bhikṣus should not mark their foreheads with ox-gallstone (gorocanā); should any do so, they shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
When the Buddha had thus prohibited marking the forehead with ox-gallstone, there was a bhikṣu who had a malignant ulcer on his forehead; he went to consult a physician, saying: "O worthy one!"
"Please prescribe a remedy for me.
The physician replied, "Noble One!"
"Apply ox-gallstone (gorocana) to the four edges of the ulcer, and it shall be cured immediately.
The bhikṣu replied, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that does not permit the application of ox-gallstone to the forehead."
The physician replied: "Venerable One!
Your teacher is greatly compassionate; he will certainly grant permission if you are ill."
Having reported the circumstances to the Buddha, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The previous rule was an initial prohibition, but now I grant a further concession: except for cases involving illness or the instructions of a physician, one may use ox-gallstone (gorocanā)."
"If one acts thus arbitrarily, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The setting was as before: the six bhikṣus of the group of six, having applied fragrant ointments to their bodies, entered among the young novices and said to them, "Young men!"
"You all may smell my incense; how does it compare?
The people replied, "How could the Elder have applied scented ointment to his body!"
He replied, "I am wearing it. The other said:
"Elder! Scented ointments are worldly adornments; how could it be appropriate to apply them? He replied:
"I have already performed what was to be done, whether it be appropriate or inappropriate.
They all held him in contempt and collectively reviled him.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
“Monks, there are these faults in a monk wearing scented ointments on his body; therefore, a monk should not wear scented ointments on his body.
Should any do so, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.”

As the Buddha had taught that one should not be attached to ointments and perfumes, at that time there was a bhikṣu who was afflicted by illness and suffering; he went to a physician and asked, "O worthy sir!"
"Please prepare a prescription and medicine for me according to my illness. He replied, "Noble One!"
"If you apply ointment, you will recover.
He replied, "O noble one!"
"Could it be that I am now to experience sensual pleasure? He replied, "Noble One!"
"This is the medicine for this illness; nothing else can cure it.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I now grant permission: when a physician prescribes it, applying scented ointment is not an offense."

At that time, a sick bhikṣu, having applied fragrant ointments to his body, sat among the assembly and preached the Dharma to brahmins and householders, or went to the homes of laypeople; when people saw this, they criticized and disparaged him.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I shall now establish the rules of conduct for bhikṣus who have applied fragrant ointments.

If a bhikṣu has applied fragrant ointment to his body, he should not enter the assembly to sit, nor should he preach the Dharma to brahmins, householders, and others, nor should he go to the homes of laypeople."
If a bhikṣu has recovered from illness, he may then wash his body and join the assembly as he pleases; he is also permitted to preach the Dharma for others.
Should one fail to follow this disciplinary procedure, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (dharma-āpatti).
At that time, faithful brahmins, householders, and others brought ointments to offer to the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus would not accept them.
The householders said,
"Noble ones!..."
Before the Buddha appeared in the world, we all regarded non-Buddhist practitioners as the places where merit was cultivated.
Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, I regard you, O virtuous ones, as the great field of merit; why do you not accept the offerings I have brought?
"How could we abandon our wholesome provisions and depart for the next world?
We pray that you will grant us your compassion and accept this humble offering. The bhikṣu replied:
"I shall wait until I have questioned the Buddha.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should accept it."
Having accepted it, the bhikṣu threw it on the ground in front of that person.
The donor replied, "Noble One!..."
"We purchased this at a high price; how can we discard it?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "One should not accept something and then discard it lightly before its owner. Instead, you may offer it by smearing it upon the ground before the caitya of the Tathāgata."

"As the Buddha has taught, one should smear the ground before the *caitya* as an offering. At that time, after the bhikṣus had received this incense, they smeared it with their hands as an offering before the hair-and-nail *stūpa*. When the donor saw this, he spoke these words: "Noble One!"
How could I not know that there is a stupa for making offerings?
My intention was to give it to you, O Benevolent One.
I have already presented it before that Buddha-stupa.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who said:
"Once you have received the incense, apply it within the room.
He then used it to smear the door panels of his dwelling.
At that time, those people, thinking it was a Buddha hall, immediately prostrated themselves; the Buddha said:
"You should not do so," and they consequently applied the plaster beside the door, which resulted in the same fault as before.
The Buddha said:
"One should place it upon the wooden panel above the wall at the head of the bed and smell it from time to time with the nose.
Any fragrant substance that, when smelled, clarifies the eyes—do not harbor any doubt regarding this."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying on Mount Śiṃśapā in the Deer Park of the Forest of Fear.
Then Prince Bodhi, having completed the construction of the Kūjanaka Pavilion, invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha to his residence to offer them a meal as a celebration of its inauguration.
When the Blessed One arrived at the residence, he took his seat with the great assembly on the ground floor of the building to eat.
At that time, while it was mealtime, Upānanda struck a pillar of the building with his own hand, causing the structure to shake.
Then the person in charge of the offerings replied, "Noble One!
Prince Bodhi has newly constructed this pavilion, adorning it with one hundred and one kinds of colors and carvings. For what reason do you, O Venerable One, wish to damage and destroy it?"
Upānanda replied, "If a poor person conceives a mind of attachment toward this [object], where will they fall after the end of their life?"
"You have again conceived a craving for this; after your life ends, you shall fall among the *mahāgalagaṇḍa* (gargantuan goiter) spirits.
When that person heard this, he was filled with extreme revulsion and disdain.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:

“Monks, there is this fault in striking a pillar with the hand; therefore, a monk should not strike a pillar with his hand. One who violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The Buddha said:
“One should not strike a pillar with the hand.”

The group of six monks immediately struck him with their fists, shoulders, backs, feet, as well as bricks and stones, shaking him about; they again incurred censure and committed an offense identical to the previous one.
The Buddha said:
"Whatever the object may be, one must not strike [another] with it."
At that time, the group of six monks again beat walls and the ground. The Buddha said:
"Even if it be other objects, one must not beat them; whoever violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma."

The setting is the same as before. At the first part of the day, the six bhikṣus took their robes and bowls and entered the city to beg for alms. Seeing the brahmins wearing the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) and receiving much delicious food when begging, they said to one another:
"Nanda and Upananda!..."
"I have now obtained an excellent expedient; my body is at ease with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*).
Thereupon, on another day, he put on the sacred thread and entered the city to beg for alms. A person of lack of faith, seeing his sacred thread, gave rise to contempt and spoke these words:
"I now prostrate myself before you."
The questions and answers were the same as before, until the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:

"For a bhikṣu to wear the brahminical thread (brahmasūtra) results in such faults. Therefore, a bhikṣu should not wear the thread; should any wear it, they shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."

The setting is the same as before. While the group of six monks were begging for alms, they saw several brahmins whose bodies were adorned with exquisite incense and flowers, and who had five-colored threads tied around their arms; having received various cakes and foods and eaten their fill, they emerged from the houses with their physical forms appearing full and robust.
The six groups of monks said to one another: "Nanda and Upananda!
This is an excellent expedient; we should do it."
Thereupon, on another day, he tied five-colored threads around his arm and entered the city to beg for alms.
When the brahmins saw him, they felt contempt and said,
"I now prostrate before you."
The group of six monks mocked and ridiculed him, as described at length above, until the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"If bhikṣus tie five-colored thread around their arms, such faults will arise; therefore, bhikṣus should not tie five-colored thread around their arms."
"If anyone ties [a cord] around their arm, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
Since the Buddha did not permit tying cords around the arms, at that time there was a bhikṣu who was afflicted by illness; he went to a physician and asked, "O worthy one!"
"My body is afflicted by illness; I pray that you will prescribe a remedy for me.
He replied, "Noble One!..."
"Take threads of five colors, enchant them with mantras, and tie them around your arm; you will surely be cured.
He replied, "The World-Honored One does not permit this."
He replied, "Your Great Master’s compassion is his very foundation; since he has granted permission due to the circumstance of illness, there is no reason to doubt it.
Then the bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to tie a string as instructed by a physician for the sake of a medical condition; there is no offense.
When the Buddha permitted tying a string on the arm, the bhikṣus placed it on the front of the right elbow, which again led to criticism. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done in that way."
He then secured it behind his elbow, but the Buddha said,
"It should not be done.
He then tied it in front of his left elbow, but the Buddha said:
"It should not be; you ought to place the left elbow behind.
Because of this, the bhikṣu’s illness was subsequently cured, and he discarded the tied thread wherever he happened to be.
When the non-humans saw this, they all felt aversion and contempt, saying:
"O Noble One! Because you tied my name with a knotted thread and used this mantra, my illness has been cured; therefore, we now treat you with disdain."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not discard it anywhere at random; if one's own illness has not yet been cured, tie it to the corner of one's robe."
"If it is well-repaired, you may place it as you wish within the crevices of the walls or pillars.
The setting was as before: while the group of six monks were begging for alms, they saw various householders with their ornaments, such as necklaces and other finery.
Then those bhikṣus took various necklaces and bracelets for their hands and feet to adorn their bodies, and said to one another,
"Is this adornment not beautiful?
At that time, the worldly travelers taunted them, saying:
“Venerable ones!
With your heads shaven and the hair in your armpits long, how can there be any dignified beauty?
Is it not the case that you are entangled by the taint of passion?”
The group of six monks remained silent.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who thought to himself:
"There is such a fault in a bhikṣu wearing necklaces; therefore, a bhikṣu should not wear various necklaces or adorn his hands and feet."
"If one intentionally wears it, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

The setting is the same as before. At that time, some thieves came and stole from the monastic treasury as well as private belongings; because there were no records, the bhikṣus did not know when the items had been lost.
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣus, you may possess seals. At that time,
the group of six [monks] made their seals out of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and jade, adorning them with jewels upon finger-rings.
Upon seeing the laypeople, he immediately extended his hand to show them his ring and wished them:
"May you all be free from illness and long-lived. The laypeople asked:
"What is that on your finger? He replied, "O noble one!"
"This is a finger-seal, permitted by the Buddha.
Worldly people mocked them, saying: "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, engage in acts of pride;
they adorn their fingers with rings made of various jewels. They are not true śramaṇas, nor are they brāhmaṇas."
When the bhikṣus had heard this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus should not wear finger-rings or jeweled ornaments; they should use five kinds of materials for their seals."
These were brass, red copper, white copper, ivory, and horn.
The group of six monks engraved images of men and women engaged in unrighteous acts upon their seals; when the laypeople saw them, they mocked them, saying:
“Do you venerable śramaṇas still possess minds of lustful desire?”
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There are two kinds of seals:
first, those belonging to the Saṃgha; second, those that are private property."

If the great assembly approves, one should carve an image of the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, with two deer placed on either side, kneeling and bowing; beneath it, one should inscribe the name of the original donor who founded the monastery.
"If it is a private seal, one should have it carved as a skeleton image or in the shape of a skull, so that upon seeing it, one may give rise to a sense of weary detachment.
The summary verse for the second section of the first chapter says:
"Trimming the nails and hair, polishing the teeth; eating small fruits in the springtime."
Eagerly listen to the five kinds of medicine and the detailed explanation of the conditions for the arising of fire.

The setting was as before. At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having constructed the Jetavana monastery for the Buddha and the Saṅgha and having offered it to the great assembly, said to his barber:
"You should now go to the Jetavana grove and shave the hair and beards of the noble assembly."
Having received these instructions, that man went immediately to the garden.
At that time, the group of six monks were stationed at the monastery gate, watching one another without ceasing.
Then, as Upānanda was pacing back and forth in front of the monastery gate, he saw the barber approaching from afar and said to him:
"Welcome! Welcome, O noble one! Why do you appear so rarely, like the crescent moon at its first emergence?"
He said, "Noble One! The householder has sent me here to shave the heads of the assembly."
He asked, "Do you know how to trim fingernails? He replied:
"Noble one! This is my karma. He replied:
"Come and try your skill.
The man then stepped forward; the Venerable One extended his hand, and the craftsman said, "Noble One!"
"How should it be trimmed?
"O Noble One! In the shape of a grain of rice."
He did exactly as instructed, and further said:
"It should be made in the shape of a human head, or like the curve of a razor, or like the edge of an axe, or like a half-moon."
Following the Venerable’s instructions, they did everything as told; afterwards, he said to them:
"You foolish men! You falsely claimed to be skillful while knowing nothing at all. You should be cut down level with the ground and released; go away quickly!"
Thus it continued until dusk, when he finally spoke of returning.
After twilight had fallen, he arrived at the householder’s residence, and the householder asked him:
"With how many people did you go to shave off their hair and beards?"
He replied: "How could I have the leisure to shave my hair along with the great assembly?
The official monk Upānanda has ordered me to remove my armor and assume various postures, as described at length above, until finally at sunset I was barely released. What else could I possibly do?"
Upon hearing this, the householder conceived a sense of aversion, thinking:
"Though he has gone forth in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, his mind is not at peace.
When the bhikṣu heard this, he informed the Buddha. The Buddha then reflected thus:
"Monks, there are such faults in clipping one's nails; therefore, monks should not clip their claws.
Should anyone violate this, they shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
Since the Buddha did not permit the clipping of nails, the fingernails of the monks all grew long. When laypeople saw them, they asked:
"Why are your nails so long?
He replied, "The World-Honored One does not permit them."
He replied, "Is it considered pure to keep one's fingernails long?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"What was previously established as a restrictive rule is now further relaxed according to circumstances.
There are two methods for clipping the nails:
first, in the shape of a razor; second, in the manner of a hatchet's edge."
The setting is the same as before. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada sent a barber into the monastery to shave the heads of the assembly; the details are as explained previously, up until he asked:
"Do you know how to polish fingernails?"
He replied, "Noble One! This is my karma."
He replied, "Come and try to see it; first it becomes yellow, then red, then white, and finally golden."
They did everything exactly as they were instructed.
He then said to them: "You foolish people!"
"His deceptive words are clever, yet he understands nothing at all; it would be best to smooth things over and let him go quickly.
When they arrived at the elder's place, what further did they intend to do?
Upon hearing this, the elder gave rise to even greater resentment, as described in detail above.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha reflected:
"There is such a fault in a bhikṣu’s polishing of his nails; therefore, a bhikṣu should not polish his nails."
"Whoever violates this shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

Since the Buddha did not permit bhikṣus to file their nails, when the bhikṣus dyed their robes or fumigated their alms-bowls, dirt would accumulate on their nails, making their appearance unsightly. When householders saw them holding their bowls while begging for food, they spoke thus:
"Noble One!..."
"Why are your fingernails so unclean?
He answered with the facts of the matter, and [the other] replied: "Noble One!"
"Why do you not scrape it off?
He replied, "The World-Honored One does not permit it."
He replied, "How can that which holds filth upon its nails be pure?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When removing impurities, one may polish the nails, but one should not rub them to make them shine for the sake of beauty.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, King Bimbisāra had this thought:
"Whenever the seasons change between spring and autumn, I shall first offer the new grain and the first fruits to the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones, and only afterwards eat them myself."
At that time, the minister presented some freshly ripened *āmra* fruits—fruits as large as peaches, whose degree of ripeness is difficult to discern.
There are four distinct varieties:
the *āmalaka*, which is as large as a jujube and fit only for medicinal purposes, was offered to the Great King.
The King said,
"Take these fruits and first offer them to the Buddha and the Sangha.
The minister then smiled, whereupon the King said:
"Why do you smile? He replied,
"Does Your Majesty think that I have not yet served the Buddha and the Sangha?"
"I have already offered it previously.
The King said, "I fear you may not know: for this reason, I now offer to the Noble Assembly a grove of fruit trees consisting of one thousand trees."
He replied, "This is indeed a wondrous matter; I truly rejoice in it.
He then immediately offered a grove of a thousand fruit trees to the holy assembly of all four directions, and further established a great assembly to celebrate and honor the field of merit.

In former times, this grove produced fruit in such great abundance that even if all the people of the kingdom of Magadha were to gather together for a great assembly and eat of these fruits, they would have been fully satisfied.

After the King had offered this grove to the Saṃgha, the bhikṣus, seeing that the fruits were small yet possessed a fragrant and delicious aroma when young, all came to eat them until they were completely exhausted.
Another king required this fruit and sent a messenger to King Bimbisāra to request an *āmra* tree.
The king said to the messenger:
"I have already given my orchard to the community of monks; you may now go there and ask for it from among them."
The messenger went to the Bamboo Grove Monastery. At that time, the group of six monks were always at the monastery gate, taking turns to keep watch without fail.
Upānanda was walking in the vicinity of the gate when the messenger arrived, prostrated at the Venerable’s feet, and said:
“Noble One!...”
"I am an envoy of a certain king; the king has sent me here to seek *āmra* fruits. If you, sir, have any, I would be grateful if you would share some with me.
Upānanda replied to the messenger, "You may now go to the orchard and take as many as you wish, according to your desire."
The messenger went to the grove and searched everywhere; seeing only bare branches and not a single fruit, he returned and reported that the empty grove was fruitless.
Upānanda then took the messenger with him into the woods, and after searching thoroughly, he said, "You may climb this tall tree."
The messenger immediately climbed up; however, not seeing the fruit, he was told again:
"Climb onto the eastern branch.
He was made to climb the southern, western, and northern branches as well. Having ascended them all without finding anything at last, he descended from the tree and asked:
“Noble one! Is it that this grove has no fruit this year? He replied:
“Worthy one! Just as there were fruits last year, so it is this year.
“If that is so, did the wind and rain cause the fruits to fall this year?”
He replied, "No. He asked:
"What was missing? They replied,
"When this fruit was small, we ate it all."
Then that messenger returned to the king's presence and reported the matter in full.
The king said, "Excellent!"
"I originally intended in my heart to have the noble assembly eat.
The messenger, feeling dejected, took his leave and returned to his own country.
At that time, there was a great assembly in the kingdom of Magadha where many people had gathered, and they asked the bhikṣu:
“Noble One! Why is it that this year none of the fruit trees in the grove have borne fruit? He replied:
“O noble one! It is not that they have not borne fruit; rather, we have eaten them all. He replied:

“Noble ones! Whenever these fruits ripened in the past, all the people within the realm of Magadha had their needs fully satisfied by eating them; yet because you have consumed them all from childhood, there are now none remaining.”
"This is not a virtuous deed.

He replied, "As for this fruit grove, the King did not give it to you or the people of the kingdom, but offered it solely to the Saṃgha; therefore, that we eat from it together—what fault is there in this?"
When the multitude of people heard these words, they all felt resentment and shame, saying:
"If even the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know contentment, how much less so we, the worldly laity?"
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"Because there is this fault in eating fruit, the bhikṣus should not eat fruit."
"If one eats it, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma. As the Buddha said:
"One should not eat fruit."
At that time, a faithful householder brought some small mango fruits to offer to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus replied,
"The Buddha has not permitted us to eat them."

The elders said, "Before the Buddha appeared in the world, we all took non-Buddhist practitioners as our field of merit," and so on, as extensively described above, until: "...out of compassion, he accepted my humble offering."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When the seeds have become hard, there is no offense in eating them.
Furthermore, a faithful householder came with ripe *āmra* fruits to offer to the bhikṣus; the details are as previously described, up until: "Please accept this humble offering of mine."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not dare to accept the food. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Once the kernels have become hard, and even until they are thoroughly familiarized, you should eat them; do not harbor doubts."
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was afflicted by illness and suffering; he went to a physician and said, "I have such-and-such a painful illness; I beg you to prescribe a remedy for me."
The physician replied, "It would be appropriate for you to consume ghee to moisten your body; I shall then administer a purgative.
He then consumed the ghee.
Furthermore, he suffered from thirst, and a physician came and asked,
"Noble One, are you well?"
He replied, "O worthy one! I am further afflicted by thirst."
The physician said,
"Take some *āmalaka* fruits.
The bhikṣu held them in his hand, and seeing this, the physician asked:
"Has your thirst been relieved?
He replied, "It has not been relieved."
The physician said,
"Venerable One! How can you not carry āmalaka fruit?"
He replied, "It is right here in my hand. The other said:
"You may place it in your mouth.
He then placed it in his mouth. On another day, the physician came again and asked:
"Have you been able to quench your thirst?"
He replied, "It is still not yet possible.
The physician said:
“Do you not have an āmalaka fruit in your mouth?
He replied,
“It is already in my mouth.”
"One should chew it. He replied, "The World-Honored One has not permitted this."
The physician said,
"The World-Honored One, out of great compassion, will surely grant permission.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should chew it.
Having chewed it, he discarded the exterior portion but did not dare swallow it; yet his thirst was still not relieved.
The physician said:
"Why do you not swallow the broth? He replied,
"The World-Honored One does not permit eating at improper times."
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I now grant permission: there are five kinds of fruit which, whether one is ill or not, and whether it is the proper time or not, may be eaten without offense."
As the Buddha has said:
"There are five kinds of fruits which, whether one is ill or not, and whether it is the proper time or not, may be eaten without offense.
The bhikṣus did not know what these five were.
The Buddha said:

"That which is called *āmalaka*—in Sanskrit, *āmala-ka*, here translated as 'remaining-sweet' (*yú-gān-zǐ*)—is abundant in Guangzhou. It is entirely distinct from the aforementioned *āmra* (mango), yet because their sounds are similar, people are often confused by them. Therefore, I have annotated this for those who observe it in the palm of their hand, along with *harītakī*, *bibhītaka*, *pippalī*, and black pepper."
"These five medicines—whether one is ill or not, whether it is the proper time or not—one may eat at will according to one's inclination;
do not harbor any doubt. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle One. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.
Volume Two, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. The Second Section of the First Chapter:

The Remaining Verses of the Summary, and the Discourse on the Causes and Conditions of the Householder Agnidatta. The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha. At that time, there was a householder in this city named Bhadra, who possessed great wealth and enjoyed abundant resources. He placed deep faith and reverence in the naked ascetics (nirgranthas). Not long after he had taken a wife, she became pregnant.

At that time, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One took up his robe and bowl and entered the city of Rājagṛha. Proceeding on his almsround, he arrived at the residence of the householder Bhadra.
When the householder saw the World-Honored One from afar, he led his wife to where the World-Honored One was and addressed him, saying: "Bhagavān!..."
"My wife is pregnant; will it be a boy or a girl?
The Buddha said, "Householder!"

"This shall certainly be a son who will bring glory and prosperity to his family; he will be fully endowed with the wondrous marks of the devas, and having gone forth to practice within my Dharma, he will sever all afflictions and attain the fruit of Arhatship."
Upon hearing this prediction, the elder immediately filled the Buddha’s bowl with pure and exquisite cakes and food, and presented it to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "May you be free from illness."
He departed from the house.
Not far from there was a naked ascetic (nirgrantha) who, seeing the World-Honored One from afar, thought to himself:
"I have only this family that regularly provides me with food, yet they too have been seduced and gathered in by the śramaṇa Gautama."
"I shall now go and inquire about the circumstances of his prediction;
what was the prophecy he received? Having arrived at the gate, he asked the householder, "Has the śramaṇa Gautama ever come here before?"
He replied, "I have come. [The other asked,] "What did he say?"
“Noble One! My wife is pregnant, and I asked her what she would give birth to.

She prophesied that she would bear a son who will bring glory to our family, one endowed with all the sublime marks of humans and devas; he will renounce the world to practice within my Dharma, exhaust all afflictions, and attain the fruit of Arhatship.”

At that time, those non-Buddhists were well-versed in calendrical calculations; they immediately observed and computed the movements of the yin and yang, finding that it was no different from what the Buddha had said.

Thereupon, they thought to themselves: "If we follow along and praise the truth of the matter, the householder will develop even greater reverence for him. We should now conceal the reality and speak falsehoods."
Having had this thought, he immediately turned his palm over and struck the man's face with it.
Upon seeing this, the elder asked,
"Noble One!..."
"You turned over your hand and wiped your face;
what were you doing? He replied, "Householder!"
"What the śramaṇa has said is half true and half false.
The householder asked, "In what way is it false and in what way is it true?"
He replied, "It is true that a male child has been born, and it is no falsehood that he will bring glory to the family.
As for 'bringing glory,' this is a synonym for fire; this son of no merit, as soon as he is born, shall consume his family."
To say that the gods possess all the sublime marks in their entirety is a false statement;
Elder, have you ever seen anyone born among humans who possessed the complete marks of a god?
To leave the household life and practice within my Dharma is also true;
yet, having been born into poverty and destitution, lacking clothing and food, one naturally turns toward the way of the śramaṇas.
To claim that one has exhausted all afflictions and attained the fruit of Arhatship is also a falsehood;
even the śramaṇa Gautama cannot sever all defilements to attain Arhatship, let alone his other disciples.
Having heard these words, the householder Bhadra became distressed and replied, "Noble One! What am I to do?"
The non-Buddhist said:
"Householder! I am one who has left the household life and upholds the prohibitive precepts; I do not speak falsely. Whether matters are true or false shall be known of itself in the future."
He then abandoned him and departed.
Sudhana thought to himself:
"The one within his belly can be killed and cast away."
He then administered an abortifacient drug;
however, as this was the child’s final birth, although he knew it was poison, it instead became a beneficial medicine.
The elder then pressed the woman’s left flank, causing the fetus to move to her right side.

When it moved from the right side to the left, the woman finally gave birth; since all the outflows (*āsrava*) of a human being have not yet been extinguished, there is absolutely no possibility that his life could have ended in the interim.
Having already passed many months, the woman’s abdomen was so tormented by the pressure that she cried out in great pain.
At that time, the neighbor heard his cries and came in haste to inquire:
"For what reason is your wife making such a loud outcry? The elder replied:
"My wife has abdominal pains and is now about to give birth.
The neighbor then returned home, and the elder thought to himself:
"I cannot harm the being within her womb; it would be better to take her to a desolate forest where no one is and end her mother's life."
They immediately went together and employed wicked means to cause her death; they then secretly brought her back to their original home and informed their relatives and neighbors:
"My wife met with misfortune and has now suddenly passed away."
At that time, all the relatives together exhausted their grief; they wrapped the corpse in five-colored silks and escorted it to the cold forest cremation grounds.

Upon hearing this, the non-Buddhists were filled with great joy and could not contain their exultation; they erected banners and streamers and entered the royal city, proceeding through every lane, alley, and thoroughfare, shouting at the top of their voices: "Proclaim thus!"

"All of you must consult together regarding the prediction made by the śramaṇa Gautama that the wife of the elder Bhadra would give birth to a son who would cause his family to flourish, who would be endowed with the wondrous marks of humans and devas, and who would leave the household life to practice within my Dharma, exhausting all afflictions to attain the fruit of arhatship. Now that the woman has died and her corpse has been sent to the cold forest, she is like a great tree whose roots have been severed; to what, then, can its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits be attached?"

It is the natural law for the World-Honored One that at all times he observes sentient beings such that there is none he does not see or hear, and none he does not know. He constantly gives rise to great compassion to benefit all, being foremost among those who provide rescue and protection; he is most heroic and valiant, his word is never twofold, and he abides in concentration and wisdom, manifesting the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*). He has skillfully cultivated the three trainings and well regulated the three karmas; he has crossed the four torrents and established himself in the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Throughout the long night, he has practiced the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); he has abandoned the five hindrances, distanced himself from the five factors, and transcended the five paths of rebirth. His six sense faculties are complete, the six perfections are fulfilled, and he universally bestows the seven riches while opening the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment. Free from the eight difficulties, he cultivates the eightfold noble path; he has forever severed the nine fetters and is exquisitely proficient in the nine meditative absorptions. He is perfected in the ten powers, and his fame resounds throughout the ten directions.
He is the most preeminent among all sovereigns; having attained fearlessness in the Dharma, he subdues the hosts of Māra and his enemies, and with a great thunderous voice, he utters the lion’s roar.
Throughout the six periods of day and night, he constantly observes the worlds with the Buddha-eye, discerning who is increasing in the roots of goodness.
Who is declining?
Who is encountering suffering and calamity?
Who is heading toward the evil destinies?
Who is mired in the mire of desire?
Who is capable of receiving transformation?
By what skillful means can they be rescued and brought forth?

He causes those who lack the noble wealth to obtain it; with the medicinal ointment of wisdom, he breaks the film of ignorance. He causes those without roots of goodness to plant them, and those with roots of goodness to cause them to increase. He places them upon the path of humans and devas, leading them safely and without hindrance toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
As it is said in a verse:
"Even if the tide of the great ocean Should ever miss its appointed time;
The Buddha, in regard to those he transforms, Never fails to deliver them at the proper moment."
"The Buddha, toward all sentient beings, With compassion never abandons them;
Thinking to rescue them from their suffering, Like a mother cow following her calf.
At that time, the World-Honored One, while on his walking path, smiled; from his mouth issued subtle light of five colors, which at times shone downward and at other times ascended upward.
The light that descends reaches as far as the Avīci Hell and other hells; those currently undergoing intense heat obtain universal coolness, while those situated in cold ice receive warmth.
Those sentient beings each attained peace and happiness, and all had this thought:
"Have you and I died from hell and been reborn in another place?"
At that time, after the World-Honored One had caused those sentient beings to give rise to faith and confidence, he further manifested other signs.
Having seen these signs, they all thought:
"We have not died here to be reborn elsewhere; rather, it must be due to the power of the majesty of the Unsurpassed Great Sage that our bodies and minds now experience such peace and happiness."

Having given rise to reverent faith, they are able to extinguish all sufferings and receive superior and wondrous bodies within the realms of humans and devas; they shall become vessels for the Dharma and perceive the principles of the True Truths.
Those who ascend reach the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, where amidst the light they proclaim the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and further recite two verses:
"You should seek liberation, And diligently practice the Buddha's teaching."
Subdue the army of birth and death, as an elephant destroys a thatched hut.
Within this Dharma and Vinaya, always remain heedful;
you shall dry up the ocean of afflictions and reach the end of suffering.
Then that radiance illuminated the trichiliocosm and returned to the place where the Buddha was.
If the Blessed One was to speak of past events, the light entered through his back;
if he was to speak of future events, the light entered through his chest.
If he speaks of matters concerning the hells, the light enters through the soles of his feet;
if he speaks of matters concerning animals, the light enters through his heels;
if he speaks of matters concerning hungry ghosts, the light enters through his toes.
If he speaks of matters concerning human beings, the light enters through his knees;
if he speaks of matters concerning a powerful wheel-turning king (*balacakravartin*), the light enters through the palm of his left hand;
if he speaks of matters concerning a universal wheel-turning king (*cakravartin*), the light enters through the palm of his right hand.
If he speaks of matters concerning the devas, the light enters through the navel;
if he speaks of matters concerning the śrāvakas, the light enters through the mouth;
if he speaks of matters concerning the pratyekabuddhas, the light enters between the eyebrows.
If he speaks of the matter of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the light enters through the crown of his head.
At that time, the radiance circled the Buddha three times and entered through his mouth. Then, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, does not smile with joy without cause or condition.
He then spoke a verse to request the Buddha, saying:
“From his mouth issue various wondrous rays of light, Flowing and filling the great trichiliocosm in manifold forms;”
Pervading all lands throughout the ten directions, like the radiance of the sun filling all of space;
the Buddha is the most supreme cause for sentient beings, able to remove arrogance as well as grief and sorrow.
Without a specific cause, he does not open his golden mouth; this smile must surely herald something extraordinary.
The serene and discerning Honored Sage, who delights in speaking for those who wish to hear, roars like the great lion king; we pray that you will resolve our doubts.
Like the King of Wondrous Mountains within the great ocean, Which does not shake unless there is a cause or condition;
You, with sovereign compassion, manifest a smile, To explain the causes and conditions for those who look up with longing.
At that time, the Blessed One said to Ānanda: “So it is, so it is, Ānanda!”
It is not without cause or condition that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, suddenly manifests a smile.
You should now inform the bhikṣus:
"The Tathāgata now wishes to go to the cemetery."
"Venerable ones, those who wish to follow may take their robes.
Then Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, addressed the bhikṣus:
"Venerable ones, those who wish to go with the Buddha to the charnel ground may take their robes."
Then all the bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Great Teacher, being himself disciplined, was surrounded by those who were disciplined; being himself tranquil, he was surrounded by those who were tranquil;
being liberated, he was surrounded by those who were liberated; being secure, he was surrounded by those who were secure; being well-composed, he was surrounded by those who were well-composed.
He was surrounded by arhats, surrounded by those who were arhats; he was surrounded by those free from desire, surrounded by those who were free from desire;
he was surrounded by those who were dignified and majestic, surrounded by those who were dignified and majestic. He was like a sandalwood tree surrounded by sandalwood trees;
like a king of elephants surrounded by a herd of elephants; like a lion king surrounded by lions; like a great bull king surrounded by cattle.
He was surrounded like a king of geese by his flock of geese, like a garuḍa by various birds, like a brahmin by his disciples, like a great physician by his patients,
like a great general by his army, like a great guide by his caravan, and like a great king [by his subjects].
Surrounded by his ministers, like a wheel-turning monarch surrounded by a thousand sons; like the bright moon surrounded by the multitude of stars;
like the solar orb surrounded by a thousand rays of light; like the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by a host of gandharvas;
like the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka surrounded by a host of kumbhāṇḍas; like the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa...
The King was surrounded by a host of nāgas, like the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa surrounded by a host of yakṣas;
like the King of the Pure and Sublime (Sudharmarāja) surrounded by a host of asuras; like Śakra surrounded by the thirty-three gods;
like the Great Brahmā King surrounded by the Brahma-hosts; and like the great ocean, serene and tranquil. Like...
Great clouds gather and hang low, like an elephant king who has stilled his wild intoxication.

His faculties are subdued and his deportment is tranquil; he is adorned with the thirty-two marks and embellished by the eighty minor characteristics. A halo one fathom wide outshines a thousand suns; he advances slowly with steady steps, like a moving mountain of jewels. Possessing the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness, he has universally cultivated boundless merit and wisdom, such that all immeasurable virtues are fully perfected.

Furthermore, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Bāṣpa, the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Kāśyapa, the Venerable Ānanda, and the Venerable Khāṇu-putra—these and other great śrāvakas, along with the bhikṣus and a vast assembly of billions of humans and devas, respectfully surrounded him as they set out for the Śītavana charnel ground.
However, there are eighteen kinds of extraordinary benefits in following the Buddha on his travels:
first, freedom from fear of kings;
second, freedom from fear of thieves.
Third, no fear of water;
fourth, no fear of fire;
fifth, no fear of hostile nations.
Sixth, there is no fear of lions, tigers, wolves, or other predatory beasts;
seventh, there is no fear of barriers or checkpoints;
eighth, there is no fear of ferry tolls or taxes.
9. No fear of lack of protection;
10. No fear of humans; 11. No fear of non-humans.
Twelfth, from time to time one obtains visions of the various devas;
thirteenth, one hears the voices of the devas;
fourteenth, one beholds great radiance.
Fifteenth, hearing the sound of the bestowal of prophecy;
sixteenth, together receiving the sublime Dharma;
seventeenth, together partaking of food and drink.
18. His body was free from the suffering of illness.
At that time, the great assembly of humans and devas followed the World-Honored One to the charnel ground; there, a cool breeze blew from all four directions.
At that time, there were two youths in the city of Rājagṛha:

one was of the Kṣatriya caste and the other was of the Brāhmaṇa caste. They both went out to play together; the youth of the Kṣatriya caste had long possessed faith, whereas the youth of the Brāhmaṇa caste lacked faith and respect.
Then the Brahmin youth replied to the Kṣatriya youth, saying: "Do you know now?

Your teacher, the Tathāgata, has granted a prophecy to the wife of the householder Bhadra that she will give birth to a son who will bring glory and prosperity to his family, who will be fully endowed with the wondrous marks of the devas, and who, having left the household life to practice within my Dharma, will exhaust all afflictions and attain the fruit of Arhatship."
"Since that woman’s body has died and been sent to the charnel ground, is not what the World-Honored One said false?
Then the Kṣatriya youth spoke these verses:
"Even if the stars and moon were to fall, And the earth, mountains, forests, trees, and the sky [were to collapse];"
"The great waves of the ocean shall all vanish at once; what the Great Sage has spoken is without falsehood.
The Brahmin youth said, "If it is so, let us go together to the Cool Grove (Śītavana) where corpses are cremated to verify its truth or falsity."
He replied, “We are traveling together.
At that time, the Kṣatriya youth saw the Blessed One from afar and spoke this verse:
“The Muni has severed all frivolous play; the great assembly of humans and devas has gathered like clouds.
He shall now let forth the most excellent lion’s roar, subduing the arguments of others without doubt.”
The Great Master now departs for the charnel ground; A cool breeze blows everywhere across the cold wilderness.
Countless sentient beings gaze upon him together, Joyfully beholding the Tamer as he exercises his supernormal powers.
At that time, King Bimbisāra heard these matters:

"The World-Honored One has prophesied that the wife of that Subhadra shall give birth to a son who will cause his family to flourish; he will be fully endowed with the wondrous marks of the devas, and having gone forth to practice within my Dharma, he will exhaust all afflictions and attain the fruit of Arhatship."

"That woman has now died and her bier has been brought to the charnel ground; the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, along with his śrāvakas and the great assembly from near and far, have all flocked to the place of mourning.

He further thought: "It cannot be without cause or condition that the World-Honored One has suddenly gone toward the Cool Grove (Śītavana). It must surely be for the sake of that wife of Bhadrika, so as to discipline those sentient beings who are connected to him through these circumstances."
"I should now go forth to witness this event together.
He immediately ordered the military regalia to be quickly readied and commanded the Crown Prince, the ladies of the inner palace, and all the attendants to depart from the city gates together.
At that time, the Kṣatriya youth saw King Bimbisāra from afar and spoke these verses:
"Now I see the lord of the land departing from the royal city, Accompanied by all his military hosts as attendants;
As I now reflect upon this great multitude, I am certain they shall all receive supreme benefit."
When the great assembly saw the World-Honored One, they cleared a path for him; the World-Honored One smiled as he entered the midst of the crowd. The naked ascetics each had this thought:
"Now that Gautama enters the assembly with a smile, could it be that this boy’s life has not yet come to an end?"
He said to the householder,
"This is a being of meager merit whose life-force has not yet ended. He replied:
“Noble One! Having now encountered this calamity, what do you intend to do? He replied:
“Householder! We are renunciants who uphold the prohibitive precepts and know only to dwell upon what is wholesome; you shall know this for yourself later.

Then the householder moved his wife’s corpse onto a pyre of wood and set it ablaze. When the fierce flames broke out, her body was completely consumed by the fire, yet the area near her abdomen remained entirely unharmed.

At that time, the mother’s abdomen suddenly split open, and from within emerged a blue lotus flower; inside it sat a child of upright and handsome appearance, sitting solemnly and alone, a sight for all to behold with joy.
At that time, when the great assembly witnessed this event, they were filled with extreme wonder; those non-Buddhists all lost their majestic splendor and simultaneously cast aside their pride.
Then the Great Master said to the elder Bhadrika:
"You may go and take the child from within the fire."
The elder still watched the face of the naked ascetic, who replied:
"If you enter the fire now, both your body and your life will be lost.
Hearing this, he was struck with fear and did not dare take his child.
The World-Honored One again commanded Jīvaka:
"You may go into the fire and take the child in your arms.
Jīvaka then had this thought:
"The World-Honored One would not have me perform such a task at an improper place or time; I should now take this child.
With a fearless heart, she then reached into the fire and drew the child out.
At that time, the devas spoke these verses:
"The Buddha commanded her to enter the fire And take up the child without fear;
By the power of the Buddha’s sovereign majesty, He was able to transform the fierce flames into a clear pool."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Jīvaka:
"When you previously entered the fire, was your body unharmed, or did any sores or blisters arise?
Jīvaka replied:
“World-Honored One!

I was born in the royal palace and raised in the royal palace; though I have previously had my body anointed with ox-head sandalwood incense, never before have I experienced such refreshing coolness as I do today.”
The Buddha said to the householder Bhadrika, "You may now take the child and return home.
At that time, the householder’s mind was corrupted by his evil views; he still did not give rise to faith, but instead turned his body back to look at the faces of the non-Buddhists.
The members of the heterodox faction replied at the same time: "O Elder!
This child is extremely lacking in merit; his nature is fierce and violent, and fire can consume all things."

That this [fire] does not burn you clearly shows that you are certainly a wretched, stubborn, and hard-hearted being suffering the pains of retribution; this is evident to all who observe you together, so there is no need for further words.
If you bring it into my house, you will surely witness disaster and peril, and your life will certainly come to an end.
"Among all things that humans cherish, nothing surpasses one's own body; yet upon hearing of impending calamity, they fail to gather and protect it.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to King Bimbisāra:
"Your Majesty should now take this child."
The king, suddenly startled and hurried, reached out his hand to receive the child and looked around, requesting the World-Honored One,
saying, "What name should be given to this boy?
The Buddha told the Great King:
"This child was obtained from within the fire; he may be named Jyotipāla (Fire-born).
The Buddha, observing the latent tendencies and inclinations of the great assembly, taught the Dharma according to their capacities.
At that time, among that multitude, there were immeasurable billions of sentient beings who attained sublime practices.
Some attain the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, or non-returning;
some further leave the household life, immediately sever all afflictions, and attain the fruit of arhatship;
others attain the roots of goodness of heat, peaks, or patience.
Some generate the mind set on the enlightenment of a śrāvaka;
some generate the mind set on the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
and some generate the mind set on unsurpassed enlightenment.
Some took refuge in the Triple Gem;
others received the prohibitive precepts and gave rise to profound faith.
At that time, King Bimbisāra entrusted the child to eight foster mothers to provide for his needs, as described in detail elsewhere.

At that time, the elder maternal uncle of the youth Agnidatta had previously gone to another region to trade goods. Hearing that his sister was pregnant, he felt great joy, thinking: "The World-Honored One has given her a prediction that she will certainly give birth to a son who will bring glory to the family," as extensively described above, up until the attainment of the fruit.
He immediately exchanged his own goods for other items and returned to Rājagṛha; upon hearing that his sister had already died, he thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One prophesied that she would give birth to a son who would attain the fruit of enlightenment—could this possibly be false?"
She consulted her neighbor, saying:
"My sister was pregnant and received a prophecy from the Buddha, which filled her with joy.
Now, hearing that she has died, it contradicts my original hope; how could the words of the World-Honored One not be true?"

The neighbor replied, "Indeed, the Great Teacher Buddha’s words are never false; however, because that husband followed the words of the non-Buddhists, he unjustly killed her until she died. Yet the child she bore possesses great majestic power, for though he remained amidst blazing flames, his body suffered no injury."
"At this time, he is being nurtured and currently resides in the royal palace.
Having heard these words, the maternal uncle went to the house of the elder Bhadra; after exchanging greetings, he said to him:
"Elder, you have acted unreasonably."
He replied, "What have I done? [The other said:

"You followed the words of a heretic with evil views and unjustly killed my sister while she was pregnant. The child she bore possesses great majestic power; though situated amidst blazing flames, his body suffered no injury."
"At present, he is being nurtured within the royal palace;
since this is the case, there is no need for further discussion.
If you bring the child here, I shall grant you my pardon; if not, I shall assemble all my kinsmen and banish you."
"By placing counting sticks on the ground, we shall enumerate your ignorance; we shall proclaim your evil reputation in the streets and crossroads, crying out:

'My sister was innocent, yet the virtuous Sudhanu has falsely put her to death! One who harms a woman should not be spoken to! And before the judges, you shall be punished according to the law for your crime."
Upon hearing this, the householder was overcome with great sorrow and distress, and he thought to himself:
"As these words of suffering were spoken, they will certainly not release me.
He then went to King Bimbisāra, prostrated at his feet, and said:
“Great King! We have related the preceding events in full, even to the point where we were punished according to our crimes; we only pray that you will grant us your favor and release the youth.
The King said:
"I did not obtain this youth from you; the Buddha, the World-Honored One, personally bestowed him upon me.
If you require him, you may go and ask the Buddha.
Thereupon, the elder went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!

My kinsmen are pressing me with harsh reproaches; they speak at length of these matters, even threatening me with punishment for my crimes. I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will grant me back this youth.”
The Blessed One thought to himself:
"If this householder does not obtain a son, he will vomit hot blood and meet his end.
He then addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go to King Bimbisāra and, bringing the householder with you, convey my words, wishing the King freedom from illness, and report:
'Great King!'"
"You should return the boy Jyotiṣka to the householder.
If that householder does not obtain the boy, he will surely die from vomiting hot blood.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having fully conveyed the Buddha’s instruction, went to the king and informed him.
The king said:
"Venerable One!
Pay homage on my behalf at the feet of the World-Honored One; I shall practice according to what the Buddha has taught."
Then Ānanda said, "May the King be free from illness," and took his leave, departing.
The king said to the elder:

"I have received the Buddha’s instruction to raise this boy, and I cherish him with great affection. Let us first make an agreement, after which I shall release him; provided he comes to see me three times each day, you may take him away as you please."
The elder replied, "I dare not disobey your command. Thereupon,
the king immediately ordered him to put on his upper garments, full attire, and jeweled necklaces, and had him conveyed to his home by means of a fragrant elephant.
It is a common occurrence among humans that while a father is still living, a son’s reputation does not shine forth.

Later, when the elder died, the youth Jyotiṣka took charge of the household affairs for himself. He conceived a profound sense of reverence toward the Triple Gem and constructed a monastery on the very spot where his father had killed his mother. He provided it with all necessary requisites in full abundance and offered it to the monastic community from the four quarters; it was named Pārśva-vana (The Flank Grove).
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The Buddha was staying at the Kalandakanivāpa Forest in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the elder Bhadra had previously dispatched a merchant to engage in trade in another region. Upon hearing that the elder had now passed away and that the youth Jyotiṣka had succeeded him in the family business, and that his reverence for the Triple Gem had become even more profound, the merchant obtained many excellent bowls made of gośīrṣa sandalwood. He then filled one bowl with precious jewels and sent a messenger to deliver it to Jyotiṣka.
Having obtained it, he placed it atop a high banner and issued a proclamation to all:

"If there are any persons—whether śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas—who, without using a ladder or steps, can take this bowl through their great power and mastery of supernatural faculties, I shall bestow this bowl upon that person."
Then, when the various non-Buddhist practitioners had risen at dawn and were going out to bathe, they saw the tall banner and said to the householder,
"What is this object?"
The householder then related the matter in detail, to which the non-Buddhist replied, "Householder, you have recently shown reverence toward the sons of Śākya; will they take it?"
Having spoken thus, he took his leave and departed.
At that time, a great number of senior bhikṣus entered the city for alms and, seeing that tall banner, all asked the elder: "What is this?"
He then answered in full detail, and the bhikṣu replied:
"How could I have displayed my own skill for the sake of a bowl?
As the Buddha has said:..."
"Concealing one's good deeds and exposing one's evil ones is the practice of those who have left the household life.
Having said this, he departed. At that time, the Venerable Daśabala-Kāśyapa passed by that way and also asked the householder:
"What is this? he asked.
He replied in full detail. At that time, the Venerable One thought to himself:
"Since beginningless saṃsāra, all the enemies of afflictions that have nurtured me, I have already vomited out and completely cast away."
"I should now accept this invitation from the elder and fulfill his wish.
He then extended his hand like the trunk of a fragrant elephant, reached up to the banner-pole to take the sandalwood bowl, and carried it back to his dwelling place.
A bhikṣu saw him and asked,
"Venerable sir, from where did you obtain this exceptionally fine bowl of ox-head sandalwood?
He then related the matter in full to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus replied:
"Venerable sir, could you perhaps manifest a supernatural power for the sake of this wooden bowl? He replied, "O Āyuṣmat!"
"I have already completed what was to be done, whether it be appropriate or not; now, what should be done?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not manifest supernatural powers before laypeople; if he does so, he commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
Now, there are four kinds of bowls:
those made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Furthermore, there are four types of bowls:
These refer to brass, red copper, white copper, and various types of wood.
Regarding the first four kinds of bowls, if one does not already possess them, one should not accept them; if one already possesses them, they must be relinquished.
Regarding the latter four types, if they were not previously possessed, one should not keep them; if they were previously possessed, one should use them as medicine bowls according to the occasion.
There are two kinds of alms bowls that may be maintained:
namely, those made of iron and those made of clay; thus should it be understood.

Later, at another time, when the boy Agnidatta had manifested all the wondrous marks of humans and devas, he traveled from the city of Campā to Rājagṛha. Along the way, there was a place where taxes were collected. A tax official who had died and been reborn as a yakṣa then appeared to his son in a night dream and said:
"After my death, I have been reborn among the yakṣas. You should construct a yakṣa shrine for me at that place where goods are taxed, and hang a bell before its door."

"If there are people who pass by carrying goods at an improper time and do not pay their taxes, the bell shall ring; they will then be summoned to turn back, and only after they have paid the dues shall they be allowed to go.
On another day, his son recounted this dream to his kinsmen, and together they inspected a strategic location where they established a shrine and hung a bell outside.
At that time, there was a Brahmin wife in the city of Campā who thought to herself:
"This Brahmin manages business everywhere, yet I constantly consume the wealth he acquires while he sits with folded hands, engaged in no productive occupation; this is improper."
She then went to the marketplace, purchased cotton wool, and had it spun into fine thread. She then had a skilled weaver weave it into a pair of fine white cloth sheets worth one thousand gold coins.
Once she had obtained the pair of sheets, she said to her husband, "These white sheets are worth one thousand gold coins; you may go to the marketplace and sell them to take the price."
If there is someone who buys it, that is well.
If no one asks for it, report:
"There is no one in the market; go elsewhere."
Her husband took it to the market to sell it, but after calling out for a thousand coins, no one offered a price;
he then cried out, "There is no one in the market!"

He then placed the cloth within the bamboo tube of his parasol handle and, together with the traveling merchants, proceeded toward Rājagṛha. Gradually arriving at the yakṣa-tax station at the shrine, he paid the tax along with the other people; as he was about to set out on his journey, the bells suspended [from his parasol] began to ring.

Upon hearing this, the tax officials said to one another, "Since the bell has already sounded, our examination of the goods is not yet complete; we should inspect them more thoroughly to ensure nothing is overlooked.
They turned the merchants back to search meticulously, examining all their wealth and property so that there was nothing untaxed, and only then did they release the merchants.
The bell rang out again; as they observed and scrutinized it repeatedly, the merchants were astonished and each conceived feelings of resentment, saying to the tax official:
"Do you wish to plunder us by means of this pretext of detaining us?"
At that time, the tax officials divided the merchants into two groups; among those in one group where there was no brahmin, they released them without making a sound.
As that first group departed, the bells began to ring again.
They divided again into two parties in this manner of departure and staying; thus, all the merchants were gone, and only the Brahmin remained alone.
The tax official seized him and would not allow him to proceed, whereupon the Brahmin said:
"Examine my person for whatever goods I may have and take them as you please."
Having searched everywhere, he let him go when nothing was found; however, the bell rang out again, so he seized him once more and said, "Brāhmaṇa!
Even if you possess wealth, I shall take no share of it. You ought to speak the truth and not deceive the spirits, for I wish to demonstrate that these deities are holy."
The brahmin said, "If my words are not false,
I shall truly repay you by drawing forth a pair of folded cloths from within the handle of my umbrella.
When the tax official saw this, he marveled at the extraordinary marvel.
“Excellent, Great Deity!
Your prophecy shall not be in vain.
Then the tax official took one bundle, opened it, and spread it out for the deity; the Brahmin said:
"You have clearly stated that you do not take taxes; why then, judging by your current actions, do you all wish to seize everything?
They replied, "Do not be afraid!"

"I do not take the object; I merely wish to demonstrate that the Great Deity’s words are not false. I shall temporarily take this single layer to repay the Deity’s kindness, and then I will return it to you.
Having accepted it, he placed it inside the umbrella tube and departed along the road.

Gradually arriving at the great marketplace in Rājagṛha, he spread out his bolt of cloth and sought a thousand pieces of gold; yet, in the end, not a single person came to offer the price. He then cried out in the market:
"There is no trade!"

At that time, the youth Jyotiṣka emerged from the royal palace, mounted upon a great elephant, and was entering the marketplace on his way back to his own residence when he heard the sound of a proclamation. He asked what the reason was for proclaiming that there would be no market.
"Summon him and question him.
When the brahmin arrived, [the king] asked:
"For what reason did you say:..."
“Is there no market in the city? The brahmin replied,
“I have a pair of fine cloths worth a thousand coins, yet not a single person has come forward to bargain with me.”
He replied, “Bring it here and let us examine it.
The other then presented it, and Agnidatta said:
"One bundle is new; one bundle has been worn.
For the one that has been worn, I will pay two hundred and fifty [coins]; for the one that has not been worn, I will pay five hundred coins.
The owner of the bundles replied:
"For what reason is this so?
I have never used it before. Jyotiṣka said:
"Let me cause you to observe for yourself and verify whether this is real or false.
