He then took one that had not yet been used, opened it, and tossed it into the air; it remained suspended like a lid and descended slowly. Next, he threw one that had already been used, and it immediately fell swiftly to the ground.
Upon seeing this, the merchant felt a sense of wonder and said,
"Householder! You possess great wisdom and spiritual insight that surpasses all others."
The youth Agnidatta replied once more:
"Those that have not been used pass over the thorns without piercing them; those that have been used are caught and held by the needles."
When the words were spoken as they were true,
the brahmin was struck with even greater wonder and replied,
"The householder’s wisdom and discernment are truly unprecedented."
According to the price agreed upon, he took the cotton cloth and departed.
Jvalana said, "You are a traveler;
I have merely offered this as a token of hospitality. There is no need for you to reduce the price; please take all one thousand coins."
The brahmin took them and departed with joy.
At that time, the elder gave the used cloth to his family to wear, while he kept the unused one for himself to use as a washing cloth.

Later, at another time, King Bimbisāra was ascending to the high pavilion together with his ministers. At that moment, the bathing garment of the householder Agnidatta, which had been hung out to dry on the corner of the tower, was suddenly blown by the wind and fell down into the king's presence.
The king said, "These garments are those worn by the gods; from where have they come?
The minister replied:
"I have heard that in the past, when King Mandhātā ruled, the heavens rained down gold and jewels for seven days. Now, as this celestial robe falls, it will not be long before gold arrives.

The King said, "I have heard that the householder Agnidatta has been prophesied by the Buddha to possess the wondrous marks of humans and devas. This exquisite celestial robe has fallen from the sky; I shall wait for him to arrive and then bestow it upon him."
When Agnidatta had arrived, the king said, "Young man!
The World-Honored One has prophesied that you possess the wondrous marks of humans and devas; this exquisite celestial robe has descended from the sky, so you may wear it."
He immediately reached out his hand and took the king’s robe; having received it, he examined it closely and realized it was his own property. He then smiled and said, “Great King! ”
"Has Your Majesty ever touched it? He replied, "I have."
He replied, "Since you have grasped my humble garment, it would be fitting for you to wash your hands.
This is not a celestial robe; it is my bathing cloth."
The king asked, "How do you know this? He replied:
“There remains one garment which I gave to my family to wear; it is similar to this one. Your Majesty may examine it.
When the king saw this, he was filled with extreme wonder and said, “Young man!...”
"How could you have manifested all the wondrous marks of humans and devas right now?
He replied, "I have already manifested them."
"If that is so, why do you not invite me to visit your home for a short while?
"If Your Majesty grants permission, I shall extend the invitation this very moment. The King said:
"You may go and prepare food and drink.
He replied, "Great King!"

"If there is someone with the wondrous marks of a human or celestial being who has appeared, he will naturally require no labor or effort; you should immediately prepare the carriage and go together to my home.
The king then proceeded to the residence and saw the women of the household working at the outer gate. The king lowered his gaze, and the elder said, "Why do you lower your gaze?"
The king said, "I am avoiding your wife. She replied:
"This messenger from abroad is not the wife of my minister.
The King said, "How rare!"
Next, he saw a woman of the inner apartments; the king lowered his gaze even further. The elder questioned him again, and the king answered as before, replying:
"This too is a messenger, not my wife."

Having heard this, the king was filled with even greater wonder; proceeding next to the middle gate, he saw that the lapis lazuli floor was as clear and still as a pure pool, and upon the gate were placed mechanical fish whose reflections appeared within.
Having seen it, the king thought it was a pool of water and immediately took off his shoes. Agnidatta said to him, "Your Majesty, why have you taken off your shoes?
The king replied:
"I am about to enter the water now and fear I may become wet," Jvalana said.
"This is not water; it is a ground of lapis lazuli."
The king asked,
"For what reason does the fish move? He replied:
"It is not a fish; it is a mechanical shadow.
The King did not believe this in his heart, so he removed his signet ring and threw it to the ground; the ring rattled and rolled away to one side.
The King marveled even more and ascended the lion throne; at that time, the women of the inner apartments all came forward to pay their respects, and before he had risen, they were all weeping.
The King asked Jyotiṣka, "For what reason do these women shed tears upon seeing me?"
He replied: "It is not that I am weeping;
rather, because Your Majesty’s garments have been perfumed by the smoke of sandalwood and aloeswood incense, the fumes have irritated my eyes and caused these tears to flow."

At that time, King Bimbisāra, experiencing celestial delights of such supreme and inconceivable excellence, became so infatuated with sensual desires that he felt no satiety; he did not return to his palace and utterly abandoned all the affairs of state.
Then the ministers addressed Prince Ajātaśatru, saying:
"The Great King, our sovereign, has entered the house where the elder Gṛhapati resides; being addicted to sensual pleasures, he refuses to return to the palace."
"I only pray that the Crown Prince will go and report this matter.
Thereupon, Ajātaśatru went at once to the King's presence and said: "Great King!"
"Why do you remain here, disregarding the myriad affairs of state?
The king said to the prince,
"Are you truly unable to attend to the affairs of the kingdom for even a single day?"
The Prince said, "Does 'Great Heaven' mean only a single day?
Since leaving the palace, seven days have already passed."
Having heard these words, the king looked at Agnidatta’s face and said,
“Is it truly already seven days? He replied:
"It is indeed so," [the monk replied]. The King said,
"If that is the case, how can one distinguish between day and night?"
Jyotiṣka replied: "Great King!
If one observes whether flowers are open or closed, whether precious gems emit light or not, and whether birds are singing or silent, one can distinguish between day and night."
The king said, "I still do not understand. He replied:
“There are flowers that bloom at night and close by day; there are those that close at night and bloom by day.
There are pearls that are dark at night and bright by day; there are those that are bright at night and dark by day.
There are birds that utter their cries at night; there are those that only sing during the daytime.”
Having heard this, the king was filled with profound wonder and replied, "Young man!
The Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, speaks without falsehood; accept everything exactly as he has predicted."
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 2;
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 3.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.

[The remainder of] "The Householder Agnidatta" follows the preceding summary verses. At that time, Ajātaśatru entered the house of the householder Agnidatta and saw a fine jewel; he then stole it and gave it to his attendant. Having returned to his own residence, he said to the attendant:
"Bring the jewel you were entrusted with earlier."
The attendant opened his fist and saw only empty hands;
he reported, "I do not know where the precious gem has gone.
The king then struck him in anger, whereupon Huosheng said:
"What fault has this attendant committed that he is suddenly subjected to such angry beating?
He replied, "I am a petty thief; this one is a great thief."
"I stole the precious gem from your house, and now this petty man has stolen it from me. Jyotiṣka replied,
"Neither the Prince stole it, nor did this thief."
"After the Prince has taken [her] back, he will soon return to his original place. He said, "Prince!"
"The wealth within my house belongs to the Crown Prince; you may take whatever you require as you please. Why, then, did you steal it?
The Prince remained silent and thought to himself:
"After my father passes away, I shall take it all."

At that time, because of the instruction of his evil friend Devadatta, Ajātaśatru subsequently committed the act of parricide against his father, the wise king, and then proclaimed himself the consecrated Great King, becoming the sovereign of the kingdom of Magadha.
He said to Jyotiṣka, "You are my younger brother; we may divide the wealth together.
Jyotiṣka thought to himself:
"His father, King Ming, killed [the predecessor] and established himself; how could he ever tolerate me?
Now this wicked king wishes to seize my residence; it is best to grant him his request first."
Having reflected thus, he said: "Great King! I previously had this intention:
that both my house and my wealth and treasures should all be offered to you."
"What further division is there?
I only pray that Your Majesty will come to my residence and I shall go to the royal palace; I would be fortunate indeed if you would grant me this permission. The King said:
"Excellent! Do as you wish.

The king then moved away, and Jyotiṣka entered the palace; all the auspicious signs within the residence were transferred into the palace. In this manner, they moved back and forth seven times, with the auspicious following Jyotiṣka and the inauspicious following behind the king.
At that time, Ajātaśatru thought to himself:
"I cannot obtain the Jewel of Fire through this means; I shall employ another stratagem to take it.
He then addressed the thieves, saying:
"You should now go inside Agnidatta’s house and steal the precious gem.

Upon hearing these words, the man fashioned an iron hook, climbed over the wall, and attempted to enter. Seeing him, the woman inside immediately cried out at the top of her voice, "A thief has entered!"
"Thieves have entered!
Having heard this, Jyotiṣka did not wish for them to leave,
and so he said, "Stop those thieves!"
He immediately became stuck to the top of the wall and could not descend; by the time dawn arrived, everyone gathered to look on and asked the thief, "For what reason have you come here?"
He replied, "The King has sent me to steal the Fire-born Jewel.
Everyone was enraged:

"This man is a villain; he has wantonly executed the Dharma King despite his innocence, and now he further causes bandits to unjustly plunder the wealth of others. This transgression is all the more grave—how can it be forgiven?"
Having heard this, the king dispatched a messenger to Jyotiṣka’s dwelling with these instructions:
“You should release him; do not inflict further harm or suffering upon him.
At that time, Jyotiṣka intended to set him free and cried out:
"The bandits have gone," he said,
and thus he was finally able to escape.
Agnidatta thought to himself:
"Since he was even capable of killing his own father, it is impossible that he would not harm me.
How could I sacrifice my life for the sake of wealth and treasures?

Rather, I shall follow the prediction formerly bestowed upon me by the World-Honored One: to leave the household life and practice within my Dharma, severing all afflictions and attaining the fruit of Arhatship."
"I should now renounce the secular life and go forth into homelessness.
Within his residence, he distributed all his wealth and treasures to the solitary and the beggars, ensuring that all who were destitute were made fully satisfied.

Then the householder Agnidatta, having taken his leave of his relatives, friends, and acquaintances, went to where the Buddha was staying. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side with palms joined in reverence, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I only pray that you will grant me permission to go forth in this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination and become a bhikṣu, and to practice the pure brahmacarya in service to the World-Honored One.
Having seen him, the Buddha said:
"Welcome, bhikṣu! You may practice the holy life."

Upon hearing these words, his hair and beard fell away naturally, as if he had been shaved seven days prior; dharma robes were upon his body and a flask and bowl were in his hands, his majestic deportment as disciplined as that of a bhikṣu of a hundred years’ standing.
The verse says:
"When the World-Honored One commanded him to come, his hair fell away and robes appeared upon his body;
immediately his faculties became tranquil, and everything was accomplished according to the Buddha’s intention."

At that time, the World-Honored One instructed him according to his capacity; he then exerted himself with skillful means and practiced diligently. He observed and understood that the cycle of birth and death within the five destinies revolves without ceasing, that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are utterly subject to decay, that loathsome dharmas are constantly harmed by others, that pleasure lasts but a moment while suffering endures through the long night, and that although there may be heavenly retribution, it ultimately ends in dispersal and extinction.

Having investigated deeply and gained this knowledge, he severed all afflictions and attained the fruit of Arhatship, endowed with the three knowledges (*trividyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and possessed of the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*). He attained the knowledge of reality as it is: "Birth has been exhausted;
the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence."

The mind is free from obstruction, like a hand waving through space; whether cut by a blade or smeared with incense, neither love nor hatred arises. Viewing gold and earth as equal and without distinction, one renounces all fame and profit; even Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas all pay him reverence.
At that time, all the bhikṣus gave rise to a doubt, thinking:
"Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can remove the net of doubt; we shall now go together to question him.
They immediately went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
“Bhagavān, what karma did the householder Agnidatta previously perform, such that as the ripening of that karma he was born into a great wealthy family and enjoyed life without lack?
Furthermore, what karma did he perform such that he was burned in a mass of fire at the same time as his mother?”
Furthermore, by what karma was he born among humans yet endowed with the wondrous marks of a deva?
Again, by what karma did he leave the household life to practice within the Buddha-dharma, sever all afflictions, and realize arhatship?
The Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus, you should all listen well:
the karma previously created by the youth Agnidatta must be experienced by him himself, as explained in detail above."
"You all should listen.

Ninety-one eons ago in a past life, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. Together with a great assembly of sixty-two thousand bhikṣus, he traveled by stages until he gradually reached a city named Bandhumatī. The king’s name was Bandhuma, and not far from there was a forest called Bandhumatīvana, where the Buddha and the bhikṣus resided."
That king possessed great merit; his realm was peaceful and secure, its population flourished, and it was free from all strife. As a great Dharma King, he was as extensively described above.
In this city there was a householder named Devabhāga, who was immensely wealthy with abundant riches and enjoyments, equal in prosperity to King Vaiśravaṇa. The householder thought to himself:

"Although I have repeatedly invited the Buddha Vipaśyin and the assembly of noble ones to partake of exquisite food and drink, I have never yet provided them with the four requisites for a three-month *varṣā* retreat. I should now invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha, and throughout the three months, relinquish all my resources to provide for their every need."

Having formed this thought, he immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha, employing skillful means, taught him the essentials of the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. Having finished speaking the Dharma, the Buddha remained silent.
At that time, the elder rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!
I pray only that you will, out of compassion and pity, accept my invitation for three months of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine."
Having seen the request, the Buddha accepted it by remaining silent.
When the householder saw that the Buddha had accepted, he prostrated at his feet and departed.
At that time, a relative of the king heard that the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, together with a great assembly, had arrived in his kingdom and was staying in a grove; he then thought to himself:

"Although I have repeatedly invited the Buddha and the Sangha to take a meal at my home, I have not yet provided them with the four requisites for three months; I now wish to invite the Buddha and the Sangha for a three-month period of offerings."
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then the Buddha taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the king, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him, before remaining silent.
The king rose, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha:

“Although I have repeatedly invited the Buddha and the assembly of monks to take meals at my residence, I have not yet provided them with the four requisites for three months. I only pray that the World-Honored One and the great assembly will, out of compassion, accept my offerings for three months, with no lack in the four requisites.”
The Buddha said, "Great King!
I have already accepted the invitation of the householder Devadatta for three months."
The king said,
"If the Buddha does not grant permission for me to receive my share of the celestial portion, I shall consult with him, and he will surely grant it.
The Buddha said:
"If he consents, I shall accept him.
Having heard the Buddha's words, the king prostrated at his feet and departed.
Upon arriving at the palace, he immediately dispatched a messenger to summon the householder Devadatta. When the householder had arrived, the king said to him:
“Householder, do you know this?
I wish to first invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha to present my offerings; you may arrange yours afterwards, for it will not be too late. He replied:
"Great King! I have already made the initial invitation to the Buddha and the Sangha; since I hold this intention, I pray that you will not go against it.
The King said:
“Householder! Although this is so, you are a person of my own kingdom; therefore, when I deliberate according to principle, I shall provide for you first. He replied:

"Great King! Although these are Your Majesty's subjects, according to principle they should have been invited first; if Your Majesty suppresses them out of hardship, it would contradict the proper way.
The King said:
“Householder! Your desire will not be fulfilled merely by passion; rather, let us take turns providing offerings day by day. Whichever meal is superior shall follow its invitation.”
The householder replied, “So be it.

Then, that very night, the householder prepared various kinds of excellent, rare, and superior foods and drinks. When dawn arrived, at the place where the meal was to be served, he filled large jars with pure water and sent a messenger to announce:
"The food and drink are prepared; may the Buddha know that the time has come.

Then, during the first watch of the day, the Buddha Vipaśyin took up his robes and bowl, followed by the assembly of monks, and proceeded to the place where the householder Devadatta had prepared the meal, where he took his seat.

Once the elder had seen that the Buddha and the Saṅgha were seated, he personally took various offerings in his own hands and presented them to the Buddha and the Saṅgha. When he perceived that the assembly was fully satiated, and they had finished chewing their tooth-sticks and rinsing their mouths, and the bowls had been set aside, he took a small seat and sat before the Buddha in order to hear the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of that elder, preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him; having taught the Dharma according to his capacity, he rose from his seat and departed.

Then the king of that country took his turn to provide offerings, immediately preparing various kinds of sustenance as extensively described before, until [the Buddha] rose from his seat and departed.
In this manner, they took turns presenting exquisite offerings, yet there was ultimately no difference in quality between them.
When the king saw this, he rested his cheek upon his hand and remained there filled with anxiety.
At that time, the ministers, seeing the king’s sorrowful countenance, said to him: "Devānampiya,
for what reason are you so distressed?"
He replied, "How could I not be anxious now?
Regarding the guests staying within my kingdom who have provided offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha, I am unable to surpass them; therefore, I harbor this anxiety."
The minister replied:

"Your Majesty, the householder has no firewood in his home to purchase for cooking; since you have forbidden all wood-sellers from selling, he lacks the fuel for steaming and thus has no means to prepare food."
The king then issued a proclamation:
"Let no one within my realm sell firewood or grass; whoever violates this shall be expelled from my country.
At that time, on the day the meal was to be prepared, the elder was unable to find firewood and consequently used *candana* sandalwood from his own home for cooking.
Furthermore, he smeared fragrant oil upon layers of fine cloth and used them to cook cakes and food; consequently, the fragrance filled the entire city.
The King, marveling at this, asked:
"For what reason is the air today so thick with fragrance, different from usual? From where does it come?"
The people reported the matter in full to the king, who said,
"I shall have no part in this now.
A minister admonished him, saying:
"Your Majesty, why do you now act in this manner?
The householder has no other offspring; once he passes away, all his property will revert to the state, allowing you to spend it as you please."
“Your Majesty should now allow him to sell firewood once more.
The King then granted permission for him to sell it.
Upon hearing that the King had permitted the sale of the wood and grass, the elder gave rise to a mind of resentment and spoke these harsh words:
"Let the king and his mother be burned together using whatever fragrant wood is currently available in my house.
On another day, the king remained sorrowful as before; when the ministers questioned him again, the king answered as he had previously.
The ministers said, "We pray that you do not harbor such grief."
"I shall employ skillful means to ensure that his offerings do not surpass those of the Great King.

On the day the king prepared the offerings, the ministers immediately cleared away all debris within the city, swept the streets, and sprinkled them everywhere with fragrant water. They burned incense until the air was filled with its pervasive fragrance, and hung banners, streamers, and silk canopies at every turn. They scattered famous flowers until they were spread everywhere, making the place as beautiful and lovely as the Garden of Joy (Nandana).

Next, he constructed a dining hall, vast and magnificent, elegant and beautiful; he further arranged seating for the meal, adorned with various precious ornaments. Upon these seats, he spread silken cloths, and applied fragrant ointments and powdered incense everywhere. The food served was exquisite and soft, like celestial nectar, with diverse flavors surpassing the world’s rare delicacies; he reverently presented these to the Buddha and the Sangha, making offerings with his whole heart.
Then the ministers together addressed the king, saying:
"We have each performed these tasks to the best of our ability, adorning the city walls and preparing these magnificent feasts; Your Majesty should now give rise to a joyful heart."
The king personally observed this and was filled with extreme wonder; he immediately commanded a messenger to go to the World-Honored One and say:
"The meal is prepared; may the Buddha know that the time has come."
The Buddha and the great assembly each took their robes and bowls and proceeded to the royal palace, arriving at the place where food was prepared; they then took their seats.
The king then ordered a consecrated state elephant to hold a hundred-ribbed parasol over the World-Honored One, while the remaining elephants each held a single parasol over the bhikṣus.
The Queen Mother personally held a precious fan to waft cool air for the Buddha, while the other ladies of the inner court fanned the assembly of bhikṣus.
The King and his ministers personally presented offerings to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, as described extensively above.
Then the householder Devadatta addressed his family members, saying:
"You should now go to the place where the King has prepared the offerings and secretly observe whether the food and drink are coarse or fine."
When the messenger arrived and beheld the magnificent feast, he forgot to return;
the second and third messengers likewise did not come back.
At that time, the elder went there in person and, seeing the lavish preparations, marveled at their rarity and thought to himself:
"These exquisite offerings can be prepared through my power, but how can I obtain the elephant and the palace ladies?
Having thought this, he returned to his own residence and told the gatekeeper:
"If you see any beggars coming here, give them whatever they need, but do not let them enter at will."
The householder entered his room and remained there, harboring sorrow.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, who constantly surveys the world with his divine eye, saw the householder in his room harboring sorrow. Discerning his mind, he thought:
"Among the fields of merit in the world, the Buddha is foremost."
"Since the celestial being Devadatta was the first to act as a great donor, I should now go there to assist him.
He immediately transformed himself into the likeness of a brahmin and went to the gate of the elder’s house, saying to the gatekeeper:
"You should now go and inform the Great Elder that a great brahmin of the Kauśika clan is currently outside the gate and wishes to see him."
The gatekeeper replied:
"The elder has ordered me to guard this gate; whenever I see a beggar who needs something, I must give it to them and not allow them to enter at will."
"If there is anyone who needs anything, let them take it as they please; why trouble yourself to see the elder's body?
That person replied, "I have no need for anything, yet I have an important matter that requires me to see the elder."
The messenger then entered and reported, saying:
"Outside there is a great brahmin of the Kauśika clan who says he has no request, but wishes to see the householder.
The householder replied:
"You may say to that person:
'If you have anything you seek, take it as you wish.
Why must you insist on seeing my body?'"
She replied: "O Mistress! I have already delivered your message exactly as you instructed."
He said, "I have an important matter that requires me to see the elder.
He then addressed his gatekeeper, saying:
"If it be so, you may let him enter. The gatekeeper led him in;
upon seeing that the elder was dwelling there filled with anxiety, the brāhmaṇa asked, "Elder! Why do you sit thus?"
"For what reason do you rest your cheek upon your hand, appearing to bear a look of sorrow?
Having heard this, the householder spoke these verses:
"If there were one who could dispel my grief, That person would be worthy of my conversation."
"If your sorrow is not dispelled, what is the use of conversing with me?
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked:
"Householder, what is the cause of your sorrow?"
"I possess a skillful means by which I can resolve this for you.
The householder then related the previous events in detail.
At that moment, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, resumed his original form and said:
"Householder! I shall cause the deity Uttara-kauśalya to come and assist you.
Having spoken these words, he vanished from sight and departed.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having arrived at the celestial palace, addressed the Deva Viśvakarman, saying:
"You should now go to Jambudvīpa and provide assistance to the householder Devadatta."
He replied, "Excellent!

Then, on the following day, the Deva Viśvakarman went to that city and manifested transformations according to his will; he adorned the streets with such extraordinary artistry that their various decorations were twice as magnificent as those of the king.

The seating arrangements in the dining hall were exquisitely crafted with celestial artistry, and all the food and drink were from the divine kitchens; the Great Elephant King held a hundred-ribbed parasol for Vipaśyin Buddha, while the other elephants held parasols for the bhikṣus.
The celestial maiden Śreṇikā held a golden fan in her hand to waft cool air for the Buddha, while the other celestial maidens fanned the assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, the king dispatched a messenger to go secretly and observe, to see what the manner of the elder’s offerings was like.
The envoy went to observe it and, seeing its wonders, forgot to return;
he then sent a high minister back, who likewise remained there as before;
subsequently, he ordered the prince to go as well, but he too did not return.
The king, marveling at this matter, immediately went in person to the gate.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw the king from afar and said to the elder:
"This is the King who has already seen the Truths; you spoke harsh and evil words to him. He is now outside the gate; go and seek his forgiveness."
The householder then went out to seek an audience with the king to offer his apologies, saying: "Great King!
I now request that you enter for a moment so that I may personally make an offering."
The king immediately entered and beheld the exquisite celestial cuisine;
struck with great wonder, he said to the elder, "It is fitting for you, O virtuous one, to provide offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks every day; this is beyond my expectations."
At that time, having prepared such wondrous and magnificent offerings for the Buddha and the Saṅgha, the elder prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and made this aspiration:

"I have now made offerings to the supreme field of merit; by virtue of this excellent cause, may I in future lives always be born into a family of great wealth and nobility, with abundant treasures and the reception of celestial marks, and may I attain the sublime Dharma to escape the entanglements of the veils."
"In this way, I shall serve my Great Teacher with a mind free from weariness.
Monks, do not harbor any other thought; the householder Devadatta of that time was none other than Jyotiṣka.
Because that king spoke harsh and evil words, he burned both his mother and himself together with sandalwood fire.
By the power of that karma, for five hundred lifetimes he was burned by fire while dwelling together with his mother, and even until the present time, they are burned in the same place together.

Because Vipaśyin Buddha received his supreme offerings and he further made a vow, through the power of that karma, he was always born into families of great wealth and nobility with abundant treasures; the various sublime marks of a celestial being appeared naturally upon him, and within my Dharma, he left the household life to practice, exhausting all afflictions and attaining the fruit of Arhatship.
"O bhikṣus! My supernatural powers and the power of my path are entirely equal to those of Vipaśyin Buddha.
You should know this: if you offer worship and service to me with a heart of profound reverence, you will certainly obtain a supreme fruit."
"If one performs purely black karma, one will obtain a purely black retribution," and so forth, as explained in detail above.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had spoken, they received it with faith and practiced accordingly.
The third section of the first chapter, summarized in verse,
says: Repairing bowls, keeping requisites, A knife and a needle-case,
Along with three types of clothing frames— These were permitted by the Great Sage.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose almsbowl had a hole. He took it with him to a smith and said, "Venerable sir, my bowl has a hole; I hope you can mend it for me."
He thought to himself:
"All these sons of the Śākyas are idlers; they do not pay wages but merely employ others in vain.
If I work for them, others will continue to arrive, and by constantly attending to their affairs, my own livelihood will be neglected without end."
"I should now wait for a while. He replied, "Noble One!"
"I do not have the leisure; you may come tomorrow.
On the following day he arrived, but was told:
"Come the day after tomorrow."
Whether early or late, he acted thus every day; by such deceitful procrastination, the bhikṣu became weary.
A bhikṣu who was his acquaintance saw this and asked him:
"Venerable one!..."
"You see him coming toward this house every day; could he possibly be one of your disciples or a close acquaintance?
He replied, "Venerable sir!"
"This family is neither my disciple nor a relative; I have a broken bowl that I wish them to repair, so they come here constantly because they seek to deceive me."
He replied, "Venerable one!
Have you not heard that it is difficult for a craftsman's son to speak the truth?"
"However, I know how to do it; if the Buddha permits, I shall mend it for you.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is a bhikṣu who is skilled at such work, he should mend his bowl in a secluded place so that if anyone sees him, no feelings of ridicule or loathsomeness will arise."
When that bhikṣu had heard that the Buddha had granted permission, he went to the skilled bhikṣu and said to him:
"Venerable sir!
The World-Honored One has granted permission; you may mend my bowl for me."
He said, "Venerable sir!
How can you mend this bowl with my finger? You must obtain the proper tools before it can be mended."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"For this reason, I now permit the Saṃgha to keep iron implements.
If anyone requires them, they may borrow and use them, returning them once the task is completed."
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus wished to cut fabric for their three robes (tricīvara), but they tore it with their hands, thereby damaging the cloth.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not tear it with one's hands; it may be cut with a knife.
Having granted this permission, a certain bhikṣu who wished to cut and tailor a robe went to a layperson and said:
"Householder!..."
"I need a knife to cut and tailor my robe.
He replied, "Take it with you."
Having finished tailoring the garment, he returned it to that person,
who replied, "This is a gift for you. He answered:
"The World-Honored One has not permitted it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit bhikṣus to receive and keep a small knife."

Having seen that the Buddha had granted permission, the group of six monks then adorned the hilt with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, various jewels, and other miscellaneous, multicolored, and wondrous treasures.
At that time, some lay travelers saw this and asked,
"Noble One! What is this?"
He replied, “The World-Honored One has permitted the keeping of a knife. The other said:
"Do you, virtuous ones, still have the affairs of desire entangling your minds?
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "Bhikṣus!"
One should not keep or use handles for knives adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, various jewels, or other miscellaneous multicolored and extraordinary treasures.
If a knife is required, it should be made entirely of iron.
It then grew very long, and a layperson asked again,
"What is this? He replied:
"This is a knife; the Blessed One has permitted its possession.
He said: "Noble one!"
"This is a large sword, not a knife.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"A bhikṣu shall not keep a long sword."
Because he made it so small that it was unfit for cutting, the Buddha said:
"You should know that there are three kinds of knives: namely, large, medium, and small."
The large ones may be six finger-widths long, the small ones four finger-widths; those between these two sizes are called medium.
There are two types of shape:
one is curved like a crow’s wing, and the other resembles a chicken feather; they should not be pointed or straight.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, when the bhikṣus were marking their three robes (tricīvara), they used bamboo pins or bird quills, whereby the robes became damaged. The Buddha said:
"One should use needles."
At that time, the group of six monks fashioned their needles from gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and various other precious gems.
When a layperson saw them, he asked, "What is this?"
He replied, “The Buddha permitted the keeping of needles.
The other said:
"The mind of the śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, is entangled with the desire for [fine] things.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not make his needle from gold or other such materials."
"However, there are four kinds of needles:
copper, iron, brass, and red copper.
A bhikṣu kept his needle in various places, whereupon it became rusted; the Buddha said:
"One should use a needle-case.
The bhikṣus did not understand how to make a case;
the Buddha said:
"There are two kinds of needle cases:

one is a hollow tube and the other is a bamboo cylinder. The use of a tube is permitted for these; as for those two types of knives, fearing that iron rust might form upon them, it is also permissible to place them inside such a tube."
The setting was in Śrāvastī. The Buddha had permitted the bhikṣus to make saṃghāṭī robes.
At that time, the bhikṣus spread their cloth upon the ground, where it was frequently eaten by insects and defiled by dust and grime.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should not be placed on the ground; you may instead make a wooden frame for the robe.
The bhikṣus did not understand, so they reported the matter to the Buddha again, and the Buddha said:
"There are two kinds of frames:
either wood or bamboo, upon which the robes are spread.
When they were pulled back and forth, the robes were damaged by the bamboo. The Buddha said:
"First one must drill a hole, then use a thread to bind them together, and finally stitch upon it.
As the Buddha has taught, there are three kinds of robes:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
The upper robe should be fitted with a top frame, but the middle and lower robes were not proportionate to it. The Buddha said:
"Three frames should be made, their sizes corresponding to the dimensions of each robe."
The summary verse for the fourth section of the first chapter says:
Looking in a mirror and reflecting in water; not using combs or brushes;
leaving long hair on the crown of the head; and the bathhouse at Nālandā.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
At the first part of the day, the group of six bhikṣus took up their robes and bowls and entered the city to beg for food.
At that time, the laypeople were opening various ornaments from within their chests and baskets.
When the group of six saw it, they took the mirror and looked at their faces to examine their forms.
Nanda and Upananda said to one another,
"We are exceedingly handsome."
The lay travelers saw this and mocked him, saying: "Venerable One!
With no hair upon your head and long hair under your arms, how can you possibly possess a dignified and upright appearance?"
He remained silent. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not look into a mirror; if he looks at his face, he commits a *vyatikrama* offense."
As the Buddha had said that one should not look into a mirror, they immediately looked into water and were ridiculed as before. The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, one should not look at one's face while standing by water."
When a bhikṣu was inspecting water for insects, he saw his own reflection and felt remorse. The Buddha said:
"Seeing one's own face while inspecting water is not an offense; do not harbor doubt."
"If one examines a sore, or observes the appearance of oneself as a youth or an elder from the past, there is no fault in looking into a mirror.
The setting of this account is the same as before.
While the group of six monks was begging for alms, they saw that another household possessed various articles of adornment; they then used their comb to groom their hair and said to one another:
“Is it well? When worldly people saw this, they mocked him as before, whereupon he remained silent.
He reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Monks, you should not comb your hair; if you do so, you commit an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
When the monks further used a brush, they were again subject to the same fault. The Buddha said:
“Using it constitutes an offense of transgression against the Dharma.”
The bhikṣus used the comb and the brush simultaneously. The Buddha said, "The offense is the same as before.
The circumstances were the same as previously described.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada spread gold over the ground to purchase the Jeta Grove; having offered it to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, he sent a barber into the monastery to shave the heads of the assembly.
When the man had arrived, the group of six asked him,
"Can you shave off all the hair except for a topknot? He replied:
"This is my craft," he said,
and immediately had him shaved and cut,
saying, "Make it large."
He further said, "Remove another portion. Thus he removed it again,
[successively] two, three, four, five, and even up to eight portions, to which the reply was given:
“Fool! You do not understand at all; have your head shaved clean and I shall let you go home.
At dusk, as he was returning home, the elder saw him and asked:
“How many people’s hair have you shaved?
He replied, “I have not had time to shave many; Upānanda has me fashioning a topknot.”
The full account continues until the evening, when they spoke of returning home; having heard this, the householder felt revulsion and disdain.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu must not carry his hair tied in a topknot on the crown of his head. Should any do so, he commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
The setting was as before.
At that time, the Venerable Gomayapicū was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, within the Jyotiṣka-rāja Garden on Mount Udakavana, inside a pigsty cave.

Later, at another time, during the month of spring when the trees and forests were in full bloom, and geese, swans, mandarin ducks, parrots, śārikas, peacocks, and various other birds were warbling everywhere throughout the groves and gardens, King Pradyota commanded the park keeper, saying:

"You must now repair and maintain the entire fragrant garden, including its waters, woods, and mountains; clear away all debris and rubble, provide abundant clean water, and station guards. I wish to go to the garden for a brief excursion."
That man respectfully assented and followed the king’s instructions exactly; having completed the construction, he returned to inform the king:
"I have completed everything as you commanded; I only pray that Your Majesty will know it is time."
The king immediately took his inner court ladies as attendants and went to the fragrant garden to play; becoming weary, he lay down and fell asleep.
At that time, the women of the inner court, who were fond of flowers and fruits, searched for them throughout the garden.
At that time, the cowherd bhikṣu’s hair and beard were long, his upper robe was tattered, and his lower garment was filthy; he sat cross-legged beneath a tree.
Seeing him from afar, the palace women were all struck with alarm and cried out, "Great King!"
"There is a ghost!
There is a ghost!
The bhikṣu immediately went and entered a cave.
Upon hearing the sound, the king immediately woke up; drawing his sword, he ran after it and asked the palace attendants, "Where is the ghost?
They replied:
"Run and enter the cave of the boar's lair.
When the king heard this, he went to the location of the cave and, grasping his sword, asked:
"What creature are you?"
He replied, "Great King! I am a śramaṇa."
The king asked,
"What kind of śramaṇa is this? He replied:
“Son of the Śākyas,” he asked,
“have you attained the fruit of arhatship?”
He replied, "I have not. [The Buddha asked:
"Have you attained the fruit of non-returning, once-returning, or stream-entry?"
He replied, "I have not.
[The Buddha said,] "Set that matter aside for now; you have attained the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna."
He replied, “In neither case may it be done.
Upon hearing this, the king became even more enraged and said to his ministers:

Thereupon, the group of six monks departed.
When he appeared before them in person, those merchants felt ashamed upon seeing him; unable to enjoy themselves, they began to criticize him, saying:
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas have come to appear at this place of song and dance."
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not manifest his body by going to places of song, dance, or performance.

If a bhikṣu performs song, dance, or recitation himself; or teaches others to do so; or collects [instruments] for himself; or manifests his body [for such purposes], he commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma."

The following is the account of the Venerable Sāhaṃja. At that time, there was a householder in Kauśāmbī named Mahāsāha, who was gentle by nature. His wife became pregnant, and the Venerable Śāriputra, knowing that the fetus in her womb would eventually be converted and attain a supreme fruit, went to his residence.
At that time, the householder had long possessed faith and sought to receive the refuges and precepts; from then on, [the Venerable] frequently went to his residence.
On one occasion, when the Venerable was traveling alone without any attendants, he arrived at the householder’s place, who asked:
"Venerable Sir!"
"For what reason do you alone have no attendants? He replied,
"O noble one!"
"How could I possibly find an attendant within this thicket of grass? It is only from among you, sirs, that I may obtain one to serve as my attendant.
They replied, "Noble One!"
"If it be so, when my wife gives birth to a son, I shall give him to you, Venerable Sir, to serve as your attendant. He replied, "O fair one!"
"May my child be free from illness," she said, and then she departed.

After eight or nine months, the elder’s wife gave birth to a son; his appearance was thin and frail, yet his voice was harmonious and elegant. When the twenty-first day had passed, she gathered her kinsmen and held a celebratory feast for them.
The father took his son in his arms and asked the assembly for a name.

The people deliberated and said, "This child’s appearance is slender, yet his voice is harmonious and elegant; furthermore, he is the son of the Elder Mahāsāṃghika. We should give this child the name Sāṃghika."
Later, as he gradually grew up until reaching childhood,
at the time for the morning meal, the Venerable Śāriputra put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city of Kauśāmbī to beg for alms, eventually arriving at the house of Mahāsāla.

Having seen him, the elder then cried out, "Welcome! He joined his palms, prostrated at the elder's feet, took the bowl, filled it to the brim with excellent cakes, fruits, and food, and presented it to him as an offering.
The youth Sāṇavāsī observed the face of the noble one, and the Venerable manifested a sign to cause the elder to remember.
The elder then said to his son:
"Before you were born from your mother's womb, I had already given you to the Venerable as a disciple; you should now follow the Venerable."

The youth, being one in his final birth, found it easy to renounce the secular life; he immediately followed the Venerable One to his dwelling place. The Venerable One then granted him the going-forth and subsequently the full ordination (*upasampadā*). Having been instructed in the Dharma according to the rules, he thereafter exerted himself with diligent ascetic practice without weariness, severed all afflictions, and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, the bhikṣu Sāṃgharakṣita chanted the Dharma with a melodic intonation; his voice was so clear and resonant that it reached as far as the Brahma Heaven.

At that moment, countless sentient beings who heard his voice all planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation. Even those among the animal realm who possessed consciousness, upon hearing that sound, did not fail to prick up their ears to listen to his wondrous melody.
At that time, the World-Honored One, because the great assembly had gathered, addressed them all, saying:
"O bhikṣus, among all my śrāvaka disciples within my Dharma, the bhikṣu Suvīra is foremost in the beauty of his voice."
Because the melodies he performed were so harmonious and elegant, they inspired a heart of joy in all who heard them.
Even those bhikṣus who had not yet abandoned desire would set aside their own duties to listen to his recitations day after day.

Later, at another time, the Great King Prasenajit of Kosala, riding upon the elephant Puṇḍarīka, accompanied by his retinue, went out from the city during the late night on some business, intending to travel to another place.

The bhikṣu Sāṇavāsi was reciting the sūtras aloud within the Jeta Grove; at that time, the elephant king heard the sound and took delight in it, leaning his ear to listen and refusing to move forward.
The charioteer immediately pushed the hook and shook his feet, but the elephant remained utterly motionless.
The king said to the charioteer, "Make the elephant move. He replied:
"Great King! Though we exert all our strength to drive him forward, he refuses to move his feet; I do not know where this elephant intends to go.
The King said:
"Go as you please. He immediately released the hook and let him go to the park, where he stood outside the monastery gate, listening intently for sounds.
Once the Bhikṣu Śāṇakavāsin had finished reciting the sutra, he spoke four verses to make this aspiration:
“Devas, asuras, yakṣas, and others who have come to hear the Dharma, you should listen with a sincere mind;
protect the Buddha’s teachings so that they endure for long, and each of you should diligently practice the World-Honored One’s instruction.”
All you disciples who have come here, whether dwelling upon the earth or abiding in the air,
should always give rise to a heart of compassion for the world of humans, and day and night abide yourselves in accordance with the Dharma.
May all worlds be ever peaceful and secure; May boundless merit and wisdom benefit all living beings;
May all karmic offenses and obscurations be completely eliminated; And may they leave all suffering far behind to return to perfect nirvana.
Constantly using the fragrance of precepts to polish and adorn the body, Always wearing the robes of meditative concentration to sustain the person;
Adorned everywhere with the wondrous flowers of Bodhi, One dwells in constant peace and happiness wherever one stays.

When the elephant king heard these verses, he knew that the recitation was finished; he immediately shook his ears, lifted his feet, and walked, letting himself be driven along as he followed the hook.
The king asked the charioteer,
"For what reason does this elephant now move according to its own will?
The charioteer replied:
"What holy being is this within the monastery?
His exquisite voice recites the scriptures so beautifully that the elephant, having heard it, has conceived a longing for it and refuses to proceed.
The King said:
"If this is so, it would be fitting to turn the elephant and visit that Honored One; I wish to personally offer my upper garment as a gift, and we may set out for that city tomorrow."
The charioteer immediately obeyed the command and turned the elephant back before they had reached their former residence.
At that time, Queen Śrīmālā, wondering at the King’s swift return, inquired as to the reason for it. The King answered her in detail regarding the aforementioned circumstances, saying: "Queen!..."
"You may stack them on top; I wish to go in person to pay my respects to that master of the scriptures.
Then Queen Śrīmālā thought to herself:
"Could it be that the Venerable Sāṃgharakṣita is reciting the scriptures with such exquisite and beautiful tones?"
However, that venerable one’s appearance and demeanor are unattractive.

Now, our Great King is by nature fond of the magnificent; if he were to see him, it would not satisfy the King's heart, and he might give rise to feelings of disdain, regretting his previous reverence.
"You should employ skillful means so that he does not go in person. He replied, "Great King!"
"You may go to that city; I shall take this cotton cloth and offer it to the Venerable One.
She replied, "Noble Lady!"
"Even if you were to take the remaining bolts, how could this object alone cause the city of Kośala to become impoverished?
The lady remained silent, and the king then took the exquisite bolt of cloth and went to the Jetavana Grove.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was walking back and forth in front of the monastery gate. Upon seeing him, the king immediately dismounted from his elephant, prostrated at the Venerable’s feet, and asked:
“Venerable Sir!...”
"Venerable sir, what sutra of the Dharma are you reciting this morning?
He replied, "Great King!"
"Why must you ask?
[He replied: "Venerable Sir!
I wish to take this robe and personally offer it as a gift."
The Venerable One thought to himself:
"The venerable Śāriputra possesses a beautiful and melodious voice; his recitation of the sūtras and dharmas is elegant and surpasses all others, yet his physical appearance is exceedingly ugly."
"Your Majesty’s nature is one that cherishes the beautiful and refined; if he were to see her, he would surely regard her as lowly and base, giving rise to thoughts of disrespect.
You should devise some expedient means so that he does not go there in person."
He said, "Great King!
You may give this robe to me; I shall offer it as a gift."
He replied, "Venerable Sir,
the Blessed One has praised giving with one's own hands as being foremost; therefore, I now wish to give it to you myself."
At that time, the Venerable Sāriputra was sitting cross-legged beneath a tree in his daytime resting place.
Then Ānanda led the king to him and said, "Great King!"
The person sitting beneath the tree was none other than the Venerable Sāriputta.

When the king approached and paid his respects, he saw that the elder’s appearance was ugly; immediately conceiving feelings of contempt and disdain, he withdrew his gaze, lowered his eyes, cast aside his robes, and departed.
When Sāṇavāsa saw the king in this manner, he spoke these verses:
“If one sees me by means of form, Or seeks me through sound;
With a mind agitated by attachment, One cannot truly see me.”
If a person knows only the internal but does not see the external,
seeking the fruit within, they are deluded by sound.
If a person knows only the external but does not see the internal;
To seek the fruit externally—this too is being deluded by sound.
If one does not know the internal, nor sees the external, such ordinary people are all obstructed; this too is being deluded by sound.
"If a person well understands the internal and likewise well perceives the external, that wise one shall attain liberation; such a one is not deluded by sounds.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:

“By what causes and conditions did the bhikṣu Sunda, whose physical form was so hideous yet whose voice was so melodious, go forth from home to practice within the Buddha’s Dharma, exhaust all outflows, and attain the fruit of arhatship?”
The World-Honored One said:
"The bhikṣu Sāṃgharakṣita must himself experience the results of the karma he has previously created.
This was explained at length, culminating in this verse:
"Even if a hundred eons pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, one must experience the retribution oneself.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should listen! Long ago, in this Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was forty thousand years, the Buddha Krakucchanda appeared in the world, fully endowed with the ten titles."
At that time, all the Buddha-activities of that Blessed One were fully accomplished, and he entered the realm of the wondrous *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

Then the king of that country, named Aśoka, made offerings to the remaining relics of the Blessed One and constructed a *stūpa*, one *yojana* in circumference and half a *yojana* in height, commissioning people to guard it while gradually completing its construction.
That man possessed a faithful mind and a virtuous disposition; he worked with diligent devotion, never giving rise to weariness or fatigue.
At that time, a laborer, seeing that the stūpa was immense in scale and height, gave rise to feelings of disdain and spoke thus to his companions:
"The King is now constructing this great stūpa; it consumes so much human labor—when will it ever be completed?"
The gatekeeper replied, "If you are unable to do it, you may leave as you please; why do you suddenly utter such words of disdain?
He remained silent and offered no reply.
The guardian wished to drive him out, but he immediately apologized and returned to his former work. Even before the stūpa was finished, he again gave rise to feelings of disdain and negligence.

The guardian struck him with a staff and drove him away, but he returned once more to apologize and was sent back to resume his original task. This continued until the stūpa was completed; those who beheld it forgot their weariness, and hundreds of thousands of sentient beings were filled with joy.
Upon seeing this, those who had been critical felt regret and remorse, thinking:
"In the past, I committed unwholesome deeds by speaking with contempt when I saw that the stūpa was so high and large.
I should now provide offerings to it."
He immediately used the wages he had earned since then to craft exquisite golden bells and suspended them atop the stupa.
You should know that the hired laborer was none other than Sāṇavāsi.
Because he gave rise to feelings of disdain toward the stupa, he has now obtained a human body that is hideous in form;
yet because he offered a golden bell, his voice is harmonious and elegant, causing all who hear it to be filled with joy.
At that time, the bhikṣus still harbored doubts and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Venerable One!
What karma did the bhikṣu Sthūlananda previously create, by the power of which karma his chanting of the Dharma resounded all the way to the Brahma-heaven?"
The Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus, you should listen to this matter.

In the past, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, endowed with the ten titles, residing at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near Vārāṇasī."
Between the city and the grove stood a tree bearing fragrant fruit, where a bird capable of singing made its home.
At that time, Kāśyapa Buddha, carrying his robe and bowl, entered the city for alms during the morning meal and passed by the side of the tree.

At that time, the bird beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, whose countenance and deportment were upright and majestic like a mountain of gold; it immediately let out a wondrous warbling sound and, after circling the Buddha three times, returned to hide within the forest.
Thus, day after day, he would watch as the Buddha passed by, circling him with mournful cries before returning to dwell joyfully among the branches.

Suddenly, one day, he was seized by a hawk; after his life ended, he was reborn into a family of great brahmins. From that time forward, he was never again conceived within inferior or base classes, and in every place where he has been born until this day, he has possessed a beautiful voice that resonates up to the Brahma-heaven, bringing delight to all who hear it.
“O bhikṣus, you should know this: that bird capable of singing was none other than Sāṃgharakṣita.
At that time, the bhikṣus again had doubts and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
“Venerable Sir!”
“By what karma did the bhikṣu Sāṃgharakṣita perform such deeds that, through the power of that karma, he became foremost among the disciples of the Buddha for the excellence of his voice?
The Blessed One replied:
“The bhikṣu Sāṃgharakṣita obtained this retribution through the power of a vow he made.”
What vow did he make?
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, Shanhe (Suvīra) went forth as a monk.
Among the disciples of Kāśyapa Buddha, his original teacher was proclaimed to be the foremost in leading others and in chanting and recitation.

However, from the time he first left the household life until his old age, although he practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*), he attained nothing. As his life was coming to an end, he made this aspiration:
"Within the holy teaching of the Buddha Kāśyapa, I have gone forth and practiced, yet in the end I have attained nothing."

"By this supreme cause, may I, as prophesied by the Buddha Kāśyapa, attain ordination within the teaching of the future Buddha Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who will appear when the human lifespan is one hundred years; and having severed all afflictions and delusions, may I realize the fruit of Arhatship."

Just as my preceptor was proclaimed the foremost among disciples for his recitation within the Buddha’s Dharma, so too am I; whenever I encounter those who have gone forth, I am called the foremost among those who lead the chant.
"By the power of that vow, he has gone forth to practice within my Dharma and is declared by me to be the foremost among my disciples as a teacher who leads and exhorts.

You bhikṣus should know this: if past karma is purely black, one receives a purely black retribution; if it is purely white, one receives a purely white retribution; and if the karma is mixed, one receives a mixed retribution."
"You all should abandon purely black and mixed karma, and cultivate purely white karma,
as explained at length elsewhere.
The setting for this account is the same as before.
At that time, when the bhikṣus were reciting the sūtras, they did not master the rhythms and tones, but spoke according to the literal phrasing, like pouring dates from one vessel into another.

Those non-Buddhists, however, chanted their scriptures with melodic intonation. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went daily to pay his respects to the World-Honored One, he heard the sound of the non-Buddhists reciting along the roadside and thought to himself:
"These non-Buddhists have left the household life within a flawed doctrine and discipline; yet as they chant their scriptures with melodic intonation, their voices and words are truly lovely."
"Our noble ones are not conversant with phonology; they merely follow the words and phrases like pouring dates from one vessel into another.
This is my concern, and I must inform the Great Master."
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling and prostrated at his feet, he withdrew to sit at one side and said:
“World-Honored One!

Those various non-Buddhists have gone forth under an evil law and discipline; they recite the scriptures with melodic chanting, their tones and words being lovely to hear. Our noble ones, however, are not skilled in rhythm and melody; they follow the sentences and the literal text like pouring dates from one vessel into another.”
"If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would graciously grant permission, may the assembly of noble ones be allowed to recite the scriptures with melodic chanting.
The World-Honored One gave his assent by remaining silent and saying nothing.
Having seen that the Buddha had silently granted his permission, the elder prostrated to the Buddha and departed.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I allow you to recite the Dharma using melodic chanting."

After the Buddha had granted his permission, the community of bhikṣus recited the Dharma with melodic chanting, as well as reading the scriptures; likewise, they did the same for requesting instruction and making formal announcements.
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada entered the monastery, he saw that the voices of the monks throughout the entire complex were clamorous and confused, and he said: "Noble ones!
This monastery was formerly a dwelling for the Dharma; today it has been transformed into a city of gandharvas."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"A bhikṣu should not recite the various sūtras and dharmas with a chanting melody; nor should he do so when reading scriptures, requesting instruction, or reporting matters—all such practices are improper."
However, there are two matters for which one may employ a melodic chant:
first, praising the virtues of the Great Master; second, reciting the *Triśaraṇa-gamana Sūtra*. For all other matters, it is not appropriate.
The Buddha permitted these two matters to be performed with a melodic chant.
They praised the Buddha’s virtues and recited the three invocations.
There was a young bhikṣu who, when performing these two tasks, did not understand how to chant; he only knew how to speak directly with a voice like that of pouring dates.
The bhikṣus said, "The Buddha permitted two things to be done with a melodic chant;
why do you not do so? They replied:
"I did not understand it previously.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should study it."
When the Buddha sent them to train, the bhikṣus practiced the sounds of chanting everywhere—in their cells, along the corridors, in the gate-houses, and in the halls and pavilions.
When the elder entered and saw this, he felt the same reproach and indignation as before, and said:
"Venerable ones!..."
They were still unable to abandon the city of the gandharvas.
They went again to inform the Buddha, who said:
"You should practice the art of chanting in a secluded place; do not dwell in public. Whoever violates this shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
The setting was as before.
A certain bhikṣu stood up from within his bowl-bag and drew out his bowl. Another bhikṣu said to him, "Venerable one!..."
"Do not stand while withdrawing the bowl. He replied,
"What is the fault?"
He replied, "Is it not a fault that he fell to the ground and was injured?
The other remained silent.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not stand while taking up his bowl, nor should he stand while placing it in its bag, washing it, or drying it."
"Whoever violates this shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The sixth subsection of the first section is summarized in verse as follows:
Treading upon robes and various bags, as well as mattresses and sitting mats.
There are circumstances for being separated from the three robes and six kinds of mental recitation rules (*cetanā-dharma*).
The Buddha was staying at the Deer Park in the Terrifying Place on Mount Gaṅgāpūrvaja.
Prince Bodhi invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha and prepared a magnificent offering in the Pavilion of Exquisite Flowers; throughout this pavilion, layers of morning-hued silks were spread everywhere.
When the World-Honored One arrived there, he saw that the area was covered by robes and did not step upon it with his feet.
At that time, the bhikṣus also did not dare to step on them. Prince Bodhi addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately step across.
The Buddha did not tread upon it; having seen this, the prince immediately withdrew the spread-out cloth, and only then did the Buddha proceed forward.
Upon hearing this, the non-Buddhists spoke these words:
“The Śramaṇa Gautama is not worthy of such offerings; the prince dares not tread upon the spread cloth.
Having understood this, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there are faithful brāhmaṇas, householders, or lay devotees who spread exquisite garments upon a path and invite a bhikṣu, saying:”

The phrase "I pray that you descend with compassion to tread upon [me]" is intended to subdue the pride and arrogance of non-Buddhists; one should cultivate the perception of the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena as a means of treading over them, and should not give rise to doubt or hesitation.
The setting was as before.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu was walking along carrying his bowl in his hand; on the road, he tripped and the bowl fell, breaking it, which caused him to lack the necessary utensils.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not carry his bowl by holding it in his hand.
He then wrapped the bowl in a corner of his robe and departed; as before, this proved inconvenient and deficient. The Buddha said:
"One should make a bowl-sack to carry it in."
When the bhikṣus carried it by hand, they incurred the same faults as mentioned above. The Buddha said:
"You should not go carrying it in your hands; you should instead make a loop and carry it by hanging it over your shoulder."
"If one acts otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The setting and circumstances are as before.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling through the human realm accompanied by a caravan of merchants. Among his traveling companions was a brahmin who suddenly fell ill with a seasonal affliction and went to a physician, saying:
"I have such an illness; please prescribe a remedy for me.
He replied, "For this illness, you should take harītakī; you will surely recover."
He replied, "I am traveling on the road; there is no place where I can seek it.
The physician said:
"The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are well-versed in all medicinal herbs; if we seek them from them, they will surely grant us what we need.
Thereupon, he went at once to where the bhikṣus were and asked, "Noble ones!..."
"Do you have any harītakī? He replied, "I have some; what would you do with it?"
He replied, "I am ill;
the physician has prescribed this for me to take. Perhaps you would grant me some?

The bhikṣu, facing him, opened his bowl-bag to search for myrobalan fruits. First he pulled out needles and knives, then extracted scraps of leather, along with various medicinal substances, clean and impure mingled together.
At that time, the brahmin, seeing their impurity, replied:
"Venerable ones! Since you bhikṣus can perform such unclean acts, I would rather die than take this medicine."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus, you should possess three kinds of bags:
first, a bowl bag; second, a medicine bag; and third, a miscellaneous bag."
At that time, the bhikṣus all adjusted the three loops evenly and placed them under their armpits, whereupon they protruded from beneath the robes and became visible on the outside.
When laypeople of lack of faith saw this, they mocked them and said,
"O Noble Ones!..."
"How could one walk with a drum tucked under the arm?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The three types [of robes] should not be worn at the same level; they should be arranged in order so that their lengths are proportionate."
He then fastened the loops, causing injury to his body. The Buddha said:
"They must be made wide; place felt inside and bind it with thread so that it does not curl or shrink."
"If one acts otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle Four. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.
Fifth Scroll.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The remainder of the summary verses (uddāna) for the sixth section of the first chapter; the setting was in the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who obtained many woolen rugs and thought to himself:
"As the World-Honored One has said:
'One should wear robes made of cut and sewn patches.'"
He then took the mat and the knife and went beneath a tree, intending to cut it.
The World-Honored One arrived at that place and asked, "What are you doing?"
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has said:
'A bhikṣu should wear the three robes made of cut and sewn cloth.'"
"I have many woolen rugs and blankets; I now wish to cut them up to make the three robes.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised those who uphold the precepts and censured those who violate them, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five kinds of items that should not be cut into pieces: [the list follows]."
All types of cloaks, including long-haired and short-haired woolen blankets, as well as various felt rugs and tattered items— if one cuts these into patches,
one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The setting was as before.
There was a visiting bhikṣu who, having some business requiring him to leave briefly, had entered the monastery without bringing his sitting mat (niṣīdana).
As the sun was about to set, the administrator said to him:
“Venerable one!
You may take the bedding. He then replied:
“I have no sitting mat; what shall I use instead of a cushion?
“If that is the case, you may take a simple bed. He then took that bed.
At that time, it was a cold night that lasted until dawn, and he became chilled; consequently, his illness flared up.
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not go outside without a sitting mat. One who violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
As the Buddha has said:
"A bhikṣu should not go out without his *niṣīdana* (sitting mat).

At that time, when the bhikṣus wished to go briefly to the villages or neighborhoods within the same city, or to visit other monasteries, or to go out for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), they would take their sitting mats with them even though they intended to return on the same day.

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who were aged, ill, and physically frail; when they needed to go out, they lacked the strength to carry their bedding and mats, causing them physical exhaustion and mental distress. They spoke thus to the other bhikṣus:
"I have a matter to attend to and intend to return immediately, yet the Great Teacher has not permitted me to leave without my bedding and mats. What should be done in such a situation?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If a bhikṣu is going to a place for daytime recreation, or is visiting another monastery briefly, or is walking in meditation within the monastery itself, or is going to a nearby village with the intention of returning immediately, he need not take his niṣīdana with him."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who, having a reason to go out for a short time and intending to return soon, did not take his sitting mat (niṣīdana).

Having arrived at his destination, he encountered other circumstances and the day turned to dusk; because he lacked a sitting mat, he returned only after nightfall and was consequently harmed by insects, wolves, and thieves.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If one’s original intention was to return, but due to other circumstances one is unable to do so, one should stay overnight there and must not travel at night. One may borrow a substitute from a fellow practitioner of the holy life to fulfill the required duties."
If you obtain one, it is well;
if not, take a seven-strip robe (*saptaka-cīvara*) and fold it into four layers to serve as a mat or cushion, sleeping little and staying awake much until daybreak.

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who borrowed an item from another; having used it as an undergarment for his bedding, it became stained with impurities. He then returned this garment to the other bhikṣu, but the latter refused to accept it.
The bhikṣu reported the matter to the Buddha, who said:
"Wash it thoroughly before returning it.
After the bhikṣu had washed it and returned it, the other still would not accept it; he reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should return the equivalent value, or offer words of apology, so as not to cause resentment.
It should be understood that when the text mentions a "sitting mat" (*niṣīdana*), it refers to one that exceeds the length of the body.
Originally, it was intended to serve as bedding for lying down, rather than for prostrating on the ground; to prostrate on the ground is a profound departure from the fundamental ritual.
As the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not go out without his three robes."

As for the phrase "at that time," it refers to when the bhikṣus intended to go briefly to the villages or hamlets within the same city, or to visit other monasteries, or to go out for walking meditation; since they planned to return on the same day, they all carried their three robes with them.
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who were old, sick, and emaciated; when they wished to go out, they lacked the strength to carry their three robes. Distressed and weary, they spoke these words:
"We have a reason to go out for a short while and intend to return immediately, yet the Great Teacher has not permitted us to go without our three robes."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If a bhikṣu is going to a place for daytime recreation, or is visiting another monastery briefly, or is walking in meditation within the monastery, or is going to a nearby village with the intention of returning immediately, he may leave his belongings behind as he pleases."

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who intended to go out briefly with the plan to return without taking his robe; when it became dusk, fearing he would be staying apart from his robe overnight, he returned deep into the night and was harmed by insects and bandits.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If his original intention was to return, but due to circumstances he is unable to do so, he should stay overnight there and must not travel at night. He may borrow the remaining three robes from a fellow practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārin) and maintain them for that purpose."
