The bhikṣus did not understand how they should maintain [the robes].
The Buddha said:
"First, one should maintain the old robe; then, having mentally relinquished it, one should maintain the new one."
However, all bhikṣus should know that there are six matters to be attended to by mind:

first, the *poṣadha*; second, the *pravāraṇā*; third, the keeping of robes; fourth, the relinquishing of the three robes; fifth, the distribution of extra robes; and sixth, the relinquishing of special invitations.
When a bhikṣu obtained cloth but had no leisure to cut, wash, and dye it, the Buddha said:

"If the conditions for sewing, stitching, washing, and dyeing are not yet complete, one may take plain white cotton or raw silk fabric; provided its value is sufficient, one may use it to make the three robes. One may even borrow the clothing of a layperson from them and maintain possession of it without offense; do not harbor any doubts regarding this."
There were some bhikṣus who, not taking their niṣīdana (sitting mats) with them, stayed overnight in other places, thinking they had committed the offense of being separated from their robes.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I have ordained that bhikṣus must not stay overnight apart from their three robes; this does not apply to the niṣīdana."
"However, monks should not intentionally fail to take it with them; there is no offense for one who forgets.
The summary verse of the seventh section of the first chapter says:
"There are five kinds of water filters; eating from a vessel in a common place."
Regarding the matters of going naked, eating and drinking, and bathing, it should be understood that the setting was in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there were two bhikṣus from the south who wished to go to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One; however, neither of them possessed a water filter, and along their route, no water could be found.
Oppressed by heat and thirst, they arrived at a pond, where one person said:
"Venerable ones!
Look quickly at the water; we wish to drink it to quench our thirst."
He immediately inspected it and saw that there were insects in the water; thus, after checking repeatedly, he found them everywhere.
The two men deliberated, saying, "Since there are insects in the water, drinking it would take life. Now, being pressed by thirst, what should we do?"
Then the young bhikṣu spoke in verse:
"Throughout hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, The World-Honored One is difficult to encounter;
I shall now drink water, Hoping to pay homage at the feet of the Great Master."
Then the Great Bhikṣu also spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata, with great compassion, takes pity on sentient beings; He has cast away all attachments to the three realms of existence.
Having received the prohibitive precepts within this teaching, I would rather give up my life than harm any living being.”
At that time, the younger one could not endure the thirst and immediately drank the water containing insects, then followed the path and departed.

The elder one, however, resolved in his heart to protect the insects and would not drink; he instead exerted himself and went to the shade of a tree, where he sat with his body upright. He focused his mind on virtuous matters until his strength failed, at which point he passed away.
By the power of this merit, they are reborn in the sublime and wondrous realm of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Whenever one is born in heaven—whether male or female—three thoughts immediately arise: "Where did I die?"
"In what place have I now been born?
By what karma was this brought about?
He then recollected that he had died in the human realm and was now born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, due to having developed the utmost reverence for the Buddha’s teachings.
Then that deva thought to himself:
"If I do not go to pay homage to the World-Honored One, it would be a lack of reverence and improper.
Having had this thought, the deva immediately adorned his body, putting on celestial necklaces of extraordinary brilliance, and filled the folds of his robe with various exquisite flowers.
Utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, puṇḍarīka flowers, and māndārava flowers came to the place where the Buddha was during the first watch of the night.
Having thus scattered celestial flowers as an offering, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side to listen to the sublime Dharma.
The radiance of that deity was so exceedingly brilliant and magnificent that it illuminated the entire Jeta Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in accordance with that devaputra’s inclinations and faculties, preached the Dharma for him, enabling him to realize the principle of the Four Noble Truths.
Thereupon, the devaputra, using the vajra-pestle of wisdom, shattered the twenty-fold mountain of the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna).
Having seen the Truths, he addressed the Buddha three times, saying:
"O Great Virtuous One!

It is through the Blessed One that I have realized the fruit of liberation; this was not something that could be accomplished by my parents, a king of men, the host of devas, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, or kinsmen."
Because I encountered the World-Honored One, my good spiritual friend, I have been rescued and drawn out from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.

I have been established in the superior and wondrous states of humans and devas; I shall exhaust birth and death to attain nirvana. Having transcended mountains of bones and dried up oceans of blood, I have used the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter the view of a self-identity accumulated since beginningless time, and have attained the fruit of stream-entry.

I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and receive the five precepts: from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall refrain from taking life, and so on, up to refraining from drinking intoxicants.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will bear witness that I am an upāsaka.
Then, before the Buddha, he joined his palms in reverence and spoke in verse:
"By the power of the Buddha, The three evil realms are forever closed to me."
I shall be born in the supreme and wondrous heavens, And forever return to the realm of Nirvana.
Relying upon the World-Honored One, I have now attained the pure eye;
Having realized and seen the principle of the True Dharma, I shall reach the very limit of the ocean of suffering.
The Buddha transcends humans and devas; he is free from the afflictions of birth, old age, and death.
Difficult to encounter within the ocean of existence, I have met him today and attained the fruit.
With my body adorned and a pure mind, I prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.
"Having circumambulated the Enemy-Remover, I shall now depart for the celestial palace.

At that time, having expressed his aspiration, the deva was like a merchant leader who has acquired great wealth, like a farmer who has gathered a bountiful harvest, like a valiant warrior who has subdued his enemies, or like a gravely ill man whose many ailments have been removed. Then, taking leave of the Buddha, the deva departed for the celestial palace.

Then the young bhikṣu gradually traveled to the city of Śrāvastī; having entered the Jeta Grove, he set aside his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and approached the Blessed One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
It is the constant custom of the Blessed One that, upon seeing a visiting bhikṣu arrive, he immediately offers consolation and asks:
"Welcome, bhikṣu! From where have you come?
In what city or country did you spend this summer retreat?"
At that time, the World-Honored One asked that bhikṣu,
"From where have you come? He replied:
“World-Honored One,
I have come from the south.
He asked again:
"Where did you observe the summer retreat this year?
He replied, "I was also in the south."
The Buddha asked,
"Did you have any companions when you traveled along that distant road? He replied:
"Yes," he replied.
The Buddha asked, "Where has he gone?"
He then related the matter in detail.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If one treats my precepts with contempt, what is the use of seeing me?"
Even if one were to see me, it would not be seeing me nor making an offering to me.
That bhikṣu sees me because he is able to uphold the pure precepts;
you, ignorant and foolish person, cannot truly see me.
At that time, the Blessed One opened his upper robe, revealing his chest for them to see, and further spoke this verse:
“Behold my body, this physical form born of parents;
It is like the color of pure gold, Due to the power of past karma.”
If one does not revere the Dharma-body, one shall not see the Buddhas;
if one realizes the Dharma-body, one attains the vision of the Great Muni.
The first is my Dharma-body; the second is the physical form.
The wise are able to know and see; they should therefore well protect their ethical discipline (*śīla*).
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, a bhikṣu violated a training rule;
because he damaged a leaf of the *elā* plant, he has now fallen among the nāgas.
At that time, the Blessed One thought to himself:
"It is because the bhikṣus do not carry water filters that such faults have arisen.
He then addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should keep a water filter.
Regarding the Blessed One’s instruction that monks should keep a water filter, the bhikṣus did not know how many kinds of filters there were.
The Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of *ra* (strainers):
first, the square *ra*; if this is for regular use, one requires three, two, or one chi of silk.
For use by the Saṃgha, it may consist of two widths of cloth, according to its size at any given time."

The nets used for this must all be made of silk; only those that are so fine and dense that insects cannot pass through them are suitable. If they are coarse or thin, they are fundamentally unfit for use.
Some people use inferior silk, loose gauze, or hemp cloth, as they originally have no intention of protecting the insects.
Second, there are the Dharma-flask and the Yin-yang flask.

Third, regarding the *kundikā* (water flask): tie its mouth with silk and fasten it around the neck with a fine cord. Submerge it in water until the mouth protrudes halfway; if it is submerged entirely, water will not enter. Once it is full, draw it out and must still inspect it for insects.

It is not merely a *junchi* (water-strainer), but simply a wide-mouthed jar or pitcher; regardless of its size, its mouth is covered with silk and tied tightly with a thin cord. Taking water as needed is extremely convenient and eliminates the need for a separate vessel for releasing living beings (*fangshengqi*), which is of great importance.

Fourth, regarding the style of this "four-measure" strainer (*sizhuoshuiluo*): it was originally unknown in the Eastern Xia (China). As described elsewhere, it is a small round silk strainer (*luozi*).

Although its purpose is largely the same, it is not the original form. Fifth, regarding the "corner-of-the-robe" strainer (*yijiaoluo*): take a piece of fine silk about one span square. It may be tied to the mouth of the jar for drawing water for use, or placed over the rim of a bowl to filter water when required.
This is not the corner of a *kāṣāya*; it is dense and oily—how could it possibly be used for filtering?
It is only because we have been lost in our direction for so long that we ask: who shall point out the way?
However, all these *lō* are currently in use in the West.
Out of compassion for all living beings, the Great Master [Śākyamuni] even prohibited the eating of meat; how could one who kills out of great benevolence ever attain Buddhahood?
Even if you must briefly go outside the monastery, you should carry your water filter (*parisrāvaṇa*), along with a fine cord and a device for releasing living beings (*prāṇamokṣaṇa*).
If you do not bring these, not only will you be held in contempt by the Buddhist teachings, but how else can you instruct and admonish your disciples?
"The practitioner should contemplate this and especially maintain protection for the benefit of both self and others.
This occurred in Śrāvastī.
There were two bhikṣus who previously harbored mutual resentment, yet they traveled together through the human world as companions.
One had a water filter and the other did not.
The one with a filter strained the water and drank it; the one without a filter then said to him, "Venerable sir!..."
"You may borrow my sieve.
But he did not give it, and thus the task was left unfinished.
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Those who harbor resentment toward one another should not travel among people as companions.
Even if such circumstances arise, they must first express mutual regret and apology before they may proceed together.
This account took place in the city of Śrāvastī.
There were two bhikṣus traveling through the human realm; one possessed a water filter, while the other did not.
The one without it asked the other:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Do you have a water filter? He replied, "I do."
He did not ask again, "Would you lend me your water-strainer?

Those who possessed strainers filtered their water and drank, while those without them asked to borrow from them; however, they refused to lend it, and because of this, resentment arose, and they said:
"You asked whether it existed or not, but you did not say you were borrowing it.
Now, to speak of 'borrowing a net' is the height of irreverence; therefore, I will not give it to you.
Thus, he was left without his object.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If any bhikṣus wish to travel and do not possess a water filter themselves, they should ask their companions:
'Do you have a filter?'"
If he says, "There is," one should further ask:
"Will you share it with me?
If he says, "I will share it," [then proceed].
"You may go along with me immediately.
[The other] said,
"I will not give it to you."
"One who [says] this should not go.
The occasion was at Śrāvastī.
There were two bhikṣus traveling through the countryside; one had a water filter, while the other did not.
The one who had none asked,
"Do you have a strainer? He replied:
"I have it. "Would you give it to me? He replied:
"Let us share it. Thereupon they traveled together.
On the way, they encountered a caravan of merchants; among them was a weaver who had to return because of his loom.
The owner said, "You previously promised me a mango; you may now give it to me. He replied:
"I permit you to share the water after it has been filtered, but do not intend for it to be kept in its entirety.
Since the resident monk had no filter, he was consequently unable to perform his duties.
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu who does not possess a *sīvanaka* (sewing-filter) asks one who has one, saying:
'Do you have a *sīvanaka*?
and if [the other] says:"
If he says, "I have it," one should further question him:
"If you return, will you give me the cloth?"
If he says, "I shall give it," that is well; if he does not give it, one should not proceed.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir,
if one lacks a water filter, is it permissible to go to another village or another monastery?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not permissible.
However, if one knows that there is a *rāka* (a type of vessel) available at that location and that no deficiency in the matter will result, there is no offense."
“Venerable sir! May two people travel together using a single *ro*?
“If there is no deficiency in the matter, they may.”
“Venerable Sir! If many people share one *ra* (a measure of cloth), or if the community of monks (*saṃgha*) does so, may they go on tour?
“If there is no deficiency, they may.”
"Venerable One! If one has no water filter, is it permissible to go along the bank of a river? "Upāli!"
If the river current is swift and no other streams enter it, one should observe every five li.
If there are other waters entering it, one should observe as they are used.
If the river does not flow swiftly, one should also observe at each location.
“Venerable Sir! When observing water, to what extent may it be used?
The Buddha said:
"It is perfectly level for one fathom. "Venerable Sir!
If water has not been inspected or filtered, may it be used?"
The Buddha said, "It must not be done;
by using it, one incurs an offense.
[The monk asked,] "Venerable Sir!"
"If the water has been filtered, may it be used without further inspection?
The Buddha said, "It may not."
“Venerable Sir! If water has not been filtered, may one examine it and then use it?
The Buddha said:
"If you observe that there are no insects, you may use it as you please.
"Venerable Sir! If one filters and observes water, is it then permissible to use?"
The Buddha said: "If there are no insects, it may be used as you please.
The Buddha then addressed Upāli:
"There are five kinds of purified water:
first, that purified by the Saṃgha;
second, that purified by an individual."
Third is purification by straining through a filter;
fourth is purification by a spring;
fifth is purification by well water.
Regarding "purification by the Saṃgha" herein: it refers to when the assembly appoints one bhikṣu to inspect the water filter, and he performs the inspection according to the Dharma.
If other bhikṣus arrive, because the water has been purified by the assembly, they may drink and use it without offense.
Regarding "purity through another": if one knows that the other bhikṣu’s precepts, views, conduct, and livelihood are all pure, there is no offense in using the water he possesses.
Regarding "purity through a filter": if this filter has never had the fault of containing insects whenever it is used, there is no offense in not inspecting it.
Regarding "pure spring water," this refers to water that is free of insects when it first emerges.
Regarding "pure well water," one takes water at dawn and observes that it is clear and free of insects; until the appearance of the morning star (the *aruṇodaya*), it may be used as one pleases.
The bhikṣus observed the water by staring for a long time, which caused their vision to become blurred when looking at objects. The Buddha said:
"One should not gaze for a long duration; one should observe for only as long as it takes for a six-oxen bamboo cart to turn around.
Furthermore, there is no offense if one observes after having attained mental purity."
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were lay devotees, brahmins, and others who offered various food vessels to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus would not accept them, whereupon they all said:
"Noble One! When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had not yet appeared in the world, we regarded the followers of external paths as the supreme field of merit.
Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, we regard those such as yourself as superior; yet you do not accept our offerings. How could this be, lest we go to the next world without provisions?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"For the sake of the great assembly, one should accept vessels.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The bhikṣu who had received the utensils on behalf of the assembly took them and placed them in the storehouse, using his own bowl to eat whenever mealtime arrived.
When the donor saw this, he asked, "I gave these utensils to the noble ones; why do I not see them?"
He replied, "O worthy one! I have placed it within the storehouse."
He replied, "Noble One! Is there no storehouse within my home?"
When we originally gave these things, we hoped that you would enjoy them, so that we might obtain the merit of their enjoyment.
Since you have received them and placed them in your storehouse, we consequently obtain only the merit of the gift, but not the merit of its enjoyment.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should accept and make use of the items offered by others.
Having followed the Buddha's instruction, they immediately accepted and used them.
Later, at another time, there was a different donor who, out of a desire for something vast and grand, offered a large copper basin.
An elderly bhikṣu received this basin as his portion; as he scrubbed and polished it with his own hands, he became exhausted. The Buddha said:
"One should appoint a person in charge of the vessels to supervise their washing and polishing."
The bhikṣus then failed to exercise discernment when appointing someone to oversee the vessels, which resulted in their damage. The Buddha said:
"One who does not possess five qualities should not be appointed if not yet appointed, nor should be allowed to act if already appointed."
What are the five? They are:
being possessed of craving, possessed of anger, possessed of fear, possessed of delusion, and being unable to remember whether [a formal act] has been performed or not.
If one possesses these five qualities, one who has not yet been appointed should be appointed, and one who has already been appointed should be made to perform [the duties].
What are the five? They are:

being free from attachment, free from ill will, free from fear, free from delusion, and being able to properly remember what has been done and what has not been done. One who possesses these qualities should be appointed.
Having spread out the seats and struck the wooden gong, and having completed the formal announcement (*jñapti*), when the assembly has gathered together, one should first ask:
"Are you, so-and-so, able to distribute the bowls for the Saṃgha?"
One who knows they are capable should reply, "I am able. Then,
one bhikṣu shall perform the formal motion (jñapti-karman):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, wishes to serve as the distributor of utensils for the Saṃgha.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and you grant permission, may the Saṃgha consent that the Saṃgha now appoints this bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the distributor of utensils, who shall serve as the distributor of utensils for the Saṃgha."
“[The motion] is thus announced.

When the *karmavācanā* is performed according to this announcement, the bhikṣus receive the vessels; once they have finished eating, they hand over the soiled vessels to the person in charge of distributing them. The Buddha said:
“Soiled vessels should be given to disciples or attendants to have them wash and wipe clean.”
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had no disciple; he washed and wiped it himself. The Buddha said:
"This person should entrust the vessel to the one in charge of distributing vessels, leaving it for him to wash and wipe."
"If the disciples and followers do not know how to wash [the bowl], this task should likewise be entrusted to those who handle the utensils.
This incident occurred in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the group of six monks were eating together from a single bowl; as they simultaneously lowered their hands into it and lifted them up, the bowl rose along with them. They said to one another:
"Behold this black bowl; it can manifest supernatural powers.
As the six of them folded their hands [in reverence], the bowl immediately fell and broke. They all laughed aloud at once.
Having seen this, the bhikṣu replied:
"Venerable one!
To have committed such a loathsome deed together should be a cause for shame, yet you instead laugh loudly. He replied:
"What have I done? Have I been drinking alcohol?
Or have I been eating onions and garlic?"
The bhikṣu replied, "This matter will not take long; you shall see it accomplished as well.
The group of six said:
"Although my bowl is broken, could it be that the potter has died and the clay has all been exhausted?
I shall simply make another; what fault is there in this?
At that time, the bhikṣus were ashamed and had no reply, so they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha then thought to himself:
"It is because bhikṣus eat in one place together that such faults arise; whoever performs this act incurs an offense against the Dharma.

As the World-Honored One had taught that bhikṣus should not eat from the same vessel, at that time some bhikṣus were traveling with a caravan. When the merchants ate in one location, the bhikṣus also ate there.

However, as they lacked sufficient utensils, they did not dare eat together; waiting until everyone had finished before eating caused such a delay that they fell behind their companions, and were consequently plundered by bandits.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If you are on the road and no vessel can be obtained, even if there are many people, they should eat from a single vessel; when one raises his hand, the next should lower his, and they must not raise and lower their hands simultaneously."
The Buddha permitted them to eat together. However, some śrāmaṇeras did not dare to eat together with the bhikṣus, and the same faults as mentioned above arose. The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should first receive the food, hold the vessel in his hand, and eat in one place together with them."
When traveling together with a *śrāmaṇera*, the procedure is the same as when traveling with a novice; the Buddha said:
"Form the rice into balls, toss them [to him], and eat.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who arrived at the place where he had family ties, and his relatives addressed him, saying:
"It has been a long time since we parted and lived apart; now that we have gathered together, you may come and eat from the same platter.
He replied, "You are a layperson and I am one who has left the home life; it is improper for us to eat from the same platter."
He remained there, overcome with grief and shedding tears.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you know that someone is earnestly inviting you to eat together, you should do so in a secluded place to avoid causing public scandal."
"First receive the food, hold the tray with your hand, and eat together;
there is no fault in this. The occasion was at Śrāvastī.
The group of six bhikṣus ate while wearing only a single lower robe (nivasana). When laypeople saw this, they said to one another:
"Who is this person eating? One man replied,
"This is a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas."
They all felt ashamed and spoke thus:
"The teacher of this sect is extremely full of shame; why then do his disciples act with such lack of conscience?
The bhikṣus reported these circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"Eating while wearing only a single skirt involves such faults as these.
A bhikṣu must not eat while wearing only a single skirt; whoever does so commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Thus spoke the Buddha.

Regarding the rule, "One should not eat with only one skirt," there was at one time an elderly, sick, emaciated, and weak person who was unable to put on another garment while eating. The Buddha said:
"One should wear a soft and smooth *saṃkakṣikā* (undergarment); in such a case, there is no offense when eating."
Furthermore, there were those who were ill and unable even to wear this *saṃkakṣikā* garment. The Buddha said:
"If one's illness is severe, one should remain in a secluded place so that others do not see one; wearing only a single lower robe (*nivasana*), one may eat as one pleases."
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
While the six bhikṣus of the group were bathing naked in the Aśvattha River, some lay travelers saw them and asked,
"Who are these people?"
Someone reported, "This is a naked ascetic bathing in the river. Others further said:
"He is a son of the Śākyas.
They all looked upon him with disdain and spoke thus:
"The teacher of this man is extremely full of shame; how can his disciples be so devoid of modesty?"
Thereupon, the Buddha gave rise to this thought:
"The bhikṣus have such faults in bathing naked. Therefore, bhikṣus shall not bathe naked;
whoever does so commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
"However, the bhikṣus should possess a bathing skirt.
When the Buddha permitted the possession of a bathing garment, the bhikṣus immediately made them double-layered. The Buddha said:

"Fearing that insects might enter, you should not hold such [a garment]. If there is only a double-layered one and no single-layered skirt, you should examine the water to ensure there are no insects."
While they were bathing, there were those who possessed only three robes; fearing that it would constitute a violation of the rules, they did not wear these robes. The Buddha said:
"One should maintain and keep them.
Furthermore, there were others who were poor and lacked such items. The Buddha said:
"If it is certain that there are none, one may tie leaves together with a cord to screen oneself from front and back; bathing in a secluded place where others cannot see is not an offense.
After the bhikṣu had finished bathing, fearing that insects might be in his robe, he did not wring out the water. The Buddha said:
"A single-layered robe will certainly have no insects clinging to it; however, when emerging from the water, you should lift it up skillfully so that no insects remain."
The summary verse for the eighth section of the first chapter says:
Beans growing in impure ground; spitting, pointing with the finger, and requesting;
one should not use copper vessels; and keeping salt and other items as provisions.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a venerable bhikṣu named Kātyāyanīputra who gave rise to many doubts regarding almost everything; for this reason, the people of the time called him "The Doubting Kātyāyanīputra."
On another occasion, he saw bean sprouts growing inside a latrine and thought to himself,
"I have destroyed a living seed.
Later, at another time, when the monastic community was making many mung-bean cakes, he did not dare to eat them.
The disciple replied, "Upādhyāya!
The monastic community has plenty of mung bean cakes; why do you not eat them?"
He replied, "How could I now possibly destroy the seeds of life?
The disciple said:
"What is this matter? He reported the situation exactly as he had seen it, and at that time, the disciple also did not dare to eat.
His other acquaintances likewise asked:
"Why do you not eat? He then recounted everything exactly as his teacher had instructed.
At that time, Kṣemadatta had many disciples; the word was passed from one to another until the entire assembly stopped eating.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Among various beans, there are unripe seeds that will sprout again even after being boiled for a long time and eaten; since these have been cooked, there is no fault in eating them."
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One:
"If a fruit tree grows on impure ground and its fruit falls onto impure ground, may it be eaten?"
The Buddha said, “One should not eat it. [The monk asked:
“If a fruit tree grows in impure ground and its fruit falls onto pure ground, may it be eaten?”
The Buddha said, "You should eat it. [The monk asked:
"If a fruit tree grows in a pure area, but the fruit falls onto an impure area, may it be eaten?"
The Buddha said,
“If it has not passed the night, you should eat.
[He asked,] “Venerable Sir!”
"If fruit from a tree in a pure area falls onto a pure area, may it be eaten?
The Buddha said,
"It may be eaten."
The setting was in Śrāvastī.

There was a brahmin who was a leader among teachers; he obtained a bull, and later obtained a cow, and again obtained another bull. In this manner, as they were passed on from one to another, the cattle eventually formed a herd.
At that time, the brahmin regarded the first bull as an auspicious omen; he immediately set it free to live out its natural life and no longer tethered it.
Later, at another time, the bull became old and infirm. Being driven by thirst, it went to the river to drink water, but fell into the mud and was unable to extricate itself.
At that time, Śāriputra was passing by nearby and saw him submerged; he then examined whether he possessed any roots of goodness.

He perceived that the ox had a karmic connection to him, so he immediately lifted it out, removed the mud, and washed it clean with water. He gave it water and fodder, taught the Dharma in three phrases, and said:
"O worthy one!..."

"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all dharmas are without self, and nirvana is bliss; you should give rise to pure faith toward me and develop a profound sense of revulsion for the realm of animals."
Having spoken these words, he abandoned him and departed.
During that night, [the bull] was devoured by jackals. The bull thought to himself:
"If my ācārya had been by my side, I certainly would not have encountered such suffering as this."
With his mind fixed upon Śāriputra with deep respect, he immediately passed away and was reborn into the family of a great brāhmaṇa.
Śāriputra then thought to himself:
"I shall now go for a moment to see that old ox."
Applying his attention and observing, he knew that [the being] had passed away;
where was he reborn?
He saw that he had gone to a brahmin family.

At that time, Śāriputra, for the sake of converting others, went to the house of a brahmin; having visited there repeatedly, both the husband and wife came to invite him to receive the three refuges and the five precepts.
Later, at another time, the Venerable One went alone to that house. The elder asked, "Venerable One, why are you alone without an attendant?
[The Venerable One] explained at length as previously described. After eight or nine months had passed, a male child was born whose face resembled that of an ox.
On the day of the full moon, when his kinsmen had gathered together, they took the boy in their arms and requested that they establish a name for him.
The assembly deliberated and said, "This child’s physical appearance resembles that of a bull-king; we should give him the name 'Lord of Bulls' (Gośālin)."
The detailed account is the same as that of Subhūṣa’s circumstances: he went forth, received full ordination, and attained the fruit of arhatship.
Due to the power of his past karma, he had two gullets in his throat:
one for spitting out what was raw, and the other for swallowing what was cooked.
Before the Buddha had prohibited eating at improper times, [the monks] would vomit their food in a secluded place and then eat it again.
After the precept was established, they vomited and discarded the food outside; consequently, lacking the nourishment of food, their bodies became emaciated and weakened.
The Blessed One, having perceived this with his knowledge, intentionally asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"For what reason is the bhikṣu Gośālīputra so emaciated and haggard, appearing far more distressed than usual?"
Then Ānanda reported the matter in detail to the Buddha, who said:

"If one has been born with two throats as a result of past karma, when food comes out, one should discard it outside two or three times; thereafter, having rinsed the mouth thoroughly, one may swallow at will. This constitutes no offense."
There were some bhikṣus who, having finished their meal, had food come back up through their throats and became doubtful, thinking:
"Will I not have committed the offense of eating at an improper time?
The Buddha said:
"If there are those of such a kind, they should rinse their mouths thoroughly;
this shall constitute no offense. After the monk Goṣṭhika had thus gone forth, many lay travelers began to feel contempt and disdain, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, practice what is unrighteous, ordaining even those with such loathsome appearances as Goṣṭhika."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"My noble disciple’s virtue is like Mount Sumeru, yet it has caused the multitude to collectively harbor feelings of disdain and contempt."
"For this reason, the bhikṣu Gomayin shall not reside in the Middle Country.
Then the World-Honored One said to Gomayin:
"From this day forward, do not dwell in the Middle Country."
"You should reside in a frontier region.
Having heard the Buddha's command, he addressed the Buddha, saying, "So be it."
“World-Honored One!
Having spoken thus, he immediately departed from the Jeta Grove and went to the Śrīṣa Palace, where he dwelt in peace and security.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“Among my disciples who dwell in the borderlands, Gopiśāla is the foremost.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:

“Venerable Gopiśāla, what karma did he previously perform such that by the power of that karma, although he was born among humans, he took the form of an ox; yet, having gone forth to practice within the Buddha’s Dharma, he attained the fruit of arhatship?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The karma previously created by the bhikṣu Gośālīputra has increased and matured; he must experience its results himself, as described at length above."
You should listen:
In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, fully endowed with the ten titles.

In the past, the owner of the ox had left the household life to practice the path under that Buddha's Dharma; his preceptor was an Arhat who was the foremost among the assembly, but having grown old and infirm, his body was so emaciated that he could not even feed himself.
At that time, Gopaka would regularly assist his teacher in collecting their alms bowls.
Once they had been thoroughly washed, he would join the other bhikṣus in one place to practice recitation.
Later, on another occasion, because the teacher was slow in eating, the washing of the bowl was somewhat delayed; thereupon, a fellow reciter asked him:
"Why have you come so late now? He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"My preceptor takes a long time to finish his meal.

On another day, after the disciple had finished eating and washed his own bowl, he went to his teacher's place; seeing that the meal was not yet finished, he became angry and said to his teacher, "Why do you eat so slowly, like an old ox?"
The teacher thought to himself:
"Since he is currently so full of anger, if I speak now, it will only cause his fury to flare up further. I must wait until his anger has subsided before I can inform him."
Once his anger had subsided, he said:
"Venerable one!
What were you saying?"
He replied, "My teacher eats as slowly as an old ox.
He [the other] said in response:
"Venerable One! Do you perhaps know who I am? He replied:
"I know that my teacher has gone forth within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha Kāśyapa;
I, too, shall go forth here. He said: "Noble son!"

"This matter is indeed true; however, among those who have gone forth from the household life, I have already completed what was to be done. I am free from all fetters, whereas you remain bound by them.
Since you have uttered harsh and evil words toward me, you ought to repent of this transgression with earnestness and a sincere heart; only in this way can such evil karma be extinguished."
When he heard this, he repented with all his heart and reproached himself. Do you know, monks?

Because of the karma created by uttering harsh and evil words toward an arhat in a former life, he has constantly taken the form of an ox for five hundred lifetimes; even until today, the residual karma is not yet exhausted, and he still maintains the shape of an ox.
"By virtue of his diligent application to the practice of recitation, he has gone forth to practice within my Dharma, severed all afflictions and delusions, and realized arhatship.
At that time, the bhikṣus again requested of the Buddha, saying:
"What karma did the bhikṣu Go-vinda perform such that he is now favored by the World-Honored One to dwell in a frontier region and is designated as the foremost there?"
The Buddha said:
"It is by the power of his aspiration.
What vow did he once make?"
He immediately left the household life under that Buddha to practice his studies until the end of his life, yet he ultimately attained nothing at all through those sublime and wondrous gates.
However, his teacher, Kāśyapa Buddha, resided among the disciples in a remote region and was renowned as the foremost in receiving robes and food.
Having seen this, he made this aspiration:
"I have gone forth from the household life to practice the path under the Buddha; yet, throughout my entire life, I have gained nothing at all through the sublime and wondrous gates."

"By virtue of this meritorious work of diligent cultivation, may I—just as the Buddha prophesied for the young brahmin—that in the future, when the human lifespan is one hundred years and the Buddha Śākyamuni appears in the world, I shall go forth under his teaching, sever all afflictions and delusions, and realize arhatship."
Just as among the disciples of my Teacher, the Buddha, those who dwell in remote regions and receive offerings of food and clothing are said to be foremost,
so too am I among those disciples of that Buddha, receiving food and clothing from remote regions in the same manner.
"By the power of that vow, he now receives this retribution.
You should know that this results from purely black karma and so forth, as explained in detail above.
This was the occasion at Śrāvastī.
The group of six bhikṣus directed others while seeking food, saying, "Give me this item" and "Give me that item," causing the food servers to lose their proper sequence.
The bhikṣus reported these circumstances to the Buddha, who said:
"A bhikṣu should not direct others while seeking food; if he does so intentionally, he commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
If there is no heat from fire, there is no offense in taking cooked food;
if the heat from fire is strong, there is no fault in taking raw food.
The setting of the occasion is the same as before.
The Venerable Upānanda went to a copper smith’s workshop and asked,
“Good sir, would you be able to make a copper bowl for me?”
He replied, "This is my own work; why should I not be able to do it?
I simply do not know what size bowl is required."
He replied, "It was made large. He asked:
“Noble One! What will you do with such a large alms bowl? He replied:
“Fool! Do you not take payment for working for me?
He thought to himself:
"What harm does it do me if he makes it large?
He then fashioned a large bowl; when the other saw the bowl, he replied, "Make another, smaller one and place it inside this large bowl."

Thus, repeating this process up to seven times, once it has been completed, he then had the disciples wash themselves thoroughly. He tied five-colored threads into a bowl-cord (*pātrakaṭaka*), placed the bowls one upon another inside the cord, and had a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) carry them away on his head.
Whenever he was invited, he would always go ahead; upon arriving at the donor's house, he would sit down and spread out his wares before him.
At that time, some lay devotees, brahmins, and others saw this and asked, "Have you now opened a copperware shop?"
He replied, "Fool! What do you know?"
1. To hold rice; 2. to store parched flour; 3. to place cakes; 4. to put fine dumplings; 5. to receive soup and vegetables; 6. to set curdled milk and cheese; 7. to invite condiments.
The laypeople said, "If that is the case,
you ought to store even more, so as to accommodate twice as much food and drink as this.
Having heard this reproach, he remained silent and offered no reply.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"Because these bhikṣus keep copper vessels, such faults have arisen.
He then addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not keep copper vessels; those who do so shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
However, there is no offense if one keeps a copper spoon, a salt dish, or a copper bowl for drinking water."
"If it is another's object, its use is likewise not a transgression.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle Five. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.
Fascicle Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The Ninth Section of the First Gate. The Summary Verse says:
One should provide a place for washing the feet, as well as a basin for rinsing them;
when it is hot, fans are permitted, and five types of whisks are allowed to ward off mosquitoes and insects.
The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣus washed their feet wherever they happened to be, causing flies to swarm and disturb the area.
When some householders and brahmins entered the monastery and saw the place where the feet had been washed, they asked,
"Venerable ones!..."
"Why are insects and flies swarming about here?
He replied, "This is where we wash our feet."
Upon hearing this, they spoke with disdain:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are all impure; wherever they may be, they wash their feet.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not wash his feet anywhere; rather, the place for washing feet should be located in the southeast corner of the monastery.
When the Buddha had spoken thus regarding the installation of a place for washing feet, the bhikṣus did not know how it should be constructed.
The Buddha said, "It should be shaped like the back of a tortoise.
At that time, the bhikṣus made them so smooth that they were unfit for wiping their feet. The Buddha said:
"It should be made rough.
This place for washing one's feet may also be used for bathing.

Such facilities exist in all monasteries throughout the Western Regions; they are not fixed in size, being constructed in open areas, ranging from as large as a bed to as small as half a mat. Bricks are piled around the perimeter to a height of about one chi.

The middle section is paved with bricks in the shape of a tortoise shell and plastered with pebbles and mud that cannot be washed away by water; a conduit is opened on the side to allow the water to flow out.
This is most essential for washing one's feet and body.
There was an elderly bhikṣu whose body was so frail and weak that he was unable to go to the place where he washed his feet. The Buddha said:
"He should keep an attendant to wash his feet, and he should have a foot-washing basin made."
At that time, having heard that the Buddha had granted permission, the group of six monks fashioned foot-washing basins out of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli.
When laypeople saw them, they asked, "What is this object?"
He replied, "The World-Honored One permitted me to have a vessel for washing my feet;
this is it. The other said:
“Noble one! Although you have shaved your hair, your greed and defilements have not been removed. He replied:
"I am treading upon your neck; what fault have I, your servant?
You are not my teacher, so why do you reproach me?
Thus he spoke with vulgar disdain.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A vessel for washing the feet should not be made of precious materials; it should be made of clay.
The bhikṣus then fashioned one in the shape of a camel, and the Buddha said:

"It is not appropriate; it should be like an elephant's foot treading upon the ground, with the center slightly raised so that the foot may find support, or one may fashion the shape of a lotus pedestal within it, which must be rough and firm."
After the bhikṣus had washed their feet, they left them wherever they were. The Buddha said:
"You should not do so. If these are communal items, they should be covered and placed in a secluded location."
"If it is personal property, place it behind the door leaf.
The setting of the story is as before.

At that time, during the warmth of spring, the bhikṣus suffered from heat; their bodies became jaundiced, emaciated, and weak, rendering them incapable of exertion. When lay travelers saw them, they asked:
"Noble one! Why is your body so yellowish, emaciated, weak, and lacking in strength? He replied:
"It is now the season of spring's warmth, and I suffer from the heat.
He said, "Noble One!"
"Why do you not hold a fan?
He replied, "Worthy sir!"
"The World-Honored One does not permit it.
He replied, "Your Great Master is by nature compassionate; if he knew of this painful heat, there is no doubt he would permit a fan."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I now permit the bhikṣus to carry fans.

When the group of six bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had granted permission, they fashioned fan handles out of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or purple lacquer, polishing them and adorning them with various colors and patterns.
When worldly travelers came and saw this, they immediately felt contempt and shame; the six groups of monks were arrogant, as described in detail above.
Eventually, the Buddha said:
"One must not use precious materials or the like to make the handles of fans."
"It should be known that there are two kinds of fans:
first, those made of bamboo; second, those fashioned from leaves.
At that time, many laypeople with faith and devotion brought various decorated and colorful fans to offer to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus would not accept it. The Buddha said:
"If you receive it on behalf of the Saṃgha, there is no offense.
This occurred at the High Hall by the side of the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.
At that time, as the bhikṣus were being bitten by mosquitoes and insects, their bodies suffered from itching and they scratched incessantly. When laypeople saw this, they asked, "Noble ones!..."
"Why is this so? He answered her in detail regarding the matter,
and she said, "Noble One!"
"Why do you not carry an object for swatting away mosquitoes?
He replied, "The World-Honored One does not permit it; the full explanation is as before."
They went on to report this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I now permit the bhikṣus to keep mosquito whisks.

At that time, having heard that the Buddha had granted permission, the group of six disciples fashioned handles from various jewels and used yak-tail hair to make their whisks. When the laypeople saw them, they spoke at length as previously described.
The Buddha further said:
"There are five kinds of mosquito-repelling objects:
the first is made by twisting sheep’s wool;"
2. made from hemp; 3. made from finely torn and folded cloth;
4. made from old, worn-out materials.
5. Using the tips of tree branches.
If one uses precious objects, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
The summary verse for the tenth section of the first chapter says:
One should tie the lower garment not too high; one should not carry heavy loads.
If ill, the use of a staff and a sling is permitted; the consumption of garlic and similar items is likewise allowed.
The setting and circumstances are as before.
As the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should assist in construction work.
On one occasion, a certain bhikṣu had to ascend a ladder; as those standing above looked down from below, they saw his body exposed and said: [to one another].
“Noble One! Only now do I know that you are a man, by virtue of your possession of the male organ.
Standing upon the ladder, he remained silent with shame.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who then reflected:
"Because the bhikṣu ascended the ladder without tying his lower robe, such a fault occurred.
He then addressed the bhikṣus:
"If anyone must climb a ladder for the sake of construction work, they should tie up their lower garment before ascending.
Furthermore, when the bhikṣus were engaged in construction, they tied up their lower garments high; seeing this, the laypeople who lacked faith mocked them, asking:
"Noble ones!..."
"Do you wish to wrestle?
He replied, "I have other tasks to attend to."
Upon hearing this, he remained silent.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one ascends by means of a ladder, one should tie up the lower garment; however, when working on level ground, one should not do so."
Regarding the instruction to "tie the lower skirt," it means to grasp the lower hem at the back of the skirt and pull it tightly toward the waist; the manner of the hem is the same as before.
When the group of six bhikṣus carried heavy loads themselves, those who lacked faith saw this and spoke thus:
"I carry heavy loads because I fear that my parents, wife, and children will not be able to survive."
"Noble one, for what purpose do you exert yourself with such personal toil? He replied:
"O fair-faced one!"
I have several reasons:
first, to make offerings to the World-Honored One;
second, for the meal of the Saṃgha.
"Third, providing for the needs of the sick.
By reason of this cause and condition, one carries a heavy burden upon the body.
He remained silent and had no reply.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not carry a heavy burden on his body; whoever does so commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
While the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, an elderly bhikṣu climbed the mountain and fell to the ground while walking up and down. The Buddha said:
"One should carry a staff.

Having heard that the Buddha had granted permission, the group of six monks immediately carved and decorated their staffs with gold, silver, and various colorful materials. When worldly travelers saw them, they all felt resentment and contempt.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus, there are two circumstances under which one should keep a staff:
first, when one is old, emaciated, and lacks strength; second, when one's body is afflicted by the suffering of illness."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who feigned old age and illness while leaning on a staff.
The other bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"If one is truly old or ill, they should request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for keeping a staff; if the Saṃgha grants it, they may keep one."

In this manner, one should request [the formal assembly]: having spread out the seats and struck the *khaṇḍi* (wooden gong), once the formal announcement has been completed and the entire community has assembled, a senior or infirm bhikṣu should squat before the presiding elder, join his palms, and make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am aged, infirm, and weak, or perhaps afflicted by illness; without a staff, I am unable to sustain myself.
I now request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the possession of a staff. May the virtuous Saṃgha grant me, the bhikṣu [Name], the formal act for the possession of a staff.
"May those who are capable of compassion do so out of their compassionate pity.
This is said three times.
Then, one bhikṣu performs the formal motion (jñapti-karman):
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu [Name] is aged and frail, or perhaps afflicted by illness; without a staff, he is unable to sustain himself.”
I now request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the carrying of a staff.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant their consent, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now grant to the bhikṣu [Name], who is aged, infirm, emaciated, or afflicted by illness, the formal act for the carrying of a staff.
The motion is as follows:
"If the Saṃgha has already performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of authorizing the carrying of a staff, there is no offense for one who carries such a staff.
The occasion for this occurred in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the bhikṣus were aged, emaciated, and lacked strength; moreover, afflicted by wind-disorders (vāta-roga), they occasionally stumbled or fell to the ground while ascending or descending Vulture Peak Mountain, causing their water jars and alms bowls to shatter completely.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "Bhikṣus, you should carry a net.

When the group of six heard this, they made nets using five-colored threads; lay travelers criticized and disparaged them, and the circumstances of their inquiry and response are as detailed as those regarding the carrying of staffs.
"If both the staff and the net are required, it is appropriate to perform the *karmavācanā*; there is no fault in this.
Once the rite has been obtained, one may carry them as one pleases without committing an offense."
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having eaten garlic, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
The Buddha said: “Bhikṣu!...”
"You may sit; listen with a single-minded focus as I preach the Dharma.
When that bhikṣu had heard the Buddha’s command, he prostrated once more before the World-Honored One and sat to one side, whereupon the Buddha preached the Dharma for him.
While listening to the Dharma, he repeatedly turned his face away, fearing that some foul odor might lightly touch the venerable countenance; this happened two or three times.
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣu!..."
"You should listen with a single-minded focus to what I shall say.
The bhikṣu likewise turned his face away three times, then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and departed.
At that time, the Blessed One, knowing [the reason] yet asked on purpose: "Ānanda,
for what reason does that bhikṣu repeatedly turn his face away while listening to my Dharma?"
Ānanda said, "Because he had eaten garlic, I feared it would offend Your Holiness’s dignity; therefore, I repeatedly turned my face away.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"O bhikṣus, do any of you eat garlic? Ānanda replied, "There are."
The Buddha said:

"Because eating garlic obstructs entry into the Noble Path, those who do not eat garlic are permitted to hear my teaching of the Dharma; by means of the vajra-wisdom mallet, they shatter the great mountain of the twenty types of self-view and attain the fruit of stream-entry."
Therefore, Ānanda! From this day forward, I establish a rule for all bhikṣus: you must not eat garlic, scallions, leeks, or their like.
Whoever eats them shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
At that time, Śāriputra was seated among the assembly and thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu has not yet seen the Truths; will he see them tomorrow?"

He then examined [the matter], yet even with clear vision he could find no causal conditions for perceiving the principles of the Truths; he then entered further into the fourth dhyāna and observed its future limit, but still did not see the day he would realize sainthood.
He then arose from meditative absorption and spoke these verses:
"Because for even a brief moment, The mind is distracted and lacks concentration,
It will cause one in future lives Not to perceive the truth of reality."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in Śāriputra’s mind, addressed him, saying: “Śāriputra!
You should not now rashly attempt to fathom the Buddha’s realm; this transcends the realm of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”

However, in the future there will be a Buddha appearing in the world named Sarvārtha; within that Buddha’s Dharma, this person will leave the household life to practice, exhaust all outflows, and attain the fruit of Arhatship.
The Buddha thought to himself:

"Because that bhikṣu has consumed garlic, it obstructs his vision of the True Dharma; therefore, a bhikṣu should not eat garlic. One who eats it commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was afflicted with a disease; he went to a physician and said, "O worthy one!
I have such an illness; please prescribe a remedy for me."
He said, "Noble one!
You should consume garlic; your ailment will be eliminated."
He replied, "O worthy one! The Buddha does not permit eating."
The physician said, "This is the medicine for this illness; nothing else can cure it.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
The physician said, "This medicine will not cure anything else; there is no offense in consuming it.
Having heard this, the bhikṣu then ate garlic within the monastery for the sake of his illness.

Whether staying in rooms, on beds, mats, or carpets; whether moving about in large or small latrines; whether entering or exiting the assembly, walking to and fro, circumambulating a *caitya*, or prostrating before an incense altar; whether passing by laypeople and preaching the Dharma for them, or sometimes accepting invitations to visit the homes of donors, or arriving at gardens, forests, or temples where crowds have gathered and immediately going among them—at every place he reached, everyone smelled the stench of garlic and felt mutual contempt, saying:
"Though these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have left the household life, they still eat garlic and their foul odor permeates them; how are they any different from us?"
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I shall now explain the rules of conduct for a bhikṣu who has an illness and wishes to eat garlic.

Any sick bhikṣu who eats garlic must stay in a room at the edge of the monastery; he must not use the monastic bedding or furniture, nor the rooms for the large or small ablutions; he must not enter the assembly, nor preach the Dharma to laypeople; he must not circumambulate the caitya, nor prostrate before the incense altar; he must not go to lay households, nor to parks, forests, temples, or places where crowds gather."
One may eat and consume them in a secluded place so that, even if people should see one, they will not feel revulsion or shame.

Once finished consuming them, one should remain in this location for seven days; if one has consumed leeks, one may stay for three days, and if scallions, for one day. Only after that may one bathe and wash one's clothes; once they have been fumigated with incense and are free of odor, one may then enter the monastery.
As prescribed above, those who do not act in accordance with this shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The first section concludes. The summary verse for the second section says:
The cow-hair [rug] and the parasol, The *pāṃsukūla* (cast-off rags), the *saṃghāṭī*, and the occasion of the *Śrīmālā*.
The renunciant’s medicinal decoction jar, the door leaf, hammer, axe, and cauldron.
The summary verse for the first section of the second chapter says:
Cow-hair [brush] and the private parts, sharing a bed, and not wearing robes alone.
"If one obtains a white garment, it should only be used after dyeing it.
The setting and circumstances were as before.

At that time, after the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had offered the Jeta Grove to the Saṃgha of the four directions, he sent a barber to the monastery to shave the hair and beards of the monks, as described in detail previously.
Upānanda asked the barber, "Do you know how to perform the 'ox-hair' cut? He replied:
"I am a skilled craftsman; how could I not understand this?
He then used shears to perform the "ox-hair cut," leaving the hair at a length of two *fēn*; this is known as the ox-hair cut.
Upānanda said, "Cut another portion.
He spoke thus until the very end, finally saying:
"You foolish man, you do not yet know how to trim hair; it would be better to shave it clean so that you may be released to return home.
The full account is as previously related, until the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not trim his hair in the 'ox-hair' style; whoever does so commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma."

"As the Blessed One has stated, it is not permitted for bhikṣus to have their hair cut in the 'cow-hair' style; yet, if a sore suddenly develops on a bhikṣu’s head, he suffers pain when shaving it with a razor."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One may use scissors to trim the area around the wound; otherwise, it should be shaved as usual.
The circumstances were the same as before.
The elder ordered his men to shave the heads of the assembly, as described in detail above.
When Upānanda saw this, he said,
"Are you able to remove the hair from my private parts for me?"
He replied, "This is my craft.

He was immediately ordered to shave [the king's head], and as before, he was driven about until evening and then released to return home; at that time, the common people looked upon him with disdain and contempt.
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not shave the hair of the three places.
One who shaves it commits a transgression of the Dharma."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who developed an ulcer in his private parts; occasionally, worms emerged, causing such unbearable itching and pain that he was unable to practice wholesome deeds.
The Buddha said:
"Those with such medical conditions should inform an elder bhikṣu, and thereafter they may have the area around the ulcer shaved by one another. Do not harbor any doubts regarding this."
The setting was as before.
The group of six bhikṣus lay upon a single bed, leaning against one another, agitated, and laughing aloud.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who thought to himself:
“There are such faults in sleeping on the same bed; those who lie on the same bed incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus were traveling through the countryside and arrived at a village where they borrowed beds from others. The host gave them one, to which they replied, “We need more.”
The host replied, "In my home, many people sleep on the same bed; why do you bhikṣus each demand one for yourselves?
What harm is there in many people sleeping together?"
The bhikṣu replied, "The World-Honored One has not permitted it.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If there are bhikṣus who, by nature possessing a sense of shame and modesty, cultivate the practice of the precepts, and who, with right mindfulness established in their hearts, spread out a cloth to lie upon and place a cloth pouch or an alms-bowl pouch between themselves and it before lying down."
"Since the bed is thus, it should be understood that the remaining mats and cushions are to be treated accordingly.
The setting of this account is the same as before.

A large number of bhikṣus were traveling through the countryside and arrived at a certain village, where they obtained a place to sleep from the house of an elder. As it was a time of cold weather, they further sought bedding materials.

At that time, the members of the household felt compassion for the bhikṣu and lent him their bedding. Whoever first obtained it would wrap themselves alone in it and lie down, while those who did not receive any had to endure the cold throughout the entire night.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not take the bedding first and sleep alone; it should be used in common, with the elder taking the upper cover.

Later, on one occasion, Upānanda received the bedding as his turn according to seniority, yet he covered himself with it, rose alone, and went for a walk, leaving the others to suffer from the cold and endure hardship during the night.
The junior monk replied,
"I am suffering from the cold, yet you, Venerable Sir,
are walking in meditation. Upānanda said:
"Who prevented you from rising to practice walking meditation?
Those bhikṣus endured the cold throughout the night.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When the community is being provided with bedding for lying down, it must cover [the body] completely. If one wishes to practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), one may wear private clothing.
If one wears communal clothing [for this purpose], one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
It was during the winter months when the bhikṣus suffered from the cold; they lay on one side with their bodies turned to one side.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada entered the monastery and, seeing the bhikṣus lying on one side, asked:
"Noble ones!..."
"The Great Master’s teaching emphasizes diligent effort; for what reason, O virtuous ones, do you lie prostrate and waste the days and hours without cultivating wholesome qualities?
The bhikṣus replied, "When the mind possesses joy and happiness, one may cultivate wholesome qualities; but we are currently suffering from the cold—how can we exert ourselves?"
"I am now frozen; who else could know this?
The elder took his leave and returned to his residence, where he provided five hundred pieces of thick white cotton cloth as robes for the assembly of monks.
At that time, the bhikṣus immediately put on their robes and went out from the monastery to wander about. When the unbelieving laity saw them, they felt disdain and shame, and asked:
"Noble ones! Have you all returned to lay life?"
He replied, "You should not speak such words; I wear these lay garments because of the cold.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is not permissible to wear the robes of a layperson.
If there is a compelling reason, one must first cover those robes with a dyed cloth before wearing them.
If it is a *saṃghāṭī* robe or a cloak, one should replace the inner layer with another object and cover the outer surface with another object, and only then put it on."
Otherwise, one will incur sin.
The second section, second sub-section, is summarized in verse as follows:
Umbrellas, no future life, singing, and not setting fire.
Wandering to seek a preceptor; one must not wear a woolen cloak turned inside out.
The setting is as before.
In this city there was a householder who regularly collected clothing and sold it to support himself.
Later, at another time, he obtained many material offerings and thought to himself:
"What skillful means might there be by which I may cultivate meritorious deeds and yet obtain even more profit?
This householder was naturally endowed with faith, and he reflected thus:

"I should now invite the Buddha and the Sangha; I shall spread exquisite robes upon their seats and provide various foods and drinks. Since this offering of food and clothing is a great field of merit, by virtue of this cause of giving, I shall obtain much benefit."
Having formed this thought, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and stood to one side. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I pray that the Buddha and the Saṃgha will come to my home tomorrow to accept my humble offering; I only beseech you with compassion not to refuse my request."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing this, the elder prostrated to the Buddha and departed. Returning to his house, he prepared various kinds of excellent food and drink, arranged a magnificent seat, and spread fine robes upon it. He then dispatched a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Buddha know that the time has come."
At that time, the great assembly all went to that house; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the steward remained within the monastery.
There are five causes and conditions for which the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, leave a steward behind to obtain food for the Buddha.
What are the five? First, the desire for seclusion and quietude, far removed from all clamor and bustle;
second, the desire to proclaim the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of the devas.
Third, it was because he wished to examine the sick person;
fourth, because he wished to examine the bedding and furniture;
fifth, because he wished to establish rules of training for his disciples.
Now, the World-Honored One has established this training rule:

when the community of bhikṣus goes to accept an invitation, they may encounter heavy rain on the way, causing their robes to become soaked. Upon arriving at the house and taking their seats, the clothing is stained wherever it rests upon those seats.
Having seen this, the householder felt extreme aversion and thought to himself:
"I have lost all my belongings; it would be fitting for me now to take these items back and give them as an offering to the bhikṣu."
Having had this thought, he said:
"Noble One! Whatever items you sit upon, I offer them all to you; please take them with you."
The bhikṣu replied, "I must wait to inform the Blessed One; I do not yet know whether he will permit it.
The bhikṣu reported the circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should know that it was not the householder’s original intention to give this gift; because it would lead to public censure, you should not accept it.
When the bhikṣus had received the Buddha's instruction, they sent a messenger to inform the householder:
"You should know that the Buddha has spoken these words:"
"It is not that this householder’s original intention was to offer these as a gift; because there is cause for public censure, they should not be accepted.
When the householder heard these words, he conceived a deep sense of reverence and thought to himself:
"If I were to sell these garments, I would not receive even half their value. It would be most appropriate if the Noble Ones were to dye them to change their color and wear them for their use."
He immediately took the robe and went to the monastery, addressing the noble assembly, saying:

"Originally I had no intention of giving away this object; however, at this time I have changed my mind and wish to offer it to the Sangha. I pray that you will accept it for me, dye it, and wear it."
"I only pray that you, sirs, will hold up the parasols so as not to let the robes become wet.
They replied, "Householder,
wait until we have consulted the Buddha."
They reported the circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"Previously, the householder had no intention to give; now, having resolved his mind, he offers it to the Saṃgha. You may accept it, dye it, and wear it; for the sake of benefiting this person, do not harbor any doubts."
"Therefore, I now command all bhikṣus to carry parasols; whoever does not do so shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

When the group of six bhikṣus heard that carrying parasols was permitted, they fashioned handles from the four precious substances such as gold, decorated them with various kinds of purple mineral pigments, and made canopies out of peacock feathers.
At that time, the laypeople and brahmins, seeing this, felt disdain and contempt; their questions and answers were as before. Eventually, the bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who said:
"A bhikṣu should not carry such an umbrella."
"However, there are two kinds of canopies:
first, bamboo, and second, leaves.
When the group of six bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had permitted canopies, they made the handles excessively long and carried them while passing through the great city.
When worldly travelers saw him, they said:
"Who is that merchant leader or great wealthy householder holding a parasol who has come from another region?
The people immediately approached him to look at and question him; once they saw he was a bhikṣu, they all felt resentment and shame. When the bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should not make the handle of a parasol too long; it should be equal in length to two cubits or the same as the canopy itself.
Furthermore, when entering a village, one should not carry a parasol.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling among the people in the company of a merchant caravan who arrived at a village where the road passed through the interior of the settlement.
A bhikṣu carrying a parasol did not dare enter the village; while traveling outside the village, he became separated from his caravan and, walking alone behind, was plundered by bandits.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who said:
"If the path is within a village, one must not hold it upright; if one carries it tilted while departing, there is no offense."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who entered a village to beg for food; because he had previously touched the handle of his umbrella, he did not dare to carry it while walking, and consequently his robes were soaked by the rain.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"A person begging for food should wash the umbrella handle clean before carrying it away. If it is certain to rain, one should leave it deposited wherever convenient; only when about to leave the village may one take it with him."
The setting was as before.

At that time, there was a wandering ascetic from the south who followed the Lokāyata school and denied the existence of future lives; his name was Udāyin. Traveling by stages, he arrived at Śrāvastī and, wishing to relieve his fatigue, entered the Jetavana Grove. He first went to the place of the Venerable Kauṇḍinya and said to him: "Bhikṣu!"
"I have studied a little of the written word under my teacher's gate, and I wish to engage in a brief discussion with you,
O worthy one. The Venerable One replied, "Brahmin!"
"Engaging in heated debate is not my practice; you may seek it elsewhere as you wish, but it is not fitting for you to remain here.
He then went to visit Aśvajit, Bhadrika, Mahānāman, Vāṣpa, Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Gavāmpati, Vimala, Subāhu, and Rāhula. Having arrived before each of them, he addressed them one by one, saying: "O Bhikṣus!"
"I have studied a little of the written word under my teacher’s gate, and I wish to engage in a brief discussion with you, O worthy one.
At that time, the venerable ones replied: "Brahmin!"
"Engaging in such heated debate is not my practice; you should seek it elsewhere and have no need to remain here.
Thereupon, he went again to the Venerable Śāriputra and asked the same questions as before.
At that time, Śāriputra immediately entered meditative concentration to observe whether the non-Buddhists possessed any roots of goodness;
he perceived and knew that they did.
To whom were these roots attached?
"I see that they belong to me.
Are there others who, through hearing the discourses and discussions, have been tamed?
He observed and knew that there were indeed others.
"When will the assembly be held?
"Within seven days.
Having understood this, he replied:
"It is a good thing that you seek a debater; let us establish a debating hall at such-and-such a place.

On the first day, the Venerable Śāriputra ascended the high seat himself and established his thesis to engage in debate with him. At the conclusion of each session, he would always leave some points unresolved. This continued for two, three, and even up to seven days, until his fame spread throughout all the kingdoms and regions; it became widely known that there was a heterodox teacher from the south, a follower of the Lokāyata school who denied the existence of future lives, named Udāyin, who was brilliant and possessed great wisdom. He traveled by stages until he arrived at Śrāvastī, where he established a point of debate with Śāriputra, and after these seven days had passed, there was still no victory or defeat.

Countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings with whom he shared a karmic connection had all gathered like clouds; some had given rise to a heart of joy, while others had previously matured their roots of goodness.
The Venerable Śāriputra then thought to himself:
"Those with whom I share a karmic connection who were to be transformed by listening to this discourse have all assembled at this time."
At that time, the Venerable One, having exhausted the meaning of his words, explained them in summary for the assembly.
Then those non-Buddhists, their minds opened through faith and understanding, rose with palms joined and spoke these words:
"Venerable Sir!..."
