"I seek to go forth in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya; I pray that you will grant me compassion and deliverance, so that I may diligently practice the holy life in the presence of the World-Honored One.

At that time, Śāriputra, knowing his resolve to be sincere, granted him the going-forth and conferred upon him full ordination (*upasampadā*), providing him with instruction according to the Dharma. He then exerted himself and aroused a courageous mind, exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*) and attaining the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, all the members of the assembly, having witnessed this event, were filled with wonder and said:
"The Venerable Śāriputra is so exceptionally wise that he has used the Dharma to subdue these arrogant non-Buddhists and caused them to go forth."

At that time, the Venerable One observed the assembly, noting the differences in their faculties and the diversity of their inclinations; he taught the essentials of the Dharma in accordance with their past conditions, causing hundreds of millions of sentient beings among those who listened to attain individual realizations—some attaining the fruit of Stream-enterer, Once-returner, or Non-returner; some leaving the household life to attain the fruit of Arhatship; and others receiving the Three Refuges along with the five precepts.
The rest of the great assembly all conceived a profound sense of reverence for the Three Jewels; with palms joined in earnest devotion, they took their leave and dispersed.
At that time, this bhikṣu reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Śāriputra does not exist everywhere, nor can anyone even be found who is his equal."
"Therefore, I now permit the bhikṣus to study the Lokāyata and other such secular treatises.

When the bhikṣus heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had permitted the study of books and treatises, they did not exercise discrimination; even those who were dull-witted and ignorant began to study secular texts. The Buddha said:
"One should not allow those who are foolish, lacking in wisdom, or lacking clarity to study secular texts."
"Only those who know themselves to possess clear wisdom, extensive learning, and a powerful memory capable of refuting non-Buddhists may study [these texts].
When those of clear wisdom constantly studied external scriptures and failed to cultivate wholesome qualities, the Buddha said:
"One should not habitually study external scriptures in this manner."
The Buddha said:
"One should divide the day into three periods: at each of two periods, one should recite the Buddhist scriptures, and during one period, one should study secular texts.
The bhikṣus subsequently divided the months and years into these three periods and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Human life is swift and uncertain from moment to moment; one should not divide it into three periods according to months and years, but rather divide a single day into three parts.
A bhikṣu studied non-Buddhist texts in the morning and read the Buddha’s sūtras in the evening. The Buddha said:
"In the first part of the day and during the middle and latter parts, one may read the Buddha’s sūtras; when it reaches the evening, one should study non-Buddhist texts."
The bhikṣus then read it for a short time, but without reciting the text, they soon forgot it. The Buddha said, "You should recite it.
They did not know when they should recite it.
The Buddha said:
"As there are three periods during the day, so too are there three times at night.
The setting for this account is the same as before.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra ordained two sons of brahmins:
one named Gavaṃdatta and the other named Gavampati; he instructed both of them in the recitation and study of the scriptures.
Later, these two traveled together through the human world and, arriving at a certain village where they received abundant offerings, they settled there.

At that time, because those two had previously studied the methods of Brahmin chanting and recitation, due to their long-standing habituation, they now performed their recitations using the original phonetic style.
At that time, one of them fell ill and suddenly died; the survivors, overwhelmed by grief, neglected their studies for a long while and eventually returned to Śrāvastī.
Having entered the Jeta Grove and rested, he went to where the Venerable Kauṇḍinya was; after completing his salutations and respects, he said:
"Venerable One, let us rehearse the scriptures together."
He replied: "Excellent! I shall recite it for you."
Having recited a small portion, he replied, "The sūtras you have recited,
Venerable One, contain errors in the text and the prosodic rhythms are not sustained, resulting in omissions."
He replied, "Son! I have been practicing and reciting this in such a manner from long ago."

He then took his leave and went separately to visit Aśvajit, Bhadrika, Mahānāman, Vatsa, Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Gavāmpati, Vimāla, Subāhu, and Rāhula; having arrived at each of their places, he addressed them, saying:
"Venerable Sirs!"
"Recite the scriptures with me. He replied, "Excellent!"
"I shall recite it for you.
Having recited a small portion—as extensively described before—until he had paid his respects and taken leave, he went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was. Once he had paid homage, he said:
“Upādhyāya! We may recite the scriptures together. He replied:
"Excellent! I shall recite for you.
As they recited together, he drew out the tones and rhythms with great length; Śāriputra’s voice, however, was twice as long, and he said:
“Great Master!
All the other venerable ones recite incorrectly; only you, my preceptor, have no error in your phonemes or phrases. He replied:
“You foolish person, you have committed an error yourself; you slander other wise ones by claiming they do not recite the sūtras well, yet those venerable elders are all free from error.
Having been thus rebuked, he remained silent and speechless.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:
"The bhikṣus recite the sūtras by drawing out the tones and melodies like songs; such is the fault. Therefore, bhikṣus should not recite the Dharma by singing or modulating their voices."
If a bhikṣu recites the sūtras with a *cāṇḍa* (harsh or discordant) voice, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).
However, if the local dialect of a region requires the drawing out of sounds, there is no offense when doing so.

Regarding the term *chanda*, it refers to the method of recitation used by Brahmins, which involves prolonging the sound and marking the pauses by pointing at the air with one's fingers; the teacher first chants, and the others follow after him.
*Vinaya-ksudraka-vastu* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, Volume Six; *Vinaya-ksudraka-vastu* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, Volume Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The second section of the second chapter, the remainder of the summary verse (*uddāna*), concerns the circumstances that occurred in Śrāvastī.
Although the six groups of bhikṣus were advanced in years, they remained constantly restless. The other bhikṣus said to them:
"You are already advanced in years, yet your restlessness has not ceased.
Having heard this, he remained silent for a moment, and then said to Nanda and Upananda:
"Those black-bowl monks are extremely meddlesome, constantly issuing admonitions. We ought to do something shameful to make them feel abashed."
From then on, they set their minds upon seeking an opportunity.
At that time, a great number of senior bhikṣus went to a forest grove and sat in meditation beneath a tree.

Then the group of six also went into the forest; seeing them in a state of meditative composure, they set fire to the windward side of three sides of the grove and stood at a distance on one side, watching from afar.
At that time, seeing the fire approaching, those senior elders all rose in alarm and fled with the smoke.
When the group of six saw this, they spoke these words:
"Venerable sirs, you are old and yet your agitation has not ceased; why do you run about so restlessly, losing all composure?"
He replied, "Venerable one!
Do you not see that a fierce fire is burning the forest? What is so strange about running away?"
The group of six replied,
"How could the World-Honored One have established these precepts during times of tranquility, only to allow their violation during times of peril?
They answered:
“Is it not you who have let loose this fire disaster?
The group of six laughed loudly and said,
“We did this intentionally to humiliate you.”
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not burn forests or wildlands.
If he does so intentionally, he commits the offense of sthūlātyaya."
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
There were two bhikṣus, an elder and a junior, traveling together through the countryside; the elder possessed many robes and requisites, while the junior had only the three robes.
The elder said to the youth, "Venerable one!
You may hold my robe-bag for me; I am now utterly exhausted and wish to rest my shoulders for a moment."
The youth replied, "I wish to offer a few words; I pray you do not reproach me.
He answered, saying:
"Speak as you wish; who would be angry with you?
He replied briefly, "Does the Elder not see that one should offer whatever one obtains to the Triple Gem—the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha? Why rely on hoarding such foolish things?"
He said, "O worthy one! If you do not hold it, who else would force you?"
"But I ask you: 'Are you my ācārya or upādhyāya that you should presume to admonish me?
" The junior monk remained silent.
The old man thought to himself, “I should now take care of this fellow.

When evening came, they stayed together at the monastery; however, the monks within the monastery had long established a regulation that no one who lacked a formal sponsor (niśraya) was permitted to stay, even for a single night.
The monastery official said to the two guests,
"Since you have newly arrived, you may request bedding.
Having taken it, the elder spoke these words:
"You may request [some bedding]," he said.
The junior monk replied, "I have not yet received formal reliance; I shall wait until I have obtained a teacher before requesting bedding."
He then went to the foremost elder among the assembly; having paid his respects, he said:
"Elder, please grant me formal reliance (*niśraya*).
The elder replied:
“O noble one! With whom have you come? He replied:
“Venerable [Name],” “Worthy one!
You should go to him and request him to be your preceptor; do not let that person speak in such a manner:”
"The Elder Maṇḍūka has broken our community of disciples.
Having heard these words, they went to others; thus it spread from one to another throughout the entire monastery, and wherever they went, they were nowhere received.
Later, he returned to his quarters, knocked on the door, and called out, saying:
"I pay my respects to the Elder. He asked:
"Who are you? He replied, "I am so-and-so."
“May you be free from illness. He replied,
“Does the Elder know?”
"This is the regulation established by the assembly of this monastery: one must not stay for even a single night without having a formal preceptor (*niśraya*).
You may grant me your formal preceptorship. He replied:
“O worthy one! This is indeed a good regulation; if the assembly does not enact it, I shall establish it for them.
You previously said to me:”
"Have you not seen how the Triple Gem keeps many foolish things?
Now he says: "I pay homage to the Elder."
"How extreme is this reversal!
Who could possibly act for one so negligent and insolent?
Follow your own inclination and seek another teacher upon whom to rely."
He remained silent and would not open the door;
sitting on the ground throughout the night, he endured suffering until dawn.
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not travel among people without relying on a preceptor.

Furthermore, while monks do not harbor a stubborn or harsh heart like a lion—maintaining resentment without relinquishing it—the Saṃgha should not arbitrarily establish such evil regulations that cause other monks to suffer affliction without cause."
"If a bhikṣu wanders among the people without a preceptor, or acts with the intent to disturb others by establishing unlawful regulations, he commits an offense against the Dharma.
While the Buddha was wandering among the people of Magadha, he stayed in the palace of the yakṣa Bhakula on Mount Makula, with the bhikṣu Nāga as his attendant.

At that time, during the dark hours of the night, as a fine rain fell from the heavens and flashes of lightning streaked across the sky, the World-Honored One was walking back and forth in meditation upon the open ground.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that until the World-Honored One has lain down to rest, his attendant must not lie down before him.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, used his divine eye to survey the lower realms and saw the Blessed One in the palace where the yakṣa Bhakula resided; during the dark of night, as the heavens rained lightly and flashes of lightning streaked across the sky, the Buddha was walking back and forth in meditation upon an open space.
"I should now pay my respects to the World-Honored One.

He then immediately transformed himself into a magnificent lapis lazuli palace, which followed his body as he ascended to hover above the World-Honored One, walking behind his Great Master as they proceeded on their journey.
In the common custom of the people of Magadha at that time, if they saw a child crying at night, they would say: "Do not cry!
The yakṣa Bakkula is coming to eat you."
At that time, Nāgaseṇa saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who, as the night deepened, did not lie down but continued walking in meditation for a long while, and thought:
"I should now employ the yakṣa Bhūtakrūra to terrify him."
Having formed this thought, he immediately donned his long-haired great cloak and, at the place for walking meditation, announced: "Śramaṇa!
The yakṣa Bhakula has appeared before you."
The Buddha said to Nāgārakṣa: "You foolish man!

You have tried to frighten the Sugata with the yakṣa Bhūkuṭī; yet the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has long since been free from fear, and even the bristling of hair and the trembling of the heart have been entirely dispelled."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing that Nāgarakṣa was performing unrighteous acts, felt aversion and wonder, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
are there also such persons as these within the Buddha-dharma?”
The Buddha said to Śakra:
“You should now know!
The house of the Gautamas is exceedingly vast and spacious; within it, there are many diverse paths for various classes of beings.”
"Do not despise this person; they shall also attain the pure Dharma in a future life.
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, departed for his celestial palace.
Then the Buddha thought to himself:
“Because the bhikṣus wear the great cloak with the fur facing outward, such faults arise.
I now decree that any bhikṣu who wears it in this manner shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.”

When the bhikṣus had heard this prohibition, they traveled among the people following a caravan of merchants until they reached a cowherd’s settlement. It being a cold night, they obtained a long-haired woolen cloak (*kambala*). The cloak had a foul odor and was infested with many lice; they wished to wear it with the hair facing outward as a covering, but fearing they would violate the precepts, they did not dare to turn it inside out.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When wearing it with the hair facing outward, one may only sit upright; walking while meditating is not permitted.
Whoever violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
The third sub-section of the second chapter contains this summary verse:
Regarding the wearing of the *kambala*—whether it is permitted or not; not placing the bowl on uneven ground;
the three types of fastenings permitted for robes; and one should know that there are likewise three types of waistbands.
The setting was in Śrāvastī. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you obtain cotton bedding, or long-haired woolen cloaks, or high-pleated garments—such items as these I now permit."

Whether for the Saṃgha or for an individual, it may be used at will; however, if it is a superior *kūṭāgāra-paṭa* (highly pleated woolen cloak), the Saṃgha is permitted to keep it, whereas an individual is not allowed to do so.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went for alms; during the first part of the day, he took up his robe and bowl and entered the city to beg for food. His upper robe fell off, so he quickly set his bowl on the ground to adjust it.
When the householders and brahmins saw this, they felt aversion and spoke thus:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are largely impure; they place their alms bowls wherever the ground is filthy and foul."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not place one's bowl on the ground; to do so constitutes a transgression of the Dharma.
However, for the sake of protecting the robe, one should attach a fastener."
The bhikṣus then sewed their robes together with thorns, which caused the robes to become damaged.
The Buddha said, "One should not do so.
They then tied them together with thread; the Buddha said:
"This too is improper; you may place a hook upon the shoulder and attach a toggle to the chest.
The bhikṣus did not know how to make the toggle, so the Buddha said:
“There are three kinds of ties: first, like a *yǎngwù* (blackberry) fruit; second, like a *kuí* (sunflower) seed; third, like a *tánglí* (quince) fruit.
He attached the fastener at the edge of the shoulder seam, which caused it to break quickly. [The Buddha said: “One should attach the fastener four finger-widths behind the seam.”
He immediately attached the toggle to the robe, causing it to tear quickly. The Buddha said: "One should make a patch and pierce holes with an awl;

place the toggle inside and tie it to form a double loop. The button should be sewn along the edge on the chest. Fold the robe three times; this is the place where the toggle and button are to be installed."
"Whoever violates this regulation shall incur an offense of transgressing the law.
The circumstances were as before, in Śrāvastī.

While a bhikṣu who was begging for alms was on his rounds, his lower garment fell down; he set his bowl on the ground to adjust it, whereupon a layperson saw this, felt disdain, and spoke these words:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not distinguish between the pure and the impure; they place their alms bowls wherever they happen to be.
When the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should fasten one's lower robe before entering a village."
He tied it with a cord, causing the garment to tear quickly.
The Buddha said, "Do not tie it with a cord; you should use a waistband.
The bhikṣus did not know how the waistband should be made. The Buddha said:
"There are three kinds of cords:
first, the oblong; second, the square; and third, the round.
If one uses anything other than these, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
The fourth section of the second door, summarized in verse, says:
The matters of Śrīmālā and Ajātaśatru; Next, the prohibition of various necklaces, Golden cords, and colored objects— None of these should be kept.
The Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, a certain village belonging to the Śākyan Mahānāman had its overseer suddenly pass away.
Then the people came and said to Mahānāman, "The village overseer has now died; please send another person to manage the affairs of the village.
At that time, a young brahmin (māṇava) was standing nearby, and Mahānāman addressed him:
“Māṇava! You go now and attend to the affairs of the village; I shall subsequently send another official.

He then departed immediately, went to the village, and conducted the inspections according to the law. The agricultural produce he delivered to Mahānāman was twice as much as that of his predecessor, yet the former showed no sign of resentment.
The Great Name asked, "Now you have sent much in taxes, double what is usual; have you not oppressed the people? He replied:
"O people! I collect taxes according to principle and do not oppress you.
At that time, Mahānāman asked the villagers:
“Does this young brahmin cause distress in the villages?
The people replied, “No one harbors any resentment toward him.”
Thereupon, Mahānāman was established as the ruler.
He administered taxes with impartiality and justice, refraining from oppression or seizure, and served as the official in charge of affairs to govern the villages and towns.
At that time, the young brahmin took a wife from a great brahmin family, and before long, he gave birth to a son.

After further months and years, he also had a daughter named Candrāvatī (Moonlight). She was raised according to the Dharma and gradually reached adulthood; she was wise and intelligent, with a countenance so surpassingly beautiful that there was no village or town where she was not praised.

Later, at another time, his father fell ill; although medicinal decoctions were administered, the illness was ultimately not cured. All the annual taxes collected in this town were exhausted for the cost of medicine, leaving nothing remaining.
He went further to borrow from other villages to use it, but his illness grew increasingly severe until he met his end.
At that time, the people of the village went to the Great Man's residence and said to him: "O Master!..."
"That official in charge of affairs has now passed away.
Mahānāman asked, "Is there an annual tax in that village?"

He replied, “During this year we collected much in taxes and levies, but because they were all spent on the cost of medicines for those who fell ill, it was still not sufficient; we have had to borrow from other villages.”
Mahānāman said, "Whatever remains may be used to repay the debt.
The people replied:
"There is nothing else remaining,
save for a wife and two children— a daughter named Candraprabhā, who is intelligent, wise, and of such surpassing beauty that there is no village or town where she is not praised."
Mahānāman replied, "Let the mother and son live as they please; you may bring the daughter Candraprabhā here.
Thereupon, the townspeople released the mother and son, and Candraprabhā was led to Mahānāman’s presence.
At that time, there was an old woman in that house who constantly performed two tasks:
first, she cooked cakes and food; second, she gathered various flowers.
Then the old woman said to Mahānāman:
"I am now advanced in years and cannot endure two tasks; let this young girl be my companion.
He replied, "As you wish."
The old woman then replied to Candraprabhā, "You may now go into the grove to gather flowers; I shall prepare the cakes and food at home.
After she had gathered the flowers and bound them into a beautiful garland with thread, she presented it to Mahānāman. Seeing it, Mahānāman was delighted and said:
"Excellent flower garlands may be left here; you may go.
He summoned his mother and asked her, "For what reason were there few flowers previously, while now they are twice as many?"
She replied, “Previously, when a relative came to my family to beg from me, I would distribute [the flowers] immediately; now I do not give them away.

Furthermore, my eyesight is dim and I cannot observe with precision, whereas this young girl’s eyes are clear and she gathers the flowers with careful discernment; for this reason, there are many flowers.”
The Great Name said:
"If that is so, let this girl remain in the garden; every day she shall gather many flowers and, having fashioned them into a magnificent garland, bring it to me."
For this reason, the girl was named Śrīmālā.
Later, when the girl took her portion of food and went toward that garden, she encountered the Blessed One entering the city to beg for alms.
On the road, Śrīmālā beheld the Buddha’s physical marks; she gave rise to a profound heart of reverence and gazed upon his venerable countenance. Standing there with thirsty longing, she thought:
“Because I have never made offerings to the true field of merit since the past, I have now obtained this state of poverty and lowliness.”
"If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would accept my food, I shall take this meal and offer it as a gift.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the girl's mind, immediately extended his alms bowl and said: "Good woman!"
"As you have thought, those who wish to offer food may place it in the bowl.
At that time, Śrīmālā took her own meal and, with a heart of reverence, placed it within the Buddha’s bowl; she prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and spoke these words:
"By this merit, may I cast off this body of a maidservant, forever leave behind poverty and suffering, and attain great wealth and nobility."
Having made this vow, she prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
On the road, she suddenly encountered a friend of her father’s; that man was skilled in physiognomy, and upon seeing that Vaśitā’s body bore extraordinary marks, he asked:
"Where are you going?"
Śrīmālā wept, and [the King] asked again:
"For what reason do you harbor such grief? She replied:
"Father! I have been taken by the one of great name to serve as a maidservant. She said:
"Little girl, extend your hand; I shall examine your marks.
She then extended her hand, and the old man, having seen it, spoke this verse:
"If upon a person's palm, There are the marks of the garland and the hook;..."
Though born into a lowly household, she shall become the consort of a great king.
If a person has the marks of city-towers upon their hands;
though born into a lowly household, they shall become the consort of a great king.
If one’s mouth is like a pond, and their voice resonates like the cry of a king of geese;
though born into a lowly household, they shall become the consort of a great king.
Do not grieve now; you will surely be freed from servitude.
"You shall certainly receive supreme wealth and honor, and you shall become the consort of a great king.
At that time, Śrīmālā took her leave of her aged father and proceeded toward the park.

Later, King Prasenajit set out on a hunting expedition with his fourfold army in full array; the horse he was riding suddenly bolted, and despite all efforts to restrain it, it could not be controlled and eventually reached the kingdom of Kapilavastu, entering the Great Name Park.
Having seen her, Śrīmālā said,
"Welcome, Great King! The King asked Śrīmālā:
"Whose garden is this? He replied,
"It is the Great Name Garden."
The king then dismounted from his horse, and the woman led him to tie it to a tree.
The king said, "Bring water; I wish to wash my feet.
The woman thought to herself:
“Warm water should be sought to wash the King’s feet.
He then went at once to fetch water warmed by the sun, filled it in a lotus leaf, and brought it to the King’s presence to wash his feet.
The king spoke again, saying, "Fetch more water; I must wash my face.
The woman thought once more:
"Washing the eyes with warm water is not appropriate.
She stirred the water with her hand until it was neither too hot nor too cold, and brought it to the king's presence.
After the king had washed his face, he spoke again to the girl:
"Bring more water; I wish to drink.
The woman then thought to herself:
"Cold water is needed to quench one's thirst."
She immediately went to the pond, drew deep water, and presented it to the king.
Once the king had drunk it, he asked the girl:
"Are there three kinds of water in this garden?"
He replied, "The garden has no three waters; it was originally a single location.
The king asked again:
"If it is but a single body of water, how did you previously obtain three distinct kinds?
He reported in full what had occurred before to the king.
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately reflected:
"This woman is skillful in means and well-versed in the proper timing.
Having thought this, he said to the woman:
"I wish to lie down; I require you to massage my feet."
Once the king had lain down, the girl massaged his feet, and the king fell asleep.
The girl then thought to herself:
"Kings are of noble and high status; they harbor many resentments, yet few show concern for others."

"Your Majesty is now asleep; I fear that wicked people may come to harm you. If I do not close the gates for Your Majesty, and some injury should suddenly occur, both I and my master will surely incur blame and punishment. Therefore, it is necessary to provide defense."
He immediately bolted the gates.
At that time, the four divisions of the army sought out the Great King and arrived at his garden, asking: "Is the King here?"
Having heard these words, the woman did not open the door; the sound of the army thundered outside, and the king was startled awake. He immediately asked the woman, "What is this noise?"
The woman said, "There are people who have come to ask where the King is; they wish to open the gate.
The King then questioned the woman:
"Who closed its door? He replied, "I closed it."
"Why have you closed it?
The woman replied,
"I was thinking to myself:"
"Among kings and nobles of high station, those who harbor resentment are many, while those who offer concern are few.

Your Majesty is now asleep; I fear some evil person may come to harm you. If I do not close the gates for the King, and you should suddenly suffer injury, both I and my master shall incur blame and punishment."
Thereupon, she immediately closed the door.
When the king heard this report, he praised her, saying:
"Excellent woman!"
"You truly have a most ingenious plan.
The King asked,
"What is your relationship to the great-named owner of this garden?"
He replied, "I am a servant of the one named Mahānāman.
The king said to the woman:
“You are no ordinary woman; you are a girl of great renown. Why do you not speak the truth?
The girl remained silent.
Then the king said to her:
"Go into the city and inform Mahānāman, saying:
'The Great King Prasenajit is within your garden.

The woman immediately went quickly and reported this to Mahānāman. Having heard it, Mahānāman prepared various delicious foods as well as fragrant flowers, and accompanied by a great multitude, he went to the garden. Upon seeing King Prasenajit, he cried out:
"Welcome, Great King!

they said, greeting one another with mutual inquiries. They then provided the king with water for bathing, followed by superior garments, fragrant unguents, and flower garlands, and served him a meal of exquisite delicacies.
After the meal, during their conversation, he asked Mahānāman,
"What is this young girl to you? He replied:
"This is a servant girl.
The King said, "She is not a servant; she is your daughter and ought to be given to me."
Mahānāman said, "There is another daughter of the Śākya clan who is several times more excellent than this one; why not take her?
The King said:
"This girl is what I require; I do not seek anyone else.
Mahānāman said, "If that is the case, I shall adorn her and provide the necessary rites to escort her to you."
The King said, "Excellent!

Thereupon Mahānāman immediately adorned the city walls and moats and swept the streets. The lady Vaśitā, fully arrayed in various necklaces and ornaments, was mounted upon a great elephant. At the crossroads, she rang a bell to proclaim throughout the entire population of Kapilavastu, as well as to those gathered from all directions:
"You should know that the daughter of Mahānāma of the Śākya clan, named Śrīmālā, is now to be sent to King Prasenajit of Kośala to serve as his chief queen."
The entire populace of the city escorted them out.
Then, King Prasenajit prepared a grand military ceremony to welcome them back to his kingdom.
At that time, the King’s mother, hearing that a maidservant had been taken as a queen, conceived a sense of resentment and thought to herself:
"This is no good son; he has merely burdened my womb.
Having been born and raised to maturity, he will ultimately become a slave's husband.
Having thought this, she remained there dwelling in sorrow.
When she was welcomed into the city, the King said to Śrīmālā, "You may now go and pay your respects to my mother.

Śrīmālā immediately went to her mother's presence, grasped her feet with both hands, and bowed her head in salutation. As her soft and delicate hands touched her mother, the latter felt a profound sense of peace in body and mind and fell asleep. After a short while, having awakened, she spoke these words:
"Beholding the beauty and touch of this maidservant’s form, she will surely cause me to lose the city of Kauśala.
At that time, King Prasenajit had two principal queens:
the first was named Vāsavadattā, and the second was named Mallikā.
Whenever the King was in the company of Śrīmālā, he would praise Varṣākārā, saying:
"Śrīmālā, you should know that the lady Varṣākārā’s countenance and deportment are transcendent."
Śrīmālā said to the king,
"When shall I be able to see you?
The king replied:
"We shall see one another before long.
Whenever he gathered with Varṣākāra, he would praise Queen Śrīmālā, saying:
"Varṣākāra, you should know that Queen Śrīmālā’s skin is so delicate and smooth as to be a rarity in all the world."
Vairāṭī said to the king,
"When may I have the opportunity to see you?
The king replied:
"I shall soon cause you to see him.
The king and the other [the minister] praised one another, causing each to conceive a sense of affection, respect, and a longing to meet.

Later, at another time when the three months of spring had arrived, the hundred species of plants flourished; in the lush forests and clear ponds, flowers and birds reflected one another’s beauty. Peacocks, parrots, geese, wild ducks, and mandarin ducks, along with various other species, warbled piteously as they flew in flocks, their voices blending in harmony.

On one occasion, the king was in a fragrant garden with his court ladies, wandering about in various places, enjoying themselves in merriment and play. While the king rested in sleep, the palace women became unrestrained; craving various flowers and fruits, they roamed about as they pleased.
At that time, Varṣākāra was weary in body and stood for a moment leaning against a branch of an aśoka tree.
As Śrīmālā passed by, she came to his side; seeing Varṣākāra, she thought to herself:
"This must be a tree deity."

She immediately prostrated at her feet; as Śrīmālā touched her, Vārṣākāra fell asleep. When the king awoke and saw from afar that Śrīmālā was still by Vārṣākāra’s side, he summoned his court ladies and returned to the palace.
Later, at another time, when the king was praising Vaśiṣṭhā in the presence of Varṣākārā, Varṣākārā said:
"When shall I be able to see Vaśiṣṭhā?
The king replied:
"You have already seen it.
Ghoṣila replied, "I have never before perceived or seen it."

The King said, “I shall cause you to remember when we met before. Recall how you went into the garden and stood for a moment leaning against a branch of the *aśoka* tree; at that time, Śrīmālā came and saw you, and her hand touched your feet.”
Varṣākāra replied, "Is that Śrīmālā? The King said:
"Yes," Khemā replied,
"I know that the King has deep affection for me, such that he could abandon his delicate and refined appearance to show such personal intimacy toward me."
The king went again to where Śrīmālā was and praised Varṣākāra;
Śrīmālā asked, "When shall I be able to see Varṣākāra?
The king replied:
“You have already seen it.
Śrīmālā replied, “I have not seen it.”
The king said,
"I am causing you to remember that you prostrated at the feet of Varṣākāra beneath the Aśoka tree.
Vaidehī replied to the king:
"Is that Vārṣika? The king replied, "Yes."
She then addressed the King, saying:
"I know that Your Majesty has deep affection for me, such that you have abandoned your exquisite complexion and physical beauty to show me such personal favor.
This was heard by all the people of the kingdom: that the Great King Śrīghoṣa had two queens.

One was Śrīmālā and the other was Varṣākārā; Śrīmālā’s skin was so soft and supple that it surpassed all others, while Varṣākārā’s deportment was such that it was difficult to compare with anything else.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying: "Bhadanta!..."
“By what karma did Śrīmālā and Varṣākārā each act, such that by the power of that karma, one has a body so delicate and soft, while the other possesses a countenance that transcends all others?
The World-Honored One replied, “Both of these were brought about, increased, and matured by their own respective karma; the full explanation is as in other [sūtras].”

"O Bhikṣus! In times past, in a great city, there was a brahmin who, shortly after marrying a wife, fathered a son. Before many years had passed, he also fathered a daughter. As they both grew up, their parents fell ill and both passed away."

At that time, having encountered such sorrow and distress, the youth resolved to go to the mountain forest; he immediately took his younger sister with him, and together they went to the woods to gather flowers and fruits to sustain themselves.
"O bhikṣus! A great black snake has five defects. What are these five?"
First, being prone to anger;
second, harboring much resentment;
third, committing evil deeds.
Fourth is ingratitude;
fifth is the poison of profit.
One should know that women likewise have five faults:
First, being prone to anger;
second, harboring much resentment;
third, committing evil deeds.
Fourth is ingratitude;
fifth is the poison of profit.
What is meant by "the poison of profit" regarding women?
Generally, women often harbor minds of fierce and intense lustful desire.
At that time, when the young girl reached adulthood, her desire grew increasingly strong, and she said to her elder brother:
"I can no longer sustain my life by constantly eating flowers and fruits; we should go among the people to seek food and drink."
Then the elder brother took his younger sister and together they left the mountain forest, going to the house of a brahmin to beg for alms; they both called out at the same time.
When the host came out and saw them, he said, "Even those who live in seclusion maintain wives."
The elder brother said, "This is not my wife; she is my own sister.
He then asked his brother:
"Have you ever been betrothed? He replied, "No."
"If that is so, why do you not give it to me? He replied,
"This has already distanced itself from the evil dharmas of the world."
The woman’s desire was intense, and she replied to her brother, "How could I not survive on the various flowers and fruits in the forest?
However, I cannot endure being oppressed by afflictions; therefore, we have left the wilderness together and come far into the human world. Now, you may give me to the Brahmin."
The elder brother said, "I truly cannot marry you; this is an evil practice and not something I would do.
You possess worldly desires, so act according to your own inclinations."
When the brahmin understood the woman’s heart, he invited her into his home and held a great assembly of his kinsmen to take her as his wife.
He then said to his elder brother, "From now on, you may live in the same residence as me; let a separate room be prepared for you."
The elder brother said, "I do not seek sensual desires; I shall delight in leaving the household life.
The younger sister said:
"Only after we have established a formal agreement may you act according to your wishes.
The elder brother said,
"What kind of agreement are you speaking of?"
The sister said,
"If you have realized the supreme fruit, you may come to see me.
The brother said:
"Excellent! It shall be as you have wished.
Having spoken thus, he took his leave and went to the hermitage to enter the religious life.

By the power of the roots of goodness from his previous lives, he spontaneously realized the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without a teacher and attained the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha. He then thought:
"I previously made a pact with my sister; I should go to see her now."

He then went to that place, ascended into the void, and manifested supernatural transformations; fire issued from his upper body while clear water flowed from his lower body. Displaying many such wondrous signs, he descended from the sky.
When all those ordinary worldlings saw the supernormal power, their minds turned back with great speed, like a massive tree collapsing to the ground; they prostrated at his venerable feet and said:
"O Elder Brother!
"Now I have attained such extraordinary, sublime, and supreme virtues. He replied,
"I have realized them."
He said, "Brother, you require food and drink for the sustenance of your body; I seek merit and wish to offer an act of worship, so please stay here. He replied:
"You have no autonomy; you may go and inform your husband.
She then said to her husband, "Do you know this now?"
"My elder brother has left the household life, perfected the prohibitive precepts, and attained the most sublime fruit, foremost in the world.
I wish to make offerings to him, yet I dare not act on my own authority; if you grant me permission, I shall provide him with food and provisions for three months."
He replied, "O noble one!
Even though he has not left the household life, although I do not wish to, I must ultimately provide for him."
"Moreover, since you have already left the household life to attain the supreme path, I shall now provide for you for three months according to your wishes.
Her husband had another wife who, seeing the food and drink being given, thought to herself:
"The family wealth is shared by all; since he seeks merit, why should I not do so as well?"
He said, "Your elder brother is also my venerable one; I wish to offer my service on alternating days. He replied:
"According to your wish.
Out of consideration for her brother's feelings, the Pratyekabuddha’s sister placed the exquisite food inside and covered it with coarse food;
she then took it and said to her former wife, "I am offering this food to my elder brother; I pray that you will rejoice in it."

At that time, when the day for offering food arrived, the former wife, wishing to protect his feelings as well, placed coarse food inside and covered it with fine food. She then took it and said to the new wife:
"I offer this exquisite food to my venerable brother; may you rejoice in it."
"O bhikṣus, you should know this:

Śrīmālā was the sister of a pratyekabuddha. Because she offered exquisite food to her brother, through the power of that merit, her body remained constantly delicate and soft for five hundred lifetimes."

The second wife, who gave exquisite food to a pratyekabuddha, is now Varṣākāra; by virtue of that karma, her physical form has been handsome and upright for five hundred lifetimes, and even in this present life, her appearance is transcendent.
"O bhikṣus, you should know this:
black karma yields black retribution; white karma yields white retribution; and mixed karma yields mixed retribution.
You should abandon both black and mixed karma and cultivate white karma," as explained at length above.
“Monks, you should train yourselves in this way.
Later on, Queen Śrīmālā became pregnant; on that very same night, the wife of the brahmin minister also conceived. Because she was pregnant, she suffered extreme hardship.

When the nine months were complete, Queen Śrīmālā gave birth to a son whose countenance was dignified and handsome, a sight that all people delighted to behold. After twenty-one days had passed, she assembled her kinsmen, intending to bestow a name upon the child.
The King said, "Let this child be brought forth and shown to the Great Queen of the State; ask her what name should be given."
The ministers followed the command and brought forth Queen Pañcāla. Then the chief queen said to the ministers, "Did I not previously say this:
'Behold the beauty and the delicate touch of this maidservant's body; she will surely bring ruin to my city of Kośala'?"
The minister replied, "Indeed there is such a saying;
before this son was even born, the Great Queen of the state had already made an inauspicious prediction, and thus this child should be named 'Evil-Born' (Duṣyanta)."

On the day of his birth, the wife of a high minister also gave birth to a son. When the month of his birth was complete, as described in detail above, all his kinsmen gathered together to bestow a name upon the child.

The people deliberated and said: "From the time she first conceived this child, the mother endured hardship; when the time came for his birth, she again encountered extreme suffering. It is fitting that this child be named Duḥkhā-mātṛ (Suffering Mother)."
Prince Aṃśumān was attended by eight foster mothers, as described in detail elsewhere.
Likewise, the infant son of Duḥkhā was provided for by eight foster mothers until he reached adulthood.

That brahmin had mastered every kind of craft and skill without exception. Later, on another occasion, Prince Duṣprasaha went out of the city with Kāḷī and others to hunt. While riding his horse, the prince suddenly galloped away and reached the Śākya grove at Kapilavastu. The park keeper then informed the owner:
"Prince Duṣprasaha has now arrived in the garden."
Having heard this, the sons of the Śākyas consulted one another, saying, "We must go out quickly;
this is the very moment we wish to slay the Wicked One (Viḍūḍabha).
Each of them prepared their armor and weapons and were about to leave the city when the elders saw them and asked one another:
“Where are you all taking your weapons? They replied,
“Prince Viḍūḍabha has come to the Śākya grove.”
The elders said, "He is a guest who has only just arrived here; since he has not yet committed any offense against us, let us be patient with him for now.
Having heard this, everyone withdrew and entered the city.
Thereafter, the fourfold army of Bandhumat searched for the prince and returned to the park, where they remained, patrolling throughout its grounds.
The park keeper then reported to the people of the city:
"The fourfold army of Bandhumat has entered the park and is causing wanton destruction."
Upon hearing this, the people’s anger redoubled; increasing their martial prowess, they all went out of the city together, intending to slaughter them.
The elders asked again:
“Where are you going now?”
He replied, "Prince Ajātaśatru has led his fourfold army, destroyed my grove, and now intends to slaughter us.
The elders said:
"For now, you must exercise patience.

At that time, Viśvantara, knowing that the Śākya forces intended to come and harm him, immediately led his troops in a swift retreat to his own kingdom. He left behind only a single man, instructing him:
"Stay here and listen in secret to whatever the sons of the Śākyas are discussing."
At that time, when the Śākya soldiers arrived at the park, they searched for him but could not find him;
seeing a certain man there, they asked, "Where is the servant’s son, Duṣyanta, now?"
He replied, "I immediately fled.
At that time, the Śākyas engaged in this discussion:
“If we were to fall into the hands of Devadatta, we would first have our hands cut off, or our feet severed, or our hearts torn out.
Now that we have fled in secret, what more can we do?”

He then ordered laborers to excavate the ground where Ajātaśatru used to walk and stay, digging to a depth of one knee. He filled the pit with other soil and demolished the wall against which he leaned. He then plastered the area with fresh mud, milk, and fragrant decoctions, and scattered various flowers and colorful ornaments throughout the garden.

While this was being done, those people left behind witnessed it all. They then proceeded to the city of Kośala and went to the place where Virūḍhaka was; they prostrated themselves in salutation and stood to one side.
Virūḍhaka asked them: "What discussion did the Śākyas have with me?"
He replied, "O Prince! Those words are poisonous and harmful; I do not dare to speak them."
Sudinna said, "He uttered evil words so that he himself might suffer for them; you may now truthfully relate what you have heard and seen, for I wish to know the deeds he has committed."
That person then explained the matter in detail as above.
Upon hearing this, Candapradyota became filled with resentment and anger, and said to those around him: "Keep this in mind!
"When my father the King has passed away and I succeed to the throne, you must recount this matter so that I may remember it; I shall surely execute the Śākyas, who were my former enemies.
Devadatta said, "Excellent, Prince!"
"Speak these words quickly; may you strengthen your resolve, for when you ascend the throne, I shall explain them to you.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle Seven. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.
Fascicle Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.

The remainder of the summary verse for the fourth section of the second chapter: An account of King Prasenajit’s faith in the Buddha and the subsequent events concerning the slaughter of the Śākyas by the wicked Ajātaśatru. Later, at another time, Prince Ajātaśatru conceived a rebellious and murderous intent, and he secretly plotted with his ministers.
The king had five hundred ministers who all followed him, but there was one minister named Dīrghanakha whom the king held in high esteem and who did not comply with his schemes.
Later, the Wicked One said to Dīrghanakha:
"Do you not wish for me to ascend the throne?"

He replied, "Prince, why do you utter such unlawful words? Your father the King is aged and will soon pass away; it is only right that you yourself should inherit the throne. Why sit here plotting treason and bringing upon yourself an evil reputation?"
"Though I am dull-witted, I privately believe this is improper.
Eṣa-jīva said, "I spoke these words merely to test your mind; you must keep your mouth shut and ensure no one hears of it."
Dīrgha replied, "I dare not disobey your command.
Later, King Prasenajit, together with the minister Dīrgha, traveled through various villages without bringing any retinue.

Having arrived there, the king saw a superior aranya—a vast, serene, and secluded place free from all impurities—suitable for practicing meditative concentration, nourishing the spirit, and advancing in one’s practice. He then said to Dīrghanakha:
"In such an excellent location as this, the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, may dwell."
"How may we humble ourselves to approach and make offerings to him?
We do not yet know where the Tamer (the Buddha) currently resides. They replied:
"Your servant has heard that the World-Honored One is staying among the Śākyas in the village of Śrāvastī.
The king asked, "How far is it from here?"
He replied, “It is three krośas from here.
The king said:
"I now wish to go and pay my respects to the World-Honored One in person.
Changxing said, "I respectfully follow Your Majesty's intention."
He immediately turned his carriage toward the Śubha Garden; having arrived there, he alighted from his vehicle and proceeded on foot, wishing to pay his respects.

At that time, the Tathāgata was within that hall, having closed the door and entered meditative absorption, while several bhikṣus were walking back and forth outside. When the king saw the bhikṣus, he approached them and respectfully inquired:
"Where is the Buddha?"

He replied, "The Buddha is within the hall, meditating in silence with the doors closed. If Your Majesty wishes to see the World-Honored One, you should approach the hall and knock gently; the Buddha will know the proper time."
The king possessed five kinds of exquisite and magnificent ornaments:
first, a jeweled crown;
second, a jeweled parasol; [and so forth].
Third, a precious sword;
fourth, a precious fly-whisk;
fifth, precious sandals.

At that time, the King desired to remove these elaborate ornaments to pay his respects to the World-Honored One; he then commanded Dīrghanakha to take charge of the five items previously mentioned and looked him in the face.
Dīrghanakha thought to himself:
"The King has entrusted me with these various objects and looks at my face; his intention is to simplify his entourage and settle his mind so as to see the Buddha. I ought to remain here."

The King then approached the hall and gently knocked on the door; the Buddha immediately opened it for him. The King then went before the Great Master, prostrated himself at his feet, and spoke these words:
"I have not beheld the Tathāgata for a long time. Now that I am fortunately able to personally attend upon your venerable countenance here, my joy is beyond measure."
The Buddha said, “Great King!
For what reason are you suddenly able to humble yourself before me with such earnest devotion?”
The king said:

"I have conceived deep faith in the Dharma of the Blessed One; because of this reverent faith, I have been moved to such earnest devotion. Furthermore, the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has well-expounded the Dharma and Vinaya, causing all the assembly of śrāvakas to practice them entirely without any opposition."
The Buddha said,
“Great King, in what dharma do you give rise to a mind of faith and reverence?”
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

In the past, I have seen various other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, relying on their meager wisdom, were arrogant and conceited; they composed treatises and books to challenge others, claiming that everyone regarded them as skilled analysts. All their followers adhered to their views, as they established their own systems of logic and constructed the premises for their inquiries."
Having done this, he thought to himself:
"I shall now go to the place of the śramaṇa Gautama to engage him in debate; if he cannot answer me, I shall humiliate him."
"If there should be an explanation that says it is thus, I shall further challenge it, saying:
'This explanation is illogical and inconsistent.
With such wrong thoughts, he came to where the Buddha was.
Having merely witnessed the majestic spiritual power of the Great Master, I still did not dare look directly upon the Tathāgata, much less confront him to engage in discussion.
Therefore, I have now conceived deep faith toward the World-Honored One; through this reverent faith, I am moved to give rise to such earnest devotion.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Awakened One, has well-expounded the Dharma and Vinaya, causing the assembly of śrāvakas to practice and uphold them all.
"Moreover, World-Honored One!"
In the past, I have seen other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, relying on their meager wisdom, were arrogant and conceited, as described in detail above.
Having themselves initiated topics for debate with the intent to challenge the Buddha, they gazed up at the World-Honored One and did not dare to pose questions; instead, they sighed in praise:

"The Great Teacher, the Dharma King, is supreme among humans and devas. His knowledge and vision penetrate all things without exception; he has uprooted their false tendencies and caused them to follow the Right Path."
Therefore, I have now conceived deep faith in the World-Honored One; through this reverent faith, I have been moved to give rise to such earnest devotion.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has well-expounded the Dharma and Vinaya, causing all the assembly of śrāvakas to practice and uphold them entirely.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

In the past, I have seen other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, relying on their meager wisdom, were arrogant and conceited, as described in detail above; they composed many treatises with the intent to come and challenge the Buddha."
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they gazed upon the World-Honored One and posed incomplete questions; the Buddha then answered them by completing those questions for them.
Having heard this, they all felt great joy, gave rise to profound faith, took refuge in the Triple Gem, and received and upheld the precepts.
Therefore, I now give rise to profound faith toward the World-Honored One; through this reverent faith, I am moved to develop such earnest devotion.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has excellently expounded the Dharma and Vinaya, causing all his disciples to practice and uphold them entirely.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
In the past, I have seen other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, possessing little wisdom, relied on their own arrogance as extensively described above, wishing to come and challenge the Buddha."
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he gazed upon the World-Honored One and posed a comprehensive question; the Buddha immediately provided a most perfect answer according to his capacity.

Upon hearing the Buddha’s wondrous meaning, he felt profound joy and, casting aside heterodox paths, he honored and followed the True Dharma. He then requested ordination and received full precepts. Diligently cultivating the holy life, before long all worldly defilements were exhausted and he attained Arhatship.

Experiencing the bliss of liberation, he thought to himself: "How long have I been in vain, losing myself and deceiving myself? Formerly I was not a śramaṇa yet claimed to be one, I was not a brāhmaṇa yet claimed to be one, and I was not an arhat yet claimed to be one."
"I am now a true śramaṇa and brāhmaṇa; I am a true arhat.
World-Honored One!
Because of this, I conceived deep faith, as described at length above.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

In the past, I have seen other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas whose complexions were jaundiced and emaciated, whose physical forms were frail and weak, and whose sense faculties were impaired, causing those who beheld them to feel revulsion."
Upon seeing this, I immediately reflected:

"Is it not that this person does not delight in the holy life (brahmacarya), or perhaps suffers from a chronic illness resulting in such emaciation, or has committed evil deeds in secret and conceals them in his heart, such that his appearance is unpleasant for others to behold?"
I then went to ask them:
"For what reason do you all suddenly lack color, your appearances so haggard that people find them unpleasant to behold? They replied to me:
“Great King! It is because of the bonds of desire that I have come to this appearance.
Having heard these words, I thought to myself:

"Those who do not sever desire have such faults as these: because those who indulge extensively in desire delight in it, they ought to experience an increase in physical strength and comeliness, yet this does not occur."

Why is this? As a king, I possess all five sensual pleasures with sovereign ease and without obstruction; thus, I ought to have attained a physical form that is exceptionally superior and transcendent.
Since it is not so, we know that the power of the body does not increase through indulgence in various sensual desires; yet foolish people all take delight in them.

I have observed that the World-Honored One’s śrāvaka disciples delight in the holy life (*brahmacarya*), their faculties being clear and pure, their countenances radiant and serene as they dwell; they always maintain a sense of vigilance and trepidation like deer dwelling in the forest, remaining pure and unadulterated throughout their entire lives, fully perfected in the stainless and pure holy life.
"Because of this, I gave rise to deep faith, as described at length above.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

I recall that once, while sitting in the main hall attending to state affairs, I saw many people who had come to me for the sake of the five desires. They were engaged in mutual litigation and disputes over the likes and dislikes of their parents, children, brothers, sisters, acquaintances, and friends; how much more so regarding others? "

Furthermore, I once saw two bhikṣus who, having engaged in a dispute with other bhikṣus, subsequently renounced the precepts. Nevertheless, those two bhikṣus were unable to utter even a slight criticism of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha; they only knew to reproach themselves, saying, "We are most wicked men, devoid of merit, and unable to cultivate the pure brahmacarya. Relying on the teachings of the World-Honored One, they remained for the rest of their lives, their minds free from transgression.
"Because of this, I have given rise to deep faith, as explained at length above.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

In the past, I saw a certain class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, having restrained their minds to dwell in tranquility and maintained the holy life for eight or nine months, were then pulled by desire; they abandoned their vows and committed defiled acts, becoming entangled in the five sensual pleasures to amuse themselves."

I have seen the World-Honored One’s assembly of śrāvakas practicing the pure and perfect holy life (brahmacarya), remaining free from any transgression of heart in accordance with the World-Honored One’s teachings for as long as they live.
"Because of this, I have given rise to profound faith, as described at length above.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

I am the sovereign of this land, known as Prasenajit. I exercise sovereign authority over this kingdom; I can take the lives of those who should not die, and I can release those who deserve death. Throughout the entire realm, there is none who does not look up to me with reverence."

Furthermore, the great ministers and prime ministers are all from prominent clans of great Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, or elders; yet when deliberating state affairs or promoting and demoting officials, they still harbor arrogance and pride during their petitions, their decorum being insufficient and thus disrupting the court protocol.

I saw the World-Honored One seated amidst a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands, surrounded as he preached the Dharma. The multitudes of devas and humans each restrained their minds to gaze upon his venerable countenance and listened together with focused attention; there was no distraction, and the assembly below was so silent that not even the sound of a cough or a sneeze could be heard, let alone any other clamor.
At that time, while the assembly was gathered, a person suddenly cleared his throat and made a sound. Those sitting nearby said to him:
"Virtuous one, please remain silent for a moment; do not cause a disturbance."
"Have you not heard how the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma is exquisite and suited to the occasion, like the finest honey?
Having said these words, he remained silent.
At that time, upon hearing these words, I thought to myself:

"The World-Honored One truly possesses great majestic power that is inconceivable; without the use of swords, staves, or severe punishments, he is able to subdue all classes of beings, who all follow and revere him."
"Because of this, I gave rise to deep faith, as described at length above.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
I have two ministers:"
One was named Kṣemadatta and the other was named Purāṇa.
Whatever land-grants, rewards, wealth, and fame those men possessed were all derived from me; since birth, they have constantly enjoyed peace and happiness.
Although they indeed remember my kindness, their heart of reverence toward the World-Honored One remains more profound.
On another occasion, I arrayed my cavalry and set out for a military expedition, wishing to test those two ministers as to which of the two—myself or the Buddha—their hearts held in higher esteem.
They went together to a private place and asked him, saying, "When you were sleeping, toward which direction did my head and feet, as well as those of the Buddha, point?

At that time, the two ministers praised the virtues of the Buddha and spoke of the True Dharma and the Sangha as fields of merit; for this reason, they had their heads toward the Buddha and their feet toward the king.

Having heard this, I revere the World-Honored One, for he possesses great power and inconceivable majesty; yet those who have obtained great renown, wealth, and peace through my favor and patronage do not show me such reverence as they do to the Buddha.
Because of this, I have conceived deep faith, as explained at length above.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

I am the King of Kośala, and the Buddha also dwells in Kośala; I was born of the Kṣatriya caste, and the Buddha is also of the Kṣatriya caste; I am advanced in years, my age exceeding eighty, and the World-Honored One is likewise, his age exceeding eighty."
I am a consecrated Kṣatriya king, and the World-Honored One is likewise the Unsurpassed Dharma King; my power compared to that of the Buddha cannot be measured by any analogy.
For this reason, I have conceived profound faith and shall extensively explain [the teachings], even to the point of practicing them all.

At that time, King Prasenajit, having extensively related before the World-Honored One these various accounts of what he had seen and heard—these wondrous and marvelous dharmas—prostrated at his feet, took his leave, and departed.
Not long after the king had departed, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should all remember what the king has said; you must receive, uphold, read, and recite this wondrous collection of Dharma."

Why is this? Because it is complete in both letter and meaning, because it accords with the True Dharma, because it brings about the fulfillment of the holy life, and because it enables one to attain the fruit of universal knowledge, perfect enlightenment, and the radiant state of Nirvana; therefore, you all should diligently practice and study it.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, all the bhikṣus were filled with joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced them accordingly.
A summary verse says:
"There are four types of persons discussed; one who dwells on desire has a thin body."
"The two ministers' reverence is exceptional; their honor for the King is not equal to that for the Buddha.
At that time, the minister Dīghāvu, knowing that the King had seen the Buddha, thought to himself:
"The King has five hundred great ministers, all of whom have gone over to Evil-Born, yet I alone do not follow him."
"How could they possibly accomplish such a great task?
Now that I return to my kingdom, I shall appoint Eḷeyya to succeed to the throne and banish both queens, Vaṃsā and Vāsabhakhattiyā, from the palace."
Having had this thought, he abandoned what he was guarding, mounted his chariot, and departed. Upon reaching Śrāvastī, he addressed Aśoka, saying:
"Does the Prince now wish to ascend the throne?"
Sudarśana said, "This is what I desire. Thereupon, Dīrghāyus,
together with his ministers, conspired to make him king and commanded the two queens to go to the old king's quarters.
Thereupon, Śrīmālā and Vāsavadattā asked Dīrghāyus,
"Where is the King now? He replied:
"The King is within the Śākya-Prabhāsa Garden.
At that time, the two queens went on foot to search for the old king.
When the Great King Prasenajit arrived outside the gate and did not see Dīrgha, he asked the bhikṣus:
“Venerable sir!
Where do you see my minister going now?
The bhikṣu replied:
"Not long after the king had entered, Dīrgha immediately mounted his carriage and departed.
Having heard this, the king proceeded on foot at a steady pace; at that same time, the Buddha was also heading toward Rājagṛha.
On the way, the king encountered Varṣākāra and others, and he asked them,
"For what reason have you come such a long distance on foot? They replied:
“Great King! The minister Dīrgha has installed Viḍūḍabha and driven us out; we have come here on foot in search of Your Majesty.
Upon hearing these words, the king said to Vaidehī:
"You have already previously received the favor and emoluments of your husband-king; now you shall return and receive the stipend of your son-king. I shall take Varṣākārā and turn back from here.
Thereupon, Vaśrabhūti returned to Śrāvastī, weeping and shedding tears as she traveled along the road back.
The King and Vassakāra proceeded toward Rājagṛha, advancing by degrees until they reached the city. Upon seeing a grove, the King halted there and said to Vassakāra:
"I shall remain here for now; you go into the city and inform King Ajātaśatru, saying:
'The Great King Prasenajit of Kośala is currently outside in the grove, wishing to see you.'"
Vassakāra then departed and saw Ajātaśatru, reporting everything as he had been told.
Upon hearing these words, King Ajātaśatru was greatly astonished and immediately said to Vassakāra:
"The King of Kośala, Prasenajit, possesses great power and his fourfold army is formidable; how is it that we did not know he had suddenly arrived?"
Vārṣākāra replied, "What great military force does the King now possess?
The Crown Prince has plotted rebellion to seize his father’s throne and claim kingship; I have merely followed the King here."
Ajātaśatru said, "If such a thing is possible,
I shall appoint him as the king of this realm, while I myself step down to become the crown prince."
He immediately summoned his ministers and commanded them, saying:
"King Prasenajit is the sovereign of a great kingdom, a consecrated king of the Kṣatriya caste; since he has now suddenly arrived here, he must be received with due respect."
"You ministers may now cleanse the city roads and lead a hundred thousand followers from the fourfold army; I wish to go in person to welcome the King as he enters.

When the ministers had received the King's command, they beat drums and blew conch shells to proclaim to the people that they were to strictly prepare the city walls and sweep the thoroughfares until they were doubly pure, like the Joyful Garden of the Lord of Devas.
King Prasenajit, having gone without food for a long time, wondered why the messenger had arrived so late; he left the park and, wandering in agitation and looking about, came upon a turnip garden.

At that time, the gardener, thinking he was an ordinary man, gave him five radishes. The king, being hungry and weak, ate both the roots and the leaves. Having eaten, he suffered from thirst and went to the water’s edge to drink excessively; consequently, he contracted cholera, his body became emaciated, and as he thought of Vaidehī, he walked forward along the road and fell down in the ruts. With the dust of the road in his mouth, he immediately passed away.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, having arrayed his fourfold army, went to the park but did not see him; he then dispatched horsemen to search for him in all directions.
One rider arrived at the radish garden and asked the gardener:
"Have you seen such a person?"
He replied, "I saw a man who came here briefly to seek radishes and headed toward the water's edge.
He then went to search and found the King’s corpse lying prostrate at a corner of the road; the messenger immediately reported this matter to King Ajātaśatru.
Having heard this, he cried out:
"Alas! Today I have once again received an evil reputation."
"I have already been notorious for harming my father and usurping his throne; now it is further said that I have killed my father’s spiritual friend.
He then set out with an immeasurable retinue toward the site of the corpse and commanded his ministers, saying:

"This King Prasenajit was a Kṣatriya, a great king consecrated by coronation. Now that he has met with such distress and passed away here, his body should be cremated according to the most magnificent rites."
Then those ministers, as commanded by the king, prepared the funeral bier with all its ornaments and escorted it to the cremation ground;
having completed the rite of incineration, the king went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
"I do not understand, Great King Śreṇika, what karma did you previously perform such that, due to eating radishes, you met your end in great suffering?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied: "Great King!"
King Prasenajit himself committed those karmic actions and now undergoes this retribution, as explained in detail above. Great King!

Long ago in the past, in a certain village, there was a brahmin who, shortly after marrying his wife, fathered a son. As the boy grew older, he supported himself by begging for alms; having obtained five radishes, he brought them to his mother.
He then said to his mother:
"I shall now bathe for a moment; please wait for my return to provide me with food. O Great King!

At a time when no Buddha was present, there appeared in the world a Pratyekabuddha who, out of compassion for the solitary and the weak, delighted in dwelling in quietude and served as a field of merit for the world.

At that time, a certain Pratyekabuddha was traveling through the countryside; in the early morning, he donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, entered a village to beg for food, and eventually arrived at that house.

When the Brahmin’s wife saw that the Pratyekabuddha’s physical form was dignified and majestic, and his six sense faculties were tranquil and subdued, she immediately took a radish and offered it to him.

At that time, the Pratyekabuddha accepted her offering and leaped into the air to perform a miraculous transformation. When ordinary people witness such supernormal powers, their minds become subdued; thus, she prostrated from afar with a heart full of great joy.
At that time, the Brahmin’s son, having finished his bath, returned home and said to his mother, "I want the radish from before.
His mother replied, "Just now a Pratyekabuddha came to beg for it; I have already given it to him as an offering."
Hearing these words, the son, being driven by hunger, gave rise to a mind of anger and a wicked thought:
"May he die from cholera caused by eating radishes."
"O Great King!
You should know now: was that child anyone else?
He was none other than King Prasenajit himself."

Because he conceived such an evil thought toward a pratyekabuddha in the past, by the power of that karma, he fell into hell for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years to undergo various sufferings; furthermore, due to the causal force of remaining karmic retribution, he has already met his death six times from cholera.
Up until now, through seven lifetimes, due to the remaining force of his residual karma, he has eaten this radish and died of cholera.
Your Majesty should know that the karmic retribution for Suprabha’s deeds is hereby forever exhausted; he shall never again undergo such suffering.
Great King, you should know this:

white karma brings white retribution, black karma brings black retribution, and mixed karma brings mixed retribution. Therefore, you should abandon both black and mixed karma, cultivate white karma, and refrain from harsh speech.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, was filled with joy throughout his body and mind; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and departed, having received it with faith.
Later, when Prince Aśoka had succeeded to the throne, he once held a court assembly in the great hall with his various ministers, and Devadatta said to him: “Great King!
Do you perhaps recall that in days of yore, before the great assembly, you uttered a lion’s roar, saying:
"When I ascend the throne, I shall first execute all the Śākya seedlings to avenge my initial grievance"?
The King asked Duḥkhilā: "Should everything I say be carried out?
Duḥkhilā replied: "Yes."
"Your Majesty has now newly ascended the precious throne; you ought to recall your former words and punish the Śākyas.
If the time arrives and you do not act, it will become a falsehood.

We pray that you issue a clear decree to select the day for the expedition, so that the fourfold army—elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry—may set forth together. Brandishing spears and armor, beating bells and sounding drums, let us depart from the city of Śrāvastī for the kingdom of Kapilavastu to annihilate the Śākyas."
At that time, King Candapradyota accepted the counsel of Vaidehī and immediately issued a decree, commanding his generals to lead troops to invade that kingdom.

The Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, who knows and perceives all things, foresaw that the Śākyas would surely perish; thus, by the side of the great road between the two kingdoms, he sat with body erect beneath a small tree that had few branches and leaves.
At that time, King Candaṣṭa saw the World-Honored One from afar and immediately approached him, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
There are many groves and gardens there, lush with shade and growth; for what reason do you abandon them to dwell here?"
"This tree has few leaves and little shade; how can one dwell here?
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
"When one has kinsmen who provide shade, why should one look back at a tree?
At that time, having heard the words of the World-Honored One, Devadatta thought to himself:
"The Śākyas of the kingdom of Kapilavastu are the Buddha’s own relatives; the Tathāgata feels compassion for them and their feelings must not be disregarded."
Having had this thought, he returned to his own country.
Later, when Duḥśīlā repeatedly urged him to exterminate them, Virūḍhaka, together with his ministers and officials, addressed the assembly of courtiers during a formal gathering, saying:
"The Śākya clansmen of the kingdom of Kapilavastu constantly say, 'We are the sons of slaves. Since their insults are so profound, they must not be forgotten."
However, they belong to the lineage of the Tathāgata; out of compassion, the World-Honored One has always restrained himself and refrained from executing them.
How, then, could one possibly repay such hateful abuse?
Kāpilāyanī replied:
"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama claims to be free from desire; one who is free from desire has no mind of attachment.
If there is attachment, then one is not free from desire."
"The paths of the clergy and the laity are distinct; Your Majesty should decide this for yourself.
He further said, "Today is precisely the time to exterminate the Śākyas."
Thereupon, Ajātaśatru desired to mobilize his fourfold army to go forth and punish them.
Before he had departed, the Buddha thought to himself:
"If those among the Śākyas in the city who have not yet seen the Truth were to engage in battle with Ajātaśatru, they would no longer be vessels capable of seeing the Truth."
He then proceeded to the kingdom of Kapilavastu; having arrived, he stayed at the Nyagrodha Park.

When the Śākyas heard that the World-Honored One had come there, they gathered in a great assembly and went to the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrating at his feet and withdrawing to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the faculties, dispositions, and past affinities of the Śākyas, preached the sublime Dharma for them.
