Among that assembly, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who attained great benefit: some attained the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship; some established the causes for becoming pratyekabuddhas, and others established the causal conditions for attaining buddhahood.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable sentient beings who took refuge in the Triple Gem, received the various precepts, and practiced the Buddha’s teachings.
At that time, the Śākyas of Kapilavastu obtained this Dharma benefit; they prostrated before the World-Honored One, took their leave, and departed.

At that time, the wicked Ajātaśatru personally led the fourfold army and stationed himself not far from the city of Kapilavastu. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"I have heard that the foolish man Devadatta has mobilized the fourfold army to come and slaughter the Śākyas. I possess supernatural powers capable of casting this host far away to other regions.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me his compassionate permission to further use my supernatural power to transform the city into iron and cover it entirely with a great iron net, so that even Devadatta cannot see the city of Kapilavastu, let alone inflict slaughter or harm upon it!"

The Buddha said, "I also know that you possess supernormal powers and have accomplished all that was to be done; nevertheless, due to the karmic burdens from previous lives of the Śākya clan, they must now undergo their retribution."
"When karma reaches maturity, it is like the flow of a torrent that cannot be restrained; one must inevitably experience its results oneself, as explained at length above.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Even if a hundred eons should pass, The karma one has created does not perish;..."
"When causes and conditions meet, one receives the retribution for oneself.
The Buddha told Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Thus you should know that all in the world receive their retribution through the power of karma."
"Born by the power of karma and sustained by the power of karma, all sentient beings follow the power of karma; they must experience the fruits of both good and evil.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, his wish unfulfilled, paid homage to the Buddha and departed.

At that time, when the Śākyas of Kapilavastu heard that King Aśoka was leading a great host of troops intending to come and annihilate them, they immediately ordered their fourfold army to array their weapons and march out of the city to resist the enemy.

They were unprepared for the assault of the evil army of the Śākyas; yet all these Śākyas had realized the vision of the Truths (dṛṣṭasatya), and they practiced no killing, employing only whips and staves. They struck and felled them by waving and brushing with their left and right hands, or they shot the bowstrings of their enemies with arrows, shooting the belly-bands of elephants and horses so that they were all severed. Or they shot the crests of helmets and the fastenings of armor so that they fell to the ground; or they shot near the ears and at the straps and girths of saddles, merely causing them to fall away without wounding the bodies or heads, nor harming their lives.
At that time, King Canda’s troops were quickly defeated and dispersed, and the Śākya youths gained victory in battle.
The entire army entered the city, closed the gates, and ascended the walls, issuing this decree:
"We must not harm Canda or his troops; whoever violates this is no longer a Śākya."
At that time, seeing that these Śākyas were all endowed with benevolence and possessed great prowess, Duṣprasaha said to Māgandikā:
"We should now withdraw our army and return for now to our own country."
Ambapālī replied, “Great King, do not worry!
The Śākyas of Kapilavastu have all realized the Truth; they would not even harm a mosquito or an ant, much less kill a human being.”
"O King, if you do not believe me, you may verify it now; in that great battle just now, not a single person was harmed.
He further established this rule:
'One must not injure the body of Ajātaśatru nor his troops; whoever violates this is no longer a Śākya.'"
Upon hearing this, Vigatāśoka remained silent.

There was a Śākya named Śyāma who was staying in a neighboring village supervising the agricultural work. He heard that Vigatāśoka had personally led the fourfold army to Kapilavastu with the intent to slaughter the Śākyas; however, he had not heard the regulations established by the Śākyas, nor had he yet realized the Truths (dṛṣṭasatya). Consequently, he mobilized his troops to launch a surprise attack on Vigatāśoka, but in his haste and reckless assault, he was utterly defeated, and nearly the entire army of Vigatāśoka was killed or wounded.
At that time, Ajātaśatru said to Vaidehī: "You previously stated:
'The Śākyas have seen the Truth; they do not harm even mosquitoes or ants, much less injure human beings.'"

"Now, even Śāṇḍa alone has brought forth troops to fight and has caused many deaths; how much more so when the other Śākyas of Kapilavastu have assembled their forces to oppose us, being difficult to withstand? It would be better to retreat for now than to perish entirely."
Dukkhā replied: "Great King!
That Śyāma came from outside and had not yet entered the city of Kapilavastu; being unaware of the proclamation, he gave rise to this sudden and violent intent for combat."
"Since there is no communication between the inside and the outside,
may Your Majesty not worry. At that time, Śvapāka the Śākya, wishing to enter the city, went to the gate and called out, "Open it!"
Then the gatekeeper asked, "Who is this? He replied:
“I am Śyāmā; you should go and inform the Śākyas.
Thereupon, a messenger was dispatched from within the city to announce:
“From this day forward, you are no longer of the Śākya clan; you may depart as you please.”
"Why is this? Because you have violated the regulations established within this city, you are not permitted to enter through this city gate. Śyāma then asked:
"What regulation has the assembly established such that you say I have violated it? He replied,
"We established a regulation not to harm the military forces of Aśoka."
"If there is one who has committed an offense, they are no longer of the Śākya clan.
He replied, "I truly have heard nothing; I pray you will grant me your forgiveness."
When he had thus entreated them in such a manner and the assembly would not permit it, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"Since you will not allow me to enter, please return my family to me.
The assembly brought them out and gave them to him.
Having obtained his retinue, he went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at His feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The Śākyas of the city of Kapilavastu have expelled me; I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will grant me His remembrance, so that I may constantly provide offerings and pay homage to the Tathāgata.”
Out of compassion, the Buddha took his own hair and nails and bestowed them upon Śaṇavāsa.
At that time, Śaṇavāsa received the Tathāgata’s hair and nails with a heart of profound reverence and departed for the kingdom of Bāhudā.
Those people heard:
"The powerful Śākyan son named Śyāma has now arrived here wishing to be our lord; shall we deliberate together on whether we may follow him?"
The people of the country all came to a certain mountain foot to deliberate upon this matter.

At that time, Śvapāka the Śākya dismissed his attendants and set them aside in one place; he himself feigned the role of a messenger carrying a letter and, with a sharp sword tucked under his arm, went to the assembly and spoke these words:
"Gentlemen, you should know that Śvapāka the Śākya possesses great power and is valiant and difficult to withstand; he has sent me to deliver this letter to you."
He asked, "For what purpose? He replied:
"He wishes to become king and rule over you all; you should take your seats and read his letter together.
The people replied, "There are no seats here; how can we sit at ease?"
He immediately drew his sword and split the boulders, making them into seats for the assembly to sit upon.
When the people saw this, they all marveled at its extraordinary nature and asked, "How many men like you are there?"
He replied, "I am merely a messenger carrying a letter; what is there to say of me? There is another person who is far superior to me.
Upon hearing these words, the assembly was all greatly struck with fear and said to one another:
"If even the messenger is thus, how much more so Śaṃba?
It would be better for us to establish him as our sovereign.
Having thus opened the seal, they drafted a reply and returned it, while addressing the messenger with these words:
"Welcome, Great King!
We have long admired your reputation and have hoped for your visit.

After Śaṃba had taken his leave, he went to his former quarters, where he arrayed his followers and marshaled his guards to enter the kingdom of Pauṇḍravardhana. Both the young and the old rejoiced; they prepared all that was required with wholehearted devotion and, selecting an auspicious day, installed him as their sovereign.

The neighboring kingdoms heard from afar that in the kingdom of Po-ju-tu (Bakuda) there was one of the Śākya clan named Shan-po (Śrībhāva), whom they collectively established as their sovereign, naming it the Kingdom of Shan-po.

After Shan-po ascended the throne, he reverently constructed a great stūpa and enshrined therein the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata to offer worship; thus, the tower was called the Shan-po Stūpa.

His consort had previously lacked faith in the Buddha; she issued a decree throughout the kingdom to establish shrines for deities, and they have continued to perform sacrifices according to secular custom down to the present day.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Scroll Eight. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.
Fascicle Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
Second Section, Fourth Subsection: A Summary Verse on the Remainder of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*. At that time, Duḥśīla addressed Māgandikā, saying:

“The Śākyas of the kingdom of Kapilavastu are brave and difficult to withstand; now they have closed the city gates and ascended the walls to defend themselves. How could we possibly succeed in killing them?”
"Now let us return home.
Kalmāṣapāda replied, "Great King!"
"Whatever great cities there may be, they shall all be destroyed through skillful means.
I have heard in the past what the ancient seers said:
'There are five matters that ensure victory over others.'"
What are these five?
The verse says:
“Cultivating conciliation and bestowing wealth, Employing deceit and practicing poisonous arts;”
"Later, we shall rely on military force; this is what a wise man does.

Following this reasoning, one should employ skillful means by first practicing deception: dispatch a messenger to him bearing the king’s command and say to him, "I have feelings of affection for you and truly harbor no ill intent.
Because of a minor matter, I wish to enter the city; I beg you to open the gates and grant me temporary admission. I shall depart immediately and will not dare to linger."
Following this plan, he went there and delivered the message as previously stated. The people within the city gathered together and deliberated:
"Should we allow him to enter, or should we refuse?"
Some said, "Let him enter. Others said:
"It is not permissible.
Or one might say:
"If you gather together in one place and cast ballots collectively, then whichever side has the majority of ballots should follow their instruction."
The assembly approved his proposal and immediately proceeded to cast lots.
At that time, the wicked Māra thought to himself:
"I have constantly followed the śramaṇa Gautama, seeking a flaw or opening, but I have been unable to find an opportunity."
"I should now slay his kinsmen; this is precisely the right time.

He then transformed himself into an elderly Śākya monk and took the voting tally as the senior-most elder. When the others saw him take the tally, they all said, "Since the venerable elder has taken it, why should we not do so?"
At that time, many people within the assembly took up the voting sticks; seeing that the sticks were numerous, they immediately opened the gates to allow the king’s army to enter.
The king said, "I have already abandoned the city of Kapilavastu; let the Śākyas be slaughtered as you please."

Having heard these instructions, the multitude unleashed the fourfold army; their banners and drums shook the heavens, and their clamor deafened the earth as they slaughtered everywhere without a heart of compassion.
At that time, having witnessed this event, Mahānāma of the Śākya clan felt profound compassion for his kinsmen; with disheveled hair, he hurried to the place where Virūḍhaka was and said to him:
"Great King, you must grant me my wish."
The king asked, "What boon do you desire? He replied:
“May you grant fearlessness to all the Śākyas.
The King said, “I cannot spare the other Śākyas; however, your family members may depart as they please.”
He replied, "I shall now enter the pond and submerge myself to the bottom; until my body has emerged, you must release all my kinsmen.
When the king heard these words, he looked at his ministers, and the ministers addressed the king:
"This Great Name (Mahānāman) was a close friend of the former king; let his wish be granted.
The king said, "If that is so, let him go for a short while."

At that time, having received permission, Mahānāman—his heart bound by grief and distress for his kinsmen—hurried to the pond and submerged himself beneath the water. He then tied his hair to the roots of a tree and died therefrom.

At that time, various members of the Śākya clan who had performed different karmic actions in the past departed from the city; some went to the Malla country, some to Nepāla, and others to various other villages, towns, and cities.
If those who shared in evil deeds in the past, even after exiting through the eastern gate, would re-enter through the southern gate;
exiting through the southern gate, they would enter through the western gate;
and exiting through the western gate, they would enter through the northern gate.
He exited through the north gate and entered through the east gate.
When the ministers saw this, they informed the king, saying:
"At this time, the Śākyas are all burning and boiling themselves."
"How is this known?
For all those who have gone out through the gates have now returned.
The King said:
"Look quickly at the Great Name; why has he been in the water for so long?
He dispatched a messenger to observe him.
Seeing that he was already dead, the messenger returned and reported:
"The King learned that he had already passed away.
The King, filled with even greater rage, immediately addressed his ministers, saying:
"Prepare a high throne; I shall ascend it and behold him for myself."
"If I do not see human blood flowing crosswise, surging like waves through the streets and alleys, I shall never leave this seat.
He then ascended the seat and gazed into the distance.
When those brave and valiant men were being slain, it was a natural law that the blood flowed sparingly; the ministers then deliberated, saying:
"Your Honors should know that this wicked king has committed a great sinful deed, making a solemn pact in the hope that blood would flow profusely."
"How could such a thing be possible?
We should take lacquer resin, boil it until it turns red, fill a thousand jars with it, and pour it out into the middle of the street; let us observe its flow, for it will not differ from blood."
He did exactly as instructed and reported,
"The blood has arrived.
Seeing it from afar, Ajātaśatru thought it was indeed blood and had this thought:
"I have now obtained what I hoped for; it is fitting that we return.

At that time, the foolish King Kalāśoka unjustly killed seventy-seven thousand members of the Śākya clan. Among these people, the majority had already realized the Noble Truths. Having slaughtered such virtuous and noble beings, he then took five hundred Śākya youths and five hundred Śākya maidens and proceeded to a park where non-Buddhist practitioners resided.
Duhkhī addressed him, saying: "These one thousand people are all enemies; why not kill them all?"
The king asked,
"How should he be executed? He replied:
"Let the herd of elephants trample them.
At that time, the five hundred Śākyas possessed great prowess; they threw the elephant down and lifted it with their hands to cast it away.
Seeing this, Dukūlā said to Aśoka:
“Great King! Do you see this valiant man?
The king replied:
"I see it. He replied, "If you abandon these followers, they will bring no benefit to Your Majesty."
The king said, "It is true.
How shall I put him to death?"
He replied, "Dig a pit in the ground and bury them with their heads protruding; then crush them from above with iron beams.

At that time, two boys ran to where the Buddha was. Then the World-Honored One, wishing to make it known that the retribution for karmic actions is not in vain, immediately used his supernatural power to transform his alms bowl so that it grew large enough to enclose the two boys; they died beneath the bowl, completely decomposed and cooked.
When the Śākyas were being slaughtered, the Buddha suffered an intense headache and immediately addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Bring me a bowl filled to the brim with water.

At that time, Ānanda presented the bowl of water; then the World-Honored One placed two or three drops of sweat from his forehead into the bowl of water, whereupon smoke immediately issued forth and a crackling sound arose, like hot iron being cast into water.
At that time, Vigataka addressed one man, saying:
"You must remain here; if the Buddha has any prediction concerning me, you must quickly return and report it.
He then took the five hundred Śākya women back to his own country.
At that time, when the bhikṣus saw this event, they were all filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
By what karma was the Buddha caused to suffer a headache?"

What further karma did the Śākyas of the city of Kapilavastu perform, such that, by reason of it, though they were truly without offense, they were summarily executed by the foolish and wicked Ajātaśatru?
The World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go and inform the bhikṣus:
'All should assemble in the park of the non-Buddhists.'"
"I shall explain for you the karmic causes and conditions of the past lives of the foolish and evil Ajātaśatru, who has slaughtered the Śākya clan.
Having received these instructions, the Venerable One went at once and informed the assembly.
Then the Blessed One, together with the bhikṣus, proceeded on foot to that garden. At that time, a brahmin on the road saw the Blessed One from afar and spoke these words:
“Gautama! The foolish and wicked Ajātaśatru has committed many evil deeds; the Śākya clan are innocent, yet they have been unjustly put to death.
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
"So it is, so it is! The foolish and evil Ajātaśatru has committed immeasurable and most grievous evil karma; the Śākya clan were innocent, yet they were slaughtered unjustly.
When the Buddha arrived at the garden and saw those boys and girls who had been ground down and still possessed a remnant of life, they all wailed and wept upon seeing the Buddha.
The Blessed One then sat down on the seat prepared for him at one side and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“The Śākyas of the city of Kapilavastu have already been slaughtered three times by their enemies, raising a great cry of lamentation.”

In the past, as a fisherman, you killed various kinds of fish; furthermore, in the villages, you harmed many people. Now, at this very moment, being slain by the Wicked King, you still have a remnant of life and let out a great cry, no different from before.

"O bhikṣus, have you ever heard of or seen any hunters, butchers, or those of similar trades, who, by means of their livelihoods involving such occupations, could attain the majestic and magnificent power of elephants, horses, chariots, or infantry?"
The bhikṣus said, "We have never heard of or seen such a thing before.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, bhikṣu!
I too have never heard of or seen such a thing—that those who live as hunters could possess such a vast and flourishing army.
For what reason?"

Because that butcher harbors a sinful mind while seeking the lives of living beings, due to this evil karma, he cannot obtain elephants, horses, chariots, or infantry, nor can he achieve great majesty or possess abundant wealth.

Why is this? Because when those animals such as sheep and other beasts are being slaughtered, they look upon that person with malevolent intent; for this reason, one does not obtain elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, or various wealth and possessions.

"O Bhikṣus! When sentient beings belonging to the animal realm merely look upon one with an evil eye, they can still cause that person to lose their fourfold army and all their wealth and treasures; how much more so for Ajātaśatru, who is foolish, ignorant, and heavily defiled by impurities—to think that by killing those trainees who possess great majestic virtue and maintain pure precepts, he could increase his elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and all his possessions, and dwell in peace without meeting with destruction or ruin—such a thing is impossible."
"You all should know that the city of Kosala is like a place where a venomous dragon casts its gaze; it shall be utterly destroyed.
Seven days from now, the foolish and evil Ajātaśatru, together with Vaidehī, will be consumed by fire, crying out in lamentation as they fall into the Avīci Great Hell to undergo extreme suffering."
"Therefore, you should understand this: if one should even harbor no evil thoughts toward withered trees, how much more so toward other classes of sentient beings!
At that time, having witnessed these events, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One:

"What karma did these five hundred Śākya sons commit in the past, such that by the power of that karma, though they were currently free of transgression, they were unjustly put to death by the foolish Duḥśīla?"
"Furthermore, by what karma was the Buddha's head afflicted with pain at the time of the slaughter?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen well, all of you, to the karma created by those Śākyas and myself in previous lives!"

When the karma performed by that person reaches maturity through the convergence of causes and conditions, it cannot be stopped—just like a torrential flood—and there is no one who can take its place, as explained extensively above.
"Even unto the karmic fruits, each shall experience them for oneself. O Bhikṣus!
Long ago, in times past, there were five hundred fishermen living along the bank of a river. At that time, two large fish entered the river from the ocean and swam upstream against the current."
Seeing the two fish, he felt great joy; together they spread a large net and captured them. Seeing that they were exceedingly large, they consulted one another, saying:
"What should we do now?"
"Since the fish is so enormous, if we were to slaughter it all at once, the meat would rot and spoil; what would be the use of that?
Another said, "Let us kill one fish for now and keep another tied in the water."
Or he said: "Both fish are large.
If you kill one, its flesh will spoil; therefore, tie it to a pillar and keep it in the water so that its life is not cut off. When you need meat, take it alive and sell it."
They all said, "So be it.
They immediately began to divide it up together, while the fish, suffering the agony of torture, let out a great cry.
At that time, among the fishermen was a young boy who, seeing such a sight, gave rise to a heart of joy.
Then the two great fish thought to themselves:
"We are truly innocent, yet we are being subjected to this extreme suffering."
"In a future age, I shall also be born in those very places where these beings are born; though they have committed no offense, I shall kill them with great cruelty.
O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts: those two fish were none other than Devadatta and Māluṅkyāputra, and those five hundred fishermen were none other than the five hundred Śākyas.

Because those five hundred fishermen caused those two fish to undergo such intense suffering, they are now being buried alive up to their necks in the earth and struck with iron plows by the wicked Ajātaśatru and Vaidehī; thus, the Śākya sons are made to endure great agony, while all the other Śākyas are those who at that time rejoiced in their actions.
That youth among the fishermen was none other than myself; because I felt joy at the sight of the fish being killed, I subsequently created that karma.
Due to that karma, although I have realized unsurpassed enlightenment, I still endure this suffering of a headache.
Had I not obtained such a mass of merit and boundless virtue, I would likewise have suffered execution along with them.
"Furthermore, you bhikṣus!
You should listen again with close attention to the karma performed by the Śākya sons of the city of Kapilavastu in past lives."

A band of five hundred thieves arrived at a village to plunder its wealth; two elders were staying on the upper floor of their residence when the thieves called for them to come down, but the elders would not descend.
The bandits spoke again, saying,
"If you do not come down, we will cause you to lose everything. The elder replied:
"I would rather face death than ever descend.
The bandits then piled up firewood and set the pavilion ablaze.
As the fierce flames soared upward and he endured the agony of being consumed by the fire, the elder made this reflection:
"I have committed no offense, yet you cause me to suffer.
In future lives, wherever you are born, I shall be born there as well, and I will repay you with such suffering.
Monks, do not entertain any other thought: those two elders were none other than Devadatta and Māluṅkyamātā, and the five hundred thieves were none other than the five hundred Śākyas.
"Because those bandits killed the two elders, these two have now in turn killed them.
Therefore, monks, by performing black karma one receives black retribution; by white karma, white retribution; and by mixed karma, mixed retribution."
"Therefore, you all should abandon both black and mixed karma, and diligently cultivate white karma.
You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, after King Canda-pradyota had slain the Śākyas, he departed for the city of Śrāvastī.

As he was about to enter the city, Prince Jetaka was on a high tower with his court ladies, playing exquisite music and enjoying the pleasures of the five senses; having heard this, Candapradyota asked, "Who is that?"
The ministers replied, “Prince Jeta. The king said:
"Summon him! Upon receiving this command, he arrived; [the king] rebuked him, saying:
"I have been exhausted by my pursuit of my enemies; why are you enjoying sensual pleasures here?"
The Prince replied, "I do not know,
Great King, who it is that is your enemy? The King said:
"The Śākyas of Kapilavastu are my enemies," [the king said].
The Prince replied,
"If the Śākyas are my enemies, who then are my virtuous friends?"
Upon hearing these words, the king became greatly incensed and said to his ministers, "This man is also an ally of the Śākyas; he must be executed immediately."
The ministers immediately executed him.

After his life ended, he was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three; as the superior rewards of his human existence were not yet exhausted, he subsequently experienced the exquisite pleasures of the celestial realm.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to proclaim this meaning, spoke in verse:
“If one rejoices in this life, one will rejoice in future lives; Because one has performed meritorious deeds, one rejoices in both.
Knowing for oneself that this joy arises from prior karma, One shall be reborn once more in the happy realms.”
If one finds joy in this life and will find joy in future lives, it is because of the merit one has created that there is joy in both;
knowing that this joy arises from prior karma, one shall further experience joy in other realms of existence.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "Bhadanta,
I do not now understand the meaning of these verses."
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!

Prince Jeta was without fault; he was unjustly executed by the foolish and evil King Virūḍhaka. Yet his superior retribution in the human realm is not yet exhausted; he shall next receive exquisite bliss in the heavens."
"It is for this reason that I have spoken these verses.
At that time, Ānanda silently accepted this with faith.
Later, on another occasion, the foolish and wicked Ajātaśatru was in the palace with his court ladies, and he began to boast of himself:
"Is there anyone in this world who resembles me in my great strength, prowess, invincibility, and the completion of my undertakings?
At that time, the five hundred Śākya maidens brought by Duṣprasaha, having heard these words, spoke together in verse:
"He is a son of the Buddha’s family, Bound by the constraints of the precepts."
"Now that you have slaughtered them all, what is the purpose of praising yourself?
When the King heard these verses spoken by the daughter of the Śākyas, he was seized with great rage and likewise addressed his ministers in verse:
"You have slaughtered the dragon but spared the dragon girl, who has thus given rise to poisonous malice toward me."
"You should quickly cut off their hands and feet, and urgently dispatch them to follow their kinsman.
Thereupon, the ministers immediately took five hundred Śākya women to the banks of the Pāṭalī pond and cut off their hands and feet; for this reason, it was called the Pond of Severed Hands and Feet.
At the beginning of various sūtras it is said: "The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, by the side of the Hand-and-Foot-Cutting Pond. This is the account of that event.
At that time, five hundred Śākya women had their hands and feet cut off and were suffering great agony; unable to endure it, they thought to themselves:

"At this moment, our bodies are oppressed by various sufferings so acute and unbearable that we can hardly bear them. Since the World-Honored One possesses great compassion, will he not deign to show us pity?"

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that there is not a single thing they do not fully comprehend. At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to great compassion; he went to that place and saw the Śākya women sitting there naked. Having seen them, the World-Honored One invoked his worldly wisdom (*lokajñāna*).
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that if they give rise to a mundane thought, even ants and insects know the Buddha’s intention;
if they give rise to a supramundane thought, even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not know the Buddha’s intention, much less other sentient beings who could possibly know it.
The Buddha thought to himself: "Excellent!
It would be of the utmost importance if the celestial maiden Śacī were to bring the robe and water here."
After the Buddha had formed this thought, the goddess Śacī immediately understood his intention and thought to herself:
"For what reason has the Tathāgata given rise to a worldly thought?"
"I know that the Blessed One wishes to proclaim the sublime Dharma for the five hundred Śākya women; they require robes and water.

He then took five hundred celestial robes and went to the Anavatapta Lake, where he drew water with his flask and returned to the Buddha's presence. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"I have now brought five hundred celestial garments and exquisite perfumed water.
The Buddha said,
"Go and comfort the Śākya women, wash their bodies, and ensure they all put on the garments."
Then Śākī performed everything in the sequence as the Buddha had instructed.
At that time, through his supernormal powers, the Tathāgata caused the suffering of those five hundred Śākya women to be entirely removed, and he said to them:
"O virtuous women, you yourselves committed these deeds which have now reached maturity; you must certainly experience the results yourselves, for no one is willing to take your place."
When the World-Honored One had finished speaking these words, he left them and departed.
Those Śākya women, having conceived pure faith toward the World-Honored One, passed away and were reborn in the palace of the Four Great Kings.
Whether male or female, those born in the heavens immediately give rise to three thoughts: "Where did I die?
Where have I now been born?"
"By what karma was this brought about?

He then recalled that he had died in the human realm and was now born in the palace of the Four Great Kings; having developed a profound sense of respect for the World-Honored One, he gave rise to pure faith.
Then those five hundred Śākya women thought to themselves:
"If we do not go to pay our respects to the World-Honored One, it would be a lack of reverence and would be improper."

At that time, after the five hundred celestial maidens had formed this thought, they each adorned themselves with various necklaces and ornaments of exquisite brilliance. Taking heavenly garments filled with wonderful celestial flowers—namely, *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, and *māndārava* flowers—they arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling past the first watch of the night. Having made offerings of the celestial flowers and prostrated at his feet, they sat to one side to listen to and receive the sublime Dharma.
At that time, the radiance of the celestial maidens blazed forth, illuminating the entirety of the Jeta Grove.

Then the World-Honored One, in accordance with the inclinations and faculties of the celestial maidens, preached the sublime Dharma to them, enabling them to realize the principles of the Four Noble Truths.

At that time, the celestial maidens shattered the twenty peaks of the mountain of the twenty-fold view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) with the vajra-pestle of wisdom and attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
Having realized the truths, they addressed the World-Honored One three times, saying:
"O Virtuous One!..."

It is by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, that I have been enabled to realize the fruit of liberation; this was not something that could be accomplished by my parents, kings of men, celestial hosts, śramaṇas, brahmins, friends, or kinsmen.

Because I have encountered the World-Honored One as my spiritual friend, he has rescued me from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts and established me in the superior and wondrous states of humans and devas; thus shall I exhaust birth and death and attain the path to nirvana, drying up the ocean of blood and transcending the mountain of bones.
Having shattered the view of a self-identity accumulated since beginningless time with the vajra-wisdom mallet, I have attained the fruit of stream-entry.

I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha and receive the five precepts; from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall refrain from taking life, up to and including refraining from drinking intoxicants.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will bear witness that I am an upāsikā.
She then joined her palms in reverence before the Buddha and spoke in verse:
"By the power of the Buddha, I have forever closed the three evil realms."
I have been born in a supreme and wondrous heaven, And shall long follow the path to Nirvana.
Relying upon the World-Honored One, I have now attained the pure eye;
Having realized and seen the principle of the True Dharma, I shall reach the very limit of the ocean of suffering.
Transcending humans and devas, free from the afflictions of birth, old age, and death;
difficult to encounter within the ocean of existence, I have now met [the Buddha] and am able to cross over.
With my body adorned and a pure mind, I prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.
"Having circumambulated the One who has Eliminated Enmity, we now depart for the celestial palace.

At that time, those five hundred goddesses, having had their wishes fulfilled—like a merchant leader who has acquired great wealth, like a farmer who has extensively harvested his field's fruit, like a valiant warrior who has subdued all enemies, or like a person of grave illness who has been cured of many diseases—were filled with great joy. They took leave of the Buddha and departed together for the celestial palace.
When the bhikṣus heard this account, they were all filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"What karma did these five hundred Śākya women commit in the past?"
By the power of that karma, he committed no transgression during this lifetime, yet the fool Duṣprasāha unjustly severed his hands and feet.
Furthermore, by what karma was he reborn in the heavens, where he heard the Buddha’s true Dharma and realized the principle of ultimate truth?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"When the karma performed by those Śākya women reached maturity, the convergence of causes and conditions was as extensively described above; all their karmic fruits and retributions were each received by themselves."

"O bhikṣus! In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Buddha, a Blessed One named Kāśyapa—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān."

These five hundred Śākya women went forth as bhikṣuṇīs within that Buddha’s Dharma; they constantly reviled the bhikṣuṇīs, both those in training and those beyond training, using words such as "cut-off hand" and "cut-off foot."
By the power of this karma, he fell into hell for immeasurable years, where he suffered the torment of being burned.

Furthermore, due to the remaining residue of this karma, his hands and feet were constantly severed throughout five hundred lifetimes, and even in this present life, he continues to suffer this same pain.
Because I gave rise to pure faith, I was reborn in the heavens.

Furthermore, because in former days I was a bhikṣuṇī who upheld, maintained, and recited the teachings of the True Dharma, I have now encountered me, heard the Dharma, and realized the principle of the Truths.
"O bhikṣus! All this is due to karma, as explained at length above.
At that time, the person who had been left behind by Candapradyota, having heard the Buddha’s prophecy, returned to Candapradyota’s presence. He then asked:
"What did the Blessed One declare concerning me? He replied,
"Great King!..."
The Tathāgata spoke, saying:
"The Kingdom of Kośala shall be utterly destroyed.
After seven more days have passed, Duṣprasaha and his mother, Pāpīmatī, will have their bodies consumed by fierce flames and fall into the Avīci Great Hell."
At that time, when Candapradyota heard what had been said, he was overcome with intense affliction and sat with his cheek pressed in his palm.
Seeing this, Duḥśīlā asked him, "Great King!
"For what reason do you harbor such grief? The King said, "O Duḥkhā!"
How could I not be filled with grief and distress?
The World-Honored One has spoken, predicting that both you and I shall, seven days from now, be consumed by fierce flames and fall into the Avīci Great Hell.
Duḥśīlā replied: "Great King!
Just as when a mendicant Brahmin enters a house to beg and, failing to obtain anything, wishes to bring about hundreds of thousands of kinds of inauspicious events upon that household."

How much more so for the śramaṇa Gautama, whose entire circle of kinsmen has been slaughtered by the king; could he not harbor words of profound resentment and, following his evil intent, utter curses?
"If the King fears, he should have a single-pillar pavilion constructed within the waters of the pond in his rear garden.
The King should go there and reside for seven days; only after the seven days are complete may he enter the city."
The king said, "So be it.
He immediately ordered a tower to be built, and he had the palace ladies, along with Dukūlā and the others, ascend the tower to reside there.
When one night had passed, Dukūla said: "Great King!
One night has already elapsed; six nights remain until we may enter the city together."
Thus, for two or three days, and even up to the seventh day, Duḥśāṇā said:
"Today we shall enter the city together in safety.
At that time, clouds suddenly arose from all four directions; as it was the women's custom to enjoy looking at their ornaments, the palace attendants said to one another:
“Once you have finished adorning yourselves, you may go into the city.
Thereupon, they adjusted their garments.

At that time, there was a woman who placed a sun-crystal gem (*sūryakānta-maṇi*) upon her couch and adorned herself. As the clouds dispersed and the sky cleared, the sunlight suddenly appeared; when it struck the precious gem, fire immediately issued forth and burned her couch. Fierce flames surged upward and instantly consumed the multi-storied pavilion.
The palace attendants scattered and fled in all directions; Duryodhana and his mother were both engulfed by the flames and sought to escape.
At that time, non-human beings barred the doors so they could not get out, and thus Duryodhana was consumed and killed by the fire.
With extreme suffering缠繞ing his mind, he cried out to the Mother of Suffering: "Alas!
I am now beset by the agony of being burned."
Dukkhā said: "Great King! I am the same in this regard."

Their bodies were scorched by a great fire until they were completely consumed; crying out in unison with loud lamentations, they fell into the Avīci Great Hell and underwent various extreme sufferings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“If one is burned in this life and will be burned in the next, it is because of the sins one has committed that one is burned in both.”
Knowing that this burning arises from evil karma, one will further be reborn in the miserable realms.
If there is suffering in this life and suffering in future lives, it is because of the commission of transgressions that both are suffering;
knowing that this suffering arises from evil karma, one will further undergo suffering in other realms.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda addressed him, saying: "Bhadanta,
I do not now understand the meaning of these verses."
The Buddha said: “Ānanda!

The fool Duṣprasaha and his mother, Kālī, have been consumed by fire and have fallen into the Avīci Great Hell. It was on account of this matter that I secretly spoke these verses, as explained in detail above.”

At that time, after King Virūḍhaka had slaughtered the Śākyas, there remained in that city various ornaments such as necklaces, bracelets, and bangles used for adorning the body. When the Śākya women saw them, they wept; filled with grief and distress, they thought to themselves:
"While those people were alive, they held the Saṃgha in high esteem. It would be fitting to take these items and offer them to the Saṃgha as a merit-making rite for their posthumous benefit."
He immediately took it and gave it as alms.
When the group of six bhikṣus received this object, they used it to adorn themselves and entered the city of Kapilavastu to go on their alms round.
Upon seeing them, the Śākya girl wept as before and said, "Noble ones!

We did not wish to behold such things; therefore, we gave these to you in the hope that you would set our grieving hearts at rest. Now, they have caused me to give rise once more to my former memories."
The group of six monks remained silent.
These bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, who thought to himself:

"Because these bhikṣus wear necklaces, bracelets, and golden-threaded belts, such faults arise. From this day forward, I shall prohibit all bhikṣus from wearing any kind of ornamental or variegated finery."
"If there be any who cling [to this], they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The summary verse for the fifth section of the second door says:
"There are five benefits of leaving the household life; not grasping money; and the bestowing of training."
The Great Assembly recited verses; the use of smoking tubes and gargling was permitted.
The setting was the city of Śrāvastī.
In a certain village there lived an elder who, not long after marrying his wife, dwelt with her in joyful harmony.
Later, at another time, the householder’s kinsmen and his wealth were completely lost; he then thought to himself:
"I am now old and can no longer seek out money and goods for my livelihood, moreover, my kinsmen have almost all died."
"I should now renounce the worldly life and go forth into homelessness.
Having formed this thought, he said to his wife,
"O virtuous lady!"
"I am already old and can no longer seek wealth or property; my kinsmen have all perished, and I now wish to leave the household life.
His wife replied, "Excellent!"
"However, you may come to consult me from time to time.
The husband replied, "So be it."
He immediately went to the Jeta Grove, approached the bhikṣus, prostrated at their feet, and said:
"Noble ones! I seek to go forth."
He replied, "O worthy one! This is a virtuous deed; do as you intend."
As the Blessed One said:
"Those who possess wisdom should delight in going forth into homelessness for the sake of seeing five benefits. What are these five?"
First, I have attained self-benefit that is not shared with others; therefore, the wise should seek to leave the household life.

Second, I know myself to be a lowly person driven by others, whereas after leaving the household life, one receives the respect, praise, and prostrations of others; therefore, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
Third, one shall attain the peace and security of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*; therefore, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
Fourth, upon the end of this life, one shall be reborn in the heavens; therefore, the wise should seek to leave the household life.

Fifth, one will always be praised by the Buddhas, the assemblies of śrāvakas, and all superior human beings; therefore, the wise should seek to go forth from the household life within the sublime Dharma and Vinaya.
"Your current resolve to seek the path is a virtuous deed.
At that time, the bhikṣu immediately granted him the going forth and conferred full ordination upon him.
After two or three days had passed and he had been instructed in the ritual procedures, he addressed him, saying:
“O worthy one! Deer do not support deer. The city of Śrāvastī is vast and spacious; it is the domain of the Buddha. You should go there to beg for alms in order to sustain your life.”

In the early morning, he took up his robes and bowl and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. There he encountered a woman whose appearance resembled that of his wife; having seen her, he thought to himself:
"Previously, I made this agreement with my wife that after I had gone forth, she would come at times to visit and inquire after me."
"Now that you have gone forth into the homeless life, you should maintain your word and your integrity;
do not cause us further distress. After receiving alms food, he returned to the Jetavana Monastery. Not long after, he said to his preceptor:
"Previously, I made a solemn agreement with my former wife that after I had gone forth, I would go to visit and inquire after her from time to time. I pray that you will grant me your permission."
The teacher said, "Go as you please; protect your own mind well. He replied:
"So be it! Having taken his leave, he departed.
Gradually traveling on, he arrived at the site of his former village; from afar, his wife saw him and came forward to meet him in haste, crying out:
"Welcome, welcome! Noble son.
He then wished to take hold of his robes and receive his bowl, but the bhikṣu said:
“O virtuous one! What do you wish to do? He replied:
"I wish to take hold of your robe and bowl.
The bhikṣu said, "Do not touch my robe and bowl."
He asked, "For what reason? He replied:
"I have been instructed by my upādhyāya to guard my mind well.
He said, "Noble son!"
"You protect your own mind; how could I possibly obstruct you!
He then took up his robes and bowl, prepared a seat for him to sit upon, brought water for washing his feet, and asked:
"What do you intend to do?"
The wife said,
"I wish to wash your feet. He replied:
"Do not touch my feet. He asked, "Why?"
He replied, "I have received my teacher’s instruction to guard my mind well.
He gave the same answer as before and then washed [the other's] feet.
Later, when he brought oil intending to anoint his feet, the bhikṣu saw him and asked;
he replied, "To anoint my feet. The bhikṣu said:
"Do not apply ointment.
The question and answer were the same as before:
"My preceptor instructed me to guard my mind."
He asked: "Noble son! Guard your own mind."
He then brought food, intending to eat from the same dish, and asked, "What is this?
The other replied:
"Having been separated for a long time and not having eaten together, I wish to eat with you.
The bhikṣu did not grant permission; the exchange of questions and answers was as before, whereupon [the other] spread out a woolen rug and said:
"Noble son!..."
"You have come from afar and are weary; I hope you will rest for a while.
Once the bhikṣu had washed his feet, he lay down to rest.
Then the other approached, wishing to lie down in the same place, whereupon the bhikṣu said:
"What do you wish to do? He replied, "Noble son!"
"Since we have not slept together for such a long time, I wish to lie down with you.
After the same exchange of questions and answers as before, the bhikṣu refused; she then came forward and embraced him.

The woman was like a poison of touch; when he was touched by her, his mind became agitated and various evil thoughts arose. They then engaged in sexual union and lived together for many days, after which he said to his wife, "I wish to return to the monastery."
The wife thought to herself:
"This man has been having secret affairs with me without others seeing; I shall now cause everyone to know of it.
The bhikṣus will surely expel him, and he will return to my place."
Having had this thought, he said: "Noble son!
You must not go empty-handed; you should take some amount of provisions and cowrie shells to accompany you."
The bhikṣu said, "It is not proper for me to handle gold, cowries, or similar valuables; how then can I take them away?
His wife said:
"I shall now devise a plan so that he does not touch it.
He then tied an object to his mendicant's staff and said,
"Take this away."
The bhikṣu then took up his staff and departed, arriving at the city of Śrāvastī.

It was the constant custom of the group of six bhikṣus to guard the gates so that no one passed by empty-handed. At that time, Upānanda was walking back and forth at the entrance of the gate; seeing from afar that bhikṣu approaching—with a head like an owl’s and long, drooping eyebrows—he thought to himself:
"Which venerable one is coming here?"
"You should go out to meet him and walk forward to welcome him," he said, "and cry out: 'Welcome!'"
"Welcome, Venerable One! The bhikṣu replied,
"I pay my respects!"
"I pay homage to the ācārya!
At that moment, Upānanda thought to himself:
"This must certainly be a mahallaka bhikṣu; he does not know his upādhyāya and does not recognize his ācārya."
"I shall now ask him from where he has come.
He then stepped forward and asked:
"Old man, from where have you come?"
He replied, "Ācārya! I have come specifically to see you."
Upānanda said: "You are a virtuous person who cherishes kindness; those who remember past favors are praised by all.
The World-Honored One has also said:"
"O bhikṣus, you should always learn to repay kindness.
If even a small kindness is repaid, how much more so a great one?
By virtue of the kindness you preserved in the past, were you not able to see your wife?"
He replied, “I saw it. He asked again:
"Have you attained peace and security?
He replied, "By your gracious protection, I have been very fortunate to remain safe and well."
"What is that object upon your mendicant’s staff?
He replied, "My wife gave me this cowrie shell as provisions for my journey."
Upānanda said, "Old man, you possess great merit;
having gone to see your wife, you have already obtained this benefit.
He then thought to himself:
"Judging by his demeanor and appearance, there must be something else afoot; I should now question him with gentle words.
That mahallaka was by nature simple-minded and straightforward, so he recounted everything he had done in detail.
Upānanda said, "What you have done should be related in full to the Upādhyāya.
Hearing this, he was delighted and went before his teacher to relate everything in detail.
The Teacher, having heard these words, informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus then reported the circumstances to the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That mahallaka did not know the gravity of the matter; he committed the offense unintentionally."
If one has not yet been instructed in the four *pārājika* rules, they do not commit an offense.
Therefore, O Bhikṣus,
as soon as you have received full ordination (*upasampadā*), you should immediately explain the four *pārājika* dharmas to them.
"If you do not speak, you shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

The remainder of the summary verse for the fifth section of the second chapter. The narrative context is set in Śrāvastī.

There was a bhikṣu named Ānanda who dwelt in a quiet hermitage; he constantly delighted in sitting in meditation, and because of his practice of concentration, people of the time called him "Ānanda, Dweller in Concentration."
As he was about to enter meditative absorption, a demoness came and invited him to engage in sexual intercourse; he joyfully refused her.

Later, at another time, as he again desired to enter absorption, the demoness returned and sat upon his lap. Thus one should know that the realm of women is a great poison that harms as soon as it is touched; once a defiled mind has arisen, they immediately engage in sexual desire together.
At that time, having engaged in sexual intercourse with joy, it was as if a poisoned arrow had entered his chest; harboring sorrowful thoughts, he said:
"I have been foolish to defile my pure conduct. Having committed this act of sexual passion, I shall return to lay life."
He further thought to himself:
"I truly have no intention to conceal anything; I should go to the Buddha's presence and explain this matter in full.
If there is a proper procedure by which I may still become a renunciant, I shall act according to the Dharma; if it is otherwise, I shall return to lay life."
He then took his dharma-robe with his right hand and covered his physical deformity with his left hand; weeping and lamenting, he went to where the Buddha was.

At that time, the World-Honored One was expounding the True Dharma to a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus. Seeing him approaching from afar, the Buddha thought to himself:
"If I do not first address that bhikṣu, saying:..."
Upon hearing "Welcome! Welcome!",
he vomited hot blood and immediately passed away.
Having formed this thought, he said to Ānanda: "Welcome! Welcome!"
"Why do you weep? He replied,
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!"
"I was joyful before, but now I am not joyful.
The Buddha said,
"What fault have you committed to speak such words?"
He replied: "World-Honored One!
I have not abandoned the precepts; it was while violating my pure conduct that I engaged in sexual intercourse."
"Although he has committed this transgression, he does not have even the slightest intention to conceal it.
The Buddha said, "Rejoice!"
"Are you able to observe the rules of training for as long as you live? He replied,
"Virtuous One!"
“I am able to uphold it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“You should know that although the bhikṣu Nandika has violated the pure precepts, because he has no intention to conceal it, this does not constitute a pārājika offense.”
"You should grant them the lifelong training rule of 'Rejoicing.
Should there be others of this kind, you should likewise grant it to them.
It should be granted in this manner:"

Having spread out the seats and struck the *khaṇḍika* (wooden gong), and having completed the formal announcement (*jñapti*), once the assembly has gathered, he should instruct the monk *Ānanda* to circumambulate and prostrate to the entire Saṃgha. Then, squatting before the senior monk (*sthavira*) with palms joined, he should make his request as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!

I, the bhikṣu Nandika, having not abandoned the training precepts but having violated pure conduct by engaging in sexual intercourse—even so much as to have no mind of concealment—now, O bhikṣu Nandika, beg from the Saṃgha the lifelong training precepts.
May the virtuous Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me, the bhikṣu Nandika, the lifelong training precepts.
A second and third time, he likewise requested in this manner.
The Saṃgha may then allow him to dwell in a place where he is visible to the eye but not within earshot, and shall appoint one bhikṣu to perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for him:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
That bhikṣu, Pārāśarika, did not relinquish the training rules and violated pure conduct by engaging in sexual intercourse; yet, he did not harbor even the slightest intention to conceal it.
He now requests from the Saṃgha the lifelong training rules.
"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha consent that the Saṃgha now bestow upon the bhikṣu Nandika the lifelong training rules.
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
Thereafter, the karmavācanā is performed.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

That bhikṣu Nandika, having failed to relinquish the training rules and having violated pure conduct by committing an act of sexual intercourse, did so without even the slightest intention to conceal it."
This bhikṣu Nandika now requests from the Saṃgha the lifelong training rules; the Saṃgha now grants the lifelong training rules to the bhikṣu Nandika.
If the venerable ones consent to granting the lifelong training rules to the bhikṣu Nandika, they should remain silent; if they do not consent, they should speak.
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner:
"The Saṃgha has already granted the lifelong training rules to the bhikṣu Nandika; the Saṃgha has already given its consent, as indicated by its silence; thus do I now hold it."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain all the rules of conduct for one who is undergoing training.
A bhikṣu undergoing training should not accept the respectful salutations, prostrations, rising to meet, or joining of palms from a bhikṣu who abides in his natural state of virtue."
When sitting together, one should not occupy the same seat as another; when sitting, one should sit on a lower seat.
One should not walk in tandem while practicing *caṅkrama* (walking meditation); if one must walk together, one should step back.
When visiting the homes of elders or Brahmins, one should not take a bhikṣu who maintains his natural demeanor as a companion; even if traveling together, one should let that person go ahead.
One should not share a room for lodging;

one should not grant others the going-forth or the full ordination (*upasampadā*); one should not accept another’s dependence (*niśraya*); one should not keep a novice (*śrāmaṇera*); one should not perform the *jñapti*, *jñapti-dvitīya*, or *jñapti-caturtha* formal acts (*karmavācanā*); and one should not be appointed as the officiant who performs these formal acts.
Furthermore, one should not be appointed to instruct bhikṣuṇīs; even if appointed, one should not go.
Upon seeing other bhikṣus who have broken their precepts, broken their views, broken their dignified conduct, or live by improper livelihoods, one should not bring them to account.
Furthermore, one must not issue various prohibitions or regulations that differ from the procedures for the *poṣadha* and the *pravāraṇā*.

Every morning, one must always rise early, open the doors, and put away the lamp-stands. One should sweep the rooms and courtyards, and smear them with fresh cow dung everywhere; one may also smear the latrines to make them clean. In all cases, earth, water, and leaves should be provided so that no necessity is lacking.

The water required may be adjusted to be either cold or warm; it should be washed clean at the water conduit. Ring the *ghanṭā*, spread out the seats and mats, and prepare various flowers and burning incense for offering.
If one is capable oneself, one should recite verses at appropriate times to praise the virtues of the Buddha;
if one is not capable, one may request another person to do so.
If it is during the summer months, one must hold a fan to fan the bhikṣus.
Whenever one wishes to sit, one should sit below the great bhikṣus and above the śrāmaṇeras.
At every time of receiving food, one should keep the mind calm and composed.
When the meal is finished, one should fold away the mats and seats, place all the eating utensils in their proper places, and sweep and sprinkle the dining area.
He should always announce the date among the assembly, making this formal proclamation:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Today is the first day of the month.

May everyone in the great assembly apply their minds with care. For the sake of the donors who have built this monastery, the deities who protect the monastery, the king, the ministers, the teachers and monks, our parents, and the donors of the ten directions, we should recite the sublime verses on the merit of giving found within the Sūtras."
"If you yourself are unable [to do so], you may request another person to act on your behalf.
This should be understood to apply to subsequent days as well.
At that time, the bhikṣus divided the dwellings among themselves and did not give any to those undergoing training (śikṣamāṇā). The Buddha said:
"One should give.
When [the monks] did not give the offerings, the Buddha said:
"One should give."
The Buddha said: "The bhikṣu undergoing training should cultivate wholesome qualities.
This practice must be followed consistently until the afflictions are completely exhausted; failure to do so constitutes an offense."

At that time, the bhikṣus acted according to the Buddha’s instructions in due order. The bhikṣu Nandika, with constant mindfulness and diligent exertion free from weariness, severed the afflictions that bind one to the five realms of existence and realized the fruit of arhatship, possessing the three knowledges, the six superknowledges, and the eight liberations.
He attained the knowledge of things as they truly are:
"Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.

With his mind free from hindrance, like a hand waving through space, he felt neither love nor hatred whether cut by a blade or smeared with sandalwood paste; he viewed gold and earth as equal and without distinction; he renounced all fame and profit without exception; and Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas paid him their respects.
At that time, having attained the fruit with joy, he continued to follow the previous regulations, not daring to violate any of the prescribed practices. The Buddha said:
"You should no longer practice those [austerities]; you should sit according to the order of seniority and dwell together with those who abide in their original nature."
The setting was in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Pilindavatsa had been afflicted by chronic illness ever since his ordination. When a fellow practitioner of the holy life came to him, he asked:
"Venerable sir, are you living in comfort? Are your daily activities light and easy? Are you dwelling in peace?"
He replied, "Venerable sir!
I am constantly afflicted by illness; how could there be any peace or happiness?"
He asked, "What is your suffering? He replied:
“I suffer from a cough.
He was asked: “What medicine have you been taking?”
He replied,
"I once inhaled medicinal smoke and thereby received healing.
[The monk asked,] "Venerable sir!"
"Why do you not take it now?
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet permitted its use."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "For those who are ill, I permit the inhalation of smoke as a means of treating disease.
The bhikṣus did not understand; they placed the medicine over a fire and simply inhaled the smoke, but it did not enter their mouths. The Buddha said:
"One may join two bowls together, pierce a hole in the top, place fire within, set the medicine inside, and inhale [the fumes].
This method was still not ideal, so the Buddha said:
"One should instead make a tube."
He made it out of bamboo, which again incurred a fault. The Buddha said:
"One should not use bamboo; it may be made of iron.
He made it too short. The Buddha said:
"Do not let it be too short.
He made it too long, so the Buddha said:
"It should not be too long; it may be twelve finger-breadths in length."
"Do not let it be sharp-pointed, nor should it be coarse or harsh. Place it over the opening of the bowl and inhale the smoke with your mouth.
After he had used it, he discarded it wherever he was;
the Buddha said, "You should not discard it haphazardly; you may make a small pouch to carry it in."
He placed it on the ground. The Buddha said:
"One should not place it on the ground so that it becomes damaged; it should be hung upon an ivory peg or a bamboo rack.
Rust then formed on the iron. The Buddha said:
"One should wipe it with ghee and oil.
Later, when it was time to use it, they found it difficult to wash and wipe clean;
the Buddha said, "It should not be washed with water; one should place it in fire to burn it for purification."
The summary verse for the sixth section of the second chapter states:
One should bathe with medicinal decoctions; Nasal irrigation and the opening of copper cups;
The use of carriages is permitted for the elderly and the infirm; And one must attend to the matters of urination and defecation.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
A certain bhikṣu, afflicted by illness, went to a physician and said:
"O worthy one!..."
"My body is afflicted by illness; please, out of kindness, prescribe a remedy for me.
He replied, "Noble One!..."
"You must bathe with medicinal decoctions before you can recover.
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet granted permission for this."
The physician said:
“Noble One! The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate; he will surely grant permission.”
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "If a physician instructs you to perform a medicinal wash, you should do so as you please.
Once the Buddha had permitted the use of medicinal decoctions for washing, the bhikṣus did not know which medicines should be used for the decoction.
He returned and said to the physician, "The Buddha has permitted me to bathe with medicinal decoctions; I do not know which medicines I should use.
The physician replied:
“Noble One! I do not know what medicine this is;
however, while reading the medical treatises of the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), I saw the name of this decoction. Since you, our Great Master, are omniscient, please explain it when asked.”
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Whatever treats wind disorders—whether roots, stalks, flowers, fruits, bark, wood, or the like—should be boiled together into a decoction to wash the body and eliminate the ailment."
When the bhikṣus washed with hot water, their skin became colorless.
The Buddha said, "Anoint it with oil.
They then applied so much of it that it stained their robes. The Buddha said:
"He rubbed it with soap powder,
yet his complexion remained lusterless. The Buddha said,
"When you are about to finish washing, place one or two drops of oil into the bathwater to make the body glossy and radiant."
Furthermore, the Venerable Pilindavatsa was ill, and when a bhikṣu asked him,
“What is your ailment? he replied:
"I suffer from a runny nose," he said.
The physician asked,
"What medicine have you been taking lately?"
He replied, "I once used it for nasal irrigation.
[The other asked,] "Venerable sir, why do you not use it now?"
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet granted permission.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there are those who are ill, I now permit the administration of ghee and oil by nasal irrigation.
When the bhikṣus simply poured it directly into their nostrils, soiling their bodies with the grease, the Buddha said:
"It should not be done in this manner."
The bhikṣus again used leaves as a vessel to pour [the water], yet the matter was still not satisfactory. The Buddha said:
"One should not use leaves.
They then poured it from within a small cloth; the fault was the same as before. The Buddha said:
"One should not use a small piece of cloth for irrigation; rather, one may use copper, iron, or tin to fashion a nasal syringe.
The bhikṣu then made it with a single nozzle, whereupon the Buddha said, "It should be made with two nozzles."
They made them sharp and coarse; the Buddha said, "Do not let them be sharp or coarse.
When a bhikṣu did not wash his hands thoroughly before irrigating his nose, the Buddha said:
"One should wash one's hands thoroughly;
only after receiving the medicine should it be poured into the nostrils.
Furthermore, Pilindavatsa suffered from thirst, and a bhikṣu came to inquire after him:
"What ailment do you have, O Benevolent One? He replied,
"I suffer from thirst, yet I have nothing to drink."
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"Keep a copper drinking cup for water.
Later, when some of Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja’s kinsmen came to hear the Dharma and had finished listening, they returned home and told their wives:
“Noble One! I have already heard and received the sublime Dharma spoken by Pilindavatsa.
His wife said:
“The Buddha has appeared in the world, and you have obtained great benefit.
The husband said,
“For what reason do you not listen to the Dharma?”
The wife said, "I am a woman;
it would be shameful for me to go out. If the noble Pilindavatsa could come here and explain it to me, I would listen and receive his teaching."
The husband then made a request on his behalf, and she replied:
"O worthy one! My body is afflicted by illness and I am unable to go there."
He replied, "Noble One! I have brought a palanquin."
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet permitted bhikṣus to ride in a carriage.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"For this reason, I permit the bhikṣus who are ill to ride in a carriage.
Once the Buddha had granted permission, Pilindavatsa immediately mounted a carriage and, accompanied by his disciples, proceeded to the place where he was invited.
At that time, the six bhikṣus encountered them on the road and asked their disciples,
"Who is this person riding in the carriage? They replied:
"This is my upādhyāya. The group of six said,
"Does the Blessed One permit the bhikṣus to ride in a carriage?"
He replied, "I grant permission.
He spoke again:
"The World-Honored One, out of great compassion, knowing that the bodies of the Śākya sons are delicate and they cannot travel on foot,
has permitted them to ride in vehicles. Then the six bhikṣus said to one another,
"We too should decorate fine litters."
On the second day, he was adorned with exquisite woolen tassels and various ornaments such as bells, and placed upon a palanquin to be carried through the streets.
When the elders and brahmins saw him, they asked,
"Noble One!..."
"What is this? He replied, "World-Honored One,
please allow me to ride in a carriage."
He replied, "Do you śramaṇas still indulge in sensual pleasures?
The group of six remained silent.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu who is not ill rides in a carriage, he commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma. There are two circumstances under which one is permitted to ride in a carriage:
[the first is when one is ill, and the second is when traveling through a dangerous region]."
"First, one who is aged, decrepit, and weak;
second, one who is afflicted by illness and lacks strength.
The setting was the city of Śrāvastī.

There was an elder who, possessing right faith, went with a faithless brāhmaṇa to the Jetavana to observe the grounds. Upon reaching the foot of a tree, they saw a place where excrement had been voided.
The brāhmaṇa said, "Elder, these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are utterly impure; they have left filth beneath the flowering and fruit-bearing trees."
The householder said, "All these noble ones are of great virtue; how could they act so indiscreetly?
It must have been a layperson performing an improper act."
While they were conversing, they suddenly saw a mahallaka bhikṣu who had covered his head with his robe and was defecating beneath a tree.
Upon seeing this, the faithless brāhmaṇa said to the elder:
"You claim that laypeople commit such impurities; look at this bhikṣu, who has covered his head with his robe and is voiding excrement beneath a tree—is he not a layperson?"
At that time, the elder was deeply ashamed and remained silent without reply.
The bhikṣus then reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not defecate or urinate beneath any forest trees; if he should intentionally violate this rule, he commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma."

After the Buddha had established this rule, while the bhikṣus were traveling on the road, they reached a large forest where the urge to relieve themselves became pressing; yet, out of respect for the precepts, they suppressed it and did not discharge their waste, which resulted in further illness.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "If bhikṣus are traveling on a journey and reach a place of great forest, they may relieve themselves as they please.

Since the Buddha had permitted them to relieve themselves in forests while traveling, there was a bhikṣu staying in a village who did not dare to relieve himself under a tree in the forest; consequently, he suffered from being scorched by the midday sun.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One may relieve oneself at will beneath a thicket of thorns.
However, Upānanda again defiled another's vegetable garden with excrement. Consequently, the Buddha established the rule that bhikṣus must not defecate or urinate upon living grass.

At that time, the bhikṣus went to a place where there was no grass and discharged their excrement, leaving it in a state of utter disorder. When the householders and brahmins saw this, they mocked them together, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have truly excellent customs; having gathered for a single meal, they likewise discharge their waste in one place."
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"For this reason, I now permit the bhikṣus to construct latrines.
They then built them outside the monastery.
At night, they encountered fearsome tigers, wolves, lions, and various bandits; they reported these circumstances to the Buddha, who said, "You should construct [a shelter] within the monastery.
The bhikṣus did not know where it should be built.
The Buddha said,
"It should be constructed in the northwest corner behind the monastery.
Again, they did not know how it should be built.
The Buddha said:
"There are two kinds of latrines:
the first is a simple shed;..."
The second type is the "side-exit" (pārśvanirgata).
Regarding the "straight hall" (ṛju-śālā), it is like a square *vīthi* (monastic cell) with the latrine situated within it.

Regarding the "side-exit," one constructs a wooden frame extending from the eaves at the rear of the room; this is enclosed with wooden boards so that the latrine is positioned within. Outside, one may install a place for washing hands and feet as well as a spot for placing the water jar. The latrine must be fitted with a door leaf and a horizontal bolt; wooden sandals should be placed outside, which one must wear upon entering.
At that time, one bhikṣu entered the latrine, and another bhikṣu entered after him.
The Buddha said: "One should not do so.
Whenever entering a latrine, one must snap one's fingers or cough; those already inside the latrine should likewise do so."
The latrine was extremely foul-smelling.
The Buddha said, "One should wash and wipe it in regular succession to keep it clean, and place leaves, soil, and so forth [on top] so as not to harm flying insects.
The bhikṣus washed the latrine with their hands while harboring feelings of disgust. The Buddha said:
"One should simply pour water and scrub with a brush; one must not use the hands.
At that time, the bhikṣus waited for a long time inside the latrine without emerging while washing their hands and feet. The Buddha said:
"Establish a place outside for washing hands and feet."
He then placed it far away. The Buddha said, "Place it nearby.
For this reason, I now permit the bhikṣus to make whatever miscellaneous items are required when constructing a latrine.

The Buddha permitted the construction of latrines. At that time, some bhikṣus who needed to urinate were also in the latrines; those who needed to defecate could not enter quickly and had to wait for a long time, which led to illness.
The Buddha said: "A separate place for urination should be constructed."
The bhikṣus did not know where it should be located.
The Buddha said:
"It should be made near the latrine; it must have a passage for water to flow out and a door-panel installed separately; the rules for its construction are all the same as those for the latrine."
The summary verse for the seventh section of the second book says:
The water jar, knowing purity and contact, May the World-Honored One live long,
Thereby the Bhikṣuṇī entered parinirvāṇa, And chewing and eating— these five are all opened.
The setting was the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, during the height of the summer heat, there was a brahmin who, being oppressed by thirst, desired to drink water. He entered the monastery and approached a bhikṣu, saying:
"I am thirsty; you, sir, should give me water."
The bhikṣu took water from the touched jar and gave it to him to drink; seeing this, the brāhmaṇa asked, "Noble one!
Is this jar pure?"
"Is this contact? He replied, "It is contact."
“If that is so, for what reason did you bring this and give it to me? He replied,
“The flask was in one place, so I brought it here.”
He replied, "Noble One!

These two jars for pure and impure water should not be mixed together; they ought to be placed in separate locations. If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas come seeking water, would it not be a source of merit to relieve their thirst?"
