The brahmin, disliking the water, did not drink it and departed.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"The great assembly should provide pure water jars to supply those who are thirsty."

The Buddha said to the great assembly, "As for the setting out of pure water," at that time there was an elder who, having heard the Buddha's permission, offered many jars and vases to the monastery. Those who had need of them would simply take them away, or the gardeners and various lay travelers would take them as they pleased.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they did not stop him; before long, all the vessels were exhausted.
Then the bhikṣus said to that donor:
"The vessels you have given away are now all broken and gone; you should bring more."
He replied, "Noble One!
I have given many vessels; why do they quickly run out?"
The bhikṣu reported the matter in detail to the donor, who said,
"Noble one! There is nothing that I do not give to ordinary worldly people."
"Why do you not prevent them from being wasted?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not neglect such things without inquiring into them; the Saṃgha should appoint a person to oversee the utensils."
After the Buddha had granted his permission, the bhikṣus did not exercise discernment when appointing [an official], but rather appointed them at will. The Buddha said:
"There are five circumstances under which one should not be appointed."
What are the five? If one possesses attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion, and furthermore does not know whether the utensils and vessels have been stored away or not—these are the [unfit].
Furthermore, there are five qualities by which one should be appointed:
If one is free from attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion, and well understands what items should be stored and what should not be stored, such a person should be appointed.
Having assembled the community as before, one should ask the candidate in the midst of the assembly:
"O Bhikṣu [Name], are you able to serve as the custodian of utensils for the Great Assembly?"
If he says, "I can," he shall instruct a bhikṣu to perform the formal motion and second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, desires to serve as the器物-custodian (bhāṇḍāgārika) for the Saṃgha.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and you grant permission, may the Saṃgha consent that this bhikṣu, so-and-so, be appointed by the Saṃgha to serve as the器物-custodian for the community."
The motion is thus made.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, wishes to serve as the steward of utensils for the Saṃgha.
If the Saṃgha permits this bhikṣu, so-and-so, to serve as the steward of utensils, let those who consent remain silent; if you do not consent, please speak.
“The Saṃgha has already authorized the bhikṣu so-and-so to serve as the custodian of utensils; because of his silence, I now hold it to be so.
At that time, someone came seeking water for thirst. The bhikṣu filled a new jar with water and gave it to the layperson, while giving the water from an old jar to the bhikṣu.
The Buddha said: “It should not be done in this way. One should provide the new vessel to the bhikṣus and give the old vessel to the laity.”
When the bhikṣus had finished using them, they would collect and store them away; however, when the laypeople finished using them, they would discard them lightly wherever they were.
The Buddha said: "All must be collected.
When the bhikṣus failed to guard them properly and they suffered loss, the Buddha said:
"A storehouse should be established.
The bhikṣus acted according to these instructions.

At that time, a caravan leader came from the north and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, intending to provide offerings for them throughout the three-month rainy season retreat. He then thought to himself:
"I shall now make offerings; I do not wish to seek various utensils from others, but shall provide them myself.

He then fashioned many food vessels out of white copper and red copper. For three months, he provided the Tathāgata and the assembly of śrāvakas with the most excellent food and drink. When the period was complete, he offered all the utensils to the community of monks.
The bhikṣus then placed these vessels inside the storehouse for earthenware; as they jostled one another, some were damaged. The Buddha said:
"Vessels made of copper and those made of earthenware should be stored separately."
At that time, a thirsty brahmin entered the Jeta Grove, approached the bhikṣus, and said:
"Noble ones! Please give me some water."
The bhikṣu then took the water jar and the rope and gave them to the brahmin, who asked:
"Noble one! What is this for?"
He replied, "I have no old water; you may draw from it yourself for use. The brāhmaṇa said:
"You, sirs, out of compassion for all sentient beings, would do an excellent service if you could prepare some water, whether a little or much,
in advance. The bhikṣus replied,
"The Buddha has not yet granted permission for this."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, who said:
"The great assembly should prepare pure water in advance.

Having heard this, the bhikṣus installed it in various places—either in the central courtyard, inside the rooms, or in front of the eaves and beside the doors—which caused the water to become impure. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done in this way; rather, a water-storage hall should be constructed.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus did not know where to locate it.
The Buddha said:
"One may construct a place for water to collect on the eastern side of the temple gate.
As the interior of the room was dark, the Buddha said:

"One should install windows; as there is mud on the floor, one should pave it with bricks and provide an outlet for the water to drain away; one should install door panels along with bolts and latches."

The water-jar for storage should not be placed directly on the ground; it should be set upon a wooden stand. If there is no wooden stand, one should use bricks or tiles. The jar should be propped with objects so that it does not lean or tip over. Whenever the water-jar becomes unclean, it should be washed from time to time.
Not knowing with what object to wash it,
the Buddha said:
"One should use a comb, a brush, and various kinds of leaves."
Although he washed and scrubbed it repeatedly, a foul odor still remained. The Buddha said:
"You should keep many vessels to hold water alternately; set one portion of them with water and let another portion dry in the sun."
He then left it out in the midday sun to dry. The Buddha said: "Dry it in the shade.
He then failed to cover the mouth [of the jar], and soil entered the vessel. The Buddha said:
"One must cover [the vessel] and not touch it with unclean hands; one should wash one's hands clean.
When he washed his hands repeatedly while touching the jar, he became weary. The Buddha said:
"If it is a clean copper or earthenware vessel, there is no offense in taking it without the fingers touching water, or by rubbing the hands with dry cow-dung powder to remove grease."
The Buddha having granted permission to prepare the water in advance, [the monks] did not know who should be made to do it.
The Buddha said:
"You should employ your disciples and followers; all the necessary items for the place where the water is to be set out must be prepared in advance."
The Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in the city of Kapilavastu.

At that time, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side; the Buddha then preached the Dharma for them.
At that time, the World-Honored One suddenly sneezed. Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One’s lifespan may be long and far-reaching, remaining for more than the duration of kalpas."
When the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs heard Mahāprajāpatī speak these words, they all raised their voices in unison to make the same aspiration as she had.

When the yakṣas and spirits of the earth heard the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs speak these words, they all raised their voices together to utter this very aspiration; and when the yakṣa deities of the sky heard the sound, they likewise uttered this aspiration.

In this way, from the palaces of the Four Great Kings, through the Heaven of the Thirty-three, Yāma Heaven, Tuṣita Heaven, Nirmāṇarati Heaven, Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and even up to the Brahmā heavens, they all heard one another’s voices and spoke these words:
“We pray that the World-Honored One’s lifespan may be long and far-reaching, remaining for more than the duration of kalpas.”
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, saying:
"You are now creating a great obstacle for all sentient beings."
Because of these words of yours, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, as well as those on earth, in the air, and even up to the Brahma heaven, have heard this statement of yours.
One should not show such reverence toward the Buddha; such reverence is not called virtuous.
Mahāprajāpatī said: "Venerable Blessed One!
How is it that by extending reverence toward the Tathāgata, one is said to have performed what is good?"
The Buddha said,
“Gautamī, you should speak these words in the presence of the Tathāgata:”
“May the Buddha and the Saṃgha abide long in this world, always remaining in harmony like water and milk, and may they cause the Great Teacher’s instruction to shine forth. Thus, O Gautamī!
"If one performs such veneration toward the Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment, this is called 'proper etiquette.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu spoke in verse:
"The Mistress of the World, Gotamī, Pays homage at the feet of the Tathāgata."
"May the Muni prolong his life, remaining for aeons to transform sentient beings.
With such earnest devotion, the Mother of Buddhas spoke these words of homage;
yet it was not fitting at the presence of the Buddha to make such a vow.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī thought to herself:

"The Buddha has praised harmony among the assembly; furthermore, while the Great Teacher still dwells in the world and the community of bhikṣus has not yet fallen into division, it is now appropriate for me to enter parinirvāṇa."
He then proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to enter parinirvāṇa swiftly.”
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One remained silent; thus it was repeated a second and a third time, and the Buddha remained silent each time.
Then Mahāprajāpatī spoke again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I now intend to enter parinirvāṇa quickly.
The Buddha said, "Gautamī!"
“Did you utter these words for the sake of nirvāṇa?
He replied, “I spoke such words for the sake of nirvāṇa.”
The Buddha said:
"Since you have already spoken these words regarding nirvāṇa, what more need I say?
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; it is entirely like this."
Then the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs spoke again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We desire to enter parinirvāṇa swiftly.”
The Buddha asked the bhikṣuṇīs,
"Did you say these words for the sake of nirvāṇa? They replied:
"So be it," the Buddha said. "Since you have spoken these words regarding nirvāṇa, what more need I say?"
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all are exactly thus.
When Mahāprajāpatī and the bhikṣuṇīs had heard the Buddha’s teaching, their hearts were filled with great joy. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and went to Nanda’s place, saying:
"Noble One!..."
"I now intend to enter nirvana swiftly.
Nanda said, "Did you say these words for the sake of nirvana?"
Having spoken thus as the Buddha had instructed, he likewise went to the Venerable Aniruddha, Rāhula, Ānanda, and even to the various elders, prostrating himself before them and saying:
"Noble ones!..."
"We intend to enter parinirvāṇa quickly.
The bhikṣu Nanda and the other elders asked,
"Is it for the sake of parinirvāṇa that you speak these words?"
He replied, “It is so. He reported this, saying:
"Since you have spoken these words regarding *nirvāṇa*, what more can we say?
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; it is exactly thus for all.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, prostrated before the senior elders and took their leave to return to their residence. Upon arriving at their own monastery, she expounded the sublime Dharma to the three assemblies of disciples for seven days.
Having heard the Dharma, they caused immeasurable sentient beings to realize vast and sublime benefits.

Each of the bhikṣuṇīs departed from the monastery and went to a secluded place, where they sat in the half-lotus posture according to their respective order; even all five hundred did so in this manner.

Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī immediately entered *samādhi*; by the power of her supreme concentration, she concealed her body from view according to her intention and ascended into the void in the eastern direction, manifesting the four dignified postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, and entering the *tejodhātu-samādhi*.

Then, from within his body, he emitted various kinds of light—blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson—all appearing simultaneously; from the lower part of his body fire issued forth while clear water flowed from the upper part, and from the lower part of his body water issued forth while fire blazed from the upper part.
As it was in the east, so it was likewise in the south, west, and north.
The five hundred bhikṣuṇīs were no different from Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī in their manifested appearance.

Then Mahāprajāpatī again entered the first dhyāna; arising from the first dhyāna, she entered the second dhyāna; arising from the second dhyāna, she entered the third dhyāna; arising from the third dhyāna, she entered the fourth dhyāna; arising from the fourth dhyāna, she entered the sphere of infinite space; arising from the sphere of infinite space, she entered the sphere of infinite consciousness; arising from the sphere of infinite consciousness, she entered the sphere of nothingness; arising from the sphere of nothingness, she entered the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, she entered the meditative absorptions in reverse order back to the first dhyāna, and there attained parinirvāṇa.
The five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, all like Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, entered the various dhyānas in both forward and reverse order and likewise passed into parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the great earth shook everywhere; the four quarters, above, and below were brilliantly illuminated, and the cries of the devas in the sky were like the beating of drums.

At that time, whatever bhikṣus were on Mount Sumeru or in other mountains, even as far as cities, towns, villages, or secluded places such as hermitages and forests, upon seeing these signs, concentrated their minds and observed; they saw that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and five hundred bhikṣuṇīs had all entered parinirvāṇa.
Then the bhikṣus again had this thought:
"Since the Compassionate Mother of the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, we should go to assist in making offerings to her śarīra."
Having formed this thought, each according to their ability, they took various types of fragrant wood and went to the place where Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the others had entered parinirvāṇa.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with Kauṇḍinya, Vāṣpa, Mahānāman, Ānanda, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the rest of the great assembly of śrāvakas, all gathered there for the purpose of making offerings to the śarīras of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the others.
At that time, King Śreṇika Bimbisāra, together with the crown prince, his ministers, and his retinue, also came to that place for the purpose of making offerings to the śarīras.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the householder Jyotiṣka, the householder Pūrvaka, and Mṛgāramātṛ, along with their respective retinues, likewise arrived at that place.
Furthermore, the great kings of various nations, together with their retinues numbering in the hundreds of thousands, all gathered there.

At that time, King Prasenajit prepared five hundred precious chariots, adorned them with various kinds of jeweled robes and ornaments, and brought along diverse fragrant flowers, banners, pennants, precious parasols, and musical instruments.

At that time, the four bhikṣus—the Venerable Nanda, Āniruddha, Ānanda, and Rāhula—carried the bier of Mahāprajāpatī; the World-Honored One also supported the bier with his right hand, while the other bhikṣus each carried the biers of the bhikṣuṇīs. With profound reverence, they provided extensive and magnificent adornments and escorted them to a broad, level, and secluded place.
At that time, the Blessed One lifted up the upper robes worn by Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Look at this! Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the others are one hundred and twenty years of age, yet their bodies show no signs of aging and are like those of sixteen-year-old maidens."

At that time, King Prasenajit and the great assembly each took various kinds of fragrant wood and cremated his body. After the World-Honored One had expounded the Dharma of impermanence for the multitude, he returned to the monastery, washed his feet, took his seat, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know this!"
All such matters arise from seeing others sneeze or spit and wishing them long life.
Therefore, monks, when another sneezes, you should not say, "Long life!"
"If you speak thus intentionally, you shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had witnessed this event, they were all filled with doubt and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, what karma did Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs perform in the past, by the power of which karma they remain free from signs of aging at the age of one hundred and twenty, appearing like sixteen-year-old maidens?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Listen well, O bhikṣus, to the karma performed by Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs; through their own karma, they shall experience its results, even unto the ripening of the fruit, which returns to themselves."

“O bhikṣus! In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Buddha, a Blessed One named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with the ten titles, who resided at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Seers near Vārāṇasī.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, having completed his work of transforming sentient beings, entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.

At that time, there was a king named Kṛkī who, in order to make offerings to the relics of that Tathāgata, erected a stūpa made of the four precious substances, one *yojana* in length and breadth, and half a *yojana* in height.
The king had a chief consort and five hundred court ladies, but as they had grown old, the king abandoned them;
they said to one another, "For what reason does the Great King now abandon us and no longer inquire after us?"
The assembly deliberated together, saying,
"It is because he has grown old in years that we do not question him.
At that time, a court lady spoke these words:
"O sisters! By practicing what karma can one avoid decay and ensure that one's aspirations are fulfilled?
The queen replied:
"If one makes offerings to the stūpa containing the relics of Kāśyapa Buddha, all one's wishes shall be fulfilled.
They all said, "Excellent!"

Having obtained the King’s permission, he immediately took various powdered incenses, ointments, flower garlands, necklaces, banners, pennants, precious parasols, and exquisite fragrant foods, and went to the site of the stupa to make extensive offerings with great reverence and offer praise. He prostrated with his five limbs touching the ground, circumambulated it to the right, and kneeling for a long time with palms joined, made this aspiration:
"By all the roots of goodness from these offerings to the unsurpassed field of merit, may I, in every birth until the end of my life, be free from the signs of old age."
"O bhikṣus! That great queen of the king and the five hundred court ladies are none other than the present Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs."
By the power of this merit, even until this present life at the age of one hundred and twenty, he has been free from signs of old age, appearing like a sixteen-year-old maiden.
You bhikṣus, you should know that all of this is due to the power of their own karma, as explained extensively before; in this way, you should train yourselves.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Blessed One had established a rule that bhikṣus should not say "Long life! when seeing another person sneeze. In this city, there was a householder who, despite having married a wife, had no son or daughter.
As his years grew old and his wealth was exhausted, he said to his wife, "I am now advanced in age and have no offspring; I wish to leave the household life.
His wife said:
"As you wish. He then went at once to the Jetavana Grove and took ordination among the bhikṣus, receiving full admission (*upasampadā*).

Later, on another occasion, when the Buddha was proclaiming the essential Dharma to the great assembly, the elderly bhikṣu sat outside the crowd. His former wife suddenly arrived; when she heard her husband sneeze, not a single one of the bhikṣus wished to say [the blessing].

"Long life! Upon seeing this, his wife could not bear it; she took a handful of earth with her left hand, circumambulated the bhikṣu’s head from right to left, and cast it away while reciting a blessing for long life.
At that time, the bhikṣus all observed the matter; his wife seized him by the arm and reviled him with harsh words, saying:

"Noble son! For what reason have you now gone forth into homelessness among enemies? In this Jetavana there are always five hundred blue-clad yakṣas; it is by my incantations and aspirations that you have been granted long life."
"If you do not do so, you will certainly have your vital energy (ojas) sucked away by the yakṣa; you should not remain here, but ought to return home.
He then led him away by the hand.
At that time, the bhikṣus said:
"O mahallaka! Stay here and do not go!
But he was unwilling to stay, so the bhikṣu seized him by one arm and dragged him.
Then the mahallaka cried out:
"I am in pain! I am in pain!"
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You may ask the mahallaka:
'Which arm is in pain?'"
"Does the pain belong to the bhikṣu who is holding her,
or does it belong to the wife who is being held?
If you say the pain belongs to the bhikṣu who is holding her, then since his mind delights in going, let him go as he pleases."
"If you say it is painful because your wife is holding you, yet your mind dwells in pleasure, you should not let her go.
Then the bhikṣus questioned him as they had been told,
and he replied, "The arms held by you, sirs, are what are painful."
He then released him to go, whereupon he returned home; because this had become a great obstacle to his renunciation and full ordination (*upasampadā*), the Buddha said:
"Elder bhikṣus all delight in long life. When such persons sneeze, one should say: 'Long life!'"
"If one does not speak thus, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The setting of this episode is the same as before.
There was a householder who harbored right faith; he went to the Jeta Grove together with a certain Brahmin who lacked faith.
At that time, a faithful householder happened to sneeze, but the bhikṣus did not say, "May you live long.
Those who lacked faith wished him longevity and said:

"Venerable sir, you have now conceived a heart of respectful faith toward your enemies; for there are always five hundred blue-clad yakṣas in this Jetavana, and it is by my wishing 'may you live long' that you have been granted longevity."
"If it is not so, you will certainly have your vital energy (ojas) sucked away by the yakṣa.
You should not remain here long; you ought to depart at once.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Ordinary people all delight in long life.
When one sees someone sneeze, one should say:
'May you have long life.'"
If any bhikṣus see an elder sneeze, a junior should rise, perform a single prostration, and say:
"Vandāmi. If a junior sneezes, the senior should say: [“Āyuṣmān edhi”].
"I am free from illness.
If one does not do so, both shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
While the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, he established the five bhikṣus in the state of right determination.

Having gone forth into the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, they were still unable to understand how to receive food and drink, how to chew and eat, or the proper conduct of their movements and deportment; so they went together to inform the Buddha:
"What should be done in these matters?"
The Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus, there are five kinds of food that may be chewed:
first, roots; second, stalks; third, leaves; fourth, flowers; and fifth, fruits."
"There are five kinds of edible foods:
first, parched grain flour; second, cooked rice; third, wheat and bean porridge; fourth, fish and meat; and fifth, cakes.
Yet they still did not know with what to season them for flavor.
The Buddha said:
"One should consume it together with milk, curd, butter, honey, fish, meat, dried meat, and various vegetables.

If these are unavailable, one may eat it mixed with water; for as long as it provides moisture and flavor to sustain a person's physical strength and complexion, one will be able to cultivate wholesome qualities."
The summary verse for the eighth section of the second chapter says:
Installing door panels, knobs, and keyholes; Leather patches, central windows, and latticed doors;
Widening the interior, door pivots, and locks; Opening and closing must be done with a "sheep-claw" bolt.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus were constructing dwellings but did not know how to install doors. The Buddha said:
"Install doors."
Furthermore, they did not install a fan, which hindered their practice of tranquil concentration. The Buddha said, "Install a fan.
They did not install a door-bolt, making it difficult to open and close the door. The Buddha said:
"One should install a door-bolt and a keyhole.
When opening it made a noise, the Buddha said:
"A leather pad may be placed over the place where the sound occurs."
The interior of the room was dark; the Buddha said, "One should install windows.
When they were installed too low, they encountered difficulties from bandits; the Buddha said:
"One should not stay too low.
He then stayed at an extremely high level, and as before, the room was dark. The Buddha said:
"One should not stay too high or too low; one must stay in the middle."
When the bhikṣus were making it, they made it wide on the outside and narrow on the inside. The Buddha said:
"It should be made wide on the inside and narrow on the outside.
Birds and small birds entered it; the Buddha said:
“Spread the net.
Once the net was spread, they still did not install the window shutters; consequently, snakes, scorpions, and other creatures came into the rooms at night.
The Buddha said, “One should install window shutters.”
When it was blown open by the wind, the Buddha said:
"One should place a pivot on top and further install a bolt.
When it was difficult to open and close, the Buddha said:
"One should open and close it using a 'ram's hoof' staff.
It is made in the shape of a small iron fork, resembling a ram's hoof. The second section, the ninth subsection, summarizes in verse:
"The iron hammer and the iron spike, the iron shovel and the wooden hoe."
Five hundred hearths, stoves, and furnaces, as well as axes and chisels, were all permitted.
The occasion was at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Pilindavatsa was ill, and the bhikṣus came to inquire after him.
"Venerable sir, what ailment do you have?
He replied, "I am suffering from a rash caused by wind."
“Venerable sir, what medicine did you recently take?
He replied, “When I was previously ill, I placed a red-hot iron hammer into water in a jar; when I rubbed and washed my body with this decoction, I was immediately cured.”
“If that is so, why do you not do it now? He replied,
“The World-Honored One has not yet granted permission.”
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I now permit bhikṣus suffering from wind-disorders (vāta-roga) to wash their bodies with water heated by an iron hammer."
Having heard that the Buddha had granted permission, the bhikṣu heated the hammer but was unable to lift it. The Buddha said:
"You should tie it with an iron chain and pull it out once it has become hot."
The bhikṣus discarded the lock along with [the rest] into the fire; it became so hot that it could not be grasped. The Buddha said:

"Leave the lock outside and do not place it in the fire. Wrap it in a lump of clay near an iron hammer, grasp the cool part, pull it out, and place it in a basin of water; you may then use it as you wish."
When it was time to use it, the bhikṣus washed the hammer clean with soap powder and cow dung. The Buddha said:
"You should not wash it again; placing it in the fire makes it pure."
At that time, the bhikṣus first warmed the water for contact and afterwards warmed the pure water. The Buddha said:
"First warm the pure water, and afterwards warm the water for contact.
If you do not do so, you shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
The setting was as before. A bhikṣu came and asked Pilindavatsa, "Venerable sir, what illness do you have? He replied:
"I have such an illness.
[The other] asked, "Venerable sir, why do you not seek medical treatment? He replied:
"Venerable one!
Previously I kept a small medicinal ladle for warming [medicines], but now that it is lacking, my illness has increased. He asked:
"Why do you not keep one now?
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet granted permission."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"For a sick bhikṣu, I permit the possession of a warming-rod.
This occurred in Śrāvastī.
There was an elder who wished to construct a bathhouse for the Saṃgha; as the charcoal within it lay scattered here and there, the Buddha said:
"Gather it together in one place."
The bhikṣus did not know with what material to make a shovel.
The Buddha said: "Make it of iron."
After the Buddha had granted permission, the forest-dwelling bhikṣus were unable to obtain iron.
The Buddha said: "Make a hoe out of wood.
When it was then destroyed by fire, the Buddha said:
"One should mix cow dung with earth to make mud and apply it before using it.
The setting was as before.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu who was suffering from illness went to a physician and asked him:
“O virtuous one! I have such an illness; please provide a prescription for me.
The physician said:
"Noble one, it should be treated in this manner.
For the sake of boiling the medicine, that bhikṣu borrowed a cauldron from the householder and returned it after he had finished.
The householder said,
"I shall now give it to you, O Noble One.
The bhikṣu said:
"The Buddha has not yet granted permission," the householder said.
"If that is so, then place it on the ground and depart."
Then the bhikṣus informed the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said, "I permit you to accept them.
At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ, having heard that the Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to keep cauldrons, sent five hundred iron cauldrons.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know what to do.
The Buddha said:
"Distribute them to the bhikṣus in successive order."
After the Buddha had sent them out, the younger monks did not obtain any. The Buddha said, "You should give them earthenware cauldrons.
The circumstances were the same as before.

There was a bhikṣu who lay upon cold ground; his food and drink did not digest, so he went to a householder’s residence and borrowed a bed and mat to serve as bedding, whereupon his illness was immediately cured.
Having used it, he returned it;
the householder said, "I now give this to you, O Noble One. The bhikṣu said:
"The Buddha has not yet granted permission.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "Accept them."
At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ, having heard that the Buddha had permitted the bhikṣus to accept beds, immediately sent five hundred beds.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
The Buddha said:
"Distribute them to the bhikṣus in order.
The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who required a hearth; having borrowed one from a householder and returned it, the householder said, "I give this to the Noble One. The bhikṣu replied:
"The Buddha has not yet granted permission.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "Accept them."
At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ likewise sent five hundred stoves, proceeding in the same manner as before to distribute them to the bhikṣus in succession.
The setting of the narrative is the same as before.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu required an axe for dyeing his robes; having borrowed one from an elder, he returned it to him.
The elder said, "I give this to you, O Noble One."
The bhikṣus replied,
"The Buddha has not yet granted permission.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"For the sake of the great assembly, you should accept that axe.
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, a bhikṣu’s bed frame suddenly broke; he borrowed an adze from a householder, and having used it, returned it.
He said, "I shall give it to the Noble One.
[The Noble One] replied:
"The Buddha has not yet granted permission.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"For the sake of the great assembly, you should accept that [gift of] digging."
The summary verse for the tenth section of the second chapter states:
Permission for axes and three ladders; bamboo, wood, and rope according to the occasion;
the method for constructing a monastery by pouring down [water]; and the account of the causes and conditions concerning Nanda.
The setting is the same as before.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu’s bed leg suddenly broke. He needed an axe for repairs, so he borrowed one from a householder and returned it to the owner, as described in detail above, until: "for the sake of the Saṃgha, he should accept [the tool]."
The setting was as before.
While the Buddha was staying in the old garden of Mṛgāramātṛ, he permitted the bhikṣus to construct monasteries and caityas.
Once the bhikṣus had built them to be very high and large, they did not know by what means to ascend them.
The Buddha said,
"Make a ladder.
The bhikṣus did not know with what materials they should make it.
The Buddha said:
"Use three kinds of materials—
namely bamboo, wood, and cord— and you should make them as you please."
The setting was in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was afflicted by the suffering of illness. He went to a physician and asked him, "Venerable sir!
Such suffering from illness has beset my body; I pray you, grant me a prescription and medicine."
The physician said:
"Venerable One! You should receive a rectal enema; it will surely eliminate the ailment."
He replied, "The World-Honored One has not yet permitted it.
The physician said:
“The Great Master is compassionate; he will grant permission without doubt.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“If there is a cause of illness, I permit the administration of enemas.”
The setting is the same as before.
As the Buddha has taught:
"When constructing a monastery for bhikṣus, the monastic cells should be made five stories high."
The Buddha hall should be seven stories high, and the gate pavilion seven stories high.
If constructing a nunnery, the rooms should be three stories;
the Buddha hall [of the nunnery] should be five stories.
"The gatehouse has five stories.
The bhikṣus did not know how to ascend it.
The Buddha said:
"One may construct a winding path leading up from the corner beside the gate; there are three types of paths, namely: stone, wooden planks, and earth.

The bhikṣus did not understand this and constructed the lower level with wood, the middle level with earth, and the upper level with stone. Consequently, the upper part became heavy while the lower part was unstable, leading to its collapse. The Buddha said:
"The lower level should be made of stone, the middle level of earth, and the upper level of wood."
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle Ten;
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle Eleven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.

The remainder of the summary verse for the tenth section of the second gate: The Nanda因缘 (Nanda-avadāna), the setting of which was at the Veṇuvana (Many-Radical Tree Garden) in the city of Kapilavastu.

The World-Honored One had a younger brother named Nanda, whose body was like the color of gold and who possessed thirty of the marks of a great man; he was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha. His wife’s name was Sundarī; her appearance was so upright and elegant that she was rarely seen in the world, her radiant splendor being so transcendent that all people delighted in beholding her.
Nanda was so deeply entangled in and attached to her that he could not part from her for even a moment; his passionate love was so profound that he intended to remain until the end of his life.
The World-Honored One, perceiving that the time had come to transform him, dressed in the morning, took up his bowl, and with the Venerable Ānanda as his attendant, entered the city to beg for alms.

Next, he arrived at the entrance of Nanda’s gate and stood there; by the power of his great compassion, he emitted golden light, which illuminated the entire interior of Nanda’s residence so that it was all like gold.
At that time, Nanda thought to himself, "A light has suddenly shone; this must surely be the Tathāgata.
He sent a messenger out to look, who saw that the Buddha had arrived. The messenger immediately returned and informed Nanda, saying:
"The World-Honored One is at the gate.
Upon hearing these words, she immediately wished to go out quickly to welcome and pay homage to the World-Honored One.
At that moment, Sundarī thought to herself:
"If I let him go, the World-Honored One will certainly allow him to leave the household life.
Thereupon, he seized his robe and pulled him back, not letting him go out. Nanda said:
"You may release me for a moment so that I may pay my respects to the World-Honored One,
and I shall return immediately. Sundarī said,
"We must first make a pact before you may go as you please."
Having applied wet pigment to his forehead, he addressed him, saying:
"You must return before this mark has even dried; if you are late, you shall be fined five hundred pieces of gold."
Nanda replied, "So be it.
He immediately went to the entrance of the gate, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, took the Tathāgata’s bowl back into the house, filled it with excellent food, and brought it back to the entrance.
The World-Honored One then departed and gave it to Ānanda.

The World-Honored One manifested a sign not to let him take the bowl; as the Great Teacher Tathāgata was so majestic and venerable that [the bhikṣu] did not dare call him back, he again handed it to Ānanda.
Ānanda asked, "From whom did you obtain this bowl? He replied:
"I shall take it from the Buddha.
Ānanda said, "It would be appropriate to present it to the Buddha."
He replied, "I now dare not lightly disturb the Great Master.
He then followed him in silence.

When the Blessed One had arrived at the monastery and washed his hands and feet, he took his seat. Nanda brought a bowl to offer to the Blessed One; when the meal was finished, the Blessed One said to him: "Nanda!"
"Will you eat my leftovers?
He replied, "I will eat them."
The Buddha then gave it to him.
After Nanda had finished eating, the World-Honored One asked him:
"Are you able to leave the household life?"
He replied, “I have left the household life.

Since the Blessed One, while formerly practicing the path of a bodhisattva, had never disobeyed the commands of his parents, teachers, elders, or other venerable ones, he was now able to speak without contradiction; he then addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Shave off the hair and beard for Nanda.
He replied, "As the World-Honored One has instructed."
He immediately ordered a barber to shave his hair.
Having seen this, Nanda said to that man: "Do you know now?"
"I shall soon become a Wheel-Turning King; if you should dare to shave my hair so abruptly, I shall cut off your wrist.
He was struck with great terror, wrapped up his tools, and was about to take his leave and depart.
Then Ānanda went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha himself went to Nanda’s place and asked him:
“Nanda, will you not go forth into homelessness?”
He replied, "I am going forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One personally took a vessel of water and poured it over his head; the attendant then shaved him, whereupon [the youth] had this thought:
"I now respectfully offer myself to the World-Honored One; let me first go forth into homelessness, and in the evening I shall return home.
Having reached the evening, he set out along the road.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a great pit along his path. Upon seeing it, he thought to himself:
“Sundarī is far away! There is no way for me to go there;
if I continue to think of her now, I may even die. If my life remains, I shall depart at dawn.”
As he recalled Sundarī, he remained in a state of grief and distress throughout the entire night.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go and inform Nanda that he is to serve as the administrator of affairs."
He immediately went to report:
"The World-Honored One has appointed you as the administrator. He asked:
"What is meant by 'one who knows affairs,' and what kind of task do you wish to perform? He replied:
"You may oversee the various affairs within the monastery.
He asked: "How should this be done?"
He replied: "Venerable ones!

Generally, one who serves as the administrator (vaiyāvṛtyakara) should, when the bhikṣus have gone out to beg for alms, sprinkle and sweep the grounds of the monastery, take fresh cow dung and apply it cleanly in successive layers, maintain vigilant care so that nothing is lost, and report any matters requiring discussion to the Saṃgha."

If there are incense or flowers, they should be distributed among the community; the doors and gates should be closed at night and opened at dawn; the places for the large and small needs of nature must always be washed and wiped clean;
and if there are any damaged areas within the monastery, they should immediately be repaired.
Having heard these instructions, he replied:
"Venerable Sir!
I shall do everything exactly as the Buddha has said."
At that time, when it was time for the morning meal, the bhikṣus took up their robes and bowls and entered the city of Kapilavastu to beg for food.
Seeing that there was no one at the monastery, Nanda thought to himself:
"Once I have finished sweeping the ground, I shall return home."
He then proceeded to sweep the ground.
The World-Honored One, perceiving this through his supernormal power, caused the cleaned area to become filled once again with filth. He then thought:
"I shall only return home after I have removed this filth."
He emptied his basket and gathered up the filth until it was gone, whereupon he thought to himself, "I shall close the door and depart.
The World-Honored One then caused one door to be closed; as soon as it was finished, he closed another door, but that door would open again, which led him to feel distress.
He further thought to himself:
"Even if bandits were to damage this temple, what harm would it do?
When I become king, I shall build hundreds of thousands of fine temples that surpass these by many times."
"I should return home; if I travel by the main road, I fear I might encounter the World-Honored One.
Having thought this, he immediately set out upon a minor path.
The Buddha, knowing his thought, came along that same minor path.
Having seen the Buddha from afar, Nanda did not wish to meet him; however, there was a tree by the roadside with branches hanging low, so he hid himself beneath it.
The Buddha caused the branches of that tree to rise high upward, and his body became visible.
The Buddha asked Nanda, "Where have you come from?"
"You may follow me. Feeling shame, he followed the Buddha.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"Since he has conceived a deep attachment to his wife, it would be well to cause him to abandon her.
For the purpose of receiving him, [the Buddha] departed from the city of Kapilavastu and traveled to Śrāvastī; having arrived there, he stayed at the Park of Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ.

At that time, Visākhā Migāramātā heard that the Buddha had a younger brother named Nanda, whose body was golden in color and endowed with thirty of the marks of a great man, being four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha; she heard that he had come together with the Buddha, thinking, "I shall go for a moment to pay my respects, and perhaps I may see him."
At that time, during the morning meal hour, Nanda took up his robe and bowl and entered the city to beg for alms. Proceeding by stages, he came to the house of Mṛgāramātṛ.
When Viśākhā saw his deportment, his excellent physical marks, and his radiant appearance, which were unlike those of others, she immediately thought to herself:
"Is this not the younger brother of the Buddha?"

He immediately conceived pure faith and prostrated at her feet; as he reached out his hand, he felt her body was soft and supple. Since women possess the "poison of touch" that causes harm upon proximity, Nanda—being by nature full of desire—conceived a defiled mind, whereupon his semen was discharged and fell upon the head of Viśākhā.
The World-Honored One, having known this, transformed that impurity into *sugandha* (sandalwood) oil. Upon touching it with his hand and smelling it, he thought:
"For what reason is there such subtle and exquisite incense oil in this place?"
"This is the Buddha’s supernormal power that has transformed these fragrant objects.
Thereupon, he gave rise to a sense of rare wonder and leaping joy, and praised him, saying:
"Excellent, O Buddha!"
Excellent, Dharma! Excellent, Saṃgha!

You have well expounded the inconceivable Dharma and Vinaya, which are able to cause men such as this Nanda, who are addicted to desire, to cast themselves into the Buddha-dharma and exclusively cultivate the holy life.
At that time, Nanda felt remorse, thinking:
"Have I not perhaps committed an offense of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* class?
He informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Nanda has committed no offense.
If there is such a person with excessive desire, he should carry [the items] in a leather pouch; do not harbor any doubt.
When the Buddha said that one with excessive desire may keep a leather pouch, the bhikṣus did not know with what kind of hide it should be made.
The Buddha said:
"Three kinds of skins should be used:
those of sheep, deer, and mice."
He then used it raw, whereupon a foul odor arose. The Buddha said:
"It should be used after being cooked; once washed, dry it in the sun.
While drying it, he saw a woman and gave rise to lustful thoughts, whereby his semen was discharged, defiling his lower robe. The Buddha said:
"One should make two:
one for drying and one for wearing.
At that time, there were those with much semen whose skins became damp and spoiled; [the Buddha said], "One should place a cloth underneath and then apply sand or soil."
At that time, there were bhikṣus who wore [the robe] while eating and while circumambulating the caitya. The Buddha said:
"Take it off and place it in a secluded spot; having washed your hands clean, eat and pay your respects."
Later, on one occasion, Nanda was sitting upon a rock and, remembering Sundarī, he drew her likeness upon that very rock.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa passed by that place, saw the drawing on the rock, and asked: "Nanda!"
"What are you doing? He replied, "Venerable Sir!"
"I am painting the form of Sundarī.
He replied, "Venerable one!"
The Buddha has dispatched bhikṣus to perform two kinds of tasks:
first, the practice of meditative concentration; second, the recitation of the scriptures.
You, however, now abandon these to paint the likeness of a woman yourself.
Having heard this, he remained silent.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"When monks engage in painting, such faults as these arise."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The foolish man Nanda has been thinking of Sundarī and has painted her image.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should not paint images."
"The one who does so shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
When the bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had prohibited painting, they did not dare to apply scented ointments at the caityas.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "For what reason are scented ointments and fragrant mud not applied to the stūpas containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata, nor sprinkled upon the ground?"
Then Ānanda reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should smear it with fragrant mud as one pleases, but one must not paint the forms of sentient beings; whoever does so shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
"If one paints a corpse or makes an image of a skull, there is no offense.
The Buddha thought to himself that Nanda was foolish, deluded, and still harbored unrelenting affection for his wife; he should employ a skillful means to cause such thoughts to cease.
He then said to him, "Have you ever seen Mount Gandhamādana before?"
He replied, "I have not seen him.
[The other said,] "If that is so, then grasp the corner of my robe."

He immediately went to seize his robe; at that time, the World-Honored One, like a king of swans, ascended into the air and proceeded to Mount Gandhamādana. Leading Nanda along, he looked around to the left and right, and beneath a fruit tree, he saw a female monkey who was missing one eye, who then raised her face and gazed directly at the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to Nanda,
"Do you see this blind monkey?
Nanda replied to the Buddha:
“I see it. The Buddha said, “What do you think?”
"Compared to this blind monkey, who is more excellent: she or Sundarī?

He replied, "That Sundarī is of the Śākya clan; her beauty and grace are supreme like those of a celestial maiden, peerless in all the world. Compared to her, the monkey does not equal even one part in ten million billion."
The Buddha asked,
"Do you see the celestial palaces? He replied:
“I have not seen it.
“You may grasp the hem of my robe once more.
He immediately took hold of the robe, and they returned as the king of geese ascends into the realm of space to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. There, he addressed Nanda, saying:
“You may go and observe the superior locations of the celestial palaces.

Nanda then went to the Joyful Garden (Nandana), the Caitraratha Garden, the Vicitra Garden, the Saṃsṛṣṭa Garden, the Pārijātaka Tree, and the Sudharmā Hall; he thoroughly inspected all such celestial parks and gardens, including the places for sporting with flowers, fruits, and bathing pools, which were filled with extraordinary delights.

Next, he entered the city of Sudarśana, where he again beheld various kinds of drums, music, strings, and flutes producing subtle and exquisite sounds; the corridors and halls were spacious and well-ventilated, with couches and curtains elegantly arranged, and in every place, celestial maidens of wondrous beauty were enjoying themselves together.
Nanda surveyed everywhere until he saw a place where there were only celestial maidens and no celestial youths.
He then asked the celestial maidens:
"For what reason do other places have men and women living together, enjoying all manner of pleasures?"
"Why is it that you see only women and no men?

The goddess replied, "The World-Honored One has a younger brother named Nanda, who has left home to follow the Buddha and is devotedly practicing the pure life; after his life ends, he shall be reborn here."
"We shall wait for one another here.
Having heard this, Nanda leaped for joy and returned quickly to the place where the Buddha was.
The World-Honored One asked him:
“Have you seen the excellent and wondrous things of the devas?
He replied, “I have seen them.”
The Buddha asked,
"What did you see? He reported to the World-Honored One exactly what he had seen.
The Buddha said to Nanda,
"Do you see the celestial maidens? He replied:
“I have seen her.
“Compared to Sundarī, which of these celestial maidens is more exquisite? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
To compare Sundarī with this celestial maiden is like comparing a blind monkey within Mount Gandhamādana to Sundarī; she does not equal even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of her.”
The Buddha told Nanda:
"One who practices pure conduct enjoys such benefits; you should now resolutely cultivate the holy life, for you shall be reborn in heaven and experience this happiness."
Having heard this, he rejoiced and remained silent.
Then the Blessed One, together with Nanda, vanished from the celestial realm and arrived at the Jeta Grove.
At that time, Nanda was practicing the holy life while longing for the celestial palace; the Buddha, knowing his intention, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go and inform the bhikṣus: 'No one shall sit on the same seat as Nanda;

no one shall walk for meditation in the same place; no one shall hang their robes on the same pole; no one shall place their alms bowl or water flask in the same spot; and no one shall recite the scriptures in the same location.'"
Ānanda transmitted the Buddha’s instructions to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus carried them out exactly according to the holy command.
At that time, having seen that others would no longer associate with him, Nanda felt extreme shame and humiliation.
Later, on one occasion, while Ānanda and the bhikṣus were mending their robes in the Hall of Service, Nanda saw them and thought to himself:
"All these bhikṣus have abandoned me and are not in my company; yet since this Ānanda is my younger brother, how could he possibly hold me in such disregard?"
He then went and sat down with him.
At that moment, Ānanda quickly rose and moved away, whereupon he said: “Ānanda!
"The other bhikṣus may well be subject to such rejection, but you are my younger brother; why do you also hold me in disdain?
Ānanda replied, "That is indeed true.
However, your reverence follows a different path, while I follow another; for this reason, I avoid you."
He replied: "What is called my path? What is your way?"
He replied, "You practice the holy life seeking rebirth in heaven, whereas I seek parinirvāṇa to eliminate the taints of desire.
Upon hearing these words, he became all the more sorrowful and distressed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts, addressed Nanda, saying:
"Have you ever seen the hells? He replied:
“I have not seen him.
The Buddha said,
“You may grasp the corner of my robe.”
Nanda immediately went and took hold of it, whereupon the Buddha led him into the hells.
At that time, the World-Honored One stood to one side and said to Nanda:
"You may now go and observe the various hells."

Nanda departed immediately; first he saw the River of Ashes, and next he reached the Forest of Swords, the River of Excrement, and the River of Fire. Entering them to observe, he saw sentient beings undergoing various kinds of suffering: some had their tongues pulled out with tongs, their teeth extracted, or their eyes gouged out; sometimes they were being dismembered by saws, or their hands and feet hacked off with axes; sometimes their bodies were pierced with spears, beaten with clubs, or stabbed with lances; sometimes they were crushed with iron hammers, or molten copper was poured into their mouths; or they were climbing mountains of knives and trees of swords, being pounded in mortars or ground on stones, or enduring extreme agony upon copper pillars and iron beds; or he saw iron cauldrons where fierce fires boiled and surging flames of hot currents cooked sentient beings—such were the sights of suffering he beheld.

Furthermore, there was another great iron cauldron in which boiling water surged and bubbled, yet no sentient beings were within it. Seeing this, [the being] became distressed with fear and asked the wardens:
"For what reason and by what cause do all the other iron cauldrons cook sentient beings, while this cauldron alone is empty, merely boiling and surging?"

He replied, "The Buddha’s younger brother Nanda aspired only to be reborn in heaven by practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) with single-minded devotion; having been born in heaven and briefly experienced its pleasures, he will, at the end of his life there, enter this cauldron. For this reason, I have now lit the cauldron and am waiting for him."
Having heard this, Nanda was seized with great terror; the hair on his body stood on end and cold sweat broke out from him as he thought:
"If she were to know that I am Nanda, I would be born within a forked cauldron."
He immediately ran in haste to the place where the World-Honored One was.
The Buddha asked,
"Did you see the hells?"
Nanda, weeping with tears falling like rain and his voice choked with emotion, spoke in a faint whisper,
saying, "I have seen it. The Buddha said:
“What do you see? Nanda then reported to the World-Honored One everything exactly as he had seen it.
The Buddha said to Nanda:
"To aspire for the human realm or to seek rebirth in the heavens while diligently practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) involves such faults as these.
Therefore, you should now seek nirvana in order to practice the holy life; do not take pleasure in birth in the heavens and thereby undergo such arduous toil."
Having heard this, Nanda felt shame and remained silent, unable to respond.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts, emerged from the hell and went to the Jeta Grove, where he addressed Nanda and the bhikṣus, saying: "Within there are three impurities:
[the impurity of desire, the impurity of existence, and the impurity of ignorance]."
"That is to say: lust, hatred, and delusion. These are to be abandoned and these should be shunned; you must train yourselves accordingly.

At that time, not many days after the World-Honored One had been staying at the Jetavana Grove, he went with his retinue to the country of Campā to dwell by the Gaggarā Pond, desiring to transform sentient beings according to their conditions.
At that time, Nanda and five hundred bhikṣus also followed the Buddha to the place where the World-Honored One was; they all prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, saw that the assembly was seated, he addressed Nanda, saying:

"I have an essential teaching, excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, with skillful phrasing and meaning—a pure, complete, and pristine holy life—known as the *Mātṛgarbha-praveśa-sūtra* (The Sūtra on Entering the Mother’s Womb)."
"You should listen attentively, apply your mind with the utmost care, and reflect upon it well; I shall now speak for you.
Nanda replied, "So be it, World-Honored One; I wish and desire to hear it."
The Buddha told Nanda:
"Although there is the mother's womb, there are those who enter it and those who do not.
How does one undergo birth by entering the mother's womb?"

If the parents, with defiled minds, engage in sexual union, and the mother’s womb is pure and her menstrual period has arrived, and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) manifests before her, one should know that at that moment it is called "entering the mother's womb."
Within this context, the form of the aggregates (*skandha*) is of two kinds: first, having upright physical form; second, having an ugly countenance.

The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) beings of the hells have an ugly countenance like that of a charred stump; those of the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*) are smoke-colored; those of the hungry ghosts (*preta*) are water-colored; those of the human and celestial realms are gold-colored; and those of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are of a brilliant white color. As for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is fundamentally no intermediate state, because they lack physical form.

Sentient beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) may have two hands and two feet, or four feet, many feet, or even no feet at all; according to the place where they are to be reborn as a result of their prior karma, the intermediate state being assumes a form corresponding to that.

If one is to be born among the gods, the head of the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) is directed upward; for humans, animals, and hungry ghosts, it moves horizontally; and for those in the hells, the head is directed straight downward.
All intermediate state beings possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and travel through the air, as if observing their place of birth from afar with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Regarding the phrase "the arrival of the menstrual period," this refers to the time of conception. Nanda!

There are some women whose periods arrive after three days, or five days, or half a month, or a full month; others may wait for a long time depending on various conditions before their menses finally arrive.

If there are women whose bodies lack majesty and who undergo much hardship and suffering; whose appearance is ugly and who lack good food and drink; and whose menstrual periods, though they begin, quickly cease—just like dry ground that dries up immediately when water is sprinkled upon it.

If there is a woman whose body possesses majesty and always experiences peace and happiness, whose appearance is upright and graceful, who obtains excellent food and drink, and whose menstrual cycle does not cease quickly—just as moist ground is difficult to dry when sprinkled with water.
What constitutes non-entry?

If the father’s semen is emitted while the mother’s semen is not, or if the mother’s semen is emitted while the father’s semen is not, or if neither is emitted, in all such cases there is no entry into the womb.
If the mother is impure and the father is pure, or if the father is impure and the mother is pure, or if both are impure, conception does not occur.
Furthermore, if the mother’s birth canal is afflicted by wind-disorder (*vāta*), or by jaundice or phlegm (*pitta-kapha*), or by blood-disorders, fetal obstructions, or fleshy growths;
or if she has taken certain medicines, or suffers from *yava-udara* (barley-belly) or *pipīlikā-madhyama* (ant-waist) swellings, [conception likewise does not occur].

The womb may be diseased; or its birth canal may be shaped like the mouth of a camel, or like a many-branched tree, or like the head of a plow, or like a chariot pole, or like a rattan cane, or like a tree leaf, or like a grain of wheat awn;
or it may be deep at the bottom, or deep at the top, or unfit to serve as a vessel for the fetus, or constantly discharging blood.
Furthermore, if the womb is like flowing water; or if it is like a crow’s mouth, always open and never closing;
or if its upper and lower parts, as well as its four sides, are uneven in width; or if it is high in some places and low in others, or convex and concave;
or if it is internally infested with worms, decayed, or impure—if the mother possesses such defects, conception will not occur.

If the parents are noble while the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) is lowly, or if the intermediate state being is noble while the parents are lowly, in such cases as these, conception does not occur.

Even if both the parents and the intermediate state being are noble, if their karma is not in harmony, conception likewise does not occur. Furthermore, if the intermediate state being lacks the two types of desire—male and female—toward the prospective parents, it will not undergo rebirth.
"Nanda! How does the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) enter the mother’s womb?

If the mother’s womb is pure, and the being of the intermediate state perceives the act of desire before him, and there are no many aforementioned faults and afflictions, and if the parents and the child possess karma that calls forth mutual affinity, only then does he enter the mother’s womb."

Furthermore, when that intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) is about to enter the womb, its mind becomes inverted: if it is male, it conceives love for the mother and hatred for the father; if it is female, it conceives love for the father and hatred for the mother. Regarding the various karmas created in past lives, it gives rise to deluded thoughts and false perceptions, imagining coldness, or imagining great winds, heavy rains, and clouds and mist, or hearing the clamor of a great crowd. Having formed these perceptions, according to the superiority or inferiority of its karma, it further gives rise to ten kinds of false conceptions.

What are the ten? "I am now entering a house; I wish to ascend a tower; I am mounting a terrace or palace; I am mounting a couch or seat; I am entering a grass hut; I am entering a leaf shed; I am entering a thicket of grass; I am entering a forest; I am entering a hole in a wall; I am entering the space between a fence."
Nanda! At that time, having formed this thought, the intermediate state being enters the mother’s womb.
You should know that what is called "receiving the womb" is named *kalala*.

The father’s semen and the mother’s blood are not other substances; rather, through the causal condition of the union of the parents’ semen and blood, they abide as the objective support and basis for consciousness. This is like the production of ghee from curd when it is placed in a vessel and churned by human effort without ceasing; otherwise, it would not arise.
You should know that the impure semen and blood of the parents, as well as the *kalala* body, are likewise so.
Furthermore, Nanda!
There are four similes; you should listen well!

Just as a worm arises depending upon green grass—the grass is not the worm, yet the worm is not separate from the grass—so too, by the conjunction of causes and conditions based upon the grass, the worm arises and its body becomes green.
Nanda, you should know!
The body of the *kalala*, formed from the father’s semen and the mother’s blood, is likewise so: through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the great elements and the sense-faculties arise.

It is like a worm that arises depending on cow dung; the dung is not the worm, nor does the worm exist apart from the dung, yet by depending on the dung and through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the worm is born with a yellow-colored body.
Nanda, you should know!

The body of the *kalala*—formed from the father’s semen and the mother’s blood—is likewise thus: through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the sense-faculties (*indriya*) arise.

It is like a worm born depending on a jujube fruit; the jujube is not the worm, yet the worm does not exist apart from the jujube. Nevertheless, by depending upon the jujube and through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the worm is born and its body becomes red in color.
Nanda, you should know!

It is the same with the *kalala* body formed from the father’s semen and the mother’s blood: through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the sense-faculties (*indriya*) arise.
Just as when worms arise from curd, their bodies appear white, and so on in detail until: through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the great elements and the sense-faculties arise.
Furthermore, Nanda!

Depending upon the impurity of the parents—the *kalala*—the earth element manifests with the nature of solidity; the water element manifests with the nature of moisture; the fire element manifests with the nature of warmth; and the wind element manifests with the nature of lightness and movement.

Nanda! If the impure *kalala* body produced by the parents possessed only the earth element and lacked the water element, it would immediately dry up and completely disperse, just like a handful of dry flour or ashes.
If there were only the water element and no earth element, it would immediately disperse like a drop of oil upon water.
Because of the water element, the earth element does not scatter; because of the earth element, the water element does not flow away.

Nanda! If the kalala-body possessed the earth element and the water element but lacked the fire element, it would immediately rot and decay, just like a lump of flesh kept in the shade during the summer months.
Nanda! If the *kalala* body possessed only the earth, water, and fire elements but lacked the wind element, it would be unable to grow and expand.

All of these arise through the mutual interaction of causes from prior karma and conditions that mutually induce one another, whereby consciousness is able to take birth. The earth element is able to support, the water element is able to cohere, the fire element is able to mature, and the wind element is able to cause growth.

Nanda! It is just as when someone or their disciple prepares granulated sugar and blows upon it with their breath to cause it to expand; its interior becomes hollow like that of a lotus root. In the same way, the internal great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—increase through the power of karma.

Nanda! It is not that the impurities of the parents alone constitute the *kalala* (embryonic mass), nor is it produced by the mother’s womb alone, nor by karma alone, nor by causes alone, nor by conditions alone. Rather, it is only through the convergence of all these various conditions that the embryo first comes to be. It is like a fresh seed that has not been damaged by wind or sun; being solid, without holes, well-preserved, and properly stored, when sown in fertile soil with moisture, and through the convergence of these causes and conditions, there subsequently arise sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit, growing in succession.
Nanda! This seed does not produce sprouts and so forth apart from the convergence of conditions.
Thus it should be understood:

It is not that the embryo arises solely from the parents, nor merely through karma and other conditions; rather, it is only through the conjunction of the causal conditions of the parents' semen and blood that the embryo comes to be.
Nanda! It is like a person with clear vision who, seeking fire, places a sun-crystal gem in the sunlight and positions dry cow dung above it; then fire is produced.
Thus it should be understood:

depending on the causal conjunction of the parents' semen and blood, there is then birth from a womb; the impurity of the parents forms the *kalala*, which is designated as "form" (*rūpa*), while sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness constitute its "name" (*nāma*); these together are called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
I do not praise this collection of aggregates, this loathsome name-and-form that takes birth in the various realms of existence, even for a mere fraction of a moment. Why is this?
To be born within the various realms of existence is great suffering; it is like excrement and filth, which is foul-smelling even in small amounts.
Thus it should be understood: even the slightest existence within the realms of rebirth is called suffering.
These five aggregates of clinging—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—all possess arising, abiding, growth, and decay.
Birth is itself suffering; abiding is itself illness; and growth and decay are themselves old age and death.
Therefore, Nanda, who would find a relish for the ocean of existence, lying within the mother’s womb and undergoing such intense suffering?
"Furthermore, Nanda! You should know this:
for any being who enters the womb, speaking in general terms, it is thirty-eight seven-day periods."

During the first seven days, the embryo resides within the mother’s womb like a wedge or an abscess, lying amidst filth as if in a cauldron. The body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) dwell together in one place, scorched by a fierce heat and undergoing extreme suffering. This stage is called *kalala*, appearing like rice gruel or curdled milk; within these seven days, it is boiled by internal heat, and the solid nature of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), the moist nature of the water element (*ab-dhātu*), the warm nature of the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*), and the mobile nature of the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*) only then begin to manifest.

"Nanda! During the second week, the embryo dwells in the mother’s womb, lying amidst filth as if inside a cauldron. The body-faculty and consciousness abide together in one place, scorched by intense heat and undergoing extreme suffering. Within the mother’s womb, a wind arises spontaneously called ‘Pervasive Contact’ (samsparsa), produced by prior karma; when it touches that embryo, it is termed ‘Arbuda,’ resembling thick curd or solidified butter. During this week, it is boiled by internal heat, and the four elements become manifest."

"Nanda! During the third seven-day period, as explained in detail previously, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called 'Sword-Sheath-Mouth' (Kṣuramukha), produced by prior karma. When it touches that embryo, it is called 'Closed Fleshy Lump' (Peśī); its shape is like an iron chopstick or an earthworm, and during these seven days, the four elements become manifest."

"Nanda! On the fourth seventh-day period, as explained in detail previously, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called 'Internal Expansion' (Antar-mukha), produced by prior karma. This wind blows upon and strikes the embryo—known as the 'Kunapa'—which is shaped like a sandalwood block or a warm stone. During this seventh day, the four elements become manifest."

"Nanda! Regarding the fifth seven-day period, as explained in detail previously, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called 'Upholder' (*saṃgrāhaka*). When this wind touches the embryo, five features appear: namely, the two arms, the two thighs, and the head. Just as when sweet rain falls from the heavens in springtime, the forests flourish and their branches grow, so too do these five features become manifest."

"Nanda! In the sixth week, there is a wind within the mother’s womb called 'Vast' (Mahā). When this wind touches the embryo, four features appear, namely the two elbows and the two knees. Just as sprouts and branches grow when rain falls in springtime, these four features likewise manifest."

"Nanda! In the seventh week, there is a wind within the mother’s womb called 'Whirling. When this wind touches the embryo, four features appear: namely, the two hands and the two feet. These four features are like a mass of foam or like water-moss."

"Nanda! In the eighth week, there is a wind within the mother’s womb called ‘Turning. When this wind touches the embryo, twenty signs appear: namely, the ten fingers of the hands and feet first emerge from it, like tree roots newly sprouting after a fresh rain."

"Nanda! In the ninth week, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called ‘Disperser. When this wind touches the embryo, nine features appear: namely, the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, along with the mouth and the two lower orifices."

"Nanda! On the seventeenth day, there is a wind within the mother’s womb called 'Hardening' (*kaṭhina*), which makes the embryo firm and solid. Then, on this seventh week, there is a wind within the mother’s womb called 'Universal Gate' (*samanta-mukha*); this wind blows upon and distends the fetal sac, just as a leather float is filled with air."

"Nanda! During the eleventh week, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called 'Pervading' (*sūcaka*). When this wind touches the embryo, it causes the embryo to become permeated, and nine apertures appear. As the mother walks, stands, sits, lies down, or performs various activities, that wind circulates and opens them up, gradually causing the apertures to enlarge."

If the wind moves upward, the upper orifice opens; if it moves downward, it passes through the lower cavity. It is like a blacksmith or his apprentice who, when fanning with a bellows, causes air to flow both upward and downward; once the wind has performed its function, it immediately vanishes.

"Nanda! In the twelfth week, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called 'Curved Mouth. This wind blows upon the embryo, forming the large and small intestines on the left and right sides like lotus fibers; thus they remain interlaced throughout the body."

During these same seven days, there arises a wind called "Hair-Piercer" (*keśa-vyūha*), which forms one hundred and thirty joints within that embryo without increase or decrease; furthermore, through the power of this wind, it creates one hundred and one points of restriction (*maryādā*).

"Nanda! In the thirteenth week, by the power of the aforementioned winds within the mother’s womb, the embryo becomes aware of hunger and thirst; when the mother eats and drinks, whatever flavors there are enter through the navel and serve to sustain its body."

"Nanda! In the fourteenth week, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called 'Needle-Mouth. This wind causes the fetus to develop one thousand sinews: two hundred and fifty in the front of the body, two hundred and fifty in the back, two hundred and fifty on the right side, and two hundred and fifty on the left side."

"Nanda! In the fifteenth week, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called ‘Lotus,’ which is able to produce twenty kinds of vessels for the embryo to absorb various nutrients. There are five in front of the body, five behind, five on the right side, and five on the left side. These vessels have various names and various colors; they may be named ‘Companion,’ ‘Strength,’ or ‘Power. As for their colors, they include blue, yellow, red, white, the color of beans, ghee, oil, curd, and so forth, with many other colors intermingling together."

Nanda! Each of those twenty vessels has forty subsidiary vessels as its retinue, totaling eight hundred inhalation vessels, with two hundred each located in front, behind, to the left, and to the right of the body.
"Nanda! Each of these eight hundred channels has one hundred subsidiary channels connected to it as its retinue, totaling eighty thousand.
There are twenty thousand in the front, twenty thousand in the back, twenty thousand on the right, and twenty thousand on the left."
