Nanda! These eighty thousand channels further possess numerous apertures—some with one aperture, some with two, and so on up to seven—each of which is connected to the pores of the skin, just as the root of a lotus has many internal cavities.

"Nanda! In the sixteenth seventh-day period [of gestation], there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called Amṛtagati (Nectar-Walker). This wind, acting as a skillful means, establishes the locations for the two eyes of the embryo; likewise, it establishes the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, the throat, and the chest, providing a place for food to be stored when it enters, and enabling the passage of incoming and outgoing breath."

For example, it is like a potter or his apprentice who takes a fine lump of clay and places it upon a wheel, arranging it according to the shape and form of the vessel he intends to produce, ensuring there is no discrepancy.

This is due to the winds of karma which are able to effect such things, arranging [the faculties] in the locations of the eyes and so forth according to their respective capacities, even to the point of ensuring that the inhalation and exhalation of breath pass through without error.

"Nanda! In the seventeenth week, there arises within the mother's womb a wind called 'Whisker-Mouth. This wind is able to make the locations of the fetus's eyes, ears, nose, mouth, throat, chest, and the passages for food and drink smooth and slippery, thereby establishing the places through which the inhalation and exhalation of breath pass."
It is like a skilled artisan, or a man or woman, who takes a mirror covered in dust and grime, and cleans it by rubbing it with oil and ash or fine earth until it is pure.
In this same way, through the wind of karma, such things are produced and arranged in their respective places without any obstruction.

"Nanda! In the eighteenth week, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called 'Stainless' (*vimala*), which renders the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) of the embryo pure. It is like the orbs of the sun and moon when they are shrouded by great clouds; suddenly a fierce wind arises, blowing the clouds apart in all directions so that the luminous orbs become clear."
"Nanda! By the power of these karmic winds, the six sense faculties of the embryo are purified in this very same way. Nanda!"
In the nineteenth week, within the mother’s womb, the fetus brings four faculties to completion:
the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue; at the time of entering the mother’s womb, it first acquires three faculties, namely the body, life, and mind.

"Nanda! On the twenty-seventh day, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called 'Solid' (*dṛḍha*). This wind produces twenty bones for the phalanges of the toes of the left foot, and likewise twenty bones for the right foot; four bones for the heels, two bones for the shins, two bones for the knees, two bones for the thighs, three bones for the pelvic sockets, eighteen bones for the spine, and twenty-four bones for the ribs."

Furthermore, based on the left hand, twenty bones are produced in the finger joints; likewise, based on the right hand, twenty are produced. There are two bones in the wrists, four bones in the forearms, seven bones in the chest, seven bones in the shoulders, four bones in the neck, and two bones in the jaw. There are thirty-two bones in the teeth and four bones in the skull.
Nanda! It is like a sculptor or his apprentice who first uses a stiff wooden frame to create the basic form, then wraps it with cords, and finally applies clay to complete the image.
The arrangement of the various bones by the power of this karmic wind is likewise so.
Among these, there are two hundred large bones, excluding the other smaller bones. "Nanda!

In the twenty-first week, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called "Arising" (*utthāna*), which causes flesh to develop upon the body of the embryo. It is just as a mason first prepares clay well and then applies it to a wall; the production of flesh by this wind is exactly like that.
"Nanda! In the twenty-second week, there is a wind within the mother’s womb called *phalgu*; this wind is able to cause blood to arise in the embryo."
"Nanda! In the twenty-third week, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called Viśodhaka (Pure-Sustainer); this wind is able to cause the fetus to develop skin."
"Nanda! In the twenty-fourth week, there is a wind within the mother's womb called *Vivardhana*; this wind can cause the skin of the embryo to become radiant and smooth."

"Nanda! In the twenty-fifth week, there is a wind within the mother’s womb called 'City-Sustainer' (Dhāraṇī-pura). This wind is able to cause the blood and flesh of the embryo to become moistened and nourished."

"Nanda! In the twenty-sixth week, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called 'Producer' (janaka), which causes hair, body hair, and nails to grow upon the fetus; all of these are individually connected by way of the vessels."

"Nanda! In the twenty-seventh week, there is a wind within the mother's womb called 'Curved Medicine' (Kuṭaja). This wind is able to cause the hair, body hair, and nails of the embryo to be fully formed."

"Nanda! Because this embryo previously committed evil karma—being stingy and miserly toward all wealth and property, stubbornly clinging to it and refusing to give in charity, and disregarding the instructions of parents and teachers—it created unwholesome karma through body, speech, and mind, which has increased day and night; thus, it shall now receive this retribution."

If one is born among humans, all the karmic fruits obtained will be contrary to one's wishes: what the people of the world consider long and desirable, for them it is short; what they consider short and desirable, for them it is long; what they consider coarse and desirable, for them it is fine; what they consider fine and desirable, for them it is coarse; what they consider close-set in its joints and desirable, for them it is widely spaced; what they consider widely spaced and desirable, for them it is close-set; what they consider many and desirable, for them it is few; what they consider few and desirable, for them it is many; those who love fatness become thin, and those who love leanness become fat; those who love timidity become courageous, and those who love courage become timid; those who love whiteness become black, and those who love blackness become white.
Nanda! Furthermore, due to evil karma one incurs an evil retribution:

being deaf, blind, mute, dull-witted, and ugly; the sounds one utters are unpleasant for others to hear; one’s hands and feet are cramped and withered, and one’s form resembles that of a hungry ghost (preta); all one’s relatives detest and do not wish to see one, let alone other people.
When one speaks of all three types of karma to others, they do not believe or accept it, nor do they take it to heart.
Why is this? It is because they have obtained such retribution due to the various evil karmas they created in previous lives.

"Nanda! Because that fetus previously cultivated meritorious deeds—being fond of giving and free from stinginess, feeling compassion for the poor and destitute, and having no mind of attachment or parsimony toward wealth and possessions—the wholesome karma he created increases day and night, and he shall receive a superior retribution."

If born among humans, all the retributive fruits one receives will be entirely to one’s satisfaction: if the people of the world prefer the tall, one shall be tall; if they prefer the short, one shall be short. One’s proportions will be harmonious, the limbs and joints well-suited, and whether in quantity, build, courage, timidity, or complexion, there will be nothing that is not pleasing. With the six sense faculties complete and a countenance so upright it surpasses all others, with clear eloquence and a melodious voice, one will possess all the marks of a superior person, bringing joy to all who behold them.
Whenever he speaks of his three types of karmic actions to others, they all believe and accept them, keeping them respectfully in mind.
Why is this? It is because he has obtained such a retribution by having performed various wholesome karmas in previous lives.
"Nanda! If the fetus is male, it remains crouching against the mother’s right flank, with both hands covering its face as it stays facing her spine.

If it is female, it remains crouching against the mother’s left flank, with both hands covering its face as it stays facing her abdomen. It is situated below the raw organs (āmāśaya) and above the digested organs (pakvāśaya); the raw matter presses down upon it from below while the digested matter pierces it from above, like one who is bound at five points and impaled upon a sharp stake."

If the mother eats too much or at times too little, she suffers distress; likewise, if she eats what is excessively greasy or dry, extremely cold or hot, salty, bland, bitter, or sour, or if it is too sweet or pungent—when eating such things, she experiences pain and suffering.

If the mother engages in sexual desire, or walks hurriedly, or at times sits in a precarious posture, or remains seated for a long time, or lies down for a long time, or leaps about, [the fetus] experiences suffering in all such instances.
Nanda, you should know this!
While dwelling within the womb, one's body is oppressed by all such various sufferings as these, which cannot be fully described.
If such suffering is experienced even within the human realm, how much more so the hardships of the evil destinies and the hells, which are beyond comparison?
Therefore, Nanda! What wise person would delight in dwelling within the boundless ocean of suffering that is birth and death, undergoing such calamities and hardships?
"Nanda! [he said].
In the twenty-eighth week, within the mother’s womb, the fetus gives rise to eight kinds of perverted perceptions.
What are these eight?

They are the perception of a house, the perception of a vehicle, the perception of a garden, the perception of a multi-storied pavilion, the perception of a grove of trees, the perception of a couch, the perception of a river, and the perception of a pond; yet in reality these do not exist, and it falsely generates such conceptual discriminations.

"Nanda! In the twenty-ninth week, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called 'Flower-Striped' (*puṣpāgra*). This wind blows upon the embryo, causing its complexion to become bright, white, and pure; or, by the power of karma, it may cause the color to be dark brown, or perhaps blue, or various other miscellaneous hues. It may also cause the body to become dry and devoid of moisture, with white light or black light emerging according to the respective colors."

"Nanda! On the thirty-seventh day, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called 'Iron Mouth. This wind can blow upon the fetus's hair, body hair, and nails, causing them to grow. The various white and black lusters all manifest according to karma, as previously described."
"Nanda! In the thirty-first week, the embryo within the mother’s womb gradually grows larger.
Thus, through the thirty-second, thirty-third, and up to the thirty-fourth week, it continues to increase and expand."
"Nanda! In the thirty-fifth week, the child’s limbs and body parts are fully formed within the mother’s womb. Nanda!"
In the thirty-sixth week, the child no longer delights in remaining within the mother’s womb. "Nanda!
In the thirty-seventh week, while still in the mother’s womb, the embryo gives rise to three kinds of non-perverted perceptions:
These are what are called the perception of impurity, the perception of foulness, and the perception of darkness; these are taught according to one aspect. "Nanda!

In the thirty-eighth week, there arises within the mother's womb a wind called 'Blue Flower. This wind is able to cause the fetus to turn its head downward, extend both arms, and move toward the birth canal."

Next, there is another wind called "Descending," which, by the power of karma, blows upon the embryo, causing the head to turn downward and the two feet upward, so that it is about to emerge from the birth canal.

Nanda! If that fetus has committed various evil deeds in previous lives and caused the destruction of another's human embryo, then by reason of these causes and conditions, when it is about to emerge, its hands and feet will become crossed and disordered, and it will be unable to turn over; thus, it shall meet its end within the mother’s womb.

At that time, there may be a wise woman or a skilled physician who applies warm ghee, elm-bark juice, or other slippery substances to her hands. She then takes a thin blade as sharp as a needle’s point between her middle fingers and thrusts it into a pit like a cesspool—dark, foul-smelling, filthy, and loathsome—which is the constant dwelling place of immeasurable worms. From this place, where putrid fluids flow constantly and where semen and blood are rotted to a state deeply loathsome, covered only by a thin skin over the sores of a body of evil karma, she pushes her hand in and uses the sharp blade to cut the child’s body into pieces and pull them out one by one.

Because of this, his mother experienced what was displeasing to her; she suffered extreme pain and hardship and consequently passed away, or even if she had survived, it would have been no different from death. Nanda!
Nanda! If that fetus is moved by the ripening of wholesome karma, even if it is positioned inverted, it will not harm its mother; it will emerge safely and without undergoing suffering or hardship.

If one does not encounter such calamities as these in ordinary circumstances, yet reaches the thirty-eighth seven-day period and is about to give birth, the mother undergoes great suffering; her life is nearly extinguished before she can finally deliver the fetus.
"Nanda! You should examine this thoroughly and seek liberation.
*Vinayakṣudrakavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*, Fascicle Eleven.
The Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume Twelve.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The Tenth Section of the Second Gate: A Summary Verse on the Remainder of the Causes and Conditions of Nanda.

The Buddha told Nanda: "All those born from a womb experience extreme suffering and distress. At the moment of birth—whether male or female—they fall into human hands; they may be wrapped in cloth and placed in the sunlight, or in a shaded place, or set in a cradle, or placed upon a bed, mat, or within one’s embrace. Through these causes and conditions, they all undergo bitter, agonizing, and most excruciating pain."

"Nanda! It is like an ox whose hide has been flayed; if it stays near a wall, it is eaten by the insects living in the wall; if it stays near trees or grass, it is eaten by the insects in the trees and grass; if it dwells in an open space, it is bitten and eaten by various insects—and thus it suffers affliction. At birth, one is exactly like this."

They are made to suffer great agony by being washed with warm water; like a leper whose skin has rotted away and from whom pus and blood flow profusely, they are further subjected to the extreme pain of being beaten with clubs and whips.
After being born from the physical body, one grows by drinking the mother's blood and impurities; what is called "blood and impurities" in the Noble Dharma and Vinaya is, in fact, breast milk, Nanda!

Since there is such boundless and extreme suffering here, with not a single thing to be enjoyed, what wise person would give rise to attachment for this ocean of suffering, constantly transmigrating without rest?
Seven days after birth, there are already eighty thousand families of worms within the body that devour it from all sides. Nanda!
There is one family of worms called "Hair-Eaters" (Keśāda) which dwells at the roots of the hair and constantly feeds upon the hair.
There are two species of worms:
the first is named Staff-Store (*daṇḍasaṃcaya*), and the second is named Coarse-Head (*sthūlaśiras*). They dwell upon the head and constantly feed upon it.
There is another species of worm named Eye-Circler (*pariveṣaka*), which dwells upon the eye and constantly feeds upon the eye.
There are four types of worms:
the first is named Expeller, the second is named Runner, the third is named Dwelling, and the fourth is named Complete; they reside in the brain and constantly feed upon it.
There is a species of worm called "Rice-Leaf" that dwells in the ear and feeds on the ear.
There is a species of worm called "Treasury-Mouth" that dwells in the nose and feeds on the nose.
There are two species of worms:
One type is named *Dūrapāta* (Far-Thrower) and the second is named *Sarvapāta* (All-Thrower); they dwell on the lips and feed upon the lips.
There is one type of worm named *Madhupatra* (Honey-Leaf); it dwells on the teeth and feeds upon the teeth.
There is one type of worm named *Kāṣṭhamukha* (Wood-Mouth); it dwells at the roots of the teeth and feeds upon the roots of the teeth.
There is a species of worm called Needle-Mouth that dwells on the tongue and feeds upon the tongue.
There is another species of worm called Sharp-Mouth that dwells at the base of the tongue and feeds upon the root of the tongue.
There is a species of worm called *Hastavartā* that dwells in the palate and feeds upon the palate.
Furthermore, there are two species of worms:
the first is named *Hastajāla* and the second is named *Ardhapuṭa*; these dwell in the palms of the hands and feed upon the palms.
There are two types of worms:
the first is named Short-Hanging, and the second is named Long-Hanging; they dwell in the wrist and feed upon the wrist.
There are two other types of worms:
The first is named Dūrabāhu (Far-Arm) and the second is named Antikabāhu (Near-Arm); they dwell in the arms and feed upon the arms.
There are two types of worms:
the first is named Jighatsa (Desire-to-Swallow) and the second is named Jighatsita (Already-Swallowed); they dwell in the throat and feed upon the throat. There are two further types of worms:
There is one named "With Enmity" and another named "Great Enmity," which dwell in the chest and feed upon the chest.
There are two types of worms:
one named "Conch Shell" and another named "Conch Mouth," which dwell in the flesh and feed upon the flesh.
There are two types of worms:
the first is named *varṇavān* (Possessing Color) and the second is named *balavān* (Possessing Strength); they dwell in the blood and feed upon the blood.
There are another two types of worms:
The first is named Brave and Strong (*Vīryavanta*), and the second is named Fragrant Mouth (*Gandhamukha*); they dwell in the sinews and feed on the sinews.
There are two species of worms:
the first is named Not High (*Anunnata*), and the second is named Downward-Mouthed (*Adhomukha*); they dwell in the spine and feed on the spine.
There are two species of worms, both named *vasa-varṇā* (fat-colored), which dwell in the fat and feed upon the fat.
There is one species of worm named *pīta-varṇā* (yellow-colored), which dwells in the yellow [bile] and feeds upon the yellow.
There is one species of worm named *muktikā* (pearl), which dwells in the kidneys and feeds upon the kidneys.
There is a class of worms called Great Pearl (*mahā-muktikā*), which reside in the waist and feed on the waist.
There is a class of worms called Not-Yet-Arrived (*anāgata*), which reside in the spleen and feed on the spleen.
There are four classes of worms:
The first is named Water-Life, the second Great Water-Life, the third Needle-Mouth, and the fourth Knife-Mouth; they dwell in the intestines and feed upon the intestines.
There are five classes of worms:
the first is named Full Moon, the second Moon-Face, the third Radiance, the fourth Radiant-Face, and the fifth Dwelling-Apart; they dwell on the right flank and feed upon that flank.
Furthermore, there are five types of worms whose names are the same as those mentioned above; they dwell on the left flank and feed upon that flank.
Furthermore, there are four types of worms:
the first is named Fore-piercer, the second Rear-piercer, the third Hard-piercer, and the fourth Dweller-in-piercing; they dwell in the bones and feed upon the bones.
There are four types of worms:
the first is named Great White, the second Small White, the third Heavy Clouds, and the fourth Foul Odor; they dwell in the vessels and feed upon the vessels.
There are four types of worms:
the first is named Lion, the second Power-Endowed, the third Swift Arrow, and the fourth Lotus; they dwell in the stomach and feed upon the stomach.
There are two types of worms:
the first is named Anzhi (Settled Intent) and the second is named Jinzhi (Proximate Intent); they reside in the matured receptacle and feed upon the matured receptacle.
There are four other types of worms:
The first is named Salt-Mouth, the second Heap-Mouth, the third Net-Mouth, and the fourth Sparrow-Mouth; these dwell in the urinary tract, feeding on urine.
There are four types of worms:
the first is named Should-Be-Done, the second Great-Doer, the third Small-Form, and the fourth Small-Bundle; these dwell in the intestinal tract, feeding on feces.
There are two species of worms:
the first is named Black Mouth, and the second is named Large Mouth; they dwell in the thighs and feed upon the thighs.
There are two other species of worms:
One type is named *Lai* (The Leper), and another is named *Xiaolai* (The Lesser Leper); they dwell upon the knees and feed upon the knees.
There is a class of worms named *Yugen* (Dull Root); they dwell upon the shins and feed upon the shins.
There is a class of worms named *Hei jiang* (Black Neck); they dwell upon the feet and feed upon the feet.

"Nanda! This body is truly loathsome and should be viewed with revulsion; within such a physical form, there are always eighty thousand families of worms that consume it day and night, causing the body to suffer from feverish distress, emaciation, exhaustion, hunger, and thirst."

Furthermore, Nanda, the mind may be beset by various kinds of suffering, affliction, sorrow, and despondency; many diseases manifest, and there is no skilled physician capable of providing a cure. Nanda!
Within this great ocean of birth and death, there are such sufferings as these; how could one find joy or delight therein?

Furthermore, one is seized by various deities and diseases—namely, those possessed by the eight classes of spirits such as devas and nāgas, as well as by ghosts and spirits up to the kaṭapūtanas, and other spirits of birds and beasts—or one is afflicted by the sun, moon, and stars. These spirits and ghosts cause various illnesses that oppress and torment both body and mind, beyond what can be fully described.
The Buddha told Nanda:
"Who would take pleasure in the cycle of birth and death, entering the mother’s womb to undergo such extreme suffering?
Thus one is born, thus one grows, drinking the mother’s milk and blood while falsely conceiving thoughts of deliciousness, and through various foods and drinks gradually reaching maturity."
Suppose one’s body attains peace and freedom from illness, with food, clothing, and comforts provided at will, and one lives to a full hundred years; yet within this life, half is spent in sleep.

First as an infant, then as a youth, and gradually reaching maturity, one is beset by sorrow, grief, calamities, and myriad diseases. The countless hundreds of sufferings that afflict the body are difficult to describe in their entirety; when the various internal pains become unbearable, one no longer wishes to remain alive and instead seeks death.
Such a body has much suffering and little joy; though it may abide for a time, it must inevitably perish.
Nanda! All who are born must die; nothing remains forever.
Even if one sustains life through medicine and food and manages to extend one's years, in the end one cannot escape being slain by the King of Death and sent to the empty field.

Therefore, you should know that birth has nothing to be delighted in; you ought to diligently accumulate the provisions for future lives and not be negligent. Exert yourself in cultivating the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and do not be indolent. Constantly delight in practicing all beneficial deeds, righteous deeds, meritorious deeds, and purely wholesome deeds.
Constantly observe that your own two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—are bound within the mind; do not allow yourself to give rise to great remorse at a later time.
All things one loves and delights in will be separated from you; according to one's wholesome or unwholesome karma, one proceeds to the next world.
"Nanda! A lifespan of one hundred years consists of ten stages. The first is the stage of infancy, when one lies in swaddling clothes.
The second is the stage of childhood, when one delights in childish play."
The third refers to youth, who experience various sensual pleasures;
the fourth refers to early adulthood, characterized by courage, vigor, and great strength;
the fifth refers to the prime of life, possessing wisdom for discourse.
Sixth is "accomplishment," meaning being able to deliberate well and skillfully devise strategies.
Seventh is "gradual decline," meaning being well-versed in ritual protocols and laws.
Eighth is "advanced age," meaning that all faculties and affairs have become weakened.
The ninth refers to extreme old age, being incapable of any action.
The tenth refers to the hundredth year, which is the stage of death. Nanda!
This is a brief summary of the general outline.

Calculating four months as one season, there are three hundred seasons within a hundred years—one hundred each for spring, summer, and winter. In a single year of twelve months, there are a total of one thousand two hundred months.
If calculated by half-months, there are a total of two thousand four hundred half-months.

Within these three seasons, there are eight hundred half-months each, totaling thirty-six thousand days and nights; since one eats twice a day, there are a total of seventy-two thousand instances of eating.

Even though there are occasions for not eating, these are still counted among the instances; as for the causes for not eating, they are: not eating out of anger or resentment, not eating due to encountering suffering, or not eating because one could not obtain what was sought; not eating due to sleepiness, observing a fast, restlessness or playfulness, or being preoccupied with affairs.
The total number of meals eaten and not eaten combined, along with the time spent drinking mother’s milk, constitutes the full span of a human life of one hundred years.
I have already fully explained the number of years, months, days, nights, and meals; you should therefore give rise to a sense of weary detachment.

"Nanda! Thus one is born, grows, and matures, and the body is subject to manifold ailments, namely: those of the head, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, teeth, throat, chest, abdomen, hands, and feet; as well as scabies, leprosy, insanity, dropsy, coughing, wind-disorders, jaundice, feverish phlegm, various types of malaria, and pain in the limbs and joints."
Nanda! The human body is subject to such sufferings of illness.

Furthermore, there are one hundred and one wind disorders, one hundred and one bile disorders, one hundred and one phlegm disorders, and one hundred and one combined disorders; in total, there are four hundred and four illnesses that arise from within.

Nanda! The body is like an abscess or an arrow, composed of manifold ailments; it does not pause for even a moment, remaining unstable from instant to instant. Its nature is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; it is constantly near death and subject to decay—a thing that cannot be cherished or protected.
"Nanda! Furthermore, there are sentient beings who undergo such suffering at birth as having their hands, feet, eyes, ears, noses, tongues, heads, and limbs severed."

Furthermore, they undergo the sufferings of imprisonment, shackles, fetters, flogging, torture, hunger, thirst, affliction, cold, heat, rain, snow, mosquitoes, gadflies, ants, wind, dust, fierce beasts, and various harsh contacts—countless and boundless torments that are difficult to describe in full.

Beings of this world constantly delight in and sink into such harsh and rigid suffering; whatever they desire has suffering as its root, yet they do not know to renounce it but instead pursue it further. Day and night they are tormented and oppressed, their bodies and minds afflicted, with an inner burning that knows no rest.

Thus, there is the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging; even the four postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—are all suffering.

If one constantly walks without standing, sitting, or lying down, one experiences suffering and no pleasure; if one constantly stands without walking, sitting, or lying down; or if one sits without walking, standing, or lying down; or if one lies down without walking, standing, or sitting—in all these cases, one undergoes extreme suffering and finds no peace or joy.
Nanda! All of these are the abandonment of suffering and the seeking of suffering; they are merely the arising of suffering and merely the cessation of suffering.

The Tathāgata, having fully understood how all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) arise in continuous succession through causes and conditions, has therefore spoken of the law of birth and death for sentient beings.

All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and not ultimately real; they are subject to decay and cannot be maintained. One should therefore seek contentment, cultivate profound weariness with them, and diligently strive for liberation.

Nanda! Within the realms of happy rebirths, the birthplaces of sentient beings are impure and their sufferings are so intense that various deceptive descriptions could never fully exhaust them; how much more so, then, can one fully describe the unbearable, agonizing torments endured by sentient beings in the three evil realms—the hungry ghosts, the animals, and the hells?
"Furthermore, Nanda!
There are four ways of entering the mother's womb.
What are these four?

First, sentient beings enter with right mindfulness, abide with right mindfulness, and emerge with right mindfulness; second, they enter with right mindfulness, abide with right mindfulness, but emerge without right mindfulness; third, they enter with right mindfulness, but abide and emerge without right mindfulness; fourth, all three stages are performed without right mindfulness.
Who is it that enters, dwells, and emerges with right mindfulness?

It is a certain class of ordinary beings who, by nature, delight in upholding the precepts and repeatedly practice wholesome qualities; who take pleasure in sublime matters and perform meritorious deeds; who are extremely well-guarded and constantly contemplate integrity; who are not negligent and possess great wisdom; and who, being without regret at the time of death, are reborn again—whether as a stream-enterer subject to seven more births, a "family-to-family" practitioner, a once-returner, or one who will be reborn only once more.

Because this person has previously cultivated wholesome conduct, at the time of their passing, although they are assailed by suffering and undergo various pains and afflictions, their mind remains undisturbed and they die with right mindfulness.

Returning once more to right mindfulness, he enters the mother’s womb, clearly understanding that all phenomena arise from karma and are produced through causes and conditions, serving as a constant dwelling place for various ailments.
Nanda! You should know that this body is a constant dwelling place for all manner of impurities; its nature is not permanent, and it is a delusive object that entices and deceives the ignorant.
This body has bones as its mechanical framework, with sinews and veins interconnected.
The various apertures are bound together by fat, flesh, marrow, and bone; covered over by skin, their defects remain unseen.
Within this hot cavern, impurities abound; hair, fur, nails, and teeth occupy their distinct positions.
Because one clings to "self" and "what belongs to self," one is constantly pulled and dragged, lacking any autonomy, and perpetually discharging tears, saliva, and filth.

It is drenched in sweat, filled with yellowish phlegm, sputum, and putrid fat; it contains the kidneys, gallbladder, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, excrement, and urine—all loathsome things—and is teeming everywhere with various kinds of worms.
Its upper and lower orifices constantly discharge foul impurities, and these two receptacles of the raw and the cooked are covered only by a thin skin; this is what is called a walking latrine.
You should observe this!

When eating and chewing with the teeth, it is moistened by saliva and swallowed down the throat; the marrow and brain mingle and flow as fluids into the belly, like a dog gnawing on a dry bone and falsely conceiving the thought that it is delicious. When the food reaches the navel, one feels nausea and it rises back up, yet one swallows it down once more.

Nanda! This body originally grows from impure and foul substances—kalala, arbuda, peśī, ghana, and praśākhā. From infancy it flows through the cycle of rebirth until old age and death, bound in saṃsāra like a dark pit or a stinking, ruined well, constantly sustained by the flavors of food that are salty, bland, bitter, pungent, sour, and so forth.

Furthermore, the fire within the mother’s womb burns and cooks the physical faculties; constantly confined within a cauldron of impure excrement, one suffers the heat and pain. Whether the mother walks, stands, sits, or lies down, it is as if one were bound by five fetters or scorched by fire—this suffering is difficult to endure and beyond all comparison.
Nanda! Although that embryo is within such a pit of filth and subjected to manifold agonies, because its faculties are sharp, its mind does not become distracted.

Furthermore, there is a class of beings with meager merit who, while in the mother’s womb, remain either horizontal or inverted. This occurs due to the power of the causal conditions of their prior karma; or because the mother’s food—whether cold or hot, salty or sour, sweet or pungent, or bitter—is not properly balanced; or because she drinks liquids in excess; or because she indulges excessively in sexual desire; or because she is afflicted by many illnesses; or because she harbors sorrow and distress; or because she falls to the ground; or because she is beaten or struck.

Due to these conditions, the mother’s body experiences intense fever; because her body is feverish, the fetus is also scorched; because it is scorched, it undergoes various painful afflictions; because it is afflicted by pain, it immediately begins to move and turn; and because it moves and turns, its body may become transverse or inverted, making it impossible for it to emerge.
There is a woman skilled in midwifery who applies ghee and oil to her hands and inserts them into the birth canal; she gently touches the fetus to settle it back into its original position.
At the moment her hand touches it, the fetus immediately experiences great suffering and distress.

Nanda! It is like a young boy or girl whose skin and flesh are sliced open by someone with a sharp knife, and then ashes are scattered upon them; because of this, great suffering and affliction arise.
The fetus’s agonizing suffering is likewise thus; although it undergoes this pain, because its faculties are sharp, right mindfulness remains undisturbed.
Nanda! In this manner, the fetus dwells within the mother’s womb and endures such suffering.

Furthermore, at the time of birth, one emerges with great hardship; driven by the winds of karma, the hands are forced together and the limbs are clenched in a fetal position, undergoing intense suffering. As one seeks to leave the mother's womb, the body is covered in livid bruises, like a fresh swelling that is difficult to touch; one is oppressed by hunger and thirst, with the mind hanging in anguish and burning with distress.

Driven out by the wind due to the conditions of karma, once it has emerged from the womb and is touched by the external air—as if being cut or smeared with ash—it experiences extreme suffering when touched by hands or clothing.

Although he undergoes this suffering, because his faculties are of the highest degree, his right mindfulness remains undisturbed; while within his mother’s womb, he knows that entering, abiding, and emerging are all entirely suffering.
"Nanda! Who would take pleasure in entering such a womb? Nanda!"
Who is it that enters the mother’s womb with right mindfulness, yet departs without right mindfulness? Nanda!

It is a certain class of ordinary beings who, by nature delight in upholding the precepts and cultivating wholesome qualities; who constantly perform meritorious deeds for superior purposes; whose minds are upright and not given to negligence; who possess a modicum of wisdom and have no regrets at the time of death; and who are either stream-enterers bound to seven more births, or "family-to-family" practitioners, or once-returners, or those separated from nirvana by only one interval.

This person had previously cultivated wholesome deeds; thus, when the time of death arrived and although suffering assailed him and he experienced various pains and afflictions, his mind remained undisturbed.

Returning once more to right mindfulness, he entered the mother’s womb, clearly understanding that all phenomena arise from karma and are produced through causes and conditions, as explained in detail above.

Even until the time of emerging from the womb, although he undergoes such extreme sufferings, because his faculties are sharp and intermediate, he enters and dwells with right mindfulness and emerges with wrong mindfulness, as explained in detail above.
"Who, indeed, would take pleasure in entering such a womb?
Nanda! Who is it that enters the womb with right mindfulness, but dwells and emerges without right mindfulness?"

Nanda! Suppose there is a certain class of ordinary sentient beings who, by nature, delight in upholding the precepts and cultivating wholesome qualities, constantly performing various meritorious deeds for sublime purposes, as explained in detail above.

Up until the time of death, they remain without regret; or, like those who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and will be reborn seven times at most, when the various sufferings press upon them at the moment of death, although they experience pain, their minds do not become distracted, and they again enter the mother’s womb with right mindfulness.
Because of these inferior faculties, one is aware at the time of entering the womb but unaware during the stay and the exit, as explained in detail above.
... up to: who would take pleasure in entering such a womb?
"Nanda! Who is it that is unrighteous in mindfulness regarding entering, remaining in, and emerging from [the meditative state]?

It is a certain class of ordinary sentient beings who delight in violating the pure precepts and do not cultivate wholesome qualities; they constantly engage in evil deeds and perform various misdeeds; their minds are not upright and they practice much heedlessness; they lack wisdom and are greedy for wealth and stingy; their hands are always clenched and unable to extend them to provide relief or charity to others; they are always full of longing and their minds are not disciplined or compliant; and they perceive and act with perversion."
At the time of death, one feels regret and remorse, and all unwholesome karmas manifest before them.
At the moment of dying, there is fierce and piercing agony; as intense suffering oppresses them, their mind becomes distracted, and due to these afflictions, they cannot remember who they are.
From where did you come?
Where are you going now, Nanda?
This is called being devoid of right mindfulness at all three times; the detailed explanation is as above. Nanda!

Although these sentient beings born among humans endure such immeasurable suffering and affliction, it is nonetheless a superior state, for a human body is difficult to obtain throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas.
If one is born in the heavens, one is constantly fearful of falling back down and suffers the pain of separation from those one loves; when one's life is about to end, other devas will say to them:
"May you be reborn in a good realm within the human world."
"What is the worldly happy destination?
It refers to humans and devas.
The human realm is difficult to attain; to be far removed from unfavorable conditions is even more difficult."
What are the evil destinies?
They are the three miserable realms.
As for the hell realm, one constantly experiences agonizing suffering that is utterly contrary to one's wishes; its fierce and piercing torments are beyond easy comparison.

Those in the realm of hungry ghosts (preta) are by nature full of anger and lack a gentle heart; they are deceitful, treacherous, and murderous, with hands smeared with blood and devoid of compassion. Their appearance is hideous, striking terror into those who behold them; even when they approach humans, they suffer from hunger and thirst and are constantly obstructed.

Those in the animal realm are immeasurable and boundless; they perform meaningless actions, meritless actions, unrighteous actions, non-virtuous actions, and lack sincere conduct. They prey upon one another, with the strong overpowering the weak. Among these animals—whether born, growing, or dying—they all dwell in darkness within impure places of excrement and filth. Occasionally there is a brief light, as seen among bees, butterflies, mosquitoes, ants, fleas, lice, and maggots; however, there are others, immeasurable and boundless in number, who grow and live in perpetual darkness.

Because in previous lives they were foolish people who did not listen to the sutras and the Dharma, allowing their body, speech, and mind to run wild; being greedily attached to the five desires and committing various evil deeds, they have been born among this class of beings to undergo the suffering of ignorance and delusion.

"Nanda! Furthermore, there are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings among the animals who are born, grow, and die entirely within the water—namely, species such as fish, turtles, tortoises, crocodiles, eels, leeches, clams, oysters, and frogs. This is due to the evil actions of body, speech, and mind committed in previous lives, as explained extensively above."

"Nanda! Furthermore, there are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings among the animals who, upon smelling the scent of excrement and urine, quickly go to those places to consume them as food and drink. These include such species as pigs, sheep, chickens, dogs, foxes, weasels, vultures, eagles, crows, flies, dung beetles, and various other birds and beasts; all of them receive such retribution as a result of the evil karma they committed in previous lives."

"Nanda! Furthermore, there are immeasurable and boundless classes of animals that constantly subsist on grass, wood, and various impurities for their food and drink—namely those belonging to the species of elephants, horses, camels, oxen, donkeys, and mules—and until the end of their lives, they undergo such retribution due to their prior evil karma."
"Furthermore, Nanda!
The ocean of birth and death is suffering!
It is painful!"

Fierce flames burn with extreme, great heat; not a single sentient being remains unburnt or unboiled. All of these result from the blazing, fierce fires of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, which greedily crave the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena before them.
Nanda! What is meant by "blazing, fierce fire"? It refers to the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion;

the fires of birth, old age, sickness, and death; and the fires of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—fires of poison and harm that are constantly burning of their own accord, from which not a single person can escape.
Nanda! Those who are indolent undergo manifold sufferings; ensnared by afflictions, they perform unwholesome deeds, revolving without rest through birth and death with no end.

Those who are diligent and energetic enjoy much peace and happiness; they rouse a courageous mind to sever the afflictions, cultivating wholesome dharmas without abandoning the yoke of virtue, never resting.

Therefore, you should now contemplate this body: its skin, flesh, sinews, bones, blood vessels, and marrow will soon disintegrate and perish. You should always maintain a single-minded focus without indolence; strive diligently to realize that which has not yet been realized. In this manner, you should train.
"Nanda! I do not engage in disputes with the world; rather, it is the world that forcibly engages me in dispute. Why is this so?
Those who know all phenomena do not dispute with others; being free from the notions of "I" and "mine," with whom would they dispute?
Because false attachments arise from views and misconceptions, I, having realized perfect enlightenment, have declared:
"There is nothing among all phenomena that I do not fully understand."
"Nanda! Is there any discrepancy in what I have said? Nanda replied:
"No, World-Honored One! What the Tathāgata speaks has no difference whatsoever."
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent, Nanda!”

What the Tathāgata speaks is invariably without discrepancy; the Tathāgata is a speaker of truth, a speaker of reality, a speaker of suchness, a speaker of non-contradiction, and a speaker of non-deception. Desiring to bring long-term peace, happiness, and great benefit to the world, he is the knower of the path, the perceiver of the path, the proclaimer of the path, the opener of the path, and the Great Guide—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Yet the people of the world are ignorant and lack faith; they are constant slaves to their own faculties. They see only what is in the palm of their hand and do not perceive the great benefit; they do not cultivate what is easy to do, but constantly perform what is difficult.

"Nanda! Let us set aside such realms of wisdom for a moment; you should now observe with the vision of your physical eyes, and know that whatever is seen is entirely illusory—this itself is called liberation."
Nanda! Do not trust me; do not follow my desires; do not rely on my words; do not observe my physical marks; do not follow whatever views the śramaṇa holds; do not conceive reverence for the śramaṇa;
and do not speak these words: "The śramaṇa Gautama is my teacher."

"However, regarding the Dharma realized through my own personal testimony, you should contemplate and examine it alone in a quiet place, practicing its cultivation constantly and extensively; following the Dharma that is the object of your mental attention, you should dwell in right mindfulness by achieving meditative visualization upon that very Dharma."
Make yourselves an island, make yourselves a refuge; take the Dharma as your island, take the Dharma as your refuge; there is no other island, no other refuge. Nanda!

"How is it, Nanda, that a bhikṣu makes himself his island and makes himself his refuge, making the Dharma his island and making the Dharma his refuge, having no other island and no other refuge? It is thus, Nanda!"

If there is a bhikṣu who dwells contemplating his own internal body, applying diligence and maintaining mindfulness to achieve correct understanding, and constantly contemplates the subduing of all anger and affliction in the world—this is called "contemplating the internal body as suffering."
If one contemplates the external body and likewise the internal and external body, it is also thus. Nanda!

Next, one dwells contemplating the body as a phenomenon of origination, and dwells contemplating its cessation; furthermore, one dwells contemplating the body with respect to both the phenomena of origination and cessation. Thus, regarding this very body, one is able to maintain right mindfulness—whether there be merely wisdom, or merely vision, or merely mindfulness—dwelling without dependence, knowing that in this world there is nothing to be grasped.
Thus, Nanda! This is called a bhikṣu dwelling in contemplation of his own internal body.
The same applies to the external body and to the internal and external body as objects of contemplation.

Next, one dwells observing internal feelings, external feelings, and both internal and external feelings; one dwells observing the internal mind, the external mind, and both internal and external minds; one dwells observing internal phenomena, external phenomena, and both internal and external phenomena.

Through diligent effort and focused mindfulness, one attains correct understanding; one constantly contemplates the subduing of all anger and afflictions in the world, abides in the contemplation of the phenomena of origination and abides in the contemplation of the phenomena of cessation. Furthermore, by contemplating the two phenomena of origination and cessation, one abides in the contemplation of dharmas; thus, one is able to maintain right mindfulness toward this very body—whether it be mere knowledge, mere vision, or mere mindfulness—and realizes that within this world there is nothing to be grasped.
Thus it is, Nanda!
This is called a bhikṣu making himself his island, making himself his refuge; taking the Dharma as his island, taking the Dharma as his refuge, with no other island and no other refuge.

"Nanda! If there is a man of upright nature who is free from flattery and deceit, and comes to me in the morning, I shall instruct him in the wholesome Dharma according to his capacity; by evening he will report what he has attained.
If I instruct him with the Dharma in the evening, he will report what he has attained by dawn."

"Nanda! My wholesome dharmas are realized in the present; they are able to remove the feverish afflictions, are well-suited to the timing, and are easy to apply as skillful means. They are dharmas of self-awakening, providing excellent protection. Having heard the Dharma taught in my presence, it accords with tranquility and can lead toward Bodhi—this is what I know."

Therefore, you should now constantly practice and study those dharmas that bring benefit to oneself, benefit to others, and benefit to both; you should diligently carry out the dharma of renunciation so that it does not pass in vain. You shall thereby obtain the supreme fruit of unconditioned peace and bliss, and by receiving from others the offerings of clothing, food, bedding, and medicine, you will cause those donors to attain great merit and blessings, and to receive a superior, noble, and vast karmic reward.
Thus it is, Nanda!
You should practice and train in this way. Furthermore, Nanda!
There is no form whatsoever that is lovely and pleasing which can remain unchanging and undecaying at a later time; such a thing is impossible.
Nor is there any possibility that one would not give rise to sorrow and lamentation, nor produce afflictions.
"Nanda! What do you think? Is this form permanent or impermanent?"
“Venerable sir! Its nature is impermanent. “Nanda!”
“Since its nature is impermanent, is it suffering?
“Venerable sir, it is suffering.”
“If that which is impermanent and suffering is a phenomenon subject to change and decay,
would my many-hearing noble disciples regard form as the self, or the self as possessing form, or form as belonging to the self, or the self as being within form?”
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
"What do you think? Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?
"Venerable sir, [they are impermanent]."
"All are impermanent. "Nanda! Since the body is impermanent, is it suffering?"
“Venerable sir! This is suffering.
“If it is impermanent and suffering, it is a phenomenon subject to change and decay.”

Do my many-hued noble disciples regard feeling and the other aggregates as "I," or as "I possess feeling and the others," or as "feeling and the others belong to me," or as "I am within feeling and the others"?
"No, World-Honored One!

Therefore, you should know that whatever forms there are—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; superior or inferior; far or near—all such forms are not the self, the self does not possess form, form does not belong to the self, and the self does not exist within form. In this way, one should examine and observe with right mindfulness and right wisdom."

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; superior or inferior; far or near—all these are not the self, nor does the self possess them, nor do they exist within the self. In this way, one should examine them thoroughly with right mindfulness and right wisdom.

If my well-versed noble disciples observe in this way, they become weary of form; they likewise become weary of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Once weary, they are no longer attached; being without attachment, they attain liberation. Having attained liberation, they know for themselves that they are liberated and declare:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."

When the Blessed One had spoken this Dharma, the Venerable Nanda was far removed from dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; and the minds of five hundred bhikṣus were liberated from all outflows.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse, addressing Nanda:
"If a person lacks a concentrated mind, They will lack pure wisdom;
Unable to sever all outflows, Therefore, you must practice with diligence."
You have constantly cultivated sublime contemplation, knowing the arising and ceasing of all aggregates;
when you are pure and perfected, all the devas rejoice.
Friends and kin share in your joy, coming and going with mutual affection.
Craving fame and seeking gain—Nanda, you should renounce these!
Do not associate with householders or those who have gone forth;
mindful of transcending the ocean of birth and death, bring an end to the limits of suffering.
First from the kalala, next the arbuda is produced;
from the arbuda, the peśī is produced; from the peśī, the ghana is produced.
As the ghana gradually transforms, the head and four limbs are formed.
A multitude of bones aggregate to form the body, all arising from the causes of karma.
The skull consists of nine joined plates; the jaw is connected by two bones.
There are thirty-two teeth, and their roots are likewise.
The auditory canals and the cervical vertebrae, the palate bone and the bridge of the nose,
the chest and the throat— these together comprise twelve bones.
There are four bones in the eye sockets, and the shoulder blades likewise form two pairs.
The two arms and the fingers together have fifty bones;
behind the neck there are eight bones, and the backbone has thirty-two—
each of these has its own foundation, their number likewise being four times eight.
On the right side, the ribs are connected in a series of thirteen;
on the left side, they likewise grow in connection, numbering thirteen bones.
These various skeletal chains are linked together in groups of three.
The two pairs of bones are hooked together, while the remaining ones do not connect.
The left and right legs and feet together have fifty bones;
totaling three hundred and sixteen, they support the interior of the body.
The bones and joints are linked together, forming the body of sentient beings;
this is what those who speak the truth have declared, and that which is known by the Perfectly Awakened One.
From the feet up to the crown of the head, it is a collection of impurities, lacking any solidity.
By these things the body is collectively formed, as fragile and precarious as a reed hut.
Without a central pin, it stands merely as a framework of bones, plastered over with flesh and blood;
it is like a wooden automaton, or like a conjured phantom.
One should contemplate this body: Tendons and sinews further entwine it, Moist skin wraps and covers it, And at nine locations there are openings of sores.
From all sides it constantly flows and overflows— Excrement, urine, and various impurities.
Just as granaries and baskets hold various grains and wheat,
so too is this body: filled with impurities within,
a mechanism of moving bones, precarious and fragile rather than solid.
Fools always delight in it, while the wise have no attachment;
mucus and saliva flow as constant impurities, and pus and blood are ever-filling.
Yellow fat mixed with breast milk, and brains fill the skull.
Phlegm and mucus flow within the chest and diaphragm; inside lie the receptacles for the raw and the cooked.
There are layers of fat and membranes, the five viscera, and all manner of intestines and stomachs.
Such foul and putrid things as these are all equally the abodes of impurity.
This body of sin is deeply fearsome; it is indeed an enemy.
Yet those who lack discernment and indulge in desire foolishly protect it at all times.
Such a foul and impure body is like a dilapidated city wall.
Day and night, one is oppressed by afflictions, In constant flux, never pausing for a moment.
The city of the body has bones for its walls, And flesh and blood for its plaster;
With greed, hatred, and delusion as its pigments, It is adorned everywhere with these colors.
This loathsome city of bones, with its flesh and blood joined together,
is constantly tormented by evil associates from both within and without.
Nanda, you should know this as I have described it.
Day and night, always maintain mindfulness; do not dwell upon the realm of desire.
If you wish to distance yourself from it, constantly practice such contemplation;
diligently seek the place of liberation, and quickly transcend the ocean of birth and death.

When the World-Honored One had finished preaching this *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*, the Venerable Nanda and the five hundred bhikṣus were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.

The Bhikṣu Nanda, having crossed the perilous and difficult places of the ocean of birth and death, reached the secure state of ultimate nirvāṇa and attained the fruit of Arhatship. He spoke this verse of self-congratulation:
"By reverently offering a bath, Pure water and fragrant ointments, And cultivating various causes of merit, I have obtained this most excellent reward."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they were all filled with doubt. To sever their doubts, they requested of the Great Master:

"Venerable One, what karma did the bhikṣu Nanda previously perform such that, as a result of its maturation, he obtained a golden-colored body adorned with the thirty marks, which was only four finger-widths shorter than the body of the World-Honored One, yet he conceived an extreme attachment to the objects of sensual desire?"
"The Great Master, out of compassion, has forcibly pulled us from the ocean of birth and death and, through skillful means, established us in ultimate nirvāṇa.
We pray that you will explain this for us.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The karma previously created by the bhikṣu Nanda has reached its fruition; its ripening has all manifested before him,” as explained in detail above.
Then he spoke these verses:
“Even if a hundred eons pass, The karma one has created does not perish;”
"When causes and conditions meet, one receives the retribution for oneself.

"O Bhikṣus! In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, when the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān named Vipaśyin. Accompanied by sixty-two thousand bhikṣus, he traveled through the human realm and arrived at the capital city of Bandhumatī, where the King resided; he went to the Bandhumatī Grove and stayed there."

At that time, that Blessed One had a half-brother who was extremely attached to the objects of sensual desire. Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, exhorted him to leave the household life within the ocean of birth and death, and through skillful means established him in ultimate nirvāṇa.

At that time, the ruler of that kingdom was named Yǒuqīn (Sakya); he governed the world according to the Dharma, and the populace was flourishing, prosperous, and at peace. There were no deceits, thieves, bandits, or epidemics, and cattle, sheep, rice, and sugarcane abounded everywhere.

The king’s half-brother was excessively addicted to sensual lust. When the king heard that the Buddha and his assembly were staying at the Veṇuvana (Sālavatīvana) Grove, he took his princes, his close ministers, and the women of the inner palace, with the common people following in attendance, and went to the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One proclaimed the sublime Dharma for the assembly of kings, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, so that they attained a supreme understanding.
However, his younger brother, being addicted to sensual desires, was unwilling to leave his door.
Then the minister’s son and his other friends, who were like dust upon his shoulder, approached him and said:
"Good friend, do you not know?

The king, the prince, along with the members of the inner court, the ministers, and the multitude have gone to the presence of Vipaśyin Buddha to personally pay their respects and listen to the sublime Dharma, thereby attaining a most excellent understanding."
"A human body is difficult to obtain, yet you have already attained it; why then do you now indulge so deeply in sensual desire that you refuse to leave your door?
Having heard this reprimand, he felt shame and humiliation, and with a reluctant air, he followed along with him as they went together.
At that time, the Buddha’s younger brother, a bhikṣu, saw his companions departing together and asked,
"For what reason are you all taking this one person along as a companion?"
Then his companion reported the matter in full, and the bhikṣu said:

"I am the younger brother of the Buddha. Formerly, when I was still a householder, I was deeply attached to the objects of sensual desire; fortunately, the Great Master forcibly led me out and established me on the path toward ultimate nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, there are others like me who are likewise foolish; it would truly be a great kindness if you, out of compassion, were to take us along by force.
We shall now go to the Unsurpassed Great Teacher, and upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, we will surely give rise to profound faith.
Then those companions went together to where the Buddha was; the Buddha, observing their kind, taught the Dharma to them in accordance with their faculties, inclinations, and dispositions.
Having heard it, they conceived deep faith, rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I only pray that the Great Master and the assembly of noble ones will come to my home tomorrow morning to enter the warm bathhouse for a wash.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing he had accepted, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet, took his leave, and departed. He then went to the King, paid his respects, and said:

"Great King! Having approached the Buddha and heard the Dharma, faith has arisen within me, and I have conceived a sense of weary detachment toward the objects of sensual desire. I respectfully invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha to come to my home tomorrow to bathe in the warm bathhouse. The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has compassionately accepted my invitation; for the Buddha is one who should be venerated by gods and humans alike. Your Majesty should now sprinkle and sweep the streets and adorn the city walls."
The king thought to himself:
"When the Buddha enters the city, I shall adorn it; yet my younger brother is addicted to sensual desires and difficult to admonish. That the Buddha has now tamed him is truly rare."
He replied: "Excellent!
You may now go and prepare the necessary items for the bathing ceremony; I shall, according to my ability, adorn the city walls and moats."
The younger brother was filled with great joy and took his leave of the king to depart.
The king addressed his ministers, saying:
"An edict should be proclaimed to inform all people:"

"Tomorrow the World-Honored One will enter the city; you who have long resided here and those who have come from afar, all of you should exert yourselves to the best of your ability to adorn the city walls, sweep the streets, and carry various incenses and flowers to welcome the Great Teacher as he enters."

The ministers, having received the King’s command, issued a general proclamation to make it known and fully proclaimed the royal decree. At that time, the multitude within the city cleared away all rubble and debris, sprinkled scented water everywhere, burned various exquisite incenses, hung up many banners and canopies, and scattered flowers as offerings, so that it was like the Joyful Garden of Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
At that time, the king’s younger brother prepared various fragrant decoctions and scented oils, adorned the bathhouse, and arranged seats and couches.

As Vipasyin Buddha was gradually approaching the city, the king, his ministers, the crown prince, the queen, the palace attendants, the court ladies, and the multitude of people all came out to welcome him; they prostrated themselves from afar at the Buddha’s feet and followed him into the city.

At that time, the king’s younger brother led the Buddha, the World-Honored One, into the bathhouse and offered scented water and other substances for his ablution; he beheld the body of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, golden in color and fully adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Having seen him, he felt great joy and gave rise to deep faith. Once he had finished bathing and put on his robes, he immediately prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and made this vow:

"I have now fortunately encountered the supreme field of merit and have offered this slight act of worship. By the power of this wholesome cause, may my body in future lives attain a golden hue no different from that of the Buddha."

Just as the World-Honored One’s younger brother, who was deeply attached to sensual objects, was forcibly pulled out and led toward the ultimate peace of *nirvāṇa*, may I likewise become a younger brother to a Buddha in the future, obtaining a golden body;
and when I give rise to attachment for sensual objects, may I be forcibly drawn out from the deep river of craving and lead myself to the secure place of *nirvāṇa*.
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any doubt: that younger brother of King Bandhumat who was addicted to sensual desires was none other than the bhikṣu Nanda.

Because in the past he invited the Buddha Vipaśyin to enter the bathhouse and bathe in fragrant water, and because of the roots of virtue from his pure-hearted aspiration, he has now become the Buddha’s younger brother with a body of golden hue."
"I have forcibly extracted you from your attachment to the objects of sensual desire, causing you to renounce the world and go forth, so that you may reach ultimate nirvana and the state of peace.
At that time, the bhikṣus again had doubts and requested of the World-Honored One:
"Venerable Sir!"
“Bhikṣus, what karma did the bhikṣu Nanda perform in the past such that he has now attained the thirty marks of a Great Man?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The deeds he performed have been explained at length as previously described.”

In the distant past, within a certain village, there was an elder of great wealth and abundant resources, lacking nothing for his livelihood. He possessed a garden where flowers and fruits flourished, with flowing springs, bathing pools, and dense groves of trees—a place fit for a renunciant to dwell in seclusion.

At that time, a Pratyekabuddha appeared in the world; out of compassion for sentient beings, he delighted in dwelling in secluded tranquility. Since there was no Buddha in the world, he alone was the field of merit.

Then, a certain venerable Pratyekabuddha, wandering through the human realm, arrived at this village. After traveling about and observing his surroundings, he reached the park. When the park keeper saw the venerable one, he said, "Welcome! Welcome!"
"To relieve his fatigue, the Venerable One dwells here.
Then, during the middle watch of the night, he entered the fire-light samādhi. When the park keeper saw this, he thought to himself:
"This Great Virtuous One has accomplished such a supreme practice."
He immediately rose in the night and went to his master, saying: "Master!

You should now give rise to a heart of joy; a great virtuous one has come to stay with me in the garden. Having perfected wondrous conduct and being endowed with supernormal powers, he has emitted a great radiance that illuminates the entire garden."
Having heard this, the householder went quickly to the garden; after prostrating at his feet, he spoke these words:
"Noble One! You seek food, and I seek the cause of merit. Please remain in this garden, and I shall constantly provide you with alms."
Seeing his earnestness, he accepted the invitation and, remaining within this grove, entered the bliss of liberation through the sublime meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
He further thought:

"This foul body of mine has transmigrated through birth and death; that which was to be accomplished has all been attained. It is fitting for me to enter parinirvāṇa and eternally realize the state of non-arising."

Having formed this thought, he immediately ascended into the air and entered the fire-light concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), manifesting various supernatural transformations. He emitted a great radiance that shone with crimson brilliance above and flowed as clear water below. Having cast off this body, his consciousness was no longer reborn, as he forever realized the wondrous realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

Then that elder took the remains and cremated them with fragrant wood, extinguishing the fire with milk. He collected the remaining bone fragments and placed them in a new jar, constructing a stūpa and hanging various banners and canopies. With deep faith and devotion, he sprinkled thirty kinds of exquisite perfumed water and made great vows, seeking the attainment of the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha.

"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts. The householder of that time was none other than Nanda. Because of his karma of offering superior and wondrous gifts with respectful faith, he now experiences the karmic fruition of having attained thirty extraordinary and sublime marks."
At that time, the bhikṣus had further doubts and again requested of the World-Honored One:
"Venerable Sir,
what karma did the bhikṣu Nanda previously perform such that, had he not gone forth and renounced the secular world, he would certainly have succeeded to the position of a Wheel-Turning King?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The karma created by Nanda in previous lives must necessarily be experienced by him in person when its retribution ripens.
[The details] are as explained above at length.

In a past age, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, endowed with the ten titles, and dwelt in dependence upon the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī.
At that time, there was a king in that city named Kṛkī, who ruled the world according to the Dharma as a great Dharma-king, as described in detail above.
The king had three sons, known as the eldest, the middle, and the youngest.
When that Buddha Kāśyapa had finished his work of converting beings, he entered Great Parinirvāṇa like an extinguished fire.

The king, filled with faith and reverence, took the Buddha’s remains and burned them with various fragrant woods—sandalwood, aloeswood, *kālānusāri*, *gośīrṣa*, and celestial incense. Once the cremation was complete, he extinguished the flames with fragrant milk. He collected the relics and placed them in a golden jeweled jar, constructing a great stūpa made entirely of the four precious substances. It was one *yojana* in length and breadth, and half a *yojana* in height. When the *cakra* (wheel) was being installed, the king’s middle son personally placed the central parasol upon it.
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts. That middle son of the king at that time was none other than Nanda.

Because of this wholesome karma of having respectfully made offerings and provided a middle parasol in the past, for two thousand five hundred lifetimes he has always been a Cakravartin King ruling over a single continent. Had he not gone forth into homelessness in this present life, he would have again become a Cakravartin King and attained great sovereignty."
At that time, the bhikṣus again had doubts and questioned the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir,
what karma did the bhikṣu Nanda previously perform such that he is foremost among the Buddha’s disciples in well-guarding the doors of the sensory faculties?"
The Buddha said, "This is due to the power of his vows.

When the bhikṣu Nanda was a layman during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he renounced the world and went forth. His preceptor was foremost among those who well-guarded the doors of the sense faculties within that Buddha’s teaching; he maintained the holy life (brahmacarya) for as long as he lived, yet he failed to attain realization in that very lifetime."
At the time of his death, he made this vow:
"I have maintained the holy life under the Buddha for as long as this body lasted, yet during my present lifetime I have attained nothing."

"By these roots of merit from my practice, may I—just as this Buddha, the World-Honored One, has prophesied that there shall be a young brahmin in a future age who will attain perfect enlightenment under the name Śākyamuni, and that within his teaching and dharma I shall leave the household life, renounce the world, sever all afflictions, and realize arhatship—become foremost among those who guard the doors of the sense faculties, just as my preceptor was foremost among those who well-guarded the doors of the sense faculties in the presence of this Buddha. May I likewise be foremost in guarding the doors of the sense faculties within that teaching."
"By the power of that vow, he is now foremost among my disciples in well-guarding the doors of the sensory faculties.

Thus, monks, if one performs purely black karma, one receives a purely black retribution; if one performs purely white karma, one receives a purely white retribution; and if one performs mixed karma, one shall receive a mixed retribution."
"Therefore, you all should abandon purely black and mixed karma, and cultivate purely white karma;
in this manner you should practice. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 12. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.
Volume Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The summary verse for the third section, which subsumes its individual subsections, says:
The three robes and a robe-rack, A temple eaves built by a riverbank,
Towels for wiping the face and body, And temple seats and knives— one should keep these.
The summary verse for the first section of the third chapter states:
The dimensions of the strips and leaves of the three robes; the bed-legs and the duster for removing dust;
the woolen rug to be placed in the walking area; and the pestle and stone—these must be permitted to be kept.
The occasion was at Śrāvastī.
As the Buddha had instructed that bhikṣus should possess khaṇḍa-cīvara (patchwork robes), the bhikṣus then proceeded to cut them; however, the long strips and short strips were not uniform.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The long strips and short strips should not be uneven; when cutting them, they must be cut evenly.
They, however, did not know how to cut them evenly.
The Buddha said:
"The long strips and short strips should correspond to their respective measurements; one may take bamboo slips to measure and cut them to the proper length before fixing them.
The circumstances were as previously described.
At that time, the bhikṣus were making cīvaras, but because the seams (pattas) were not uniform, they were not well-proportioned. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When making robes, the seams should be uniform."
The bhikṣus did not know what was meant by "similar.
The Buddha said:
"One may take a piece of bamboo to measure the width of the leaf, and then cut it accordingly."
The Buddha said, "One should measure the leaves. At that time, the bhikṣus made the leaves excessively large.
The Buddha said, "They should not be made large.
Furthermore, there are three characteristics of leaves:"
These are categorized as large, medium, and small.

The large is four finger-widths wide, or as wide as a crow’s outstretched feet; the small is two finger-widths wide, or as wide as the surface of a thumb; that which is between these two is called medium.
The bhikṣus sewed and patched their robes on impure ground, whereupon they became stained and soiled. The Buddha said:
"One should wipe the ground clean with cow dung and prepare a maṇḍala; once it has become pure, one may make the robe upon it."
The Buddha said that for one constructing a maṇḍala, cow dung is difficult to obtain; the Buddha then said:
"One should sprinkle the ground with water, sweep it clean, and lay out the cloth."
The setting was as before.
At that time, the bhikṣus made pointed bed legs, which consequently damaged the floor. The Buddha said:
"They should not be sharp; they should be made flat."
Nevertheless, damage still occurred.
The Buddha said, "One should make a bag of chaff and place it under the bed, or wrap [the vessel] with torn cloth.
The setting of the occasion is the same as before.

There was a brahmin who, having traveled outside the city and become utterly exhausted, entered the Jeta Grove when the time for the meal arrived. Seeing that a place for eating had been prepared with exquisite mats and seats and fine food and drink set out, he felt a sense of wonder and gave rise to a heart of faith and reverence. He immediately removed his upper robe, spread it over the seat where the presiding elder was to sit, and departed through the gate.
Later, at another time, the robe became soiled and greasy; the person in charge of monastic affairs spread it out beneath his seat.

Subsequently, for some other business, that brahmin came to the monastery and went to the dining area. Not seeing his robe where the senior monk sat, he searched throughout the area in order until he saw it spread out beneath the seat.
He thought to himself:
