"My robe is new and of high value; for what reason has it become so defiled today?
He decided to wait a moment to investigate the cause.
When he saw the administrator having arranged the seats and then grasping his robe to sweep the ground, he perceived the cause of the defilement and said to the administrator,
"Do you not understand this minor matter?"
"One should first sprinkle water, then sweep until it is clean, and only afterwards spread out one's seat; because you do not understand this, you have caused damage to my robe.
Having conceived a sense of resentment and shame, he abandoned [the place] and departed.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"At every place where food is served, one should first sprinkle water and then sweep it clean; only after that should seats be spread, for then it will be in accordance with the Dharma."
At that time, the administrator spread his seat-covers upon a dusty seat, which subsequently became heavily soiled. As the fault was the same as before, the Buddha said:
"First you should sweep and wipe the bed and seat, and only then spread the felt mats."
The bhikṣus did not know with what to wipe [the furniture], so the Buddha said:
"One should use a single garment to wipe the beds and seats.
At that time, the administrator used a fine garment to wipe them, so the Buddha said:
"One should use old cloth.
When the attendant used old cloth to sweep, it soon became tattered and was all discarded. The Buddha said:
"One should not discard it immediately; tear it into small pieces and tie them to the end of a staff to use for sweeping beds and seats."
After a long time, finding them unusable, he eventually discarded them. The Buddha said:

"Even if they are no longer fit for use, you should not discard them. You should chop them up and mix them with mud or cow dung to fill the holes in pillars or plaster over the cracks in walls, so that the merit and benefit of the donor may increase for a long time."
The setting was as before.
At that time, there was a young bhikṣu who was performing walking meditation (caṅkrama) in a certain place; as he walked, he caused the ground to become damaged.
At that time, there was an elder who entered the monastery and toured it everywhere. Upon reaching the place where [the monks] practiced walking meditation, he had this thought:
"If even the ground is like this, what must the feet of the Noble Ones look like?"
Having had this thought, he asked: "Noble One!
Who has caused damage to this place?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"This is precisely where I practice walking meditation.
The householder replied:
“The ground is already like this; what then of your feet?
I would be so fortunate as to lift your foot for me to examine it.
He then raised his foot to show him that it was pierced through by the skin.
Upon seeing this, the householder gave rise to a heart of compassion and replied, "Noble One!
I have a woolen rug; I wish to spread it for you to walk upon so that your feet will not be harmed."
He replied, "Householder, the Buddha has not yet granted permission."
He said, "Noble One!
Your Great Master is by nature compassionate; he will surely grant this."
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I now permit those bhikṣus who are diligently exerting themselves through walking meditation to possess woolen rugs; they may do so as they please without offense."
He returned and informed the householder, who immediately prepared a seat for him; the bhikṣu then accepted it.
After he had stood upon it for a long time, it was consequently split into two pieces, each lying on one side.
Later, when the elder returned and saw the rug in such a state of disarray,
he asked, "Venerable sir!
For what reason has the woolen rug fallen into such ruin?"
"If you see a place that has been torn, why do you not sew it up and repair it?
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"What the householder has said is truly excellent!"
If one sees a place that has been broken, it may be sewn and repaired, or patched with materials.

If it is shattered and beyond repair, one should mix it with mud or cow dung and apply it as a coating upon the walking path (caṅkrama), thereby enabling the donor to increase their field of merit (puṇyakṣetra).
The setting is the same as before.
A certain bhikṣu, being ill, went to a physician and said:
"O worthy one!..."
"I have such an illness; please prescribe medicine for me.
He replied, "Noble one!"
"By taking this medicine, you shall recover.
He then prescribed the remedy.
Upon returning to his dwelling, he needed a mortar and pestle to prepare the medicine; he therefore went to another house to borrow them temporarily, and the person there lent them to him.
Having finished grinding the medicine, he returned the stone to him and said, "Noble One!
I give this to you; take it back with you as you please."
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep one.
[The other said,] "If that is the case, you may leave it on the ground."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I now permit you to keep pestles, stones, and their shafts; if others offer them, you should accept them as you please."
The second sub-section of the third chapter contains this summary verse:
Clothes-racks and lanterns, Do not let insects cause injury;
Open the three-sided hut when it is hot, And one may mark Nanda’s body.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
A bhikṣu left his robes wherever he happened to be, and they became soiled with grease and were bored through by insects and ants.
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not place clothing anywhere at random; one should instead make a clothes-rack.
The bhikṣus then pierced the walls to hang their robes, causing the walls to be damaged. The Buddha said:
"One must not pierce the walls. When first constructing a monastery, one should leave wooden sockets when building and place poles for the robes upon them."
At that time, the bhikṣus placed poles inside their rooms but did not construct them under the eaves.
The Buddha said, "Construct them under the eaves as well; do not let necessary matters be neglected.
The circumstances were the same as before.
The Buddha said that one should make a clothes rack; however, when a bhikṣu in an araṇya found no bamboo, the Buddha said:
"One should take a rattan vine and tie it across to hold the robes."
Or perhaps there was no kudzu vine; the Buddha said, "Use a rope as a support.
The setting for this account is the same as before.
As the Blessed One said, when one recites a sutra in the darkness of night, a snake may come upon him while he is reciting; seeing it, the youth was startled and cried out in great alarm, shouting:
"Long-backed one!"
"Long-spine!
At this, all the ordinary bhikṣus were struck with terror, causing the listeners to abandon their practice.
When the matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should light a lamp while reciting the scriptures.
When monks lit lamps during the summer months and harmed insects, the Buddha said:
"One should make a lamp-shade."
The bhikṣus did not know how they should proceed.
The Buddha said:

"One should make a cage out of bamboo strips and cover it with thin layers of cloth. If these are difficult to obtain, use pieces of mica. If even those are hard to find, one should make a 'hundred-eyed' jar."
The bhikṣus did not understand how it should be made.
The Buddha said:
"Have a potter make it in the shape of a lantern, with many small holes pierced along its sides."
Since it was difficult to find a potter, the Buddha said:
"One should take a jar or pitcher, break off its bottom, and pierce a hundred holes in its sides; having placed a lamp inside, one should then turn it downward and close it."
"If insects enter through the holes, they should be covered with paper, silk, or thin materials.
The setting of this account is the same as before.
At that time, during the height of summer, the bhikṣus suffered from the heat; their bodies became withered and yellow, and they grew weak and emaciated from illness.
At that time, the Blessed One, knowing [the situation], intentionally asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"For what reason are the bodies of these bhikṣus withered, pale, sickly, emaciated, and lacking strength?"
Then Ānanda reported the matter in detail to the Buddha, who said:
"A cooling shelter should be constructed.
The bhikṣus did not know how it should be made.
The Buddha said:

"One should construct a three-sided shelter near the exterior of the monastery; its three sides should have walls erected with an open, unenclosed front to allow the wind to pass through freely, unlike the monastery itself which has walls on all four sides."
The bhikṣus then constructed walls on the inside and placed pillars for walking on the outside.
The Buddha said, "Place the pillars in the middle.
They still did not open windows and consequently suffered from heat and suffocation. The Buddha said:
"Place it at the window.
When he placed it at the window, it was sometimes too high or too low;
the Buddha said, "It should be level with the bed."
When various birds and sparrows entered the room, the Buddha said:
"One should install window lattices so that they cannot enter.
When wind and rain blow and splash in, one should install window shutters."
When the bhikṣus were eating with the doors closed and the room was dark, the Buddha said:
"Open the doors during mealtime.

When the bhikṣus were hot within their own rooms, if they wore only the lower garment (antarvāsaka) and the monastic shoulder-cloth (saṃkakṣikā), reading and reciting as they pleased, preaching the Dharma, or making robes and so forth, there was no offense in any of these four modes of conduct (īryāpatha).
The setting was as before.

At that time, after the Blessed One had shaved Nanda’s hair, ordained him, and conferred upon him full ordination (*upasampadā*), he led him to Mount Gandhamādana, to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, and to the hells (*naraka*). Having traveled about and observed these places, he returned to the Jeta Grove.

Some visiting bhikṣus did not recognize Nanda; seeing his body golden in color and adorned all over with the thirty marks, an elderly bhikṣu, upon seeing him, thought he was the Tathāgata and rose to welcome him. Only after they recognized him did he feel regret.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should make a mark upon Nanda’s robe as a sign; if there is anyone else with such a person, one should likewise mark them."
"This is the Perfectly Awakened One; this is another person.
The third section of the third chapter, summarized in verse, says:
"By the riverbank, the tooth-stick was prepared; Rāhula was sent out the door."
"Whether it is appropriate to speak or inappropriate to speak, these two modes of conduct should be practiced.
This occurred in Śrāvastī.

At that time, a group of bhikṣus by the River of Supreme Wisdom (*Jyeṣṭhā-nadī*) applied themselves with skillful means and diligent cultivation, exhausting all afflictions and realizing the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, the bhikṣus were dignified in their deportment and deliberate in their actions, such that they inspired profound respect and faith in all people.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The dwelling place of the bhikṣus by the banks of the Vipāśā River is near that village; all the people there have obtained great and wholesome benefit."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard the words of the Blessed One, immediately understood their meaning; for, having long served as the attendant to the Great Master, he would understand them at once whether he heard their words or observed their gestures.
"If the Blessed One wishes to see me, he will speak words of praise. Once the Venerable One had understood this, he sent a message to the bhikṣu by the riverbank, saying:
"O venerable ones!..."
"The World-Honored One has praised us and desires to see us; you, sirs, may come.
Having heard this, they spoke to one another:
"The Buddha has spoken words of praise regarding us; we must surely meet him—what should we do?"
One person replied,
"What else is there to do? We shall go."
Consequently, they failed to examine what ought to be done; for even an Arhat cannot know in advance without such examination.
They further deliberated together, saying, "It would be a good thing to go."
He then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Virtuous ones, you should know!
The Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, has praised us and desires to see us; we may go now."
The bhikṣus said, "If it is so,
we shall go together. They then followed one another along the road, traveling by stages until they reached Śrāvastī.
The resident bhikṣus came out to welcome and greet them, and there was a great clamor outside the monastery.
Having heard it, the Blessed One, knowing the reason, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"Why is there such a great clamor outside the monastery?"

Ānanda said: "The assembly of bhikṣus from the banks of the Vipāśā River have all come together and are staying outside the monastery; everyone inside the monastery has gone out to welcome them, and their mutual greetings have caused this commotion."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go and inform the assembly of bhikṣus by the banks of the River Jyeṣṭhā: 'All of you should return; do not remain here.'"
At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the Venerable One went to where the bhikṣus were and said to them:
"Venerable ones, you should know!
The World-Honored One has given this command: 'You all should return; do not remain here.'"
When he had heard this, he took up his robes and bowl and traveled among the people.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"In whatever village or settlement there may be a bhikṣu dwelling by the side of the river Prajñāvatī, all the people living near that village will obtain great and wholesome benefit."

When Ānanda heard this, he returned once more with a message; the bhikṣus came again, and this happened up to three times, whereupon the bhikṣus took up their robes and bowls and departed once more for the human world.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The bhikṣus residing at the hermitage by the banks of the Vipāśā River have all obtained benefit.
When Ānanda heard the Buddha’s repeated praise, he reported it with faith. Those bhikṣus then said to one another:
"Venerable one!
Why does the Blessed One praise us for desiring to see him, sending us back to the Buddha's presence after we have already gone there?
It must be because he intends to inform many people so as to send us away; therefore, it would be appropriate for me now to depart in silence without informing anyone."
Then the bhikṣus, taking their robes and bowls, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"You should now seek out a secluded and quiet room and arrange seats and mats for me and those bhikṣus by the banks of the Śubhavastu River."
The Venerable One, having received these instructions and completed the arrangement, returned to the Buddha’s presence and said:
"Venerable Sir,
I have finished preparing the place in one location."
“The Buddha alone knows the right time.

At that time, the World-Honored One went to the dwelling place of the bhikṣus by the banks of the Śubhavatī River. Having washed his feet outside the gate, he entered a room, sat down upon a seat, crossed his legs, straightened his body, and established himself in mindfulness before him.
At that time, the bhikṣus also each washed their feet, entered their rooms, and sat down, abiding in the presence of mindfulness.
Then the Blessed One entered the first dhyāna;
the bhikṣus by the riverbank also entered the first dhyāna.

The World-Honored One emerged from the first dhyāna and entered the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; he then entered the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness, and finally entered the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The bhikṣu by the river did likewise, following the World-Honored One as he entered and emerged from these various meditative absorptions.
The World-Honored One emerged from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and entered the concentration of nothingness;
the bhikṣus also emerged from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and entered the concentration of nothingness.
...until he entered the first dhyāna;
the bhikṣus likewise entered the first dhyāna.
The World-Honored One thought to himself:
"When I enter the first dhyāna, the bhikṣus also enter the first dhyāna; and so on, until when I enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the bhikṣus also enter this concentration."
"I shall further enter and emerge from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception down to the first dhyāna, and all the bhikṣus shall likewise do so with me.
Now, I should enter the first dhyāna by means of another mode of manifestation, such that it becomes a state beyond the reach of the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas."
Having formed this thought, he immediately entered that meditative absorption. At that time, the bhikṣus said to one another:
"Venerable sirs, you should know!
The Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, abides in his own absorption; we too may abide in our own absorptions."
He then entered his own meditative absorption.
When the night had turned to dawn, the World-Honored One emerged from that concentration; the great assembly had all gathered, and the Buddha took his seat among them.

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes to bare his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha:

"Venerable World-Honored One, you have repeatedly praised those bhikṣus by the River of Supreme Wisdom and expressed your desire to see them; yet, though those bhikṣus have all come here, they have not received your inquiry."
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
I have already finished speaking with those people; we have mutually comforted one another according to the noble speech and the noble Dharma and Vinaya.”
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I do not yet understand what is meant by ‘the noble speech, the discipline, and the mutual greetings of the Dharma.
[The Buddha replied: “Ānanda!”

Just as I, together with all the bhikṣus, having washed our feet outside the door, entered the rooms one after another and sat down upon our seats, each sitting upright and abiding in present-moment mindfulness, I entered the first dhyāna;
the bhikṣus by the riverbank likewise entered the first dhyāna.

Emerging from the first dhyāna, I entered the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; then I entered the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness; and finally I entered the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The bhikṣus by the river did likewise, following me as I entered and emerged from these various meditative absorptions.
Emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I entered the sphere of nothingness;
then I further entered the first dhyāna, and these bhikṣus likewise entered up to the first dhyāna.
Ānanda! I had this thought:
‘I should now enter the first dhyāna by means of another mode of appearance, such that it would not be within the range of experience of Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas.’”
Having formed this thought, he immediately entered that meditative absorption.

At that time, the bhikṣus by the riverbank said to one another, "The Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, abides in his own meditative absorption; we too should abide in our own meditative absorptions."
"Ānanda! This is what is called mutual consolation through the noble speech and the noble Dharma and Vinaya; having offered such consolation, I [have finished].
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, Great Virtue!
You have comforted me with noble words and the noble Dharma and Vinaya.
It is most excellent, Blessed One!”
"The Noble One comforts the noble Dharma and Vinaya.

After the Blessed One had thus comforted the bhikṣus by the river with the noble language and the noble Dharma and Vinaya, the sound spread everywhere, and people from all directions said to one another:
"The Buddha is comforting the assembly of bhikṣus by the river with the noble language and the noble Dharma and Vinaya."

Having heard this news, the various householders and brahmins all came to pay homage to the bhikṣus by the riverbank; however, as these bhikṣus were proclaiming the essential points of the Dharma for the householders and brahmins, foul breath issued from their mouths.
At that time, those people looked around to left and right and said to one another,
"From where does this foul odor come?
The bhikṣus replied:
"This foul odor issues from my mouth," he said,
addressing him: "Noble One!"
"How can it be that you do not chew tooth-sticks every day? He replied, "I do not."
He asked, "For what reason? The bhikṣus replied:
"The Buddha has not yet granted permission. He replied, "Noble One!"
"Can one attain purification without chewing a tooth-stick?
At that time, the bhikṣus remained silent and offered no reply.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“The reproach made by that brahmin householder was entirely appropriate.
In another place, I have already instructed the bhikṣus to chew tooth-sticks, yet you were unaware of this; therefore, I now decree that all bhikṣus should chew tooth-sticks.”
Why is this? There are five benefits to chewing a tooth-stick. What are these five?
First, it can eliminate jaundice;
second, it can remove phlegm and mucus;
third, it ensures that the mouth has no foul odor.
"Fourth, one can consume food and drink;
fifth, the eyes become clear and bright.
The Buddha prescribed that bhikṣus should chew a tooth-stick every day. At that time, a young bhikṣu was chewing a short piece of wood in a public place.
When the Blessed One arrived there, the bhikṣu felt deep shame upon seeing the Buddha and said,
"I ought not to have spat out my tooth-stick before the Blessed One."
He immediately swallowed it, and it became stuck in his throat.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that they never lose mindfulness; at that time, the World-Honored One extended his left hand—which was produced from immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits, marked with the revolving *svastika*, capable of removing fear and bestowing peace—and grasped the youth’s head. He bent a finger of his right hand and inserted it into the youth’s mouth, hooking out the tooth-stick along with the blood.
The Blessed One asked,
"What have you done? The bhikṣu reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
“There are such faults for one who chews a tooth-stick in an open place.
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“A certain youth, while chewing a short tooth-stick in an open place, gave rise to this fault.”
"Therefore, monks, one should not chew a tooth-stick in a public place, nor should it be a short piece. Any monk who violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

Regarding the Buddha's instruction that a monk should not sit in a public place to chew a tooth-stick, there was at that time a young monk who sat before an elder to chew his tooth-stick. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
"There are three matters that may be done in a secluded place:
namely, defecating, urinating, and chewing a tooth-stick.

When the Buddha stated that one should not use short pieces as tooth-sticks, the group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) began using long pieces as tooth-sticks. Upon seeing this, the other bhikṣus were filled with resentment and reproached them, saying:
“Venerable ones!
Do you perhaps intend to play with sticks?
They replied:
"In Buddhism, rinsing the mouth is a ritual; how can it be considered a frivolous play?
Have you not seen how one who was nearly at the point of death while chewing a short tooth-stick was saved by the Buddha's protection and preserved his remaining lifespan?"
"How could it be that you have some desire regarding my robes and bowl,
wishing for me to die early so that we may perform the *karmavācanā* together?
However, there is a beneficial purpose for long-toothed wood:"
"First, you may light the cauldron to cook rice;
second, you may whip the junior disciples.
Upon hearing this, they all remained silent.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not use a long strip as a tooth-stick; one who chews a long strip commits a *vyatikrama* offense.
The bhikṣus did not know the proper length for a tooth-stick, so the Buddha said:
“There are three kinds of these: namely, long, medium, and short.
The long is twelve finger-breadths; the short is eight finger-breadths; those between the two are called medium.

When the Buddha said that one should chew the tooth-stick in a secluded place, there were at that time those who were old, sick, or frail, and unable to go to a hidden, secluded spot. The Buddha said:
"A sick person should be permitted to keep a basin for rinsing the mouth.

The bhikṣus then used ordinary earthenware basins and placed them inside their rooms; however, when they were touched by feet, the basins would tip over, and the flowing water would soil the floor. The Buddha said:
"The basin for rinsing the mouth should be shaped like an elephant's footprint."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who sought a basin but found no place for it.
The Buddha said, "One should chew the tooth-stick near the water drain.
The bhikṣu chewed it from a distance, not close to the mouth of the drain. The Buddha said:
"One should keep it within one cubit of the edge.
When the Buddha taught that one should chew a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), the bhikṣus did not know how to scrape their tongues; consequently, their mouths remained foul-smelling. The Buddha said:
"Having finished chewing the tooth-stick, one must scrape the tongue."
The bhikṣus did not know with what to scrape their tongues.
The Buddha said:
"You should keep a tongue-scraper."

The Buddha permitted the keeping of ear-pickers; consequently, the group of six bhikṣus fashioned them from gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. When the brahmins and householders saw them, they asked, "Noble ones!..."
"What is this? He replied, "O worthy one!"
The World-Honored One has ordered me to use a tongue-scraper. He said,
“Do you, a śramaṇa son of the Śākyas, crave sensual pleasures?”
The group of six monks remained silent.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There are four kinds of tongue-scrapers that a bhikṣu should keep."
"What are the four?
They are copper, iron, brass, and red copper.
At that time, the bhikṣus made them sharp, and they injured their tongues while scraping them. The Buddha said:
"One should not use it for sharpening.
However, as these four types of tooth-sticks are difficult to find, the Buddha said:
"One should split a tooth-stick, bend it, and use it to scrape the tongue."
The bhikṣus split the tooth-sticks and used them directly, which caused sores on their tongues. The Buddha said:
"After splitting the tooth-stick, rub the two pieces against each other; once the splinters have been removed, you may then use it."
After the bhikṣu had finished chewing his tooth-stick, he did not know to make a sound and discarded it in silence; it consequently fell upon the head of a protective deity of the monastery.
The deity felt resentment and shame. The Buddha said:
"One must not discard it in silence; one should make a sound. If one does not make a sound, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma."

The bhikṣus made a sound only when discarding a single item, such as a tooth-stick, but they did not make a sound when discarding anything else, such as during the time of defecation or urination, or when spitting, vomiting, purging, or spitting out water.
The Buddha said: "In all such matters involving the discarding of things, one must make a sound."

Since the Great Master had established the rule that one must always chew tooth-sticks, the bhikṣus, while traveling on the road, were unable to find them when they urgently needed them and consequently did not eat. The Buddha said:
"One should not abstain from food."

If tooth-sticks are unavailable, one should use soap-nut powder, earth, or dried cow dung; having rinsed the mouth thoroughly with water three times, one may eat as desired without further hesitation.
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra had two śrāmaṇeras:
one was Cunda, and the other was Rāhula.
Later, at another time, the Venerable Śāriputra, wishing to travel among the people of the human realm, said to his two disciples:
"I wish to wander freely among the people; will you two remain here?"
"Are you going?
Cunda replied, "Upādhyāya, I wish to follow you."
Rāhula said, "Upādhyāya, I am staying here. Śāriputra replied:
"If this is so, to whom shall you entrust me?
He replied, "I shall entrust myself to the Venerable Udāyin; I will dwell in dependence upon him."
He replied: "Rāhula! He is an evil man; I fear he will act unlawfully."
He replied, "Upādhyāya!
I regard him as my father; how could he do anything wicked?"
He then entrusted him with the task of traveling among the people.
Just after he had departed, Udāyin said to Rāhula,
"Come here and perform such-and-such a deed."
He replied, "I did not. Udāyin spoke angrily:
"You fool! If you will not even do this, how could you ever be willing to do anything else? Rāhula replied:
"Are you perhaps my preceptor or my teacher? Udāyin’s anger flared up even more;
he seized him by the neck, pushed him out through the temple door, and stood outside the gate weeping.
At that time, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī arrived with five hundred female disciples to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet;
seeing him weeping, she asked, “Noble Rāhula, for what reason are you weeping?”
She replied, "Gautami!
The Venerable Udāyin gripped my neck with his hand and pushed me out of the monastery."
He thought to himself:
"I ought not now to abandon the Son of the Buddha and go elsewhere.
He immediately stood there, surrounded by his disciples.
Next, the Great King Prasenajit, Lord of Kośala, intending to enter the grove to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet, saw Rāhula and engaged in the same dialogue as before. The king thought to himself:
"I ought not now to abandon the Son of the Buddha and the Mother of the Buddha to go elsewhere."
They immediately stood surrounding him.
Next, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada also entered the grove and paid homage at the Buddha’s feet; seeing Rāhula, he engaged in the same dialogue as before. The householder thought to himself:
"I ought not now to abandon the Son of the Buddha, the Mother of the Buddha, and the Great King, the sovereign of the land, to go elsewhere."
They immediately surrounded him and stood there.
At that time, a great crowd had gathered outside the gate, creating a clamor.
The World-Honored One, the Great Teacher, knowing this, intentionally asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"Why is there such a great clamor with many people gathered outside the gate?
Venerable Ānanda respectfully reported all these matters to the Blessed One.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Is it true that there is a bhikṣu who has driven another bhikṣu out of the monastery? He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"This is indeed the case. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"A bhikṣu may exercise authority only over his own cell, not over the entire monastery. He must not drive another bhikṣu out of the monastery; one who violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (dharma-āpatti)."

Since the Blessed One had prohibited the expulsion of bhikṣus from outside the monastery, the bhikṣus did not dare to reprimand their own disciples or followers; consequently, they became negligent regarding the rules and were unwilling to practice them. The Buddha said:
"They must indeed be reprimanded."
The bhikṣus did not know how to reprove him.
The Buddha said:
"There are five methods of reproving:..."
First, not speaking with them;
second, not instructing them;
third, not sharing in communal use.
Fourth, to obstruct their wholesome activities;
fifth, to refuse to grant them formal reliance (*niśraya*).
Regarding "not speaking together," this refers to not engaging in verbal exchange through questions and answers.
"To not provide instruction" means that one does not offer guidance regarding matters of benefit or harm.
"To not share in the same enjoyments" means that one should not accept any service or offerings, nor should there be any exchange of food, clothing, or the Dharma.
"Prohibiting virtuous activities" means not allowing any practice of wholesome qualities or superior deeds to be performed.
"Withdrawing the support" refers to severing the relationship of mutual dependence between teacher and disciple, such that they no longer share the same quarters.
Regarding what the Buddha said concerning those who should be rebuked: if a bhikṣu rebukes someone without first investigating the matter, the Buddha said:
"One should not rebuke someone immediately upon the occurrence of the matter."
If there are five conditions, only then should one reprove them. What are these five?
First, lack of faith;
Second is indolence;
third is harsh speech;
fourth is a lack of shame and remorse.
"Fifth, associating with evil friends.
At that time, the bhikṣus would only begin to reprimand [the offender] when these five conditions were met; if they were not all met, they would not reprimand him. The Buddha said:
"If even one of these five conditions is present, you must immediately reprimand him."
When the disciples were being rebuked, other bhikṣus proceeded to take them under their protection. The Buddha said:

"If, when one is being rebuked by one's preceptor or instructor, others provide protection with the intent to cause division, this is a means for breaking the Saṃgha and constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense."

The Buddha said that he should not be accepted. At that time, the bhikṣus all refused him; because of this, the difficult-to-tame man became even less respectful, and some left the country while others returned to lay life. The Buddha said:
"One should have the bhikṣus instruct him in repentance so that he may develop a mind of respect."
He then dispatched one who was unskilled to that person's side and said:
"Venerable One!
Your preceptor summons you to seek his favor."
He became even more arrogant. The Buddha said, "A skillful bhikṣu should be instructed to teach him how to repent and cause him to give rise to a profound and earnest resolve.

At that time, when his original teacher saw him come to offer an apology, he did not exercise discernment but immediately accepted and pardoned him; consequently, the student was unable to progress in wholesome qualities.
Furthermore, there was a youth who, because of this, returned to the secular life; the Buddha said:
"One should perform *kṣamā* (confession) when endowed with five qualities:
first, having faith;"
Second, they exert diligence;
third, they give rise to reverence;
fourth, their mouths utter pleasant words.
"Fifth, associating with virtuous friends.
The Buddha said:

"Among these five, even if one possesses only some of them, it is still permissible to perform confession (kṣamāpana). However, it is not appropriate for bhikṣus to reprimand those who do not deserve reprimand; those who do so commit an offense against the Dharma (dharmātikrama)."
To fail to reprove one who deserves reproval is also a transgression of the Dharma;
to tolerate one who should not be tolerated is a transgression of the Dharma;
and to fail to tolerate one who should be tolerated is likewise a transgression of the Dharma.
If any of the five factors of the aforementioned dark side manifest, and the person shows no reverence in their mind, they should be expelled;
however, if it is known that they harbor kindness and compliance, they should be forgiven.
"If one possesses the five black dharmas, they may be expelled; if they are not expelled, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The Buddha commanded that they be expelled, and they were immediately expelled naked. The Buddha said:
"They should not be made to leave naked."
If it is a śrāmaṇera, one should provide him with a water filter, a water flask, and the two robes (upper and lower), and only then allow him to depart.

If it is one who has received full ordination, or one intended for full ordination, one should provide him with the six requisites and dismiss him from the monastery; he must not be allowed to leave in his bare body. The six requisites are: the three robes, a sitting mat, a water filter, and a water flask.
"You possess two things, namely pure contact.
The summary verse for the fourth section of the third gate says:
Building monasteries, installing eaves and nets, and extensively arranging places for sweeping the ground.
Seeking the Dharma, two youths spoke; in the heat, one should construct a dwelling.
The occasion was at Śrāvastī.

As the Buddha had said, bedding under a tree is pure and easy to obtain; a bhikṣu may rely on this for going forth and receiving full ordination (upasaṃpadā) to become a bhikṣu. If a long-term benefit such as a separate room or a multi-storied pavilion is obtained, all of these may be accepted.
When a bhikṣu was constructing a monastery but failed to install a foundation and steps, nor a projecting eave, the Buddha said:

"First, one should install a foundation and steps reaching up to the height of the knees. Upon this, place thick planks and erect pillars; then install the bracket-sets, capitals, beams, and rafters in their proper sequence. Lay flat boards on top, and cover the boards with bricks. Over these, again mix crushed bricks with mud and ram it down very firmly; finally, apply a coating of lime plaster mixed with salt."
Since it is so for the first layer, one should understand the others by analogy: having installed the railing, one should fasten cross-beams and nails to the pillars to prevent them from falling.
At that time, when the bhikṣus were eating there, birds and sparrows came and disturbed them; therefore, one should install a net.
Not knowing what constitutes a net, the Buddha said: "There are five kinds of nets: [the net of desire, the net of form, the net of existence, the net of views, and the net of ignorance]."
"They are made from hemp, ramie,芒 (máng), reed, and the bark of the mulberry tree, etc.
Although they were able to make nets, they did not know how to install them. The Buddha said:
"Attach small iron rings to the four corners of the net; use a convenient method to hang it up so that it does not rot from the rain."
"Later, when birds still enter while he is eating this food, cover it with an object; once he has finished eating, open it again.
While the bhikṣu was eating, a dog came and stood before him, hoping for leftover scraps. The bhikṣu gave nothing to it, and its hopes being frustrated, the dog died.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Whenever you eat, set aside one handful of food as an offering for the animals.

At that time, whatever food and drink the forest-dwelling bhikṣu produced, he gave it only to the jackal, excluding the other crows and birds. The crow then became resentful and, making its own cawing sound, addressed the bandit leader, saying:
"There are many gold treasures with the bhikṣus in the forest.
The thief understood the language of crows; he went to where the bhikṣu was and demanded gold from him, to which the bhikṣu replied, "I have none."
He immediately struck and reviled him, whereupon the bhikṣu said: "Alas, O man!
For what reason do you strike me?"
He replied, "You possess much gold; why do you not give some to me? The bhikṣu said:
“I dwell in the forest; where could I have obtained gold?
Please do not strike me unjustly.
The bandit said:
"You certainly have gold; if you do not give it to me, I shall surely take your life.
The bhikṣu said, "One who harbors anger toward me has falsely made these words; he must certainly be my enemy. I pray that you will report this truthfully."
The thief said, "The crow told me. The bhikṣu said:
"Because he harbors resentment. He asked,
"For what reason?"
The bhikṣu recounted the preceding events in full.
The bandit leader said,
"Venerable sir, had you not told me everything, I would certainly have executed you unjustly."
Having realized this, he released it.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"When a bhikṣu practices giving with a narrow-minded focus, such faults arise. Therefore, you should know that when setting aside food, one should give universally to all living beings and not restrict it to a single class."

One may moisten the rice with water; as for the cakes, they must be broken into small pieces and scattered upon the ground. One should eat them as one pleases and must not prevent others from doing so.
If one does prevent them, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
When a bhikṣu was building a dwelling, rain fell and water flowed in from the sides of the eaves, causing damage. The Buddha said:
"One should construct a hanging screen to block it."
The bhikṣus did not know how to construct a screen.
The Buddha said:
"Use wooden boards."
He then blocked it entirely, causing the area to fall into darkness. The Buddha said:
"One should not block it entirely; a space for light should be left.
However, it was difficult to find suitable boards.
The Buddha said:
"Mats made of reeds and the like may be used temporarily as screens.
Once they became damp from the rain, insects and ants began to breed; the Buddha then said:
"It is safe during the summer rains; at other times, one should depart.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-ksudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 13. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-ksudraka-vastu*.
Volume Fourteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
The Third Section, Fourth Sub-section: The Remaining Verses of the Summary (Uddāna); the Setting is the Same as Before.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada would go every morning to the Jeta Grove to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One; having paid his respects, he would sweep the grounds of the monastery.

On one occasion, the householder was unable to enter the monastery due to other business. As the World-Honored One was walking to and fro, he saw that the ground was not clean and, giving rise to a worldly thought, he reflected thus:
"How can I cause Śakra, Lord of the Devas, to come from Mount Gandhamādana bringing a broom?"
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they give rise to a mundane mind, even ants know their intention;
yet if they give rise to a supramundane mind, even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot comprehend it, let alone others who could fathom it.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having perceived this through his divine knowledge, thought to himself:
"For what reason has the Great Teacher given rise to a mundane thought?
He then saw that the World-Honored One was personally desiring to sweep the grounds of the Jeta Grove.
Having understood the Buddha’s intention, he went to Mount Gandhamādana and took five hundred exquisite brooms, as light and soft as cotton, and stood before the Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause those beings who delight in merit to plant pure karma within the supreme field [of merit], personally took up a broom and intended to sweep the grove.
At that time, the great śrāvakas—Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Ānanda, and the others—having witnessed this event, all took up brooms and together swept the grove.
Then the Buddha, the World-Honored One, together with his noble disciples, having finished sweeping everywhere, entered the dining hall and took their seats.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five benefits for one who sweeps the ground."
What are the five?
First, the purification of one's own mind;
second, the purification of the minds of others.
Third, all the devas will rejoice;
fourth, one plants the karma for physical excellence;
fifth, after the end of this life, one shall be reborn in the heavens.

Later, when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada entered the grove, he heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, along with his great disciples, had personally taken up brooms to sweep the entire grove. He then thought to himself:
"The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, and the assembly of noble ones have personally taken up brooms to sweep the Jetavana Grove."
"How would we dare to tread upon it with our feet?
At that time, the elder stood there unable to move forward out of shame and trepidation. Knowing this, the Buddha intentionally asked the bhikṣus, "Who is standing there?"
The bhikṣu replied, "Venerable Sir! This is the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Having heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the great disciples were each personally holding brooms to sweep the Jetavana Grove, he was overcome with shame and trepidation; he stood right there and did not dare to move forward."
The Buddha told the householder:
"You should proceed while reciting the sūtras and the Dharma.
Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, reveres the Dharma, all the Arhats likewise revere the Dharma.
The elder then recited a verse and proceeded to the place where the Buddha was; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the sublime Dharma for him, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him.
At that time, having heard the Dharma, the elder departed with joyful leaps after paying his respects.
Then all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"How extraordinary, O Great Virtuous One!"
"You have personally conceived a mind of respect for the True Dharma, praising and honoring it.

The Buddha said, "Now, the Tathāgata is free from passion, hatred, and delusion; he is far removed from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and suffering; he possesses all-knowledge and has attained mastery over all objects. That you hold the Dharma in high esteem and praise the True Dharma is not yet considered rare."

"You all should know that in the past, while I was still possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion; had not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, and death; and was currently subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction—I sacrificed my own life for the sake of the Dharma."
Listen well now, and I shall explain it to you.

Long ago, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who ruled the world according to the Dharma; the people were numerous, peaceful, secure, and prosperous, as has been described at length elsewhere.

At that time, King Brahmadatta had deep faith in the True Dharma; by nature he was virtuous and benevolent, benefiting both himself and others. He felt compassion for all beings and constantly practiced giving; possessing great loving-kindness and compassion, he was free from attachment and never harbored any stinginess.
Later, at another time, the king’s principal queen suddenly became pregnant; she then conceived a strange thought and desired to hear the sublime Dharma. The queen said to the king:
"Your Majesty, command a physiognomist to inquire into the reason for this."
He addressed the King, saying:
"It was because of the noble embryo conceived by the Chief Queen that such a thought arose.

Thereupon, the Great King immediately sought the Dharma; he commanded his ministers to fill chests with gold and distribute it throughout the entire realm to offer for the sake of the Dharma, yet in the end he did not achieve his heart's desire.
When the moon was full, he gave birth to a son whose countenance was transcendent and who was endowed with all the marks; the details are as described elsewhere.
The king thought to himself:
"This child is handsome and pleasing to behold; even before his birth, he longed for the sublime Dharma. Now that my kinsmen have gathered together, what name shall we give him?"
The ministers addressed him, saying:
"Since the prince, even before his birth, longed for the sublime Dharma, he should be given the name 'Seeker of the Sublime Dharma' (Dharmapriya).

The King ordered eight nurses to nourish and attend to him, as described at length elsewhere, until he was like a lotus emerging from the water; as he gradually grew older, he constantly sought the sublime Dharma, yet ultimately his heart’s desire was not fulfilled.
After the king passed away, he succeeded to the throne and addressed his ministers, saying:
"You must seek the Sublime Dharma for my sake.
Having received this command, the ministers took golden caskets and traveled throughout Jambudvīpa, searching everywhere, yet they could find no such Dharma.
The minister addressed the king, saying:
"We have searched everywhere, yet no such dharma can be found.
At that time, King Dharmagaveṣin, his wish unfulfilled, was constantly filled with grief and distress.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, perceived through his divine insight that the king was harboring distress for the sake of seeking the Dharma; he then thought to himself:
"Though the king acts thus, it is not yet known whether he is sincere or false; I should go and test him."
He then transformed himself into a great yakṣa, raising his hands and staring with wide eyes in a terrifying form; standing before the king, he spoke this verse:
"Those who constantly cultivate wholesome dharmas And do not commit any evil deeds, Will always enjoy peace and happiness Both in this life and in future births, whether awake or asleep."
Upon hearing this verse, the king was filled with great joy and said to the yakṣa,
"Virtuous one, please recite this gāthā for me once more.
Thereupon, the yakṣa replied to the king:
"If the King will follow my words, I shall explain them for him. The King said, "So be it."
"I pray that you will proclaim it for me; I shall follow your words without opposition.

Then the yakṣa said, "Great King, if you truly delight in the Dharma, you may prepare a fire pit and cast yourself into it after burning charcoal for seven days and seven nights until fierce flames arise; I shall then preach it to you again."
Upon hearing these words, the king’s joy redoubled, and he replied to the yakṣa,
"I shall not dare to disobey.
The king immediately issued a proclamation to be made known throughout the kingdom:
"Because I delight in hearing the sublime Dharma, seven days from now I shall enter a fire pit; all those with a karmic connection who desire to behold such a rare wonder may come to see me."
Once the decree had been proclaimed, the entire kingdom came to know of it, and immeasurable sentient beings all arrived at the appointed time.

Moved by the king’s profound reverence for the Dharma and his utmost sincerity, there were further immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas in the void, playing drums and music, singing songs, and making offerings of incense and flowers to celebrate this rare event; all gathered together, moved by the king’s profound sincerity.
When the yakṣa’s seven days had elapsed, he ascended into the air and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"The appointed time has arrived; you may now enter the fire pit.

At that moment, the Great King established his crown prince to succeed him to the throne and summoned all his ministers to offer their congratulations. Together they took their leave, and as he drew near the fire pit and stood upon its edge, he spoke this verse:
“‘Such a blazing pit of great fire, with crimson flames like the sun that terrifies all people—I now joyfully cast myself into it;
for the sake of the Dharma, I have never felt regret or fear.’”
Although I now stand within this pit of fire, I shall resolutely seek a rare and wondrous thing:
may the merit of this act support all sentient beings, and may these fierce flames be transformed into a sublime lotus pond.
When the Great King had finished speaking these verses, he threw himself into the fire pit.
As soon as his body descended, the great fire pit was transformed into a lotus pond, cool and lovely; at that moment, the Bodhisattva’s body remained unhurt.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing that this was a rare occurrence and that humans and devas were paying him homage, resumed his form as Śakra and spoke these verses once more to the king:
"Always cultivate wholesome dharmas, And do not commit any evil deeds;
In this life and in future births, One shall always be at peace, both waking and sleeping."

At that time, having received these verses, the Bodhisattva emerged from the pond, inscribed them upon golden leaves, and distributed them throughout all the cities, towns, and villages of Jambudvīpa, making them known to all so that everyone might practice and study them.

"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any doubt: the King Dharmaparyeṣin of that past time was none other than myself. For the sake of seeking the Dharma, I even cast away my own life; how much more so now, when one should not fail to show reverence for the sublime and wondrous Dharma?"
Therefore, you all should practice and study this.

I shall revere, make offerings to, honor, and praise the sublime Dharma; thus, dwelling with sincerity according to the Dharma, one will be fully endowed with both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

As the Blessed One had said that there are five benefits to sweeping the ground, some elderly bhikṣus abandoned their practice of meditation and recitation and entered the Jeta Grove to sweep the ground themselves.
The Buddha said: "I spoke thus regarding those in charge of administrative affairs, not regarding the elder bhikṣus who are practitioners."
"However, for those who have gone forth in the noble Dharma and Vinaya that I rely upon, there are two types of activities:
first, the practice of meditative concentration; second, recitation and study.
When the bhikṣus heard the Buddha making this secret statement regarding the *karmadāna*, the *karmadāna* was unable to sweep the entire grounds of Jetavana.
The Buddha said:
"One should sweep according to necessity.
On the eighth or fifteenth day of the month, one should strike the *ghanṭī* and assemble the entire community of monks to perform the sweeping together."

At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣus engaged in talk concerning worldly matters while sweeping the ground. Consequently, the guardian deities of the monastery, non-human beings, and other members of the Dharma assembly heard these frivolous discussions and gave rise to feelings of disdain and contempt.
The Buddha said, "You should not do so; you should either speak the Dharma or maintain noble silence.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had finished sweeping the ground, dust covered their bodies. When people who lacked faith and respect saw this, they felt contempt and disdain. The Buddha said:
"Once the floor has been swept and the filth removed, one should wash the body.
If one does not wash, one should moisten the hands with water and wipe away the dust and grime.
Washing the hands and rinsing the feet should be done as is customary."
The Buddha said:
"On every eighth and fifteenth day, one should inspect the bedding and seats.
When the bhikṣus performed this task collectively, the Buddha said:
"It should not be done so. You should have your disciples examine it thoroughly, for fear there may be fleas, lice, or filth.

As the Buddha had said, when he saw that people were treading upon the ground after it had been swept clean while they were reciting scriptures, the bhikṣus sprinkled the ground and then swept it cleanly to create a maṇḍala; when others saw this, they did not dare to step upon it with their feet. The Buddha said:
"One should recite a gāthā and then step over [the threshold], for there is no offense; do not harbor doubts.
One should know that this applies to all incense altars, palaces, flagpoles, caityas, and the images or shadows of the Tathāgata: one must recite a gāthā before stepping upon them with one's feet."
"If you do not do so, you shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

At that time, there was a king in the north who sent two youths to King Prasenajit as a national gift: one named Bhaddālika and the other named Puṇḍalika. Of these, Bhaddālika was skilled in preparing food and drink, while Puṇḍalika was proficient in arranging beds and seats.
Generally, the people of frontier lands are prone to gluttony; whenever they wander about, they enter the markets and take others' fish and rice to eat as they please.
At that time, the owners of the food immediately beat them severely.
Then the two youths returned to the king’s presence and said, “Great King!
We previously went into the marketplace to fetch a small amount of fish and rice; at that time, the householders beat us severely, leaving us so exhausted that we were nearly dead.”
Having heard these words, the king issued a proclamation to the people of the market:
"You should all know that you must personally guard your own food and drink; you must not strike these two children of mine under any circumstances."

Later, at another time, after the king had concluded his court business and was resting for a while, the two boys were each on one side, massaging and moving the king’s feet. Seeing that the king did not speak, one said, "The king is asleep."
The second replied, "It is so.
Upon hearing this, the king gave rise to a thought:
"Could it be that these two are having a private conversation?
He then feigned sleep to eavesdrop on what they were saying.
At that time, Dāsaka said to Palaga:
"Is there a future world?
He replied, "How could there be a future world?"
Then Vālaka asked Dāsaka, "Is there perhaps any arhat in the world? Dāsaka replied:
"There is no fruit of arhatship in the world.
When the king heard these words from the two youths, he thought to himself:
"These two youths have both given rise to wrong views."
"One holds the view of nihilism (ucchedadṛṣṭi), and the other holds wrong views (mithyādṛṣṭi).
The king informed his ministers, and the ministers spread the word until everyone far and near within the kingdom knew that the two princes were people of evil and heterodox views.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, clearly proclaiming among the great assembly and uttering a lion’s roar, spoke these words:
"Whoever passes away within my residence shall surely be reborn in heaven."
Having heard these words, the king thought to himself:
"If the householder comes, I shall entrust these two boys to him.

Later, on another occasion, Anāthapiṇḍada came to the king's presence; he brought his young son along, carrying his own seat. Once the boy had been seated, the child immediately went outside to play with other children.
After the young boy had departed, the King thought to himself,
"Now is precisely the right time.
Entrusting the two boys to one another, he then secretly told the gatekeeper:
“Elder’s son, do not let him enter. The gatekeeper followed these instructions and would not allow him in.
After the elder had sat for a long time, he thought of returning home; rising from his seat, he looked back toward the servant boy.
The king asked,
"Householder, what do you have in mind? He replied:
“Great King! I am seeking a messenger boy.
The king said:
“Householder, I have two children whom I now entrust to you; you may take them and lead them away.
Observing the king’s intention, he accepted them with a respectful bow, and further thought to himself:
“For what reason has the Great King entrusted these two children to me?”
He further reflected, "Previously these two held wrong views; now the King has tested me and sent them away.
At that time, the elder immediately returned home with them.
Once they had arrived at the house, he commanded the steward, saying:
"Give all the things required by these two youths.
He further addressed the people at the marketplace:
"If these two youths have anything they need, you may provide it; I shall record the price clearly and repay you double."
Then the two youths went to the storehouse keeper’s quarters; they obtained everything they required according to their wishes and said to the keeper, "Will you give us everything we seek?"
He replied, "I will give them all.
The youth asked again:
“Who sent such [a message]?
He replied, “It was the householder.”
The two boys said to each other, "The elder is no different from our parents; he never refuses anything we ask for.
On another occasion, as they were walking together into the market, people saw them from afar and all called out to the two boys:
"Come to my place and eat as you please.
The two boys replied, "In the past, when we saw you from afar, each of us covered our food trays; today, when we looked from afar, you called for us all."
"It is not without reason; please explain it to us.
The men replied, "In the past, you ate one [portion] by force without paying its price. Now, the elder has returned that value twofold. It is for this reason that we have invited you to eat."
Having heard this, the two boys said to one another again,
"The elder is compassionate and looks upon us with deep affection.
They then returned and informed the elder.
"If there is any work to be done, please entrust it to me.
He replied, "Wait for now; I shall have you do it later."
Later, the householder took those two boys into the Jeta Grove and had them both take brooms to sweep the grounds of the Saṃgha.
Having some business that required him to return to his own home, he said to the two boys:
"I must depart on account of some business; you should remain here and sweep the monastery clean, removing all filth and refuse. Only after you have completed this task may you return home."
Once the ground was purified, they wished to clear away the refuse; however, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the refuse proved inexhaustible.
At that time, these two youths were filial and respectful toward their master, and they exerted all their sincerity and strength to clear the refuse without ceasing.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda,
“For these two boys, you should leave some leftover food.
Then Ānanda left some leftovers for them to eat, and the two boys thought to themselves:
"I must finish clearing away the refuse before returning home; I shall not eat this leavings-food of the noble one.

By the Buddha’s supernormal power, when he cleared the eastern side, the refuse reappeared on the western side; when he cleared the western side, it reappeared on the eastern side. Thus he labored in hardship until the sun was about to set.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"These two boys shall stay near you tonight.
You, moreover, must inform all the bhikṣus: [that they should likewise accommodate them]."
"I have previously taught that one should conceal good deeds and reveal evil ones; for the sake of causing these two youths to abandon their wrong views, it is fitting to manifest their goodness.
You bhikṣus who have attained meditative concentration, remain in such concentration throughout the first watch of the night."

When Ānanda had thus proclaimed the Buddha’s teaching, the bhikṣus immediately during the first watch of the night emitted rays of light or manifested wondrous signs. Having seen this, the two youths said to Ānanda, “What is this?”
Ānanda said, "He is an Arhat manifesting various supernatural transformations.
Then the two boys said:
“Venerable One! Are there any Arhats in the world? Ānanda replied:
"Did you two not witness this with your own eyes?
Why do you harbor doubts?
Thus, these two had previously held wrong views, claiming that there were no Arhats; now, upon seeing the supernatural power, their wrong views ceased and right view arose.
In the middle watch of the night, the Buddha gave rise to a worldly thought:
"How can I cause Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas to come here?
The detailed explanation is as above.
At that time, the hosts of devas, perceiving the Buddha’s mind, all came to where the Buddha was; due to their majestic power, there was a great radiance.
Having seen it, the two youths asked Ānanda, "What is this light?"
He replied, "This is because Brahmā,
Śakra, and the other hosts of devas have come to the Buddha's dwelling, manifesting this radiance. He asked:
“Venerable One! Is there a future world? He replied:
"Since you have seen this with your own eyes, why do you harbor doubts?

Those two youths had previously held wrong views, believing that there was no future life; now, upon seeing the celestial hosts, they immediately conceived right view at that very moment. Deeply rejoicing within themselves, they both went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, in accordance with his faculties and nature, taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; through instruction, exhortation, benefit, and joy, he caused him to attain awakening. With the vajra-wisdom mallet, he shattered the twenty kinds of mountain-like false views regarding a self-existent body and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having attained the fruit, he again prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to go forth and receive full ordination within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata, becoming a bhikṣu and diligently practicing the holy life.”
The World-Honored One then addressed them, saying:
"Welcome, Dāsaka and Palaga! Practice the holy life."

At that moment, as soon as the Buddha had spoken, the hair and beards of those two fell away of their own accord, and alms bowls and robes appeared in their hands; they were like those who had been shaved for seven days, and their deportment and dignified bearing were equal to those of a hundred-year-old monk.
The verse says:
"When the World-Honored One commanded him to come, his hair fell away and robes appeared upon his body;
his deportment was like that of a centenarian, and everything was accomplished according to the Buddha’s will."

At that time, the World-Honored One personally instructed those two bhikṣus; they practiced with diligent effort without weariness, and before long they attained the fruit of arhatship, as described in detail elsewhere, until they were venerated by all the gods, including Brahmā and Śakra.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had ordained Dāsaka and Palaga and caused them to leave the household life, King Prasenajit, having heard of these matters, felt a sense of disdain and shame, thinking:
"How is it that the World-Honored One has ordained these people of wrong views and caused them to leave the household life?"
"This is not a virtuous matter; it is known by all that this person holds such wrong views.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One thought:
"Among my assembly, my śrāvaka disciples have exhausted all afflictions, and their merit and dignity are as venerable as Mount Sumeru."
"How can the King give rise to such thoughts of contempt?
This would be a great error.
I should now manifest the superior virtues of those two individuals."
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada came, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side, listening as the Buddha taught the Dharma to instruct, benefit, and gladden him.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent.
The elder immediately rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and said:
"World-Honored One!
I pray that the Great Master and the assembly of noble ones will deign to visit my home tomorrow to accept a modest offering."
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing this, the elder prostrated to the Buddha and departed.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go and tell Dāsaka and Palaka:
'You two should go to the house of the elder tomorrow to perform the water-offering for the assembly.'"
At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the Venerable One went to the two men and delivered the Buddha’s teaching in full.
Having received the Buddha’s command, the two men replied,
“Venerable One!...”
"As the World-Honored One has instructed, I shall respectfully carry it out.
He then thought to himself:
"For what reason does the World-Honored One set aside all those of senior and middle standing, and instead show such special consideration toward us two, commanding us to serve the water?"
"Is it not that the World-Honored One wishes to manifest his supreme virtues through me?
We ought to fulfill the World-Honored One's wish.
Thereupon, that night, the elder prepared various kinds of pure and exquisite food and drink, namely the five types of solid foods and the five types of chewed foods.
Then, early in the morning, having prepared the seats and arranged the water vessels with all their ornaments, he sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The food and drink are ready; we pray that you will know the time."

At that time, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and together with the assembly of bhikṣus, proceeded to the house of the elder. Upon arriving at the place where the meal was being served, he took the seat that had been prepared.
When the great multitude had all taken their seats, the elder again dispatched a messenger to inform King Prasenajit, saying:
"Today, in my own home, I have invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a modest offering. I pray only that Your Majesty will deign to come and share in this joy."

When the king heard this, he immediately accompanied the crown prince and the ladies of the inner court as his retinue, proceeding to the house of the elder to join in the expression of sympathetic joy.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated at his feet and sat down.

At that time, the Venerable Dāsaka stood before the elder; holding a water flask in his hand, he empowered it with supernatural power so that the poured water flowed from top to bottom, allowing them to wash their hands in succession.

At that time, the Venerable Pālaka stood before the lower seats; wielding the power of spiritual mastery, he took pure water from his flask and caused it to flow in succession from the bottom to the top, rinsing their mouths one by one.
At that time, when King Prasenajit saw this event, he thought to himself:
"Who is this venerable elder bhikṣu who has dared to manifest such supernatural power in the very presence of the Buddha?"

He immediately rose and went to the side of the junior monk to look for water, where he saw Pālaka holding a water jar. He then went further to the side of the senior monk to look for water, where he saw Vatsaka standing with a water jar. Struck with great wonder, he extended his right hand and uttered words of praise:
"How marvelous, O Buddha!"
How rare is the Dharma!
How excellent is the True Dharma!
It is able to cause Dāsaka, Palaga, and others, in this very life, to abandon their sinful views and realize such supreme virtues.

When the elder saw that the great assembly was all seated, he personally served them various foods and drinks with his own hands. Once the assembly had eaten their fill, washed their hands and rinsed their mouths, and finished chewing their tooth-sticks, they set aside their alms-bowls. The elder then took a small mat and knelt before the Buddha to listen to the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to King Prasenajit and the great householder according to their capacities, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them; he then rose from his seat and departed.
When the bhikṣus had returned to their quarters, they were all filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."
What karma did these two, Dāsaka and Palaga, previously perform such that they were born in a border region—one holding nihilistic views and the other holding heterodox views?
Furthermore, what karma did they perform such that they went forth in the Buddha’s Dharma, severed all afflictions, and attained arhatship?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"These two individuals have brought to maturity the karmic results of the deeds they themselves committed. As explained at length previously, up until the point that the retribution must be experienced by oneself."
Listen attentively.
In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world.

At that time, these two individuals entered the Buddha’s Dharma to become renunciants. Traveling together as companions to a frontier country, they practiced meditative concentration on their own without a teacher to instruct them. Although they had no actual realization, they developed a sense of conviction that they had attained it. At the time of their death, they slandered the Noble Dharma and gave rise to wrong views, speaking thus:
"The Buddha Kāśyapa deceived the world; he claimed to have exhausted all afflictions and attained Arhatship."
"I have not been able to exhaustively sever all afflictions; how then could any other person have attained arhatship?
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor such doubts. Those two who practiced meditative concentration without a teacher in the past were none other than Dāsaka and Palaga."

Because they slandered the sublime Dharma and gave rise to wrong views, they fell into the evil realms for a long period of time; furthermore, throughout many lifetimes they constantly dwelt in border regions with minds inclined toward wrong views, and even in this present life, they have again been born in a border region with a mind inclined toward wrong views.

Because those two had studied, recited, and mastered the principles of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination, as well as the distinction between the possible and the impossible, through the power of that karma they went forth in my Dharma to practice, and having exhausted all afflictions, they attained arhatship.

Practicing meditative concentration without a teacher carries such faults; therefore, you should not practice concentration on your own without a teacher. If you practice it recklessly, you will incur an offense against the Dharma.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.

A certain householder had constructed a small cell in a forest hermitage, and at that time a bhikṣu resided there. Being oppressed by the heat of the spring season, his complexion became withered and yellow, and he was emaciated and lacking his usual luster. Desiring to move to another dwelling, he went to inform the householder:
"May you protect this place; I wish to travel elsewhere."
The householder asked,
"What is lacking that you wish to travel elsewhere?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I have no lack of anything; however, because it is hot at this time of year, my dwelling is somewhat difficult to inhabit.
The householder replied, "If you fear the heat, I shall construct an earthen cave for you."
He replied, "Householder! The Buddha has not yet granted us permission."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "Those who require earthen caves may build them as they please.
The elder built one for them, but when the summer months arrived, it became damp and was no longer fit to dwell in. Later, the bhikṣus said to the elder:
"I wish to travel elsewhere.
The same exchange of questions and answers took place as before; however, because the ground was damp and his phlegm-related illness had increased, he was unable to remain there.
The elder replied:
"If that is the case, we shall build a great hall.
The bhikṣu replied, "The World-Honored One has not yet permitted it."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You may build it as a large hall.
The elder then constructed it; however, because there was no eaves, the pillars were unstable and on the verge of breaking. He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Secure the eaves.
If you fear they may collapse, you should install diagonal braces and nail them down.
The summary verse for the fifth section of the third gate says:
Rock salt should be placed inside a horn; medicinal vessels should be kept on a woolen rug;
when seated upon a substitute seat while reciting the scriptures, one’s feet should be supported by an object.
This account was given while the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Pilindavatsa had been constantly afflicted by illness ever since his ordination. A fellow practitioner came to inquire after him, saying: "Elder!..."
"Are the four great elements at peace?
He replied, "I am afflicted; how could there be any peace?"
He asked again,
"Elder, what medicine have you been taking lately? He replied:
“I once consumed rock salt.
[The physician asked: “If that is so, why do you not consume it now? He replied:
"O Noble One! The Buddha has not yet granted permission.
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to keep sāmudra salt.
The bhikṣus stored it in various places, whereupon it eventually melted away. The Buddha said:
"It should not be stored in such an improvised manner; one should rather keep it in a tube."
He then placed it in a bamboo tube, but it was again lost.
The Buddha said, "One should use a horn tube to place the salt inside.
He subsequently used a new horn, which caused it to become foul-smelling. The Buddha said:
"One should wash it with water boiled with cow dung until it is dry and undamaged.
Regarding the Buddha’s instruction that rock salt should be placed inside a horn, [the monks] did not know how to place a lid on it, so dust and dirt entered;
the Buddha said: "Use a lid."
The bhikṣus did not understand; the Buddha said, "You should indeed use horn.
At that time, Pilindavatsa suffered from an ailment; as with the previous dialogue, he required a medicinal bowl, and the Buddha said:
"One should keep [a rug]. This occurred in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was an elder who, shortly after marrying, had a son. As the boy grew up, he eventually went forth into homelessness within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya; however, he slept only on an empty bed, as he did not yet possess a woolen rug or mat.
Later, when the elder entered the monastery to tour and observe, he saw that his son was lying on a single bed with no woolen rugs or mats at all.
He said, "Noble son!
All the other bhikṣus have woolen rugs and mats; why do you have none?"

He replied, "Most of these people were long-standing renunciants who came here first and have been accumulating [possessions]; I am newly renounced from the secular life, and for that reason, I have none yet. He answered:
"If that is so, my house has fine woolen carpets that could be used for spreading out and lying upon.
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet granted permission."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to use woolen rugs.

The bhikṣus then lay down on them without any cloth beneath, and as they slept naked upon them, they became covered in much grime and oiliness. When a householder entered the monastery and saw their filthy condition, he did not recognize them and asked his son:
