"Did you obtain another mattress?
He replied, "It is the old one."
The father asked,
"For what reason has she become so defiled? She replied:
"Because there was no protective lining, it has become soiled.
His father said, "This is an expensive item; you should now use it with a protective lining."
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Even though it is one’s private property, one must still place a lining beneath it; if one does not do so, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.”
The setting is the same as before.
The Buddha said,
"Those who are to recite the sūtras should ascend the high seat."
When that person sat upon the lion throne, his two feet hung down and became weary.
The Buddha said, "A footstool should be made.
The bhikṣus did not understand; the Buddha said:
"If the seat is not to be moved, it should be made of brick; if it is to be moved about, it may be made of wooden boards.
Although it is difficult to lift when made of boards, one may attach iron rings to each of the four corners so that it can be carried away at will."
At that time, there were monks seeking merit and lay travelers with faith who smeared fragrant mud upon the tops of his feet. The reciter of the sūtras did not dare to step on them. The Buddha said:
"One should place grass or leaves beneath them before stepping; do not harbor any doubts."
The setting was as before. The Buddha said, "Construct a footstool.
The bhikṣus in the forest found such an object difficult to obtain, and their feet became weary from hanging down; they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Use stones to support your feet.
The sixth section of the third door, summarized in verse, says:
A thin and coarse face-towel, a spittoon along with a body-cushion,
an iron trough for the foundation of the site, and a sun-crystal for washing clothes.
The circumstances of these matters occurred in Rājagṛha.

Pilindavatsa was constantly afflicted by illness, and his head and face were greasy and unclean. The questions and answers were the same as before, until [the Buddha] asked, "What did you previously carry, Elder?
He replied, "I carried a face-towel."
"Why do you not carry it now?
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet granted permission."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Whether one is ill or not ill, one should carry a face cloth.
The circumstances of the setting were the same as before.
Pilindavatsa’s body was yellow from the heat; the questions and answers were the same as before, until [the Buddha asked], "What did you previously wear, Elder?
He replied, "I wore thin, light clothing."
"Why do you not carry it now?
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet granted permission."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"During the heat, one should wear thin and light clothing.
This occurred in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu suffering from phlegm who discharged saliva and mucus on both sides of his bed, leaving it unclean.
As dawn was about to break, a disciple entered the room to pay respects and inquire after his well-being; the disciple’s forehead became smeared with the mucus and spittle.
When the bhikṣu saw him and questioned him, he answered according to the facts.
The bhikṣu said,
"I shall examine it for myself."
He then entered the room and saw that snot and spittle were scattered in disarray upon the edge of the bed; he informed the bhikṣus, causing them all to feel disgust and shame:
"How can a bhikṣu spit and sneeze such impurities within the monastic quarters?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This is not a place where mucus or saliva should be discarded; one must not discard them there.
If one is in the dark and does not strike the ground with one's head to perform prostration, but must nevertheless pay respect, one should say with the mouth:"
"Vandana. Whenever one has a request to make, it should always be done in this manner.
If one suffers from a cold such that saliva and nasal mucus flow out, one should receive them with a vessel.
When placing vessels, they became tilted and became even more defiled. The Buddha said, "You may place them on a support.
They placed them on a circular cord, yet they still tilted; the Buddha said:

"As for the spittoon and the vessel for rinsing the mouth, their shape should be like an elephant's footprint with the bottom convex and facing inward; they should be placed on the ground so that they are stable.
When discarding the spit-water, one should immediately withdraw [the vessel]. The Buddha said:
"Place an object inside the basin."
The bhikṣus did not understand; the Buddha said:
"One should cut grass and place it inside, or put sand, soil, and so forth.
When many flies settled upon it, the Buddha said:
"You should fan it away.
When there was a foul odor in the basin, the Buddha said:
"It should be washed from time to time."
After washing them, he did not dry them in the sun, which caused insects to breed.
The Buddha said, "Dry them in the sun.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu whose saliva would not stop flowing; while waiting for the vessel to dry, his affairs were neglected. The Buddha said:
"One should keep two basins and use them alternately.

When a bhikṣu was reciting scriptures or walking in meditation beneath the eaves and happened to spit or discharge nasal mucus, he discarded it wherever he stood. The Buddha said: "You should not do so;
one who discards it in such a manner incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (vayatikrama)."
"However, within the monastery, a spittoon should be placed beneath each of the pillars at the four corners; if there is anyone who needs to spit, they may discard it here.
This account took place in the city of Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Lomaśoṇita (Hair-and-Blood). In five hundred previous lifetimes, whether being born or dying, he had constantly dwelt in hell. Later, having been reborn in the human realm within a household, he was always fond of adorning his body and indulging in play and pleasure without satiety, never thinking of hell.

Later, at another time, he left the household life to practice within the Buddha-dharma. Seeing the Buddha preaching the Dharma, he heard the teachings of the Tripitaka concerning the sufferings of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and the distinctions between humans and devas. When he heard about the hells, the extreme suffering became manifest before him; blood flowed from all the pores of his body, his robes were stained with it, and they constantly emitted a foul odor.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "A bhikṣu such as this should keep an undergarment.
The bhikṣus then wore it over their outer robes, which led to public derision and censure; the Buddha then said:
"One should wear it inside.
When his body was itchy and he used this robe to rub against it,
the Buddha said, "One should not do so."

"If there is thick blood, one should prepare a decoction with tree leaves and wash it away slowly; as for the undergarment worn next to the body, it should be washed, dyed, and sun-dried at regular intervals.
This account was given while residing in Rājagṛha.
The Venerable Pilindavatsa was constantly afflicted by illness. His fellow practitioners questioned him as before, up until the point where they asked: "What did the Elder previously carry?"
He replied, "I once used an iron trough to hold medicinal decoctions for immersion.
[The Buddha asked,] "If that is so, why did you not bring it with you?"
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet granted permission.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A sick person should keep an iron trough.
This occurred in Śrāvastī.
At that time, when the rainy season was upon them, the bhikṣus circumambulated the caitya with their feet soiled by mud. The Buddha said:
"One should lay down bricks, strike them with mud mixed with crushed bricks on top, and then apply a coating of lime mortar.
As the stupa was large and difficult to cover entirely, the Buddha said:
"It should be leveled to the height of one fathom."
"This too is difficult to procure," [the monks said].
The Buddha said, "Use wooden boards.
Again, these were difficult to find, so the Buddha said:
"Place bricks at every step.
As the monastery gates and the grounds within the monastery were often muddy and treacherous, the Buddha said:
"One should act according to the principle as described above."
The setting was as before.
A certain householder had constructed a small hut in a quiet grove, where a bhikṣu resided.
It being the season of cold, the bhikṣu’s body became emaciated from the chill; he came and said to the householder:
"I wish to travel elsewhere. He replied, "Noble One!"
"Is there anything lacking?
He replied, "There is no shortage,
but it is simply because of the bitter cold."
The elder said, "Virtuous one, stay here; I shall give you a sun-crystal so that you may always obtain fire. He replied:
"Householder! The Buddha has not yet granted permission. He replied:
"The Buddha, out of great compassion, will surely permit its use.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one requires a sun-gem (sūryakānta-maṇi), it is permitted to keep it so that fire may be produced at any time."
The householder then gave it to the bhikṣu for his use.
At that time, a band of five hundred thieves intending to attack a small city passed by the bhikṣu’s location and said to him,
"We need fire."
He replied, "There is none at present.
The bandit said:
“From where can fire be obtained? He replied,
“O worthy one!”
"There is a sun-crystal (sūryakānta-maṇi) capable of producing fire.
He then pointed out its location. The bandits went away, broke into the city, and returned here intending to seize the crystal.
They asked, "Where is the crystal?"
The bhikṣu showed him the jewel, and the thief took it and departed.
Afflicted by the cold, the bhikṣu went to the householder’s place and said, "I am cold."
He related everything as previously described.
The householder asked,
"Where is the pearl?"
He replied, “A thief has taken it away. The elder said:
"This precious object was not carefully held; it would be a great pity if a thief were to take it away.
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This precious jewel should not be shown to a thief; you should give it to a fire."
"Just as with the sun-gem, so it is with the moon-gem.
The setting and circumstances were the same as before.
At that time, the six groups of bhikṣus had a washerman launder their robes; however, the washerman had received many other people's clothes and had not yet finished washing them.
Then, after the sun had set, Upānanda took some old clothes and went to the laundry place,
saying, "Wash these for me. They replied:
"There are many robes here; they shall be washed tomorrow.
He then became angry, and she said:
"Do not be angry!"
"You may leave it here and depart; I shall wash it for you now.
He then left the garment there, soaking it together with many other clothes. Consequently, the red dye ruined the other garments.
Seeing him standing there with his cheek pressed in his hand in distress, many people who came upon the sight all mocked and censured him.
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"Because of washing clothes, public censure has arisen."
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Upānanda has defiled others' garments with red dye; therefore, a bhikṣu should not cause another to wash or launder garments dyed red. One who does so incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
When the group of six heard this, they took a white-robed layperson and had him wash [the robes]; he then beat and pounded them, causing the garments to be damaged and torn. The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should never have a washerman wash his robes."
The setting was as before.

Having heard that the Buddha did not permit them to have others wash their clothes, the group of six monks took their garments to a laundry place; wrapping their heads with cloths, they washed their own clothes by the edge of a pond, which drew the ridicule of the people who saw them.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not go to a laundry place to wash his own clothes; whoever does so commits a *vyatikrama* offense."
The setting was as before.
A bhikṣu beat and pounded his robes upon a large wooden board, thereby damaging them. The Buddha said:
"You should not do so. You should soak them in warm water within a basin and wash them clean with your own hands slowly."
The Buddha ordered him to wash with his hands, but the bhikṣu was unable to do so;
the Buddha said, "Use your feet.
At that time, there was one who was unable to use either his hands or his feet, whereupon the Buddha said:
"Let another wash it; you should inspect it yourself.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudrakavastu*, Fascicle 14. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudrakavastu*.
Fascicle Fifteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Order.
The seventh subsection of the third section; the summary verse says:
Wiping the body, treading on a snake’s hood, A stone vessel giving rise to doubt,
Many kinds of dyed robes, And painting monasteries according to one's whim.
The occasion was at Śrāvastī.
After the bhikṣus had washed themselves, they put on their robes while their bodies were still wet; consequently, the robes became discolored and malodorous.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"You should keep a towel for wiping the body."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had no towel available. The Buddha said:
"After washing, squat on the ground for a short while; wipe your body with your lower robe (*nivāsana*), and then put on your upper robe."
When the bhikṣus had dust and dirt upon their leather sandals, they beat them to remove it, which caused the lacing to break.
The Buddha said, "One should not do so.
Later, when they washed them with water, the sandals became even more rotted and damaged. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; rather, one may wipe it with a damp cloth.
Therefore, a bhikṣu should carry an item for wiping shoes. Regarding the "washing skirt" (*nivasana*):

one may use a piece of silk cloth approximately one and a half *fang* (cubits) in width and six *chi* in length. It should be wrapped crosswise around the waist and tucked in so as not to slip out; no additional belt is required, for this is the custom of the Western Regions. This was when the Buddha was at the side of the Kakutthā Pond in the kingdom of Campā.
At that time, there was a nāga girl whose faith was pure and virtuous, but her son lacked faith and did not follow the Dharma and Vinaya. His mother then exhorted him to listen to the Dharma, saying:
"My son, you should now go before the Noble One to hear the True Dharma, so that you may obtain merit."
The son did not change his original form but went to the place where the sutra was being recited; when the young bhikṣu saw him, he was struck with terror and cried out:
"Long-waisted one! Long-waisted one!"
The other bhikṣus who had not yet abandoned desire all became terrified; they immediately tied a cord of hair around the dragon's neck and cast him outside the monastery.
When the son returned home, his mother saw him and asked, "Did you go to the place of the Noble One to listen to the True Dharma?"
He replied: "Mother! There is no need to speak of such a person who lacks compassion and love."
The mother asked, "What improper act did he do toward you?
She then explained in detail how the hair-rope had injured her neck. The mother said:
"For this reason, he is called a noble one; if you were to kill anyone else, there would be no doubt that they would do the same to you.
The son remained silent.
Then his friends all mocked him together, crying out:
“Broken Neck.
When he was seen being teased, his body became yellowish and emaciated, and his strength grew weak.
Seeing this, his mother asked him, “Why has your body become so withered and pale?”
She replied, "Mother!
A close acquaintance constantly taunts me by calling me 'Broken-Neck'; out of shame, I have become so emaciated."
The mother said, "It was because you did not change your original form that you incurred this misfortune; had you changed your form before leaving, you would not have been caught by the hair-rope.
You may now change your form and go to listen to the sublime Dharma; whatever you hear and see will accord with your heart's desire."
"If you listen while hiding your body according to its natural form.
Lacking faith, he did not follow his mother's words and remained silent.
His mother thought to herself:
“The noble one has bound the neck of this nāga prince with a woolen cord; for those who wish to hear the Dharma, this creates an obstacle. I shall now go to inform the Buddha.
Having passed through the first watch of the night, he emitted light from his body and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
Due to the radiance of that nāga girl’s body, the Gagā Pond was illuminated all around. The nāga girl said to the Buddha, “Venerable Sir!
My son did not believe;

I exhorted him to listen to the Dharma, and when he arrived at the place where the sutra was being recited, the Noble One saw him and immediately bound his neck tightly with a cord of hair and cast him outside the monastery, so that his neck was injured.”
When his friends saw him, they mocked him, shouting, "Broken-neck! Because of this ridicule,
his body became withered and yellow, and his physical strength was utterly depleted.
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will briefly issue a prohibition among the assembly of noble ones, so that the sons of the nāgas shall not be bound with hair-ropes out of compassion!
Having understood this, the World-Honored One accepted the request by remaining silent.
At that time, the dragon girl paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, the World-Honored One took his seat before the assembly of monks and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Last night, a dragon girl came to my place; having prostrated at my feet, she withdrew to sit to one side."
By the radiance of his majesty, the sides of the pond were completely illuminated and became bright; he then said to me:
"Venerable One!

My son was without faith, so I urged him to listen to the Dharma. When he reached the place where the scriptures were being recited, you, O Noble One, saw him and immediately bound his neck tightly with a cord of hair and cast him outside the monastery, whereby his neck was injured."
When his friends saw him, they mocked him, crying out, "Broken-neck! Because he was thus ridiculed,
his body became withered and yellow, and his physical strength was utterly depleted.
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will briefly issue a prohibition among the assembly of noble ones, out of compassion, so that the sons of the nāgas are not bound with hair-ropes.
He then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“For what reason have you committed such an unrighteous act as to cause those nāgas and spirits to conceive feelings of contempt, thereby leading to the eventual extinction of the True Dharma?”
Therefore, O bhikṣus, do not bind dragons or snakes around their necks with woolen cords.
When you see them approaching, you may snap your fingers and say: "O noble one!"
"Go toward a place where you cannot be seen.
It is well if he follows these words and departs;
if he does not depart, take a staff with a ram's horn, gently pry open his head, place him inside a jar, pierce a hole in its side, cover the opening with an object, and carry him outside.

If there is no such staff, one should tie [the person] around the neck with a soft cord or similar item and pull them out; if even this is unavailable, one should gently press down with a staff, bind the neck with a rope, lift [the body] and place it inside a jar, and discard it outside as previously described.
He discarded it among the grasses; the snake unleashed its wrathful fire to burn the grass, and the snake also died. The Buddha said:
"One should not discard [waste] within the grasses."
After he had discarded it in an open space and had not been observing for long, various insects came to swarm and devour it.
The Buddha said:
"Once you have discarded it, you should not depart immediately. You may discard it in an open space, but you must wait until it has entered its hole before you may leave."
The setting was in Rājagṛha.
In that city there was an elder who was skilled in stone craftsmanship; he manufactured various stone vessels and sold them as needed, thereby acquiring great wealth. He then thought to himself:
"By what means can I perform meritorious deeds that will yield inexhaustible benefit in this very life?"
"I should now invite the Buddha and the Sangha to my home for offerings; by eating and drinking from stone vessels, I shall acquire abundant merit and gain endless benefit."
He then went to where the Buddha was and related everything as above, until the Buddha and the assembly had all arrived at the house and were seated.
The elder then took new vessels and distributed them to the senior monks, while giving the old vessels to those in the lower seats.
The bhikṣu was filled with doubt and refused to accept it.
The Buddha said, "Since the source is pure, you should accept it; do not harbor any doubt.
The elder made offerings until everyone was fully satisfied. The Buddha preached the Dharma for them and departed from his seat.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
When the bhikṣus required dye, the World-Honored One permitted it.
However, when the bhikṣus boiled wet dyestuffs, the color was ruined. The Buddha said:
“Dry it in the sun and then boil it for use.
When it was dried in the midday sun, the dye turned out poorly.
The Buddha said, “One should not dry it by exposing it to the midday sun.”
When he hung the robes in the open air to dry until mold appeared on them, the Buddha said:
"Do not hang them in direct sunlight, nor in excessive shade; dry them according to the season.
Furthermore, when he boiled the robes together with dye-wood and thereby damaged the robes, the Buddha said:
"Boil the dyeing liquid separately.
Having boiled it once, they immediately discarded it. The Buddha said:
"Discard it only after boiling it three times."
The bhikṣus boiled the broth three times and placed it all in one location. The Buddha said, "Place each of the three separately.
They were unable to distinguish which was the first, the middle, or the last. The Buddha said:
"He recorded the sequence by writing characters.
When the bhikṣu poured the dye onto the robe, the Buddha said:
"This should not be done; first place the dye in a basin, and only then put the robe into it."
Consequently, they applied too much liquid, which ran off while the cloth was drying.
The Buddha said, "One should not apply too much.
At other times, they dyed too little, causing the garment to become mottled. The Buddha said:
"One must not be excessive in either quantity or deficiency; one should exercise moderation.
When robes were dried on the ground, they became soiled with dust. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
He then spread it out to dry upon a bundle of grass, but the dye flowed toward one side.
The Buddha said, "It may be hung on a rope or upon a pole.
He then draped it over a rope, but the color did not penetrate through the center. The Buddha said:
"One may drape the robe over the cord and secure it with bamboo clips; if one fears damaging the robe, substitute the clips with other materials.
The bhikṣus did not turn it over frequently, so the liquid flowed toward one side. The Buddha said:
"One should turn it over frequently."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was making a heavy, large robe; after dyeing it, he placed it upon a cord, but its weight was too much for him to bear. The Buddha said:
"Spread it out upon grass to dry, and you must turn it over frequently."
There were those who dyed old robes with fresh dye, and those who threw new robes into old dye. The Buddha said:
"New robes should be dyed with fresh dye, and old robes with old dye; one should not act otherwise."
There were those who hung new clothes in the shade and dried old garments in the sun;
the Buddha said, "Place the new ones in the sun and the old ones in the shade."
When dyeing the robes, they used the third decoction first to dye the robes, followed by the middle, and then the first. The Buddha said:
"First the first, then the middle, and finally the last."
When the dyeing was finished, they did not rinse it with water, so the colors were mottled and uneven.
The Buddha said, "One should rinse it with water.
The bhikṣus rinsed it with water on the very day it was dyed. The Buddha said:
"One should wait until tomorrow.
While he was dyeing the robes, wind and rain arrived; the bhikṣu was terrified and did not know where he should spread out the garments to dry them.
The Buddha said:
"One should place it before the eaves.
He then dyed his robes right there in front of the eaves, causing the dye to stain the ground.
Seeing this, a lay traveler asked, "Venerable sir, for what reason is there blood on this spot?"
He replied, "It is not blood; it is my place of defilement.
Thereupon, they gave rise to derision and loathing.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"In places where robes are dyed, one may either smear them with cow dung or wipe them with earth.
The circumstances were the same as before.
After the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had constructed this monastery and offered it to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, the walls remained unpainted; he then thought to himself:
"I shall now invite the Buddha so that I may have the monastic quarters painted."
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to one side, and said:
“Venerable Sir!
The walls of the monastery have not yet been painted; I now wish to paint them.”
The Buddha said, "As you wish.
The elder did not understand and came to inform the bhikṣu; the bhikṣu, however, did not know what pigments to use.
He then went to inform the Buddha, who said:
"Excellent! The elder did not know; since you have now asked again, one should employ four colors: [red, yellow, blue, and white]."
"Use blue, yellow, red, white, and various other colors to fill out the paintings.
The third section, the eighth sub-section, is summarized in verse as follows:
"Requisites for building monasteries; the etiquette for piercing beds and paying respects."
One should keep a separate set of robes for shaving the hair, and hang flower garlands at the place where one sleeps. The setting is as before.
In this city, there was a householder who provided food to the bhikṣus; they frequently visited his home and eventually established him in the precepts of taking refuge.
Later, on another occasion, when [the Blessed One] was teaching the seven types of meritorious actions with material basis, he replied:
"Noble One! I wish to apply my mind to the cultivation of one such meritorious action."
The bhikṣu replied, “Excellent! It should be done.”
He asked, "Noble One! What shall I do?"
He replied, “It may be used to construct a dwelling for the community of monks.
“Noble One! [he said.]
"I currently possess the funds to build a monastery, yet I lack a virtuous companion to assist me in its construction.
He replied, "Householder!"
"You, O Benevolent One, should prepare the materials; I shall assist in the construction.
"Excellent, O Noble One!"
He then handed over the money and goods.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This property belongs to the Saṃgha of the four directions; how can it be spent to manufacture utensils?"
"I shall seek it out elsewhere. Later, the householder thought to himself:
"The money and goods are stored within my treasury.
At that time, the householder reflected thus:
"The Noble One has kindly built a monastery for me; let us go and observe its condition.
Upon arriving there, they found no construction at all. They asked the bhikṣu, "He promised to build a monastery for you; why is it empty and nothing?"
He replied, "Since there are no tools, with what shall we construct it? He answered:
"What is being done with the donated goods? He replied,
"The goods are in the storehouse."
The householder said,
"It would be appropriate to use these materials to construct various utensils. He replied:
"This object belongs to the Saṃgha of the four quarters; I do not dare to use it.
The elder said, "The monastery was originally intended for the monks of the four quarters; what fault is there in using its funds?"
He replied: "Householder!
I shall go and inform the Buddha; I will act according to his instructions."
The householder said, "Go as you please and inform him.
He then informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"This material is for making utensils and repairing the monastery.

At that time, while the bhikṣu was constructing the monastery, he went from house to house begging for alms. When the elder saw this, he marveled and asked, "Since you are building a monastery for me, why are you going about begging?"
"The money and goods in the temple may be used for food and drink; if they are insufficient, I shall bring more.
He replied, "How could I alone consume the property of the four quarters?"
The householder said, "Our intentions are in accord; what fault is there in this?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I shall ask the Blessed One.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Those who perform construction work should eat from the property of the monastery."
Although he heard that eating was permitted, he still consumed coarse food;
the Buddha said, "One should not eat coarse food.
He then prepared superior food, and the Buddha said:
"One should not skip the superior [meal], but should observe the established custom of other monasteries for food.
The setting and circumstances were as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who suddenly suffered from abdominal pain; he had to go out and return repeatedly, which caused him great exhaustion.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who said:
"Make a hole in the bed and turn it over from time to time.
He then made a hole by boring through a fine bed. The Buddha said:

"One should take the old bed; if it is woven of rattan, one should cut it to form holes, and if it is braided with cords, one should split it open to create cavities. After the illness has been cured, one should repair it according to the circumstances."
Because the lower part of his body turned repeatedly due to the pain from the wound, the Buddha said:
"One may place soft material around the edge of the bed opening; when impurity falls to the ground, it should be caught in an earthenware basin, and one must not lift [the body] high."
The excrement was foul-smelling and discarded outside, and as they searched for other basins in succession, no vessels could be found. The Buddha said:
"One should not discard them all; rather, one may keep individual basins, wash them, and dry them in the sun."
"A second basin should not be provided with tree leaves.
Although the basin has been washed, if the foul odor does not depart, it should be smeared with oil.

Following the Buddha’s instruction that one should attend to the sick, at that time both junior and senior bhikṣus all came to inquire after his illness. When the juniors arrived, they would prostrate to the patient; when the seniors arrived, the patient would pay respects to them. Because of this reciprocal reception, his suffering from illness increased even further. The Buddha said:
"Since his body is impure, he should not pay homage; since one's own body is defiled, it is improper to pay homage to another, and even if another pays homage, one should not accept it.
Should anyone violate this, both shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One:
"As the Blessed One has said:
'If one is not pure, one should neither accept prostrations nor prostrate to others.'"
"O Virtuous One! How many kinds of impurities and defilements are there in total?
The Buddha told Upāli:
"There are two kinds of impurity:
first, the impurity of chewing and eating; second, the impurity of defilement.
What is called the impurity of chewing and eating refers to chewing tooth-sticks and consuming various foods, such as roots, fruits, cakes, and vegetables."
Whether during the act of eating or after having finished eating, as long as one has not yet rinsed the mouth with pure water, it is called impure.

That which is defiled and impure refers to the times of voiding excrement or urine, attending to unclean places, and shaving the hair; until one has thoroughly washed and rinsed the mouth, it is all termed impure.
"When one receives a prostration or performs a prostration while in such states of impure contact, both parties incur an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

The Buddha’s explicit and clear teaching states that this practice is not employed here [in this land], which has caused these rules to be entirely submerged; the circumstances for this are the same as previously mentioned.
The Venerable Upāli requested the Blessed One, saying:
"Bhadanta, as the Blessed One has said:..."
The brahmin Puṣpa spoke thus, saying: "Gautama!

When I am riding in my carriage, whether I am holding the horse's reins or raising my whip to give a loud crack, at that moment may it be known that I, the brahmin Puṣpa, prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and inquire after his well-being."
He further said: "Gautama!

If you see me walking along the road, whether I am removing my leather sandals, stepping aside to avoid the path, or extending my arm, at such times you should recognize my salutation and inquiry as before."
He further said, "Gautama!

Should you at any time see me conversing with someone among my own assembly, whether I shift my seat, remove my upper garment, or take off my turban— at that moment, as before, let it be known that I am offering my respectful greetings."
“World-Honored One!
I do not yet know whether, within the holy teachings of the Tathāgata, the method of paying homage is also the same as this.
The Buddha told Upāli:
"One should not perform prostration in such a manner; for whenever one says with the mouth,
'I now pay homage,' this is merely an act of verbal homage."
If at that time one bows the body and says,
"Vandāmi," although this is a form of salutation, it is not yet complete.
However, Upāli! Within my Dharma and Vinaya, there are two kinds of salutation. What are these two?
First, one places the five wheels upon the ground; second, one grasps the calves with both hands, and in both cases says aloud:
"I now prostrate. The other says:
“Be free from illness.
Otherwise, both shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

The setting of the narrative is as before. At that time, the bhikṣus would shave their hair and beards while wearing whatever robes they had on, and then put those same garments back on to eat their meals and pay homage to the Great Master.
Those who lacked faith saw this and felt contempt and shame, saying:

"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are truly impure; they take the very robes used for shaving their hair and eat from them, yet they still don these garments to pay respectful homage to the Great Master."
"How should we show him respect?
The bhikṣus asked the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not shave the hair and beard while wearing only one of the three robes."
"However, one should separately keep a garment for shaving the hair—namely, the *maṇḍala-kaṭhina* (the patched strip)—and one should remove the beard and hair while wearing this garment.
At that time, there were those who were so impoverished that such a garment was difficult to obtain;
the Buddha said, "One should use a *saṃkakṣikā* (a side-covering cloth) to shield the body while shaving."
When the shaving of their hair was finished, the bhikṣus did not wash themselves; when the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not even know to bathe after shaving their beards and hair; they are truly loathsome."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When the shaving of the hair is finished, one should bathe.
At that time, there were those who were old and infirm with failing strength, or times when water was difficult to obtain; the Buddha said:
“Those of this class should wash five limbs:
namely, the head, along with the hands and feet.
The setting and circumstances are as before.
At that time, there were devout brahmins and householders who came with exquisite flower garlands to offer to the bhikṣus, but none dared to accept them.
The laypeople replied,
"Noble ones!..."
The full explanation is as above, up until: "How could I now possibly abandon all wholesome qualities to go to the next world?
I pray that you will accept them.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Seeing that a flower garland has been offered, it is appropriate that you accept it.
Having accepted it, he discarded it wherever he was; seeing this, the other said with reproach:
"I purchased these flowers at a high price to offer them to you; for what reason do you discard them so recklessly?"
The Buddha said,
"One should not discard it recklessly.
The bhikṣu then used it to hang upon a hair-and-nail stūpa as an offering, whereupon the other said:
“Noble ones! Is it that I have not seen the stūpas of hair and nail?
I have already made offerings to the stūpas in the past; I now bring them here specifically to present them to you, venerable sirs.”
After the bhikṣus had received it, they hung it above the door of their quarters; when laypeople saw it, they assumed it was a Buddha hall and paid it homage. The Buddha said:
"Do not place it outside the door; you should place it inside the room."
Because he placed it in an exposed area, the same fault as before was incurred. The Buddha said:
"It should be placed in a screened location; one may occasionally smell its fragrance, for such fragrant substances can benefit the faculty of the eye."
The bhikṣus did not know what constituted a secluded place.
The Buddha said:
"It may be hung at the head of one's bed."
The summary verse for the ninth section of the third gate says:
Giving fine seats and beds; Fragrant clay and bowl-cases;
Oil vessels, Dharma discourse, and conduct; Cloth bags and carrying three ropes.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one obtains an excellent bed or seat, the Saṃgha should accept it; it is not permitted for an individual."
"One may obtain a large couch; this too belongs to the Saṃgha and not to an individual.
The setting of the story is the same as before.
When laypeople with faith and reverence came to offer high-quality fragrant clay to the bhikṣus, none dared to accept it.
The lay traveler reported, saying: "O Noble One!
I now take you as my field of merit," and so on, as extensively described above, up until: "How could I now abandon all wholesome qualities and depart for the next world?"
"I am fortunate that you will accept it for me.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You should accept it."
Having accepted it, he immediately threw it on the ground in the other's presence, whereupon the latter gave rise to reproach and disdain, saying:
"I purchased this incense at a high price, yet you now cast it away!"
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not discard it.

He then instructed that it should be used to smear and polish the hair-and-nail stūpas, as explained at length previously, up until: "Having received it, one should place it by the side of one's head and smear it upon the walls; from time to time one should smell it with the nose, for all such fragrant substances can cause the eyes to become clear."
At that time, a faithful householder invited the community of bhikṣus to his home for a meal; he offered fine fragrant clay to smear upon the feet of the bhikṣus, yet none dared to accept it.
He replied, "Noble One!
There are Brahmins who possess faith and reverence; when others give them fragrant clay, they apply it to their heads or rub it upon their bodies."
"I revere you, sirs, and have applied fragrant paste to your feet; why do you not accept it?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "Accept the fragrant paste for anointing the feet."
Having accepted it, they threw it away. When the laypeople saw this, they spoke at length as before:
"Excellent! You gentlemen should accept it for me."
Upon arriving at the monastery, he acted as he pleased.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"As before, one must not discard things directly in front of others."
The setting was as before.
At that time, the bhikṣus placed their alms bowls in various locations, causing them to be damaged. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"One should not place alms bowls in various locations; one should construct a bowl-casket."
At that time, the bhikṣus made holes through the walls; the Buddha said, "It should not be done in this way.
When first constructing a monastery, one should provide places for bowls to be kept within the various rooms."
The Buddha said that one should construct a bowl-cavity (*pātra-kośa*). Since forest-dwelling bhikṣus had no place to construct such a cavity, the Buddha said:
"One should weave a basket using rattan vines or grass ropes, and smear it with cow dung or wipe it with mud."
As he placed the bowl inside, dust and soil entered it. The Buddha said:
"One should instead fashion a lid like this and close it; one must not leave it on the ground.
It is appropriate to tie a cord to it and hang it from a tree branch."
When a bhikṣu went out and carried it with him, those who lacked faith saw it and together raised derision, asking: "Venerable One!
Is that object you are holding a chicken coop, or a place for keeping a monkey?"
The Buddha said:
"When you go out on a journey, you should not take it with you; it may be left in its original place.
The circumstances of this incident were the same as before.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling through the human world who arrived at a village seeking a place to stay. Once the host had granted him permission, he washed his feet and then requested oil from him.
A daughter in that household came with oil to offer it as alms; the bhikṣu, having no vessel, reached out his hand to receive it, whereupon the woman replied, "Noble one!
Though you know how to beg for oil, you do not know how to hold a vessel."
She replied, "Sister! The Buddha has not yet granted permission."
The woman remained silent.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should carry an oil vessel."

Having heard that the Buddha had granted permission, at that time Upānanda took his two disciples with him; each carrying an oil vessel, they went about begging for oil. A certain woman came with oil to offer it, but seeing that the vessels were extremely large, she beat her breast and said, "Noble One!"
"Who can give enough to fill this large oil jar?
The bhikṣu said, "How strange! What stinginess!"
"Give as you wish; there will be other faithful brahmins and others who will surely fill it to the brim.
The woman remained silent.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not beg from others carrying a large oil vessel.
After the Buddha had prohibited large ones, they carried small vessels instead; however, the amount used for begging oil was insufficient. The Buddha said:
"One should not carry an extremely small vessel."
However, there are three types of vessels:
the large is two *śu* (measures), the small is one *śu*, and those between the two are called medium.
One should keep [vessels] in this manner.
The setting was as before.
There were two bhikṣus, one old and one young, traveling along a road while speaking improper words. At that time, there was a yakṣa who lacked faith; hearing what they said, he thought to himself:
"These sons of Śākya are traveling along the road discussing what is not the Dharma; I should now suck away their vital essence."
He followed after him immediately and thought to himself:
"The previous matter has already passed and cannot be pursued; I shall instead utter wicked words and suck his vital essence."
As they were traveling along together, they encountered a yakṣa who was a person of faith.
He asked them, "Where do you wish to go?
They answered him in detail regarding their situation, and he replied:
"These two practitioners will surely discuss the Dharma; you should wait for a moment and not pursue the bhikṣu. Let me first engage in conversation with you.
He replied, "Friend!"
"I shall certainly not let these two go.
Then the two yakṣas followed behind them.

Those two bhikṣus spoke words that were contrary to the Dharma; having reached a fork in the road, one went toward the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden and the other toward the Lady Migāramātā’s residence. At that time, the junior one prostrated at the feet of the senior elder and said:
"Go well," the Elder replied,
"O Venerable One!"
"May you be free from illness; do not be negligent.
Then the two bhikṣus each departed by their respective paths.
That non-believing yakṣa, assuming a fierce and imposing form, intended to suck away their vital essence. Thereupon, the yakṣa who had arrived later spoke, saying:
"You should not now act so hastily; those two bhikṣus have already preached the sublime Dharma, yet you yourself do not understand it and needlessly give rise to anger.
He asked again: "What is this Dharma?"
“Have you not heard the Great Cloud Sūtra say:
‘Be free from illness, and do not be negligent’?
To be free from illness is what the Buddha calls a great benefit;”
Heedfulness is the root of all virtues.
As the World-Honored One said:
"If one is not heedless, One can attain the deathless state."
"If one acts with negligence, one will ultimately return to the path of death.
Having heard this Dharma, he felt joy in his heart and returned along the road.
Later, the yakṣa thought to himself:
"This is precisely what I ought to do; I should now go and inform the Blessed One.
Having arrived at the Buddha's dwelling and prostrated at his feet, he sat to one side and said:
"Venerable Sir!..."
There are yakṣas who are lords of non-human beings and harbor faith and reverence for the Buddha’s Dharma, yet there are also yakṣas who harbor nothing but disbelief.

Generally, the yakṣa hosts have little respect or faith in the Buddha’s Dharma; they fear that if bhikṣus speak improper words while traveling along the road, the yakṣas might hear them and perform harmful deeds. We pray that the World-Honored One will enjoin the bhikṣus to maintain right mindfulness and refrain from speaking improper words while traveling along the road, out of his great compassion.
The Blessed One, having understood this, accepted [the invitation] by remaining silent.
Then that yakṣa, knowing that the Buddha had consented, prostrated at his feet and departed.
At that time, after the yakṣa had left, the Blessed One sat upon his seat in the midst of the great assembly and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I have heard the yakṣas say this:
'If a bhikṣu speaks improper words while on the road and proceeds along the path, the faithless yakṣas will watch for an opportunity to strike him.'"

"That which you have done is improper; when those who have gone forth travel along the road, they utter speech that is contrary to the Dharma. Therefore, I now establish the rules of conduct for all bhikṣus when traveling along the road."
When a bhikṣu travels along a road, there are two things he may do:
first, engage in formal discourse; second, maintain noble silence. At a place of rest, he should recite this noble verse:
"The pleasures of the five worldly desires, Or even the pleasures of the various devas..."
Compared to the bliss of the total exhaustion of craving, it does not equal even one-thousandth part.
Because of accumulation, suffering arises; from suffering, accumulation arises again.
By means of the Eightfold Noble Path, one can transcend and reach the sublime state of Nirvana.
"Whoever practices giving will certainly obtain its benefit;
if one gives for the sake of happiness, one will surely attain peace and joy in the future.
The setting of this episode is the same as before.
When a bhikṣu had finished making his three robes and placed them upon his shoulder while traveling along the road, they became damp with sweat and stained by dust. The Buddha said:
"One should carry them away in a bag placed upon the shoulder."
The bhikṣus did not know how to make the bag.
The Buddha said:
"It may be three cubits long and one and a half cubits wide; fold it at the one and a half cubit [width] and sew it together."
One end had its opening shaped like an elephant's trunk; the Buddha said, "It should not be like this;
the opening should be made in the middle.
Dust still entered even though they did not install a fastening; the Buddha said:
"One should install fasteners and loops.
A bhikṣu placed his regularly used robes at the bottom and his non-regularly used robes on top; when he took them out, they became entangled and disordered. The Buddha said:
"The regularly used ones should be on top, and the non-regularly used ones should be at the bottom."
The setting is the same as before.

At that time, a band of robbers plundered people on the road and entered a village; the villagers rushed out in competition to pursue them, but the robbers were defeated and scattered, seeking refuge wherever they could find it.

At that time, the bandits sought water but lacked a rope and a bucket. The bandit leader ordered a man to climb a tree and look into the distance, saying, "If anyone comes, you may borrow what they have as needed.
Seeing a bhikṣu approaching along the road, they then said to one another, "A Śākyaputra is coming;
he is likely preoccupied with his affairs and must have a bucket and a rope. It would be well if he has them."
"If he does not have it, we shall tear open his belly and drink his blood.
Having made this resolution, they remained there watching from afar.
When the bhikṣu arrived, they asked him:
"Noble one! Do you perhaps have a well-rope and a water jar? He replied:

"I have none. When the bandits heard this, they immediately became agitated; each took up a sword or staff and looked about to the left and right. Among them was a leader who was an Arhat, and he immediately observed: "For what reason do these people each hold swords and staves?"
Seeing that those bandits intended to kill the bhikṣu, he said to them,
"Why have you, sirs, become so agitated?
When they had reported the matter in full, the Elder said:
"Do not worry, sirs; I shall provide for all of you. You will certainly obtain clear water and may drink as much as you desire.

He then took the waist-bands belonging to the bhikṣus and joined them together, further securing his alms-bowl by tying it firmly to them. Lowering it into the well, he drew water at will; having inspected it to ensure there were no insects, he allowed them to drink their fill.
The people, filled with joy, replied:
"Noble ones! Had there been no water, we would have killed you without a doubt."
"Excellent, Noble One! You should take hold of the well-rope.
The bhikṣu replied, "I shall comply with your words."
The bandits then prostrated at his feet and departed along the road.

At that time, the bhikṣus also all drank water; they filled their kuṇḍikas and added water to their water-pots (kamaṇḍalu). The spouts of the kuṇḍikas were closed and the mouths of the water-pots were open as they followed the path ahead, gradually reaching the Jeta Grove.
Having seen him, the bhikṣu greeted him, saying:
"Welcome! Welcome!"
"Have you all found a safe path along the way?
They then related everything in detail.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Therefore, I now permit the bhikṣus to carry well-ropes.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus carried extremely long ropes. The Buddha said, "It should not be done thus."
He then made it extremely short. The Buddha said, "It should not be done so.
There are three kinds of cords: [the long, the medium, and the short]."
This refers to long, medium, and short.
The long is one hundred and fifty cubits; the short is ten cubits; those between the two are called medium.
In some places where there was sufficient water, they still used a long rope; the Buddha said:
"One may measure the terrain, and its length and breadth should be adjusted according to the occasion.
The summary verse for the tenth section of the third chapter says:
"One should keep a razor, as well as items such as nail clippers."
A bed frame with a reclining pillow, and scented soil may be used according to one's preference.
The circumstances were as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose hair had grown long; he went to a barber and said:
“O worthy one! Shave my hair. He then thought to himself:
“The Śramaṇa son of the Śākyas uses force to compel people to work, wasting their labor for no reward at all.
He then took a blade and polished it for a long time, thinking to himself:
“If I shave him quickly, someone else will come; in this way, he will cause delays and ruin my household business.”
He replied, "Go for now; I shall come later in the afternoon."
He followed those words and arrived, yet [the Buddha] spoke again,
saying, "In the afternoon.
When the afternoon hour had arrived, he spoke once more, saying, "Tomorrow morning."
He constantly spoke deceptively and ultimately did not shave him at all.
A learned bhikṣu asked him,
"Venerable one!..."
For what reason do you come to this house so frequently?
Are you a kinsman, or are you an acquaintance?
He replied, "No.
It is simply because my hair has grown long and I wish to have it shaved; that man deceived me, and for this reason I have come here repeatedly."
The acquaintance replied,
“Have you not heard? It is difficult for those skilled in arts and crafts to speak the truth.”
"I understand how to shave hair, but the Buddha has not yet granted permission.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who said:
"If there are bhikṣus who know how to shave hair, they should do so with one another in a secluded place; do not allow laypeople to witness it and cause them to give rise to derision."
When that bhikṣu had heard this instruction, he went to his acquaintance and said, "Venerable one!
The Blessed One has granted permission; you may now come and shave my hair for me."
He replied, "Excellent!
Although the Buddha has granted permission, how could one shave a person's hair using only a finger? One requires a razor, a whetstone, as well as tongs and a nail-clipping knife."
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I now permit you, for the sake of the Saṃgha, to keep a razor for shaving hair along with whatever other necessary items are required."

The Buddha was staying at the Mahāvana Kūṭāgāraśālā in the city of Kapilavastu. After the Buddha had permitted one person from each household of the Śākya clan to go forth into homelessness, their beds had no supports for the feet, and they could not sleep in peace.

However, whereas his limbs were previously supple and the things upon which he lay were entirely magnificent, at present he lies uncomfortably on a low bed and lacks much digestive heat; he then went to a physician and asked, "O worthy sir!..."
“I lack the necessary medicinal power; I shall instead provide a prescription.
The physician replied, “I shall go with you to inspect the room where you reside and determine how the bed upon which you lie should be arranged.”
Seeing that the head of his bed was low, he said, "Venerable One!
Because the head of your bed is low, it causes the heat of the four great elements to diminish; you should place a footrest beneath the legs of the bed."
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet granted permission.
[The other said,] "The Buddha is greatly compassionate; he must surely grant permission."
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who said:
"You should place a footrest upon the bed where you lie.
He acted according to these words, yet his illness still did not subside.
He asked the physician again for a remedy, and the physician said,
"When you lie down to sleep, you should place a pillow beneath your head. He replied:
“The Buddha has not yet granted permission.
[The monks] explained at length as above, and the Buddha said:
“When lying down, you should place a pillow beneath your head.”
The bhikṣus did not understand how it should be made.
The Buddha said:
"The method for making a pillow is as follows:"

The object used is four cubits long and two cubits wide; the four-cubit length is folded into two layers and sewn into a pouch, which is filled with cotton絮 so that it may be used to support the head.
The setting was in Rājagṛha.
Pilindavatsa was habitually afflicted by illness; the details are as explained above, up until he asked:
"What did you previously carry?"
He replied, "In the past, I used scented soil.
He reported this, saying:
"Why do you not carry it now?
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet granted permission."
He reported the circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"For the sake of the cause and condition of illness, you may use fragrant soil as a support.
This concludes the third section of the Miscellaneous Rules (Kṣudraka-vastu).
The summary verse for the fourth section says:
The Elder and the Wall-Fence, The Causes for Breaking and Nursing the Sick,
Caṇḍāla, Pig, Sugarcane, and the Monastery, The Alms Bowl, Reliance, and the Method for Planting Trees.
The first sub-section of the fourth section is summarized in verse as follows:
The Elder speaks in turn; Or one may stay together until the end;
Filtering to make non-time-appropriate gruel; And no restriction on the location.
As the Blessed One has said, the *poṣadha* (confession of purity) should be performed every half-month; however, the bhikṣus did not know whom to designate to recite the precepts.
The Buddha said:
"The *sthavira* (senior elder) should be appointed; at the time of the *poṣadha*, the *sthavira* shall always recite them."
At a certain residence, the Elder was unable [to recite the precepts].
The others said to him, "The time for the recitation of the precepts is approaching;
why do you not review them? He replied:
“Venerable One!
I myself lack the power; what should I do?
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the Elder is unable, the second should speak.
Again, in another residence, the second was unable, as explained in detail above.
"If the second is unable, let the third do it."
Furthermore, there was a residence where the third [requirement] could not be fulfilled; the details are as explained above.
The Buddha said: "The bhikṣus should take turns reciting the precepts.
When the bhikṣus took turns reciting them, some were capable while others were not.
Those who are capable may explain it for them, while those who are not capable do not know how.
The Buddha said:
"Those who are not capable should seek out those who are capable to explain it for them."

Furthermore, in certain residences where it was the turn of one who was unable to recite the *Poṣadha* to do so, they sought out another person, but that person refused. Not knowing what to do, they asked the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Those capable of reciting should always be invited in advance."
"As the World-Honored One has said, the senior monk (sthavira) should recite the precepts; if the senior monk is unable, the second may be appointed.
If the second is unable, the third shall be made to do so."
If this is not possible, they should take turns performing it.
If this too is not possible, one should seek someone capable, or perhaps invite someone regularly to do so.

There was once a monastery where not a single person could recite the entire Prātimokṣa; however, its senior monk (*sthavira*) could recite the four *pārājika* rules, while the others could not recite anything at all.
At that time, the bhikṣus ceased reciting the precepts. The Buddha said: "One should not suspend the recitation of the precepts altogether;
rather, they may be recited according to what each individual has memorized. The Elder (upādhyāya) should recite the four *pārājika* rules;

the next seat should recite the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; the next seat should recite the two *aniyata* rules; the next should recite the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; the next should recite the ninety *pāyattika*; the next should recite the four *pratideśanīya*; the next should recite the *śaikṣa* rules; and the next should recite the seven *pratikṣepaṇīya* rules."
"One should recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra in this manner; one should not fail to recite it.
This occurred while the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying:
"As the Buddha has spoken of 'beverages for the proper time' and 'beverages for the improper time,' what constitutes the proper time?
What constitutes the improper time?
The Buddha said:
"That which has not been strained is for the proper time; that which has been purified by straining is for the improper time.
Furthermore, it is purified by sprinkling it drop by drop with water.
The setting and circumstances are as before.

At that time, the group of six monks was constantly beset by many evil desires and the stain of avarice; they improperly utilized other residences at all times, or during the designated periods for specific rooms, or during the day, or on account of their personal acquaintances.
What is meant by "all"?
This refers to my dwelling place during the spring, this during the summer, and this during the winter; these are called "all seasons.
What is meant by "delimitation"?
"This is my room; this is another's room.
What is meant by "the division of time"?
"This is the dwelling place for the morning; this is the dwelling place for the afternoon."

What is the time for friends? This is the place of my preceptor; this is the place of my teacher; this is the place of my disciple; this is the place of my student; this is the dwelling place of my acquaintance.
Because of this, many people came and went, causing disturbance to the bhikṣus.
When they reported these circumstances to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not establish such restrictions within his own residence; whoever violates them commits an offense against the Dharma."
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudrakavastu*, Fascicle Fifteen; *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudrakavastu*,
Fascicle Sixteen.
The Fourth Section, Second Sub-section: A Summary Verse states: Fences and enclosures;
nuns and shaving implements; Not wearing clothes that have been beaten or polished.
"Even when receiving a small amount, one should divide it equally; one should know the proper ritual for washing and cleaning.
This occurred in Śrāvastī.
After the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had donated the monastery, many people—both monastics and laypeople—began coming and going. The householder thought to himself:
"Now that this monastery garden has become a public thoroughfare, it would be appropriate for me to build a high wall all around it.
He then went to the Buddha's presence and said,
"World-Honored One!"
"Now this monastery garden has become a great thoroughfare; I wish to erect a wall around it, but I do not know if I may do so?
The Buddha said, "Householder!"
"You may do as you please.
The householder then enclosed the area on all four sides with walls; when the summer rains arrived, the water could not flow out and caused the ground to become submerged.
Later, when the householder came to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet, he saw that the water had filled [the cell] and thought to himself:
“Previously, I built this wall without providing a drainage aperture, which has caused the water to fill up. If the Buddha permits it, I shall make an aperture to allow the water to flow out.”
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "Let the water flow as you wish.
At that time, the calves rubbed against the wall or gored it with their horns; when the elder saw this, he thought to himself:
"Although I have built a wall, I have not yet made a wooden fence.
As explained in detail above, the Buddha said:
"One should make a wooden fence."

At that time, some wicked people stole the wood and took it away. When the householder returned and saw that the fence had been plundered by thieves and was scattered in pieces everywhere, he informed the Buddha of the matter:
"I shall install a moat outside the fence."
The Buddha said, "Do as you please.
The householder immediately dug a moat all around the perimeter outside the fence.
The setting is as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Tiśyā whose hair was extremely long; she went to a barber’s place and requested him to shave her head.
He thought to himself:
"The Śākya women are forcing me to do this," as explained at length above.
The Bhikṣus were requested [by the Buddha]: "It is permitted for the Saṃgha of Bhikṣuṇīs to possess items such as hair-cutting tools; they should shave one another's hair in a secluded place.
The circumstances of the setting are the same as before.
After the World-Honored One had granted Nanda permission to go forth, Sundarī prepared a fine Dharma robe, polished it until it was bright and clean, rubbed it with her teeth, and sent it to Nanda.
Having received them, Nanda donned these fine robes and, holding up his excellent alms-bowl, strode about before the great assembly.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who thought to himself:
"Because of wearing fine robes, such faults arise."
He addressed the bhikṣus:

"This is contrary to the Dharma and should not have been done. This foolish man Nanda, wearing these robes and carrying a fine alms-bowl in his hand, racing ahead of the assembly, has acted contrary to the Dharma."
"If there is a bhikṣu who wears a garment that has been beaten smooth, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

Once the Blessed One had prohibited the wearing of beaten-smooth garments, faithful brahmins and householders brought such garments as gifts for the bhikṣus. The bhikṣus did not accept them, as explained at length above:
"How could we proceed to the next world without the provisions of merit?"
"I pray that you will accept it.
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"Accept it as you wish."
"Once you have received it, remove the sheen from the cloth and use it as you please.
The bhikṣu rubbed the cloth with his hands, yet the sheen would not go away. The Buddha said:
"Place it in the open air; wait for it to become damp, then rub it."
This, too, could not remove it. The Buddha said: "Soak it with water.
This, again, did not entirely remove it. The Buddha said:
"If it has been soaked in water, you may use it as you please; do not harbor any doubts.
If faithful Brahmins, householders, or others offer well-washed and finished robes to the community, they should be used according to the aforementioned rule."
The setting was as before.
At that time, the brahmins and householders of this city were gathered together in a public assembly hall at a central location, conversing among themselves, and said: "Do you all know?"
"The śramaṇa Gautama and his disciples do not share the gains and offerings they receive equally, unlike the followers of other paths.
At that time, there was a brahmin in the assembly who previously lacked pure faith, and he said to the people:
"Tomorrow, you should all go together with me to personally observe whether Gautama and his followers are indeed impartial or not."
The people said, "Excellent! Thereupon,
the brahmin took a pair of white cotton cloths into the Jeta Grove and immediately offered those cloths to the Saṃgha of the four quarters in the presence of the presiding elder.
He said, "Venerable One!
I offer this cotton cloth to the community of monks for them to use as they please."
The Elder replied:

"Great Brahmin, may you be free from illness and live long. This gift of yours is an adornment of the mind and an aid to the mind; it will skillfully support supreme concentration and lead to the attainment of wondrous Bodhi, whereby you shall receive excellent garments among gods and humans."
When the brahmin heard these words, he feigned respect, paid his respects, and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"You should inform the bhikṣus: [as follows]."
"That brāhmaṇa came specifically to the monastery seeking a point of fault, yet he has offered this cotton cloth.
You bhikṣus should divide it equally and each take a small portion; you may use it to patch robes, or for buttons and loops, or simply as much as fits the hand to serve as a support for your bodies."
Then Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, addressed the bhikṣus:
“The World-Honored One has given this command:
‘That brahmin has come seeking a point of vulnerability.’”

The cotton cloth that has been offered should be divided equally among you all; each of you should take a small portion, using it either to patch robes, to make fastenings and buttons, or as a square handkerchief, according to your needs for sustaining the body.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus replied to the Venerable One,
“We shall practice according to the instructions of the Blessed One.
Having received it, the bhikṣus immediately divided it equally and made use of it as before.
On the following morning, that brahmin stood at the city gate. At that time, the bhikṣus, taking up their robes and bowls, entered the city to beg for alms.
Having arrived at the gate, the brahmin said:
"Noble ones!..."
“I have given this fine cotton cloth; how will you venerable ones make use of it?
A certain bhikṣu replied to the great brāhmaṇa, “Once the Saṃgha has received it, we shall divide it equally among ourselves; my own portion was used to patch my torn robes.”
One person replied,
"That which I have obtained I use as a fastener.
Another person replied:
"What I have obtained is only as much as the palm of my hand, which I shall enjoy according to my own needs.
When the brahmin heard these words, he thought to himself: "What we have been saying was all false;

we were merely slandering the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, by claiming they do not share their gains equally. Now, having personally verified it, I know that these bhikṣus are men of virtue; they are truly impartial and free from favoritism. It would be fitting for me to go forth among them."
Then, having conceived faith, the brahmin went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and said to the Buddha:

"I pray only that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will grant me permission to go forth within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination and become a bhikṣu, and to diligently cultivate the holy life under the World-Honored One."
The Buddha said to the brahmin: “Excellent, excellent!

That you are able to give rise to this most sublime resolve to seek renunciation is well. The wise understand that those who have gone forth possess five benefits, as explained at length below, up until the point where the World-Honored One and the noble sages all praise them; therefore, one should seek renunciation.”
The World-Honored One then addressed the brahmin, saying: "Welcome, bhikṣu!

At that moment, he became a renunciant and attained full ordination. Exerting himself with right mindfulness and unremitting vigor, he shattered the wheel of birth and death within the five destinies—as extensively described before—severed all afflictions, and realized the fruit of arhatship, until even Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas paid him their respects.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Benefiting others and receiving with moderation brings such advantages as these. Therefore, bhikṣus, if you obtain cakes or food—even if it is as small as a tree leaf—you should divide it among the assembly. If you obtain clothing—even if it is as little as enough to serve as a lamp wick—you should likewise divide it among the assembly."
The setting was as before.
At that time, there was a brahmin in this city who constantly delighted in purity and longed for the life of a renunciant. He then thought to himself:
"Is there perhaps a method of purification that satisfies my mind? If so, I shall go forth into homelessness according to that dharma."

That brahmin traveled abroad in search [of a teacher], journeying through the various sites where non-Buddhist practitioners and brahmins cultivated their disciplines. He saw some who, having finished defecating or urinating, did not wash themselves; others entered a pool and cleansed themselves with a hundred clods of earth. Seeing such impurity or such excessive ritualism, he found none of it to his satisfaction, as there was no place of refuge.
Then the brahmin thought again:
"I have examined them all thoroughly, yet none has satisfied my mind; there is only the śramaṇa son of the Śākyas whom I have not yet gone to observe."
He then proceeded to the Jetavana Grove, where he saw the Venerable Śāriputra carrying a water-pot with a capacity of three *śeṣas* toward the place for evacuation. Having seen him, he thought:
"This is the foremost disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama; I shall observe how he performs his purification."
He immediately followed after him.
Since an Arhat cannot observe the mental inclinations of others when not in meditative absorption,
Śāriputra, seeing that man following him, concentrated his mind and observed why this Brahmin was following him.
I then realized that this person sought purity of heart, wishing to observe my good and evil deeds.
Furthermore, I observed whether this person possessed roots of goodness and with whom they were connected.
He then perceived that this person possessed prior roots of goodness and was connected to him.

Having made this observation, he immediately placed his dharma robes upwind; he wore only the *saṃkakṣikā* and the lower garment (*antarvāsaka*). Next, on a brick or stone to one side, he arranged seven heaps of powdered earth in a single row, each about the size of half a peach.
Furthermore, one should arrange seven heaps along this side, and place another heap separately on the opposite side.
Taking a tally stick and three clods of earth,
one enters the latrine without closing the door, using skillful means so that they may see from afar at a distance.

When the evacuation was finished, he used a counting-stick to wipe his body; then, taking a piece of earth with his left hand, he washed downward to cleanse himself, and again took another piece of earth to wash the area of the urinary passage.

Once it has been purified, next take a portion of earth and wash the left hand thoroughly. Holding the water flask with the right hand, go to the place where the earth is located and rest the flask upon the left thigh so that the water flows out obliquely. If there is a three-pronged wooden stand, it is essential to place [the flask] upon it. First, take seven portions of earth and wash the left hand with each one; then, take another seven portions of earth and purify both hands with each one. Wash and wipe both arms until they are also clean and bright. Finally, take one portion of earth and use it to wash the water flask.
When his business was concluded, he departed with serene and dignified deportment, wearing his dharma robes; thereafter, he washed both feet with water.
Next, he went into his room and took water from a pure flask, rinsing his mouth two or three times before finally engaging in his various activities as he pleased.
When that brahmin saw this, he conceived a deep sense of faith and thought to himself:
"How excellent is this essential Dharma! Nothing else can surpass it.
Even if an outsider were to cleanse themselves by washing with a hundred measures of earth, it would not equal the son of the Śākyas who requires only two weeks."
Having formed this thought, he prostrated at the feet of Śāriputra and said:

"Noble One! I now wish to go forth under the Venerable One in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination to become a bhikṣu, and diligently cultivate the holy life with heedfulness."
Śāriputra replied: "Excellent, excellent, O brāhmaṇa!"

That you are able to give rise to such an excellent resolve is a virtuous deed; as the Buddha has taught, those possessed of wisdom should delight in leaving the household life because they perceive five benefits.
What are the five? First is the merit of renunciation; it is my own self-benefit and not shared with others. Therefore, the wise should seek renunciation.

Second, one should know for oneself that while previously a lowly person driven by others, after having left the household life, one receives offerings, prostrations, and praise from others; therefore, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
Third, when one’s life here ends, one shall be reborn in the heavens and remain free from the three evil realms; for this reason, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
Fourth, by renouncing the secular world, one departs from birth and death and shall attain the secure, unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*; for this reason, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
Fifth, one will always be praised by all Buddhas, the assembly of śrāvakas, and all superior persons; therefore, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
You should now contemplate these benefits and, with a heart of profound sincerity, cast off the worldly snares to seek great merit.

Having spoken these words, he immediately granted him the going-forth and the ten precepts, followed by full ordination. He was instructed and exhorted according to the Dharma, practicing with diligent application; he severed all fetters and delusions, realized the dharma of non-arising, and attained the fruit of Arhatship. Free from the defilements of the three realms, he viewed gold and earth as equal and indistinguishable; whether cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance, he harbored no dualistic thoughts. Like a hand waving through empty space, his mind was free from obstruction; with great wisdom, he shattered the shell of ignorance, becoming fully endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the four unhindered analytical knowledges. Regarding any attachment to existence within the three realms, and all gain, offerings, and honor, he abandoned them all without exception, becoming an object of praise for Śakra and the various devas.
Śāriputra, together with his arhat disciples, personally approached the Buddha and prostrated at his feet, reporting the aforementioned matter in detail.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“You have been able to use such skillful means to guide sentient beings into my Dharma; because of this, the establishment of the precepts for the sake of purity will bring boundless benefit and merit.”

Examining these holy teachings, the direct words from the Golden Mouth of the Buddha, it is clear that they ought to be practiced and followed; in principle, they cannot be contravened. However, because the texts of the various Vinaya schools of the past contained omissions and gaps, and although a small portion has been transmitted, its full purport remains incomplete, leaving students without a reliable standard to rely upon.
