Consequently, for seven hundred years this dharma remained incomplete; some used bamboo tubes or troughs as substitutes, while others used silk cloths to wipe their bodies or rubbed their hands on stones. Originally, there was no provision for using earth, so that what was intended to achieve purity instead resulted in defilement. This was entirely contrary to the original method.

Now that this has become as clear as a bright mirror, let it be whether they practice or not, according to their own reverence or negligence. At that time, all the bhikṣus had doubts and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"By what causes and karma did the Venerable Śāriputra, through pure means, tame and attract that brahmin, enabling him to go forth and reach the state of parinirvāṇa?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“It is not only today that I have subdued this man and brought him to peace and happiness; in the past, through pure deeds, I have already disciplined and guided him, causing him to abandon his band of thieves, take refuge in the Triple Gem, and uphold the five precepts.”
"You all should listen.

Long ago, in a certain village, there was a brahmin whose wife gave birth to a daughter of exquisite beauty. When she had grown up, while the maiden remained at home, a band of five hundred thieves plundered the village at night."
At that time, the leader of the bandits was oppressed by thirst and required water; entering the brahmin’s house, he saw the young girl and said to her: "Young woman!
I am now oppressed by thirst; bring me some water."
The woman said, "Wait a moment!
She immediately hurriedly lit a lamp, fetched water, and examined it; then the leader of the bandits asked:
"What do you observe? He replied,
"I observe water."
He asked, "What is there to be observed? He replied:
"I fear there may be grass or hair [in the water], which would cause harm when you drink it.
He replied, "I am a mad bandit wishing to destroy your village; by this logic, you ought to give me poison. Why worry that grass or hair will cause me harm?"
Hearing these words, the woman spoke in verse:
"Whatever a thief may do, he wrongfully seizes the wealth of others;
whether you act or do not act, I shall always proceed according to the Dharma."
"Having ascertained that the water was pure, she offered it to him.
When the bandit leader had finished drinking the water, he felt great joy and said:
'Young woman!'"
"You are my sister; do not harbor such heterodox thoughts.

The woman said, "I truly have no need for such a thief as a brother—one who constantly harbors the intent to plunder the property of others. When the owner sees him, he shoots him with a poisoned arrow, and upon meeting such a death, the suffering is beyond words. Hearing that my brother has perished, my grief and sorrow have doubled."
"If you, O virtuous one, can now take refuge in the Triple Gem and uphold the five precepts, I shall become your sister.
The bandit then spoke these pleasing words to his daughter:
"Your words are most excellent; I shall do as you say."

The girl immediately explained the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts to them, causing them to give rise to faith; the bandits then received and upheld these, and together they sought the way back home.
"O Bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts: the bandit leader of that time was none other than this Brahmin, and that young girl was none other than Śāriputra."
In the past, because he perceived water as pure, he caused bandits to receive the precepts, abandon evil, and take refuge.

Now, by means of this method of ritual purification, he causes them to give rise to a sense of the marvelous, pull themselves out from the river of craving, ascend the shore of Nirvana, bid a long farewell to the sea of suffering, and eternally realize non-arising.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know! This is a constant practice that must always be kept in mind. Such purification brings great benefit, rendering the body clean so that the devas will pay it honor."

Therefore, from this day forward, whether you be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, all who take refuge in me and accept me as their teacher should wash yourselves clean just as Śāriputra has done.

If a person does not perform such purification, they should not circumambulate the stupa or walk its paths; it is improper for them to pay homage to the Buddha or recite the scriptures; they should neither pay homage to others nor receive homage from others; they should not eat food, nor sit upon the monastic beds, nor enter the assembly.
Because the body is impure and not in accordance with the Dharma, it causes the devas to see [the practitioner] and feel no joy; consequently, all dhāraṇī practices they maintain will lack efficacy.
Should anyone violate this, they incur the offense of duṣkṛta.

If one prepares offerings for a vegetarian feast, transcribes scriptures, or fashions images without having washed and purified oneself, the merit obtained will be meager due to such negligence and disrespect.
If one does not chew a tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha) in the morning or after midday, it is improper to eat and the fast is not accomplished; one incurs the same fault as mentioned before.

"You all should rely upon my instructions; do not deceive yourselves by practicing impure dharmas, for through indolence and negligence you will become those of inferior conduct and shall fall into the evil realms."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, all the bhikṣus were greatly rejoiced and practiced accordingly in accordance with the Dharma.
The third sub-section of the fourth chapter contains this summary verse:
"Regarding the need for replacement when damaged, Mingyue heard it and immediately took charge."
Based on the knowledge of distinctions, three people sat together to listen.
The setting was at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus were wearing old, worn-out robes and had no sense of care for them; consequently, the edges and borders of the robes were all frayed and falling apart.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Bind it with thread wherever it has been damaged.
Although the horizontal threads were bound, they would sag downward again; therefore, vertical threads were added to bind it so that it would be secure. The Buddha said:
"One should regard the saṃghāṭī robe as if it were one's own skin.

At that time, the bhikṣus had no other robes and constantly wore the great outer robe (saṃghāṭī). Sweat flowed from their armpits and soaked the garment, making it foul-smelling and impure, which caused the robe to quickly fall into disrepair.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You may attach a separate patch to the sides near the armpits.
The bhikṣus did not know how to apply the patch.
The Buddha said:
"Use a material one cubit and a half in length and one handspan in width to make its patch.
The Buddha said:
"One should not patch it with white material; rather, one should use dyed cloth.
He used the color of a *kāṣāya* robe, and the Buddha said:
"One should not use this *gandha* color, for fear it might stain other garments."
"It has been dyed with red stone and red earth.
The bhikṣu sewed it on, whereupon the Buddha said:
"It should be roughly drafted."
He then placed a patch on one side. The Buddha said:
"Patches may be applied to both edges; it may be worn even when turned inside out.
If there is an odor, it should be torn open and washed from time to time."
The setting is the same as before.

There was a brahmin who, shortly after marrying a wife, had a daughter born to him whom he named Candraprabhā (Moonlight). As she gradually grew up, Mahāprajāpatī ordained her and conferred upon her full ordination (*upasampadā*).

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, leading five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha preached the Dharma for them until he sat in silence.
At that time, having heard the Dharma, Mahāprajāpatī rose from her seat, adjusted her robe over one shoulder, joined her palms in reverence, and said:
"World-Honored One, you have already taught the Vinaya for the bhikṣus; we pray that out of compassion you will likewise teach it for the bhikṣuṇīs."
The Buddha said:
"There is no such possibility that the Tathāgata, the Great Teacher, would personally expound the Vinaya dharma before nuns.
However, if there are among the community of bhikṣuṇīs those who can retain it after hearing it but once, I shall speak for them."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Candraprabhā was seated among the assembly; she immediately rose, joined her palms, and said:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will speak for me, so that I may receive your venerable words and understand them upon hearing them once.”
The Buddha explained it for her, and she understood it all at once without omission.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Among the community of śrāvakī bhikṣuṇīs in my Dharma, Candraprabhā Bhikṣuṇī is foremost among those who understand upon hearing it just once."
The Buddha thought to himself:

"A bright moon does not exist everywhere that one may seek it, nor can even something resembling it be found. Therefore, bhikṣus should also receive and uphold the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya to preach it for the bhikṣuṇīs, and they should further instruct them and provide answers when questioned."
Having reflected thus, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Regarding the matters as I have reflected upon them, I shall answer whatever questions are asked.

As the Blessed One has said, by relying on the precepts and abiding in the precepts, one cultivates the Dharma—whether it be meditative concentration or wisdom—in accordance with the principle of reality.
This nun Candraprabhā has followed my example.

By relying upon the precepts and abiding in the precepts, she has applied herself with vigor through the union of concentration and wisdom; exerting right effort as extensively described before, she attained the fruit of Arhatship, destroyed the wheel of the five destinies, and emerged from the ocean of birth and death. As extensively described, she even came to be honored by all the gods, including Śakra and Brahmā.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:

"What karma did this Bhikṣuṇī Candraprabhā previously perform, such that through the ripening of that karma, she attained great wisdom and great eloquence, was declared foremost among those who hear and retain the teachings, and having gone forth to practice within the Buddha's teaching, severed all afflictions and realized arhatship?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This nun Candraprabhā has brought to maturity the karmic fruit of actions she previously committed; the full account is as in other [cases]. You, bhikṣus!"

In the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago, when the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Vipaśyin, fully endowed with the ten titles. Accompanied by sixty-two thousand bhikṣus, he went to the city of Bandhumatī and dwelt in the Vanavāsin Forest.
At that time, there was an elder in that city who, not long after marrying a wife, had a daughter born to him.

As she gradually grew up, her father, being faithful and respectful, went to a bhikṣuṇī convent during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and presented his daughter to the community of nuns as a gift for the *pravāraṇā*, providing them with knives and needles.
At that time, seeing this virtuous deed, the girl felt great joy in her heart and said to her father:
"I too shall follow my inclination and perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony together with the community of nuns."
The father said, "Excellent! Do as you wish."

The girl immediately took knives, needles, gold, silver, precious jewels, and various other items, offering them to the assembly of nuns for the purpose of the *svairī-karman* (the rite of free distribution). She then joined her palms in prostration before the head of the assembly and made this vow:

"By virtue of all the roots of goodness from this reverent and meritorious gift made to the assembly of nuns, may I, in future lives, attain great wisdom and great eloquence, and be fully endowed with the power of hearing and retaining."
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thought: the woman of that time was none other than Candraprabhā.

Because of the roots of virtue she cultivated by distributing knives and such among the community of nuns in the past, and because she further made this great aspiration, 'May I in the future attain great eloquence and be fully endowed with the power of hearing and retention.'"
Due to those karmic conditions, she now undergoes this retribution.

Furthermore, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, she left the household life to practice as a bhikṣuṇī; she maintained the precepts without flaw for the remainder of her life, yet ultimately attained no realization.
At that time, her preceptor was foremost among those who heard and retained the Buddha’s Dharma; then, her disciple made this aspiration:
"My preceptor is foremost in the mastery of dhāraṇīs within this Dharma."
As the Buddha prophesied that in the future, when the human lifespan is one hundred years, there will be a Buddha appearing in the world named Śākyamuni, within his Dharma I shall go forth as a monk.
"The Buddha has also prophesied that among the assembly of nuns, I am foremost in dhāraṇī.
Due to the power of my past vows, I now receive this retribution.
You should know that if one performs purely black karma, one obtains purely black retribution; the details are as explained previously."
"Therefore, you all should practice and study this.
The setting was as before.
A young bhikṣu was traveling through the human world together with an elderly bhikṣu until they reached Śrāvastī.

At that time, the elder bhikṣu went to the house of Mṛgāramātṛ, while the younger one went to Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Having requested a certain bhikṣu to serve as his preceptor (niśraya), he resided there for some time and said to his teacher: "Ācārya!..."
"I have placed my robes and bowl in that monastery; I shall go there briefly to retrieve them.
He replied, "Son!"
"Go with him and return quickly.
He replied, "He has no other business; he will return immediately."
Having prostrated at his feet, he departed.
Upon arriving there, the community already had a regulation:
"If one stays for even a single night without a preceptor (*niśrayācārya*), one must not remain."
He then went to the bhikṣus to take them as his preceptors.
When dawn broke and he wished to depart, he went to his teacher’s cell, knocked on the door, and entered, saying:
"I pay homage to the Ācārya; are you well in body and spirit?"
The teacher said,
"It is not peaceful.
He then thought to himself:

"The Teacher now has an illness; for me to abandon him and depart would be improper. Because of this, the World-Honored One established the rule that one must rely on another and look after one another. I should now remain here until he recovers, and then I shall go."
He then provided for his needs, and the illness was eventually cured.
[The monk] said, "Please inspect my bedding; I wish now to depart.
[The other] replied:
"Son! Are you not lacking anything? He replied:
"I have no lack of anything; however, it was not my original intention to stay here. I came only for a short time to retrieve my robes and bowl.
Yet there is a regulation in this community:
'Even if one stays for only a single night, one must seek formal reliance (niśraya) upon a preceptor.'"
I was apprehensive that the community would request me to serve as their preceptor; seeing that my teacher was ill, I thought to myself:
"My teacher is suffering from illness; for me to abandon him now and depart would be improper."
He related his intention in full.
The Master said:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Venerable one!
A co-resident disciple should attend upon and serve his preceptor and instructor in this manner.
Any other co-resident disciples should likewise act toward their two teachers in the same way."
"Cultivating wholesome dharmas like a lotus emerging from the water—this is a virtuous matter; you should go with a good heart, always remaining heedful and never being negligent.
He then prostrated at his teacher's feet, took his leave, and departed. Gradually reaching the Jeta Grove, he arrived at his teacher’s location, joined his palms in reverence, and paid homage.
The teacher said, "Welcome, venerable one!"
"Why have you been so late?
He then related the matter in its entirety, and the teacher said,
"Excellent, venerable one!"
"Since you are able to treat your teacher with such reverence and respect,
your roots of goodness will cause you to flourish day and night, like a lotus in water.
The teacher thought to himself:
“Is it because he previously relied upon him, or should he be granted [the precepts] again?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“If there is a reason for his temporary departure and he intends to return immediately, he should rely upon his original teacher; there is no need for the precepts to be granted again.”
The setting is the same as before.
There was a bhikṣu who was devoted to the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). A junior bhikṣu requested him to serve as his preceptor (*niśraya*), and he accordingly agreed to do so.
He then had this thought:

"As the Buddha has taught: 'It would be better to be a butcher than to allow others to go forth or receive full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) without instructing them; as it is with those one dwells with, so it is with one's own disciples.'"
"I am practicing meditative seclusion and have no occasion for instruction; it is fitting that you entrust this to another person to teach the recitation.
He then approached a bhikṣu and said, "Venerable One!..."
"Teach him how to recite the scriptures. He replied,
"Let us make an agreement together, and I shall teach him to read."
"If there should be anything lacking that you require for service,
I shall not oppose it. He replied,
"If there is anything deficient, I myself shall provide it."
He then instructed him in his studies.

Later, at another time, the student fell ill; his preceptor provided for him according to the Dharma, and he subsequently recovered. However, when the preceptor himself fell ill, the student did not turn back to look after him, and this continued for three times without him attending to him.
Finally, [the preceptor] said to him: "Go away and seek another preceptor."
He replied, “I have relied upon you for support; this kindness has flowed to me so that I lack nothing at all. Why do you now drive me away? He answered:
"You have no lack, whereas I have a lack.
Your suffering from illness I shall personally attend to.
Though my own illness has reached its third stage, I have never once looked back."
"You have committed such an act of disrespect; if there is anyone who will take you as their *niśraya* (preceptor/sponsor), you may stay with them.
Upon hearing this, he remained silent and was unable to offer a reply.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"You may provide service and attendance to your preceptor; you should regard your preceptor as no different from your own father and mother. Whoever violates this shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."

At that time, there was an ācārya who taught recitation and fell ill; his disciple who had received the Dharma from him did not attend to him during his sickness. When the teacher’s illness had subsided and the disciple returned to inquire about the scriptures, the teacher said: "Go away!"
"I have been suffering from illness and have never looked after you; who else could possibly teach you how to study? You should seek someone else to instruct you.
Again, there was no reply.

The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said, "One should provide service and attendance to the *niśraya-ācārya* (preceptor), and one should also provide for the *adhyāpaka-ācārya* (instructor). Later, at another time, both the preceptor and the instructor fell ill simultaneously; [the disciple] did not know whom he should serve and attend to.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one is capable, both may attend to him; if one lacks the strength, one should provide for the one who serves as the *upādhyāya*.
If there is no one to teach and recite with him, he may dwell wherever he finds himself; however, if there is no *upādhyāya*, it is not permissible for him to remain."
The setting is the same as before.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who ordained another and conferred full ordination upon him, yet he immediately abandoned him and traveled elsewhere. He did not provide for his disciple with food, clothing, or the Dharma; consequently, the disciple sought refuge elsewhere, where his [new] teacher supported him with food, clothing, and the Dharma.
As the Blessed One has taught, there are four means of integration: giving, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.
At that time, the disciples felt a redoubled sense of reverence toward their teacher and had no desire to be separated from him.
Later, at another time, when his preceptor had finished his travels and returned to the Jeta Grove, the young bhikṣus all rose to welcome him, while those who were elderly cried out, "Welcome!"
When his former disciples saw him, they did not rise from their seats.
The bhikṣus said to them:
"When seeing a venerable one approach, those who are young all rise to welcome him; as for the elderly, they merely say: "I see you, Venerable One."'"
"Welcome. "For what reason do you now see your own Teacher coming and yet remain seated without rising? Is this not contrary to reason? He replied:
"Could it be that they, having ordained me and granted me full admission, might provide for me with food, clothing, and the Dharma, so that I may remember them, see them, and welcome them?"
The bhikṣu replied: "Do not speak such words!
As the Buddha has said:"

"Furthermore, if there is a person who relies upon a teacher, shaves off their hair and beard within the Buddha-dharma, dons the dharma robes, and leaves the household life to practice with pure faith, that person shall not be able to repay the teacher's kindness even by providing the four types of offerings for as long as they live."
"Your statement is not reasonable.
He then remained silent.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"When a disciple or follower sees their teacher, they must immediately stand up; however, if they see their preceptor (upādhyāya) or the one upon whom they rely (niśraya), they shall relinquish [that reliance].
Regarding the Buddha's statement that one "relinquishes reliance" upon seeing the preceptor, the bhikṣus did not know how this was to be understood.
It is related in detail as follows. The setting is the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had a young man as his attendant (niśraya). When half a month had passed and it was time for the Poṣadha ceremony, he went to his teacher and said:
“Ācārya! I now pay homage and have a request to submit: I wish to observe the poṣadha.
The teacher says:
"O virtuous one! For what reason have I become your teacher? He replied:
“I shall take you as my ācārya for dependence.
The teacher said:
“If you are so arrogant and disrespectful, who would grant you dependence?”
"Go as you please and seek another teacher elsewhere.
He then remained silent.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
“Because the bhikṣus do not pay homage to their preceptors three times each day, such faults arise.
Therefore, it should be known that disciples and followers must approach their two teachers to offer salutations three times every day.”
He then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Therefore, you disciples and followers should approach your two teachers to pay them homage three times every day."
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who acted as the preceptor for a young novice, caring for him and providing for his needs with affection as if he were his own son.
Later, when that disciple encountered some other business and had to go elsewhere, he addressed his teacher, saying:
“Ācārya, please inspect the dwelling and bedding; I now wish to travel among the people.
The teacher said:
"Is there nothing lacking for you, my son? He replied, "Ācārya!"
"I have no lack of anything; however, I wish to travel about various places in the human realm and shall return before long.
He replied, "Go, my son; if you feel regret along the way, you may return immediately."
He replied, "Excellent! I shall return at once in accordance with your instructions."
Having reached the halfway point, he immediately felt regret and thought to himself:
"I have provided for all my teacher's needs; it would be improper for me to abandon him and go elsewhere. I should now turn back."
He then returned to his dwelling.
When the master saw him, he asked, "You have come back again; is there something you have forgotten?"
He replied, “I have not forgotten anything; however, while on the road, I thought to myself:
‘My preceptor provides me with whatever I require; what further need is there for me to travel abroad?’”
"It is for this reason that I have returned.
The Master said, "Excellent!"
The teacher further thought:
"Should he remain under his previous dependence, or should I grant him a new one?
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the preceptor has a mind of attachment while the disciple has no mind of attachment, this is called 'not relinquishing the dependence.
If the preceptor has no mind of attachment while the disciple has a mind of attachment, this also is called 'not relinquishing the dependence.'"
If both individuals harbor feelings of attachment, it is not termed "renunciation.
If both individuals renounce [the relationship], it is termed "loss of reliance.
The setting and circumstances are as before.

There was a bhikṣu who served as the leader of a group; for many years, they had studied and recited together under him. At one time, the teacher suddenly fell ill with a seasonal affliction, yet those students who were his pupils did not look after him, and this continued for three such occasions without any showing of concern.
Later, when his illness had subsided, the disciples all came to request of their teacher, saying:
"Instruct us in study and recitation. Or they said:
"Recite for me," the teacher said. "Venerable one!
[the student replied.]
"I am afflicted by three defilements, yet none of you turn their backs to look upon me.
If there is anyone who, seeing such arrogance in you, can instruct you, you may go to them to engage in recitation."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The teacher who instructs them in recitation should also attend to them.
When they did all of these things, their wholesome qualities were impaired; the Buddha said:
"It should be done by turn.
At that time, there was an elderly, emaciated bhikṣu who had already taken up residence;
the others informed him, "Elder, it shall be your turn tomorrow."
He replied: "Why do you provide direct service to the Teacher?
You remain at ease while I constantly attend to and nourish him."
The people replied, "This is a virtuous deed, just as the Buddha has said:
'To care for a sick person is to care for me.'"
"O virtuous man, you may do as you wish.
He then provided [the necessary supplies], and because of this, the illness was cured.
He came to invite the Master, saying:
"Teach me to recite the scriptures. He replied,
"Wait a moment!"
"It is not yet your turn.
Later, he requested of the Master, saying,
"Please teach me how to recite from memory."
He replied, "It is not yet your turn.
He then answered his teacher:
"The responsibility for attending to and providing for [the master] falls upon me; the others shall take turns in the sequence for reciting and teaching the scriptures.
You should dwell here well while I go out on a journey.
The Master said:
"Stay for a while!
Whatever you require, I shall provide it all for you.
He remained silent.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"The constant attendant must not be treated like others; do not allow his duties to be neglected, and let others take turns following him.
At that time, there were two men:
One was intelligent and one was dull-witted.
When the teacher bestowed [the teachings] upon the intelligent one, the text was lengthy; consequently, the dull-witted one fell behind. The Buddha said:
"You should bestow them again in succession."
The setting was as before.

The six bhikṣus of the group went to the house of their disciples; they brought out a bed for them to sit upon, and all six sat together on it. The bed then broke, whereupon they all laughed aloud at once.
Other bhikṣus saw this and said to him:
"Venerable one!
To commit such an unrighteous act and yet feel no shame, you even laugh loudly!"
They replied together,
"How could we possibly drink alcohol or eat onions and garlic?
He reported this, saying:
"This too shall surely be done before long.
He asked, "In what way am I unrighteous?"
He replied, "How could you not see that the bed is broken and heavy? He answered:
"How could it be that the wood is exhausted and the skillful craftsman has passed away?
He then remained silent.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not have six people sit together on a single bed.
They then had five people, which was still subject to the same fault as before; with four people it was likewise so. The Buddha said:
"There should not be four."
If three persons may sit upon a single bed, or two persons may sit together on a large wooden stool, while only one may sit on a small one;
whoever violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The fourth section of the fourth gate, summarized in verse, says:
Nursing the sick except for natural transgressions; One about to be ordained should not climb trees;
Kings and ministers do not receive the precepts; One should not perform the act of cutting off a hand.
The setting was as before.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One:
"As the Buddha has said:"
"If one sees a sick person, they should provide for them.
[The monks asked,] "With what things should they provide such service?
The Buddha said:
"Upāli! With the exception of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), you may provide all other pure items as you wish.
The setting of this account is the same as before.

At that time, the Venerable Upānanda had a śrāmaṇera who wished to receive full ordination. The preceptor immediately summoned a karma-master, a private instructor, and seven other monks; taking the śrāmaṇera along with the items for the seat, they first went to the ritual platform to sweep the ground and spread the mats.
When the people had not yet arrived, Upānanda looked around and, seeing that the trees were in bloom, immediately commanded the śrāmaṇera:
"You may gather some flowers and go to give them to the community of monks."
He then climbed a tree and fell to the ground, injuring his hand and thus failing to complete his full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "You should know this!"
Just as the eldest son of a wheel-turning monarch, who is about to receive consecration and is next in line for the royal throne, is protected with redoubled care during this time,
so too should one who desires full ordination be well-loved and protected.
Therefore, one must not allow a person who is about to receive full ordination to climb a tall tree; whoever causes them to climb shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The setting of this episode is the same as before.

There was a householder named Viśāla who was entrusted with matters by King Prasenajit. On one occasion, having committed an error, he was rebuked by the king. The householder then thought to himself:
"Since it is difficult for any sovereign to maintain his reign for long, it is fitting that I should avoid him from afar; I shall now go to seek ordination.
Having thought thus, he went to the Jetavana Grove.

The group of six bhikṣus would always have one person stationed by the door; at that time, Upānanda was standing at the entrance and, seeing Pūrṇa approaching, addressed him with pleasant words: "Welcome!"
"Why is it so difficult to behold, appearing like the new moon? He replied,
"Venerable One!"
"How can one not have heard the saying of the world's people:
'One pays respect when meeting someone rarely, but treats them with contempt upon seeing them often'? He asked.
"Vast One! For what reason have you come? He replied:

“O Noble One! Any king is difficult to serve for long; though one may gain his favor now, it ultimately leads to the destruction of one’s own body. I wish to renounce the household life—would you be able to deliver me?”
He replied, "O worthy one!

To be able to give rise to such a mind is an exceedingly virtuous deed. For all who go forth into homelessness, there are five benefits, as extensively explained elsewhere; they are praised by all Buddhas, śrāvakas, and wise ones."
"Now is precisely the right time.
He then led him away, granted him the going-forth, and conferred full ordination upon him.
At that time, King Prasenajit asked his ministers, but they did not see Mahādeva.
"Did you encounter some illness?
He replied, "He has no ailment;
it was because the Great King rebuked him that he departed immediately, went to the Jeta Grove, and became a renunciant."
The king asked, "Who has done this? They replied:
"Venerable Upānanda. Upon hearing these words, the king harbored resentment in his heart and sent a messenger to inform him:
"Venerable One!..."

"Those whom I have rebuked have already been ordained; now you may ordain me, as well as Prince Aśoka, Queen Śrīmālā, and the courtesan Vāsavadattā, so that we may all go forth together. You may then declare yourself king and rule over the city."
The messenger went to the monastery and related the King’s words in full.
Upon hearing these words from the King, Upānanda replied to the messenger, saying:
"Take my words and report them to your King:..."
"Come to the monastery and take Āṣāḍha, Vaśiṣṭhā, and Varṣākāra—all of them—into the monastic order; I shall serve as king. What harm would there be in this?"
"How could I have gone to his house to entice him with grand promises to leave the household life?
He came to me of his own accord seeking refuge; I then delivered him, benefiting him according to the occasion and thereby attaining boundless merit."
Upon hearing these words, the king gave rise to even greater derision and suspicion.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"There is such a fault in ordaining the king’s ministers; therefore, one should not haphazardly ordain such persons."
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know that Upānanda is a foolish man! He ordained the minister Viśāla, causing the King to give rise to resentment.
Therefore, bhikṣus should not ordain ministers into the homeless life; when someone comes to request ordination, you must interrogate them [as follows]:”
"Are you not a minister of the king?
If one grants ordination without making such an inquiry, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

After the Buddha had established this rule, there were foreigners who arrived whom no one recognized, and whose home kings had not previously granted permission. When they went to the bhikṣus and requested ordination, everyone felt doubt and hesitation and did not grant them ordination. The Buddha said:
"If there are such persons from foreign lands, they should be granted ordination; do not harbor any doubt.
The setting for this account is the same as before.

On one occasion, the Venerable Ānanda, having recently shaved his beard and hair, dressed in his robes and carrying his alms bowl in the early morning, entered the city to beg for food and proceeded along the main street.
There was a brahmin who was a great scholar; in a fine, spacious, and lofty hall, he was teaching five hundred brahmin youths to read the Four Vedas.

At that time, the teacher was arrogant and self-important, lacking in propriety; harboring a malicious disposition, he held others in contempt. Upon seeing the Venerable Ānanda, he commanded his disciple, saying:
"Can you not strike this bald śramaṇa on the head with your hand?"
He replied, "I can.
Then that disciple, obeying his teacher's command, struck the Venerable’s head with his fist.

At that time, Ānanda looked around in all four directions; the brahmin became even more enraged and distressed, and again ordered his disciple to strike him on the head. The Venerable One thought to himself:
"Why did I look around?"
"You should depart in silence.
Having arrived at the Jetavana, finished his meal, and washed his bowl, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Venerable ones!..."
"One should not go to such-and-such a street or lane. He asked:
"What fault or danger is there?"

He replied, "There was a brahmin there who was by nature malicious and unacquainted with etiquette; while instructing his disciples in the recitation of the *vidyā* treatises, he had one disciple strike my head with his fist."
The bhikṣu asked, "What offense have you committed to cause him such resentment? He replied:
"I am both without fault and with fault.
He asked, "What is the meaning of this?"
He replied: "I originally committed no offense when he struck my head; it was because I looked back that he struck me again.
Thus, the former act was without fault, while the latter constitutes an offense."
When Upānanda heard this, he asked,
"Venerable sir,
what were you saying?"
He replied, "There is a small matter. Upānanda said:
“I have heard it briefly; I pray that you will explain it further.
He then explained it in detail.
At that time, Upānanda nodded his head three times and, uttering an assent with his voice, thought thus:
"I shall now personally subdue that petty man.
He had the barber shave his head both forward and backward until it was clean, rubbed it with oil, and in the early morning, donned his robes and took up his bowl, entering the city of Śrāvastī.
Gradually, he arrived at the place where the brahmin was teaching; however, as the brahmin had other matters to attend to, he had not yet seen the bhikṣu.
At that time, Upānanda was walking back and forth right in front of him. Seeing this, the brahmin called out to a disciple, saying:
"Go and strike that shaven-headed śramaṇa!"
Having heard these words, Upānanda said to the brahmin,
"You ignorant fellow, why do you send another instead of coming yourself to strike me?"
The brahmin, seized by great anger, immediately departed and struck him on the head with his fist.
Upānanda then seized him by the arm and replied, "You fool!"
"Upānanda has been struck by you; I shall now take you together to the King.

He then seized his arm and dragged him forward. The Brahmin cried out loudly, calling for his disciples to come, and seizing one of his other arms, they pulled him along. As others continued to arrive, they all were likewise dragged away.
Upānanda possessed great physical strength; he dragged both the brahmin and his five hundred disciples all the way to the king’s gate.
It was the natural habit of the group of six that whenever they harbored anger, the royal palace would tremble as they reached the king’s gate.
Having observed these signs, the king said to his attendants, "Did any of the holy Six Groups of Monks come out as we were observing?
He immediately went out to look and saw Upānanda arriving at the gate accompanied by five hundred sons of Brahmins; he returned and informed the king.
"The noble Upānanda is now outside the gate.
The king said, "Call him in."
He then met him face-to-face and asked, "Great King!
Had the noble Ānanda not gone forth as a renunciant, what rank would he have been entitled to?"
The king said:
"Noble One! He shall become a Wheel-Turning King."
“What kind of person are you, Your Majesty?
He replied, “I am an attendant.”
He further said:

"The King previously established a decree: 'Regard the bhikṣus as if they were crown princes, and regard the affairs of the bhikṣuṇīs as equal to those of the queens and consorts. This matter is granted exemption and does not apply equally to others."

"The King holds us both in equal affection; yet there was a brahmin who, defying the King's command, struck the head of the Venerable Ānanda with his fist. He, in turn, harboring anger, struck me on the crown of my head. Was this action appropriate?"
Upon hearing this, the king was greatly incensed and commanded his attendants, saying,
"You may go now and cut off the hands of this brāhmaṇa.
The minister then led the brāhmaṇa to the streets and informed the public of what had transpired.
At that time, his parents, along with other kinsmen and friends, all came together, weeping with tears falling like rain, wailing aloud and speaking these words:
"Alas, our son! Alas!"
"Alas, my son! They all proceeded together and addressed the judge, saying,
"Excellent, Great Minister!
"My son has committed an offense, and the King has ordered his hand to be severed.
Since he has violated the laws of the state, this is not an unjust punishment.
However, as a Brahmin, my son relies on his right hand for his livelihood; if you were instead to sever his left hand, it would truly be a gracious act of leniency."
Upon hearing this, the minister immediately cut off his left hand.
Later, at another time, when the Brahmin’s hand wound had gradually healed, he covered his left hand and raised his right arm to point at the sections as he recited the scriptures.
Seeing him from afar with his hand raised, Upānanda became even more incensed; returning to the king's presence, he said:
"Great King! It is the law for a king that his commands must not be disobeyed, for in this lies true happiness."
Although the king knew that such a thing did not exist in his kingdom,
he replied, "Noble one,
what business do I have?"
He replied, "Previously,
you issued an edict to have the hands of the brahmin cut off, yet those hands appear intact.
The king summoned his ministers and questioned them, saying:
"Brahmin, why did you not cut off your hand?
He replied, "I have already cut it off."
“If that is so, Noble Upānanda was seen by the people raising his hand to teach them how to read.

The minister replied, “I saw his parents weeping and exhorting him, saying, ‘All Brahmins live by their right hands; it would be fortunate if you were to cut off your left. For this reason, he immediately cut off his left hand.”
The king said, "His parents cut off his left side; now, by my command, you shall cut off the right side as well.
He then went and executed the execution.
At that time, the brahmin stood with his arms hanging down, as he was now without both hands. Later, when Upānanda passed by his side, he asked him:
"Why do you hang your hands, not striking my head as you did in the past?"
Upon hearing this, he was distressed and remained silent, unable to respond.
Then the brahmins, elders, householders, and the entire multitude were filled with reproach and shame, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, lack compassion; they dispatch others to carry out executions and perform such cruel deeds as cutting off the hands of others."
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"When a bhikṣu severs another's hand, such faults arise; therefore, a bhikṣu should not sever the hands or feet of others."
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The foolish Upānanda has committed an act unbecoming of a śramaṇa and improper to do; having gone forth from the household life within my Dharma, he has performed such an evil deed."
"If there is a bhikṣu who severs a person's hands or feet, he incurs the offense of thullaccaya.
All these bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!"
"For what reason did the Venerable Ānanda protect that brahmin, while Upānanda, harboring a desire for retribution,
cut off his hand? The Buddha said,
"It is not only today that Ānanda has given rise to a mind of protection, and Upānanda has carried out an act of retribution by severing his hand."
"You all should listen.

In the distant past, there was a garden filled everywhere with flowers, fruits, and bathing pools. At that time, a hermit lived there, subsisting only on roots and fruits and drinking water for his own contentment; he wore nothing but skins and had no further desires, sitting cross-legged beneath a fruit tree to contemplate the meaning of the Dharma."
Above, a monkey climbed for fruit and caused it to fall, striking his head.
At that time, the hermit spoke a verse, saying:
"I never conceived the thought To cause you to die in suffering."
"Because you have committed this transgression yourself, you shall surely reap the retribution of losing your life.

At that time, the hermit had previously been a close friend of the hunter. The hunter went out to that forest and arrived beneath a fruit tree; finding the hermit absent as he had gone away on some business, the hunter took a moment’s rest there under the tree.

Then that monkey took a large fruit and struck the hunter on the head. Since the hunter’s head was previously hairless, as soon as the fruit fell, blood began to flow from his head. Tormented by the pain, he raised his head to look at the tree and saw the monkey leaping upon its branches. He immediately drew his bow and shot it with a poisoned arrow; the monkey fell from the tree and died as a result.

"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts: the hermit of that time was none other than Ānanda; the monkey of those days was none other than this brahmin; and the hunter was none other than Upānanda."
At that time, he was protected by Ānanda and rejected by Upānanda; even until now, it remains the same—one protects and one rejects.
From this one should know that the causal conditions of prior karma are never lost;
this has been explained at length elsewhere. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 16. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.
Volume Seventeen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
The fourth section, fifth subsection: A summary verse says:
Caṇḍasodāyin [took] the great robe for temporary use;
Sermuvasuta took a bowl with the thought that it was his own property;
Aśvagupta took his own robe with the thought that it was a thief's.
This verse and its detailed explanation do not differ from those concerning the precept against stealing; therefore, they are not repeated here, and may be understood by consulting them.
The summary verse for the sixth section of the fourth chapter states:
Pigs, sugarcane, and *tāla* fruit; The woolen cloak and the return of Kālī.
One should place knives and needles [in a case], and not use vessels made of lapis lazuli.
The setting is as before.
At that time, during a year of famine, there was a thief who stole another's pig, went into a dark forest to slaughter and eat it, and then cast away the bones, head, and hooves before departing.

It was the constant custom of the group of six monks to rise early in the morning, ascend to the upper story of the monastery, and look out in all four directions; if they saw smoke from afar or flocks of crows descending in disorder, they would immediately call one another to go together and observe.
Having seen smoke rising from the dark forest and crows descending, they then said to one another:
"Nanda and Upananda! There must certainly be something edible there; we should go, for we may obtain something."
Upon arriving there, they saw pig bones and heads and feet;
they said to one another, "These discarded things are quite sufficient!
We may boil them and eat."
He then proceeded to cook it himself.
At that time, the owner of the pig followed his tracks and arrived; seeing him cooking the meat, he said, "Venerable One!..."
"It is not appropriate for one wearing the robes of a Great Sage to act in this manner.
He replied, "O Noble One!"
If I were to engage in the act of killing, could I not have taken the exquisite flesh of fine deer or gazelles for my food?
Why would I have taken this pig’s bones, head, and feet to boil and eat?
Someone stole some choice meat and ate it; the remaining bones and hooves were discarded by him as refuse. What offense have they committed against me?
He replied: “Noble One!...”
"However, one who has gone forth from the household life should not perform such loathsome acts.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not take discarded items in such a manner; whoever does so commits a transgression of the Dharma."
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, there was a thief who took another's sugarcane; having finished eating the middle portion, he discarded both the root and the tip.
As the group of six monks were walking along, they saw this and said to one another:
“Venerable sir!
There are many discarded items; let us collect them together.
And so they collected them.
At that time, the Lord of Ikṣvāku followed their tracks and arrived; seeing those six groups of monks gathering the remaining sugarcane together, he said to them:
"Noble ones! You wear the robes of great sages yet perform such unrighteous deeds."
He replied: "O worthy one!
If I were capable of committing theft, how could I not have taken fine sugarcane to eat as I pleased, instead of taking what others had discarded?"
"However, there was someone who stole these sugarcane stalks; we have taken them, eating the good parts and discarding the bad.
What fault is there in this? He said:
"Noble one! This act of disparagement is not something that should be done by those who have gone forth.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not take discarded items (pāṃsukūla) in such a manner; whoever does so commits a transgression of the Dharma.
The setting is as before. At that time, there was a thief who took tāla fruits from a dark forest, selecting the good ones to eat and discarding the bad ones.
The group of six monks saw these discarded items while traveling; the circumstances were identical to those regarding the sugarcane, leading eventually to their being rebuked by the laity.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Those who take them shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
The setting was the same as before.

At that time, there was a young perfume-seller in this city who possessed a fine woolen cloak (*kambala*) for which he felt such great affection that it surpassed all other possessions. Later, he fell ill; although medical treatment was administered, it was ineffective, and his end drew near.
He then gathered his kinsmen and said to them: "After my death, do not cremate me with fire. Instead, wrap my body in this woolen cloak and cast me into the forest wilds."
The relatives present together comforted him, saying:
"You need not fear; how could it be that everyone who falls ill must die?
Before long, you shall naturally recover."

However, as his life came to its end, it was difficult to sustain; his breath suddenly ceased because he had conceived such heavy attachment to the woolen cloak. After his life ended, he was reborn among the *vighna* spirits known as those with great goiters (*mahāgalagaṇḍa*).
At that time, the relatives adorned the funeral bier with five colors of silk and, having wrapped the corpse in a woolen shawl, carried it to the cemetery.
Upon seeing this, the bhikṣu said to the bhikṣu Kāla-nanda of the Śmaśāna:
"Venerable one!..."
There was a perfume seller who died of illness; his body was wrapped in a fine woolen cloak and discarded in the forest. This is a *pāṃsukūla* (refuse-rag) that you may go and take.
He then went quickly to the charnel ground and took the woolen cloak.
At that moment, the non-human being raised the corpse and firmly seized the cloak, saying these words: "Noble Kāṇa!"
"Do not take my cloak.
For those in the charnel ground generally possess great courage; he then replied to the spirit, "Fool!"
"Because of your attachment to your woolen cloak, you were born among the hungry ghosts; do you now wish to go further to the hells?
You should let it go now.
Kṛṣṇa, out of love and attachment, struggled with the ghost, but the ghost kicked him and forcibly dragged him away toward the Jetavana Grove.
At that time, the corpse-demon’s anger intensified further; he pursued [the monk] without ceasing and said, "Noble One!
Return my woolen cloak to me!"
He did not accept the invitation and entered the monastery.

However, the Jetavana Grove was protected by many devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and other great deities; this ghost, being of little merit, did not dare to proceed further and remained weeping before the gate of the monastery.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"For what reason are non-human beings weeping before the gate?
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The bhikṣu Kālakalpa has taken that woolen cloak.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"Observe how this non-human being has developed such deep attachment; if he does not obtain the cloak, he will surely vomit hot blood and die immediately."
He said to Ānanda, "You should go at once and tell Kāḷaka Udāyin to return the non-human fur cloak; if he does not give it back, he will vomit blood and die."
Having given him the cloak, he ordered the messenger to proceed ahead to that grove and say,
"Lie down," and afterwards cover him with the cloak.
Then Ānanda delivered the Buddha’s instruction to the bhikṣu Kāla-nandika, as described in detail above, until the point where [the robe] was later covered with a woolen cloak.
Having heard this, Kāla-nandika said to Ānanda,
“I shall not dare to transgress what the Buddha has taught.”
He replied to the spirit, saying, "The one who loves the woolen cloak may go ahead.
Upon reaching the forest, he sent it to lie down; as soon as it was told to do so, it lay down, and he covered it with the cloak.
At that time, the non-human being stepped upon the bhikṣu Kālika with its foot; Kālika possessed great strength and barely escaped death.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"A bhikṣu should not take garments from a cemetery at will, nor should he give them away in such a manner. When taking a garment, one should proceed from the feet toward the head; when giving a garment, one should proceed from the head toward the feet."
Bhikṣus, you should know:
there are five faults regarding robes from a charnel ground. What are these five?
First, foul colors; second, a foul odor;
third, lack of strength.
Fourth, it is infested with lice;
fifth, it is possessed by yakṣas.
One should not take the clothing from a corpse that has no open sores on its body.
Having heard that the Buddha had established this rule, the group of six monks immediately took a dog and departed. Those who lacked faith mocked them, asking:
"Venerable ones! You are taking a dog toward that empty forest; will you perhaps kill the animal?"
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not take a dog along.
[A man] then wounded him with a knife and took his robe; the Buddha said:
"It should not be done like that.
If insects or ants have damaged the body [of the robe], one should take it up later.
Having obtained the robe, he put it on immediately as he pleased; the Buddha said:
"You must not wear it immediately; you may place it in a thicket for seven or eight days. Once it has been dried by the wind and sun, you may then wash, dye, and wear it."
He immediately donned it and entered the monastery to circumambulate and prostrate before the *caitya*.

The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "I shall now establish the rules of conduct for a bhikṣu from the Śmaśāna (Cemetery). A bhikṣu from the Śmaśāna who wears the garments of the deceased must not enter the monastery, nor prostrate before the *caitya*; if he wishes to prostrate, he must remain at a distance of one *vyāma* (fathom). He shall not occupy monastic quarters, beds, or mats; he shall not sit in the assembly; he shall not preach the Dharma or its meaning to laypeople; and he shall not go to the homes of the laity."
If there is a reason that necessitates going there, one should stand outside the gate.
If the host commands one to enter, one should reply:
"I dwell in the charnel ground."
If they say, "I have now obtained great benefit and merit, for I am fortunate that the noble one, who is superior to many people,
has come to my house," upon hearing these words, he should immediately enter the house, but not sit upon a bed or seat.
If someone calls for you to sit, reply:
"I dwell in the charnel ground.
If they speak of the difficulty of encountering such a person, you should then sit; do not harbor any doubt.
"If a bhikṣu in the Śmaśāna does not follow this instruction, he commits a *vyatikrama* offense.
The setting of the occasion is the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣus placed their knives and needles in various locations, where they were damaged by dirt. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not place it anywhere at random; rather, it should be placed upon a needle-cloth.
The bhikṣus did not understand how this should be done, so the Buddha said:
"One should apply felt or use yellow beeswax rubbed onto cloth to wrap the knives and needles; then they will not become tarnished.
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Tullānandā had previously stored some imitation glass vessels. A certain bhikṣuṇī, oppressed by thirst and wishing to drink water, went to that bhikṣuṇī’s place and asked:
"Noble One! I am oppressed by thirst; I have brought this lapis lazuli vessel with the intention of drinking water. He replied:
"This is a vessel; you may take it and use it.
When she used it, it fell to the ground and broke.
At a later time, Pūtanā remembered the borrowed vessel and immediately asked her for it back:
"Give me back my vessel," he said.
The other replied, "Noble one!"
"If you hold it loosely and it falls to the ground and breaks, you must make another one and return it.
He replied, "Give me back my original object."
Thus, for a long time, they repeatedly disturbed one another.
They informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha thought to himself:

“Since there are such faults when a bhikṣuṇī drinks water from a lapis lazuli vessel, a bhikṣuṇī should not drink water or eat food from such a vessel; if she makes use of it, she incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.”
The summary verse for the seventh section of the fourth book says:
One should paint throughout the monastery; lighting fires and bathing;
not treading on leaves with bowl-water; and eating while wearing shoes are not permitted.
The setting is the same as before.
After the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had offered his park, he thought to himself:
"If it were not painted and decorated, it would not be magnificent; if the Buddha permits it, I wish to adorn it."
He immediately went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"Paint as you wish.
Having heard the Buddha’s permission, he gathered various pigments and summoned a painter, telling him:
"This is colored pigment; it may be used to paint within the monastery.
He replied, "From where shall we work?"
"What do you wish to paint?
He replied, "I do not yet know; I shall go and ask the Buddha."
The Buddha said: "Householder!

On both sides of the doorway, you should depict yakṣas holding staffs; next to one side, depict the manifestation of great supernatural powers; on the other side, paint the wheel of saṃsāra with its five destinies; and beneath the eaves, paint the accounts of past lives."

Beside the door of the Buddha Hall, paint a Mālādhara Yakṣa; in the lecture hall, paint an elder Bhikṣu proclaiming the essential points of the Dharma; in the dining hall, paint a Piṇḍapātra Yakṣa; beside the door of the storehouse, paint a Ratnadhara Yakṣa; in the water hall, paint a Nāga holding a water jar and wearing exquisite necklaces; for the bathhouse and the fire hall, paint according to the ritual methods of the Devadūta Sūtra; and depict various hells in great detail. In the infirmary, paint an image of the Tathāgata personally tending to the sick; in the places for excrement and urine, depict the forms of corpses in a terrifying manner; and within the private chambers, one should paint white bones and skulls.
At that time, having heard this from the Buddha, the householder prostrated at his feet and departed. He then followed the instructions to paint and decorate [the monastery].
Once the painting was complete, there was a monk who did not exercise mindfulness, who lit fires in various places, and the smoke damaged the paintings.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit the bhikṣus to construct a fire-hall.
If there is a need, one should kindle a fire therein and not in any other place; whoever does so shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
At that time, there was a sick person who required fire; however, he did not dare to light it beneath the eaves of the room.
The Buddha said, "You may light it outside the monastery or in the courtyard of the monastery; wait until the smoke has cleared before bringing the fire inside."
The setting was as before.
The bhikṣus bathed beneath the eaves, and the moisture damaged the murals on the walls. The Buddha said: "You should not do so."
"One may bathe within the monastery near a corner, facing the Buddha image, or one may construct a separate bathing room.
When there was mud in the room, the Buddha said:
"Bricks should be laid and a drainage outlet for water should be made."
"If there is impurity, one should wash and clear it out from time to time, or go near a water channel for the purpose of bathing.
The setting is the same as before.
In this city, there was a brahmin whose son fell ill; he went to a physician and asked:
"My son has such an illness; please provide a prescription for him.
The man, being faithful and respectful, replied:
"Virtuous one, you may go to the community of noble ones and beg for bowl-water; if you use it to wash his body, he will surely recover."
When the brahmin had heard this, he departed and went to the Jeta Grove, where the group of six monks was at the gate.
Seeing the brahmin, Upānanda said to him, "Welcome!"
"Why do you appear so slow, like the new moon? He replied,
"I pay homage to the Noble One!"
"I have indeed rarely come before, and it is my good fortune to meet you today; had I come frequently, you would have conceived a sense of contempt for me.
He asked, "For what purpose have you come?"
He replied, "Venerable Sir!
My son’s illness is grave; I went to consult a physician, and he said:"
"If one were to beg for water from the bowls of the Noble Assembly, one's illness could be cured.
I have therefore come to beg; I pray you will grant me this. Upānanda replied:
“Wait a moment; I shall fetch some water.

He then entered the monastery, finished his meal, washed his bowl, and took the remaining cakes, parched grain, vegetables, fruit, and various leaves, mixing them with water. Carrying it out of the monastery, he addressed the brahmin, saying:
“This is the water from my bowl; you may take and use it.”
He said, "Noble One!
My son would rather die than use such impure things as these to wash his body."
Upānanda said, "If your faith is as firm and accomplished as you claim, then your son should likewise recover from his illness.
At that, the brahmin felt a deep sense of contempt.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:

"Because of placing unsuitable items in the alms bowl, such faults as these arise. Therefore, I now command all bhikṣus not to place unsuitable items within their bowls; whoever does so shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
However, I shall now establish the rules for the proper procedure when bhikṣus offer water from their bowls to others:
one must first wash the bowl three times, fill it with water, and then consecrate it by reciting verses from the Buddha’s sūtras over it several times before offering it.
"If you do not comply, you shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The setting and circumstances were as before.
At that time, whenever the bhikṣus ate, they would step on the leaves used to replace their bowls with their feet; seeing this, lay travelers mocked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are truly impure; they eat while treading upon the leaves on which their bowls were placed.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not tread upon leaves while eating; whoever does so commits a *dharmātikrama* offense."
The Buddha was staying in Vaiśālī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who ate while wearing leather sandals; some lay travelers criticized him, saying, "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, eat in an impure manner."
The Buddha said, "One should not eat while wearing shoes in this manner; whoever does so commits a *vyatikrama* offense.
At that time, the sick monks removed their leather sandals to eat, which caused their illnesses to worsen. The Buddha said:
“If a sick person does not remove their leather sandals and steps upon them while eating.
The summary verse for the eighth section of the fourth gate says:
“Crossing over great thieves without a bowl; the rainy season retreat without a formal preceptor;”
"Five years of sharing the same provisions; one should not carry heavy burdens.
The occasion was at Śrāvastī.

Upānanda had ordained a disciple who had no bowl to give him. When the assembly was eating, each person washed their own bowl and placed it in a clean spot before going out to pay homage to the stūpa. Upon seeing the bowls, the newly ordained monk thought:
"This bowl is vacant; I shall take it now and return after the meal.
He then intended to take the bowl of the Elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya, whereupon the others replied, "Venerable One!..."
"This is the Venerable One's bowl; you should not take it.
He then took the bowls of other Venerables, such as Aśvajit and Bhadrika.
The bhikṣus asked:
"Do you have no bowl? He replied, "I have none."
“Who was it that first gave you an almsbowl and ordained you? He replied, “My preceptor, Upānanda, ordained me.”
The bhikṣus mocked and reproached him, saying,
"Aside from that man of evil conduct, who would not give his bowl to another and allow them to go forth?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not grant ordination to another without providing them with an alms bowl; whoever does so incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
Whenever one wishes to grant ordination to another, one must first provide them with the six requisite items: the three robes, the sitting mat, the alms bowl, and the water filter."
The Venerable Upāli requested the Blessed One, saying:
"If one knowingly confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon someone who lacks a bowl, does the ordination become valid?
The Buddha said:
"It is accomplished.
Those who receive it incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
"Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, using either a small bowl or an excessively large bowl, or even a white bowl, confers full ordination (*upasampadā*). Is the full ordination accomplished?"
The Buddha said:
"It is accomplished.
Those who receive it incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, there was a great thief who, while stealing another's property, was discovered by the owner; having abandoned the goods and fled, he went to the Jetavana Grove.
Being exhausted from his journey, he stopped beneath a tree and sat with his cheek resting in his palm.
At that time, during the first part of the day, Upānanda took up his robe and bowl and entered the city to beg for food; on the road, he saw a thief and asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, “I am a poor man. He asked:
"If that is so, why do you not go forth [into homelessness]?
He replied, "I shall discuss going forth only after I have related my circumstances; I am a great thief—who would take me in?"
He replied, "The teaching of the World-Honored One takes compassion as its priority; who would not feel pity and welcome one another?
You must resolve to do so, and I shall grant you ordination."
“Excellent, Noble One! I shall now leave the household life.
Upānanda immediately granted him the going forth and the full ordination, and said to him:
“O worthy one! Have you ever seen a deer capable of supporting other deer?
The city of Śrāvastī is vast and spacious; it is the very place where our ancestors once roamed. You should go there to beg for alms in order to sustain yourself.”
Having heard these words, during the first part of the day, he took up his robes and bowl and entered the city to beg for alms.
As he was wandering through the streets, the laypeople all recognized him and said to one another,
"This is a great thief who has now gone forth as a monk."
They further mocked him together, saying: "Excellent!

These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, know this man to be a great thief and yet they have allowed him to leave the household life. By day he patrols the houses and becomes thoroughly familiar with their locations; by night he acts as a thief, stealing the property of others."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"There are such faults in ordaining bandits as monks.
He then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If one is a great thief, do not grant him ordination; whoever does so shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, not knowing the man was a thief, did not grant him ordination, whereupon the man created obstacles and deviated from the path to liberation. The Buddha said:
"If you know he is a thief, do not grant him ordination."
If you do not know [the answer], you should give it as you please.
If someone comes seeking to go forth, you should first ask them:
"Are you not a great thief?"
"If one does not inquire about their renunciation, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The setting of the narrative is the same as before.
At that time, there was a residence where a certain bhikṣu had many disciples who came to rely upon him for instruction.
When this teacher passed away, they had no one to rely upon and said to one another,
"Since we have no one to depend on, what shall we do?
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

“Those disciples should further seek out virtuous persons, provide them with excellent quarters, exempt them from administrative duties, and ensure that their attendants and bedding are all provided without deficiency.”
If it is obtained, that is well.
Should it not be available, the bhikṣus must not perform a second poṣadha ceremony at this location; any who violate this shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who wished to take up residence at a certain dwelling place, but his preceptor suddenly passed away. The people deliberated, saying, "What should we do?"
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"These individuals may likewise seek a teacher for dependence (niśrayācārya) and receive the same provisions as before.
If they obtain one, it is well."
"If such [a person] is not present, a bhikṣu should not observe the summer retreat there;
one who violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who had entered the prior summer retreat at a certain residence. An ācārya upon whom he relied fell ill and died, whereupon the people deliberated, saying:
"What should I do? he asked the Buddha. The Buddha said, "You should seek out a preceptor (niśrayācārya) and provide for him as before."
If one obtains [a preceptor], it is well.
If there is none, the bhikṣus at that time should seek a preceptor from another location for the subsequent summer retreat.
One who violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (dharma-āpatti).
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who was staying for the latter part of the summer retreat (paścimā varṣā) under the guidance of a single teacher, but that teacher subsequently passed away.
The Buddha said:
"For two months, you may stay together, examining one another and dwelling with vigilance; once the two months have passed, you shall have a person to rely upon, who will provide for you as before."
If there is none, one must not wait beyond the second *poṣadha*; one should instead seek a teacher for reliance (*niśraya*) in another location.
One who violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (*dharmāpatti*).
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who had received full ordination at a certain residence, and when his original preceptor passed away, he did not know what to do.
The Buddha said:
"All duties shall be performed exactly as before for the *upādhyāya*; should anyone act contrary to this, they shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
The setting was as before.
In a certain village, there was a great householder who constructed a dwelling complete with all necessary provisions and offered it to the Saṃgha of the four quarters.

Later, at another time, he was arrested by government officials. Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu abandoned the monastery and departed elsewhere; consequently, the property belonging to the Triple Gem was stolen by bandits.
When the householder was released, the bhikṣu learned of it and returned to inquire:
"Householder, you previously knew [of my departure] and abandoned the monastery, thereby losing the articles for our use."
The householder said, "For what reason,
O Noble One, have you abandoned the monastery and traveled elsewhere? He replied:
"I heard that the Elder was seized by the King; my heart was filled with fear, and I immediately fled.
He replied, "Though I am confined, my other kinsmen are surely not all under arrest. They are able to provide for me, so why such haste?"
Upon hearing this, he remained silent.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not flee."
One should ask the abbot’s kinsmen:
"The abbot has been detained; are you able to provide for and support him?
If they are able, that is well.
If one is unable [to do so], one should dwell for five years or more, maintaining oneself by begging for food as circumstances permit.
It is well if the monastery head departs;
if he does not depart, then for five years within that vicinity, one shall share the same *lābha* (alms-offerings) while performing the *poṣadha* separately.

The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) should be performed as follows: having spread the seats and struck the *gandī* bell, and after the formal announcement has been made, when the entire assembly has gathered, one *bhikṣu* should perform the *jñapti-karman* (motion) in this manner:
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!..."
If the donor who has built a monastery at this residence is now detained by a king or by bandits,

and if it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha allow that this residence and that [other] residence shall share the same distribution of alms (lābha) but perform the Poṣadha separately for a period of five years.
"Thus it is announced.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
The donor who has constructed this monastery at this present residence has now been detained by either a king or bandits.
The Saṃgha shall now, for five years, share the same distribution of alms (lābha) between this residence and that residence, while performing the Poṣadha ceremony separately.

If it is agreeable to the venerable ones that, for five years, the same alms-food be shared while the Uposatha be performed separately at this and that location, let them remain silent; if it is not agreeable, let them speak.
"The Saṃgha has already completed the act of sharing the same *lābha* (alms) and performing separate *poṣadha* at this place and that place for five years.
Since the Saṃgha has granted its consent by remaining silent, I now hold it to be so."
"If, after five years have passed, the owner comes, that is well.
If he does not come, even until ten years have passed, one should act in this manner: sharing the same *lābha* (material gains) but performing the *poṣadha* separately."
It is well if the master returns;
if he does not return, one may entrust all bedding and miscellaneous belongings to a nearby monastery, securely lock the monastery gate, and depart as one pleases.
"When the owner arrives, all entrusted items must be returned to him.
If they are returned, it is well; if they are not returned, the bhikṣu incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
The setting of this episode is the same as before.
When the six groups of bhikṣus carried heavy loads upon their own bodies, lay travelers saw them and immediately mocked them, saying:
"We laypeople have parents, wives, children, kings, officials, and others who provide for us; it is only fitting that we ourselves carry our own burdens."
“Virtuous one, for whom are you now performing such toil?
Hearing this, he remained silent.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu must not carry heavy burdens upon his body; whoever does so commits a transgression of the Dharma.
When the group of six bhikṣus heard this regulation, they immediately began carrying heavy loads on their heads, backs, waists, and hips, which again invited derision and censure.
"One should not carry a heavy burden in such a manner; the one who does so incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The summary verse for the ninth section of the fourth chapter states:
"Seeking the six requisites through the four reliances; stealing a bhikṣu’s robe;"
The five types of entrustment differ; one must know the methods for dyeing [robes].
The setting and circumstances are as before.
At that time, there was a brahmin who wished to seek ordination and went to the Jetavana Grove.
Having entered the monastery, he saw the bhikṣus holding their staffs and carrying their alms bowls, intending to go out for alms.
Upon seeing the bhikṣus, he thought to himself:
"I shall now ask them where they are going."
He asked, "Noble one, where do you wish to go?"
He replied, "I am going on almsround. He asked:
“Do all the bhikṣus beg for their food?
He replied, “Those who are of great virtue and well-known to the public mostly receive food brought by donors; those who are not well-known go out themselves to beg for food.”
He thought to himself:
"If I were to leave the household life, how would it differ from begging for food?
To come and join the disciples of the Śākya son would not exempt me from toil."
He further thought to himself:
"I should now ask another bhikṣu: 'Is it solely for the sake of seeking alms that one goes forth into homelessness, or are there other matters as well?'"
He then went to another person; having seen him, that person asked, "Why have you come now, O worthy one? He replied:
"Noble ones! There is a matter that requires your presence, which I wish to inquire about:
upon what basis do you have gone forth into homelessness?"
He replied, "An excellent question.
Please sit down comfortably; I shall explain it for you."
