That person, desiring to seek the going forth from home, prostrated and sat down.
The bhikṣu replied:
"For one who goes forth within the Buddha-dharma, there are four reliances; through the going forth and full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), one becomes a bhikṣu."
"What are the four?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

'Wearing rag-robes is pure and easy to obtain; sustaining life by begging for food, dwelling under trees, and using discarded medicines are pure and easy to obtain. By relying on these, one leaves the household life and becomes a bhikṣu.'"
When the brahmin heard these words, he replied: "Noble One!
Who could possibly make their living by relying on this?"
"My original intention was to seek ordination; seeing that this is so difficult to accomplish, I shall now take my leave.
Thus, [the former wife] became a great obstacle to his going forth and receiving full ordination.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:

"There is such a fault in first teaching the four reliances to those who have not yet left the household life; therefore, when a bhikṣu sees one who has not yet left the household life or received full ordination (*upasampadā*), he should not explain the four reliances to them, but may do so only after they have received full ordination."
"One who speaks beforehand incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma. The setting is as before.
There was a householder who, not long after marrying his wife, fathered a son; as the boy gradually grew up...
His father rebuked him with anger, whereupon he thought to himself, "It is difficult to serve one's father; I should instead go forth into the religious life.
He then went to the Jetavana Grove.
At that time, Upānanda saw him and asked,
"Why have you come? He replied:
"I wish to leave the household life.
He replied, "This is a virtuous deed, as the Buddha has said:"
"Indeed, there are five benefits for those who have left the household life, as extensively explained before and praised by the Buddha.
However, one who has left the household life must obtain the six requisites."
He asked, "What are the six? He replied:
“[I have] the three robes, the alms bowl, the water filter,
and bedding. He replied, “I have none.”
Upānanda said, "Go for now; I shall seek out the six requisite items you need.
He then took his leave and departed.
Knowing that his father had already abandoned him, he did not return to his original home but went instead to the house of his relatives.
When his kinsmen learned that this son of a wealthy man wished to leave the household life to become a renunciant, they would not allow him to go and immediately arranged for him to marry.
The Venerable Upānanda, having obtained the six requisites, entered the city at another time to beg for alms; seeing that boy, he said to him:
"O fair youth!"
"I have obtained the six requisites; you may come now, and I shall ordain you.
He replied, "Noble One!"
"I have also obtained the six requisites that are required. He asked,
"What are these six items?"
He replied, "They are what are called the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Upānanda asked:
"What is this? He replied, "My kinsmen have taken a wife for me who is complete in her six sense faculties; therefore, I am currently unable to go forth."
Because of these circumstances, it subsequently became a great obstacle to his going forth and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, if a poor person comes wishing to go forth and receive full ordination, you should lend him the six necessary requisites."
Why is this? It is truly difficult to encounter the opportunity to go forth and receive full ordination within the sublime Dharma and Vinaya, thereby attaining the nature of a bhikṣu.
Once fully ordained, one should subsequently seek out and restore to others their original property.
The setting was as before.

At that time, a large number of bhikṣus were traveling through the countryside when they encountered bandits on the road who plundered all their clothing and requisites. The bandits went to the Jeta Grove to sell the stolen goods, while the robbed bhikṣus also arrived at the grove. Upon seeing their own robes and bowls, they recognized them all and immediately cried out to the people, "Seize the thieves!"
"Thieves! Our robes and bowls were stolen by you! they cried out.
Their clamor was heard from afar, and the thieves immediately fled in all directions.
The bhikṣus each took their own robes and bowls and stayed wherever they were, thinking to themselves:
"Should these various items be taken back?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not be alarmed; that which has been stolen is indeed his own property.
Regarding the Buddha’s statement that "that which has been stolen is indeed his own property," there was once a bhikṣu traveling through the human realm who had his belongings seized by bandits.
When a thief’s hand touched the robe or alms bowl of a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu immediately discarded it, thereby depriving himself of its use.
The Buddha said:

"A bhikṣu who has lost an object should not hastily form the intention to relinquish it. As long as the thief’s mind is not at ease and he has not yet formed the thought that the object belongs to him, the bhikṣu should take it back when he sees him."
Again, there were bhikṣus who encountered bandits as before; the bandits went to the Jeta Grove and sold their belongings.

When the bhikṣus saw the clothes, they recognized them all and seized the bandits, delivering them to the royal court. Thereupon, the bandits were shackled and beaten with clubs, subjected to torture and interrogation, and endured manifold sufferings.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One should not hand over the thief to the government officials; rather, one should preach the Dharma to him and beg for the goods from him. If he does not give them, one should return half the value."
If he still does not give it, one should pay him the full price. Why?
Because it is difficult to obtain robes and bowls that are complete.
The setting was as before.
At that time, the bhikṣus used cow dung soil, tooth-sticks, and various dye solutions; when they went outside, they discarded them without any sense of regret or attachment and departed.
At that time, although the bhikṣus saw that [the robes] had been discarded, they harbored doubts and none dared to use them; consequently, they became moldy and ruined.
The bhikṣus then reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Use them with the thought that they are for a friend."
There are five kinds of persons to whom one may entrust one's belongings as trusted friends:
first, those who possess a heart of mutual affection and compassion;
second, those who are close and have become dear confidants.
Third, they are those who are respected;
fourth, they are those with whom one has long shared intimacy;
fifth, they are those who hear of the use of their own wealth and feel joy in their hearts.
Regarding these five types of persons, although one does not ask their owner, there is no fault in using their property at that time.
Furthermore, if one observes and knows that an object has been discarded by another, there is likewise no transgression in using it as if it were ownerless.
The setting was as before.

Since the Buddha had permitted the dyeing of robes, they began to dye them on the open ground and at walking paths outside the monastery; consequently, the robes became soiled with dust and dirt, and were dampened by wind and rain.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You may perform the dyeing within the monastery.
While they were dyeing inside the monastery, the dye fell upon the ground like the color of blood. When laypeople saw this, they spoke as follows:
“Venerable One! Are cattle and sheep slaughtered here? He replied:
"It was not that I killed a living being; it was a drop of dye that fell to the ground.
He replied, "Noble One!"
"Why do you not sweep up the dye that has fallen on the ground?
The Buddha said,
"You should clean it by smearing cow dung and mud over the stained area until it is pure."
He then applied a heavy coating that damaged the lime-plastered floor. The Buddha said:
"The lime-plastered areas may be washed with water; the remaining areas should be plastered.
Should one act contrary to this, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
The summary verse for the tenth section of the fourth chapter says:
One should know the method for planting trees; Regarding the thief’s robe and performing miracles;
If one obtains an upper garment, One should not cut away the border.

The setting was the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha. At that time, after the Blessed One had caused Śakra, Lord of the Devas, to attain the vision of the Truths on Mount Vaipulya, King Bimbisāra established a great Dharma assembly at this very spot. All the people of Magadha gathered there like clouds; however, as there were no trees on the mountain, the multitude became distressed by the heat when they assembled.
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Excellent, worthy ones!..."
"One may plant trees for shade in this place.
He replied, "The World-Honored One has not yet permitted it."
He replied, "O noble one! What is it that you have transgressed?"
The bhikṣus remained silent.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to plant trees."
The bhikṣu planted the tree and then abandoned it and departed; consequently, the tree withered and died.
When the multitude of people returned for their assembly in the second year, they were again oppressed by the heat as before, and asked:
"Noble One!..."
"Did you plant the trees first?
He replied, "I have already planted them."
[The questioner asked,] “Why are there none now?
He replied, “Once the seeds were sown, they were abandoned and not guarded; consequently, they were trampled and many more have withered and died.”

The laypeople said, "When you were first born, O virtuous ones, had your parents not nurtured you, you would surely have perished; a tree must be protected and tended until it is large enough to stand on its own."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"One should not plant a tree and then abandon it to depart.
The bhikṣus did not know how to nurture and protect it.
"In the winter months, they may be damaged by frost; you should cover them with straw.
When wild fires then burned them, the Buddha said:
"You should build a wall of brick around the four sides to protect them."
Furthermore, they were injured by the heat; the Buddha said, "One should provide windows and holes.
During the summer rains, water collected like in a granary, causing the floor to rot and collapse; the Buddha said:
"In the summer, one may remove the surrounding walls, provided that water channels are opened.
When the trees were not yet large and they were discarded as before, resulting in the same damage, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"I shall now establish the rules for planting trees: if it is a flowering tree, one may depart once flowers have bloomed; if it is a fruit-bearing tree, one must depart only after it has borne fruit."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had an urgent matter requiring him to travel, yet he did not know what to do.
The Buddha said:
"He should entrust his affairs to a monastery attendant or a close friend and then depart as he pleases."
The setting was as before.

At that time, the King of Gandhāra in the north sent a woolen cloak with fine hair (*urṇā-śāṭaka*) as a gift to King Bimbisāra. Having received it, the king presented it to the Venerable Pilindavatsa, who then donned it and departed for the forest hermitage (*āraṇya*).
When the bandits heard of this matter, they said to one another, "The king has obtained an upper robe and offered it for the Venerable One to wear at the āraṇya;
what should we do with such an excellent object?"
One man replied, "We should go and seize it; what else is there to say?
They then went at night to the āraṇya and knocked on its door with a staff. The Venerable One asked:
“Who are you? He replied, “Noble one!”
"I am a bandit. He asked, "What do you seek?"
He replied, "I wish to take the upper robe.
[The other said,] "If that is the case, stretch out your arm through the window."
The thief then reached out his hand; at that moment, the Venerable One formed a thought of empowerment:
"May this woolen cloak not be cut or burned, and may it not be exhausted as it comes forth."
The thief then drew out one side; as he pulled it incessantly, it became a vast mass that showed no sign of exhaustion, yet when he tried to cut it with a knife, the blade could not wound it.
He then tried to burn him with fire, but the fire would not take hold;
he said, "Venerable Pilindavatsa!
Why do you trouble me?"
He replied, "Fool! Since you do not trouble me, why should I trouble you?"
"Exert all your courage and strength to pull it out; I will never let go!
The robbers said to one another, "The Venerable One possesses great supernatural powers; we are no match for him. We should flee and hide so as not to be captured by the king."
He then cast off his woolen cloak, vanished from sight, and departed.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who thought to himself:
"Because one dwells in an araṇya while wearing a superior cloak, such faults as these arise."
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Pilindavatsa has acted improperly; he wears this expensive upper robe while dwelling in an araṇya. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should not wear such an expensive upper robe while dwelling in the wilderness."
"If anyone [acts] thus, they shall incur an offense against the Dharma.
If a forest-dwelling bhikṣu obtains such a fine cloak, he should wear it within a village and have someone guard it.
Later, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu obtained a fine cloak from another and left it in the house of a layperson; he himself went into the forest, and consequently, it was eaten by insects.
The Buddha said:

"It should not be done in this way. One should place bitter gentian leaves, or assafoetida, or *kairava* (bitter *dhava*) leaves inside the robe; if these are unavailable, one should place it on a rack and dry it in the sun from time to time."
The setting was in Śrāvastī.

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada used to come regularly to pay homage to the Buddha and the various venerable ones. At that time, as it was a cold day, he saw the bhikṣus lying prostrate with their backs arched.
When the elder saw that he was not cultivating wholesome qualities but was sleeping wherever he happened to be, he asked:
"Noble one! The teaching of the Blessed One is for exclusive and dedicated cultivation."
"For what reason, Noble One, do you cast aside your virtuous qualities and lie down wherever you please?
He replied, "Householder!"
"I am enduring the suffering of the cold; what leisure do I have to practice exclusively?

Having heard this, the elder prostrated and took his leave. Upon arriving at his residence, he brought five hundred pieces of white cotton cloth for robes and offered them to the Saṃgha within the monastery.
Having received it, the bhikṣu cut away the threads and fringes, dyed it with red ochre, and wore it as he pleased.
Later, when the elder came to the doors of the various cells and saw that the cloak had completely disappeared from where it had been folded, he asked: "Noble one!"
"I gave you a cloak; why do I not see it now?
The bhikṣu answered the matter in detail, and [the other] replied: "Noble One!"
"I have such a superior and exquisite upper robe; for what reason has it been torn and ruined?
I only wish that you would leave me this remnant to use.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Items belonging to the Saṃgha must not be divided; they should be used as they are.
One who divides them incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma. — *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 17.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 18.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
The summary verse for the fifth section says:
Incinerating the corpse, interrogating, and the three turnings;
Expiation with forfeiture, my death, the boundary, and the bhikṣus; It is improper to use the five kinds of skins.
The first sub-section of the fifth gate is summarized in verse:
Incinerating the corpse, reciting the Threefold Homage; Maudgalyāyana dies from being struck;
One should not construct on a large scale; Obtaining many precious treasures.
The setting was in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a householder in this city who, not long after marrying his wife, fathered a son. As the boy grew older, he went forth into homelessness within the Buddha’s Dharma, but fell ill and died.
At that time, the bhikṣus immediately discarded the corpse along with its robes and bowl by the side of the road.
A layperson saw this and spoke these words:
"The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have abandoned the deceased body and departed."
Someone said, "I shall try to observe him. Having seen him,
he recognized him and reported to the people, saying:
"This is the son of that householder," they all said, feeling resentment:

"Among those who have gone forth as monks under the Śākya sons, there is no one to provide for him. Had he remained a layman, his relatives would surely have performed the funeral rites for him according to the Dharma."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"When a bhikṣu has died, you should perform offerings for him.
The bhikṣus did not know how to make these offerings.
The Buddha said,
"It should be cremated.
The Venerable Upāli then requested of the World-Honored One:
“If it is as the Buddha has taught that there are eighty thousand families of worms within this body, how can it be burned?
The Buddha said, “These various classes of worms are born along with a person’s birth and die along with their death; there is no fault in this.”
"If there are sores on the body, one must observe it to ensure there are no insects before it may be cremated.
When they were about to cremate [the body] but could find no firewood, the Buddha said:
"It may be discarded in a river."
"If there is no river, dig the ground and bury it.
During the summer months, when the earth is damp and teeming with insects and ants, the Buddha said:
"In a secluded thicket, have them lie on their right side with their heads facing north, supporting their heads with a bundle of grass, and cover their bodies with grass or leaves."
"The bhikṣu escorting the funeral procession should have a capable person recite the *Sūtra of the Threefold Exhortation on Impermanence* and speak verses (*gāthā*) for the sake of his blessing.
When the task is finished, they should return to the monastery; they must not fail to bathe and disperse as they please. When the people saw this, they mocked them, saying:
"The sons of Śākya are utterly impure; they remain near a corpse without bathing their bodies."
The Buddha said, "You should not do so; you ought to wash your bodies.
They then washed together, whereupon the Buddha said:
"If those who have touched a corpse shall wash themselves along with their robes, while those who have not touched it need only wash their hands and feet.
When they returned to the monastery and did not pay homage to the caitya, the Buddha said:
"One should pay homage to the caitya."
The setting was Rājagṛha.

At certain times, the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to observe the five realms of existence—hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas—and as they traveled about surveying them, they reached the Avīci Hell.
Then Śāriputra said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Venerable one!
You ought to extinguish the suffering of these fierce flames for the sake of this being in the Avīci hell."

When Mahāmaudgalyāyana heard these words, he immediately ascended into the air and caused a torrential rain to pour down upon the great hell, with drops as thick as axle-trees; yet the fierce flames within the hell caused the rain in the sky to vanish wherever it fell.
Then, having seen this, Śāriputra said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Venerable friend, stop!
I shall extinguish the fire."
He replied, "As you wish.

Thereupon, Śāriputra entered the samādhi of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-samādhi*) and caused a great rain to pour down, turning the ground of the Avīci Hell into mud; all attained coolness and were granted relief from their suffering.

He then saw the non-Buddhist Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who, due to having preached evil and false teachings to others in the past, had received a massive body as retribution; upon his tongue were five hundred iron plows that were furrowing it until blood flowed. Seeing the two Venerable Ones, he addressed them, saying:
"Great Virtues!..."
"Virtuous ones, if you go to Jambudvīpa, convey my words to my disciples, saying:

'Because I spoke false doctrines and deceived others when I was alive, by the power of that evil karma I have fallen into the Avīci Hell; upon my tongue there are five hundred iron plows, which furrow it until it bleeds as I endure extreme suffering.'"
"However, when you made offerings at my original stupa, my physical pain increased even more intensely; from this day forward, do not make offerings.

When the two elders heard these words, they accepted them in silence. They vanished from the hell and arrived in Rājagṛha; the two followed one another into the city, where they encountered various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) along the way, all of whom were of the sort who carried staffs and wore their hair in topknots.
The non-Buddhists deliberated, saying,
"We wish to strike those śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas.
One person replied:
"Now is precisely the right time; however, do not strike him until he has committed an offense, lest you cause him harm—do not permit it.
Let me first question him; if his answers accord with my wishes, that would be well.
If they do not satisfy my mind, it will not be too late to strike him."
Śāriputra arrived first and asked,
"Bhikṣu! Is there any śramaṇa among the Saṃmītiya community?"
Śāriputra thought to himself, "With what intention does he question me?
Perceiving that [the monk] wished to strike him,
he immediately spoke these verses, as the naked ascetic (nirgrantha) claimed for himself a life of right livelihood (samyagājīva):
“In the assembly of those with right livelihood, there are no śramaṇas; within the assembly of Śākyamuni, there are śramaṇas.
If an arhat possessed craving, then there would be no ordinary, deluded person.”
At that time, the non-Buddhist, not being familiar with the meaning of the verses, replied to the Venerable One,
"Since you have praised me, you may go as you please. Thereupon,
the Venerable One proceeded along the road.
As the Venerable Maudgalyāyana’s past karma was about to ripen, he approached with slow steps; seeing him, the non-Buddhist immediately asked:
"Bhikṣu! Is there any śramaṇa among the Saṃgha of Right Livelihood?"
If one does not observe beforehand, even the wisdom of an Arhat will not function; he replied:
"Is there truly any śramaṇa within your assembly?
As the Buddha has said:
"This is the first śramaṇa; this is the second śramaṇa; this is the third śramaṇa; this is the fourth śramaṇa. Apart from these, there are no further śramaṇas."
"Brahmins possess only their empty names; though they are called śramaṇas and brahmins, they lack the reality [of those titles].
Thus, among gods and humans, as well as within the assembly of śrāvakas, I utter words that are non-deceptive and let out a lion’s roar."

"Furthermore, your teacher Pūraṇa, because he preached evil and false doctrines among human beings to deceive and delude them, has been reborn in the Avīci Hell and received a vast body. Upon his tongue there are five hundred iron plows that furrow it until it bleeds, causing him to suffer extreme agony. He sends me this message:

'Because I preached evil and false doctrines among human beings to deceive sentient beings, I have now fallen into an evil realm and am suffering from my tongue being plowed. I inform all my followers: you must no longer make offerings at my stūpa; whenever offerings are made, the pain in my body increases twofold. From this day forward, remember my instructions.'"
Upon hearing this, the people were filled with indignation and spoke thus:
"All you people, you should know!
This shaven-headed śramaṇa has not only forcefully argued against us regarding our faults, but he has also slandered our great teacher. What shall we do now?"
One man replied, "We must give him a thorough beating; what more is there to say?
Is it not true that we agreed to beat anyone who commits an offense? Now that he has slandered our Great Master, this is a grave transgression, so it is only right that he be beaten."
The assembly immediately struck the Venerable’s body with sticks until his entire frame was mangled and cooked, just like a beaten *mṛdaṅga* drum that instantly falls apart.
At that time, Śāriputra, wondering why he had not come back from behind so late, went to look for him. Seeing his body shattered like a beaten *mṛdaṅga* drum spread upon the ground, he asked:
"Venerable friend!..."
"What is the meaning of this? He replied, "Śāriputra!..."
"This is the ripening of karma; what do you think should be done?
Śāriputra said, "Venerable friend!"
"Is it not the case that the Great Master declared among his assembly of śrāvakas that you were foremost in supernatural powers?
How is it that you have come to this? He replied, "Because I am sustained by the power of karma, I cannot even recall the character for 'supernatural' (ṛddhi), much less manifest such powers."
Then Śāriputra wrapped his body in a seven-striped robe and carried him to the monastery like an infant.
The people gathered in astonishment and asked Śāriputra,
"Venerable One, for what reason has your body come to such a state?"
He replied, “The Daṇḍapāṇi heretics beat me until I was thoroughly bruised.
He then slowly lowered his lower garment and placed it gently upon the ground.
At that time, the bhikṣus asked Śāriputra:
"Did the Great Master not declare among his assembly of śrāvakas that the Venerable Maudgalyāyana was foremost in supernatural powers?"
He replied: "I speak the truth;
you, sirs, should know this! The power of karma is supreme.

Yet Mahāmaudgalyāyana possesses great vital strength; with the big toe of his right foot, he kicked the palace of Śakra, the Lord of Devas, whom he had conquered in battle, causing it to shake until it was on the verge of collapsing. Among the śrāvakas, the Tathāgata has praised him as having great majestic power and being foremost in supernormal powers (ṛddhi)."
"However, due to the power of karma from previous lives, I cannot even remember the character for 'spirit' (shen), let alone manifest supernormal powers!
At that time, Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:

"With this impure and useless body, I have personally served the Buddha as his attendant, carrying out his instructions to the best of my strength and ability without any transgression. Yet I have repaid but little of the kindness of the Buddha, the Lord of the Teaching; who can ever fully repay the gratitude owed to such an ocean of virtue?"
"I can no longer bear this body; having developed a profound sense of weary detachment toward this vessel of boundless suffering, I shall seek tranquility and have no need to linger.
He then maintained his life-force (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) while relinquishing his vitality-force (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*).

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had not yet attained the noble path; having witnessed these events, he was overcome with profound distress and gave rise to the aspiration for renunciation. He immediately went to a forest hermitage, accepted humble bedding, lived with few desires, and secluded himself from the world to cultivate tranquility exclusively.

At that time, throughout Rājagṛha and all other inhabited places, everyone heard that the non-Buddhist ascetic Daṇḍapāṇi had beaten the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana until every limb and joint was completely mangled and crushed like a beaten reed.
Then Śāriputra wrapped him in his own robe like an infant and carried him to the Bamboo Grove; with only a remnant of life remaining, he suffered extreme agony and was soon to die.
At that time, a great assembly of hundreds of thousands gathered at the Bamboo Grove. The ministers reported to the King:
"The ascetic Dandapāṇi has beaten the noble Mahāmoggallāna until every limb and joint of his body was shattered like a crushed reed."
At that time, Śāriputra wrapped him in his own robe as if he were an infant and carried him to the park; with only a remnant of life remaining, he suffered extreme agony and was soon to die.

Having heard this, the King was deeply moved by grief and pity. He immediately gathered with the ladies of the inner court, the crown prince, the ministers, and all the people of the city, and they went together as a cloud-like assembly to the Bamboo Grove. Upon seeing the King, the people cleared a path for him; he approached the Venerable One with tears streaming down his face like a great tree collapsing to the ground, grasping his feet and wailing with a sobbing voice:
"O Noble One!..."
"For what reason have you suddenly come to this place? He replied, "Great King!"
"This is the ripening of karma created by this very body in a previous life; what do you think can be done?
The King, overcome with extreme rage, commanded his ministers:
"You must immediately gallop out in all directions to search for that heretic. If he is captured, place him in an empty room and burn him with fire."
The Venerable One replied, “Great King,
you ought not to do such a thing.”
"The karma I previously committed flows like a torrent, pouring down upon my own body; it is not for another to receive in my stead.
The king replied to the minister, "If this is so, the sovereign's command is difficult to disobey. However, once he is captured, you must cause him to leave the country."
The king spoke again, saying:
"Whatever I possess, I offer all to the Noble One; may you accept and use it as you please.
Thus spoke the king.

“Noble One! Is it not true that the Great Teacher has declared you among his disciples of the śrāvaka assembly to be foremost in supernormal powers? Why, then, do you not fly through the air when encountering such suffering?”
He replied: "Great King!
This is what the Great Teacher has taught; yet, sustained by the power of karma, I cannot even recall the word 'divine' (deva), much less manifest supernormal powers."
The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, does not speak with duplicity; he personally uttered this verse:
"Even if one passes through a hundred eons, The karma one has created does not perish.
When the causes and conditions meet, One must receive the retribution oneself."
"I am now receiving the retribution; what more can I say?
At that time, King Ajātaśatru covered his tears with his robe and commanded the physicians, saying:
"If you do not restore the noble one’s entire body and all his limbs to their former state within seven days, I shall confiscate your current stipends and emoluments."
He further commanded a high minister to personally attend to his needs; having paid his respects with great earnestness at the Venerable’s feet, he took his leave and departed.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to Śāriputra:
"Venerable friend, you should know this!"
I pray you, grant me your compassionate forgiveness! I pray you, grant me your compassionate forgiveness!
I shall now enter parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing this, Śāriputra said to him:
"The two of us both sought the sublime Dharma; we left the household life at the same time, realized the Deathless together, and shall both enter parinirvāṇa together."
Śāriputra said, "I shall do as you say!
When the Venerable Aśvajit heard that Mahāmaudgalyāyana had undergone such physical suffering, he went to him and offered his condolences, saying:
"Venerable one, you should know:
Neither on a mountain nor in the midst of the ocean, nor in any place upon earth,
nor even within the sky, can one escape the results of one's prior karma."
"Just as a shadow follows a person, there is nothing that remains fixed;
yet good and evil karma do not perish—this is what the Unsurpassed Honored One has taught.
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Śāriputra, having prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Aśvajit, circumambulated him three times to the right and said:
“Ācārya! What was to be done has been accomplished; this is my final farewell.
I shall now enter the realm of cool nirvāṇa, free from the remainder of the aggregates.”
At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit addressed Śāriputra:
“The task you were to perform has been accomplished; you have been able to turn the wheel of Dharma following the Sugata.
Now, as he desires to enter nirvāṇa, the world’s Dharma-general and lamp of light shall go out.”
Once those physicians had received the king’s command, they deliberated among themselves, saying, “The King has issued a strict edict;
what do we intend to do? One of them said:
"What do you know? The Noble One is advanced in years and has been severely beaten with a staff; he is like a crushed reed—how can he be healed?
However, this Venerable One possesses the power of great compassion; we take refuge in him, and he will surely bestow his grace upon us."
The people said, "This is a wise plan.
They immediately went together to the place where the Venerable One was, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"The Great King has issued a general command to the physicians:
'If within seven days you do not restore the limbs and joints of the Noble One to their former state, I shall confiscate your current stipends and emoluments.'"

"However, as the Venerable One is advanced in years, this grievous injury is difficult to heal. I pray that you will grant me your compassionate skillful means so that my stipend and emoluments may not be revoked."
Then the Venerable One replied to the physician, saying:
"If it is so, you should go and inform the King:
'After seven days have passed, the noble Maudgalyāyana will enter the city of Rājagṛha to wander for alms.'"
The people, delighted by these words, went together to the king’s residence and said to him:
“O Holy One! After seven days had passed, Maudgalyāyana entered the city of Rājagṛha and proceeded to beg for alms.”
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and said, "If it is truly so, then how excellent!

When the seven days had passed, by means of his supernormal powers, he stilled his pain and entered the city of Rājagṛha; proceeding on almsround, he eventually arrived at the gate of the great king’s palace.
Having seen him, the gatekeeper went in and reported to the king, saying, "The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana is now at the gate, wishing to see the Great King.

Upon hearing these words, the king was overcome with joy; he rose quickly, prepared a seat, and went out to the gate. Seeing the Venerable one prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, the king paid him reverent homage and invited him to enter and take his seat. Having sat down, the king addressed him, saying:
"Noble One! Is your health and well-being at ease?
The Venerable One replied:
"Great King, you should listen!
'What use have I now for this body of pus and blood, bearing manifold sufferings without rest?
Now that the venom of the viper has been entirely eliminated, I shall proceed in peace toward the city of Nirvāṇa.'"
Within the city of Nirvana, all afflictions are severed; All sufferings born of dependent origination are entirely absent.
The Buddha and the assembly of noble ones dwell therein; Ignorant beings caught in the cycle of transmigration cannot enter.

"Great King, you should know that this is the retribution I must undergo for my past karma. My body is like a crushed reed, beyond all medical treatment; even the Great Physician-King of old could not have restored it to health."
"May all the physicians be released," [the king] said.
The King replied,
"Release all the physicians."
Having heard this, the king’s tears flowed profusely as he rose to prostrate at the Venerable One’s feet. The Venerable One said to him, “O King, do not be heedless!
Having briefly expounded the Dharma, he took his leave and departed.
At that time, Śāriputra entered meditative concentration and observed: for what reason did the Venerable Maudgalyāyana enter the city to beg for alms despite having encountered such suffering?
He then perceived that [Maudgalyāyana] was about to enter parinirvāṇa.
After the Venerable Śāriputra saw Maudgalyāyana being beaten, a sense of sorrowful longing arose within him and he was stricken with illness. He thought to himself:
"If the venerable Maudgalyāyana enters parinirvāṇa, what purpose would there be for me to remain?"
"I should now first enter parinirvāṇa.

Having formed this thought, he went to the Venerable Ānanda to take his leave, as described at length in the Sūtra. Next, he went to the Blessed One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"I have upheld the Buddha's teachings and expounded them to others according to my ability."
Having served the noble assembly, he harbors no attachment to his own body.
Having brought his personal duties to completion, he has cultivated the practice for nirvāṇa;
in the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, he follows the right path without deviation.
"I have no attachment to birth, nor do I have any sorrow regarding death;
therefore, I am in nirvāṇa, and there is no bliss greater than this.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"Why is it that you, amidst such a sublime Dharma, come last and depart first?
At that time, Śāriputra joined his palms in reverence and spoke in verse:
"I could not bear to see the Buddha enter nirvāṇa; The sublime Maudgalyāyana was likewise."
The Tathāgata, the General of the Dharma, has now completed his task; therefore, I have first realized parinirvāṇa.
Now I address the Great Sage, the Honored One among Men: I now wish to go to my place of birth;
there I shall preach the essentials of the Dharma for my kinsmen, and then cast off this saṃsāric body of the five aggregates.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"Do you desire nirvāṇa?
Śāriputra replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I wish for parinirvāṇa.
He asked again:
"Do you desire nirvāṇa?
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "Sugata!"
"I wish to enter parinirvāṇa.
He further addressed Śāriputra:
"If you also wish to enter parinirvāṇa, [know that] all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and subject to the law of arising and ceasing; according to your own desire, what more need I say?"
Then Śāriputra, having finally paid homage to the Buddha with palms joined in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right and took his leave.
He then went to Mahāmaudgalyāyana and said to him:
"Venerable friend!"
"I have a grave illness; do you know of it?
I now wish to go to the village of Nālada to teach the Dharma to my kinsmen and shall there attain parinirvāṇa."
He replied: "Venerable sir,
you may do as you please."
"I shall do likewise; having gone to the village of Vanakhaṇḍa and taught the essentials of the Dharma to my kinsmen, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Next, he went to Nanda, Ānanda, Aniruddha, Kṣemaka, Bhadrika, Rāhula, and the other great śrāvakas, bidding them all farewell and saying:
"I wish to enter parinirvāṇa."
Then that venerable elder said, "Be careful!

Śāriputra’s attendant, Cunda, went with the assembly of bhikṣus to the village of Nālada, about twenty li southeast of the Nālandā Monastery; the Venerable Rāhula also followed behind with the assembly of bhikṣus.
Then Śāriputra addressed Rāhula with words of loving-kindness, saying:
"If one aspires to seek liberation, One should know that all things are entirely impermanent;
There is nothing in the world worth craving— One must certainly contemplate this and not be negligent."
Form and life are impermanent and devoid of joy, Like drawings upon water that do not remain for even a moment;
To realize that all things are like dreams, The gathering of precarious lives is likewise so.
Revere the Buddha, revere the Dharma, and make offerings to the Saṅgha; take the Buddha’s treasury of the True Dharma as your refuge.
Rāhula, act according to my instructions: you should draw near to those who are senior.
Regarding the points of doubt within the Tripiṭaka teachings, there is none other than myself who can answer them!
If there are such matters, you should question the World-Honored One; he shall resolve your doubts for you and proclaim the true meaning.
The Venerable Rāhula replied:
"Observing this sequence, I see that the Buddha will also not remain for long;
like a tree whose four branches have been burned, how could its trunk endure for much longer?"

Then Rāhula prostrated at the feet of Śāriputra, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having realized that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, he immediately turned back and departed.

The Venerable Śāriputra, taking the novice Cunda as his attendant, traveled through the human realms of Magadha and eventually arrived at the Uruvilvā forest north of the village of Nālada, where he took up residence. There he expounded the essential teachings of the Dharma to his kinsmen, establishing them in the Three Refuges and causing them to receive the five precepts.

When they heard that Śāriputra was about to enter parinirvāṇa, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings gathered like clouds. The Venerable One observed that this assembly of people was capable of being transformed; he taught the Dharma through skillful means in accordance with their faculties, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them. He caused those sentient beings to attain either the stage of *uṣmagata*, or the stages of *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgradharma*; or to attain the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, or *anāgāmin*; or to leave the household life and attain the fruit of an *arhat*; or to plant the seeds for unexcelled bodhi, or to plant the seeds for the state of a pratyekabuddha or a śrāvaka.

At that time, after the Venerable One had delivered his kinsmen and inspired pure faith in the great assembly, he ascended into the void during the first part of the day, emitted great radiance, manifested various miraculous transformations, and entered the realm of the wondrous Nirvana without remainder.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, the great earth shook violently; flames blazed forth from the four quarters, meteors fell, and celestial drums resounded in the void.

The assembly of bhikṣus—some in Uttarakuru, Pūrvavideha, or Aparagoyānī, others dwelling on the seven mountain ranges of Mount Sumeru, or on the cliffs, caves, and riverbanks of the Snowy Mountains and Gandhamādana—were all practicing meditation in their respective locations, experiencing the bliss of liberation.
At that time, when those people saw the earth tremble, they thought to themselves:
"For what reason has the great earth suddenly shaken?
Composing their minds, they observed and saw that their preceptor had already entered parinirvāṇa; they all then thought:
"I ought not now to dwell securely in Jambudvīpa without a preceptor.
Having thought this, eighty thousand arhats, who were the venerable one's disciples, simultaneously entered parinirvāṇa.

At that time, during the first watch of the day, Mahāmaudgalyāyana took up his robe and bowl. Sustaining his body through supernormal power, he entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms in sequence. Having returned to his original location and finished his meal, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and approached the World-Honored One. After prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying: “This body is entirely a mass of pus and blood;
It is without solidity, fragile, and constantly trembling. Like a poisoned cake, I have cast it aside; I only pray that the Great Teacher will compassionately forgive me.”
Furthermore, he spoke in verse:
"I now have no debts; my mind is fully satisfied.
In the boundless ocean of birth and death, I have left fear behind and ascended to the further shore."
"My companion Śāriputra, whose great wisdom was perfected, has already entered parinirvāṇa.
I shall now follow after him; I pray only that the Great Hero may know this.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Do you desire nirvana?
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"I wish for parinirvāṇa.
He asked again,
"Do you wish for parinirvāṇa?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "Sugata,
I wish for parinirvāṇa."
He asked again:
"If you wish to enter nirvana, know that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and subject to the law of arising and ceasing; according to your desire, what more need I say?"
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana, as a final act of homage, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined in reverence, circumambulated him three times to the right, and took his leave.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana then proceeded to the village of Vanavāsa; having expounded the essentials of the Dharma for his kinsmen—as described in detail previously—he caused countless beings to receive the refuges and precepts, to resolve their minds on awakening, and to attain the fruits of the path.
The Venerable One then entered parinirvāṇa in the late afternoon; all his disciples, seventy-seven thousand arhats, simultaneously entered parinirvāṇa as well.

After the two holy ones had entered nirvana, their kinsmen, brahmins, householders, and others collected their bodily remains and constructed stūpas; all these people performed sublime deeds conducive to rebirth in heaven and liberation.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda and Rāhula, having heard that Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana had entered parinirvāṇa, wept with tears filling their eyes. They went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and stood together to one side. The Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have heard that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have passed away; my entire body and mind are shaken through and through.
My vision of all directions is utterly darkened, and even if I were to hear the Dharma, my mind would be bewildered."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those two people, saying:
"Do not give rise to distress; all who are bound by affection must part.
I have already explained this to you, therefore do not grieve."
"Those who are born cannot escape death; the world is impermanent and unstable.
Wandering through the five realms of rebirth, none shall ever remain.
Then, having performed the cremation and offerings for his upādhyāya, the śrāmaṇera Cunda took the remains of the bone-relics (śarīra) along with the robes and bowl, and set out for Rājagṛha.
Having arrived at his dwelling, he set down his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and went to where the Venerable Ānanda was. After prostrating at his feet, he sat to one side and said:
"Venerable sir, do you know?"
"My preceptor, the Venerable Śāriputra, has already entered parinirvāṇa; here is his remains along with his three robes and alms bowl.
Then Ānanda immediately took Cunda and went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have heard that Śāriputra has passed away; his physical form is like that of a fool."
Unable to distinguish the directions, his mind found no understanding upon hearing the Dharma.
"Now the śrāmaṇera Cunda has come to me and spoken thus:
'Venerable Sir, do you know?'"
"My preceptor, the Venerable Śāriputra, has already entered parinirvāṇa; I have already cremated him as an offering and taken his bodily relics, and I have brought both his robe and bowl here."
"Now, what do you intend to do?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Does the Bhikṣu Śāriputra intend to enter nirvāṇa along with the aggregates of the precepts?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Do you mean that the aggregate of concentration,
the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation enter into nirvāṇa?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Furthermore,

is it by means of the Dharma I have personally realized and taught— the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path— that one carries this Dharma into nirvana?"
"No, World-Honored One! The Venerable Śāriputra did not bring these untainted aggregates of Dharma and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment into nirvāṇa."

However, the Venerable Śāriputra is endowed with ethical discipline and extensive learning; he has few desires and is content, delights in the practice of tranquility, and is ever diligent and courageous. He possesses present mindfulness and right situational awareness, as well as swift wisdom, liberating wisdom, penetrating wisdom, wisdom of great benefit, vast wisdom, profound wisdom, incomparable wisdom, and the wisdom of emptiness. He reveals, exhorts, encourages, and inspires others; whatever he hears, he fully understands, and when proclaiming it before the assembly, his mind is free from timidity.
However, Śāriputra and I shared the Dharma together; now that he has entered parinirvāṇa, this recollection causes me grief, lamentation, and unhappiness.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not grieve, lament, or be unhappy. It is impossible for such a principle to exist; it is not possible that a phenomenon born of conditions could be made to abide eternally."
Since you already know that the nature of all phenomena is eternally subject to decay and destruction, you should not feel sorrow or distress. Ānanda!
I have previously taught in various places that all matters of affection and joy are entirely impermanent and ultimately end in separation.

It is like a great tree whose roots are planted deep and firm; though its trunk, branches, twigs, flowers, and fruits are all abundant and full, those branches that reach upward will inevitably break first;
it is like a great mountain of jewels, where the peaks that are highest and most precipitous will inevitably fall first.
Now it is likewise: while the Buddha, as the foremost leader of the community of bhikṣus, currently dwells in the world, Śāriputra has already entered parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
"Wherever Śāriputra goes, his fame will fill that region, and I shall have no cause for anxiety.
Therefore, do not give rise to sorrow now; such is the nature of the world—that it ultimately ends in separation."
Whether I am present in this world or have passed away, you should know this:
take yourselves as your island and yourselves as your refuge; take the Dharma as your island and the Dharma as your refuge, for there is no other island and no other refuge.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
You should take yourself as your island, and so forth, until you have no other refuge; however, among my disciples who follow the Dharma, those who are able to uphold the precepts are the foremost.
How is it that a bhikṣu makes himself his island and makes himself his refuge, making the Dharma his island and the Dharma his refuge, having no other island and no other refuge?

If there is a bhikṣu who contemplates the internal body and diligently practices right mindfulness, knowing that all the world gives rise to the afflictions of anger, sorrow, and delusion; or [contemplating] the external body, or the internal body, or both the internal and external bodies—and so on, as extensively explained—likewise contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena while diligently practicing right mindfulness, knowing that all the world gives rise to the afflictions of anger, sorrow, and delusion: this is called "making oneself an island," and so forth, up to "having no other refuge."
When Ānanda had heard what the Buddha said, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew, and departed.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
“Noble One!...”
"What karma did Maudgalyāyana previously commit that caused his body to be crushed by the non-Buddhists?
The World-Honored One replied, "O Bhikṣus!..."
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, what one has done oneself must be experienced by oneself; no one can take it upon themselves. This is explained at length...

Long ago, in a certain city, there was a brahmin whose wife gave birth to a son. When the boy had grown up, his father took a wife for him. The son developed an intense attachment to his new wife and grew resentful toward his mother. He failed to show her respect, and his mother rebuked him, saying: 'You love your wife and act in opposition to me.'"
Upon hearing these words, the wife gave rise to an evil thought:
"This old woman, whose own beauty has long since faded, cannot even for a moment part from her own husband, yet she now forcibly speaks of faults against my lord."
From that time forward, he constantly sought out his mother’s faults.

Later, on another occasion, the wife saw her mother-in-law engaged in some private, illicit act; she then informed her husband, and they both became filled with resentment and anger. The son said to his wife:
"This foolish old woman still does not rest her mind; she imposes harsh verbal demands upon me, though I am but a youth."
He then gave rise to an evil mind and uttered cruel words:
"How might there be a man of great strength who could strike that body until it is shattered like a reed being beaten?

Monks, do not harbor doubts; the Brahmin’s son of that time was none other than Mahāmaudgalyāyana. Because he conceived an evil thought toward his parents and spoke meaningless words, for five hundred lifetimes his body was constantly struck and shattered like a reed being beaten. Even now, in this final birth, though he is foremost in supernatural powers among my disciples, the śrāvakas, he still undergoes this retribution.
Therefore, you should know: the karma previously created must necessarily be experienced by oneself; no one can take its place. Thus it should be studied in detail, as extensively explained.
Having heard this, the assembly of bhikṣus received it with devotion.
Then the bhikṣus again requested of the Buddha, saying:
"By what cause and condition did the various non-Buddhists not strike Śāriputra, but instead harm Maudgalyāyana?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only today that I release one and strike another; it was likewise so in the past.
You should listen!

In the distant past, in a certain village, there was a large group of boys playing together. Seeing two young brahmin students (maṇava) coming along the road, they said to one another, "Let us beat these two men now."
They further deliberated together, saying:
"It would not be appropriate to strike him immediately; rather, we should question him.
If he is to our liking, we shall not administer the rod; only if he is not to our liking may we then strike him."
One person asked, "When does the cold occur?
Another māṇava thought to himself:
"What do you mean by asking this?
Seeing that his opponent’s posture suggested he intended to strike him, he immediately replied:
"I ask not whether it be winter or summer; I only require that the wind arise."
"When there is wind, cold arises; without wind, cold is certainly absent.
Upon hearing these words, the youth released him.
He then questioned the second man, who replied:
"In winter months cold is certain; in summer time cold does not exist.
All people recognize this fact, yet the ignorant give rise to doubt together."
"When the youths heard this, they became angry and resentful, beat him severely, and departed. O Bhikṣus!
He who let them go at that time was none other than Śāriputra; he who was beaten was Mahāmaudgalyāyana. It is just as it is now."
At that time, the bhikṣus again had further doubts and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"How extraordinary, O Great Virtuous One!
The Venerable Ānanda was overcome with great grief and distress, yet the World-Honored One, through his great compassion, was able to provide him with consolation and resolution."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"My now dispelling Ānanda’s sorrowful thoughts is not yet something rare; in the past, I have already removed his grief for him."
"You all should listen!

In a past age, in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśī, there was a king named Brahmadatta—[and so on, as extensively described]—the realm was prosperous, joyful, and peaceful. That king had a son named Sujāta."

Sujāta had a son of handsome appearance; when his kinsmen gathered together to beg for a name for him, they deliberated, saying, "Since he is the grandson of the King of Kāśī, he should be named Kāśisundara."

Later, at another time, Prince Sujāta suddenly passed away. Out of his deep affection for his son, King Brahmadatta took the corpse in both arms and wailed with bitter lamentation; beating his breast and crying out loudly, he was overcome by grief and fainted.
At that time, Kāśisundarī possessed skillful wisdom and thought to herself:
"The Great King is so distressed that he may even lose his life; I should now resolve his knot of grief."
He immediately went to the king’s presence, prostrated at his feet, and said:
“Great King! I have a request.”
The king asked, "What do you desire? He replied:

"Build me a chariot with the sun and moon as its wheels; it must be exquisitely crafted and brought here swiftly. If you do not provide it, on the seventh day my chest shall burst and I shall meet my end."
Upon hearing this, the king’s anxiety and fear increased all the more, and he said to his son:
“Who has committed this useless act? It is the speech of a fool;
I know for certain that I am incapable of it, yet they insistently desire me to search for it.”
The son replied: "Great King, I am not the fool; it is you, O Lord of the Land, who are the fool.
Embracing this stinking corpse of flesh, you call out to your son with bitter lamentation."
Just as the sun and moon emerge, they shine universally upon the world;
able to dispel the darkness of the four quarters and bring forth great radiance.
Now the Father King knows not that his son has departed to be born in another realm.
In the hells, among animals and hungry ghosts, and within the divergent paths of humans and devas—
do not fixate upon these improper objects, O King of Men; contemplate well and with diligence,
let your mind be settled, for only the Dharma is worthy of refuge.
When the king heard the youth’s words, his body and mind were filled with joy;
he extracted the poisoned arrow of sorrow and cast away the corpse of his son.

"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts: the one who was Kāśisundara at that time was none other than myself; Sujāta was none other than Śāriputra; and King Brahmadatta was none other than Ānanda."
Then he spoke in verse:
"The prince was my very self; My father was Śāriputra;
Ānanda was Brahmadatta— One should know these as matters of the past."

At that time, the World-Honored One departed from the city of Rājagṛha and traveled toward the kingdom of Kośala, wandering through the human realm until he reached the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was making offerings of incense and flowers to the bodily remains of Śāriputra. When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that Śāriputra had already entered parinirvāṇa and that the Venerable Ānanda was personally making offerings to his bodily remains, he [went to him].
He then went to that place, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Noble One, do you know?"

The Venerable Śāriputra has now entered parinirvāṇa; he was one whom I previously held in high esteem, for whom my reverence deepened over the long course of days and nights. You shall take his remains and offer worship to them wherever you go.
"I also have a mind that wishes to offer worship; I only pray that you will grant it to me.
He replied, "Householder!..."
"I am likewise; there is no way for me to associate with those whom I have previously revered.
[The Buddha] spoke at length until Anāthapiṇḍika went to where the Buddha was and said, "World-Honored One!..."
"I only pray that you will compassionately grant me the bodily relics of the Venerable Śāriputra, for I wish to offer them worship.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"To offer worship to the relics of one who shares the same holy life is not yet an offering made to the Tathāgata, nor is it a repayment of his kindness."

If one is able to perform such deeds, this is truly making an offering to the Tathāgata and repaying his great kindness; that is to say, being able to grant others the going forth and the full ordination (*upasampadā*), or providing them with a preceptor (*niśraya*) and instructing them in recitation, exhorting them toward meditative reflection, and leading them to seek the path of liberation exclusively so that their lives are not spent in vain.
Why is this? Ānanda!

Throughout three incalculable great eons, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, underwent immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of difficult practices and ascetic austerities for the sake of all sentient beings, before finally realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Ānanda! By relying on me as their spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), all sentient beings shall attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
"Therefore, you should now give the bodily remains of the Elder to him so that he may make offerings to them.
Having received the Buddha's instruction, Ānanda then took the bodily remains and presented them to the Elder.
For what reason does Ānanda not oppose the Buddha’s teaching?

Just as when the Buddha formerly practiced the bodhisattva path, he never opposed any instruction given by his parents, teachers, or elders in positions of respect; likewise, there is now no one who dares to oppose his teaching.

At that time, having obtained the bodily relics, the elder paid homage to the Buddha and departed. Carrying them back to his own residence, he placed them in a high and prominent location; together with his household and all his kinsmen, they offered full worship with every kind of incense, flowers, and exquisite objects they possessed.
At that time, the people within this city all heard that the Venerable Śāriputra had already entered parinirvāṇa at the village of Nāla in the kingdom of Magadha;
that his bodily relics were entrusted to the novice Cunda by Śāriputra, who in turn delivered them to the Venerable Ānanda;

and that the Venerable Ānanda had brought them here, as the Buddha had commanded him to bestow them upon the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, so that he might take them back to his home and together perform offerings to them.

At that time, King Prasenajit, Queen Vāsavadattā, and Queen Vārṣākārī, together with the elders who were upāsakas, the laywoman Viśākhā, and the rest of the assembly, all carrying incense, flowers, and exquisite offerings, went to the elder’s residence to present their offerings collectively. Some among them, having previously attained realization of the Path through Śāriputra, also came to offer worship out of remembrance of his past kindness.

Later, on another occasion, when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had some business and had to leave, he locked the gate and departed. At that time, the great assembly, carrying offerings, arrived at the gate; seeing it closed, they all raised voices of reproach, saying:
"For what reason does the householder obstruct the path to merit?"
When the elder returned, his family members told him:
"Many people came wishing to offer their worship; seeing the gate locked, they all raised voices of reproach, saying that you were obstructing their meritorious deeds."
Having heard this, the householder thought to himself:
"This is indeed the occasion; I should go and inform the Buddha.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat down to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
A great multitude of people, feeling deep reverence for the bodily relics of the Venerable Śāriputra, have come to my home, each bringing various exquisite offerings to present in worship.”
"I had other business and left after locking the door; when people came and saw it, they all spoke with resentment, saying:
'The elder has closed the door and blocked our path to merit.
If the Buddha would permit it, I now wish to erect a stūpa for the Venerable’s relics in an open and spacious place, so that the multitude may make offerings according to their wishes."
The Buddha said,
"Householder! Do as you please."
The householder then thought,
"How should this be done? The Buddha said:

"One should construct a foundation using two layers of bricks; next, install the body of the stūpa and place an inverted bowl (pātra) upon it. Its height may be adjusted as desired, and on top one should place a flat coping (maṇḍala), one or two feet high and two or three feet square. Measuring its dimensions accordingly, erect a wheel-pole (cakra-yaṣṭi) in the center, and then attach the parasol-discs (chattra)."
"As for the number of tiers in its parasol-umbrella (*chattra*), it may be one, two, three, four, or even up to thirteen, followed by the installation of a precious vase.
The elder thought to himself:
"Is it only Śāriputra who is permitted to construct such a stūpa?"
"May others also obtain [the merit]?
He then went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha told the elder:
"If one constructs a stūpa for the Tathāgata, it should be made complete in all its parts, just as previously described."

If it is for a Pratyekabuddha, do not place a jeweled vase; if it is for an Arhat, the *cakra* (wheel) should have four tiers; for a Non-returner (*Anāgāmin*), three; for a Once-returner (*Sakṛdāgāmin*), two; and for a Stream-enterer (*Srotāpanna*), one. For an ordinary person or a virtuous layperson, there should merely be a flat top with no wheels or canopy.
“As the Blessed One has instructed, it should be done in this way,” [the monks said]. But the bhikṣus did not know how to arrange them.
The Buddha said:

“The stūpa of the Great Teacher should be placed in the center of the Dharma-seat where the Blessed One resided; the great śrāvakas should be on both sides; and the other venerable elders should be arranged according to their seniority.”
“Ordinary people and virtuous layfolk should remain outside the monastery.
Once the elder had completed the construction of the stūpa, he addressed the Buddha, saying,
“If you would grant me permission, I shall establish a great festival of offerings to celebrate the stūpa of the Venerable Śāriputra.”
The Buddha said, "Do as you wish.

At that time, King Prasenajit heard that the Great Householder had invited the Buddha, wishing to hold a celebratory assembly for the stūpa of the Venerable Śāriputra; the king then thought to himself:
"I shall assist in this undertaking.
He then rang a bell within the city and made a general proclamation:

"To all persons currently within the city, as well as merchants and traders from the four distant regions—if any among you come to witness this Dharma assembly, you may trade whatever goods you have for sale according to your own inclination, and no taxes shall be levied upon them."
At that time, there were five hundred merchants who encountered a black wind within the great ocean, which threatened to destroy their ships.

Those people had previously received the precepts for refuge from the Venerable Śāriputra and each had recited them; furthermore, relying on the mutual assistance of the devas, they were able to emerge from the great waves and arrive here in safety.
Hearing that King Prasenajit had given such instructions, they all formed this thought:
"The king attained this exalted position due to his past karma; now, without weariness, he further practices the giving of alms."
"How can we fail to cultivate merit?

Thinking thus, the merchants all together gave rise to a heart of reverent faith; they immediately took many gold, silver, rare treasures, pearls, shells, and jade, and with all their hearts made offerings within the Dharma assembly, then departed after relinquishing them.
Having received them, the bhikṣus did not know how to dispose of the items.
The Buddha said:
"Conch shells that are capable of being blown should be given to the image of Jambudvīpa for its use."
Of all other precious treasures remaining, a certain amount should be set aside for the necessary repairs of the Śāriputra stūpa.

If there are garments suitable for hanging as offerings, a certain amount should be set aside to be hung as silk banners on fast days (*poṣadha*). As for the remaining items—clothing, folded cloths, money, cowries, and so forth—the monastic community present should divide them among themselves, for it is proper that wealth belonging to fellow practitioners (*sabrahmacārin*) be used collectively.
This distribution is made based on the property of the Śāriputra Stūpa;
if it were the property of a Buddha Stūpa, all of it would be used for the stūpa.
The second sub-section of the fifth gate is summarized in verse as follows:
Interrogation for the sake of recollection, asking whether one consents,
not performing the instruction, the *poṣadha*, and the *pravāraṇā*.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, without careful examination based on what was seen, heard, or suspected, proceeded to interrogate other bhikṣus.

Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus were each filled with shame; their bodies became emaciated, their complexions grew pale and sallow, and their physical strength diminished. Consequently, they were unable to recite the scriptures or engage in proper reflection. Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, a bhikṣu shall not interrogate another bhikṣu based on what he has not carefully examined through seeing, hearing, or suspecting."
If one reproaches another in such a manner, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (*dharmāpatti*).

Just as it is with reproaching, so should it be understood that [the same applies to] calling to mind, inquiring after one's welfare, failing to provide instruction, performing the *poṣadha*, or the *pravāraṇā*; these should all be understood as analogous cases, and they likewise constitute offenses of transgression against the Dharma.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudrakavastu*, Fascicle 18; *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudrakavastu*, Fascicle 19.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The third subsection of the fifth section; the summary verse says:
The Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma three times; Having first delivered the five bhikṣus, [he established the Saṃgha].
Without addressing him by name or clan, [the Buddha] proclaimed this concise teaching at Kuśinagara.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Bhagavat was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five bhikṣus, saying:
"O bhikṣus! This is the Noble Truth of Suffering.
By attending appropriately to the Dharma as it has been heard, one can give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening."

"O bhikṣus! Regarding these noble truths—the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering—through appropriate mental attention, they give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening."
“O bhikṣus! This noble truth of suffering is a dharma to be fully understood; thus it should be known.
By applying correct attention to the teachings as they have been heard, one can give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.”
“O bhikṣus! This noble truth of the origin of suffering is a dharma that must be fully understood; it is to be abandoned in this way.
By applying correct attention to the teachings as they have been heard, one can give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.”
“O bhikṣus! This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is a dharma to be fully understood; thus it should be realized.
By attending appropriately to the dharma as it has been heard, one can give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.”
“O bhikṣus! This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is a dharma that must be fully understood; thus it should be cultivated.
By attending appropriately to the teachings as they have been heard, one can give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.”
"O bhikṣus! This noble truth of suffering is a dharma to be fully understood; thus it has been known.
By attending appropriately to the teachings as they have been heard, one can give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening."
“O bhikṣus! This noble truth of the origin of suffering is a dharma to be fully understood; it has been thus abandoned.
By attending appropriately to the teachings as they have been heard, one can give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.”
“O bhikṣus! This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is a dharma to be fully understood; it has been thus realized.
By applying correct attention to the teachings as they have been heard, one can give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.”
"O bhikṣus! This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is a dharma that has been fully understood; thus it has been cultivated.
By attending appropriately to the teachings as they have been heard, one can give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening."

"O Bhikṣus! If I had not fully realized these four noble truths through their three turnings and twelve aspects, then vision, knowledge, wisdom, and awakening would not have arisen in me; I would not have attained liberation of mind through the abandonment of defilements amidst this world with its gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, and I could not have realized unsurpassed bodhi."

“O bhikṣus! Because I have understood these four noble truths through their three turnings and twelve aspects, vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening were all born within me. Thereupon, amidst all the world with its gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, I abandoned the afflictions and attained liberation of mind, whereby I was able to realize unsurpassed bodhi.”
When the Blessed One had spoken this Dharma, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya and eighty thousand devas were freed from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
The Buddha said to Kauṇḍinya:
"Do you understand this Dharma? He replied:
“I have understood,
World-Honored One!
“Have you understood this Dharma?”
He replied: “I have understood, Sugata.”
Because Kauṇḍinya had understood the Dharma, he was therefore named Ājñātakauṇḍinya; "Ājñāta" means "understood.
At that time, the yakṣas dwelling on the earth, having heard what the Buddha said, raised a great voice and proclaimed to humans and devas:
"O worthy ones, you should know!"
The Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, where he extensively turned the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects.

By this, he brought great benefit to the entire world—including its devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—and caused his fellow practitioners of the holy life to swiftly reach the state of peace and *nirvāṇa*. Thus, humans and devas increased while the asuras decreased.
When that yakṣa had thus proclaimed, all the devas in the sky and the hosts of the Four Great Kings heard and knew it.

In this manner, it was passed on in an instant throughout the six heavens of the desire realm; in a mere moment, its resonance reached as far as the Brahmā heaven. Having heard it, the assembly of Brahmās likewise proclaimed it everywhere, as extensively described before.
For this reason, this sutra is called "The Turning of the Wheel of Dharma in Three Turns.
At that time, the five bhikṣus, along with humans, devas, and others, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.

When the Buddha had thus turned the wheel of dharma three times for the five men, causing them to go forth, receive full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), and become bhikṣus, those five bhikṣus frequently addressed the Tathāgata by his personal name, his clan name, or as "Venerable One" (*āyuṣmat*).
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should not address the Tathāgata by his personal name or clan name, nor call him 'Venerable One. Why is this?"
If there is a bhikṣu who addresses the Tathāgata by name, by clan, or by the title "Venerable," this person is a fool!
For a long night he will undergo much suffering and bring about what is not beneficial.
"Therefore, you should no longer address the Tathāgata by name or by other such titles; if you do so again, you shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

When the Buddha had thus declared that one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma for addressing the Tathāgata by name or otherwise, there was at that time a young bhikṣu who, with the exception of the Blessed One, addressed other elder bhikṣus by name or even by the title "Venerable" (Āyuṣmat).
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A junior bhikṣu should likewise not address a senior by name, clan, or as 'Venerable Friend' (āyuṣmat)."
However, there are two ways of addressing others: either as "Venerable" (bhadanta) or as "Fellow in the Holy Life" (āyuṣmat).
A junior bhikṣu should address an elder as "Venerable," while an elder should address a junior as "Fellow in the Holy Life."
"If you do not do so, you shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
While the Buddha was staying between the twin śāla trees at Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas, the World-Honored One, on the verge of parinirvāṇa, addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I have already extensively proclaimed the Vinaya Piṭaka for you; I have never spoken of it in brief."
I shall now further explain its concise teaching; you should listen attentively, reflect well, and apply your minds with the utmost care.
O Bhikṣus! There may be occasions when there is a matter regarding which I have neither previously prohibited nor permitted.
However, regarding this matter, if it contradicts what is impure and accords with what is pure, then this is pure and should be practiced.
If it contradicts what is pure and accords with what is impure, then this is impure and should not be practiced.
"This may be respectfully upheld; do not harbor any doubt.
The fourth sub-section of the fifth gate, summarized in verse, says:
"Not dividing items subject to forfeiture; keeping mosquito nets as one pleases."
A tripod made from a three-pronged staff; the *kaṭhina* robe should be spread.
The occasion was at Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed the offense of possessing an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*) and incurred its forfeiture. He then took the robe and offered it before the presiding elder (*sthavira*). Upon seeing this robe, the administrator (*vaiyāpṛtyakara*) thought to himself:
"Today the Saṃgha has acquired much property; we may sell it and divide the proceeds.
Thereupon they immediately put it up for sale and shared the proceeds among themselves.
Consequently, that [monastery] was left in ruin.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
