"There was such a fault in relinquishing the cloth that had been forfeited to the Saṃgha; therefore, one must not relinquish a forfeited cloth to the Saṃgha."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the past, when a bhikṣu committed an offense requiring the forfeiture of a robe, he would forfeit it to the Saṃgha, whereupon it was distributed among them, resulting in his subsequent lack of necessities.
Therefore, one should not forfeit [an item] to the community of monks; rather, it may be given to an individual."
If there is no one who knows [the rules], even if it is relinquished to the Sangha, it should not be divided.
If one relinquishes an extra robe to the assembly of monks and they immediately divide it, both of these parties incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

The Buddha said, "Regarding the relinquishing of extra robes to another person: at that time, there was a bhikṣu who had committed an offense regarding extra robes and relinquished his robe to someone ignorant of the rules. Having received the robe, that person remained silent and did not know how to return it."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should send another person to instruct those who lack knowledge; if they return it, that is well.
If they do not give it back, one should take it by force and maintain possession of it."

"This relinquishing of the robe is a formal ritual act; it is not a complete gift. However, when relinquishing the robe, one must first seek out those who know the Dharma, and only then should it be relinquished.
This account was set in the city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, as the bhikṣus were being bitten by mosquitoes and gnats, they scratched their itchy bodies until blood flowed from all over them.
When lay travelers saw this, they asked the reason for it.
The bhikṣus answered them in detail, and they said:
“Noble ones! Do you not keep mosquito nets? They replied:
“The World-Honored One has not permitted this; what then should we keep?
They replied, “The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate; he should grant permission for this.”
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow the bhikṣus to possess mosquito nets.
The bhikṣus did not know how they should make them.
The Buddha said:
"It should be twelve cubits in circumference, with a canopy placed upon it.
The canopy shall be four cubits long and two cubits wide; depending on the height of the body, a corded strap shall hang down from it."
He sewed it straight through, leaving no opening for mosquitoes and insects to enter again. The Buddha said:
"One should not sew it entirely; one should leave a small portion unsewn to serve as a flap for a door. When it is hot, one should use a fan."
"If mosquitoes enter from the bottom, you may press them down with a felt mat or other materials so that they do not get inside.
The setting of this account is the same as before.
Regarding the Buddha’s instruction that water should be strained, at that time the bhikṣus grew weary from holding the strainer with their hands; the Buddha said:
"Bind it to a staff and open the *kara* to draw water.
Even when used in this manner, they were still weary;
the Buddha said, "Carry a three-pronged staff and bind [the vessel] to the staff with a rope."
The cord would not stay in place, so the Buddha said:

"One should pierce three holes near the top and thread the cord through them to tie it; alternatively, one may attach iron rings to open the three strands wide, using two of the rings as loops to receive the water."
When pouring water, it overflowed and flowed onto the ground. The Buddha said:
"Pour the water with care so that it does not overflow.
When there was no handle on the bottom of the jar, it tilted over wherever it was placed. The Buddha said:
"Place a ring [on the spout] so that the jar does not move.
As the water passed rapidly through the filter without pausing, it caused the insects to faint;
the Buddha said, "One should place an object inside the filter."
The bhikṣus did not understand; the Buddha said:
"Either sand or dry cow dung should be moistened with water and placed within the filter.
When the water still did not stay, the Buddha said:
"One should construct a water-receptacle.
The bhikṣus did not know how to construct the vessel.
The Buddha said:
"There are two kinds of vessels:
namely, copper and earthenware.
Because the bhikṣus grew weary from holding their bowls with their hands, the Buddha said:
"One should not hold it in one's hand.

Instead, one should pierce three holes around the rim of the bowl and tie it with a cord, suspending it from a three-pronged fork so that it is securely fastened. One should place a corner of a strainer inside the vessel to preserve the lives of the insects."
"If the water does not flow through because the strainer is too fine, you should strike the outside of the strainer with a smooth stick.
A bhikṣu looked at the water inside a jar that was not yet full and could not see the insects. The Buddha said:
"Pour water into the jar until it is full so that it remains still; only then may you observe it."
When there was dust on the water and the insects could not be seen, the Buddha said:
"Remove the dust before examining them; when showing small insects to others, point with your finger."
Because small insects move so swiftly that they cannot be seen clearly, the Buddha said:
"One should point them out using the tip of a blade of *māṇa* grass or a stalk of straw.
When a bhikṣu catches insects, he covers the mouth of the well with a strainer; although many of the insects fall into the water, they mostly faint or sometimes die. The Buddha said:
"One should construct a release-vessel and submerge it in the water.
The bhikṣu then used this jar, lowering it full and drawing it out full; the insects remained as before. The Buddha said:
"One should use such a vessel to hold the insects when lowering it, and once it reaches the water, cover it [with insects] and draw it out empty."
The bhikṣus did not understand and [asked], "Should we make separate devices for releasing living beings?
At that time, there were times when no such devices could be obtained;
the Buddha said, "One may tie a net with a rope and skillfully cast it down, then pull it out after judging that the insects have departed."
As for this vessel for releasing living beings, it has long been practiced in the Western Regions (India), and everyone there understands it.
In the Eastern Land (China), however, it has previously been neglected; therefore, its ritual must be explained in detail, for without a full exposition, one cannot achieve understanding.
The vessels for use may be made of copper, iron, clay, or wood.

If one intends to carry them with one, they may be made of copper with a capacity of two or three *sheng*; these are the small copper jars used in the past. One should attach a copper handle so that it can pass through the hand, and on one side of the base, a copper hook must be installed to hold the tip of a small bamboo chopstick.
When departing to beg for alms, he passes the rope through his left arm and covers it with his robe, carrying the bowl in his right hand.

Having obtained food, he proceeds to a certain house and sets down his alms-bowl. Taking a single strand of clean rope about as thick as a sinew, he lowers it into the well according to its depth to draw water from the jar. After filtering it through a small strainer until he has obtained a sufficient amount, he immediately hooks one end of the rope onto a hook and fastens it tightly. He pulls up the rope until it is level with the mouth of the jar, and then fastens a small iron hook onto the rope.
When lowering the hook, ensure it remains level and does not tilt; furthermore, prepare everything in advance so that nothing must be sought at the last moment.

Cover the insect jar with a small strainer, lower it slowly until it reaches the water, release the hook, and pull up the rope to turn it over. Rinse it thoroughly two or three times before finally drawing it out of the well.

This is the ritual for begging for alms. If one is in a monastery, one should cover [the vessel] with an iron jar using the usual well-rope; the arrangement is mostly as before, with a slight difference: one attaches an iron ring to the bottom, large enough to accommodate three fingers, and hooks the jar-hook inside it to lift it up and tie it level. As before, one places the hook and covers the insects within; then, lowering it until it reaches the water level, one overturns it according to the prescribed method. Even if it is a deep well, this may still be done.

If one keeps a separate rope, it may cause unnecessary trouble; if the well is deep, one might instead use a basin to collect the water, or carry it to a river or pond. Once the water has been drawn, the vessel must be washed; such is the proper method.

Since the compassionate teachings of the Tathāgata take mercy as their foundation, the precepts he established distinguish between offenses that are transgressions by nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and those prohibited by convention (*prajñapti-sāvadya*). Among these, while conventional prohibitions are light, natural transgressions are grave; within the category of natural transgressions, taking life is the foremost. Therefore, it is only logical for the wise to preserve and protect [life].
If one considers this to be a minor matter, what could be more serious?
If one is able to practice it, one will obtain the karmic fruit of long life in the present life and shall be reborn in the Pure Land in a future life.

Furthermore, in the land of China, there are over four hundred cities, and those who have left the household life number in the tens of thousands; yet, those who pay heed to the matter of filtering water are few. Because long-standing customs give rise to habitual negligence toward Buddhism, it is impossible to visit every door and transmit this orally to each individual; I therefore hope that fellow practitioners will instruct one another in succession.

Even if one has mastered the Tripitaka and attained realization through the four dhyānas, maintaining the contemplation of non-arising and clarifying the mind within the principle of emptiness, if one does not protect life, one cannot escape the Buddha’s reproach; who then shall take upon themselves the first of the ten evil offenses?

Furthermore, for instance, when one sees a butcher leading sheep into a temple, they do no more than release a few mouths to live out their natural span, with the assembly watching together and snapping their fingers in praise; yet how could they know that within the rooms, thousands and tens of thousands of lives are killed daily by the use of water?
Having understood the teachings and principles, one ought to investigate them minutely and examine them closely, protecting oneself and benefiting others through skillful guarding and reflection.

Furthermore, there are those who cause people to plow fields and sow crops, seeking meager profits while failing to see the great transgression involved; thus both land and water are harmed, and countless living beings are killed.
As for these transgressions and faults, what can be done?
One simply knows that one must fold one's hands at the gate of the underworld and submit to whatever judgment others may pass.
Thus, a sutra says:
"One who takes life shall fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; even if they should obtain a human birth, they will be short-lived and plagued by many illnesses. Alas!
Who would wish to undergo such suffering?
"If there is anyone capable of doing so, excellent!
Most excellent!

We shall together establish a bond of compassion at the first assembly under the Dragon Flower; as this is detailed extensively in other biographies, I shall not trouble you with it here. At that time, whenever the bhikṣus finished using their strainers, they would not wash them frequently, nor wring them out, nor dry them in the sun, nor turn them over, causing the strainers to deteriorate quickly. The Buddha said:
"Whenever one uses a water-strainer, one should wash it and so forth.
If one does not do so, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was filtering water for a large assembly; as the number of followers was great, he became weary. The Buddha said:
"If the assembly is large and the water supply is insufficient, one should construct a water-straining vessel.
The bhikṣus did not know how to make it,
so the Buddha said:

"If made of copper, iron, or earthenware, it should be shaped like a cauldron; at the bottom, there should be a hole about the size of a cup. It should be fashioned in the shape of a lotus pedestal four finger-widths high, with many holes on top about the size of thick chopsticks."
"Wrap it with layers of felt or use silk cloth, bind it with fine cord, and filter water through it. When finished, wash it and cover it as prescribed above.
At that time, the bhikṣus hung lice, bedbugs, and various other insects on the ground and discarded them; they immediately fell into a state of fainting distress.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"No living being should be discarded by hanging, nor should they be cast away haphazardly wherever one happens to be.
Place the lice in old cloth; if such cloth is unavailable, place them in a hollow in a tree."
Place the bedbugs from the crevices of the wall within fresh green grass; if there are none, place them in a cool, shaded spot.
If there are other insects as well, they may be settled in whatever location is appropriate for them.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One:
"May one drink water that has been filtered but not inspected?
The Buddha said:
"No, because it has not been inspected.
"Venerable sir, can water that has not been strained be drunk if it has been inspected?"
The Buddha said:
"It is attained, because of contemplation.
The setting of the occasion is the same as before.
As the Buddha had taught, once the communal summer retreat was concluded, the *kaṭhina* robe should be spread.
When King Prasenajit heard that the Buddha had granted permission, he sent a *kaṭhina* robe as an offering to the Great Assembly.
Queen Vaidehī, Queen Vārṣākārī, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, and the various lay devotees of faithful conviction all sent many robes to provide for the use of the Saṃgha.
At that time, the bhikṣus took only one robe to perform the kaṭhina ceremony and returned all the others to their owners.
When the king heard this, he replied:
"Noble ones!..."
"We have already relinquished these items to the Saṃgha; how can we now take them back again?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"Therefore, I now permit the bhikṣus to accept and take possession of these robes. According to the number of robes received, one should appoint many people to act as the 'robe-distributors' (cīvara-vistāraka). They should take one of them and perform the formal ritual of acceptance and maintenance (dhāraṇa), while the remainder should be set aside and stored, to be used as the property for the Saṃgha's rainy season retreat (varṣā-lābha)."
The fifth section, the fifth sub-section, is summarized in verse as follows:
"Entrusting after death; the death of the person to whom one has entrusted [the object];
entrustment across different regions; and if one dies, [entrusting] to another person."
The setting was in the city of Śrāvastī.

At that time, there lived in this city an elder who had fathered three sons. The youngest of them went forth into the Buddha’s Dharma and wandered among the people; not long after he had departed, the father fell ill. As death approached, he summoned all his kinsmen and addressed his two sons, saying:
"Bring everything that belongs to the household here."
He then gathered them together and divided [the inheritance] into three portions, saying, "Give one portion to each of my two sons, and give the remaining one portion to the one who has gone forth.
Having made this arrangement, he passed away.
As it is said in a verse:
"All accumulations come to an end; All that is lofty must fall;
All meetings end in separation; All who have life return to death."
At that time, the two sons performed the cremation according to the Dharma and dwelt in profound grief. When the one who had gone forth heard that his father had passed away, he thought to himself:
"I have brothers; I should now go home and preach the Dharma for them."
Having arrived at the house, the brothers met and together expressed their grief; the elder brother said, "Brother, you need not weep.
On the day our father passed away, he left behind one portion of his property for me to give to you."
The younger brother thought to himself:
"As the World-Honored One has said, what is given after death does not constitute a valid gift.
He therefore did not accept it.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When a layperson dies, they possess a mind of expectation; when a bhikṣu dies, his mind is free from expectation.
This is the case for a layperson who has a mind of expectation: there is no fault in taking [the property], and it may be used as one wishes."
The setting was as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was afflicted with illness; he said to another bhikṣu:
"You must attend to me well; I have robes and a bowl which shall belong to you."
He then attended to him, but before long, the monk passed away.
Seeing that his body was dead, he took the deceased's robes and bowl and placed them in his own room. At that time, the bhikṣus came together to inquire:
"Where are the robes and bowl of the deceased now?"
He replied, "She has already given it to me," and related the matter in full.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"That foolish person, while still alive, did not give anything; why does he only bestow gifts after death?
There is no such rule that one should give only when dead."
"One should claim those items and divide them among the great assembly; they should be distributed according to the standard share.
The setting and circumstances were as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, while sorting through his robes and belongings in the presence of another bhikṣu, suddenly passed away.
That bhikṣu then took those items and placed them in his own room; having carried the corpse away and cremated it, he returned to his room.

At that time, the administrator entered the deceased’s quarters and, observing them in order, saw the robe, the alms bowl, and the water-strainer. He immediately took these items and brought them to the assembly.
The bhikṣu asked, "This item has been brought; there are many other items remaining—why have you not brought them? He replied:
"There is only this in the room; there is nothing else.
Another person replied, "There is a bhikṣu who is his close friend; if you ask him, he will know whether it is there or not."
When asked, he replied, "I distinguished it for myself; I took that robe.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This is a formal act; it should not be left as it is, but may be taken back and shared.
The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was distributing robes in the presence of another; that person suddenly passed away, whereupon this bhikṣu took the robes and offered them to the Saṃgha.
The great assembly asked,
"Whose property is this? He replied:
"I have made a formal assignment of this object to him; he has since passed away, so I shall take this object and relinquish it to the Great Assembly.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The procedure should indeed be thus; although the object was formally assigned to him, it does not belong to him, and you may take it for your own use."
The setting was as before.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who had distributed clothing items to another bhikṣu, but that recipient suddenly returned to lay life.
Later, the former bhikṣu remembered: "That certain bhikṣu once had his clothing items distributed by me."
"Although I have returned to lay life, those goods belong to me;
I ought to go and reclaim them. Having arrived there, he said: "Noble One!"
"Venerable One, you previously sorted my clothing for me; you may now give it back to me.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought:

"Because the bhikṣus have designated that other bhikṣu as the person of trust, they then proceed to sort the clothing in his very presence; such is the fault. Therefore, I now decree that bhikṣus shall not sort clothing in the presence of the person to whom it was entrusted. Whoever does so shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma (dharma-āpatti)."
The setting was as before.

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who was distributing clothing items to another bhikṣu. This recipient was a quarrelsome person who constantly engaged in disputes and disturbances with the bhikṣus; having become filled with anger and resentment, he intended to leave. When the one distributing the clothing saw him depart, he wept and said to him, "Do not go!"
Although they tried to detain him with great persistence, he was unwilling to stay.
The people said to him:
"Do not detain him; he is fond of quarreling and disturbs the multitude."
He replied, "How could I not remain? I am constantly sorting these robes here; there is no one elsewhere to whom I can entrust them."
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the bhikṣu to whom the entrustment is made should reside even beyond the seas, provided he is still alive, there is no fault in designating him as the trustee from afar."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in a very distant land who designated another bhikṣu as his trustee; however, that person subsequently passed away.
When the first bhikṣu heard the news, many days had already elapsed, and he did not know what to do.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Once you have heard this for the first time, all items, whether new or old, should be entrusted to another person.
The summary verse for the sixth section of the fifth gate says:
Not granting consent (*chanda*) outside the boundary; not passing on [the consent] when about to depart;
and performing the *poṣadha* and the *yathā-sukha* (as-pleased) procedures—those who violate these all incur faults.
The setting and circumstances are as before.
At that time, although the six bhikṣus were outside the boundary, they also conveyed their consent (*chanda*) to those within the boundary.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not convey consent to those within the boundary while remaining outside the boundary."

Seeing that the Buddha did not permit it, at that time there was a bhikṣu who wished to go outside the boundary; as he was about to set out, the Saṃgha had business to attend to, so the group of six [monks] then forcibly compelled him to convey his *chanda*.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Those who wish to go outside the boundary should not take the *chanda* (consent).
Having heard this, the group of six monks subsequently gave *chanda* to one another outside the boundary, even to the extent that all six of them passed it on to each other in turn.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not convey the consent (*chanda*) by passing it from one person to another outside the boundary; whoever does so incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).
The setting and circumstances were as before.
As the Blessed One said that the precepts should be recited every half-month, the group of six monks then sought to confer purity outside the boundary. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done in this way."

Furthermore, regarding taking the *chanda* (consent) of one who is about to travel, or successively taking the *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi* (purity) outside the boundary, as explained in detail previously, the Buddha said:
"None of these should be done; whoever does so incurs a *dharmātikrama* offense."

As the Buddha had taught, when the *varṣā* retreat was concluded, the bhikṣus were to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony regarding the three matters—what was seen, heard, or suspected; however, the group of six bhikṣus then performed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony outside the boundary.
Furthermore, one should not leave behind those who are traveling, nor should one pass them from one boundary to another; all such actions are prohibited as previously stated.
The summary verse for the seventh section of the fifth gate says:
"One should know the number of persons; according to one's wish, one may distribute the voting sticks."
One should not sit together with laypeople; seniority should be determined according to the number of years since ordination (*varṣa*).
The setting and circumstances were as before.
At that time, there was a brahmin in this city who, having gone out on business, entered the Jeta Grove and felt a sense of wonder:
"I shall now inquire how many people currently reside in this monastery.
Having seen the bhikṣu, he asked him the number of residents, and the bhikṣu replied, "I do not know."
The brahmin said, "The entire military host of King Mahāsudassana of the kingdom of Kosala may still be counted, but for what reason can the number of monks within the monastery not be ascertained?"
He remained silent and offered no reply.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who said:
"You should know the number of people."
The bhikṣus then counted them one by one individually; at times, they would lose count by counting on their fingers and fail to remember.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should use tally sticks."
Having completed the total count, he informed the assembly so that they might know.
The bhikṣus did not know when they should perform the counting;
the Buddha said:
"One should count them during the period of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat).

Furthermore, there was an elder who entered the Jeta Grove and saw the bhikṣus diligently engaged in study and recitation, their minds focused in silent contemplation. Having witnessed this, he conceived deep faith and, wishing to know the number of the Saṃgha so as to provide them with midday meals, asked the bhikṣus:
"How many people are there in total residing at this place?"
He reported the number, and having paid his respects, he departed.
Once he reached his home, he informed his family members, saying:
"I wish to invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha to my house for a meal tomorrow; there are this many people. You should prepare everything accordingly for the assembly of monks."
He replied, “Very well! and immediately prepared various offerings within his home.
Then, when the assembly had gathered, that householder went to the monastery and informed the monastery official, saying:
"Venerable sir, you should respectfully inform the Saṃgha on my behalf: 'The householder so-and-so will invite the Buddha and the great assembly to his residence for a meal tomorrow.'"
Having thus informed him and received his leave, they departed.
Meanwhile, other bhikṣus arrived at the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden from the human realm.

That morning, the householder prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink throughout the night; he arranged seats, set out water jars, tooth-sticks, and cleansing powder, and in the morning sent a messenger to inform the Buddha and the assembly, saying:
"The time has arrived; we pray that you will deign to come.
At the first part of the day, the community of bhikṣus took their robes and bowls and went to the house of the elder.
At that time, the Great Master remained at the monastery and sent someone to fetch food.
There are five causes and conditions for which the Tathāgata, the Great Teacher, does not personally attend an invitation. What are these five?
First, he remains in solitary meditation.
2. preaching the Dharma for the sake of devas;
3. attending to the sick;
4. inspecting bedding and seats.
5. Regarding the formulation of the training rule (*śikṣāpada*).
Here, "for the purpose of" means that he wished to formulate a training rule.

At that time, the householder calculated the number of monks and prepared seats accordingly; he did the same for the food and drink. When he saw many people arriving at his residence, he informed the *karmadāna* (steward), saying:
“Venerable One! I have prepared the number of people based on what you previously informed me; now that it has exceeded that number, what should be done?
The steward replied:
"A guest has newly arrived; you must feel joy.
He replied, "If you had spoken first, I would have prepared the meal."
The bhikṣus remained silent.
At that time, some in the great assembly were fully satiated, while others suffered from hunger.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“The steward should observe the number of guests and inform the donor.
Furthermore, when another bhikṣu arrived during the midday meal, the Buddha said:
“This too must be informed.”
I shall now explain the rules of conduct for the foremost elder among that assembly.
The elder should first observe the disciples and the food and drink.
If there are many people but little food, he should inform the donor, saying:
"O Noble One! People eat little while receiving much; you should distribute it equally.
If there is someone who eats little but receives much, he should say:
"O Worthy One! There is abundant food and drink available for you to take as you please.
If the senior monk (upādhyāya) does not examine the situation well or does not act according to what has been prescribed, he incurs an offense against the Dharma (dharmāpatti).

Furthermore, when arriving at the house of a donor, one must inspect the water for insects, as well as the tooth-sticks and powdered earth, ensuring they are all fully prepared and not lacking; before and after eating, one must wash the hands and rinse the mouth according to the proper rules.
"If they do not exercise supervision, both the senior and the junior monks shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The setting of the occasion is as before.
At that time, the six groups of bhikṣus were sitting on the same seat as various laypeople; when those with faith and reverence saw this, they laughed in derision and said:
“Noble one! You are a renunciant who constantly practices the holy life; how can you sit on the same seat as one who constantly engages in sexual desire and impurity?”
Upon hearing this, he remained silent.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"The words of those faithful laypeople are reasonable; therefore, bhikṣus should not sit on the same seat as laypeople. One who so sits commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
Having heard that the Buddha had established this prohibition, he nevertheless sat together with a śrāmaṇera.
A believer said to him, "Venerable sir, you have already received full ordination; why do you sit together with a junior disciple?"
He replied, "This is not a layperson, but one who has left the household life; what fault is there in this?
Upon hearing this, the other remained silent.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Furthermore, one should not sit on the same seat as those who have not yet received full ordination.
After the Buddha had prohibited this, an elderly bhikṣu sat on the same seat with a junior, and another junior sat in the same place with an elder, neither showing respect to the other.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"The old and the young should not sit together in a mixed assembly. Those with no years of seniority may sit together with those who have two years of seniority; those with one year of seniority may sit together with those who have two years of seniority; and from two years of seniority onwards, they may all sit together with those who have three years of seniority."

After the Buddha had established this rule, the bhikṣus found themselves in lay households where they could only sit on the same seat as those who had spent three or more summer retreats (trivārṣika), making seats difficult to obtain. The Buddha said:

"If seats are difficult to obtain within a lay household, one may even sit on the same seat as one’s preceptor (upādhyāya) or instructor (ācārya), provided that a physical object is placed between you; do not harbor any doubts about this."
The summary verse for the eighth section of the fifth chapter states:
One should not occupy a seat reserved for storage; One should not entice others to seek the status of a śrāmaṇera;
One should not make vows regarding gambling objects; Nor should one eat the remains of a tiger’s prey.
The setting was as before.

At the time of listening to the Dharma, one should arrange the seats; at that time, there was a śrāmaṇera who sat upon a soft seat and consequently fell asleep, whereupon he lost control of his bowels and defiled the cushion.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A śrāmaṇera should not sit upon a soft cushion.
At that time, when the venerable Śāriputra’s śrāmaṇera, Cunda, came to listen to the Dharma, the bhikṣus gave him a stiff wooden stool and told him to sit, asking:
"Venerable sir!
Why have you given me such a hard seat? He replied:
"The Buddha prohibits soft seats.
The śrāmaṇera replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"How could I possibly be like those who possess such faults?
The Buddha said, "If there is one who applies their mind to seeking tranquility, you should provide them with a soft seat; for others, it is not appropriate."
The setting was as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who rebuked a śrāmaṇera and subsequently expelled him; the śrāmaṇera remained outside the gate of Jetavana, weeping.
When Upānanda saw him, he asked:
"Why are you crying? He replied,
"I have been rebuked by my teacher."
He replied, "Come, my son! I shall give you robes,
an alms bowl, a bowl bag, a waistband, and whatever else you may require, so that you lack for nothing."
He then summoned him back to his quarters and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"When reprimanding a disciple, one should not abandon them completely; rather, one should employ the method of 'releasing with the halter,' maintaining a heart of affection while intending to eventually gather them back in. You should have the bhikṣu speak with the śrāmaṇera."
He said, "I no longer require that preceptor.
Venerable Upānanda provides me with everything I need; I shall not go back to my former teacher."
Upon hearing this, the teacher spoke with words of reproach and indignation:
"I ordained him, yet Upānanda has lured him away.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu must not entice the disciples of others; whoever entices them away commits a thullaccaya offense, for this is a means of causing schism in the Saṃgha.
The setting of the缘 (nidāna) is the same as before.

At that time, when the group of six had some business to attend to, they would immediately invoke the Triple Gem—the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—as an oath, or they would invoke their upādhyāya or ācārya as an oath.
When faithful laypeople heard these incantations and oaths, they spoke as follows:
"We, who are mere worldly folk, do not even cite the Buddha or our teachers as a pledge; why do you, who have left the household life, cite the Buddha and your teachers to make such an oath?"
"This is improper.
He remained silent and offered no reply.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"Although worldly people may feel reproach or shame when circumstances require it, those who have left the household life originally seek truthful speech and should not engage in oaths; if one does so, they incur an offense against the Dharma."
The setting was as before.
At that time, whenever the six bhikṣus had business to attend to, they would immediately use their robes, alms bowls, waistbands, and other belongings as stakes for gambling.
When the laypeople saw this, they were filled with derision and shame, saying:
"How can you, venerable sirs, act like worldly folk?
To come here on some business and then gamble for robes and bowls—this is not reasonable."
He replied: "What is unreasonable about this?
Could it be that you eat scallions and garlic and drink alcohol?"
He remained silent. The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is indeed appropriate that laypeople should feel reproach and shame; a bhikṣu should not gamble with objects. One who does so commits a *vyatikrama* offense."
The setting was as before.

Every morning, the group of six bhikṣus would stand atop the monastery pavilion and gaze out at the wild fields from afar; whenever they saw smoke rising or observed birds descending, they would immediately go to those places to see what was there.
Once, having witnessed this event, he went in person to observe it; seeing the remains of meat left by a tiger in a thicket, he joyfully took them and brought them into the Jeta Grove.
The tiger, following its scent, arrived at the location of the monastery and howled loudly outside the gate during the night.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason has the tiger come and howled so loudly?"
Ānanda said: "The remaining meat that the tiger had hidden was brought to the monastery by the Venerable Upasena.
The Buddha said:
“Monks, did you eat the tiger’s leftovers?
They replied to the Buddha, “We did.”
“Ānanda! Just as the lion king, having killed a fine deer, devours its choice meat and drinks its fresh blood before casting it aside and departing;

whereas the tigers, having eaten their fill of flesh, hoard up the leftovers—therefore, bhikṣus do not eat what has been left over by tigers. One who eats it incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.”
However, I shall now establish the rules of conduct for the senior elders among the assembly.
Whenever a senior elder is seen consuming meat, he should be asked:
"What kind of meat is this?"
"Is it not the remains of a tiger?
Or is it not food that should not be eaten?
If one accepts [the food] without asking these questions, one incurs an offense against the Dharma (vayadharmika-āpatti).
The summary verse for the ninth section of the fifth chapter says:
It is not permissible to hide one's own body; One should not fail to announce [one's arrival] and so forth;
If one obtains a cloak of high value, One should sell it and share the proceeds equally.
The setting is as before.

In a certain city there was previously a monastery. At that time, Nanda and Upananda, while traveling through the countryside, arrived at this monastery just as the great assembly there had received a large amount of offerings.
At that time, although the bhikṣus saw these two and knew of their evil conduct, not a single one among them offered to relieve their fatigue.
Then Upānanda said to Nanda: "Ācārya!..."
"These black-bowl monks are constantly full of arrogance; we should create some cause for them to be troubled.
Let us first hide our bodies together in a secluded place and observe how they distribute the shared requisites."
He replied, "Excellent! It should be done in this way."
He then concealed his body and secretly observed the distribution of the goods.
Having seen how it was divided, he said, "This division is improper; this is an unjust distribution."
"Venerable sir, you may inform the assembly that you wish to share out the robes.
He replied, "I was not present at the time of distribution; from where have you come now?"
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When you wish to divide the profits, first inform the assembly, saying:
'The Saṃgha possesses property that is now to be divided among all; no bhikṣu should depart hastily.'"
Then the bhikṣus gathered the items together once more and announced to the entire assembly that food should not be distributed; they then divided the items.
At that time, those two men hid their own shares again, and when the assembly had finished the distribution, they emerged as before and declared:
"This division is invalid."
He replied, "I have already informed the assembly; from where have you two come? The two men said:
"Even though it has been announced, you may still strike the *gandī*.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must announce the formal declaration and then strike the *gandī* before the items can be distributed."
Then the bhikṣus again collected the items and informed the assembly, striking the *gaṇḍī* once more before dividing the goods among them.
The two men hid themselves again and only emerged after the division was complete; they were reprimanded as before.
The people replied,
"How could you not have heard the announcement to the assembly and the sound of the *gandi*?
They then informed him, saying:
"Even though you have informed the assembly and struck the *gandi*, how could you, O virtuous ones, proceed to distribute voting sticks?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"After having made the formal announcement and struck the *gandi*, you may then proceed to distribute the voting sticks; only then shall the items be divided."
Then the bhikṣus again gathered the items; having completed the three matters as before, they hid them once more and only emerged after the distribution was finished.
As before, they were rebuked. The people said, "Venerable ones!..."
"For what reason do you thus cause distress to the Saṃgha?
Since the announcement has been made, the gaṇḍī struck, and the voting sticks distributed, you have not revealed yourself; wait until it is concluded before coming forth. He replied:
“Virtuous ones, why do you say that we have disturbed the Saṃgha?
How could you possibly act in such a manner before the assembly?
This is entirely unnecessary; I shall now depart.”
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Even when performing the three acts, one must still act in the presence of the assembly; if it is not before them, then it need not be granted.
This is called 'proper distribution'; do not harbor any doubts."
"However, monks must not intentionally cause trouble for the Saṃgha; if one does so intentionally, they commit an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The setting of this episode is as before.

At that time, after the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had finished donating the monastery to the Saṃgha of the four directions, he used various exquisite pigments to paint both the interior and exterior. When the people of this city heard that the householder had completed the murals, they vied with one another to come and view them, until hundreds of thousands of people gathered within the monastery.

Within the city there was a great brahmin, a man of such eminence that he was held in high esteem by the multitude. Having obtained a single-fur cloak from the royal household, he immediately donned it with a sense of pride and began to tour the Jetavana Grove, observing the monasteries. Struck by a sense of the extraordinary, he then offered the fur cloak to the Sangha of the four directions; although the text here mentions "the four directions," the intended meaning refers to the *pratyutpanna* (present) Sangha, not the permanently resident monks.

As the Buddha taught, even down to garments currently being worn, one should cut them into wicks for lamps and share them equally; thus, the bhikṣus proceeded to cut their heavy woolen cloaks into pieces and distributed them among the community.
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself during the night:
"That is a superior woolen cloak; I ought to pay its price and redeem it.
Rising at dawn, he entered the monastery and went to its gate, where he saw the bhikṣus and asked them:
“Noble one! What use will people have for this woolen cloak I am giving?
The bhikṣu replied:
"You may rejoice; let us cut it up and divide it among the assembly.
One person said, "I shall make a cap from it."
One said, "Make boots. Another said:
"Adjusting the waistband. Another says:
"Wiping the bowl-cloth."
He replied, "Noble one! That was a fine cloak; why have you torn it apart?"
"It would be appropriate to sell it; once the money and coins have been obtained, they may be shared among the assembly.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"What that brāhmaṇa has said is reasonable. Therefore, bhikṣus, when you obtain such a high-value woolen cloak, you should sell it for money and coins before sharing it."
The summary verse for the tenth section of the fifth chapter states:
One should not use the five kinds of skins; the same applies to other similar types.
If one suffers from hemorrhoids, one should wear sandals made of bear skin.
The setting was as before.
At that time, the six bhikṣus said to one another:
"Nanda and Upananda, we have obtained the price for cakes from every person in this city."
"However, we have never seen him give anything to the elephant trainers at the royal court; we should go there now and seek it from him, for he might perhaps grant us some.
One man replied, "We should do exactly as you say."

However, one must first devise a modest plan: take a lion’s skin and make shoes from it, then walk upwind of the place where the elephant is tethered; when the elephant smells the scent, it will immediately flee in terror.
He replied: "Excellent plan!
I shall go now to beg from him; if I succeed, it will be well."
"If you do not give it to me, it will not be too late for me to fear the elephant.
Thereupon, at dawn, he went to the elephant trainer's place and said, "O worthy one!"
"O virtuous ones, why are you so utterly devoid of a mind seeking merit?
Have you never bestowed upon us even a small amount of the value of cakes or fruit? They replied:
“Venerable ones!
How could we possibly be dependent upon you, such that we should provide you with the price of cakes and fruit?
Having heard this, the group of six monks nodded their heads in agreement, dismissed them, and departed.
Thereupon, on another day, he put on a pair of lion-skin sandals and stood upwind from where the elephants were.
At that time, when the herd of elephants caught the scent of the lion, they lost control of their bowels and urine and fled in terror.
At that time, the elephant trainer used his hook to strike the elephant's head but could not make it stop; seeing this from afar, the group of six addressed him, saying:
"Worthy sir! Pull hard!"
"Pull quickly!
He replied, "The hook and the spade cannot hold it; how can I pull it by hand?"
The group of six replied,
"We can cause him to stay.
He answered, saying:
"Noble One! If you can cause us to abide [in this], it would be a great kindness.
The group of six said:
They made a mutual covenant, saying, "If you can pay me the price for these cakes and fruits, I shall allow you to stay.
He replied, "I will give it to you immediately."
He then hurried to a position downwind from the elephant; as the elephant could no longer smell his scent, it ceased its panicked flight.
The elephant trainers asked him, "Venerable One!..."
"Are you skilled in incantations? He replied,
"I possess no extraordinary arts."
"If that is so, how can you cause the elephant to be afraid or not afraid?
He then told the elephant trainer the truth, and the trainer said,
"Noble One!..."
"How can you all commit such an unrighteous and harmful act?
If the royal elephant, the most excellent of its kind, should become terrified by this and flee into the mountain forests, you will surely incur a great punishment."
Upon hearing this, he smiled and remained silent without speaking.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"It is because the bhikṣus wear lion-skin shoes that such faults have arisen."
He then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"From this day forward, you must no longer wear shoes made of lion skin. Should anyone wear them, they shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
Hearing that the Buddha did not permit it, he then made shoes out of tiger skin. The Buddha said, "This also is not permissible.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of animal skins with claws and fangs that should not be used: namely, those of the wise elephant, the wise horse, the lion, the tiger, and the leopard."
After the Buddha had refused, the Venerable Upāli requested of the World-Honored One:
"If there are other types of skin from clawed or fanged creatures, may these be used?"
The Buddha said:
"It should not be used either.
One who uses it incurs the offense of duṣkṛta."
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu afflicted with hemorrhoids who went to a physician and said,
"O worthy one!"
“I have hemorrhoids; please provide a prescription for me.
He replied, “You should make shoes from bear skin; when you wear them, the illness will be cured.”
He replied, "The World-Honored One has not yet permitted it.
The physician said:
"The Buddha is greatly compassionate; he will surely grant permission.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "One who is ill should wear it."
"Multiple layers are difficult to obtain," the Buddha said.
"If there are none, one should take a single layer together with wool to serve as the sole of the sandals.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 19.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu,
Fascicle Twenty-three,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The summary verse for the sixth section says:
Tendon of a wild beast is not permitted; The lamp-light and the heroic;
The *dhāsa* and the rules for nuns; Because of the granting to Gautamī.
A nun should not precede an elder; she may provide other bedding, but it is improper to soil it with splashed water. This should be understood as the sixth general point.
The summary verse for the first section of the sixth chapter states:
Boots laced with the sinews and hides of fierce beasts, those that cover both the front and the back,
and those with two points or a pointed tip— none of these boots are permitted.
The circumstances were in Śrāvastī.
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not use the skins of the five fierce beasts that possess claws and fangs, namely: the wise elephant, the wise horse, the lion, the tiger, and the leopard."
At that time, the group of six monks used sinews from those animals, which again constituted an offense.
The Buddha said: "Do not use these sinews to sew shoes.
The group of six monks then used leather thongs, which constituted an offense as before; they further used animal hides to patch their shoes, whereupon the Buddha said:
"None of these are permitted for use.

One should know that regarding footwear and similar items—whether they cover the front, cover the back, have two points at the tips, or are made of hemp sandals and various boots—one must not wear them; to do so constitutes an offense against the Dharma."
"Except for two or three layers of leather sandals.

People from the Western Regions do not wear such items as these. However, if one lives in a cold foreign land, one may wear them for the sake of sustaining life, provided the mind remains inwardly restrained. A verse says:
When the Four Great Kings were first born, Their radiance illuminated everywhere.
Because of this matter, his parents each established a name for him.

At that time, while the Bodhisattva was in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, there was a king in the city of Rājagṛha named Mahāpadma. He ruled the world according to the Dharma; the people were numerous, living in peace, security, and abundance, free from all thieves and bandits.

The king of Śrāvastī was named Brahmadatta; the king of Caṇpā was named Mahācakra; and the king of Kauśāmbī was named Śatānīka. These four kings were all Dharma-kings who transformed the world through the Dharma, as has been explained at length elsewhere.
At that time, while in the celestial palace, the Bodhisattva observed the world through five matters.
What are these five?
First, he observed his distant ancestors.
2. Contemplation of the time;
3. Contemplation of the region;
4. Contemplation of the nearby clans;
Fifth, contemplating his mother:
the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm purified her womb three times; then, while Lady Māyā was reclining, she saw in a dream a six-tusked white elephant descending into her womb.

At that time, the great earth shook in six ways, emitting a great radiance that filled the world, surpassing the light of the gods; even the dark places between worlds, where neither the sun nor the moon shines, became entirely clear, so that all sentient beings were able to see one another.

When the Bodhisattva was born as described below, the four great kings all gave birth to their own crown princes; they beheld a great radiance like the color of molten gold and each said to themselves:
"It is by the majestic spiritual power of the son born to me that the heavens and earth have been made to shine with such rare and marvelous brilliance."
Each was given a name to correspond with these auspicious omens.
Then, the Great Lotus King addressed the assembly, saying:

"When my son was born, he was like the radiance of the sun, illuminating heaven and earth with a brilliance so wondrous and extraordinary that he should be named 'Shadow-Victorious' (Vijitāvin); in Sanskrit, his name is Bimbisāra."
King Brahmadatta addressed the assembly, saying:
"When my son was born, his radiance was extraordinary, illuminating the entire world; therefore, my son shall be named Prabhāsa."
The Great Wheel-Turning King addressed the multitude, saying:
"When my son was born, he was like the light of a great lamp that illuminated everywhere; therefore, my son shall be named Dīpaṃkara (Light-Maker)."
Then King Śatānīka addressed the assembly, saying:
"When my son was born, his radiance was like the rising sun, illuminating everything clearly; therefore, I shall name my son Prabhāsa."
Each [of the gods] claimed it was due to their own power, yet none knew it was through the might of the Bodhisattva.
The internal summary verse says:
"Guarded by the gods within his womb, Upon birth, he stepped upon lotus flowers."
Raising his hand, he alone was proclaimed supreme; as he was bathed, flowers and robes fell [around him].

At that time, when the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, commanded four celestial sons to each hold weapons to guard his mother, so that neither humans nor non-humans might cause her harm.

When a bodhisattva dwells in the womb, he is not defiled by the impurities of the blood within it; just as a collection of various jewels placed together in one place does not stain one another, so too is it with the bodhisattva in the womb.

Furthermore, just as a person with clear vision can distinctly discern a pure, exquisite lapis lazuli gem placed upon five-colored cloths, so too does the mother clearly perceive the interior of her womb.

Although she carried the fetus in her womb, her body experienced no fatigue; naturally, she observed the five precepts for as long as she lived—namely, abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking intoxicants—and she maintained a mind free from lustful attachment toward all men.
When the ten months were complete, she went to the Lumbinī grove and, grasping a branch of an *aśoka* tree, stood for a brief moment; then the Bodhisattva was born from her right side.
At that time, the great earth shook in six ways, emitting a vast radiance no different from when he had entered the womb.

When the Bodhisattva was born, Śakra personally received him with his own hands and placed him upon a lotus flower. Without requiring assistance, he took seven steps upon seven lotuses and, surveying the four directions, pointed toward the zenith and the nadir, speaking these words:
"This is my final birth-body; in the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the most honored."
The Brahma King held a parasol and the Lord of Devas grasped a fly-whisk; in the midst of the void, the Dragon Kings poured forth water—one warm and one cold—to bathe the Bodhisattva.
At the time of his initial birth, before his mother, a well appeared spontaneously, from which fragrant springs surged upward for him to enjoy as he wished.

Furthermore, from the sky, various devas scattered down *utpala* flowers, *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, and *pundarika* flowers, along with various other kinds of wondrous powdered incense; celestial, exquisite music spontaneously resounded, and wonderful celestial garments and necklaces fell in profusion from the air.
There were further numerous wondrous and auspicious omens, as described in other places.
A summary verse states:
Asita beheld the marks; Nālāda exhorted his teacher.
Five hundred auspicious omens appeared before him, and his father, the King, bestowed upon him three titles.
At that time, in a great mountain to the south, there was an ancient seer named Asita, who was well-versed in the timing of the formation and destruction of the world-systems.

At that time, there was a man named Nārada, who was clever and possessed of eloquent wisdom; he came frequently to pay his respects and engage in discourse with the seer Asita regarding the matters of the world’s formation and destruction.

Having heard this, he was filled with grief and lamentation; he immediately went forth as a renunciant in the presence of that seer. Later, at another time, while staying together with this seer in a stone cave, he saw a radiance illuminating the place with extraordinary and marvelous signs. He then spoke a verse, questioning his teacher:
"Why does this radiance, Shining everywhere like the sun, Pervade these mountain forests? How is it that such a marvel has suddenly appeared?"
The seer replied: "If this were the sunlight, it would be scorching; yet now this coolness manifests as a marvel.
This must surely be the Unsurpassed Muni, revealing such an auspicious sign upon first emerging from his mother’s womb."
This is the sign of the Bodhisattva’s emergence from the womb; its light is pure and rare in the world.
Like golden radiance filling the ten directions, it soars forth, illuminating the three realms of existence with complete clarity.
Narada said to his teacher, "Upādhyāya! If this is so,
we should go together now to see the Bodhisattva."
The Master said: "Do you know now?

The Bodhisattva possesses great majestic power, and immeasurable devas have all gathered like clouds. Although we have come here to pay our respects at his crown, there is no way for us to do so; wait until he has entered the city and been given a name, and when he emerges again, I hope to welcome him."

When the Bodhisattva was born, five hundred attendants headed by Chandaka were born simultaneously; five hundred handmaidens headed by Chanda were also born at the same time. Five hundred superior elephants and five hundred stallion horses were all born, five hundred hidden treasures spontaneously opened up, and the kings of neighboring countries all presented tribute.
Having seen this, the minister addressed King Śuddhodana, saying: "Great King! Today the national destiny has flourished;

the birth of the Prince has brought forth auspicious omens in their entirety. Five hundred male attendants and five hundred female attendants have been born; five hundred superior elephants and five hundred superior horses have each appeared; five hundred hidden treasures have spontaneously manifested; and rare treasures from the tributary states of all nations have gathered together."
Having heard this announcement, the king’s heart leaped with great joy, and he said to his ministers:
"Since all matters have been accomplished following the birth of the prince, it is fitting that we establish a name for him: Sarvārthasiddha (in Sanskrit)."
"This was the Bodhisattva’s first bestowal of a name, titled 'The Accomplisher of All Deeds.
At that time, the Bodhisattva mounted a carriage made of the four precious substances and entered the city of Kapilavastu, followed by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of humans and devas."
The Śākyas are by nature arrogant and habitually talkative; yet when the Bodhisattva entered the city, they all remained silent—the Sage was without speech.
Having seen this, the King addressed his ministers, saying:
"The Śākyas are by nature arrogant and habitually talkative, yet when the Prince entered the city, they all remained silent."
"The Muni remains silent; therefore, the Prince should be named Śākyamuni.
This was the second name established for the Bodhisattva.

At that time, there was an ancient yakṣa residing in this city named Śākyavardhana, whom the people of the time revered and honored with a temple and sacrifices. Whenever a child of the Śākya clan was born, they would bathe them thoroughly and carry them to the yakṣa’s abode to pay their respects.
Then King Śuddhodana filled the Prince’s mouth with the finest ghee and honey and said to his ministers,
"Take the Prince to pay homage to the yakṣa.
When the ministers had carried him there, the yakṣa saw the Prince from afar and immediately manifested himself, going before the Bodhisattva and prostrating at his feet.
The minister returned and informed the king; having heard this, the king gave rise to a sense of wonder and said:
"Now my crown prince is even more exalted than among the heavenly deities; one should establish a name for him called 'God Among Gods' (Devātideva)."
This is the third designation given to the Bodhisattva.
The internal summary verse says:
Entrusting him to his mother to raise the Prince, and causing him to observe the marks of a Great Man.
Asita traveled from afar and personally beheld the form of the Muni.

At that time, the father-king entrusted the prince to various foster mothers, who bathed him at the appropriate times, nursed him, and provided him with food and drink, constantly ensuring he was safe, peaceful, and that his body and mind were contented and joyful.
The foster mother then anointed his body with the finest unguents and, having adorned him with various necklaces and ornaments, presented him to the King, his father.
The King then took him in his arms, gazed upon him, and was filled with joy.
He then summoned all the brahmins, as well as everyone in the kingdom who was skilled in interpreting signs and portents or proficient in calculation, and commanded them:
"Gentlemen, you should examine him closely. I have heard that ancient seers spoke thus:
'One who possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man has two possible destinies:'"
If he remains a householder, he shall become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four continents and transforming the world through the Dharma.

He will possess the seven treasures—namely, the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the minister of the treasury treasure, and the minister of the military treasure—and will be endowed with a thousand sons who are brave, robust, loyal, and capable of subduing enemies. Throughout the entire realm within the seas, there will be no afflictions or distress; the people will dwell in abundance, joy, and peace.
"If he goes forth from the household life, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and attains equal and perfect enlightenment, he will possess great renown that fills the world.
When the physiognomists heard what the king said, they all observed him together and said to the king:

"It is exactly as the Great King has stated. If one is endowed with the thirty-two marks, there are only two possibilities: either a Wheel-Turning Monarch or a Buddha—up to and including having great renown that fills the world."
The King asked again, "What are these marks?

At that time, the physiognomists answered him fully, pointing out each of the thirty-two marks individually. Since they are already extensively detailed in other sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras, and there is no difference in the facts, I have not troubled myself with translating them here.
At that time, the seer Asita said to Nārada: "Māṇava!
Recently, the Bodhisattva has already entered the city and established three names; we ought to go there to pay our respects and behold his countenance."

Each mounted upon their supernormal powers and soared into the air; however, by the majestic spiritual power of that bodhisattva, they were brought to within about one *yojana* of the city of Kapilavastu, whereupon they lost their supernormal powers and proceeded on foot.
Having entered the city and arrived at the king’s gate, he said to the gatekeeper:
"Go and inform the king:
'The seer Asita has now arrived at the gate.'"
The messenger went and informed the king, who said,
"Let him enter. Who would dare to obstruct a great seer?"
He immediately went to the king's location.
When the king saw the seer arrive, he called out from afar: "Welcome!"
"May you be blessed with auspiciousness.
Having washed his feet, he had him seated upon a magnificent lion throne. After the king had prostrated at his feet, he addressed him, saying:
"O Great Sage!..."
"What brings you here?
The seer spoke a verse, saying:
"O Lord of the Land, I have now arrived, desiring to see the Prince."
Beholding the Honored Muni, the foremost among all teachers.
The King said,
“The Prince has fallen asleep.”
He replied, "Although he is asleep, I wish to see him for a moment.
The king then took him up and showed him to him.
Seeing that the Bodhisattva’s eyes were not closed, the seer spoke this verse:
"A noble steed does not sleep much; He sleeps for but a moment at midnight.
Since the task to be accomplished is not yet finished, Why do you sleep so soundly?"
The seer asked again:
"What did the diviners and physiognomists predict?
The king replied:
“The Great Seer described his marks, saying:
‘He shall become a Wheel-Turning King and transform the four continents.
The Seer then replied to the king with a verse:
"The marks [of a wheel-turning monarch] are often spoken of erroneously; in this final age, there is no wheel-turning monarch.
Because you possess these superior karmic conditions for merit, you shall sever the afflictions and attain Buddhahood.
Had you been transformed as a ruler of the four continents, the marks of a wheel-turning monarch would not have been so manifest."
"The marks of a Great Master are clearly manifest; there is no doubt he will attain Buddhahood.
Having observed the signs of his future Buddhahood, the seer further examined how soon he would attain the unsurpassed nectar and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma.
He then saw that in twenty-nine years he would leave the royal city and, after six years of ascetic practice, would attain perfect enlightenment.
He further observed how long his own life would last and whether he would be able to see the Buddha.
Knowing that he could not see the Buddha, he was overcome with grief and distress, his tears filling his eyes.
Seeing him filled with sorrow, the King spoke a verse, asking:
“Whether man or woman comes to behold [the Buddha], All find joy pervading their entire body and mind.”
"O Benevolent One, you have now personally observed that his marks are not those of an ordinary man; for what reason do tears fill both your eyes?

If the marks of the Prince were not auspicious—signifying a short life, much illness, and inauspiciousness—I pray that you, Great Seer, will speak according to the truth, so as not to increase the sorrow and exhaustion of my heart."
The seer replied: "Even if a thunderbolt were to descend from the sky, coming upon the Prince's person with terrifying force,
it could not harm the Unsurpassed Honored One of the Munis by even so much as a hair."
Even if a fierce fire with soaring flames and winds, or a sharp sword as cold as frost should appear before him;
even if poison and black snakes were to arrive all at once—at the Prince’s dwelling, they would all vanish away.
I grieve that I died too soon and did not see the Buddha; my tears fill my eyes and are difficult to restrain.
Having abandoned the unsurpassed Dharma, I passed away before it; no undertaking has yet been brought to fulfillment.
This one possesses great merit that dispels all afflictions; having realized the Dharma of Ambrosia, he acts as a Teacher.
If you can hear his teachings and practice according to them, you shall all return to the state of quiescent nirvana, free from conditioned existence.
Upon hearing that the Crown Prince had realized the Dharma of Ambrosia (*amṛta*), the king remained silent and spoke no word.
For all worldly people are disturbed and distracted by perverse minds; their speech is flatterous and deceptive, unable to accord with reality.
Then that seer said to the king:
"Recently, Great King, you have often thought to yourself:
'When shall I be able to let the seer Asita enter the city on foot so that he may meet with me and all the people may pay him their most earnest respects?'"
"Out of compassion for me, you have traveled here on foot; now that my business is concluded and I am about to depart from the city, you should clear away the debris and thoroughly repair the town.

At that time, King Śuddhodana commanded his ministers to strictly prepare the roads and issued a general proclamation throughout the city for all to join in the restoration. The streets and main thoroughfares were swept clean and polished; they were sprinkled with sandalwood-scented water and strewn with *campaka* flowers. Banners and canopies reached toward the sky, and fragrant incense smoke filled the paths, such that all who saw it rejoiced as if in the Nandana Grove.
He further sent out those ringing bells to proclaim everywhere:
"All people should know—whether you reside within the city or have newly arrived from other regions—let everyone take heed that tomorrow at dawn they shall witness the Great Seer depart."
Having heard this, the multitude each set out on their way; beholding the Rishi as he stepped forth from the city gates, they were all filled with a sense of wonder and longing, and returned home.

At that time, the Rishi Asita returned to his mountain abode and focused his mind upon meditative stillness. Through the skillful means of wisdom, he exercised his supernormal powers, yet as his life was drawing to a close, he fell ill; despite the application of medicine and nourishment, he had but a few moments remaining.
Then Nalada came and prostrated at his teacher’s feet, saying: “Great Master!
I originally left the household life seeking the flavor of the Deathless; I pray that you will graciously share with me what you have attained.”
The teacher said: "I am the same as you;
when we originally left the household life, our intention was to seek the nectar of immortality (amṛta), yet in the end we have gained nothing and spent our lives in vain.
By the side of the Snowy Mountains, in the city of Kapilavastu, a prince appeared in the world, whom the physiognomists all predicted:"
"When he attains perfect enlightenment, he shall be known as the Teacher of Gods and Humans and called the All-Knowing One.

You should seek to go forth under him; casting aside arrogance, you should practice humility, diligently cultivate the holy life with heedfulness, and at that time, you shall obtain the flavor of the Deathless."
He spoke in verse:
"The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter; to have met him now is most rare.
Do not be negligent, but seek with a sincere heart; you shall obtain the flavor of the deathless nectar."
Having spoken these words, he immediately passed away. As a verse says:
"All accumulations are dispersed; what is lofty must fall."
"All meetings end in separation; all who are born must return to death.

At that time, after the seer Asita had passed away, his disciple Nālada cremated him according to the Dharma. Having completed the funeral rites and cast off his grief, he went to Vārāṇasī and lived among the other seers.
Narada was originally of the Kātyāyana clan; because of this, people of the time called him the Rishi Kātyāyana, and the multitude all held him in high esteem.

At that time, the crown prince born to King Uśīnara was named Dīpaprakāśa. The king entrusted him to eight nurses to care for him, and his upbringing was provided without deficiency. As he gradually grew older, he became widely proficient in the arts and sciences; there was nothing required of a scholar or a warrior that he did not master.
When the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni engaged in the play of childhood, Prince Dīpaṃkara likewise engaged in the play of childhood.
When the Bodhisattva received the consecration of a crown prince, Prince Dīpaṃkara also received the consecration of a crown prince.

When the Bodhisattva went out through the four gates and beheld the afflictions of old age, sickness, and death, he conceived a sense of weary detachment toward his three consorts—namely, Queen Go-pālā, Queen Mṛga-dā, and Queen Yaśodharā—and as leaders of six thousand court ladies, they were all abandoned by him; in the middle of the night, he leaped over the city wall and departed.
He went to an empty forest to cultivate the life of a renunciant; relying on a seer, he studied a sublime concentration and became free from the desires of the desire realm.
Next, he studied the concentration of nothingness under Udraka Rāmaputra and severed the desires of the sphere of nothingness.
Finding no further guide, he practiced asceticism with single-minded devotion for six years; yet, as he did not attain distinct realization, he considered it fruitless.

He then relaxed his discipline and indulged himself, partaking of fine foods, anointing his body with ghee, bathing in warm water, and entering a village where, at the home of the two cowherd girls Nandā and Nandabalā, he consumed sixteen times more than usual of the most excellent milk-rice.

The Naga King Kālika paid him honor and praise; from Śubhavyūha he took auspicious grass (*kuśa*), went to the foot of the Bodhi tree, spread the grass himself, and sat cross-legged with body upright and mindfulness established, thinking and saying:
"If I do not completely exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*), I shall never break this cross-legged posture."

At that time, the Bodhisattva, having subdued thirty-six billion kṣoṇīs of māras with the weapon of his compassionate mind, realized unsurpassed wisdom; he accepted the invitation of Brahmā and proceeded to Vārāṇasī to turn the Wheel of Dharma in three revolutions and twelve aspects.

At that time, King Dīpaṃkara also received the consecration to the great sovereignty; he governed by means of the Dharma, and the people of the kingdom of Uśīnara flourished, being secure, peaceful, and prosperous, as has been described at length elsewhere.

By the power of the king, the common people sang songs and held festivities one after another, making offerings everywhere to the supreme celestial deities; they dug five hundred ponds and five hundred canals so that the people might enjoy them without any lack.
The second sub-section of the sixth chapter, summarized in verse, says:
Dīpāyana attained kingship, Possessing five extraordinary things;
Due to recounting these wondrous events, The land of Gandhāra is explained at length.
At that time, King Dīpaṃkara possessed five supreme treasures. What were these five?
The first was a preeminent bull elephant named Veṇuśikhin.
Second, the preeminent female elephant named Bhadrā;
third, the preeminent camel named Sāgarapāda;
fourth, the preeminent horse named Vastraprīvaka.
Fifth, the superior messenger was named Flying Crow (*Pakṣin*). As for their speeds:

an elephant travels one hundred stations (*yojana*) in a day and night; a female elephant travels eighty stations in a day and night; a camel travels seventy stations in a day and night; a horse travels fifty stations in a day and night; and Flying Crow travels twenty-five stations in a day and night.

Although that king possessed such superior things and enjoyed happiness and security, his four elements became unbalanced and he suddenly fell ill with insomnia; because of this disease, he developed an aversion to clarified butter (*sarpis*) and a craving for wine.
At that time, the physicians prepared various kinds of exquisite medicines, mixing them with clarified butter (*sarpis*) and boiling them, then presented them to the King to take as medicine.

The King refused to use them; however, when the Crown Prince and those in the inner palace all learned that the medicinal butter could cure insomnia, they each offered it to him, yet the King became even more averse to sleep.
The king then issued a decree, saying:
"If anyone shall utter the name of 'ghee' in my presence, his head shall be severed.

Since the king could not sleep, he engaged in amorous play with the women of the inner palace during the first watch; at the hour of midnight, he went to the stables for elephants and horses to conduct an inspection; and during the last watch, he inspected the various treasuries. Carrying a sharp sword himself, he questioned the night-watchman, saying:
"Who is awake? If he does not answer when asked for the first and second time, one should temporarily tolerate it; however, if he does not answer by the third time, one shall cut off his head.
Because of this cruelty, the name "Dīpaṃkara" (Lamp-Light) was obscured, and by adding other characters, he was called "Caṇḍa-pradīpa" (Fierce Lamp).
On another occasion, King Dīpaṃkara addressed his chief queen and the ladies of the inner court, saying:
"I am personally awake; why are you all asleep?"
He replied, "Great King! I too am awake."
Thus, they were unable to sleep throughout the night and said to the king:
"If we are made to remain awake all night, there will be no way for us to satisfy Your Majesty’s wishes; furthermore, this lack of sleep will cause us to neglect our duties."
The king said,
"If it were not for your karma, who else would be fit to do so? He replied:
"The Crown Prince ought to do so.
Thereupon, the King immediately went to inform the Crown Prince, saying:
"Why have you not awakened?"
He replied, "I was keeping watch. Later, when he was unable to do so, he addressed the king, saying:
"If you always cause me to remain on guard, I shall neglect my royal duties; this is not my concern.
The king asked, "Then who else should do it?"
He replied, "The ministers should perform this.
The king then immediately went and informed the ministers, saying:
"Why do you not remain vigilant? He replied,
"I am indeed vigilant."
Later, being unable to do so, he said to the king:
"If you constantly require me to serve as your watchman, who will assist the king in transforming the world according to the Dharma?"
"This is not my business," the king said.
"Who else, then, should do it?"
He replied, “The disbanded soldiers should do it.
The king then went at once to where the disbanded soldiers were and said to them:
“I am alert; for what reason are you not being alert?
Later, when they were unable to do so, they said to the king:
“If you always require us to remain alert, how can we fight against others as your king?”
"This is not my affair," the King said.
"Who else, then, should do it?"
He replied, "The common people should do it.
The king then went at once to where the common people were and engaged them in the same dialogue as before.
At that time, the people of that country were keeping watch in rotation to maintain vigilance.
It was the turn of the young incense-seller; he thought to himself, "The king is cruel and violent; he might even kill me."
