Thereupon, in the middle of the night, he rested his cheek in his palm and brooded in sorrow.
At that time, a friend of his saw him and asked,
"Venerable sir, why are you so sorrowful?"
He then answered his acquaintance in detail regarding the matter.
The acquaintance replied, "There is a man named Gandhāra not far from your home; why do you not seek him out for the purpose of providing watchfulness?"
The youth replied, "If I cherish my own life,
how could he possibly be willing to do so for me?
Even if he were asked, he certainly would not be able to do it."
He said, "If you give me money and goods, I will certainly do it for you.
He then went to seek them.
That man replied,
"If you can give me five hundred gold coins, I shall do it for you," and he immediately granted him permission.
The Gandhara said, "For now, you may take half; if my life is spared, it will not be too late to return it.
But if I die, this shall belong to you, to be used as you please."
He then gave him half.
Having received the money, he purchased much wine, meat, and various cakes and fruits; he fed all the king’s staff and ensured they were fully satiated, then said to them:
"The King has ordered us to remain vigilant; it is my turn for watch duty."
He asked the people,
"How did the Great King carry out the act of awakening?
They all reported the circumstances in full detail.
The Gandhara said,
"I would be grateful if you would consider this for me. They replied:
"We have been granted this exquisite meal by Your Majesty; while it has not yet been digested within our bellies, why should we not do [your bidding]?
He asked, "What is it that you wish us to do for you?"
He replied: "If the King comes and asks,
'Who is keeping watch?'"
"Then, call me to wake me. He replied, "So be it."
At that time, during the middle watch of the night, the Gandhara wound a woolen blanket around his knees and sat down to sleep for a short while.
The King amused himself with the palace women during the first watch, inspected the elephants and horses during the middle watch, and then, during the last watch, questioned the sentries.
The men replied: "Gandhara!"
"You must wake up and not sleep; the Great King wishes to come.
He then became alert, and the King said to him:
"Who is it that has awakened me?"
Upon hearing this, the Gandhāra thought to himself:
"If I were to answer immediately when first addressed, later on it would not be so; they will certainly cut off my head and cast it to the ground."
He did not respond.
The king called out again:
"Who is keeping watch?"
He remained silent. A third time, he was addressed:
"Who is it that keeps watch?"
He replied, "Great King! I am a Gandhara."
The king said: "Gandhāra! What were you thinking about?"
He, being wise and well-versed in speaking of worldly affairs, replied:
"Great King! I am reflecting upon worldly matters."
The internal summary verse says:
The owl, the crane, and drinking milk; the *māṣa* grass, tail and body equal;
mottled with the same color as the fur; the sand basin and the water not overflowing.
The distinctions between salt, flour, and water, And the transformation of clothing and tiles into dust—
These are called the ten matters That the people of Gandhāra contemplate.
The King said:
"What are you contemplating regarding worldly affairs?
Ghaṇṭāla replied, "There is a marvelous thing in the world: for instance, whether an owl has feathers or not, when weighed on a scale, their weight is identical."
The king asked, "Is this matter true? He replied:
"The King should witness it with his own eyes.
The King said, "If that is so, it is well; I shall observe it for myself."
The Gandhara arrived at dawn with an owl; he weighed it before the king and then removed its feathers, whereupon the weight became identical.
The king asked, "What is the reason for this?"
He replied, "It is fanned by the wind.
The King said:
"You possess wondrous wisdom.
He replied, "It is because of the King that it is so."

Then Gandhāra, having spent the night in sorrow, rubbed his head with his hand and returned to his former residence.

At that time, the young incense-seller brought back the remaining half of the goods to Gandhāra; meanwhile, those in the kingdom who were on their turn for watch duty all hired Gandhāra for five hundred gold coins to ensure his vigilance as he kept the night watch.
During the final watch of the night, the king asked,
"Who is awake? They replied:
"I am a Gandhāra. The king asked, "What are you thinking?"
He replied, "Great King! I am reflecting on worldly affairs."
The king asked,
"What is this worldly matter? He replied:
"A long-necked white crane was given water mixed with milk to drink; it drank only the milk, leaving only the water behind.
The king asked, "Is this fact true?"
He replied, "Your Majesty shall witness it with your own eyes. The King said:
"If that is so, it is well.
At dawn, he brought the crane before the king and had it drink; the result was exactly as he had said.
The king asked, "What is the cause for this?"
He replied, "The nature of the bird's saliva is acidic; when it drinks milk, it turns into curd, leaving the water behind.
The King said:
"You possess wondrous wisdom.
He replied, "It is because of the King that this is so."
The king remained silent.
Later, on another night, the king asked:
"Who is keeping watch?"
He replied as before:
"I am keeping watch. The king said:
"What are you thinking? He replied, "Great King!"
"I am reflecting on the affairs of the world. The king asked,
"What are these worldly affairs?"

He replied: "In the world there is the *śara* grass; when it is struck with an object and compared with one that has not been struck, if they are weighed on a scale, their weight is identical. This is not the case with other types of grass."
The king asked, “Is this matter true? He replied:
"The King should witness it for himself. The King said,
"If that is so, it is well."
At dawn, he took the *māṣaka* grass and struck it against the king; he then weighed it on a scale, and it was exactly as he had said.
The king asked, "What is the reason for this?"
He replied, “When it is struck, wind enters.
Thereupon, the king remained silent.
Again, on another night, the king asked once more:
"Who is keeping watch? They replied:
“I am a Gandhāra,” he replied.
The king asked, “What were you thinking?”
He replied, "I was reflecting on worldly affairs.
The king said:
"What is this worldly matter?
He replied, "There is a report that the tail of a *lingshu* (spirit-mouse) is equal in length to its body."
The king asked, "Is this matter true? He replied:
"The King should witness it for himself. The King said,
"If that is so, it is well."
At dawn, he brought the mouse and compared it with the king; it was exactly as he had said.
The king asked, "What is the cause for this? He replied:
"I saw it beneath a tree during the springtime; its tail was level with its body.
Thereupon, the king remained silent.
On another night, the king asked again.
He replied,
"I am here to provide a warning.
The king said:
"What are you thinking about? He replied,
"I am thinking about worldly affairs."
The king asked,
"What is this worldly matter? He replied:
“Great King! I am thinking of the pheasant;
on its body, for every patch of variegated color, there is still that many stalks of downy feathers remaining, with the exception of its tail.
The King said:
"Is this matter truly so?
He replied, "Your Majesty should verify it for yourself."
The king said, "If that is so, it is well.
At dawn, he obtained a pheasant; when presented to the king, it was indeed just as had been described.
The king asked,
"How do you know this? He replied:
"I previously knew this by calculation.
The king said,
"You possess wondrous wisdom."
He replied, "It is because of the king that it is so.
The king then remained silent.
Again he asked, "Who is keeping watch? He replied:
“I am a Gandhāra. The king asked,
“What were you thinking about?”
He replied: "Great King!
It is like a bowl filled with sand; when water is added until the bowl is full without overflowing, the sand and water occupy the same space without obstructing one another."
The king asked, "Is this matter true? He replied:
"The King should witness this for himself.
At dawn, he immediately filled a basin with sand and poured water into it until it was full; yet the water did not overflow. The King then remained silent.
Again, the King asked:
"Who is it that has awakened?
He replied, "It is I who have awakened."
The king asked again,
"What were you thinking about? [He replied,] "I was thinking about worldly affairs."
“What is this worldly matter?
“I thought that if one were to mix one *droṇa* of salt with one *droṇa* of water, the water would not increase in volume.
The King said:
"Is this matter truly so?
He replied, "Your Majesty should verify it for yourself."
At dawn, he mixed water with salt and the king tested it himself.
The king asked, "Why is this? He replied:
"Salt comes from water; when it meets water again, it returns to its original state.
The king then remained silent.
The king asked again:
"Who is awake? He answered as before.
The king said:
"What are you thinking about? He replied,
"I am thinking about worldly affairs."
The king asked,
"What is this worldly matter? He replied:
"I thought that if I were to mix one sheng of water with one sheng of flour,
they would not cohere," the king said. "Is this actually true?"
He replied, "Your Majesty shall witness it for yourself.
At dawn, he brought water and flour and mixed them together before the king to test them.
The king asked,
"For what reason? He replied:
"I am originally from that country, and many there eat parched grain; I have often seen such things.
The King said, "You are capable of remembering past events."
He replied, "This is by the power of the Great King.
The king then remained silent.
The king asked again:
"Who is keeping watch? He received the same answer as before, up until: "What is the state of the world's affairs?"
He replied: "I see that worldly people constantly engage in the labor of weaving on shuttles day and night; yet I do not know where the silk, cloth, brocades, and embroideries thus produced go to?"
The king said,
"I too do not know where this object has gone. Ghaṇṭāla replied:
"These various objects will ultimately return to earth.
The King said, "It is exactly as you say; they will ultimately return to earth."
The king asked again:
"Who is keeping watch? He received the same answer as before.
...up to: "What is the worldly matter? He replied:
"I see that various potters and others in the world work ceaselessly day and night to produce many earthenware vessels, yet they do not know where these objects go."
The king replied, "I too do not know where he has gone! The Gandhara said:
"These various objects have been transformed into mud.
The King said, "As you have said, they have rotted into mud."
The internal summary verse says:
King Candraprabha personally questioned his mother, And learned she was born from a scorpion;
He gave her five hundred pieces of gold And drove her out of the country.
At that time, having seen that Gandhāra possessed great wisdom and skillful eloquence in responding, the Great King questioned him further:
"You possess much wisdom and are able to comprehend the various affairs of the world; what is the cause for my inability to sleep?"
The Gandhara said:
"I pray only that Your Majesty will remit his punishment and grant him fearlessness; then I shall venture to speak for the King."
The king said, "I grant you fearlessness; speak as you wish.
Thereupon, the Gandhara addressed the king:
"The King was born from a scorpion. The King said,
"You are now insulting me."
The Gandhara said, "Since the King commands me to speak the truth, how could I dare to revile you? If you do not believe me, wait until tomorrow morning and the King shall verify it for himself.
The King replied:
"Very well.
When daybreak arrived, the Gandhara dug a pit in the ground, filled it with cow dung, and placed bedding upon it; he then had the king lie down to rest, and the king immediately fell asleep.
The king, though having realized this for himself, still doubted whether it was true or false; he then entered the palace and asked his mother, saying:
"I now have a matter that must be inquired about; you should speak truthfully—whence was I born?"
The mother said: "Great King!
Grant me now fearlessness, and I shall speak for you."
The king said,
"Grant your mother fearlessness. She then replied:
"In the past, when your father, the King, had many court ladies and was away on a journey to another land for many years, a desire arose in me. Suddenly seeing a scorpion, I thought to myself:
'This is a man; would it not be pleasant for me to engage in sexual union with him?'"
"At that time, the scorpion transformed into a man and had intercourse with me; I then became aware of my pregnancy, and from this you were born.
Having heard this, the king thought to himself:
"That Gandhāra possesses great and clear wisdom; he is able to know that I was originally born from a scorpion."

"I have granted him fearlessness such that he cannot be executed; now you should grant him a generous reward and cause him to leave the country, ensuring that no one among the people learns of this matter."
He then immediately granted five hundred gold coins to the Gandhara and ordered him to leave the country.

The internal summary verse says:
Pracaṇḍa and Upavāṇa, Kanakavarṇa and Aṅgulimāla;
Narada attained the fruit, and Sunakṣatra held oil in his bowl.
At that time, King Pracaṇḍa thought to himself in silence:
"I am now afflicted by this disease of insomnia, which I perceive to be increasing daily; what means should I employ to bring about its cure?
I ought to summon the physicians within the kingdom to treat this illness of mine."
Having had this thought, he summoned all the physicians and addressed them, saying:
"I have this illness that prevents me from sleeping; you must treat it together."
The physicians said to the king:

"This illness is extraordinary; none of us is able to cure it. However, in Rājagṛha, King Bimbisāra has a son named Jīvaka, who is renowned among the great masters of medicine and possesses such great wisdom that he is capable of curing this disease."
At that time, King Pradyota dispatched a messenger bearing a letter to King Bimbisāra.
The letter read: "I address King Śreṇika!
Please have the great physician Jīvaka come for a brief meeting; I wish to have him treat a certain ailment, so I hope you will not refuse me."
"If he does not come, we must store up much fodder, grain, and troops to welcome him.
When King Bimbisāra had finished reading the letter, he was overcome with great sorrow; resting his cheek in his palm, he thought to himself:
"If I send my son, I fear he may return again; I must comply with his request immediately, for then my realm will become a tributary state."
"If we do not grant it, that kingdom’s army is powerful and will double its harassment.
Seeing the King's expression of distress, Śivaka knelt and said to him,
"For what reason are you so dejected?"
The king said, "Because of your many skills and mastery of these arts, you have caused me great distress; what other way do you know?
He then addressed the king again, saying:
"Please tell us of this matter.
At that time, the father-king related the contents of the letter in full.
Having heard it, Jīvaka addressed the king:
"May you grant us your instructions; we shall carry them out according to your command.
The King replied: "O son!..."
That King Candraprabha is by nature extremely violent and cruel; regardless of whether an act is good or bad, he kills anyone as soon as anger arises in him.
I fear that he might commit an unrighteous act and unjustly slaughter you.
Jīvaka said: "If one cannot protect one's own body, how can one be called a physician?
I pray only that Your Majesty do not give way to grief; I shall go to meet that appointment."
The king said: "Act according to your will!
You must guard yourself well, lest I, the people of the kingdom, and those of the inner palace, both great and small, be filled with anxiety."
He spoke again to the king, saying:
"I pray that you do not harbor grief; such a thing is certainly impossible.
I shall observe the progression of his illness and employ skillful means to ensure that he does not become angry."
The king remained silent.
Then Jīvaka asked the messenger,
"What illness does King Candraprabha suffer from now?"
"What food is suitable for him?
What is unsuitable?
At that time, the messenger fully described the symptoms of the illness.

Having heard this, the Great Physician prepared a medicinal ointment with clarified butter; its color was like the color of wine, its taste like the taste of wine, and its fragrance like the fragrance of wine.
Once it had been compounded, he chose an auspicious day and arranged favorable omens; bidding farewell to his kinsmen, he set out with the messenger and traveled toward the kingdom of Uśīnara.

On his way, he arrived at the city of Kanyākubja. In that city there was a medical apprentice who, hearing that the Great King of Physicians intended to travel to the kingdom of Ujjayinī, presented him with a harītakī fruit. Once they had exchanged words, they became fast friends, bound by an unbreakable bond.
He asked the youths, "King Candraprabha is afflicted with such an illness; why do you not provide medical treatment for him?
The youths replied:
"The illness from which that king suffers prevents him from sleeping; he should be treated with ghee (*sarpis*).
However, the king detests ghee and loves only wine, and his nature is violent and cruel.
If anyone speaks of ghee before the king, he immediately has their head cut off. Because these physicians know the king's wicked nature, they have all fled and dispersed, and none dare to treat him."
At that time, the King of Physicians replied to the youth:
"Dharma-brother!
You should know that for the sake of that king, I have blended medicinal paste with ghee such that it is indistinguishable from wine; you may come with me to him."
"If I manifest signs and provide instructions through skillful means, you may administer the medicine after careful consideration; you may remain here while I go out.
Once the King’s illness has been cured, I shall reward you, and I will also cause that king to grant you many gifts."
The youth said, "Very well.
Thereupon they set out together and gradually reached the royal city.
At that time, when King Pracaṇḍa heard that the King of Physicians had arrived, he thought to himself:
"Since this Jīvaka is both a prince and a king of physicians, one should receive him with grand ceremony and welcome him into the palace."

At that time, the king immediately ordered the city walls and gates to be magnificently adorned and the streets to be repaired and lined with ceremonial insignia; the king, the crown prince, the various officials, and the common people all went out to welcome him.
At that time, the King of Physicians, surrounded by a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people, entered the city together with them.
Then, after the King of Physicians had rested, King Candraprabha greeted him with a joyful countenance and, offering words of consolation, asked:
"I suffer from the disease of vigilance and cannot sleep; it has now become extremely severe, so you should provide a remedy for me."

The King of Physicians replied: “I shall treat you; however, I require medicinal herbs. These herbs are mostly found in various kingdoms and other cities. Only I recognize them, while others do not; or others may know them while I do not; or we both may know them. Some are nearby, while others are far away. I only pray, Great King!”
"Take this excellent mother-elephant and ride it as you please.
Then the king replied, "Excellent!"
"As you wish," the King commanded the elephant trainers, saying,
"If the Great Physician requires a noble and well-trained elephant for riding, you must not obstruct him at all."
He addressed the great ministers and the gatekeepers, saying:

"The King of Physicians may depart at dawn and return at noon, or depart at noon and arrive at night; whenever he rides his noble and excellent elephant to enter or exit, do not obstruct him in any way."
Having received the king’s command, the ministers and gatekeepers did not dare to detain or obstruct him.
At that time, the King of Physicians mounted the elephant-vehicle and traveled back and forth, sometimes during the day and sometimes at midnight without regularity, yet no one found it strange.
Then King Prabhāsa said to the King of Physicians,
"Why do you not provide medical treatment? He replied:
"Your Majesty, please bathe.
After the king had bathed, he was served food.
When the king had finished eating, Jīvaka addressed the king:
"I have now obtained the finest and most excellent wine from the kingdom of Magadha; Your Majesty may drink it.
At that time, King Candraprabha was filled with great joy and said, "Bring it here!"
At that time, the King of Physicians directed his attendant boy to manifest signs and instructions to fetch a certain amount; once the king had obtained the medicine, he immediately consumed it.
Having taken the medicine, the king then fell fast asleep.

At that time, having realized the king was asleep, the King of Physicians mounted an elephant and fled. When midnight arrived, the king awoke from his sleep; he immediately belched, and the smell of ghee reached him.
The king then became greatly incensed and commanded his attendants:
"Quickly seize and bind Upatiṣya; I shall have his head cut off!
At that time, the men all went to arrest him, but upon learning that he had already fled, they addressed the king, saying:
"He cannot be found now; he has fled far away.
The King grew even more enraged and summoned Piliyakkha, saying:
"Mount the great elephant Veḷuvana and pursue the physician at once! Bind him by the neck and bring him back; I shall have his head cut off."
"If you see him, he will understand his illusory arts; do not accept any medicinal substances he may give you.

At that time, having received the king's command, the flying crow mounted the foremost elephant and hurried to pursue him. Following the tracks of the elephant, he reached the Āmalaka grove, where he overtook him and called out, "Great Physician!"
The king called out, "Come quickly!
They replied, "Why must you be so urgent?"
"Come and eat this āmalaka fruit.
The flying bird replied, "I have received a command from the King: 'Do not accept anything given by one who understands the arts of illusion.'"
He replied, "You need not fear; since you are now hungry and thirsty, I shall take one *āmra* fruit and we shall each eat half.
The flying crow then thought:
"If we eat it together as one portion, how could there be any magic?

The King of Physicians took an *āmra* fruit and first ate half of it; he then concealed the remaining half within his fingernail, cut that half so that the medicine entered inside, and held it out to the flying crow.
The flying crow accepted the fruit and ate it immediately.

At that time, the crow had previously suffered from leprosy; once he had eaten the fruit, the medicine coincided perfectly with his ailment, so that he immediately experienced upward vomiting and downward diarrhea, unable to control himself.
The King of Physicians entered the village and addressed the villagers, saying:

"This is King Candraprabha’s foremost great elephant, as well as the noble female elephant Bhadrā and the messenger Kāka; you must look after them well and ensure they are not lost, for should any harm come to them, you will surely incur a heavy penalty."
Having given these instructions, he departed on his way. The men, following their orders, nursed the flying crow until its illness was cured.
Once the young physician had treated King Candraprabha and the king’s illness was healed, the flying crow returned to the king's presence. Seeing it, the king asked, "Where is the physician?"
The flying crow replied,
“What does Your Majesty intend to do with the physician once he is captured?
[The king said,] “When I have seized him, I shall cut off his head.”
He replied, "The King’s illness has now been cured, and my leprosy has likewise been removed; we ought to receive a reward, so for what reason should I be beheaded?
When the King heard these words:
“Excellent! Excellent!
Grant him a generous reward as you wish, to repay his great kindness.”
The flying crow immediately wrote an imperial edict to inform the King of Physicians, saying:
"You are a King of Physicians and deserve a heavy reward.
For what reason have you fled?"
"Please come at your convenience to receive the King's rewards.
Jīvaka sent a reply by messenger, stating:

"By the Emperor’s grace, my wealth and treasures are not lacking. If Your Majesty feels such joy toward me, I pray that whatever gifts you intend to bestow upon me be instead returned to that young physician."

At that time, the Great King bestowed much wealth and goods as rewards upon the physician’s apprentice; he also dispatched an envoy to deliver a large piece of fine cotton cloth, worth one hundred thousand taels of gold, to the Physician King.
When Jīvaka obtained the robe, he thought to himself:
"This is fit for the King to wear; who else is worthy to receive it?
Then he further thought:
"The Blessed One is the unsurpassed Great Teacher and my father; it is fitting that I offer this to him.
Thinking thus, he went to where the Buddha was and presented the cotton cloth to him.
When the World-Honored One saw the offering, he said to Ānanda, "You should use this cloth to make a cīvara.
Thereupon, Ānanda immediately cut and sewed it into the three robes for the Buddha; when there was a remainder, he informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You and Rāhula should wear these as appropriate.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda made two garments, one upper and one lower, for himself, and further made a *saṃkakṣikā* robe for Rāhula.

Furthermore, one should know the account of the causes and conditions concerning the Naga Elapatra. Formerly, above the palace of the Tuṣita Heaven, there was a written dialogue of the Buddha’s words, which in verse said:
"In what place is the king supreme?"
Attached to what is defiled, finding defilement even where there is none—what is it that makes one a fool?
Where does the fool grieve?
And where does the wise person rejoice?
"Who brings together those who are separated? Who is said to be blissful?
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had not appeared in the world, no one would have been able to receive the meaning of this verse, nor would there have been anyone to explain it.
When a Buddha appears in the world, there are those capable of receiving and upholding his teachings as well as understanding their meaning.

At that time, the Northern Yakṣa Heavenly King Vaśavartin had occasion to go to the Tuṣita Heaven palace; seeing this verse of inquiry, he was struck with wonder. He committed the text to memory but could not understand its meaning, so he carried it back to his own palace and inscribed it upon a wooden board.
At that time, in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, there was a long-resident nāga king named Elāpattra, who had long cherished the hope of when he might behold the World-Honored One appearing in the world.

At that time, that dragon king had a yakṣa friend named Golden Light who, having gone to the abode of the Northern Guardian Vaiśravaṇa, saw these written verses upon a wooden tablet; he immediately committed them to memory but was unable to understand their meaning.
Then this yakṣa took it to the kingdom of Takṣaśilā and presented it to the Nāga King Elāpattra, saying to him:

"Friend! This is the Buddha’s teaching; its profound meaning cannot be understood by anyone. You should commit these dharma verses to memory and, carrying this golden casket filled with gold, travel throughout all kingdoms, villages, towns, and cities, proclaiming these words:"
"If there be anyone capable of explaining the meaning of this verse, I shall grant them a golden casket as an offering.
If there is no one in that place who can understand it, you may say:
"This place has no people; it cannot be called a kingdom or a town."
Having uttered this proclamation, he proceeded once more to other places.

Upon hearing this, the Dragon King respectfully received the verses of the sūtra; he immediately transformed himself into the form of a young brahmin (*māṇava*), carrying a golden casket, and traveled through various kingdoms, cities, towns, and villages. Gradually arriving at the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, he stood at a crossroads within the city and proclaimed these words:
"All you people currently residing in this city, as well as the merchants and travelers coming from the four distant quarters, listen to my words!"
He then recited the verse:
"This riddle-verse was brought by me from the future; whoever can solve it shall be given this golden casket as an offering.

Thereupon, an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of people gathered like clouds. Among them were those of great intelligence and vast learning whose pride was aroused, as well as others who, upon hearing it, felt a sense of longing and were struck with extraordinary wonder; yet, there was no one capable of explaining it.
The Dragon King proclaimed:
"Since there are no wise people in Vārāṇasī, this is not a city.
Then all the brahmins and householders replied to the young brahmin (māṇava):
"Do not utter such a proclamation; this is not a city. Within this city of mine dwells a person of supreme wisdom who resides in an araṇya; wait for him to arrive, and he shall explain this meaning."
Question: "What is his name? Answer:
“His name is Nārada. “If that is so, I shall wait for him now.
At that time, Nārada, having gained faith, came from the forest retreat.
Then that emanated nāga stood before him and said, "Great Seer!
I have now brought these verses of inquiry here; if anyone can explain them, I shall offer a golden casket as an act of worship."
When Nalada had heard this, he committed it to memory and said to the young brahmin (māṇava),
"I shall explain it for you. He asked:
“When? He replied, “After twelve years.”
He said, "Great Seer! The time is far too long."
He spoke again, saying, "Six years. He replied:
“Too long. “Three years, one year, six months, three months, one month, half a month, or even seven days. He said:
"Great Seer! I shall wait for seven days," the transformed dragon replied.
“Great Seer, do as you wish!
I shall first offer my sincere devotion.
At that time, Nalada, who had previously been a close friend to the five bhikṣus, went to them and informed them:
"A certain young brahmin, carrying this verse and holding a golden casket, came to where I was and spoke these words:
'Whoever can explain this verse, to them I shall give this golden casket as an offering.'"
"However, those verses contain little text but great meaning; they are profoundly deep and difficult to understand.
What should we do now? The bhikṣu replied, "Narada!"
"You should go to the Buddha's presence and inquire [about this]. Nalada said,
"O virtuous one!"
"Has the Buddha appeared in the world? He replied,
"He has appeared."
He asked, "Where do you reside? He replied:
"In the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana. Upon hearing this, his heart was filled with great joy;

he immediately hurried to the place where the Bhagavān was. There he beheld him, his body resplendent with the thirty-two major marks, adorned with the eighty minor signs, and encircled by a halo extending one fathom. His brilliance surpassed a thousand suns, his form was like a mountain of jewels, and his physical appearance was so exquisite that his mind and spirit were utterly tranquil.

Having personally beheld him after twelve years of practicing meditative concentration, he gave rise to a sense of rare wonder, like a childless man suddenly obtaining a son, like a poor person finding a great treasure trove, like a crown prince succeeding to the royal throne, or like a sentient being who has long accumulated roots of virtue first seeing a Buddha; at that time, Nārada’s profound joy was exactly like this.
Gradually approaching the Buddha’s presence, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

The World-Honored One, according to his inclinations, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the distinctions of his faculties (*indriya*), taught him the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths as was appropriate for him, so that he might attain realization and understanding.

Having heard the essential points of the Dharma, he used the vajra-wisdom mallet to shatter the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Having realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) and perceived the true truths, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“World-Honored One!
"I wish to go forth within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha, to become a bhikṣu, and to firmly cultivate the holy life.
The Buddha said, "You previously promised to explain the meaning of the verses for the māṇava; you should first go there and speak for him, and only after that may you go forth."
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Although I have attained such wisdom and insight, I do not yet understand how to explain the meaning of these verses; since I lack eloquence, what benefit would there be in my going?"
The Buddha said:
"You may go there and speak these words:
'You should recite the verse of inquiry for me.'"
If he has spoken thus, one should answer in this way:
“The sixth king is supreme.
To become attached at the very place of defilement, to give rise to defilement where there is no defilement—this is called a fool.”
"The fool grieves over this; the wise person rejoices in this.
That which is beloved can be separated from; this indeed is called peace and happiness. If he should say this:
"I cannot understand it.
He then spoke further in verse:
"If a person hears these wondrous words, and having understood them, practices the supreme concentration;..."
"If one hears what is of incomplete meaning, that person does so out of negligence.
If he hears this verse, he further says:
"You have now spoken the Buddha’s words, yet I am not yet familiar with their meaning."
"Delusion prevents one from understanding; you should quickly act to dispel their doubts.
"While saying these words, you may use your nails to cut the leaf in front of them."
If one were to ask further,
"Has the World-Honored One appeared in the world?
one should reply:
"Already emerged. If one asks: "Where?"
He replied, "It is in the Deer Park.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Nalada went to where the young brahmin was and spoke these words:
“You may speak in verse.
He then replied with a verse, recounting the matter in detail, even reporting that the Buddha was in the Deer Park.
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"If I were to manifest my original dragon body before Nalada, he would surely despise me.

If I were to go to the World-Honored One in the form of a brahmin, there is a great brahmin in Vārāṇasī who understands the Three Vedas and the Four Treatises; if he were to see me in the guise of a young brahmin student (māṇava), they would all harbor contempt and say: 'The brahmins are born of a noble lineage; why do they humble themselves and approach the Gautama?'"
He further thought:
"If I go to the World-Honored One in my original dragon body, there will be many enemies of dragons who may create obstacles; I should now approach the World-Honored One as a Wheel-Turning King."

He immediately manifested as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), with the seven treasures leading the way and ninety-nine koṭis of soldiers and banners in attendance. A thousand sons surrounded him in the shape of a half-moon, each adorned with various kinds of precious objects.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable varieties of non-Buddhist śramaṇas and brahmacārins, a multitude of hundreds of thousands acting as attendants, who held a hundred-branched parasol over the king’s head; their majestic radiance was as brilliant as the sun and moon as they proceeded to the place where the World-Honored One was.

At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma before an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands. When the great multitude saw from afar the Wheel-Turning King surrounded by an army of immeasurable hundreds of thousands, they were struck with wonder and said to one another, "From where has this Wheel-Turning King come?"
"Never before seen in this world—
could it not be that the Brahmā kings and others have come to make offerings?
At that time, some among the people were filled with longing and, giving rise to greedy attachment, wished for the king’s body, each conceiving different thoughts.
The king went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed him, saying: "You foolish man!"

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, you received the Buddha’s prohibitory precepts but were unable to maintain them; consequently, you broke the precepts and experienced this inferior rebirth as a long-lived nāga.
Why now do you again give rise to a deceitful mind to mislead my assembly?
"You may now restore yourself to your original form.
The Dragon King addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"I am a dragon body with many enemies and malevolent beings; I fear that sentient beings may come together to harm me.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vajrapāṇi, saying, "You should protect this dragon king and not allow him to be harmed or distressed."
Then Vajrapāṇi, having received the words of the Blessed One, followed behind him to provide protection.

At that time, the Nāga King rose from his seat and went elsewhere, where he resumed his original form; his body had seven heads and was immeasurably vast and long. His head rested upon the city of Vārāṇasī, while his tail reached Takṣaśilā, a distance of two hundred *yojanas*. Due to his former evil karma, a great *uḷūka* tree grew upon each of his heads; shaken by the wind, they caused pus and blood to flow, which defiled his body with a foul and loathsome stench. Constantly, various insects, flies, and maggots covered his entire body, devouring him day and night, causing others to feel contempt and making it unpleasant for them to behold him.
At that time, the Dragon King approached the World-Honored One in his own true form, prostrated at His feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

When the great assembly saw this dragon body—so terrifying and fearsome that even those who had abandoned desire felt dread, let alone those who had not—they beheld its coarse and rough scales all split and cracked, with festering wounds from which pus flowed in various colors; its body was uneven with protrusions and depressions, and its form was so vast that how could they not be struck with alarm?
They all said to the Buddha,
"What is this object that has come before the World-Honored One?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:

"This was formerly the body of a Wheel-Turning King. You all have conceived feelings of attachment and delight toward his life, death, prosperity, and splendor; yet this is his original form, while that was a transformation. Due to the retribution of past evil karma, he now undergoes this suffering."
When those people had heard what the Buddha said, they each harbored grief and distress and remained silent. The Dragon King addressed him, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me a prophecy as to on which day I shall cast off this dragon body."
The Buddha told the Dragon King:

"In the future, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, a Buddha shall appear in the world named Maitreya, complete with the ten titles; he shall bestow upon you the prediction that you will escape your dragon body."

At that time, the Dragon King immediately wailed and wept before the Buddha; from the eyes of all his heads, tears issued forth simultaneously, forming fourteen rivers that flowed with a swift and startling torrent.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Cease for now! Do not weep so profusely with unceasing tears, causing the kingdom to fall into ruin."
The nāga addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In my original heart, I do not harm even the smallest life, much less damage a kingdom.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and suddenly vanished.
At that time, the great assembly was filled with doubt and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What evil karma did this dragon commit in his past lives?
Why does a tree grow upon his head and pus and blood flow from his body? [They spoke at length as described above.]
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:

"If you wish to know the causes and conditions of this dragon’s past lives and how he obtained this body of suffering through retribution—he himself created it and must experience it himself; there is no one else who can receive it on his behalf."
As explained at length above, the verse says:
"Even if a hundred eons should pass, The karma one has created does not perish;
When the causes and conditions converge, One must receive the retribution oneself."
“O bhikṣus! You should listen with a single-minded focus to what I shall say.

Long ago, in the past, during the Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa, fully endowed with the ten titles, who dwelt in dependence upon the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī.”

At that time, this nāga went forth into the Buddha’s Dharma to practice the path; he was well-versed in the Tripitaka and fully trained in the gates of meditative concentration. In a secluded place, beneath an udumbara tree, he practiced walking meditation to exert himself with diligence.

At that time, a leaf from a *khadira* tree struck his forehead, yet he endured it immediately. Later, at another time, his mind became weary and he arose from meditative concentration; rousing his mindfulness, he began to walk in meditation (*caṅkrama*). A leaf once again struck his forehead, causing him extreme pain. Giving rise to a mind of anger, he used both hands to break off a leaf from the tree, threw it to the ground, and spoke these words:
"What fault did the Buddha Kāśyapa see in an insentient object that he established this training rule (*śikṣāpada*), causing me to suffer such pain?"

"Because he destroyed the precepts with a mind of fierce poison and hatred, after his life ended, he fell among these nāgas; a great *uḷumpa* tree grew upon his head, from which pus and blood flowed out, attracting many insects, flies, and maggots that fed upon him, making the filth and stench extraordinary."
"Monks, what do you think?
Is this bhikṣu who was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, practiced in meditation, and destroyed the *hiṇṭāla* leaves anyone else?
It is none other than this nāga here."
"Monks, you should know that black karma brings black retribution, white karma brings white retribution, and mixed karma brings mixed retribution.
Therefore, you should abandon black and mixed karma and cultivate pure white karma. [The Buddha] then spoke verses as before.
At that time, the seer Nalada approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What I previously promised, I have now completed; I wish to go forth and train within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!"
"I permit you to go forth and practice the holy life.

Upon hearing these words, his hair and beard fell away naturally, as if he had been shaved seven days prior; dharma robes were upon his body and a water jar and alms bowl were in his hands, his dignified demeanor as solemn as that of a bhikṣu of a hundred years' standing.
The verse says:
"When the World-Honored One commanded him to come, his hair fell away and robes appeared upon his body;
his faculties immediately became tranquil, and everything was accomplished according to the Buddha’s will."
At that time, when the bhikṣus saw that Nalada had already gone forth, they did not know how to address him by name.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This bhikṣu’s family name is Kātyāyana; you should take this family name as his name."
Then the bhikṣus immediately addressed him by that name.
At that time, the Buddha said to Kātyāyana:
"In this world, there are two bases of reliance: [the Dharma and the Saṃgha]."
That is to say, there are the views of existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, being bound by the fetters of afflictions, one constantly adheres to these two views; with afflictions not eliminated, one perpetually harbors pride, arising together with suffering and perishing along with suffering.
"You, Kātyāyana! Through the absence of doubt and hesitation, wisdom has arisen within you, and right view has become manifest just as it was seen by the Buddha. Why is this?"
Having correctly known and seen the phenomena of arising in the world, the worldly adherence to the view of non-existence no longer arises;
having correctly known and seen the phenomena of cessation in the world, the worldly adherence to the view of existence no longer arises.
Kātyāyana! Do not cling to these two extremes. The Tathāgata always teaches the Dharma by relying on the Middle Way, which is:

because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. That is to say: conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is grasping; conditioned by grasping is becoming; conditioned by becoming is birth; and conditioned by birth arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering comes into being through continuous succession.

Because this does not exist, that does not exist; because this ceases, that ceases. That is to say: because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; because volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases; because consciousness ceases, name-and-form cease; because name-and-form cease, the six sense bases cease; because the six sense bases cease, contact ceases; because contact ceases, feeling ceases; because feeling ceases, craving ceases; because craving ceases, clinging ceases; because clinging ceases, existence ceases; because existence ceases, birth ceases; because birth ceases, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering is utterly dispersed and extinguished.

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, Kātyāyana, while still seated, perceived through insight the cycle of birth and death within the five destinies, as well as the conditioned nature of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. His mind opened and his intellect awakened; he severed all afflictions and realized the fruit of Arhatship, endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations. He attained true knowledge, realizing:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."

The mind is without obstruction, like a hand waving through space; whether cut by a blade or smeared with incense, neither love nor hatred arises; viewing gold and earth as equal and without distinction, one renounces all fame and profit; thus, Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas pay him complete respect.
Because the Buddha bestowed upon him the name Kātyāyana, from that time forth he was known as Mahākātyāyana.

At that time, many people in the kingdom of Uśīnara died of pestilence; funeral biers followed one another and corpses covered the fields, so that both the king and the people were filled with grief and distress.
The minister said to the king:
"Your Majesty should now cultivate various meritorious deeds. Or it is said:
"Make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas," or say:
"One may perform incantations and medicinal rites."

Having heard this deliberation, the king offered prayers and performed all the rites for averting calamities, hoping to eliminate the pestilence and bring peace to the people. He then addressed the gatekeepers, saying:
"You must know that if any śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others should enter the city who are able to eliminate the pestilence, you shall immediately inform me."
At that time, the Tathāgata, the Great Teacher, knowing that many people in this land were afflicted by pestilence and that countless had perished, desired to save and have compassion for them.
It is the constant law of the Unsurpassed World-Honored One that there is nothing in the world he does not hear or see;
he constantly gives rise to great compassion to benefit all beings, being the foremost among those who provide protection and the most heroic and valiant.
Without dualistic speech, abiding in concentration and wisdom, they manifest the three types of supernormal knowledge; they skillfully cultivate the three trainings and harmonize the three karmas;
they cross the four torrents and establish themselves in the four bases of psychic power; throughout the long night, they practice the four means of attraction;
they abandon the five hindrances, distance themselves from the five factors, and transcend the five paths; their six sense faculties are complete, and they fulfill the six perfections.

Perfected, he universally bestows the seven riches and opens the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment; detached from the eight worldly dharmas, he reveals the path of the eightfold rightness;
having forever severed the nine fetters, he is luminously proficient in the nine meditative absorptions; filled with the ten powers, his fame resounds throughout the ten directions;
among all those who possess mastery, he is most preeminent; having attained fearlessness in the Dharma, he subdues the hosts of Māra and his enemies, shaking the great thunder.
He utters the lion’s roar and, throughout the six periods of day and night, constantly observes the world with the Buddha-eye:
who is increasing?
Who is declining?
Who has encountered suffering and calamity?
Who is heading toward the evil realms?
Who is mired in the quagmire of desire?
Who is capable of receiving transformation?

By what skillful means can they be rescued and delivered so that those who lack the wealth of the noble attain the wealth of the noble; so that the cataracts of ignorance are shattered by the medicinal collyrium of wisdom; so that those without roots of goodness may plant them, and those with roots of goodness may cause them to further increase; and so that they are placed upon the path of humans and devas, proceeding safely and without hindrance toward the city of Nirvana?
As it is said: "Even if the tide of the great ocean Should ever miss its appointed time;
The Buddha, regarding those he transforms, Never fails to deliver them at the proper moment."
Just as a mother has an only son and constantly protects his life,
the Buddha’s compassionate concern for those he transforms exceeds even that.
The Buddha’s loving-kindness toward all sentient beings never abandons them.
"Thinking to rescue them from their suffering and hardship, as a mother cow follows her calf," the Buddha had this thought:
"Who is capable of taming King Mahātejas of the country of Oḍḍiyāna, along with his harem, court ladies, and the common people?"
The Blessed One, perceiving that the bhikṣu Mahākātyāyana was capable of subduing them, immediately said to him:
"Mahākātyāyana! You should go and observe the city of Uśīnara, so that King Prabhāsa, the ladies of his court, and all the common people may attain peace and happiness."
The Venerable One replied to the Buddha, "As the World-Honored One has instructed.

Then, when morning dawned, the Venerable One took up his robes and bowl and entered Vārāṇasī to wander for alms in succession. Having finished his meal, he took up his robes and bowl and, together with five hundred bhikṣus, set out for the country of Uśīnara, passing through the country of Caṇpaka on the way.

At that time, there was a brahmin in this city who was an old friend of the Venerable One; he had a daughter whose appearance was upright and whose beauty was peerless, her hair being so lustrous and radiant that it had no equal, and for this reason she was named "Wondrous Hair" (Sunanda).
A musician came from the south; seeing that the woman Miāofa had exceptionally beautiful hair, he went to the brahmin and said:
"O Great Brahmin!..."
"I require this girl's hair; you may sell it to me for a price of one thousand gold coins.
The Brahmin replied, "According to the law of the Brahmins, one should not sell one's hair. Why do you now speak such unrighteous words?"
His wish not being fulfilled, he departed in silence.

Later, at another time, his father passed away. When his mother heard that the noble Mahākātyāyana, together with five hundred followers, had arrived in this country and was staying not far away, she was filled with grief and sorrow because her husband had recently died.
Hearing that the Venerable One had arrived, she grew even more distressed, resting with her cheek pressed against her palm.
Seeing her mother sorrowful, the girl Mālinī asked her the reason:
"Mother, for what reason do you now sit with your cheek pressed against your palm, harboring such grief?"
The mother said, "Noble Mahākātyāyana! You were a close friend of my late husband.
Now that you have come here, because your father has passed away and our family is impoverished, I am unable to provide even a single offering; for this reason, I am filled with grief."
The girl said, "If that is so, let a musician buy my hair for a price of one thousand coins; you may take that money to provide for your offerings.
My hair will grow back again later; I pray you, Mother, do not worry."
When the mother heard these words, she knew he possessed pure faith; she went to the man who delighted in pleasure and said to him:
"O worthy one! You previously sought to purchase my daughter’s hair for a price of a thousand coins; if you truly require it, you may pay back that former price."
He replied, "Old mother!
At that time we required this hair, but now it is of no use; if you wish to sell it, you may take half the price."
He replied, "As you wish," and immediately paid the price and took the hair away with him.
At that time, the Venerable One traveled to that city and stayed in a secluded place with a settled mind. The Brahmin’s wife approached the Venerable One, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Noble One!..."
"Is your journey safe?
My husband was acquainted with you, Venerable Sir, during his lifetime; I would be grateful if you would show me your compassion and accept my humble invitation for tomorrow at noon.
The Venerable replied:
"My assembly is extremely large; how could we possibly save them all?
He asked, "O Noble One!"
“How many people are there?
He replied, “There are five hundred.”
He replied, "Very well! The Venerable remained silent.

At that time, the old woman, knowing she had been invited, prostrated at his feet and departed. She immediately prepared various offerings within her home; when the clear morning dawned, she spread out mats and seats, set out jars of pure water, and went to inform him:
"The meal is ready; may the Noble One know the time."
Then, at the time for the morning meal, the Venerable One took up his robe and bowl and, accompanied by five hundred people, went to the woman’s house and sat down upon a seat.

Seeing that they were seated, the old mother personally served them various kinds of excellent food and drink with her own hands. When they had finished eating, chewed their tooth-sticks, rinsed their mouths, and set aside their bowls, she took a small mat and sat down to listen to the teaching of the Dharma.
The Venerable One, wishing to preach the Dharma for him, asked:
"Where is your daughter Māṣa now? He replied:
"Her appearance was disheveled, so I did not dare come at once.

Although an Arhat does not know unless he observes, he immediately concentrated his mind and observed the girl's heart; knowing it to be extremely pure and virtuous, he said, "That girl’s heart is good; you may summon her here."
He immediately ordered her to leave the room and go to the Venerable One; with a heart of profound reverence, she prostrated at the Venerable One’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
Her mother said, “This is a beautiful lock of hair; though I know it is a trivial thing, I request that you accept it as a daughter for the Venerable One.”
The mother spoke again with urgency:
"Since we are related by blood, there must be matters concerning our kinship that require consultation; to whom does this daughter now wish to be given?"

The Venerable replied, “We who have left the household life should not inquire about worldly matters; nevertheless, this girl shall certainly obtain five hundred sets each of internal and external ornaments and jewelry, and five large villages shall be granted as her fief.”
The mother said, "I am of a poor household; who would grant such an excellent thing to me?
The Venerable One replied:

"Do not speak such words. This woman’s merit is lofty and far-reaching; because she has offered worship with a profound and pure mind to this supreme field of merit, she will surely obtain this extraordinary retribution. Do not harbor grief or distress."
The mother remained silent.

The Venerable One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the mother and daughter with the teaching of the sublime Dharma; having finished speaking, he rose from his seat and departed, traveling by stages until he reached the country of Uśīnara.
As soon as he entered the city, all calamities and afflictions were for the most part eliminated.
At that time, the gatekeeper went to inform the king, saying:
"Does Your Majesty know this?"
There were five hundred men of extraordinary appearance; as soon as they entered the city, all calamities and afflictions were for the most part extinguished.
The King said, "This is truly a virtuous matter; offerings should be presented to them."
Then the brahmins came and said to the king:

"We have labored with great hardship day and night; it is through our power that this calamity has been half-eliminated. Before long, it shall be entirely eradicated. For what reason do you now say it is due to that bhikṣu?"
The bhikṣus offered their blessings to the king, saying,
"May you be free from illness and enjoy long life!
Having done so, they took their leave of the king and departed.
The king said to his ministers:
"The gatekeepers informed me:
'There were five hundred men of extraordinary appearance; as soon as they entered the city, all calamities and epidemics were for the most part eradicated.'"

The Brahmins said, "We have exerted ourselves with extreme hardship day and night; it is through our power that these calamities and obstacles have been half-eliminated. Before long, they shall all be completely eradicated, not by anyone else."
"I do not know now whose power this is.

You all should take the bhikṣus and the brahmins to the elephant stable; in that impure place, give them coarse rice cakes with vinegar-water to eat together. When they have finished eating and are departing, both parties should ask:
'How was the food provided by the Great King today?'"
The ministers replied to the king, "It shall be done accordingly.
They immediately prepared food in the elephant stable as instructed. When the elephants had finished eating and were leaving, the gatekeeper first asked the brahmin:
“How was the food today at the King’s offering that you have received, sirs?
They became greatly incensed and cried out in a loud voice:
“We observe this as contrary to the Dharma; this poor king has provided only coarse cakes and foul gruel with vinegar and water to the Brahmins—what merit can there be in such a thing?”
Having heard this, the disciple remained silent.
After he had departed, another bhikṣu arrived and asked: "Noble one!"
"What was the flavor like of the offerings provided by the king?
He replied, "O worthy one!"
"What has been bestowed by a donor should be consumed by the recipient; it is sufficient to sustain the body throughout the day and night.
At that time, the gatekeeper entered, saw the king, and reported both accounts in detail. Having heard this, the king again addressed his minister, saying:
"You should now once more prepare fine food in a clean place within the elephant stables, and then ask him the same question as before."
He immediately prepared excellent seats in a clean place and respectfully offered fine food. As he was about to depart, he asked the same question as before, to which the brāhmaṇa replied:
"O sir!..."
"It is as if a consecrated Kṣatriya great king had prepared such exquisite food; one would obtain immeasurable merit.
The disciple replied, "The culinary affairs of the royal palace are difficult to standardize; why did you not show contempt for them today?"
He then departed in silence.
Next, a bhikṣu arrived, and when questioned, he answered as before.
A gatekeeper entered, saw this, and reported the matter to the king:

The king issued another command, and as it was with the elephant stables, so it was with the horse stables; the questions and answers regarding the pure and the impure, the refined and the coarse, were similar.
Having heard these words, the king thought to himself:
"The community of bhikṣus is the true field of merit, not the brahmins."

He then conceived deep faith and immediately went to the place where Mahākātyāyana was, prostrated at his feet, and sat down. At that time, the Venerable One taught the Dharma to the king, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, after which he remained silent.
The king again prostrated at his feet and said:
"Venerable One!
I pray that you and the assembly of noble ones will, out of compassion, come to my palace tomorrow to accept a meal of coarse food."
The Venerable One gave his silent consent.

Having seen that he had accepted, the king paid his respects and departed. That very night, he prepared exquisite food; having risen at dawn, he arranged the seats and set out pure water vessels. He then sent a messenger to inform the Venerable One:
"The meal is ready; may the Noble One know it is time."
At that time, during the first part of the day, the Venerable One took up his robes and bowl and, accompanied by the bhikṣus, went to the place where food was being served and took his seat.

The king ordered musicians to play various musical instruments, and songs and dances broke out all at once. The Venerable One and the assembly of monks sat upright with composed countenances, having withdrawn their sense faculties. When the sound of the drums and music ceased, the king asked the Venerable One:
"How were the pipes and music to listen to?"
The Venerable One replied:
"Great King! Only those who have seen and heard shall know good and evil."
The King said,
"While one might not know the internal darkness of the sense faculties, why is it that when the mind races toward external objects, one does not hear or see?
Desiring to make the King fully comprehend this matter, the Venerable One employed a skillful means and addressed him, saying:
“O King! Is there currently anyone who ought to be executed?
The king replied:
"What do you require? He replied:

"Your Majesty may fill a bowl to the brim with oil and place it within his hands, then have a man follow behind him brandishing a sword to frighten him, but you must not cause him harm; then report back, saying:"
"If even a single drop of oil falls upon the ground, I shall cut off your head.
He was then allowed to walk about freely; furthermore, many courtesans were placed before him as they performed various kinds of music. Upon returning to this spot, he asked the oil-carrier:
"Were the beauty of the women and the music pleasing?"
"Only then will genuine faith arise within me.
Having heard this instruction, the king performed everything exactly as told, in due order.
When the man arrived, he asked:
“Are the beauty, appearance, and music excellent?
He replied, “Great King!”
"Only those who see and hear it will know what is good and what is bad.
The King said,
"Since you possess eyes and ears, why do you not see and hear it?"
He replied: "Great King!

If even a single drop of oil from my bowl were to fall, that man wielding the sword would surely behead me and leave my corpse lying across the ground. At such a time, fearing the bowl might tip over and fearing my head might fall to the earth, I would have carried it back with single-minded devotion and great hardship; how would I have had the leisure to observe the beauty of the lady’s appearance or the quality of her singing and dancing?"
The king then remained silent and speechless.
The Venerable One asked:
"Did Your Majesty see it?"
The king said, “I have seen it.
“Great King! [he continued.]

This person, fearing the great suffering that might befall them for the sake of a single lifetime’s life, maintains earnest and correct mindfulness, refrains from indulgence, and well protects themselves.

How much more so should I, a bhikṣu, who has renounced all song and dance, considering these to be causes of suffering throughout many lifetimes; how could I ever allow myself to again desire to see or hear them?
The King observed the oil bowl and scrutinized the situation; he conceived a redoubled sense of reverence toward the Venerable One.

At that time, the Crown Prince, the various kings, the women of the inner palace, and the commoners and citizens all came to join in the celebration, making offerings of various kinds of superior food to the Bhikṣu.
When the assembly had finished eating, chewed their tooth-sticks, rinsed their mouths, and cleared away the bowls, the king sat on a low seat before the Venerable One and asked him:
"Is there perhaps another place where such exquisite food and drink are offered to five hundred noble ones as is given to us?"

The Venerable One said, "Your Majesty is the sovereign of the kingdom who governs a hundred cities; whatever you think of comes to you, lacking for nothing. Thus, it is no wonder that you provide superior food and drink for five hundred monks."

When I came from a certain village yesterday, there was a young girl in a household who, out of resentment toward her own poverty, cut off her own hair and sold it for five hundred gold coins. She then prepared a magnificent meal as an offering of respect for my assembly; this is truly rare.
Upon hearing these words, the king thought to himself:
"The price of that woman's hair is five hundred [pieces of gold]; she is difficult to compare with even the celestial maidens. I must examine closely who she is."
"I shall take it; however, as the Venerable One’s virtue is so high, it would be difficult to pose questions to him.
He then commanded a messenger, saying:

"You may now go and follow the path by which the Venerable One came. In which village or town was there a woman who sold her hair for five hundred gold coins to provide a meal offering for the Venerable Mahākātyāyana?"
"Whose daughter is she?
I must see her. Knowing the king's mind, the messenger set out to inquire, traveling from place to place until he eventually reached the city of Kanyakubja.

Having arrived in the city, he searched everywhere until he learned its location; as it happened to be exactly where he had been seeking, he rested for a moment and then went to the brahmin’s house, standing at the gate. Seeing his mother come out, he asked, "Are you well?"
The mother then asked,
"Virtuous one, having come here now, what do you seek? He replied:
"I desire her exquisite hair for the sake of a marriage. He asked, "For whom?"
He replied, "She has been taken as the queen of King Candraprabha.
His mother said:
"Excellent! However, the bride-price is not small; I fear the matter will not succeed.
The messenger said:
“How much wealth does he possess?

The mother replied, “His inner ornaments number five hundred, and his outer necklaces are likewise; he holds five great villages as his fief. To him who obtains these things, I shall give my daughter.”
Having heard this, the messenger hurried back to report to the king, saying: "Great King!
I have found the girl."
The king asked,
"What were you saying together? He replied:
"I shall inform my mother that I have taken her as queen.
The king asked,
"Did she demand a bride-price?"
The messenger then related the matter in full.
Having heard the report, the king said:
"Give him whatever he requests, however much it may be."

The messenger, bearing the king’s command, returned to the girl’s family; they gave their mutual consent, selected an auspicious day, and prepared the ceremonial rites on a grand scale. With a vast army arrayed in full splendor with banners and drums, he set out from the city of Caṇpā and proceeded toward the kingdom of Ujjayinī.

Once she had entered the city, on that very day all pestilences were entirely eliminated; the realm became peaceful and the people lived in security and happiness. Because of this auspicious response, they collectively named her Lady Anle (Peaceful Bliss).
