At that time, King Caṇḍapradyota resided in the city of Ujjayinī. There was a householder who, not long after marrying his wife, left her at their home while he himself went abroad with merchandise to engage in trade.

After her husband had departed, the wife indulged herself in food and clothing; her afflictions grew intense, and she eventually ascended the pavilion to gaze upon men everywhere, looking out ceaselessly day after day.

Later, at another time, King Candraprabha was passing by the house riding upon a magnificent fragrant elephant. Upon seeing him, the woman conceived a mind of lustful attachment and cast a flower garland from afar toward the king, where it landed upon his shoulder.
The king immediately looked up and saw a young girl whose countenance was upright and whose radiance was transcendent; she glanced to her left and right, considering herself peerless.
Having seen her, the king knew that her mind was filled with passion, and he addressed her, saying: "Young girl!
"If you have such affection for me, why do you not come out for a moment?
She replied, "I am but a young wife and have no means of leaving; if Your Majesty has such concern for me, you may deign to visit my humble abode."
The king’s mind was so captivated that he could not advance; he immediately dismounted from his elephant and entered her residence. Once his joy was fully satisfied, she conceived.
There are five qualities of a wise woman:
first, she knows whether a man has lustful intent or lacks it.
2. Knowledge of the seasonal conditions;
3. Knowledge of the time of conception and that it is the fetus of such-and-such a person;
4. Knowledge of whether it is male;
5. Knowing that it was a girl, he then addressed the king, saying:
"Does Your Majesty know this now? [That it is a girl.]”
"I am already pregnant.
At that time, the king immediately gave her a necklace of superior pearls and told her:
"If you give birth to a daughter, you may keep it for yourself; if it is a son, give this necklace to him and send him to me."
The woman respectfully assented, and the king departed.
After several months had passed, the signs of pregnancy became manifest on her exterior. Then, a letter arrived from her former husband, informing her:
"May you be at peace; I expect to arrive in my native land before long."
Upon hearing this, the woman was filled with great sorrow and sent a messenger to inform the king:
"I am already pregnant; now that my former husband is about to arrive, what should I do?"
The king sent a messenger, saying:
"You may set your mind at ease; I have a skillful means to ensure that he does not come.
The woman then remained silent.
The king sent him a letter, saying:
"I now require such-and-such items; you may travel far to a certain place to seek them and bring them back.
Having traveled a great distance, a full year passed. When the woman’s months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose appearance was so handsome as to be rare for the age.

As dawn was about to break, she filled her mouth with clarified butter and honey; she placed soft cotton inside a chest, cradled the child within it, and covered it entirely with fine white woolen cloth, lacing it over with strings of pearls. She sealed the chest tightly, fastened it securely with crimson cords, and marked it with a seal of purple mineral pigment.

She then instructed a maidservant, saying: "Take this chest to the king’s gate. Wipe a platform clean and place the chest upon it; then set a lamp nearby and stay there. When someone comes to take it away, you may return."
The messenger acted according to his instructions.
At that time, a herd of oxen came out along the road; when they reached the location of the chest, they surrounded it and would not proceed.
King Candraprabha and Queen Sukhā, observing from atop a high tower that the herd of oxen was standing encircling the chest, commanded a messenger, saying:
"Look outside the gate; for what reason is this herd of oxen gathered and standing there?
The messenger replied, "At the gate there is a chest, bound with crimson cords and sealed with purple mineral lacquer."
The king said, "Bring her here at once.
The lady addressed the king:
"The King should give me whatever is within the chest.
The King said, "As you wish."
When the messenger arrived at the king’s presence carrying the casket, he opened the seal and beheld the pearl necklace as well as the infant.
Recognizing the pearl necklace, the king declared, "This is my son."
He embraced the child and handed him to the lady, saying, "This is your son.
Having received him, the lady immediately offered this prayer of blessing:
"May my son live long!
Now, what name shall we give this child?
The king said:
"A child of merit has been protected by a cow;
he should be named Gopāla.
Furthermore, as Queen Kṣemā personally nurtured him, she too changed her name to Gopāmātā, "Mother of Gopāla."

At that time, in the north, there was a king of Takṣaśilā named Parantapa; the kingdom he governed was peaceful, secure, and prosperous, with a flourishing population—as described at length elsewhere—and its gardens and trees were always in bloom with fruit. Rain fell in season, and alms were easily obtained.
Later, on another occasion, while the king was enjoying himself at will upon a high tower together with his ministers, he addressed them, saying:
"Is there any other kingdom that resembles my own realm in its abundance, prosperity, and security?"
The minister replied:

"There is a king of Uśīnara named Caṇḍapradyota; his realm is likewise prosperous, peaceful, and secure, with flowers and fruits appearing without end, no different from here. A merchant from there has arrived at this place."
The king sent for him, and when he arrived, the king questioned him in detail. Upon hearing of his great wealth and prosperity, the king conceived a sense of envy and said to his ministers:
"Gentlemen, prepare the troops; I wish to wage war against him."

The king himself then personally marshaled his fourfold army and marched toward the kingdom of Uśīnara, gradually reaching that city; he plundered it without restraint and acted with such irrational cruelty that the people could no longer endure life.

When King Prabhāsa heard that the bandits had arrived, he likewise arrayed his fourfold army and went forth to engage them in battle; however, as Prabhāsa was no match for them, his troops were scattered, and he fled on a single horse toward another place.

Arriving at a desolate wilderness, he saw a plowman named Vardhana who was personally engaged in plowing. Observing that the man’s countenance was different from that of others, the king immediately asked him:
"You are a brave and sturdy youth; have you ever heard it said that King Maṇicūḍa fought with King Candraprabha, and that Candraprabha was utterly defeated? Do you know of this matter?"
He replied, "I have heard this matter, but I do not yet know whether it is true or false.
He [the other] replied:
"It is not false.

The plowman, moreover, did not know that this man was King Candraprabha, so he replied to him, "King Candraprabha resides in his own kingdom, while this man is but a traveler who has been humiliated and forced to flee everywhere; what use are ministers and generals to him?"
"O King, had you previously taken me as your own fang and claw, I would have long ago bound the neck of Pūrṇabhadra with a stout rope and dragged him into the city.
Before he had finished speaking, his wife arrived bringing food in a vessel made of sewn leaves. As the husband washed his hands, intending to eat, he looked toward the king and said:
"Noble and valiant man, judging by your appearance, you seem to be hungry. I am but a poor man with this coarse meal; I hope you will not disdain it, but will partake of its flavor with me."
At that time, King Pradyota immediately thought to himself, "If I do not eat, I shall perish of hunger.

He then dismounted from his vehicle and took the seat upon the saddle-cloth; having washed his hands and feet, he ate together with him in one place. His wife then poured wine from a cracked-rimmed earthen bowl and made him drink it.
The king thought to himself:
"Although I know the cup is chipped, I shall drink from it at the unchipped portion.
The king was possessed of wise strategy and well-versed in the affairs of his time; he reflected further, saying:

"If I were to drink from the unbroken part, I fear that person might think I am treating them with contempt; it would be better for me now to drink from the broken part, so as to cause him to feel deep affection for me."
At that time, the plowman first drank from the broken vessel himself to ward off the poison, then passed it to the king; once the king had received it, he drank from the same broken vessel.
The farmer thought to himself:
"This great man’s heart knows no barriers; he drinks from the same well as I do when my supply is low. I ought now to feel deep reverence for him, so that our friendship may endure and not be lost."
Having reflected thus, he said to his wife: "O fair lady!

This great man is my dear, trusted, and intimate friend. You should take him to our former humble home, anoint his body with oil, bathe him with warm water, provide him with food and drink, and let the horse drink its fill and graze on water and grass as it pleases."
The wife then took him back home and did everything exactly as he had said; they were in perfect harmony, and she provided him with all his necessities.
At that time, King Pūrṇavijaya had a small subordinate kingdom called Kāśa, which came to plunder and exploit the common people.
Then the ministers wrote a letter to inform the king, detailing the matter in full, and requested that he reflect well upon it. At the end of the letter, they composed a verse, saying:
"Just as Your Majesty diligently subdued other kingdoms, So too should you diligently protect your own realm."
At that time, after King Parākrama had read the letter, he thought to himself:

"If I were to lead my army back to my own country, everyone would say that I have been defeated by the enemy and fled back to my capital. It would be best for me now to establish friendly relations with him before returning to my former residence."
He then sent Śraddhā to report to King Candraprabha: "My friend! That which has already passed cannot be pursued;

you should come out for a moment, for I long to see you. As for all other matters of victory or defeat, there is no need to discuss them. I hope we may sit close together with our robes intertwined to express our mutual trust, as we did in the past, before I return to my own city."
Having received his message, the ministers deliberated together:
"If we report to the King that [the horse] is not here, he will certainly deceive us; we should devise a skillful means to answer according to the current situation."
He composed a letter in reply, saying:

"My friend! Since you have understood that the contents of this sealed letter are sincere and the depth of my feelings profound, and since the matter is indeed as it is and you can be free from hesitation, though the two nations are gathered together and each harbors doubts, even if this opposes your intentions, I have no leisure to go forth."
"However, this prince is named Go-pāla; let him come out to meet you so that we may express our mutual joy and he may go or stay as he pleases.
At that time, Go-pāla was immediately sent out to see Pūrṇajit. Once their joyful intentions were fully shared, the military siege was lifted, and the banners were turned back toward his own kingdom.
At that time, King Pracaṇḍa and his ministers deliberated together, saying:
"The enemy forces from other lands have already dispersed like rain; we must urgently seek out our own king."
Cavalry messengers were dispatched in all directions, both far and near, to search for him.
When King Candraprabha heard that Pūrṇajaya had already withdrawn his troops and departed, he addressed the plowman Vardhaka, saying:
"I am now free from fear; I bid you farewell and shall return home."
"If you enter the city, you should pass by my house. He replied, "Great man!"
“I am not even familiar with your honorable name; how shall I visit your residence at a later time?
The King replied, “Who, indeed, does not know the house where I dwell?”
"When you enter the city, you should ask thus:
'Where is the house of the man with many horses?
" Having given this instruction, he spurred his horse and proceeded until he reached the main gate of the city, where he addressed the gatekeeper, saying:
"You should know now that if anyone comes to inquire about the House of Many Horses, you may bring them to see me.
Having said this, he entered the palace.
Later, on another occasion, there was a great festival in the city of Uśīnara, and people from far and near all flocked to the city.
Then the husband and wife of the plowman said to their husband:
"Today there is a great festival in the city; we shall now go to see the gathered crowds, and on that occasion, we will also inquire about the house of the man with many horses."
The husband said,
"O fair-faced one! How can it be said that all noble gentlemen possess such reality?"
One may encounter such a person in three circumstances:

first, when defeated in battle by another; second, when deceived and humiliated by another; and third, when, as a ruler, one loses both family and state. Beyond these, how else could one encounter them?
The wife said,

He spoke again, saying:

He replied, "I have come specifically to seek an audience.

The King commanded the women of the inner court, saying:
"These are my parents. Whatever they require—food, drink, clothing, bedding, or male and female servants—you must provide it all."

He replied, "Great King! I am a plowman;

The king said, "You need only attend the assembly; I shall cause him to show you respect.

The minister said, "A certain high official has now passed away; his wives, concubines, slaves, and servants remain in his residence.
The king said:
“Please grant this house, my wife and children, along with all other property to Vaḍḍha.
Having obtained the house, he asked Vaḍḍha,
“Have you been well lately?”
He replied, “The members of my household treat me with contempt because I am a plowman.
The king said:
"If it be so, when you are bathing, I shall send for you, and you must say:
'Wait until I have finished my bath; then I shall go to see the king.'"
Vardhana replied, "How could I possibly disobey the Great King's command? The King said:
"This was my instruction; truly, there is no fault in this.
Furthermore, when you wish to eat, I shall send a messenger to summon you, and you should reply:
'Wait until I have finished eating; I shall go to see you of my own accord.'"
"When it is time for you to eat, I shall come to your residence and dine with you.
He replied, "Great King!"
"How could I ever presume to eat together with the King?
The King said, "There is no fault in my granting permission; when one acts in this manner, all show him respect."
Upon hearing the command, Upacāra went to the palace.
Just as he was washing himself, the King sent a messenger to summon him, saying:
"There is an urgent matter; you must come at once."
When the messenger arrived to deliver the message, Saṃpāka replied,
"Wait until I have finished bathing before you go."

After the messenger had departed, the people within the residence said to one another, "Now this master of the house has defied the royal command; by giving rise to such arrogance, he has invited calamity upon himself."
They also said to one another:
"It is not that those of noble lineage become arrogant and haughty merely because they have attained power for a short time.
The family members further said:
"Sisters, you should know!
All who ascend to heights must inevitably fall. This man will surely meet execution by the king this very day; the matter will not be delayed.
Having finished bathing and grooming, he did not go to the king's appointment, but instead went directly to eat.
The king again sent a messenger with the message:
"There is business; you should come at once.
Although he heard the king's command, he replied:
"Go now; you may depart only after you have finished eating.
The messenger went and reported this to the king. Having heard it, the king himself mounted a great elephant and went to that residence, where he asked, "Bhandu!"
"Do you wish to eat now?
He replied, "I wish to eat."
The king asked, "Did you not invite me? They replied:
"Please, come and take your meal.
The people within the residence said to one another,
"Our patriarch’s conversation with the king was as casual as if they were equals."
Each gave rise to a sense of wonder and looked up at one another.
The king then immediately washed his hands and feet and ate together with them in one place. When the residents of the house saw this, they were all struck with fear and said to one another:
"We have previously held these men in contempt as mere plowmen; yet now we see them eating together with the king."
They further deliberated together, saying:
"What do we know of how to proceed?

Since the King has shared a meal with us, this matter must not be treated lightly. From now on, we should not show him disrespect; if we fail to show him reverence, we will certainly invite calamity."
The assembly agreed with his words and together felt a sense of awe and reverence.
At another time, the king asked again: "Is it well?"
He replied, “There is a high minister who is a relative of the king; he constantly insults and reviles me—how could there be anything good about him?
The king said:
"If I were to speak further, it would lead to obstruction; as for whether to proceed or retreat, you should know that for yourself.
He replied, "As for what I have done, I pray the King will not hold me accountable."
The King said, "I have no cause for reproach.
On another occasion, as Vaḍḍha was traveling along the road, he saw two boys who were poor and had no relatives; they were playing by the way with a slingshot and pellets.
At that time, a maidservant passed by nearby carrying a water jar on her head.
One boy said, "I shall shoot a dry pellet at the jar to make a hole.
Another person then said:
"It is not particularly remarkable that one shoots a dry ball to make a hole; it is truly a marvelous feat to shoot a wet ball and seal that hole.
Having thus deliberated together, he immediately shot a dry ball to create a hole, and then shot a wet ball to seal it so that it closed.
At that time, Vaḍḍha saw the matter from afar; a sense of wonder arose in him, and he thought to himself:
"I can have these two young boys assist me in subduing those royal kinsmen and clearing away their insults."
He asked the two boys, "Whose sons are you? They replied:
"I have no kinsmen; I sustain my life according to the circumstances.
He replied, "If that is so, you may live together with me under my care."
He replied, "As you command.
Once he had been accepted into the community, [the Master] asked him:
"What more shall I do? He replied, "You need only practice archery;
later, if you see someone quarreling with me, you should take a pellet smeared with filth and shoot it into their mouth."
He replied, "I can.
Later, when he was engaged in a dispute with a relative of that king, the youth used a foul pellet to strike him from a distance into his mouth.
He immediately spat it out, covered his mouth with his hand, and hurriedly ran outside; because of this humiliation, he no longer insulted him.
The King asked again: "Are you well?"
He replied, "The king's inner women treat me, a plowman, with equal contempt.
The king said:
"If it be so, when I enter the palace, you shall come to the gate and ask: 'Where is the King? If he says:"
"She is inside. You may say to her:
"You have abandoned the myriad affairs of state and remain unaware of them; staying constantly within the inner palace, how can you manage the business of government?"
"Furthermore, when you saw me staying inside, you were sleeping with your feet dangling on my bed in the side chamber; I myself went out the door to lift your feet so that you could get back up."
He replied: "Great King!

How could I have two heads so that you might raise your foot over me? The positions of sovereign and minister are distinct, and their ranks differ by a vast margin; since our current relationship is already obstructed by human propriety, how could such a thing as this even be possible?"
The king said, "She is my beloved; what fault have you committed?
When she acts in this manner, the women of the inner palace would not dare to treat you with contempt."
He remained silent. Later, at another time, he entered the inner palace and asked, "Where is the King?

He performed everything according to the King's instructions, even to the point of lifting the King's foot. When the women of the inner palace saw this, they were all unable to endure it and wished to insult him; however, the King said:
"Do not do this! She is my beloved; what fault has she committed?
Thus they said to one another.
"We have all seen that this man is cherished by the king; we ought not to treat him with further contempt, for if the king learns of it, he will inflict punishment upon us.
From that time forward, they all showed him respect.
At another time, the king asked, "Is it well? They replied:
"It is well that we have found this opportunity.
King Candraprabha was by nature fond of female beauty; while conversing with his youths on worldly affairs atop a high tower, he addressed them, saying:
"Do you know of any city where there is a beautiful woman?"
Some say: "Kanyākubja. Others say: [Kurukṣetra].
"Leave the city of Vyāghrapura. Some said: "Let us not speak for now of other cities or kingdoms;

within this very city there is a courtesan named Bhadrā, whose beauty and majesty are peerless in the world, like a celestial maiden in the palace of Śakra, or like the sunlight outshining all the stars."

Upon hearing these words, the king’s joy redoubled beyond his usual state; bewildered and losing his composure, he longed to see him. That very night, he cast off his royal robes and donned the clothes of a commoner, taking five hundred gold coins with him, and went to the house of Bhadraśrī.
Having seen him, she joyfully cried out, "Welcome!
and instructed her maidservant, saying, "Bathe this gentleman thoroughly.
The maid then followed her instructions, bathing him and rubbing his body.
At that time, another man arrived at the entrance carrying five hundred gold coins and announced,
"I wish to stay the night. Now,
it was the constant custom of this courtesan to kill the one who arrived first whenever someone else came later, so that she might enjoy her pleasure with the newcomer.
At that time, a maidservant saw King Candraprabha; his countenance was so lovely that it was unlike that of ordinary people, and she immediately shed tears, thinking to herself:
"Is this man not of the Kṣatriya caste? His appearance is so upright and handsome that he is peerless in the whole world. How could a courtesan give rise to such an evil mind and unjustly kill him?"
The tears she shed fell upon the king’s body.
The king looked up at her and asked,
"Why have you suddenly shed tears?"
He replied, "There is nothing.
The king, harboring a sense of doubt, questioned him repeatedly and more intensely.
"You must tell me; there must certainly be a reason for this.
He then proceeded to explain the matter in detail.
The king immediately asked:
“O maiden! I have lost my way; is there any expedient by which I might escape? She replied:
"Men with swords stand at all four sides of this house, guarding it together so that there is no way to escape;
yet there is an exit that is utterly foul and loathsome—so why even mention it?"
The king said, "Point out the location, whether it be good or bad; my life must be preserved. He replied:
“There may be a way to escape from that place, but it is a latrine hole nailed shut with iron nails; if you can pull them out, that will serve as a path.
The king said, “Go point out the location, and I shall try to pull them out.”
The woman pointed out the location; the king threw himself down and pulled at the nail in the latrine hole, yet despite exhausting his strength, he was unable to extract it.

At that time, not far outside this wall, there lived a brahmin who was well-versed in the science of stellar omens. In the middle of the night, he went out and looked up at the Milky Way, while his wife followed behind him carrying water.
The brahmin said to her, "You should know now that as I observe the constellations, the king has met with great peril and his suffering is extreme."
The wife said, "Why speak of the state's secrets?
If others were to hear this, you would surely suffer execution."
The brahmin said, "I have received this protection solely because of the king; while the king undergoes hardship, I remain at peace.
He then stood in the courtyard, gazing afar at the constellation of calamity while reciting prayers.

The king heard their voices from within the latrine hole; exerting all his strength, he shook the nail and pulled it out, whereupon he emerged. He then crawled through the hole following the excrement, his body smeared with filth, until he painfully reached the outside, at which point the heavenly signs were finally altered.
At that time, the brahmin, seeing that the stars had shifted, said to his wife:
"Although the king has suffered, he has now escaped; that he remains alive is a source of great fortune for me."
The king then hurriedly entered the city in secret and went to the residence of Lady Anle.
Startled by his sudden arrival, the lady asked him:
"Heaven is impartial; what is the meaning of this?"
The King then related the matter to her in full detail.

Upon hearing this, the Queen wept with tears streaming down her face; she immediately scraped away the impurities with a bamboo scraper, first washing her thoroughly with fragrant earth, then bathing her with various kinds of scented powders and exquisite perfumed waters. Next, she wiped her body, applied unguents, and dressed her in fine garments. After she had rested for a short while until dawn, the Queen sat in the main hall and addressed her ministers, saying:
"All the masters of Yin and Yang who are skilled in the stars and the calendar must be summoned and assembled."
The minister immediately summoned them all, and the king asked him:
"What was the matter last night? He replied:
"The King was safe and sound during the night, with no other occurrences.
The King said, "In such-and-such a quarter there is a brahmin who is well-versed in astrology; he should be summoned here."
He immediately dispatched a messenger to the brahmin’s residence to announce:
"The King summons you!
The brahmin then put on his robes and set out for the King's presence, whereupon his wife said to him:
"I have already informed you previously; why speak of matters of state secrecy?
Because you did not heed my words, you have now been summoned for questioning.
The Brahmin then examined the day and hour and, finding no ill omen, said to his wife:
"You need not fear; all of this is auspicious.
He proceeded to the king's location, and as soon as the king saw him from afar, he cried out in a loud voice:
"Welcome, Great Teacher!"
"You may sit close by.
The brāhmaṇa then offered a blessing:
"May the King's life span be long and prosperous."
He took his seat and sat down.
After resting for a short while, the king asked: "Brahmin!"
"Do you understand astrology?
He replied, "According to my limited ability, I am somewhat familiar with it."
The king said, "Great Master!
What was it like for me last night?"
He replied, "Great King, you encountered extraordinary peril last night and suffered greatly; it was only by the power of Your Majesty’s merit that your life was barely preserved.
Having heard this, the king addressed his ministers, saying:
"As the Great Master said:
'Last night my life was nearly lost.
Since these practitioners of yin and yang are unskilled in calendrical calculations, from this day forward their stipends and emoluments shall be abolished."
"The courtesan Bhadrā should have her hair tied to the hoof of a vicious horse and trampled to death; the house she inhabits shall be ploughed by donkeys.
As for the maidservant of her household who washed me, command her to enter the inner palace so that she may attend to matters of state."
Then the ministers did everything exactly as the king had instructed.
The king asked the brahmin, "Since you were concerned for me and I have survived, I now wish to repay your kindness; what is your wish?"
He replied: "Great King!
Allow me to inquire briefly with my family, and then I shall come to fulfill my wish."
The king said, "As you wish," and immediately returned home to tell his family:
"The King has granted me a boon, providing everything I require according to my wishes. As for you all, what does each of you desire?
His wife said, "And what do you yourself desire, my lord?"
He replied, "I wish for the five great villages to be my perpetual fief.
His wife said:
"If it be so," he said, "I desire a hundred female cows to provide me with a constant supply of milk and curd.
His son replied,
"I wish for a superior horse-drawn chariot to serve as my vehicle."
The woman said,
"I wish for exquisite necklaces adorned with jewels.
Her maidservant said:
"I wish for a fine whetstone for incense; this is what is required for preparing food.
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself:
"Since this is the case, it would not be appropriate to state my request directly; I should instead seek this boon from the king by means of a verse."
He then went to the king’s presence and addressed the Great King, saying:
“Regarding all the petitions within my household, I beg that your majesty will grant me leave to exhaust my words; I shall briefly compose verses to set forth these matters:
‘I pray for five fiefdoms, And a hundred head of cattle for my wife.’”
The son desires a horse-treasure chariot; The daughter loves various necklaces;
In the house there is a maidservant Who needs stone for grinding incense.
Since such are their wishes and requests, May Your Majesty, out of compassion, grant them.
When King Pracaṇḍa heard these words, he replied with a verse, granting their wishes:
"I grant you five fiefs; To your wife, a hundred cows;
To your son, a chariot drawn by a horse-treasure; And to your daughter, various necklaces."
"The small maidservant in my household is given a fine stone for grinding incense;
since she has this aspiration and request, I shall cause it all to be fulfilled.
The King said to his great minister:
"Whatever you desire, you may have it all. The king said to the brāhmaṇa, "Great Master, let us govern the affairs of state together;
with a sincere heart, assist me in deliberating upon the myriad matters of government."
He replied, “Great King!
I am a brahmin; by principle, it is not appropriate for me to know the affairs of state.”
The king then forcibly appointed the brahmin as a high minister of state.

A neighboring realm of the king’s named Kāśa was in rebellion; consequently, he ordered Vaḍḍha to lead an army to attack it. Having defeated that army and captured much booty, he stationed his troops in the open country and was about to enter the city.
When the King heard that [the youth] was coming, he mobilized his army and went out in person. Seeing the young girl Kṣānti covered in many scabs and sores, he asked Vaḍḍha:
"Is there any man who has slept and stayed the night with this daughter?"
She replied, "Not only will she share my bed with joy, but in the end, she will even ride upon her husband's back, making him bray like a donkey.
The King said:
"How could such a thing possibly be true?
He replied, "Your Majesty shall witness it for yourself."
Then, Vardhana immediately entrusted the young girl to the physician, saying:
"You should treat her well and provide a generous payment for the medicine; I shall have no stinginess regarding whatever you may require."

The physicians treated him until he was completely restored; subsequently, they nourished him with clothing and food according to his wishes, so that his countenance became lovely and extraordinary compared to ordinary people.
At that time, Vaḍḍha took her as his daughter and named her Śrīprabhā.
Vaḍḍha said to her:
"If I invite the King to our home for a meal, you must adorn yourself with all manner of necklaces and ornaments and present yourself before him."
The woman accepted her instructions.
Later, Saṃpāka respectfully addressed the king, saying:
"I pray that Your Majesty would deign to visit my humble abode for a short while."
The king said,
"Since you did not invite me, by what means could I have gone? He replied:
"I invite you to come this very evening; tomorrow, we shall proceed to your residence.
The King said, "Excellent!"

Vardhana then prepared an extensive array of sumptuous meals and set out rare delicacies; he invited the King into his residence, bathed him with scented water, and presented him with priceless garments. When the meal was nearly finished, they sat together in refined conversation.
Then the maiden Jyotiṣkā, from within the curtain, threw a small ball toward him from afar; she immediately drew back the curtain and said to her father, "Catch my ball and bring it back.
When the King saw that the young girl’s countenance was of transcendent beauty, he conceived a lustful desire for her and asked Upacāra:
"To whom does this belong? He replied,
"It is my daughter."
He asked, "Have you already given it to another? He replied:
"Not yet," [the man] replied. The King said,
"Why have you not given it to me?"
He replied, "If Your Majesty does not disdain her, you may take her away as you please.
The king then prepared a grand display of ceremonial rites and took her into his harem.

It is the constant law of the world that when one obtains something new, one discards the old and no longer enters the former chamber; having become attached to the starlight, all other matters have been neglected.
Ghaṭīkāra thought to himself:
"This is precisely the right time; what was said in the past should now be carried out."
He asked Jyotiṣka, "Can you ride upon the king's back and make him neigh like a horse? He replied:

"Wait while I consider whether I can do it or not. Generally, a woman of wisdom understands things naturally without needing instruction; she then put on soiled clothes and lay down upon a broken bed. When the king came and asked, "What is the meaning of this? she replied: The king said, "I have heard that you are a woman of great wisdom. Why have you put on these dirty clothes and lain upon this broken bed? She replied, "Great King, I am indeed a woman of wisdom, but I do not know how to perform such a task. Therefore, I have put on these dirty clothes and lain upon this broken bed. The king said, "If you truly do not know how to do it, I shall go elsewhere and seek another woman. She replied, "Great King, please do not go elsewhere. Allow me three days to consider whether I can do it or not. The king agreed and departed. On the first day, she went to the marketplace and purchased a large quantity of fine cloth. On the second day, she went to the market and bought various kinds of fragrant flowers. On the third day, she went to the market and purchased all manner of rare and exquisite items. Having finished her purchases, she returned home and prepared a magnificent feast. She then had the king summoned and led him into the inner chamber. There, she spread out a clean and beautiful bed, covered it with fine silk, and adorned it with various precious ornaments. She then took off her own garments and put on the finest robes, adorned herself with exquisite jewelry, and sat upon the bed. She then addressed the king, saying: "Great King, please enter the inner chamber and sit upon this bed. The king entered and sat upon the bed. She then spoke to the king, saying: "Great King, I have heard that you are a man of great wisdom. Why do you sit upon this bed with such a heavy heart? The king replied, "I am indeed a man of wisdom, but I do not know how to perform such a task. Therefore, I sit here with a heavy heart. She replied, "Great King, please do not be distressed. He replied: "Great King!
It is because the deva is angry with me that I have now encountered this calamity."
The king asked,
"What did you pray for when you were among the gods? He replied:
"When the King sent my father to wage war against Kāśī, at that time I made a prayer to the gods:
'If my father leads his army to conquer that kingdom and returns in safety, then when I am married, may the husband I obtain ride upon my back and make the sound of a horse.'"
"The King has now taken me as his consort and possesses an abundance of women; who could fulfill my long-held vow for him?
Indeed, when one is led by sensual desire, there is nothing one will not do.
He replied:
"O lady! That which you seek is indeed for my sake."
"I pray that you may be free from illness; I shall do everything for you.
He remained silent and said nothing. The king asked, "Why are you silent?"
"Did you perhaps have some further prayer or aspiration directed toward the devas?
He replied, "I had no other request or aspiration; however, at that time, I again thought to myself:"
"Let the Brahmin ministers offer prayers of blessing, and have musicians play the lute.
The King said, "This may also be done."
"Brahmin minister, those who are my own dependents may seek out one among them who plays the lute.
He replied, "I shall seek one for you."

At that time, there was a merchant from the kingdom of Gandhāra who, carrying various goods, arrived at the city of Ujjayinī. He subsequently became intimate with a courtesan; having developed such deep attachment that his mind became disordered and deluded, he exhausted all his wealth, and his family members and servants fled to various places.
At that time, seeing his destitution, the courtesan said to him, "Virtuous sir!
I have no fields to cultivate, nor do I have a shop for trade; I rely solely on the gathering of friends and associates to sustain my life."
"If you have wealth or goods, you may bring them here at once; if you have none, you must go, for we must accommodate future guests.
He replied, "I am poor and have nothing; even if I did have something, what would I use it for?"
"However, I feel deep affection for you; please grant me your acceptance and do not drive me away with harshness. Only when you permit me to stay in your house will I know that you truly love me.
The courtesan said, "If you can do everything according to my word, then I shall allow you to reside here."
He replied, "I have done it all.
At that time, driven by lust, the courtesan, having finished defecating, placed a date pit upon her excrement and said:
"You may bite out the pit of this jujube with your teeth.
He then bit it out, whereupon the woman stepped on his waist and spine with her foot and said, "You wretched creature!
Why do you commit such an evil act with your mouth?"
"You are an unclean person; you must leave me," he said, and immediately drove him out of the house.
That man’s former occupation was playing the lute (*vīṇā*), so he sustained himself by means of his musical voice.
The King replied to Vaḍḍha, saying:
"Your daughter has made such a prayer to the gods; as for the Brahmin minister, I already have one myself, but where can a lute player be sought?"
He replied, “There is a Gandhāra man who plays the lute for his livelihood; he will have his eyes covered with silk and be led into the palace.
The King said:

"Act accordingly. The king and his ministers ascended the seven-storied palace, whereupon they commanded the minister to relate the matter in detail; then, Paṇḍaka covered his eyes with a cloth and led him up to the palace.

At that time, Jyotiṣkā donned bright white garments and mounted the king’s back; the minister Śuddhakarman offered prayers for the king’s blessing, the lute emitted its sound, and the king let out the neigh of a horse.
At that time, the Gandhāra thought to himself:
"How could there be the sound of a horse on this seven-storied palace? It must be my companion being deceived by a woman.
With these thoughts arising from his heart, he sang this song:
"This matter is very similar; this matter is known to all:
wealth is entirely lost, and its foul seeds defile one's teeth.
At that time, he played the lute with his hands while reciting these words without ceasing. The King then asked:
"The lyrics are extraordinary; what meaning do they hold?
He then reported the matter to the king in detail, and the king thought to himself:
"This man knows me; it is not fitting for him to remain here."
He then gave him five hundred gold coins and drove him far away out of the country.
Later, a minister admonished [the king], saying:
"In all matters concerning the governance of a kingdom, do not allow yourself to be deceived and toyed with by women."
Upon hearing this, the king felt inward shame and remained speechless.
The king then commanded Upacāra, saying:
"The Brahmin minister has mocked me; are you capable of causing his wife to shave his head?"
He replied, "I shall try to observe it.
He then went into the house and asked his wife:
"The King has been subjected to direct mockery by the brahmin; do you have any skillful means by which you might cause his wife to shave off his hair?
He replied, "There is no need for preliminary talk; we shall see after it has been shaved."
The husband said, "If you can do this, it would be a fine thing.

A wife with deep affection for her husband will surely have a husband with deep affection for her; thus, his wife immediately became close friends with the wife of a high minister. Once she had gained her favor, she told her:

"Though he speaks with words of affection, how could he possibly surpass me?
I always hold sovereign power over my husband; no one else can exceed me. She replied:
"If you have authority over your husband, try shaving his hair; I now suspect you will certainly be unable to do so.
She replied, "Just wait until it is finished, and then you shall know whether I can or not."
His wife immediately put on old and tattered clothes and lay upon a single bed, groaning as she remained there.
The minister asked, "For what reason are you like this?"
He replied, "The celestial deity is angry with me.
He reported this, saying:
"Is it that because your family is poor you are unable to fulfill your vows, causing the celestial deities to harbor resentment toward you?
Whatever you request shall be granted in its entirety, so that the deities may be delighted and your sufferings eliminated."
He asked, "What do you concede regarding the self (ātman)? He replied:

“Previously, when my husband was still at home and had not yet entered government service, as soon as the King first summoned him, I prayed to the gods, saying: ‘May my husband be sent on this royal mission; may his endeavors meet with success and he return in safety. If these prayers are fulfilled, I shall shave his hair as an offering to the heavenly deities.”

"Since that time, my household has flourished and I have become immensely wealthy; yet, greedy for pleasure, I forgot to offer sacrifices to the gods. Because of this arrogance, I have incurred the wrath of Heaven. I am now certain to die—by what path can I seek life?"
The husband said, "What you have requested from the gods has already been granted to me; you should inform the King, and he will arrange everything for you.
His wife then sent a message to the wife of Puṣkarasārin, saying:
"I have already given my husband's consent to do everything for you.
Upon hearing this, the wife informed Vaḍḍha:
"The minister’s wife has sent a message; my husband has already granted his permission, pending a brief audience with the King."
Uttara entered the audience hall and informed the king:
"The task is accomplished; please do not doubt it further.
Should the minister arrive, may you be made aware of this matter."
The King said, "I already know; there is no need for you to trouble yourself with such instructions.
At that time, the minister came to the King's presence and addressed him, saying:
“Great King! I have a prayer to offer to the devas, for which I must remain within my chambers for six months. I pray that you will grant me your favor and permit me to fulfill this request.”
The king said, "Excellent!
Upon returning to his palace, he immediately shaved his hair; however, filled with shame, he did not go out.
His wife sent a messenger to inform Saṃpāka’s wife, saying,
"The head has already been shorn.
The wife informed Saṃpāka, and Saṃpāka reported it to the king.
Upon hearing this, the king was greatly delighted and immediately ordered a messenger to summon his ministers. At that time, Saṃjīvaka taught the two boys to recite a song, which said:
"If she be a beautiful girl from a noble family, Can she cause a man to act according to her will?"
"From atop the seven-storied tower, the sound of a horse's neighing is heard; look at this minister, whose head has been shorn!
At that time, the minister, hearing the King’s summons, donned his cap and entered.
Having arrived at the king’s location, they were commanded to sit to one side; those two youths then sang this song:
“If she be a beautiful woman of noble birth, Can she cause a man to act according to her will?”
"From atop the seven-storied tower, the neighing of horses is heard; look at this great minister—his head has been shaved!
One of the youths immediately approached and removed the minister’s hat; seeing that he had no hair, the court officials present clapped their hands and laughed aloud.
The minister, inwardly filled with shame and outwardly abashed before others, bowed his back and lowered his head, offering no word in reply as he departed.
At that time, having completed his task, Puṣpasena boasted of his own prowess, proclaiming to the assembly:
"If one is thus mocked by a woman, how could one possibly accomplish the great affairs of state?"
In a secluded place, the king said to the minister,
"Are you capable of causing Saṃgharakṣita to suffer humiliation? He replied:
"Great King! Let me first observe whether I am capable or not.
His sister's son, who was highly skilled in the arts of illusion, said to him:
"Every time the minister Pihgala-gupta attends the court assembly, he constantly mocks and ridicules me. If you can perform an act that humiliates him, it will remove this great shame of mine."
He replied, "Uncle! Allow me to deliberate upon how this matter should be handled."
Having reflected thus, he replied, "It is somewhat so.

He then employed his illusory powers to manifest a vast caravan of merchants; within a great heap of excrement, he conjured a dwelling, and from withered bones, he fashioned a merchant's wife whose countenance was so upright and beautiful that all who saw her were filled with delight.
According to the laws of the king’s realm, whenever a large caravan of merchants arrived at the city, either the king himself would inspect the taxes or he would appoint Bṛhaspati to receive them.
At that time, the king did not go out, so he ordered Bṛhaspati to receive the taxes.
Having arrived at the camp, he asked,
"Which is the chamber of the merchant leader?
They then pointed it out to him.

Having entered the inner chamber, he saw the mistress of the merchant’s household, whose appearance and deportment were so lovely as to be capable of deluding the human heart; upon merely seeing her, he was immediately overcome with passion and said, "Young woman!..."
"If you can share this pleasure with me, I shall release all your merchant companions from the payment of customs duties.
He replied, "As you wish."
He replied, "It should not be during the day; you may wait until the night.

The magician immediately concealed the daylight and made it night. Gopāla then engaged in unrighteous conduct with the illusory woman; as he embraced her by the throat with his arms, she fell into a deep sleep, whereupon the magician finally released his magical arts.
At that time, as Vaḍḍha was cradling those dry bones and lying amidst a heap of filth, the minister departed and said to the king:
"Your Majesty, please deign to turn your carriage for a moment and grant us an audience with Vaḍḍha."
The king went outside the city; having arrived there, he snapped his fingers to wake him and said, "Bāḷhika!
Do you eat meat after engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman in the wild?"
When Vaḍḍha saw this, he thought to himself, "Such mockery as this is the work of the King;
what use have I for living like this?
It would be better to die than to seek life further."
He further thought to himself:
"To give up one's life is extremely difficult; I should now depart and go to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana to seek ordination from him."
He immediately went forward to pay his respects and said,
"Virtuous One! I wish to go forth into the homeless life."

The Venerable One immediately granted him the going forth and conferred upon him the five precepts and the ten precepts; subsequently, having conferred full ordination and given a brief instruction, he had him read the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
At that time, King Pradyota, being unable to find peace of mind because he no longer had Upacāra, subsequently ordered him to return to secular life and settled him as he had been before.

The internal summary verse says:
The hunter Govinda dies; Vāsavadattā is released and returns to the palace;
Candraprabha goes toward Takṣaśilā; the killing of a man; the eight dreams.
At that time, King Candraprabha, after rising from sleep, had this thought:
"Will Prince Govinda be able to exercise the wisdom and capability to succeed to the royal throne after my passing?
I should now test his strategic intelligence.
He then had a messenger summon him and said:
"I have some minor affairs within the inner palace that must occupy me for seven days; you may temporarily take charge of state affairs in my stead.

The prince immediately accepted the command and oversaw the government. He administered rewards and punishments appropriately regarding what was beneficial and what was not. When those guilty of wickedness were seized and brought before him by the officials, the prince saw them and asked the man and woman:
"Do you love one another?"
He replied, "We love one another.
Having heard this, the Prince told his ministers:
"Since they love one another, why not let them follow their desires?
He then told his attendants,
"From this day forward, do not prohibit illicit affairs."
Having heard this, the people gave rein to their passions and committed transgressions at will.
The Prince constantly scrutinized state affairs with great rigor.
After seven days had passed, the King personally left the palace and asked Vaḍḍha:
"After my passing, will Prince Govinda be able to succeed to the throne?
Puṣpasena replied,
"He shall indeed succeed, yet he will permit those who engage in illicit affairs to commit evil."
The king asked,
"For what reason?
Vardhana answered the matter in full, and the king thought to himself:
"Is Prince Govinda free from jealousy toward other women, or is he likewise free from jealousy even toward his own wife?
I shall put him to the test."
At that time, there was a guest from Gandhāra in the north staying in the city; the king, having heard that he was wise, told him:
"You should engage in unrighteous conduct with the chief queen, Gopā."
Upon hearing this, he immediately covered his ears with his hands and said,
"If such an evil deed is committed, I shall have no way to live.
The king said:
"It is necessary for the king's business that this be done; there is no fault in this, for if one does not do so, it would constitute a violation of your command.
He replied, "Great King!"
"It must indeed be so; this task is too urgent for haste, and it requires a gradual sequence before it can be accomplished.
The King said, "I shall act according to whatever sequence you require."
He replied, "Great King!
First, construct a large shop near his residence; Your Majesty should provide me with the value of the goods. By employing this expedient, I hope that we may gradually become acquainted."
The king immediately provided him with money and goods as requested; he then built a shop, collected various merchandise, and laid out a grand display of fine wares.
At that time, a maidservant belonging to the Prince’s consort’s mother came to the shop to purchase various perfumes and medicines.
Then the Gandhara asked his maidservant,
"Young girl, for whom did you buy this?"
He replied, "I have been sent by the mother of Gopi’s wife to purchase this. He asked:
"What is that mother's name?
He replied, "Her given name is so-and-so."
He replied, "Her name is the same as my mother's; I now regard her as no different from my own mother.
He then took a small portion of the payment and gave him many fragrant items in return.
When the servant girl had returned home, her mother asked her:
"For what reason was the wealth you previously brought back so small, while today it is so great?
She answered her mother in detail regarding the aforementioned matters, and the mother said:
"Excellent! That is my son.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time; seeing that the goods were many, he rejoiced from afar.
Later, the shopkeeper said to her maidservant,
"You may inform my mother that I wish to have an audience.
The maidservant then informed the mother, who said:
"Come as you please," the maid replied upon her return. Thereupon, she took many fragrant offerings and went to that house. Upon seeing one another, she embraced her mother and wept.
Her mother asked, "Why do you weep?"
He replied, "The mother's features are identical to those of my own mother; a feeling of sorrow arose within me, and for this reason I wept.
His mother said:
“I am your mother; do not trouble yourself further with weeping.
Thus, they came to feel a profound depth of mutual affection.
Gopāla’s wife stood by their side, and her mother said:
"Come here! This is your elder brother; you should grasp his feet and pay him respectful homage.
The girl did as she was told.
He then asked his mother,
"What is this girl's name?
When she answered with her name, he replied:
"My elder sister-in-law was also named thus, and since her appearance is similar,
she must be my sister-in-law. His mother said, "Excellent!"
From that time forward, his compassion and concern for her increased manifold.

Once he had arrived at the house, the shopkeeper, harboring deceitful intentions, feigned illness and lay down to sleep. At that moment, the maidservant came to purchase ointment, and he said to her: "Young girl!"
"I am extremely distressed by my illness; why does my mother not come for a brief visit?
She replied, "She is unaware of your ailment; I shall return and inform her."
The maidservant returned and informed her mother, who immediately came to inquire, asking:
"My beloved child!
What ailment do you have?"
He replied, "I am suffering from extreme exhaustion.
His mother said:
"One should consult a physician and administer medicine according to the illness. She replied, "Mother!"
"This is not a case for medical treatment; because of this illness, my life will surely come to an end.
His mother said, "Do not grieve.
What skillful means can be employed to cause your illness to be cured?"
He replied, “There is medicine that can cure this illness, yet there is no means by which it may be obtained.
His mother said:
"I shall provide for you everything that you require. She replied, "Mother!"
"If I could obtain the pleasure of union with the Great Queen Gopā, my illness might be cured.
When his mother heard this, she was greatly incensed and said, "You wretched man, you who desire the King's consort— why do you not simply die?"
He immediately shook out his robe, abandoned it, and departed.
At that time, the shopkeeper again practiced deception and drew up a contract, stating:
"After my death, the house and all its property shall be given entirely to the mother of that Prince’s consort."
She then took the letter and gave it to her mother. Once the mother had finished reading it, her anger was immediately dispelled, and she thought to herself:

"I harbored resentment and came away from her in rejection, yet she has instead shown me even greater devotion; her affection and sense of duty are unceasing and difficult to find its equal. For this reason, I shall go to see my daughter to inquire after her, lest she should lose her life because of this."
He immediately called his daughter and said to her:
"The shopkeeper has been a long-standing friend; he is your uncle. He is currently beset by illness—have you not gone to visit him even for a moment?"
He replied, "Mother! Are there no physicians to treat his illness?"
The mother said, "His illness is difficult to cure and may even lead to death. I have heard him say:
'If I could obtain my elder sister-in-law and enjoy love with her, this illness might be removed.'"
The woman then said in anger:
"This poor and wretched man wishes to commit an illicit act with the Queen; why does he not meet his end this very day?"
The mother said, "Nobility and lowliness are not fixed; you now seem to understand this. But who was the progenitor of Grandfather? He replied:
"I do not know," [the queen] said.
Her mother replied, "He was born from a scorpion; now that he has become king with a great host of troops, your husband—born of the wife of a householder—shall also become king."
"You may enjoy amorous dalliance with him; if you have a son, he shall become king—what harm is there in this?
Because of his mother's persuasion, he finally consented to the union.
The mother then sent a messenger to inform Gandhāra, saying:
"Seeing your earnestness, I have already given my daughter's consent; you yourself know the proper time, so you may come to her.
Upon hearing this, the shopkeeper informed the king that the matter was about to be finalized, and he briefly allowed Govinda to leave the house.
The king thought to himself:
"After my death, Gopāla shall become king, and Gopāla’s son shall succeed to the imperial throne.
If a Gandhāra man fathers a son with the queen, that child might become king and sever my lineage. I should give him medicine so that he does not father a son."
He then gave him the medicine and said to Ghaṇṭāla,
"Take this medicine first when you engage in unrighteous conduct with that woman.
The King replied to Govinda:
"Stay for a short while and do not return to your home; I have another plan. He then did not go.
Gandhāra took his medicine and had sexual intercourse with the woman, and they both fell asleep together. The king thought to himself:
"He has finished his duties," he replied, saying, "Gopāla!"
"You may return home.

Once he had arrived at the residence, he saw that Gandhāra and his consort were sleeping together with their arms hanging down; the Prince immediately raised their hands and covered them with his garment.
The two of them slept together throughout the night until dawn;
then, thinking, "Is there no one who saw us?
they immediately returned to the shop.
When the next day arrived, the king said to the crown prince,
"Last night I dreamed that your wife was having an illicit affair with another man. He replied:
"The Great King saw this in a dream; I have witnessed it with my own eyes.
The King asked, "How did you see it?"
He then related the matter in full.
The king asked,
"Do you harbor no jealousy toward that woman?"
He replied, "I have none. The king said:
"What is the reason for this?
He replied, "Great King,
please listen for a moment!"
"Since my birth, I have known the matters of past lives.
I recall that in the past, I was the wife of a merchant; my husband took his goods to engage in trade in another region.
I said to my husband:"
"I wish to follow you in practice.
Her husband said,
"Who will provide for you and attend to your needs?"
"Because of this hardship, we cannot travel together.
The wife then wept. Seeing this, the others said to the caravan leader:
"The virtuous wife weeps, wishing to go with you.
The merchant leader reported the difficult circumstances in detail, and the others said, "Let her simply be taken along; we shall provide for her needs."
He was then led away.
On a perilous road, there were five hundred bandits who came to raid the merchant caravan and killed the merchant leader.

At that time, the five hundred bandits committed sexual misconduct with the women; subsequently, the bandit host raided the merchant camp again and captured a young girl, with whom they all fell in love.
When the wife saw this, jealousy arose within her,
and she thought, "Is this woman vying with me for my husband?
She immediately ordered someone to throw her into an empty well, whereupon her life came to an end.
"Great King!
She who was my wife in the past was none other than myself.
I recall that in former times, even when I engaged in sexual desire with five hundred thieves, my heart was not yet satisfied; how much less could it ever find satisfaction with a single man?"
Recalling this matter, I no longer harbor feelings of jealousy toward women.

Observing this, I know that in the world, fools often take their wives and place them within palaces to guard them; it is only logical that men should protect women, for how could women be permitted to guard men?
The king said, “It is truly as you say;
to be able to sever the heart of envy is a difficult thing in this world. Although there is such a principle, I am unable to practice it.
At that time, there was a hunter in the city of Uśīnara whose wife was beautiful and whom he cherished with the utmost affection. Desiring to go out hunting, he thought to himself:
"If I leave my wife to go to the mountain forest, I fear she will engage in various unrighteous acts with others;
if I do not go, we shall have no other means of livelihood and will both perish. It is fitting that we take her with us and travel together through the wilderness."
They immediately went together and lived in a grass hut, killing various birds and beasts for the sake of hunting and selling them to provide their sustenance.
Later, on another occasion, King Caṇḍapradyota went out on a hunt; his horse bolted and galloped to the hunters' location, where the hunters recognized him and called out from afar: "Welcome!"
The king then dismounted from his carriage and rested in the shade of a tree. The hunter thought to himself:
"How could I now offer old, stale meat to the Great Anointed King?"
"You should take a new one to serve you.
He then took his bow and arrows and went into the wilderness.
There, the king looked around and saw a young woman of lovely appearance; a mind of lust arose within him, and being entangled by desire, he committed an unrighteous act with her.
At that time, the hunter returned home carrying fresh meat he had obtained; seeing his wife engaged in illicit acts with the king, he was filled with rage and thought to himself:
"This king has transgressed the law; he must now be put to death."
He further thought, "How could I harm the Great King for the sake of a mere woman?

At that moment, a lion suddenly appeared and killed the hunter. As he was about to die, he conceived a heart of compassion toward the king and was consequently reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
When the king saw that her husband was dead, he thought to himself:
"I have had intimate relations with this young woman; it would not be right to cast her aside lightly.
He immediately comforted her and placed her by his side.
Then the king’s ministers, searching all around, arrived together at the king’s location and asked,
"Whose daughter is this?
The king replied:
"This is within my domain; why is it necessary to ask about this?
It would be appropriate to take him away and place him in the inner palace.
Having finished his excursion, the King returned to the city gates.
However, there were many palace women within the royal palace, and the king thought to himself:
"If this hunter could not even protect a single young woman while living alone in the forest wilderness, how much less can I guard so many palace women?"
He immediately shook his bells, blew his horns, and beat his drums, proclaiming throughout the city:
"All people, take heed!

Whether you are long-time residents or recent arrivals, all should listen to these words: I now release all the women within my inner palace; let them go wherever they please and act as they wish, engaging with outsiders as they see fit, without it being considered a transgression."
He further addressed the women of the inner apartments, saying:
"I now release you; go out from the palace at night to enjoy yourselves as you please, but as soon as the drum sounds, you must return inside."
"If anyone violates this, I shall take your life.
However, all women delight in men, especially those confined within the royal palace.
At that time, the palace ladies all went out at night to seek men, wandering wherever they pleased according to their desires.
Only Queen Anurādhā, the mother of Govinda, and Queen Tiṣyarakṣitā remained outside the palace to protect the king’s feelings.
The king said to Anurādhā,
"You may go outside and seek another husband."
He replied, "I truly cannot abandon the King to go outside and seek out another person.
Then the King spoke again to Queen Śrīprabhā:
"Why do you not go seek another man?

Thus, because her youth, beauty, and passion were difficult to restrain, she constantly harbored feelings of affection for other men; though she remained within the palace, her heart longed to go outside. Hearing the king’s repeated warnings, she silently accepted his words, and that very night went to the marketplace.
Seeing a perfume seller there whose countenance was handsome, she said to him, "You should engage in acts of love with me."
He replied, "Hold this lamp for me for a moment; I must calculate the total cost before I can act as you wish.

Since the man had received so many items, it was difficult to complete the accounting all at once. He calculated throughout the night until dawn, but once the drum sounded, he had no leisure to remain.
Having cast the lamp on the ground, Starlight was about to leave when the man said, "Stay for a moment;
let us enjoy each other's company. She replied:
"I cannot remain here any longer.
The King has issued a command, and the drum has sounded: 'Those who do not enter the palace shall have their heads cut off. Since I possess no second head, how could I possibly stay much longer?"
She then took her leave and departed.
When the king saw her, he asked, "Jyotiṣprabhā! Why have you come?"
“Have you been enjoying yourself with outsiders?
She replied, “I have had no leisure.”
The king asked, "What is the meaning of this?
He then explained everything in detail to the king in sequence, and the king remained silent at that time.
The King issued a solemn decree as before, proclaiming:
"All palace women are released to associate with outsiders at will during the night.
This report was heard from afar and spread throughout other regions.

At that time, King Pradyota of Kauśāmbī, having heard that King Candraprabha had issued such an edict allowing all the women of the palace to go out at night for private trysts, asked his minister Yaugandharāyaṇa:
"I have heard that King Candraprabha has released all the palace women to follow their own inclinations. I wish to go there for a while to enjoy their company."
He replied, "That King Candraprabha constantly harbors resentment toward Your Majesty; if his enemies were to hear that you have come in person, they would surely act unrighteously."
He replied, "A man must decide between good and evil when undertaking a task; you should remain here while I go elsewhere for a time. He answered:
“Great King, your mind is set; who would dare detain you?
I only pray that you will exercise great caution on your journey ahead.

At that time, King Pradyota was deeply infatuated with female beauty; disregarding the minister’s admonition, he proceeded toward the city of Ujjayinī. There, in the middle of the night, he beheld the maiden Tārāvalī. Having learned her identity and observed that her countenance was so exceptionally distinguished as to be peerless in all the world, he addressed her:
"The beautiful woman of the Kṣatriya caste, Jyotsnā, come and enjoy yourself with me.
She replied, "As you wish!"
"You may spread out the mats and seats.
The King said, "You may spread them out."
At that time, the two men were each filled with pride and did not spread out their bedding.
When the night had passed into dawn and the drums began to sound, the woman was about to depart, whereupon the king said: "Wait!"
"We may enjoy each other's company.
She replied, "The King has issued a command and the drums have already sounded; those who do not enter the palace shall have their lives cut short. I have no leisure to remain here any longer."
Jyotiṣka then immediately removed the golden ring from the king’s finger and departed carrying it in his hand.
King Prabhāsa also returned to his own city.
The king asked Jyotiṣka:
"Can you obtain a man with whom to enjoy sexual pleasure? She replied, "I cannot."
When asked why, he then explained the circumstances in full sequence and produced the ring, saying:
"This is that person's property which I have taken off and brought here."
Having read the seal, the king said to Udayibhadra:
"King Prasenajit has entered the city with a great host while no one was on guard; he has been secretly seeking amorous pleasure with my palace women. How could I possibly let him go?"
He replied, "Great King!
This person has come here in secret; I was not aware of it beforehand. If he comes again, I shall certainly not let him go."
When King Pradyota returned and learned of this, he informed his minister Yaugandharāyaṇa as previously described. The minister admonished him, saying:
"Previously, the king departed in secret without being noticed by him, which allowed him to return safely to his own city."
"At this time, that king is providing extreme security; if you go again, it will certainly not be safe. It would be better not to go.

Although the minister earnestly remonstrated, the king would not accept his words. Once the king had set out, the minister followed him, and they arrived at the city of Uśīnara, where they stayed within a single residence.
Having awakened Vaḍḍha, he ordered many strong men to stand guard with drawn swords by his house and told them:
"If any woman comes out from this house, let her go; do not let any man go."
At that time, Yaugandharāyaṇa, perceiving the gravity of the situation, thought to himself:
"I must not remain silent and abandon the King while he faces such peril; by what means can I cause him to escape?"
He then immediately ordered the king to dress in the clothes of a maidservant and place a water vessel upon his head; he had people follow behind him, driving him along with a staff, and said:
"Go fetch water and return quickly; the king awaits you for rinsing and washing."
At that time, the guards, thinking he was a maidservant, did not stop him; having reached the edge of the pond, he abandoned the jar and fled.
When Puṣkarasārin entered the palace and could not find the king, he saw only Yukenana and immediately brought him before the king, saying:
"It was solely because of this man that King Udayana escaped."
Then Yu Jian-na stepped forward and addressed the king, saying:
"I have hitherto been sustained in life and limb by Your Majesty's grace; it is precisely appropriate that I should now escape.
Yet these ministers receive their stipends and fiefs from Your Majesty—if they allow me to flee, how can this be considered right?"
The king then severely rebuked Vaḍḍha, saying:
"How could it be that while an enemy kingdom has come here to harm the king, you have openly allowed him to escape?"
"If you can obtain it through other means, that would be well; if not, you shall receive the ultimate punishment.
Having heard this, he was struck with alarm and sought a means.
At that time, a master craftsman from the south had newly arrived there, and Ghaṭīkāra asked him:
"Do you possess the skill and wisdom to create such and such mechanical devices?
He replied, "I shall first attempt to learn how to make them, hoping for success."
At that time, Vaḍḍha then hid the royal elephant Mahāpaduma from Mount Veṇu and made a proclamation throughout the city and its districts:
"The great elephant Mahāpaduma from Mount Veṇu has escaped to a foreign land; his whereabouts are unknown."
When those far and near had all heard this report, they told the craftsmen:
"You should construct a wooden mountain-elephant.
They immediately fashioned a mechanical elephant according to these words; fifty men were placed within it, and much elephant dung and water were stored inside the elephant. Then they said:
"You should activate the mechanism so that this elephant may go and stay not far from Kośāmbī.

If the king comes with his fourfold army to see it, the elephant may return; but if he comes alone, seize the king immediately, place him inside the elephant, and run back to our own country with all haste."
Upon hearing these instructions, the craftsmen acted accordingly and caused the great elephant to arrive and stay at a short distance from Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the cowherds, shepherds, and various laborers, seeing the elephant’s extraordinary appearance, all gazed upon it together;
some said, "This elephant has come from the mountain forests."
He further said,
"This is the great elephant lost by King Candraprabha, which has come from afar to this place.
Someone came to inform the king of these circumstances.
"I have heard that King Candraprabha possesses a great elephant named Veṣṭhila, which is unsurpassed in the world.
By the power of the king’s merit, it has come here of its own accord; people from near and far, numbering ten billion, have all gathered to behold it."
Upon hearing this, the King was filled with great joy and said to Yukṣaṇa:

"You must immediately beat the drums to proclaim throughout the imperial capital that the fourfold army shall assemble together, carrying many nooses. Leading a multitude of people, we shall go out from the city gates to capture the great elephant."
The ministers followed the King’s instructions and carried them out in succession; their retinue gathered like clouds in the outskirts of the wilderness.
At that time, seeing the King’s army approaching, the people within the elephant enclosure fled. The chief minister reported:
“Your Majesty already knows well how to bind an elephant; by what means can we entice it so that it comes near?”
The king said, "Withdraw the fourfold army; I shall go alone to see him.
Thereupon the multitude withdrew and the king proceeded alone, taking his exquisite lute, Miāoxiǎng (Wonderful Sound), with him as he advanced.
The elephant’s female keeper, seeing the king arrive alone, immediately stopped the elephant.

When the king reached the elephant’s side, the attendants emerged, seized him, and led him inside; they then activated the mechanical mechanism, which moved like a swift wind as they returned to their own country.
When King Prabhāsa had been captured, a great multitude of soldiers all raised a loud cry:
"The king has been seized by bandits!
The king has been seized by bandits!"
Thereupon, they increased their troops and pursued him as far as the border of his kingdom.
The ministers said, "Since we have reached another territory, it is not appropriate to enter further; we should all return. As for the King, who has been captured, let us devise other means."

At that time, King Prabhāsa was captured by his enemies and brought to the city of Ujjayinī. The minister Puṣpasena led King Prabhāsa into the presence of King Caṇḍapradyota and addressed him, saying:
"Great King!..."
"This is King Prabhāsa.

Upon seeing him, the king was filled with joy; he struck the bells and beat the drums, and the masses of people rushed forward like clouds, filling the streets and roads by the hundreds of thousands and millions.
The king commanded Udayana, saying, "Cast that Prabhāsa away according to the laws of the kingdom."

The minister said, "This King Prabhāsa is well-versed in the subtle arts of elephant training. If Your Majesty were to kill him, these techniques would perish along with him. Furthermore, it would not be difficult to have someone approach him to learn them until all the wondrous skills are mastered and he can then be dismissed."
The king said, "If that is so, you may learn it yourself. He replied:
"This person is none other than the Great Teacher from whom I have received my training; how could I possibly harm him?
Since such a thing exists, it would contradict the ways of the world. The King said:
"Who is capable of being enrolled in this study?

He replied, "It is well known to all that Princess Gopā is by nature diligent and industrious, and possesses penetrating insight; let her be enrolled in the study so that she may master its subtleties."
The king approved of her plan and said to his daughter:

"There is a man endowed with eighteen kinds of inauspicious marks who is well-versed in the treatises on training elephants. You may learn from him behind a curtain; I shall gradually learn it after you. It would not be fitting for you to see the face of that wicked man; if you were to see him, you would certainly die, without a doubt."
He then immediately studied the text from behind a curtain.
At that time, Yu-ken-na (Yaugandharāyaṇa) was in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī and thought to himself:
"I should now seek news of the king; if his life remains, I shall provide the conditions for his release from bondage, but if he no longer exists, I must seek another successor."
Yugandhara’s younger sister was named Suvarṇamālā; she was clever and affectionate, and her intelligence surpassed that of her brother.
She replied, “Little sister!
"You should now go to the city of Ujjayinī to inquire after the king’s condition.
If his life remains, you must create the conditions for his release from bondage; but if he has passed away, another successor must be established."

Having heard this, she remained silent and reflected inwardly upon the matter. She then changed her clothes to assume the form of a female non-Buddhist ascetic, sustained herself by begging, and wearing worn-out garments, she gradually made her way to the city of Ujjayinī.
There she asked the gatekeeper, "Is the Great King Prabhāsa still alive?"
The gatekeeper replied,
"What enmity or malice does that king have toward you? He answered:
"Kill the husband and his son, and seize their wealth and property.
The gatekeeper said, "The King is not yet dead; he is currently teaching the princess the scriptures on how to train elephants."
In this manner, they inquired at all four gates of the king’s palace, receiving identical answers each time.

They then employed various means to seek out someone who could meet with King Prasenajit; concealing their shadows and hiding their forms, they looked about in every direction, made a soft sound, and asked: "Great King!"
"I have now attained existence.
She too was struck with alarm and looked around in every direction, replying:
"Little sister!..."
"For now, she has not yet passed away.
He then devised another pretext to observe Devadatta closely and asked, "Young girl!
