“From whom do you now learn the art of training elephants? She replied, “Mother!”
"There was a man endowed with eighteen kinds of inauspicious marks, and I studied under him from behind a curtain.
He replied, "How could there ever be a man endowed with eighteen kinds of inauspicious marks?"
This is King Mahāpraṇāda, whose appearance is upright and handsome, endowed with all the marks of excellence, and rare in this world.
Who, moreover, has deceived you into speaking such evil words?
"If you say it is false, lift the curtain and see for yourself.

Upon hearing these words, her heart was filled with joy; she immediately lifted the curtain and beheld the King’s countenance. A passion arose within her like a fierce wind, and she replied, "O Mother!"
"It is indeed as you have said. Is there perhaps some expedient means by which the lord of the land might be made to unite with me?
Her mother replied, "I shall now tell you:
even if one were to seek far and wide, such a person would be difficult to encounter; how much more so since he is your own beloved, making him the most fitting partner for you."
"This is the consecration for a Kṣatriya king; I have devised this expedient to bring it into accord with your heart.
Once these words were exchanged, they immediately united in joy; thus, Devadattā and the king became deeply enamored of one another.
At that time, Suvarṇamālā quickly dispatched a messenger to inform her elder brother, saying:
"Please set your mind at ease and do not worry further; Princess Devī is learning the art of training elephants from King Prasenajit."

Having received this message, the elder brother donned five kinds of ornaments for seclusion, covered himself with a grass garment, and assumed the name Vasantaśrī. Feigning madness, he proceeded to the city of Ujjayinī; there, in the streets, alleys, and public squares, he would lie down or stand up, uttering delirious words and singing this song:
"In spring one may sport; In spring one may find delight. I am Vasantaśrī herself; Come, let us enjoy our pastimes together."
If there is someone who recognizes him, saying,
"This is Yaugandharāyaṇa," they will immediately understand the secret signs of the golden necklace and seek him out.
If they do not recognize him, they will say,
"This is a madman," and refuse to accord him any consideration.

Wherever he went, whether to the residences of royal families or high ministers, he obtained food and clothing to stave off his morning hunger; gradually, he managed to seek out King Pradyota and briefly presented his proposal for discussion.
Later, the girl Devadattā said to Pradyota:
"If my father learns of this, he will surely execute me with severe punishment; it would be best for you to prepare a means of escape beforehand."
Dīpaka replied, "If that is so, you may now say this to the king:

'I have studied the training of elephants and read the texts, yet I have not personally witnessed their galloping and charging. I pray that Your Majesty grant me a noble female elephant so that I may ride it at will and observe whether its movements accord with the written treatises.'"
He then presented this proposal to the Great King for his consideration. The King said to the elephant keeper:

"The noble and virtuous mother-elephant may be given to Devadatta to ride as he pleases; whether he returns from morning until midday, or arrives at dusk and departs at nightfall, or travels back and forth without a fixed schedule during the first watch and the latter part of the night, or returns at midnight or arrives at dawn."
At that time, Yaugandharāyaṇa devised a plan to escape; he loaded elephant dung upon his back and departed through the city gate. A gatekeeper asked him, "Spring Flower!
What are you doing with this dung?"
He replied, "The royal family has established a feast to provide for the *pramoda-piṇḍa*.
People called this a madman's talk and paid it no heed.
He wrapped the dung in grass, hung it from a tree branch along the road to Kauśāmbī, and carried out the elephant urine in jars.
When his disciples saw him and asked about it,
he replied, "The royal family is holding a festival, and this will be used as a beverage."
Everyone laughed at this, and no one took it seriously.
He returned to the road and hung the jar from a tree branch.

At that time, King Śīlāditya, along with his minister, Suvarṇamālā, and Devadatta, had made an appointment for a specific time and place, and they did not deviate from it. Then King Śīlāditya and Devadatta mounted the royal elephant and arrived at the appointed place. The minister, Suvarṇamālā, and the lute player Svarasundarī all set out together, filled with joy. The king then played the lute, and the minister sang this song:
"Riding together upon a noble elephant, playing harmonious and wondrous melodies:
Devadatta and Vasanta-dattā, dancing with their hands, returned home together.
The King himself acted as the caravan leader, and they were able to return to Kauśāmbī."
"Having fulfilled my loyal minister's wish, let us sing long songs and enjoy ourselves.
After Udāyin departed, he lost track of the time and did not enter the palace. King Candapradyota said to Gṛhapati:
"For what reason has Devadatta not entered for so long?"
Gopa then searched for him; knowing that he had already fled, he informed the king, saying:
"King Bimbisāra has mounted the noble elephant Bhaddavatiya and, together with Devadatta, has escaped from the city."
Hearing this, the king was shocked and enraged, and he declared:
"You must quickly mount the great elephant of Veṭhadīpa and pursue that wicked man, bringing him here to see me!
He then mounted the great elephant and set out along the road.

The great elephant galloped along, keeping its eyes on him in hopes of catching up; however, Yaugandharāyaṇa immediately took some elephant dung from a tree branch, threw it upon the ground, and departed.

The great elephant then sniffed the scent and refused to proceed further. During this brief interval, the female elephant had moved far away, yet after traveling many *yojanas*, the elephant returned and caught up with them once more.

Yugandhara took a jar of elephant urine and threw it upon the ground; the great elephant smelled it again and was able to proceed further until he reached his own border, where his mind was freed from sorrow and fear.
At that time, Vaḍḍha thought to himself:
"This is another's territory; it is best that I return, lest this great elephant also be taken away.
Since his wishes were not fulfilled, he returned home in disappointment.
Upon arriving at his capital city, the king asked him,
"What news do you have? He replied:
"He has already fled to his own country; there is no one left to pursue.
The king then rested his cheek in his palm and remained there in sorrow.

At that time, King Prabhāsa, having returned to his native land, was restored to life after death. He immediately invited śramaṇas, brahmins, merchants, noble kinsmen, acquaintances, and the poor and destitute who had no support. From far and near, they rushed like stars to the king's presence, where he extensively practiced the giving of alms and held a great assembly.
He enjoyed himself at will with Queen Devadatta; later, while playing with her on the upper terrace, he said:
"I employed a deceptive artifice to bring you here."
The lady said, "My father also employed deceptive arts to imprison Your Majesty's person, managing to keep you alive only by such means.
The king said:
"If I do not bring your father here to the kingdom of Kauśāmbī to serve as a weaver, I shall no longer be known as King Prabhāsa.
With this thought, he remained silent, harboring resentment and anger.
Then King Prabhāsa said to Yaugandharāyaṇa,
"Are you able to dispel my sorrow? He replied:
"What do you intend to do?
The king replied,
"I shall bind a long rope around the neck of Prabhāsa, drag him here, and force him to learn the craft of weaving."
He replied, "Since the noble and virtuous elephant Devadatta has returned safely with me, is this not the end of my sorrow?
As Your Majesty has said, I shall consider it further to see whether I may obtain [the horse]."

Having devised this plan, he informed the king that he could depart. He then gathered the goods required for the city of Uśīnara, sought out a capable merchant leader, and found a beautiful woman; he had her fully adorned with necklaces and ornaments to serve as the wife of the merchant leader.
Having performed these tasks, the caravan set out and gradually reached the city of Uśīnara.
When King Caṇḍapradyota heard that a great caravan had arrived at his city, he went out in person to inspect them and collect the tolls.
Having arrived at the camp, he asked, "Where does the merchant leader reside?

Guided by those who pointed the way, the king went there, opened the door, and entered. Proceeding straight into the central courtyard, he beheld the merchant leader’s wife; her countenance was exceptionally distinguished, such as he had never seen before, and her exquisite adornment was utterly beyond anything found among men, with no one in this city able to equal her. The king conceived a lustful intent and addressed her, saying:
“O virtuous one! Come and enjoy yourself with me.
The woman said:
"This is the bedding; use it as you wish.

Since he was already entangled by the fetters of lustful defilement, there was nothing he would not do; he immediately sat and lay down with her to engage in sexual intercourse, his mind so clouded and deluded that he could no longer distinguish between before and after.

The merchant leader immediately covered [the body] entirely with cloth, had four men carry the bier, and while the great assembly sang songs, they departed through the rear gate of the city of Uśīnara and proceeded on their long journey.
At that time, some of the attendants shook their bells and sang this song:
"A mosquito among men can devour the moon; King Vaiśravaṇa is dragged away by his creditors;
The earth, the trees, and the sky— A courtesan can carry away even the Fierce Light."
At that time, all the merchants within the city, seeing this joyous celebration, said, "The caravan is about to depart," and they all followed along.
The people of the city were entirely unaware of the king’s destination; Bṛhaspati, finding the king strange, searched for him everywhere.
Those traveling merchants brought King Candraprabha along until they gradually reached the kingdom of Kauśāmbī. The ministers congratulated him, saying: "Great King!
Your royal lineage shall flourish and all your wishes shall be fulfilled, for King Candraprabha has arrived here."
The king said, "Bind him with shackles and chains and compel him to learn the craft of a weaver; furthermore, do not allow anyone to inform Devadatta.
Later, while the king and Devadatta were together on a high tower enjoying themselves as they pleased, King Candraprabha left the weaver’s workshop due to some minor business.
At that time, Devasmitā saw him from atop the tower in the distance and said to Devadatta, "Do you recognize that man?
The King’s former concubine, Sthūlanandā, gazed at him closely; she then recognized him, her tears fell upon her breast, and she thought to herself:

"Now that this wicked king has brought my father to such a state of distress, if I do not kill this evil king, I shall no longer be called Devadatta; though I commit the killing, I shall ensure he remains unaware."
The King, being of sharp faculties, perceived his resentment and said to the minister:

"I have already settled my vengeance against Candraprabha; you should now bathe his body, prepare a sumptuous meal of fragrant food, and escort him back to his own country with full ceremonial honors."
Because he followed the king’s instructions and released them all in succession to allow them to return, Devadatta then thought to himself:

"If I were to employ a means for his murder right now, he possesses such evil intelligence that he would immediately become suspicious; therefore, let us first pass the time and wait for another day."
They forced themselves to speak and laugh to dispel their sorrowful feelings.
Suddenly, Tianshou put on soiled and tattered clothes and lay upon a broken bed; seeing this, Chuangguang asked, "What is the reason for this?"
He replied, "A celestial deity is angry with me.
The king said:
"Madam, what deficiency do you have such that your wish remains unfulfilled? She replied,
"That which I previously promised can never be obtained."
The king said,
"What have you promised that causes you such premonitory anxiety?
Whatever your heart desires, I shall provide it all for you."
He replied: "In the past, when my father imprisoned Your Majesty, I made this petition to the deities:

'If I and the King reach Kauśāmbī in safety, I shall abstain from food and drink for seven days and seven nights. When those days have passed, I will take a fine flower garland and wind it from the tips of my toes up to my neck, and place you upon a litter atop the city wall.'"
"I have already established a great assembly of offerings for the King, commanding a multitude of brahmins numbering a full thousand to perform extensive acts of worship.
Great King, you now possess many ladies of the inner palace; how could you possibly harbor any further anxiety regarding me?"
"By this calculation, it is certain that death will come; there is no doubt.
The King said, "This is precisely what you have prayed for on my behalf from heaven. You need not worry any further; I shall do everything for you."

From that time forward, he devised a means to kill them: he tied two puppies beneath the city wall and fed them fine meat every day. As they grew, they eventually became so large that they could eat as much meat as a human body.
He then made a solemn vow with the king to abstain from both food and drink for seven days. During the night, Devadatta secretly ate his fill.

For the duration of the seven days, the king resolved not to eat; his body became so emaciated that he could no longer support himself. When the seven days were complete, Devadatta summoned the garland-makers and said, "You must quickly produce many fragrant garlands using coarse thread and bring them to me."
He commanded Yujianna, saying:

"Today the Great King’s period of observance has come to an end; you should adorn the city walls and moats and extensively prepare for a great assembly of almsgiving, providing for more than a thousand Brahmins."
The various ministers each hurried about, desiring not to let anyone know of the secret affairs within the inner palace.

At that time, Yu-kyen-na (Yaugandharāyaṇa) carried out all the imperial commands: he swept and scrubbed the streets, sprinkled them with scented water, and ensured that there was nowhere not pervaded by the fragrance of incense burners and precious canopies. Flowers of various kinds were scattered everywhere until they filled the air; it was most delightful, like the Garden of Joy (Nandana). In every place there were various drums and music, their sounds blending in harmony as dancing girls performed with graceful movements.

While this commotion was occurring, Devadatta immediately led the King up to the top of the city wall, forced him to lie on the ground, and wound a flower garland around him from his feet to the crown of his head until there was no empty space between them; he then pushed him over.
Once they had fallen to the base of the city wall, the two dogs devoured the flesh and blood until it was entirely gone, leaving only the remaining white bones.
At that time, crows, ravens, eagles, vultures, jackals, and their like ate the meat, while birds and beasts licked and pecked at the skeletal remains.

At that time, all the people within the great city were struck with alarm and terror, as it was rumored that the Great King had personally ascended the city wall to observe the assembly, only to fall from its corner and die thereupon, his body being devoured by dogs.
Upon hearing this, the multitude raised a cry of lamentation; tearing their hair and beating their breasts, they filled the city with clamor.
At that time, the bhikṣus all dispersed in every direction, some heading for other places and others proceeding to the Jeta Grove.
The various ministers gathered together and deliberated:
"For what reason has the Great King ascended the city wall himself?
For what cause does a dog come from below the wall to eat?"
The ministers deliberated together and, upon seeing the thread from the flower garland, realized that Devadatta had certainly devised this evil plot in advance to kill their Great King.
Having conceived a fierce anger, they constructed a chamber of lacquer resin, caused Devadatta to enter its center, and set it on fire; he suffered there and died.
Thus, one knows that the mutual retribution of enemies has no day of rest.
At that time, all the bhikṣus gave rise to doubts and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"O Bhadanta!..."
"What karma did King Prabhāsa previously create,
by the power of which he was born to be devoured by dogs?
The Buddha said:

"O Bhikṣus! This King Prabhāsa encountered the ripening of the causes and conditions of karma he himself created in the past; it has manifested before him like a torrential flood that nothing can obstruct."
"Who shall take upon themselves the karmic results of King Prasenajit’s actions? O Bhikṣus!

Whatever karma one performs does not ripen within the external four great elements; rather, one experiences the retribution of pleasure and pain only within one's own aggregates, elements, and sense bases. As it is said in a verse:"
"Even if a hundred eons were to pass, The karma one has created does not perish;
When causes and conditions converge, One must experience the retribution oneself."
"O Bhikṣus! In the distant past, in a certain capital city, there lived a brahmin minister.

At that time, when no Buddha had appeared in the world, a Pratyekabuddha had manifested in the world—one who felt compassion for the poor and delighted in dwelling in solitude; he was the sole field of merit in the world."

A certain pratyekabuddha, wandering through the human realm, arrived at this city and stayed overnight in a secluded grove; when dawn broke, he took up his robes and bowl and entered the city to beg for alms.
At that time, the minister led his dogs out of the city to hunt; seeing this Pratyekabuddha, who was free from all fault and possessed the marks of a great man, he released the dogs to devour him.
"O Bhikṣus! What do you think?
Do not harbor other thoughts; could that great minister be anyone else?"
The present monk Devarāja was once a person who,
in the presence of a faultless holy man, released a dog to eat him.
By the power of this karma, for five hundred lifetimes he constantly met his end by being eaten by dogs.
"O bhikṣus, you should know this!

If one performs purely black karma, one will obtain a purely black retribution; if one performs purely white karma, one will obtain a purely white retribution; and if one performs mixed karma, one will obtain a mixed retribution. For this reason, you should abandon both black and mixed karma, and instead cultivate white karma."
"O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, King Pradyota of Kauśāmbī died, and King Candapradyota of Ujjayinī dwelt in peace and security, free from all enemies.
Once, while on a high palace terrace, he engaged in improper conversation with his ministers and asked them,
"In which city or village is there a beautiful courtesan?"
Someone said: "Great King!

There is a king named Pūrṇavijaya in the city of Takṣaśilā. In that city, there is a courtesan of exquisite beauty who possesses sixty-four arts; among all the men within this great earth, there has never been one who did not become infatuated upon merely seeing her."
As soon as the king heard this description of her beauty and wisdom, he conceived a deep attachment and said to Vaḍḍha:
"Even if one were to search far and wide, a woman such as this would be difficult to find; I shall now go there myself to enjoy her company."
He replied: "Great King!
That King Maṇicūḍa has been an enemy of yours for a long time; he currently resides in Takṣaśilā."
"If the King goes in person, they will surely perceive it as an improper act when they understand the timing.
He replied, "My intention is now set; the matter must not be contravened."
"You remain here; I shall depart!
He replied, "Your Majesty's command is difficult to disobey; you may go as you please, but you must be cautious."
Then the king mounted the great elephant Veṣmanta and proceeded toward that city; on the way there was a mountain of stone pestles, where he stationed the elephant and entered the city himself.
Having arrived there, he immediately removed the exquisite pearl necklace from his neck, worth ten million, and gave it to that courtesan, whereupon they engaged in sexual intercourse.
At that time, the ministers, the populace, and the brahmins of the city of Ujjayinī were astonished that the king was nowhere to be seen and wondered where he had gone.
They said to one another:
"The King is no ordinary person; his departure will surely be known by others.
They further said:
"The King already possesses such abundance within his inner palace;
what more could he possibly seek? They replied again, "We ought to go together and ask Puṣkara."
They immediately went together to him and asked,
"Great King, we do not know where you have gone? He replied:
"Why do you all so urgently wish to see the King?
Be patient for a while longer; you shall see him before long. They asked:
"When can they be seen? He replied,
"In twelve full years."
All the people, filled with indignation, replied:
"You have now killed the king and wish to establish yourself; how can you utter such unrighteous words?
If you see the king within seven days, it will be well; if you do not, we shall install another king and end your life."
Having heard this, Poṣaṇa remained silent, dwelling in a state of sorrow.
At that time, the chief queen of Govinda’s mother saw that Poṣaṇa was distressed and addressed him, asking:
"For what reason are you now so filled with anxiety and fear?"
He replied: "O Lady!
When the Great Brahmin and the various ministers spoke thus, reporting all that had occurred, how could my heart remain free from sorrow?"

The lady said, "You may mix honey with clarified butter and smear it upon parched barley grains; place them in a golden platter and carry it to the stall of the superior horse. Kneel before him and speak these words:
'If there is anyone capable of traveling to the city of Takṣaśilā today, they may eat this parched barley mixed with honey and clarified butter from the golden platter.'"
Although the horse heard this announcement, it did not eat a single morsel.

At that time, there was a thin and weak old horse standing apart to one side with its ears drooping; [the king] then went to its place and, holding a golden platter in his hands, acted exactly as previously described.
Having heard these words, he went to the tray and ate it all.
He then reported this matter in detail to the lady. The lady said:

"You may go and saddle [the horse]. If you see any unusual signs, you need not be afraid; you should manifest a heroic and fierce bearing before them. For those who possess courage, no creature can deceive them."
He immediately went to him, lifted the saddle, and was about to place it on; however, the horse suddenly became agitated and transformed its appearance, saying:
"O man! Have you ever seen such a horse before?"
He then drew his sword and replied,
"O Yakṣa Jīmūta! Have you ever before seen such a horseman?"
He replied, “I did not see it. He was told:
“Horse-King Yakṣa!
It would be well if you could depart without violating the established rule; if you do not go, I shall sever your head, and its blood shall flow upon the ground.”
He replied, "Sir!
Let us make an agreement: I shall go for you, but do not bring me back here again."
He replied, "Go as you please; I shall not betray your trust.
He then mounted the horse and gradually arrived at the city of Takṣaśilā.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu, Fascicle Twenty-three.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu,
Fascicle Twenty-four.
The *Saṃgraha-gāthā* precedes this.
At that time, King Pracaṇḍa was in the house of a courtesan in Takṣaśilā; seeing Puṣkarasārin approaching, he asked:
"Why have you come? they asked.
He then answered them fully regarding the matter.
The king said, "I am currently enjoying myself; when the seven days are complete, we may go together."
When the full term had expired, he went to Mount Śilāmuṣala and mounted his elephant himself; the elephant then let out a great roar.
Not far from there was a man skilled in interpreting signs who, hearing the sound of the elephant’s cry, spoke thus:
"I can discern the intent of an elephant's cry by listening to it. This one will travel a hundred *yojanas* in a day and return to the Southern Sea to drink water and satisfy its thirst."
Upon hearing these words, Vaḍḍha immediately mounted the elephant together with the king and proceeded along the road.
When they reached a potter’s house where there were unbaked earthenware vessels, the elephant stepped on them with its foot, causing the potter to look on in distress.
Poṣadha said, "There are such people who subsist by means of the earth.
The King then became suspicious in his heart and thought to himself:
"Vardhana, this statement of yours mocks me; I alone subsist upon the land of the kingdom—what is the meaning of these words?
I shall remember them later.
Having said this, he departed in silence.
Furthermore, while on the road, he saw a wagtail bird that had laid eggs across the path; when an elephant stepped on them, they were crushed, and the bird cried out in grief.
Upon seeing this, Vaḍḍha spoke these words:
"This should not have been done; it has brought about sorrow and lamentation."
The king again thought to himself:
"These words are yet another way of mocking me.
Entering the house of a courtesan is improper; I shall remember this well hereafter."

He set out along the road and, further along the way, passed beneath a tree while riding an elephant. On a branch of that tree was a black snake, which lowered its body and extended itself downward, intending to bite the King. Upon seeing this, Bhaddāli immediately drew his sword and cut it into several pieces;
as it lay coiled on the ground, Bhaddāli said, "This was not what should have been done, yet you forced yourself to do it."
The king again thought to himself:
"These words are yet another mockery of me; I shall remember this after a third time.
On another day, the elephant then moved swiftly, refusing to go slowly.
Just as they were about to reach the city, Vaḍḍha addressed the King, saying:
"Previously, a physiognomist spoke these words:
'The elephant will travel a hundred *yojanas* and then return toward the Southern Sea to drink water and satisfy its thirst.'"
"Seeing that he is traveling so swiftly, he will certainly not stop; we must embrace a tree branch and let ourselves down.
The King and Vaḍḍha embraced a branch and descended, entering a garden where they allowed the elephant to run away as it pleased.
The King said to Vaḍḍha:
"You may go now and secretly inform Anuruddha, saying:
'I have arrived and am currently in the Fragrant Garden.'"
He immediately went and related everything in detail; having heard his report, the king was filled with boundless joy.
At that time, the king felt ashamed and did not approach the main gate, but instead sought to enter the palace through a water-window.
At that time, there were two women who did not recognize him as the king, and they said to one another,
"I have heard that the Great King has already arrived.
One of them said:
"I was merely thinking that it had entered through this window.
Upon hearing these words, the king thought to himself:
"I ordered Saṃvahaka to inform the queen in secret, yet she has spread the word throughout the city at her own whim."
On another day, unable to bear it in his heart, he said to Puṣkarasārin:
"You have repeatedly uttered various kinds of useless and malicious words toward me to mock me; do I alone enjoy the entire earth?"
In such-and-such a place, you spoke these words:
"These people enjoy the great earth to sustain their own lives.
Furthermore, in such-and-such a place, you spoke these words:
"This should not be done, for it leads to sorrow and lamentation.
Thinking, "I should not go to the courtesans' quarters," he further spoke these words at a certain place:
"This was something that should not have been done, yet you forced yourself to do it.
Was it not improper for me to go to the place of the courtesan?
Furthermore, while you and I were in the Fragrant Garden, I sent you alone to secretly report to the Lady, saying:
"I have now come and am staying within the park.
If you were to announce this throughout the city, it would be doing me no good.
Terrified and alarmed, Upacāra spoke these words:
"May the spirits and deities together bear witness and clearly discern my heart; I truly do not reproach the King.
Previously, at a potter’s workshop, I saw an unbaked earthen vessel being kicked and broken by an elephant's foot, and seeing the potter’s distress, I spoke these words:
'These people depend upon the earth and its soil for their livelihood.'"

Along the way, I saw a small bird that had laid its eggs upon the road; as the elephant walked by, it stepped on and crushed them, whereupon the bird cried out in grief. Seeing this, I spoke these words:
"This creature has produced its offspring in an improper place."
Later, seeing a snake descend from a tree branch intending to bite the king, I cut it into several pieces on the ground and spoke these words:
"You have forcibly acted where you ought not to act."
Regarding these matters, I speak straightforwardly; it is not to disparage the King.
Furthermore, as for the claim that he was sent into the palace to secretly inform the Queen, who then spread these words throughout the city, this too is not so.
"I entered alone to speak in private with the lady; how would I dare do anything harmful to the King?

The King said, "Even if you were to plead your case and claim it was no fault of yours, when I was about to enter the city through the small gate, I personally saw two women making such statements. One said:"
"Your Majesty, please come.
Another said, "Enter by this path."
"If you do not speak, how will she know?
He replied, "She is a flying ogress who has hidden her body to listen secretly to the sound of the king's voice; thus, this is not an unprofitable act on my part."
The king said, "You have committed no fault now; you may set your mind at ease and need not be afraid.
Furthermore, after I have departed, there was a brahmin who said:"
"If the King does not come, we must kill all others who are established [in his place]; now is precisely the time. He replied:
“Brahmin, wait a moment; first we shall kill this evil man who flies through the air.
The king said, “How could he possibly be killed?”
He replied, "I shall devise a plan to kill and eliminate her.
The king said:
"Eliminate evil and practice good.
At that time, there was a son of a high minister in this city who was previously well-versed in mantras.
Manibhadra went to him and asked, "A flying ogress is ravaging living beings; how can you devise a plan to ensure she is completely eliminated?"
He replied, "Father! I am able to capture him."
He then cut off the hand of the corpse and transformed it into an *utpala* flower.
He gave it to a man and told him, "Take this to the marketplace and sell it; however, do not give it to anyone who comes to buy it with money."
"Regarding those who laugh, record their names and note their physical appearances.
The man followed these instructions one by one, and within this city, he recorded the names of five hundred people who laughed.
Having heard this, the king replied to Vaḍḍha, "There are so many people; how can they be killed? He answered:
"I understand the skillful means; Your Majesty need not worry.
The King said, "Do as you see fit."
He then prepared a site by the city wall, having it thoroughly cleansed, and issued a proclamation:
"The King now intends to hold an unobstructed great assembly (*anavadya-mahāpariṣad*) to pray to the celestial deities; you sisters should all assemble here."
Upon hearing the king’s command, the women gathered together with the intent of seeking wealth; though they had no names on the list, they came out of greed, numbering more than five hundred.
The sons of those ministers bound him with magical cords and compelled him to stay; then, Jīvakambala ordered his men to take up knives and slaughter them all.
The King said:
"Although this sorcerer has been eliminated, there are still many Brahmins remaining."
He immediately ordered that this be proclaimed everywhere:
"I have committed immeasurable unwholesome karma by killing five hundred flying yakṣiṇīs.
For the sake of rescuing me, you all should come daily to a single place to receive food."
Upon hearing this, they were all delighted and came to receive [the offerings].
The king commanded his gatekeeper, saying:
"As for the assembly of brahmins who come to receive food, you must count them well and report back to me."
The disciples respectfully assented, and the king further commanded them,
"All you people of the city and its districts should prepare the finest food to offer as alms to the brahmins.
At that time, the brahmins, out of greed for delicious food, accepted the king’s invitation and all assembled together.

When they had finished eating and were about to depart, the gatekeepers counted them and found there were eighty thousand in total; they immediately informed the king, saying, "The number has reached eighty thousand.
Upon hearing this, the king reflected:
"How can one kill many lives at once? he asked.
He then ordered that while each of the brahmins was eating, a butcher should stand behind them with a sword in hand and say:
"If you hear me make the sound 'take the curd,' you must all sever their heads simultaneously."
Having been thus instructed, they acted according to his words, even going so far as to sever all their heads.
When the king had thus slain the many brāhmaṇas, that very night he saw an earthquake in a dream; the six-syllable sound emerged from the earth, and the six-syllable sound issued from the sky.
Furthermore, there are eight dreams.
Regarding the six characters for "earthquake," they signify: "The six [realms] are without self; my base mind is as such.
Regarding the six characters for "emptiness emerging," they signify: "Who among all is now equal to that self?"
What are the eight dreams?
They are as follows: first, seeing white sandalwood incense paste smeared over one’s entire body;
second, seeing red sandalwood scented water poured over one’s body.
Third, he saw fire blazing upon his head;
fourth, he saw two large venomous snakes hanging from his two armpits;
fifth, he saw two carp fish licking his two feet.
Sixth, he saw two white geese flying through the air toward him;
seventh, he saw a massive black mountain approaching head-on;
eighth, he saw a white gull drop excrement upon his head.
At that time, having had these many such dreams, the king was struck with great terror and his hair stood on end; he thought to himself:
"Could it be that because of these matters my royal throne will be lost, or my life forfeited?"
He then summoned a Brahmin skilled in interpreting dreams and informed him of it. The Brahmin thought to himself:
"This is a favorable dream for the King; I must declare it to be inauspicious.
If I say it is favorable, his arrogance will increase further and his evil views will grow, leading to the further execution of other Brahmins."
Having had this thought, they consulted together and replied,
"Great King! This is not a favorable dream."
The king said, "Tell me, what will be the retribution? He replied:
"This dream portends that the sovereignty of the kingdom will decline and that my own life shall come to an end.
Upon hearing this, the king was overcome with great distress.
At that time, the king further thought to himself:
"Is there any expedient means by which my life may be preserved and my royal throne not lost?
I should now go to the Venerable Kātyāyana to inquire about my fortune; could this not be an ill omen for me?"
Having arrived there, he prostrated with his head at [the Elder’s] feet, sat to one side, and reported everything concerning the dream.
The Venerable replied: “Great King!
"Have you perhaps asked about this matter elsewhere? He replied, "Noble One!"
He asked about others as well. "From whom did you ask? He replied:
“At the place of the brahmin. “What did he predict?
The king then reported in full what had been said by him.
The Venerable One replied:
“Great King! They constantly indulge in sensual pleasures and aspire only to rebirth in heaven; what else could they possibly know?”
The dream Your Majesty has had is an auspicious omen; there is no need for alarm or fear. You shall not lose your throne or meet with death because of this. Why is that?
As for the six sounds heard by Your Majesty from the earth, what is their premonitory significance?
Thus it should be understood that this is a mutual admonition for kings, intended to cause them to reform their evils and follow what is wholesome.
In the past, there were six kings who ruled the world unrighteously; when their bodies perished and their lives ended, they fell into hell.
This first king, undergoing extreme suffering within hell, spoke this verse, which begins with the word "Six" (Ṣaḍ):
"For sixty-six thousand years, I was burned and boiled in hell;
Now experiencing extreme suffering, I do not yet know when it shall end."
The second king also spoke in verse, which is the second "No" (Mu):
"There is no end to suffering; Even when the sun has set, it is not known.
We are all likewise the same, This being due to our past evil karma."
The third king also spoke in verse, which is the third instance of the word "I":
"The food and clothing I obtain, whether by right or by wrong,
Are enjoyed by others while I alone suffer calamity."
The fourth king also spoke in verse, namely the fourth line beginning with the character "vile" (鄙):
"Vile is my physical life, That there are things I cannot relinquish;
I do not bestow food and drink upon others, Causing this body to be of no benefit."
The fifth king also spoke in verse, which is the fifth character, "Mind" (Citta):
"Mind constantly deceives me, Perpetually dragged by ignorance;
When suffering in the hells, No one is willing to take my place."
The sixth king also spoke in verse, namely the sixth syllable "Ja":
"If I am born in the human realm, I shall constantly cultivate all manner of virtues;
By the power of such meritorious karma, I shall surely attain rebirth in heaven."
"Therefore, these six sounds manifest his past karma.
Furthermore, Great King,
as for these six sounds in the air, whose omens are they?"
It should be understood in this way:
within the king’s residence there is a large bamboo pole, upon which many minute insects feed; that which is soft has been entirely consumed, leaving behind only what is hard and rigid.
The insects were distressed, fearing their lives would not be spared; they spoke this verse together to inform the master of the house—this was the first word, "zhū" (all).
"All soft parts have been eaten, And only the tough skin remains;
May Your Majesty know our distress, And provide us with other [food] instead."
“The King removed the old bamboo and installed new ones, which enabled many insects to survive.
Furthermore, Great King!
The King has a groom named Upaka, who was previously blind in one eye.”

That man, day after day, broke the eggs within the crow’s nest. When the crows saw their offspring dead, they were filled with resentment and cried out in unison, reciting this verse; this was the second instance of the word "Who."
"Who else could act for me by piercing a man until his eyes go blind,
rather than killing my sons and grandsons, thereby removing the sorrow and affliction from my heart?"
"Your Majesty should restrain him and prevent this from happening again.
Furthermore, Great King!
In the royal park there is a pleasure pool, its waters originally full to the brim, inhabited by many fish, turtles, and frogs; there was a white heron that constantly fed upon those fish."
Now the pond has dried up and is without water; seeing this, the bird gave rise to lamentation and spoke a verse, which is the third [verse beginning with] the character "Ping" (Level):
"The level ground was once ever-filled with water, Where many fish and turtles abounded;
I took them as food to sustain my body, But now the water has all vanished."
"Your Majesty should now add water to it and drive the birds away. "Furthermore, Great King! In this kingdom of yours there is a great mountain called Bhīṣma.

Upon it dwell a male elephant and a female elephant who are both blind from birth. They have only one son who constantly serves them. For the sake of his parents, he went out to seek food and encountered a female elephant; following her, he was gradually enticed to a park where he was subsequently bound. Remembering his parents, he was filled with grief and remorse, refusing to eat grass or drink water, and spoke these verses—this being the fourth verse beginning with the word 'Now' (jina)."
"Now my parents are solitary and alone; born blind, they have no guide.
Dwelling deep within the mountains, with no food, who will care for and nourish them?"
"Your Majesty should now order that elephant to be released so that it may rejoice together with its parents.
"Furthermore, Great King!

In Your Majesty’s residence there is a bound deer; having been separated from its former herd, it has conceived distress in its heart and speaks this verse, which is the fifth instance of the syllable 'that' (pa)."
"The entire herd enjoys happiness, roaming at will among water and grass;
only I am bound in restraint, harboring sorrow alone day and night."
"Your Majesty should release him and allow him to go to the mountain forests.
Furthermore, Great King!
In Your Majesty’s palace there was a goose that had been tied up; looking up at the sky, it saw a flock of geese flying away, and feeling distressed, it spoke this verse:
This refers to the sixth character, "I" (吾). [The verse says:
"When the flock of birds has all departed, / And their drinking and pecking follow their own whims;
/ What sinful karma is there in my person?"
"Bound as we are, life is weary.
"The King should give rise to a heart of compassion and likewise release us.

Furthermore, Great King, regarding the eight things you saw in your dream, what are their portents? As for seeing white sandalwood-scented mud smeared all over your body: it is a sign that a king from a superior region will send a great white woolen cloak to present to Your Majesty!
"Now that he has reached the halfway point, he will surely arrive here after seven days; this is a preliminary omen.
Furthermore, as for seeing red sandalwood scented water sprinkled upon his body: it means the King of Gandhāra is sending a cloak of red-furled precious wool to present to Your Majesty!"
"Now that we have reached the halfway point, it shall also arrive here seven days from now; this is a premonitory sign.

Furthermore, as for seeing fire burning upon the head: the King of Pañcāla is sending a golden wreath to present to Your Majesty, and it is coming along the road; it shall also arrive here seven days from now—this is a premonitory sign."

"Furthermore, as for seeing two large venomous snakes hanging down from both armpits: this is an omen that a King of China has sent two precious swords to present to Your Majesty; they will arrive in seven days, traveling along the road."

"Furthermore, as for seeing two carp licking his two feet: a king from Siṃhala Island has sent a pair of precious sandals to offer to the Great King; they are traveling by way of the road and shall arrive in seven days—this is a premonitory sign."

"Furthermore, as for seeing two white geese flying through the air and coming toward us: this is an omen that the King of Tukhāra has sent two fine horses as a gift to the Great King; they are traveling along the road and shall arrive in seven days."

"Furthermore, seeing the Great Black Mountain approaching directly before us is an omen that the King of Kalinga has sent two great elephant kings as tribute to Your Majesty; they are traveling by way of the roads and shall arrive in seven days."
"Furthermore, as for seeing white gulls dropping excrement upon their heads, this is an omen concerning Queen Anala, the mother of Gopāla; Your Majesty should know this yourself."
"Nevertheless, Your Majesty should not give rise to further ill-will toward the brahmin.

When King Caṇḍapradyota heard these words, he leaped for joy as if one returning from death to life; filled with deep faith, he prostrated at [the monk's] feet and departed. Returning to his palace, he followed all the instructions of the Venerable One exactly as taught.

He separately placed large bamboo, blocked the horseman, filled the dried-up pond with water until it was full, released the elephant and the deer, and set free the tied geese; when the seven days had passed, everything arrived exactly as he had foretold.
Having seen this, the king conceived even greater reverence for the Venerable One and thought to himself:

"All the auspiciousness within my palace is brought about solely by the power of the Noble One’s merit. For now, I shall offer him the great woolen cloak I have recently obtained as an act of worship; later, I shall offer the throne of kingship to the Venerable One."
He then said to the messenger,
"Take this woolen cloak and present it to the Venerable Kātyāyana.
The messenger then took it and offered it to the Venerable One.
Next, he addressed Queen Śrīmatī, Queen Tārā, Prince Govinda, and the minister Pālaka, saying:
"Gentlemen, you should know that all the great kings currently ruling in these various kingdoms—
"All have brought tributes from their respective kingdoms to present to me;

you may take whatever you desire as you please. At that time, Queen Anurādhā took the golden garland; the junior queen Jyotiṣprabhā took the red-furred woolen cloak; Prince Govinda took the two horses; Vaśabha took the two swords; the minister took the jeweled sandals; and the King himself took the precious elephant.
At that time, King Pradyota had finished distributing the five precious gifts offered by others among them all; he then went to the Venerable One, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and said:
"Virtuous One!..."

“Your compassionate deeds are vast and profound; it is difficult to describe them all in detail. I respectfully hold the sovereignty of the kingdom and offer it to you, Venerable One. I only pray that, out of compassion and pity, you will graciously accept it.
The Venerable One replied, “The World-Honored One has given instruction forbidding bhikṣus from accepting royal thrones.”
The king said, "If it be so, you shall receive half the kingdom. He replied:
"This too is not permitted," [the monk] said.
The King replied, "If being a sovereign of a kingdom is what the Buddha forbids, then there should be no harm in enjoying the five desires; I shall offer them all to you."
He replied: "Great King! The Buddha does not permit any sensual desires whatsoever."
The king said:
"Since you do not accept this, please accept all my enjoyments, superior luxuries, and personal requisites, and use them as you please."
He replied, "Great King! Wait while I inform the Buddha."
The King said, "Please the Buddha as you wish.
At that time, the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī; since there is nothing the Great Teacher does not know or see, he then had this thought:
"Even if Kātyāyana has no personal need for these requisites or superior enjoyments, he should nevertheless accept them for the sake of future bhikṣus."
Having formed this thought, he gave rise to a conventional mind.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas:
whenever they give rise to a conventional mind, even ants and insects come to know the Buddha’s intention.
When he gave rise to the supramundane mind, even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas were unable to comprehend it, let alone animals.

At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One, knowing Kātyāyana’s intention from afar, gave rise to a mundane mind and immediately caused Kātyāyana’s divine ear and divine eye to hear and see one another.
At that time, the Venerable One addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
May a bhikṣu accept articles for ordinary use as well as articles for superior use?”
The Buddha said:

"Out of compassion for the bhikṣus of future generations, and so that the merit and reward of donors may increase, I now permit the Sangha of the four directions to accept items for general use and superior use; this does not apply to individuals."
"In this context, 'enjoyment' refers to villages and fields;
'superior enjoyment' refers to cattle, sheep, and the like.
Having thus requested the World-Honored One, the Venerable One addressed King Caṇḍapradyota, saying:

“The Blessed One has already granted permission for the Saṅgha of the four directions to accept and utilize [requisites] and superior enjoyments, out of compassion for the bhikṣus of future generations and so that the merit and reward of donors may increase.”

Thereupon, the king immediately built a great monastery for the Venerable One; he provided him with all four types of requisites in full abundance and bestowed fields, lands, oxen, and livestock upon the Sangha of the four quarters.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"I now first permit upāsakas to offer articles for the use and enjoyment of the Saṅgha of the four quarters among the śrāvakas; this refers to King Prasenajit of the city of Ujjayinī, who was the foremost."

Furthermore, it was first permitted for an upāsaka to offer cakes and food to the Saṃgha of the four quarters of śrāvakas, beginning with King Bimbisāra, the sovereign of Magadha at Vulture Peak Mountain.
Furthermore, I first permitted the upāsakas to provide bedding and requisites for the Saṅgha of the four quarters of all śrāvakas, with the householder Anāthapiṇḍada of Śrāvastī as their leader.
Furthermore, I first permitted upāsakas to construct vihāras for the Saṃgha of the four quarters of śrāvakas, with the elder Bhadra of Vārāṇasī being the foremost among them.
The preceding verses are summarized as follows:
“Candapradyota gave all things; Bimbisāra first offered cakes;
Regarding bedding and seats, it was Anāthapiṇḍada; and Sudatta constructed the monastery.”
At that time, King Candraprabha was once eating his evening meal within the palace together with Queen Sukhāvatī; the king was by nature fond of curd.

The queen stood before the king holding a bowl of curd. At that moment, the starlight passed in front of the palace eaves, which were draped with a cloak of exquisite jewels; the color of the cloak shone through like a flash of lightning, illuminating both the king and the queen so that they were clearly visible.
When the lady saw the light, she was greatly startled and marveled, asking, "Great King!
What is this brilliant illumination?"
"Is this a flash of lightning,
or is it the flame of a lamp? He replied:
"This is neither lightning nor the flame of a lamp;
rather, it is the radiance of Starlight as she passes by here, draped in her precious brocade cloak.
The king said:
"To discard such a precious brocade and refuse to take it, only to accept this golden wreath, is truly a lack of discernment. Is there no golden wreath in my palace?
Who says that a woman from a foreign land can know what is fine or coarse?"
He replied: "Great King! How could such wisdom possibly exist [in me]?"
"Is it not that Your Majesty commanded the taking of the woolen cloak?
The King said, "He took it himself; it was not my command."
The king and his consort, having thus come to treat one another with contempt, were overcome by anger and resentment; she then took a bowl of curd and hurled it at the king’s head.
The king had previously suffered from a protruding forehead, and being wounded by the bowl, he rubbed it with his own hand and said:
"My head is split, blood flows, and my brain is exposed; I shall certainly die now, and there is no way to escape. Before my life is severed, I shall kill her first."
He then commanded Vaḍḍha, saying:
"You should now put this useless woman, Anuruddhā, to death.
Upon hearing this, Vaḍḍha thought to himself:

"The King holds you in such deep affection that these words were uttered suddenly out of a fit of resentment; you should not terminate his life so precipitously. Wait until his anger has subsided, and only then kill him after examining his intent—it will not be difficult. For now, keep him in a secluded place and do not let the King see him."
Having formed this thought, he said,
“So be it; I shall kill him immediately,” and then he concealed [the victim].
Once the king’s anger had subsided, he asked Vaḍḍha,
"Where is Queen Kṣemā now? He replied:
“Great King! Having received Your Majesty’s command to execute him, I have obeyed Your Majesty’s word and already taken his life.
The king said:
"This is an extraordinary matter; we must also put to death myself, Prabhāvatī, Prince Govinda, and a high minister. You shall yourself be consecrated as the sovereign of this great kingdom.
As for his act of insolence toward me, let it serve as a warning so that he may deliberate more carefully in the future; how could it be appropriate to carry out execution on account of this alone?"
Udayin said: "Your Majesty, please listen to a parable, for those who possess wisdom understand a matter through the words of a parable.
A summary verse states:
The pigeon died, its body raw; the three kinds of difficulties were not applicable;
observing it without weariness, he did not sleep—these seven verses are collected in total.
The first internal summary verse says:
"The wood pigeon has died within the forest; the monkey has perished beneath the tree.
Within this world and the world beyond, one should recognize these four blind darknesses.
"Great King! [he said.]
In times past, there was a famous mountain where the springs flowed with clear, cool water and the fruit trees flourished in full bloom.
At the top of a great tree, two doves lived together in a nest they had built; they gathered fine fruits and filled their nest with them, and the male dove said to his mate: "O fair one!"

The fruit stored herein should not be eaten haphazardly; rather, one should first seek other things to temporarily sustain the body, and only when encountering wind or rain such that food and drink are difficult to obtain may it be shared and consumed.
He replied, "A good thing. However,
it was subsequently exposed to the wind and sun until it became parched and withered, so that there was a deficiency within the nest.
The male dove asked, "I told you before:
'You must not eat the fruit; you may only consume it when the time of wind and rain arrives.'"
"For what reason have you come to eat fruit alone?
He replied, "I did not eat fruit."
He asked, "I previously filled this nest entirely with fruit; now that it is deficient, where has it gone if it was not eaten? He replied:
"I do not know for what reason we have been deprived of food. Both doves said,
"We did not eat."
The two birds’ dispute led to such a commotion that the male dove pecked at the female’s crown with its beak until she died.
The male dove remained by her side, watching over her until he grew weary; suddenly, as it began to rain, the fruits filled the nest once more. The male dove thought to himself:
“Now the nest is full again; clearly, she did not eat them.”
He then approached the female dove and apologized, saying:
"O lovely, variegated dove, please rise quickly; The fruit missing from the nest was not for you to eat.
Now see that what was sparse has become full as before; May you now forgive me for this transgression."
At that time, various devas in the sky, having seen this, spoke in verse:
"You who once shared the company of the fine-textured partridge, Delighting in dwelling among the mountains and forests;
Now, being foolish and lacking wisdom, You grieve in vain after having killed him."
At that time, Vaḍḍha spoke two verses:
"Just like that foolish pigeon, Who killed its own kind without cause;
Unaware that its life had come to an end, It repented and felt deep sorrow."
The Great King is likewise like him; though innocent, he has been driven by anger toward those he loves.
Having already ordered their execution, he needlessly gives rise to grief and affliction for himself.
"I shall speak another parable so that the King may understand."
Furthermore, Great King!
Long ago there was an elder who, when autumn arrived, took yellow beans on his shoulder and went to a field intending to sow them; he set them down beneath a tree at a place where he could turn back.
A monkey on the tree came down to steal some seeds; having taken a handful, it climbed back to the top of the tree.
While climbing up, it dropped a single seed, yet it let go of the full handful and descended the tree to search for that one yellow bean.
The elder saw this and immediately struck him with a staff, whereupon he died.
At that time, there was a tree spirit who, seeing this, spoke a verse:
"Just like that foolish monkey, Who cast away the handful to seek a single grain; [He has lost both for the sake of one.]”
"Because of this, he was beaten by others, and his suffering led to his death.
"The King previously sent me to kill the Queen; for the sake of a minor moment of anger, he has lost a great benefit. Now that I seek to see him again, can it be possible?"
The King said to Vaḍḍha,
"For what reason did you kill the Queen on a single word? He replied:
"Does Your Majesty not hear this: 'The Great Teacher has no duality; that which he utters is but a single word.
It is certain and never inconsistent; so too is the speech of the King.'"
The King said, "My mind was darkened and confused, and I ordered the lady to be killed;
you immediately followed my words— how could that be considered right?"
Udayin said, "Does Your Majesty not hear that there are two kinds of darkness in the world?
He then replied with a verse:
“Great King, you should now know that there are two kinds of darkness in the world:
first, those who are blind from birth; second, those who do not understand the Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding this life and future lives, there are again two kinds of darkness:”
The first is the view of evil; the second is the destruction of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
The secondary internal summary verse says:
"Nakedness is empty and useless; a pestle and mortar should be used as one."
Suffering and harm give rise to doubt; matters of contempt must be handled gradually.
The King said to Vaḍḍha:
"You have killed Queen Kṣemā; I am now left naked."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not hear that there are three naked bodies in the world that do not constitute auspicious signs?
What are these three?"
“As a river without water leaves one with bare skin, so it is when a kingdom lacks a sovereign;
when a woman’s husband has perished, she has no place of refuge to turn to.
The King said:
"You have killed the queen, leaving the palace entirely empty.
He replied, "Does Your Majesty not know that there are three other kinds of emptiness in this world?"
What are the three?
"An ox that is slow on the road, food that lacks variety in flavor,
and a house with a wanton woman— these three are empty."
The king said,
"That beloved lady had not yet fully enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses, and you have nonetheless killed her. He replied:
“Does Your Majesty not hear that there are three things in the world that are likewise never put to use?
What are these three?
‘The fine clothes of a charcoal-seller; the shoes of a washerman;”
"One should know that while the woman is within the royal palace, she has no enjoyment [of it]. 'Great King!
Not only these three, but there are another three kinds that are not enjoyed.'"
What are the three?
"In a secluded ravine, spring flowers bloom; a young woman maintains her chaste heart.
Her husband has gone far on a military expedition; she passes day and night in solitude."
The king said, "You acted with such recklessness as to kill my consort; your crime deserves the punishment of the pestle and mortar. He replied:
"O King, have you not heard that there are others who likewise deserve the mortar and pestle?
The carpenter who does not examine his work well, the tailor who uses long thread,
and the charioteer who does not inspect his carriage— these three deserve the mortar and pestle."
"Great King! It is not only these three that ought to be placed upon the pestle and mortar; there are another three kinds as well.
What are these three?"
"The messenger sends another messenger, and that one sends another to have yet another do it;
the young girl loves to act wantonly—these three should be placed upon the pestle and mortar.
Your Majesty, it is not only these three; there are three others who likewise deserve the pestle and mortar."
What are the three? "One who grazes cattle within the fields, one who shaves his head and dwells in the forest thickets,
and one who constantly stays at his wife's family home— these three should be treated as a pestle and mortar."
The king said, “I have uttered but a single word, and you have already killed my lady; this is truly a great suffering! He replied:
"Does Your Majesty not hear that there is another certainty in the world, which consists of three things?
What are these three?
'Once a king has uttered a word, once a woman has been wed.'"
"As soon as the Noble One appears, these three will become one.
The King said:
"You have now brought this calamity upon yourself; having received but a single word from me, you have gone and killed my consort."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not hear that there are three things in the world that create their own harm?
What are these three?"
“The weak man who dons armor, the one without companions who possesses much wealth,
and the aged man who keeps young wives— these three bring about their own ruin.
The King said:
"I now suspect that you harbor some other intention; how could you kill the lady with such a single-minded resolve?
He replied, "Does Your Majesty not know that there are three types of people in the world who cause others to doubt them upon seeing them?"
What are these three?
"To see a person of shallow wisdom practicing superior conduct; to see a brave and strong man without a single scar;
and to see an old woman speak of her chastity—these three can cause others to fall into doubt."
The king said, "You treat me with extreme contempt; why did you so recklessly kill my queen? He replied:
"O King, have you not heard that there are three things in this world by which one is held in contempt?
What are these three?
'To speak much when there is nothing to say, and to wear soiled and tattered clothing.'"
"Not going when invited to another's house—these three things cause one to be despised by others.
The King said:
"You wish to gradually increase my enemies; having killed my beloved wife, what else remains?"
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not hear that there are three further matters that must be approached gradually?
What are these three?"
"Eating fish must be done gradually; climbing a mountain is likewise so.
Great matters are not accomplished abruptly—these three require gradual progress.
The summary verse for the third internal section says:
There are three kinds of foolish people, and there are three distinct types of sowing discord.
One of inferior quality should be torn apart by chariots; one should know that this concerns matters of treachery and deceit.
The King said:
"You are a fool; how could you kill my beloved wife?
He replied, "Does Your Majesty not know that there are likewise three signs of folly in this world?"
What are the three? "Entrusting one's affairs to those with whom one has no mutual understanding, serving those of impulsive temperament,
and abandoning others in haste— these are called the three marks of folly."
The king said,
"You are the one who sowed discord between me and my close friend and caused the murder of my consort. He replied:
"Does Your Majesty not hear that there are also three kinds of estrangement in the world?
What are these three?
'Not associating with a true friend, or else being too intimate.'"
"Seeking at improper times; these three you should abandon.
The King said:
"You are a base person, for you have killed my consort."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not hear that there are yet another three kinds of inferior persons?
What are these three?"
"One who covets the property of others, clings with attachment to their own wealth,
and feels joy at the sight of another's suffering— such a person is of the lowest class.
The King said:
"You deserve to be torn apart by chariots for killing my queen.
He replied, "Does Your Majesty not know that there are three other instances where one deserves to die by being torn apart by chariots?"
What are the three?
"One who is naturally clumsy yet builds mechanical contrivances, one who paints without knowing colors,
and a strong man lacking skillful means— these three all deserve to die."
The king said, "You are a great traitor; you have killed my queen. He replied:
"Does Your Majesty not hear that there are yet three other types of deceitful things?
What are these three?
'A woman who has married three times, And one who left the household life and returned to secular life.'"
"A bird caught in a net escapes its cage and flies away; these three ways of escaping deceit.
The summary verse of the fourth section on internal matters says:
"Difficult to obtain for the sake of others; matters concerning the solitary are mostly false."
"Since you have acted in opposition and struck me repeatedly, it is useless for you to lose your livelihood.
The King said, "The lady was difficult to find; you have now killed her."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not hear that there are four other things in the world that are difficult to obtain? What are these four?"
"A rabbit's head rarely yields horns; a tortoise's back rarely yields hair;
a wanton woman rarely serves one man; and a clever child rarely speaks the truth.
The King said:
"You killed my lady for the sake of another's business.
He replied, "Does Your Majesty not know that there are four other kinds of actions performed for the sake of others?"
What are the four? "To receive deposits for others, to act as a guarantor or witness,
to provide provisions for a journey where no road exists— fools engage in such deeds."
The king said,
"You have killed my queen and left me all alone. He replied:
"Does Your Majesty not hear that there are four further matters concerning solitude? What are these four?
'When born, one comes alone; when dying, one departs alone.'"
"Suffering is experienced alone, and wandering in saṃsāra is undertaken alone.
The king said:
"What you have done is much in vain and little in substance; you have killed my consort."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not know that there are four other things that are largely empty and very little substantial? What are these four?"
"To practice poverty and beg from others, like fish eggs or jujube blossoms;
for autumn clouds to rise heavily—these are empty and of little substance.
The King said:
"What you have done is profoundly contradictory; you have killed my queen.
He replied, "Does Your Majesty not know that there are four other kinds of contradictory matters?"
What are the four? "Light and shadow,
as well as brightness and darkness, day and night, and wholesome and unwholesome dharmas—
these four in the world are always mutually contradictory phenomena."
The king said,
"You deserve to be beaten severely for killing my queen. He replied:
"O King, have you not heard that there are four further instances where striking is appropriate? What are these four?
'Cloth is beaten to produce luster; A donkey is beaten so it may walk.'"
"As a wife beats her husband, she must follow him; as a drum is struck, it immediately resounds.
The King said, "Since you have killed my consort, you shall be executed."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not know that there are four further ways in which things are lost? What are these four?"
"The wind rises and the dust is stirred away; the multitude loses the sound of their song.
One who serves without purpose acts in opposition to virtue.
The King said:
"You have committed an improper act by killing my lady. He replied,
"Does Your Majesty not know that there are four other kinds of improper acts?"
What are the four? "A king who utters falsehoods, a physician afflicted by cholera,
a śramaṇa who gives rise to anger, and a wise man who engages in deluded folly."
The king said, "You have done me no good; you have killed my queen. He replied:
"O King, have you not heard that there are four further things that are of no benefit?
What are these four? 'A lamp beneath the sun, rain falling upon the great ocean, [a flower in the sky, and a childless woman conceiving]—these four things are useless.'"
"Eating to satiety and eating again, serving those who are inactive.
The summary verse for the fifth section on internal matters says:
"One should not serve those who do not observe [the rules], nor those who are unwholesome; they should be sent away."
Terror, lack of joy, and abandonment; thirsting remembrance and inconceivable sorrow.
The King said:
"You have done what should not be done; you have killed my consort."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not know that there are four further things that ought not to be done?
What are these four?"
"To teach forcefully when uninvited, to preach the Dharma to one who is asleep,
to seek what should not be sought through forceful means, and to wrestle with strong youths.
The King said:
"You are unfit to be looked upon; you have killed my wife.
He replied, "Though I am unfit to be looked upon, there are four other things that are worthy of being looked upon."
What are the four? "The battle of a hero is worth seeing; / A spell that removes poison is worth seeing;
/ A feast with kinsmen is worth seeing; / One who can expound the meaning is worth seeing."
The king said,
"That you have killed the queen is an unwholesome deed. He replied:
"O King, have you not heard that there are four other kinds of unwholesome things? What are these four?
'One who stays at home but does not work diligently, and one who has left the home life but still harbors desire.'"
"The lord of the land did not deliberate; it was the one of great virtue who acted out of anger.
The King said, "Since you killed my consort, you ought to be driven away."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not know that there are four further matters for which one should drive [the vehicle] away?
What are these four?"
“The charioteer caused the carriage to tilt; he did not understand the measure of the ox’s strength.
The cow yields much milk; the wife has long resided with her kin.
Thus spoke the King.
"You killed my lady, and seeing you, I was struck with terror. He replied,
"Does Your Majesty not hear that there are four other things for which one should not fear, yet one fears?"
What are these four?
"The wren and the lark, the white gull and the gray goose;
these four kinds of birds always harbor a fearful heart."
The king said, "I have no queen, so my heart finds no joy; why then did you kill her? He replied:
"O King, have you not heard that there are four things that bring no joy? What are these four?
'A monkey finds no pleasure in the village; a fish or turtle finds no pleasure on a rocky mountain.'"
"Thieves have no place in a meditation hall; a madman loathes his own wife.
The King said, "You deserve to be cast out for killing my consort."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not know that there are four further matters that ought to be abandoned?
What are these four?"
"For the sake of the household, one person is abandoned; for the sake of the village, a household is abandoned;
for the sake of the state, a village is abandoned; and for the sake of oneself, the entire earth is sacrificed.
The King said:
"You have killed my queen, and my longing for her shall never reach satiety. He replied,
"Does Your Majesty not know that there are four other things that can never be satisfied?"
What are the four?
"Fire has no limit for grass; likewise, one who lusts after another's wife;
drinking from the cupped hands when thirsty; and drinking another's wine—these are difficult to satisfy."
The king said,
"That you have killed my queen is a matter difficult to conceive. He replied:
"O King, have you not heard that there are four further inconceivable matters?
What are these four?
'The anger of a sovereign is difficult to fathom; One may suddenly encounter bandits on the road;'"
"The women of the household were quarreling when inconceivable offerings arrived.
The King said,
"That you killed the Queen is truly a cause for grief."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not know that there are four other matters that cause grief? What are these four?"
An aged man harboring lustful desires, A wicked wife sent away by her husband,
A courtesan whose youth has faded, And one who leaves the home-life with a mind full of anger—
These four kinds of matters are all truly pitiable.
The sixth internal summary verse says:
Lack of contentment with pleasing things, Playing together, seizing property,
Not competing together, harboring ill will, Having no support, having no companion, and lack of faith.
The King said, "I never tire of gazing upon Lady Anle; you must kill her. She replied:
"O King, have you not heard that there are five things that can never bring satisfaction? What are these five?
'The sovereign of the land and the king of elephants, the famous mountains and the great ocean;'"
"The physical marks and signs of the World-Honored One—when one contemplates them, there is never weariness.
The King said: "The lady was lovable, yet you have killed her."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not hear that there are five other kinds of delightful things? What are these five?"
“Of beautiful countenance and born of a noble lineage, gentle and never doing evil,
with all the virtues of a wife complete— such a person is truly lovely.
The King said:
"I should not have engaged in play with you; you have killed my lady.
He replied, "Does Your Majesty not know that there are five other things with which one should not engage in play?"
What are the five? "A small child, a venomous snake, a eunuch, a son born of a paramour,
and one who lacks discernment according to circumstances— these are not those with whom one should play."
The king said,
"To kill the lady is to deprive me of my wealth. She replied:
"O King, have you not heard that there are five others who seize people's wealth? What are these five?
Dancers and musicians, physicians, Thieves, and prison wardens."
"Those who enter and exit the royal palace—these five robbers of people's wealth.
The King said:
"You have killed my consort; you are no longer fit to contend with me."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not know that there are six further kinds of non-contention? What are these six?"
"The very wealthy and the utterly poor, the lowly and the most noble,
the extremely distant and the extremely near— these six should not contend.
The King said:
"You harbor an evil intent; you have killed my lady.
He replied, "Does Your Majesty not know that there are six other kinds of people who possess an evil intent?"
What are the six? "Though seeing one another, they do not look at each other; they act in opposition and do not associate;
they delight in speaking of others' faults; they expect a reward for giving wealth to others."
"Though you give, you do so with the intent to take back; this is the mark of an evil mind.
The king said, "You have killed my consort; I am left without refuge."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not know that there are seven further things that are without refuge?
What are these seven?"
An aged and sick monk, a wicked king, An elderly head of household with foul speech,
One unacquainted with the Dharma and Vinaya, A grave illness without medical treatment,
And one who does not rely on the instructions of the Venerable One— These seven are without refuge.
The king said,
"Since you have killed my consort, you are no longer fit to be my companion. He replied:
"Does Your Majesty not know that there are seven further kinds of people who are unfit to be companions?
What are these seven? "The playful man, the actor, The gambler, and the harlot,"
"Those addicted to wine, thieves, and eunuchs— these seven do not make companions.
The King said,
"Since you killed my consort, you are no longer fit for confidential trust."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not know that there are seven further things that are difficult to entrust with confidence?
What are these seven?"
"Deep water reaching up to the throat; monkeys, elephants, and horses;
black snakes with bristling hair; and a face contorted with sparse whiskers and beard—regarding these seven matters, one should know that they are difficult to rely upon."
The seventh internal summary verse says:
Not sleeping and not desiring, the nine afflictions and lack of compassion,
the ten evils and the ten contradictions, and the manifestation of the Ten-Powered Lady.
The king said,
"Because you killed my consort, I cannot sleep. He replied:
"Does Your Majesty not hear that there are eight other things in the world that cause people to lose sleep? What are these eight?
'Fever, emaciation, and coughing; poverty, illness, anxious thoughts, and extreme resentment.'"
"With a heart struck by terror, dragged away by bandits— these eight matters cause one to lose sleep.
The King said,
"Since you have killed my consort, I no longer desire you."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not know that there are eight further things that are undesirable?
What are these eight?"
“Illness, old age, and death; famine; separation from what is loved and meeting with enemies;
being struck by hail and the ruin of one’s country—these eight things are undesirable for people.
The King said:
"You have caused me great distress by killing my queen.
He replied, "Does Your Majesty not know that there are nine kinds of causes for distress in the world? When such matters as these arise, one must practice forbearance."
What are the nine? "If one loves my enemy, or hates my good friend, or hates my own self—
whether [the act] has already been done, is being done now, or will be done in the future,"
"If these nine matters manifest before you, you must open your own understanding;
do not give rise to resentment again, for it only brings distress to yourself and others.
The King said:
"You lack compassion; you have killed my lady," [the man] replied,
"Does Your Majesty not know that there are ten kinds of beings in this world who are devoid of compassion?"
What are the ten? "Slaughterers of oxen, sheep, chickens, and pigs; bird-catchers, fishers, and hunters of wild beasts;
those who set snares for rabbits, thieves, ringleaders, and butchers—these ten types of evil ones lack a heart of compassion."
The king said, "You are a wretched and evil man; you have killed my queen. He replied:
