"Does Your Majesty not hear that there are ten evils among men? What are these ten?
'Having an evil reputation and foul speech, lacking shame and modesty; turning one's back on kin and abandoning kindness, devoid of compassion.'"
"Violent thieves and pilferers make it difficult to provide food; constantly uttering perverse words—this is the tenth.
The King said, "You have committed an act of contradiction; you are not to be trusted, for you have killed my consort."
He replied: "Does Your Majesty not know that there are ten further contradictory matters which are not to be trusted?
What are these ten?"
"The so-called sun, moon, fire, Water, a young girl, a woman, A bhikṣu, a brāhmaṇa, And a naked ascetic, human excrement— Among these, that which is contrary to the sun is as follows:
in winter it stays near [the earth] yet does not burn excessively; in spring it stays extremely far away yet can burn with a scorching heat."
Regarding the contradiction with the moon: when it is a thin crescent in the beginning, everyone bows and pays homage to it; yet when it becomes full and large, no one offers such homage.

Regarding the contradiction with fire: for instance, one suffering from a feverish illness must further apply heat through fire-therapy, or as when a wound is treated with fire-cauterization and only then heals.

Regarding the contradiction in the characteristics of water: for example, during the winter months, the water in ponds is so cold and frozen that no one drinks it, whereas well-water, though warm, is drunk and used by all.
In the month of spring sunshine, the water in ponds becomes warm and everyone drinks from them together.
Although well water is cold, people do not enjoy drinking it; this is discussed according to the customs of Western countries regarding what is contrary or compliant.

As for the characteristics of a young maiden who is contrary: while she is unmarried, she constantly longs for her husband’s family; yet once she has been married away, she frequently weeps and yearns for her original home.

Regarding women acting contrary [to expectations]: when a woman is young, everyone delights in seeing her, yet she walks along with her robes and shawls covering her body; once she has grown old and people no longer delight in seeing her, she then goes along the road with her head and face exposed.

Regarding the contradiction concerning bhikṣus: when they are young, the food and drink they consume all possess flavor; though it is digested once eaten, they cannot obtain enough. When they grow old, the food and drink they consume all lack flavor; though they cannot digest what they eat, they receive abundant offerings.

Regarding those who act contrary to the Brahmins: when a young child is seven years old and has not yet developed lustful intentions, they cause him to receive the precepts and practice the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) exclusively for five years; yet when he reaches his prime and lustful passions flourish, they fail to restrain him and instead allow him to engage in misconduct.
Regarding the contradiction of being naked: for example, a naked ascetic (nirgrantha) wears clothes when inside a room, yet upon going outside, he instead becomes naked once more.
Regarding the contradiction with human excrement: when the excrement is moist, it floats upon the water; yet when it dries, it sinks back down again.
These are called the ten kinds of contradictory phenomena.
The king said, "Bṛhaspati! There is no need to discuss such matters for now."
"I now ask you again; you should answer truthfully: by what power did you kill my lady?
He replied, "Great King!"
"In what place could I possibly have the power to dare harm the Queen?
Great King, you should know this!

That Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—now has the noble Kātyāyanīputra as his disciple. The power of wisdom possessed by that Blessed One is entirely unobstructed; having become a Wheel-Turning King and accomplished the preeminent state of the ten powers, he possesses great wisdom and turns the Great Brahma-Wheel, uttering the lion’s roar amidst the fourfold assembly."
This may rightly be called possessing great power.
What are the ten? They are:

the power of knowing, as it truly is, what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*). Because one has accomplished this supreme state of the power of knowledge, one possesses great wisdom and turns the Great Brahma-wheel, uttering the lion’s roar amidst the fourfold assembly; this is the first power.

Furthermore, he knows, as it truly is, the karmic retributions of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time—including their locations, activities, causes, conditions, and maturations; this is the second power.

Moreover, he knows, as it truly is, the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and samāpattis, as well as the afflictions and their purification; this is the third power.
Furthermore, knowing, as they truly are, the distinctions among the faculties and natures of all sentient beings is the fourth power.
Furthermore, knowing, as they truly are, the inclinations of all sentient beings is the fifth power.
Furthermore, knowing various worlds as they truly are is the sixth power.
Furthermore, knowing the universal movement throughout all places as it truly is is the seventh power.

Furthermore, he recollects and knows all his various places of birth in previous lives—namely, one birth, two births, up to ten births, twenty, thirty, up to a hundred births, a thousand births, ten thousand births, immeasurable tens of thousands of births, through eons of formation and eons of destruction, even up to immeasurable eons of formation and destruction—all of which he recollects:

"Such was my kind, such was that being; my dwelling place was named so-and-so, of such-and-such a clan; such was my food and drink, the suffering and pleasure I experienced, and such was the length of my life; dying here and being born there, in such a region and country, in such a former place of birth"—all these he recollects in detail, knowing them as they truly are. This is the eighth power.

Furthermore, having attained the pure divine eye, which transcends that of humans, he is able to observe the births and deaths of all sentient beings, their forms and colors—whether beautiful or ugly—their lineages—whether low or high—and their rebirths in good or evil realms as they proceed according to their karma; he knows this all exactly as it is.

If there are sentient beings who commit evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, revile and disparage the noble ones, and give rise to wrong views, then by reason of these evil karmas as causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are born in hell;

if there are sentient beings who perform good deeds of body, speech, and mind, do not revile the noble ones, and give rise to right views, then by reason of these good karmas as causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are born in the heavens—knowing this as it truly is, as extensively explained before, is the ninth power.

Furthermore, having attained the exhaustion of all taints (*āsrava*), one attains liberation of mind within the untainted state; being able to personally realize and witness the perfected Dharma, one knows according to reality, as extensively explained before: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence"—this is the tenth power.
Having attained this supreme excellence of power, endowed with great wisdom, he turns the Great Brahma-wheel and lets out a lion’s roar amidst the fourfold assembly.
Great King!
"This is because the Tathāgata possesses great power that none others can surpass; this is what is called 'having power.
When Upacāra had thus explained these essential points, King Mahātejas remained silent and offered no reply.
Upananda thought to himself:
"Since the King remains silent and says nothing at all, what is the use of deceiving one another for so long?
I should now take the lady out."
He immediately appeared before him.
With tears filling his eyes, he prostrated himself before the king and paid homage at his feet, expressing his gratitude with these sublime verses:
"Your Majesty, you should understand that impermanence is the family law handed down through successive generations."
The King’s law is to always harbor patience when seeing evil; may the Great Lady of the Realm deign to forgive me.
Your Majesty has previously heard the sublime words of the world, which I have briefly set forth through this exchange of questions and answers.
If the King’s power can subdue even a great mad elephant, how much more so this matter of a wayward wife?
"In honoring my husband, she was endowed with the virtues of a wife; from beginning to end, we were united as one in this alone.
For my sake, she hesitated and deliberated as our master; may this lady now find favor and forgiveness."
At that time, the King, seeing this, was filled with great joy and replied to Puṣya with a sublime verse:
"Because you have uttered such beautiful and wondrous words, It is clear that you harbor feelings of affection for me;
I now grant you the city of Kanyākubja as a reward, And I forgive the Lady Anurādhā."
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudrakavastu*, Fascicle 24; *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudrakavastu*, Fascicle 25.
The third sub-section of the sixth chapter, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by imperial decree, contains this summary verse:
"Valiant One and the Precious Vessel; Sublime Light in the Āraṇya."
Because he was able to restore life, the physician was released; those who harm the multitude were not spared.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the High Chamber Hall beside the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.
Then, a great number of brahmins, elders, and others were gathered in a large assembly hall, engaging in discussion and all saying these words:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is constantly possessed by sensual desire, and his assembly of disciples is likewise full of greed.
When these words were spoken, the elder Vīrabhadra, who was also seated among the crowd, heard this and replied to the people:
"This matter is not yet known; I shall cause you all to witness it for yourselves."
Is the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, one of many desires,
or one of few desires?
And is it the same for the assembly of his śrāvakas?

The householder returned home and, having surveyed all his gold and silver vessels, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and after inquiring after his well-being, sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the sublime Dharma to that elder, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him, and then remained silent.
The elder rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I pray that you will deign to show your compassion and, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, accept my humble offering at my home tomorrow.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
When the elder knew that the Buddha had accepted, he took his leave and departed.
The householder also invited the various non-Buddhist practitioners and said to them:
"Tomorrow I have invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to my home for a meal; you gentlemen may likewise partake of food there with them."
Next, he went to the brahmins and householders within the city and informed them, saying:

"I have invited the Buddha and the community of monks, as well as the assembly of non-Buddhist practitioners, to take a meal at my home tomorrow; you gentlemen may also come together to join in this act of sympathetic joy and make offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha."

That night, the householder prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink, both solid and soft; at dawn, he arranged the seats and provided the necessary items, such as water basins, tooth-sticks, and bean-flour powder. Having completed these preparations, he sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The food and drink are ready; may the Buddha know that the time has come."

At that time, the World-Honored One, accompanied by the assembly of noble ones, took up his robe and bowl during the first part of the day and proceeded to the place where the elder had prepared offerings, taking his seat. The elder, together with the brahmins and lay devotees, then brought excellent vessels made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—most exquisite in quality—and desired to serve them in succession to the Buddha and the Sangha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should now go and inform the bhikṣus:
'This is the intention of the householder to test you by offering four jeweled trays; none of you should accept them.'"
The Venerable Ānanda received the instruction and announced it; however, the bhikṣus followed the instruction so strictly that not a single one would accept his vessels.

Seeing this, the householder immediately took red and white copper vessels and distributed them in succession, offering and serving exquisite food with his own hands until everyone was fully satisfied.
When the meal was finished, and he had chewed his tooth-stick and rinsed his mouth, he put away his bowl and utensils. The householder then took a low seat and sat facing the World-Honored One.
The Buddha taught him the Dharma, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening him; having also recited the verses on giving and the *Dhāraṇī*, he departed from the house.

At that time, the various non-Buddhist practitioners all assumed improper postures and sat in disorder according to their own whims, rather than following the prescribed order. The elder then said to the gatekeeper:
"If you see any of these non-Buddhists leaving the gate carrying vessels made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or crystal, you must seize them."
If one says,
"The householder gave it to me," the answer is:
"I am offering you a temporary meal, not a permanent gift.
If you do not return it, I shall beat you, seize you, and forcibly take back the vessel.
The elder then presented a bowl made of the four precious substances to the non-Buddhist practitioner, who immediately cried out loudly for it.
"Give me a golden platter," or he might say:
"Hand me a silver vessel."

Thereupon, they fell into a chaotic fray, their anger and rivalry erupting together; they struck with staffs, seized one another by the hands, pummeled with fists, and trampled with feet, mutually insulting one another in a manner utterly unsightly.

When the elder saw this, he manifested an expression of wrathful alarm and commanded them to cease. He then served them food in succession, and once they had finished eating, each took his vessel and departed.
The disciples tried to stop him, and he replied, "The householder gave it to me; why do you stop me? They answered:
"You may give us food for a short while, but this is not a permanent gift; you should stay here and then depart.
He refused to stay, so the gatekeeper struck him, causing a great commotion that echoed outside.
When all the men, women, and children residing in the city of Vaiśālī heard of this matter, they all gathered like clouds. The elder addressed the people, saying:
"Virtuous ones, do you perceive any difference between the Buddha and his bhikṣus and the assembly of the non-Buddhists?"
He replied, "I saw it. The elder said:
"The Buddha and the noble assembly are of few desires and content; they do not, like the base and evil laws of the non-Buddhists, employ such means to entice and lead others.

Consequently, those people redoubled their deep respect for the Buddha and the Sangha, and their sincere faith flourished even further. Even those who were without faith or were neutral began to give rise to respectful and faithful hearts toward the Buddha and his assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having arrived at his dwelling and washed his feet, sat upon his usual seat amidst the great assembly. Once seated, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"The practice of few desires brings such supreme benefits; therefore, bhikṣus, you must not eat from vessels made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or crystal. Should anyone eat from such vessels, they shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
"If it is one who has abandoned desire, they may act according to the host's intention.

If it is an ordinary person, they may go to the heavens or to a dragon palace; when food is prepared through the power of that person's meritorious karma, all the vessels are made of exquisite jewels such as gold, with no other materials mixed in. Fearing that he might commit an offense, the bhikṣu did not dare to take and eat it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If no other utensils can be obtained at that place, one should take food even from a vessel made of gold or jewels; do not harbor any doubt about this."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a householder in this city who was immensely wealthy with vast riches and abundant enjoyments, like King Vaiśravaṇa. Not long after he had taken a wife, she became pregnant; on that very day, her physical appearance and radiance became extraordinary compared to her usual state.

After the moon was full, she gave birth to a daughter whose countenance was upright and beautiful, a sight that all people delighted to behold; her complexion was radiant and her features were complete in every excellence. On the day of her birth, the room was illuminated as if by the light of the sun, and an auspicious reputation spread throughout the city.

The people deliberated together: "A certain elder has given birth to a daughter whose appearance and demeanor are exceptionally distinguished; all who see her delight in beholding her, for her physical marks are perfectly complete. At the moment of her birth, there was light in the room like that of the sun, and every day for many thousands of people, moved by a sense of wonder, gathered at the elder’s house to behold this rare marvel."

At that time, there was a physiognomist from another region who was well-versed in omens; hearing of these wonders, he also went to observe them. Having seen such a rarity, he looked around in all directions and said to the people: "Do you not know?..."
"This girl possesses marks that are entirely without peer in the world; according to the manuals of physiognomy, she is destined to share amorous pleasures with five hundred men.
The people replied, "Considering these extraordinary marks, five hundred is hardly enough to be called remarkable."
The prediction made by the physiognomist was heard throughout the four quarters, and people vied with one another to come and observe her, until the streets were choked with crowds.
At that time, after twenty-one days had passed, the elder held a great celebration and summoned his kinsmen to name his daughter.
They all asked, "What name should this girl be given?"
They all said, "At the time of her birth, the chamber was illuminated as if by sunlight; therefore, this girl should be named Prabhāvatī.
The elder then appointed eight nurses to look after her together, as described at length elsewhere.

As she gradually grew from childhood, her countenance became elegant and exquisite, and her refined demeanor surpassed all others. She mastered every form of music, both wind and stringed instruments; radiant and resplendent, her silken garments were fragrant, illuminating her own residence with such brilliance that she resembled a celestial maiden dwelling within a wondrous flower garden.

Behold this extraordinary form; her countenance is lovely, her majestic radiance preeminent and peerless in all the world. Even if reclusive sages or those who have transcended desire were to behold her, they would still be moved to give rise to defiled lustful thoughts; how much more so would young men, who have accumulated afflictions since beginningless time and whose sensual desires are flourishing, not become infatuated?
Her father, along with his family members, kept watch day and night with such strict vigilance that he could not find any opportunity to sleep.

At that time, the Crown Prince and ministers of King Prasenajit, the Lord of Kośala, as well as other kings and princes, all came together to inquire after her and seek her hand in marriage. However, because the physiognomist had predicted that the girl of Wondrous Light would engage in sexual acts with five hundred men, they all felt revulsion and shame and did not form matrimonial alliances with her. Nevertheless, the house was filled with people both inside and out; everyone gazed through the doors, windows, and lattices, and despite the thorough defenses, it was difficult to prohibit their scrutiny.
Having seen this, the elder feared it would bring calamity upon his family; finding no peace of mind, he immediately thought to himself:
"My daughter has grown old; although she is not of a suitable match, I shall give her to whoever seeks her."
Everyone felt ashamed and no one came forward to receive him with respect.
Thereupon, seeing that no one would take him in, the elder’s heart was filled with distress; he was gripped by the suffering of illness, and his physical form grew emaciated and weakened.

At that time, there was a householder in this city who was immensely wealthy and possessed vast riches. Not long after he married a wife, she died; thus, in succession, he sought further wives, yet the second, the third, and so on up to the seventh all died from illness.

Because the evil karmic tendencies resulting from the short-lived wives he had taken in previous lives were now manifesting, people at that time gave him the nickname "Killer of Wives" (Bhāryāghātaka).

Living alone, the elder Killer of Wives found it difficult to survive and sought another woman. He went to her family home to inquire about the marriage, and her parents replied, "How could we possibly wish to kill our own daughter now?"
He then further reflected and sought out widows, but the people replied,
"How could we now wish to kill ourselves?
The elder, unable to find a wife anywhere, finally abandoned his search for a spouse and went instead to dwell with heterodox śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and various other practitioners of the holy life.
The elder thought to himself:
"My father was formerly a lay follower (*upāsaka*) belonging to the Buddha; why should I further trouble myself by following various non-Buddhist paths?
It would be fitting for me now to dwell together with the disciples of the Buddha, gradually extending my offerings until I eventually go forth into the homeless life."
He then went repeatedly to the Jeta Grove.
An old acquaintance asked him,
"Do you frequently enter the monastery seeking to go forth?"
He replied, "I am currently without affairs; I have already left the household life, so why trouble myself further?
The other asked him the reason for this.
He replied:
"One wife of mine died, and I took another, who also perished; this happened a second, a third time, up to seven times.
The people of the world have given me the name 'Wife-killer,' which is entirely brought about by the evil karma of my previous lives. I reflect upon this myself:"
"My father has already surrendered himself to the Buddha; where else could he go?
Thereupon, she immediately resolved her mind and threw herself among the bhikṣus.
Her acquaintance replied:

"Although I know this to be so, the principle of having a wife must ultimately be fulfilled; if there are no sons or daughters, the lineage will surely perish, and it may be permissible to seek other various types of women."
He replied: "What do you wish for?
However, all those who have made requests say: "
"Would I ever wish to kill you?
[She replied: "If that is so, why do you not seek among the widows? He answered:
"I was also seen by him.
He said: 'How could I possibly kill myself?'"
"If that is so, why not go and seek the beautiful maiden Sunetra?
He replied, "The physiognomist prophesied she would have five hundred men; how could we allow our house to become a brothel?"
"All men have completely abandoned it. He replied,
"Since you possess faith, who else would dare to enter?"
"Except for the bhikṣus who come from time to time to visit,
you may now ask him. He replied:
"He is very unwilling to take me as his wife.
She replied, "He too is weary and burdened; perhaps we may be a match for one another."
The elder immediately went to that house; when the father saw him, he exclaimed:
"Welcome! What do you seek?"
He replied, "In my heart there is a wish, yet I have not dared to speak it.
His father said:
"What harm would there be in speaking of it? He replied,
"I wish to seek out Miaoguang (Wonderful Light) to be my bride."
He replied, "I give her to you.

He immediately prepared grand ceremonies and took the girl in marriage; with chariots and horses, he welcomed her back to his home, where he entrusted her with all the keys and locks belonging to the household, saying:

"O noble one! It is the long-standing custom of my household to take refuge in the Buddha and the Sangha; they are our field of merit, and there is no other destination for us. You should provide them with offerings from time to time."
He replied, "Excellent! I shall do as you say."
At that time, the elder invited monks to his house for meals every day.
Suprabhā herself constantly provided offerings with her own hands; whenever she saw a monk whose countenance was handsome and whose complexion surpassed all others, she would take note of him.
At that time, the elder had some business requiring him to go out briefly, so he said:
"O virtuous one! I have a matter to attend to in such-and-such a place and must depart; you must continue to serve the field of merit without interruption."
He replied, "It is so.
The householder went again and informed the bhikṣu, saying:
"I have other business that requires me to go elsewhere; I only pray that the Noble One will come to my home for a meal every day.
He replied, "May you be free from illness; I shall come for the meal."

After the householder had departed, the bhikṣu went to the residence; at that time, because her husband was absent, Sunetra displayed her charms before the bhikṣu, assuming a seductive and coquettish manner.
Having seen this, the bhikṣus each finished their meal and returned to the monastery, where they said to one another: "Do you know?
Our faults have been revealed; what should we do now?"
One person said, "I shall not go tomorrow; what would he do there?
Another person replied:
"I am a beggar; I shall go begging for alms. The people said, "Very well."
The next day, not a single bhikṣu went there. Later,
when the householder had finished his business and returned home,
he asked Sunetra, "Does the noble one, a field of merit, come regularly to eat?"
He replied, “They came for a meal one day and have not returned since.
The householder reflected:
"Could it not be that this woman displayed flirtatious and lustful gestures before the Noble One, and he did not come because he feared the fault?
Thinking thus, she went to the monastery and earnestly invited him again.
He replied, "I am a mendicant; you may rely upon the established rule."
He said, "Noble One! I have already reflected upon this;
I shall not act as I did before, lest further faults and afflictions arise."
The bhikṣu accepted it, and the man prostrated and departed.

On another day, when the bhikṣu went to take his meal, the elder sent Suvarṇaprabhāśrī into the room and closed the door from the inside; the elder himself stood outside the door and personally served the food.
While the bhikṣu was eating, Subhāṣita conceived a conceptualization within his mind regarding the interior of the room:
"Such are the feet of this noble one; such are his waist and back; such are his chest, neck, face, and eyes, up to the very crown of his head."

As he thus applied his mindfulness and engaged in such discrimination, an extremely heavy passion arose within him; he was then consumed by the fires of desire from both within and without, and with sweat streaming from his entire body, he suddenly passed away.
When the bhikṣu had finished eating, he rinsed his mouth and washed as usual; having recited a verse for him, he took his leave and departed.
The householder opened the door and called out to Suprabhā, saying, "Come forth; I wish to eat with you."

Once she had passed away, there was no sound or movement; the elder entered and saw her prostrate on the ground. Thinking she was merely asleep, he wished to rouse her, but only upon pushing and stroking her with his hand did he realize she was dead. Weeping bitterly and piteously, he told his family members:
"I am a person of meager merit and lowly station that such a precious daughter has suddenly abandoned me. You must inform our relatives that the girl has died."

The kinsmen having assembled, they all came to wail and weep; beating their breasts in anguish, they threw themselves upon the ground, or uttered words of abuse against the elder. Thus, amidst such commotion, the day drew to a close; they then adorned the funeral bier with five-colored fabrics and conveyed it to the cemetery.
At that time, not far from the grove, there was a band of five hundred thieves who had come to settle there after committing robberies elsewhere.
A man on the road, having seen the thieves' camp, thought to himself:
"The beautiful woman Prabhāvatī has now passed away; her kinsmen from all directions have escorted her to this grove. Lest these thieves cause some calamity here, I should go quickly to inform them."
Arriving at the grove, he announced:
"Not far from here, five hundred bandits intend to come; you must leave immediately so that they do not harm you.

Upon hearing this, the relatives made grand preparations for the funeral rites and, having stationed guards to protect them, entered the city together while suppressing their grief and wiping away their tears.

The bandits eventually reached the edge of the grove; those guarding it fled to various places, while the bandits, seeing the various kinds of ornaments from afar, all went together to look at them, none of whom failed to be struck with wonder and astonishment.

They removed their clothes and examined her together; although her spirit had departed, her countenance remained as solemn as if she were alive. Observing that her features were no different from when she was living, they said to one another:
"This woman’s beauty is such as we have never seen before; even if one were to search far and wide, a peer such as this would be difficult to find."
Each gave rise to a defiled mind and together committed an unrighteous act; they immediately collected five hundred gold coins, placed them at his side, and departed.

When dawn broke, the news spread far and wide that although Sunetra was dead, his remains were still able to accommodate five hundred men who obtained five hundred gold coins. The community of bhikṣus also heard and learned of this.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"What karma did Subhāṣita perform in a previous life to be endowed with such radiance?
At the time of his birth, his entire chamber was illuminated; now, though he is dead, he has shared [his wealth] with five hundred people and obtained five hundred gold coins."
The World-Honored One said:
"O bhikṣus! The karma created by the girl Prabhāvatī in her previous life must necessarily be experienced by herself."
"When the fruit of retribution ripens, no one can take its place in one's stead," and so on, as extensively explained above. You should listen!
During this Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, endowed with the ten titles, and resided at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī.

At that time, there was a king in this city named Kṛkin, who was a great Dharma King; the realm was peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, free from all bandits and thieves, as described at length elsewhere.
Then, when the World-Honored One’s work of transformation was completed, like a fire whose fuel is exhausted, he entered the wondrous realm of Nirvāṇa without remainder.

At that time, the king and all the people extensively offered worship to the Buddha’s remains; once the cremation was completed, they collected the relics and erected a stūpa one yojana in length and breadth and half a yojana in height.

A householder’s daughter, seeing the majestic form of the stupa, felt a profound sense of longing and reverence. She then fastened a bright mirror within the *cakra* (the rotating wheel) of the stupa and made this great vow:
"May I, in future lives, wherever I am born, have light shining forth like the sun, emerging from my very body."

"O bhikṣus! The householder’s daughter of former times was none other than this very Miāoguāng (Wonderful Light). Because of the power of her vow made when she hung up the mirror in the past, she has now obtained this fruit: her body is like the light of the sun, and at the moment of her birth, its radiance filled the entire room."
Furthermore, you should know that although his body was dead, five hundred people gathered together to engage in sexual union with him and gave him five hundred gold coins.
You should listen to this past causal connection!
In the past, there was a king of Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta who was a great Dharma-king, as described in detail previously.

At that time, in this city, there was a courtesan named Bhadrā, whose countenance was so upright and beautiful that all people delighted in seeing her; she had previously been in a relationship with the king’s own maternal uncle.
At that time, there were five hundred cowherds who went to a fragrant garden to enjoy themselves in merriment. They said to one another, "Within this garden we have everything we need;
our only lack is a young maiden with whom we may take pleasure. We should seek one out and bring her here."
The assembly all said, "Excellent.
Whom do you wish to bring here?"
They all said, "Excellent," and immediately went to his location and reported this to him.
“Maiden! Come to the fragrant garden so that we may enjoy ourselves together. She replied:
"If you obtain a thousand gold coins, I shall go with you; otherwise, I will not go.
He replied, "Take five hundred for now; once our pleasure and games are over, I shall return the other five hundred."
The woman said, "As you wish.
The men immediately gave her five hundred [pieces of gold] and informed her.
"Go ahead; once I have prepared my incense, flowers, and clothing, I shall follow immediately.
After the men had departed, the woman soon gave rise to this thought:
"If I have illicit relations with those five hundred men, will I be able to survive?"
"Since five hundred have already been detained, what should we do?
He then devised a stratagem:
"The King’s maternal uncle was once an associate of mine; if we rely upon him, he might perhaps provide us with relief."
She then sent a maidservant to her maternal uncle with these words:

"I suddenly lost my mind and agreed to take five hundred gold coins for amorous play with five hundred men. If I have intercourse with those five hundred men, it will be difficult for me to survive; however, if I do not go, I shall be fined double the amount of gold."
"I once shared a close and harmonious relationship with my maternal uncle; how can we devise a plan to resolve this?
The maid returned and related everything in detail. Relying on the King's authority, the uncle neither allowed his daughter to leave nor did he return the money.

At that time, there was no Buddha in the world; rather, a Pratyekabuddha had appeared in the world. Compassionate toward the poor and destitute, he relied on humble bedding and ate whatever food he happened to receive; he was the sole field of merit in the world.

At that time, this pratyekabuddha was traveling through the human realm and arrived at Vārāṇasī, seeking a secluded place to dwell in peace. He saw five hundred people gathered together in one spot; observing that the Venerable One’s body and mind were both tranquil and exceptionally distinguished from the common crowd, they realized, "This is truly a field of merit, difficult to encounter. We should offer him sustenance to plant seeds for future causes."
They immediately consulted together and prepared a fine meal, filling their bowls to the brim and reverently offering them to the Sage.

It was the constant custom of the Pratyekabuddhas not to preach the Dharma with words, but rather to inspire virtuous thoughts by manifesting physical signs; he thus ascended into the air and displayed various supernatural transformations, emitting streams of fire and water from his upper and lower body.

When the ordinary people saw this supernatural power, they immediately conceived faith and reverence; like great trees collapsing, they prostrated their entire bodies before that superior person and each made a grand vow:

"Having offered worship to such a true field of merit, by this root of goodness, we pray that we may, even at the cost of our own lives, pay five hundred coins to have sexual union with the virtuous courtesan."

"O Bhikṣus! You should know that the virtuous woman of former times was none other than this very woman, Prabhāvatī; and those five hundred people of old were none other than these five hundred bandits."

Due to the merit of making offerings to the Noble One and by the karmic force of his aspiration, as he transmigrated through the cycle of birth and death, for five hundred lifetimes he constantly engaged in unrighteous conduct together with five hundred gold coins; even until today, the courtesan Prabhāvatī, though her life has ended upon that very corpse, still engages in evil deeds together with those gold coins.
Therefore, you should know that no one can take upon themselves the karmic results of another's actions; this is explained at length, even down to a single verse, as previously stated.
You should abandon black and mixed karma and cultivate pure white karma; in this manner you should train yourselves.
When the assembly of bhikṣus had heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One reflected thus:
"Because the bhikṣus accept food and drink in such households, there arise these faults and calamities."
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Because the maiden Prabhāvatī gave rise to discriminatory thoughts toward a bhikṣu, she consequently met her death. Therefore, you should not go to such households to accept their offerings, lest you incur this fault."
"If there be a bhikṣu who visits such a household and gives rise to faults, he shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, there was a certain bhikṣu who was a practitioner of meditative concentration; he would frequently go to an araṇya to cultivate dhyāna and reflection.
At that time, there was a māra-daughter who conceived an unrighteous thought and invited the bhikṣu to eat; the bhikṣu did not accept.
She spoke these words:
"Venerable One, if you do not accept [my invitation], I shall do you harm."
He replied, "Sister!
Since I am one who upholds the precepts, what power do you have to cause me harm?"
He immediately made a sound of indignation in her presence, and from that time forward, he constantly sought an opportunity against her.
Once, while that bhikṣu was in a secluded place with his body wrapped in a patched robe, he suddenly fell asleep. Seeing this, the māra-maiden thought to herself:
"This is precisely the moment for me to take my revenge."

He then lifted the bhikṣu up onto the upper terrace where King Bimbisāra was staying. As the king was fast asleep, he placed the bhikṣu upon him. The king immediately woke up in alarm and asked, "Who is this?"
He replied, "I am a śramaṇa. He asked:
“Who is this śramaṇa? He replied,
“He is a son of the Śākyas.”
The king said,
"Noble One! For what reason have you come here?"
He then related the matter in detail to the king, who said:
"Why do you dwell in this place of fear and hardship?
Had I not yet conceived faith in the Buddha, your life would certainly not have been spared, and the holy teaching would also have been brought to ruin."
Having heard these words, he returned in silence and informed the community of bhikṣus.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"This fault has arisen because bhikṣus have taken up residence in a place of fear and danger."
He then addressed the bhikṣus:

"King Bimbisāra has rightly spoken regarding this reproach. Therefore, bhikṣus, you must not dwell in such places of fear and danger; should any remain there, they shall incur an offense against the Dharma."
The setting was as before.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had developed an abscess. A physician-king, having come upon seeing his ailment, immediately lanced it; however, having some other business, he departed without applying medicine. Consequently, the bhikṣu’s pain increased further.
At that time, seeing his suffering, the bhikṣus said to one another:
"Venerable ones! If there is anyone who knows how, please relieve his pain."
At that time, a young bhikṣu immediately prepared it for him.
The King of Physicians thought to himself:
"Previously, when I lanced the abscess, I did not administer the healing medicine; now I ought to give it."
He immediately went and asked,
"I have lanced the abscess but have not yet applied the healing medicine. He replied:
"It has been done. He asked, "By whom?"
He replied, "It is this youth.
The King of Physicians examined him and, knowing he was a suitable candidate for the medicine, said:
"If on another day I am not present, you should administer it in this manner.
He replied, "I shall temporarily practice this method as appropriate for the time being; however, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has not yet granted permission."
He replied, “The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate; he will surely grant permission.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there are bhikṣus who are skilled physicians, they should administer medicine to them in a secluded place so that laypeople do not see them.
If one performs such treatment in an exposed area, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, certain brahmins and lay devotees of pure faith came to the monastery and asked the bhikṣus:
"I have such-and-such an illness; what medicine should I take and what food should I eat?"
At that time, the bhikṣus did not understand the physician and remained silent; the skilled physician likewise harbored doubts and did not provide an explanation.
Consequently, the lay travelers departed displeased.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is a bhikṣu who is well-versed in medical prescriptions, he should explain them for him; this constitutes no offense.
The setting and circumstances were as before.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had manifested his great supernormal transformations, subduing the non-Buddhists and bringing joy to humans and devas, all the non-human beings from various foreign regions—whether they resided in cities, towns, or villages, or even in the midst of the world—all came together to Śrāvastī.

The World-Honored One, the Great Teacher, constantly receives offerings of food, drink, and clothing from devas, nāgas, yakṣas, the great King Prasenajit, Lord of Kośala; Queen Śrīmālā; Queen Vāsavadattā; the old friend Yajñadatta; Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ; and furthermore, from the rest of the great assembly who have come together, all of whom he causes to be fully satisfied.

There were also non-human beings who developed deep attachment and dwelt there, no longer returning to their former abodes. Whenever they gave rise to desire, they would immediately transform themselves into the likeness of husbands and engage in sexual acts with those women. The sons and daughters born to them took on the forms of non-humans, with hands, feet, heads, and faces unlike those of human beings; some had eyes that were dark red, some had large heads and short bodies, some had hair that was purely blue-black, and some had hair that was a mixture of yellow and other colors.
When his mother saw him, she was struck with great terror and abandoned the child in a perilous place.

When that non-human father saw his son, he infused him with vital energy; at the time of birth, the child might have appeared in human form, but as he grew up, he took on the appearance of a non-human being. His mother likewise abandoned him as before, but when the ghost-father saw him, he nurtured and raised him until he reached adulthood.
When the group of six saw this, they said to one another:
"Nanda and Upananda! Those black-bowl monks have stolen our disciples; once they have raised them to maturity, they take them away."
"I shall now gather in such disciples as these, so that those with black alms-bowls will no longer be able to entice them away.
Then, during the first part of the day, Upānanda took up his robe and bowl and entered the city for alms. Along the way, he saw a man with yellow hair and thought to himself:
"A person of such appearance is not one whom those with black alms-bowls would support; if he leaves the household life, I shall ordain him."
He then approached him and asked:
"Virtuous one! Whose son are you?"
He replied, “I have no one to rely upon; I am all alone.
[The other asked,] “If that is so, why do you not leave the household life?”
He replied, "Who else would serve as a preceptor for my elderly self to allow me to go forth? He then said:
"O noble one! The Great Master’s teaching takes compassion as its supreme principle; if you are able [to fulfill this], I shall serve as your preceptor for going forth.
He was filled with joy and followed him to the monastery, where he immediately granted him the rites of going forth (*pravrajyā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā*).
After instructing him in the practice of the Dharma over the course of several days, he said:
"O worthy one! Have you not heard that deer do not raise deer? The land of Śrāvastī is vast; go to the places where your father used to travel and sustain yourself by seeking alms."
On another day, he took up his robes and bowl and entered the city to beg for food. At that time, a woman came out with alms-food to offer it;
seeing that bhikṣu, she pressed her chest and said to him, "Who has allowed you, one with yellow hair, to go forth as a renunciant?"
He replied, "Upādhyāya Upānanda. He then said:
"Except for those who commit evil deeds, who else could cause such harm to the teachings of the World-Honored One?
Those who lacked faith gathered along the roads and in the villages to mock him, saying:
"The conduct of the Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, is contrary to the Dharma; even those with yellowed hair have been ordained as renunciants."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"Because the bhikṣus have ordained such persons as these, this fault has arisen; therefore, bhikṣus shall not ordain those with yellow hair."
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"When lay travelers rebuke [a candidate], it is indeed appropriate for them to do so according to the Dharma. Therefore, a bhikṣu should not grant the going forth to those who disparage the Dharma."
"If anyone acts as such, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
As the Buddha has said:
"Those of such a kind are not to be granted ordination."
The bhikṣus did not know what was meant by "those who disparage the assembly of the Dharma.
The Buddha said,
"There are two kinds of base and evil persons who bring disgrace upon the assembly of the Dharma."
What are these two? First is lineage; second is physical appearance. Regarding lineage:

this refers to those of lowly and humble descent, impoverished and of common stock, who subsist by manual labor and lack sufficient food and drink; or those such as the Caṇḍālas, Rukkasas, wood-workers, bamboo-workers, laundrymen, liquor-sellers, hunters, and the like—this is called a base and evil lineage.

What are the physical characteristics? They are as follows: hair that is yellow, blue, red, or white; hair like elephant fur; or being hairless; a head that is coarse, long, or flat; a donkey’s head; a pig’s or dog’s head; ears like those of various animals; or being earless; eyes afflicted with various diseases such as being yellow, red, too large, or too small; blindness or deafness; dental disease; or being toothless; a loss of the male organ, both organs, or the downward-drooping wind-disease; or being entirely without them; a body that is too stout or too thin; emaciation; a loathsome complexion; or being deprived of hands or feet; or suffering from scabies, leprosy, and other such ailments. All these are prohibited by the Great Sage and should not be ordained.
As it is said in a verse:
"You have fully received the precepts within the most excellent teaching;
You should uphold them with a sincere heart, For an unimpeded body is difficult to obtain."
"Those who are upright leave the household life; those who are pure receive full ordination.
These are the words spoken by those who speak truth, known by the Perfectly Awakened One.
At that time, Upānanda took his yellow hair and sold it to a jester, whereupon the Buddha said:
"If one sells hair, one incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
The fourth section of the sixth chapter, summarized in verse, says:
"The three cases of *dhāsa* and so forth are the same; [the offenses for] forgetting the context and for questioning."
The Greatly Powerful Great Medicine, with a blade, descended from the celestial palace.
The setting was the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli had two novices:
One was named Dāsaka and the other was named Palaga; these two were close friends whose affection was unyielding.
One said to the other:
"You may receive full ordination; as for myself, I shall serve both my preceptor and you, ensuring that neither lacks for anything."
Having heard these words, he spoke in the same manner; at that time, these two men protected and cherished one another so that not a single person among them received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Then the Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying: "Bhadanta!..."
Is it possible for one preceptor (upādhyāya), one private instructor (ācārya), and one ritual master (karmakāraka) to simultaneously confer full ordination (upasampadā) upon two disciples at once?
The Buddha said,
“Yes. [The interlocutor asked,] “Which of these two is greater?”
The Buddha said, "There is no distinction between great and small. [He asked again:
"May I receive the precepts together with three others?"
The Buddha said, “Yes.
[The interlocutor asked,] “Among these three, which is the greatest?”
The Buddha said,
"There is neither great nor small.
[He asked again,] "May one receive the precepts together with four other persons?"
The Buddha said:
“It is not permitted. Why is this?”
"One should not perform a *karmavācanā* with a group that does not constitute a formal assembly, for it contradicts the principle.
If one acts in such a manner, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
"World-Honored One!"

"Since these individuals have all received ordination at the same time and there is no distinction of seniority among them, how should they pay respects to one another, serve as administrators (*karmadāna*), and receive the benefits of the community?
The Buddha told Upāli:
"These individuals should not pay formal salutations to one another. If they act as administrators or receive the benefits of the community, they may accept them as assigned by others."
The setting was as before.
At that time, Upāli requested of the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir!"

In future ages, people will be prone to forgetfulness and possess little power of mindfulness; they will not know in which regions, cities, towns, or villages the World-Honored One preached which sūtras.
"What training rule (*śikṣāpada*) shall be established? How should this be done?
The Buddha said:
"In the six great cities, it is said that there is no offense in speaking [of the name] wherever the Tathāgata long resided at a great *caitya*.
If one forgets the names of kings and so forth, whom should one speak of?"
The Buddha said:

"As King Prasenajit, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, and the female lay follower Viśākhā have spoken, so should it be understood; in other regions, one should speak of them according to the respective kings and householders."
“If one speaks of events from former causes and conditions, where should they be said to have occurred? “One should say:
‘In Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta, a householder named Saṃtati, and an upāsikā named Poṣadha.’”
"Speak at the appropriate times.
[The interlocutor asked: "If one is unable to memorize the sūtras, how should one uphold them?
The Buddha said:
"One should write it on paper and recite, study, and uphold it.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 25. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.
Fascicle Twenty-Six. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. The Fourth Section of the Sixth Chapter: The Remaining Verses of the Summary;

The Matter of the Buddha Manifesting Great Supernatural Powers. At that time, the Bhagavat was dwelling at the Bamboo Grove Monastery (Veṇuvana) by the Kakrandaka Pond in Rājagṛha. At that time, the king, ministers, brahmins, householders, lay devotees, and all the inhabitants of the cities, towns, and villages—including merchants and caravan leaders—collectively honored, revered, and made offerings to the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, and the assembly of bhikṣus. They obtained abundant gains of food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and other necessities for the body.

However, the various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) were not honored by the king, his ministers, or the brahmins, nor did they receive food, drink, or even the basic necessities for sustaining their bodies.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"For a long night I have troubled the Gautama but could find no opportunity; I should now cause distress and confusion among these various non-Buddhist practitioners."
At that time, the six teachers, including Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and the others—who, though not omniscient, harbored the pride of being omniscient—also resided in dependence upon Rājagṛha.

The Māra Pāpīyān immediately transformed himself into the form of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and went to the place of Maskarī Gośālīputra; there, he manifested various supernatural transformations before him, emitting water and fire from his body and causing rain and thunderbolts to fall.
Then Makkhali Gosāla asked, “Pūraṇa!
Are you able to accomplish such rare and extraordinary virtues as these?”
He replied, "I have realized it thus.

He then went to the place of Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, then to the place of Ajita Keśakambala, then to the place of Kakuda Kātyāyana, and then to the place of Nirgrantha Jñātiputra; before each of them, he manifested various supernatural transformations, emitting water and fire from his body and causing rain, thunder, and lightning.

Furthermore, he transformed himself into the form of Makkhali Gosāla and went to his location; there, before him, he manifested various supernatural transformations, emitting water and fire from his body and bringing down rain and thunder.
They all asked, "Makkhali Gosāla, have you accomplished such rare and extraordinary virtues?"
He replied, "I have realized it.
Then he again transformed himself into the form of Śreṇika Bimbisāra’s son; they all went to that place and spoke at length as before, until finally he replied:
"I have realized it.
Next, he again transformed himself into the form of Ajita Keśakambala, as previously described.

Next, he again transformed himself into the form of Kakuda Kātyāyana, and next, he again transformed himself into the form of Nirgrantha Jñātiputra; in each case, he manifested various supernatural transformations before them, emitting water and fire from his body and causing rain, thunder, and lightning to fall. They all asked:
“You have been able to realize such rare and sublime qualities.
He replied, “I have realized them.”
Having seen this, they all formed this thought:
"They are all endowed with great majestic power and superior strength; were it not for me alone, no one would lack such majesty and virtue."
At another time, these six great teachers gathered together in the hall of recitation and engaged in a discussion, all saying:

"In the past, we were all honored, revered, and venerated by kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, and merchant leaders; we received abundant gains of food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and other necessities for the body."
"At this time, we no longer receive such respectful offerings; our food, drink, and clothing have all been cut off.
However, you should know that the śramaṇa Gautama is respectfully honored by various kings and others, and his requisites for sustaining the body are entirely abundant."
"We should, by means of our supernatural powers and spiritual strength, summon the śramaṇa Gautama to come and compete with me in the higher dharmas.
If Gautama displays one miraculous transformation, I shall display two;
if he displays two, I shall display four."
If he manifests four, I shall manifest eight;
if he manifests eight, I shall manifest sixteen;
if he manifests sixteen, I shall manifest thirty-two.
"However, regarding the superhuman states manifested by Gautama, I shall excel what he has done two-fold and three-fold.
Then those six teachers went to King Bimbisāra; having offered blessings to the king, they spoke these words:
"Great King, you should know!"

We possess great supernormal powers and great wisdom; the śramaṇa Gautama likewise claims to possess great supernormal powers and great wisdom. We pray that Your Majesty will grant permission for those who possess wisdom to compete with this wise man in the display of supernatural transformations and the dharmas of a superior person.
"If that śramaṇa manifests a single transformation, I shall manifest twice or three times as many supernatural feats.
If he travels halfway along the road, we shall likewise go halfway with him to compete in our supernatural powers."
At that time, King Bimbisāra replied to the six teachers, saying:
"Though you live, you are no different from corpses; how can you invoke the Tathāgata by means of the Dharma of a superior person?"
Upon hearing these words, they all took their leave and withdrew.

Later, at another time, the King went out from the great city and proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling for the purpose of paying his respects. The six masters then encountered King Bimbisāra on the road and spoke as previously described at length, requesting a contest of supernatural powers.
The King said, "You have spoken twice now; the matter cannot be pursued."
"If you speak further, we shall expel you from the boundary.
He then departed in silence; having reached his dwelling place, he returned once more to deliberate with them, saying:
"You honorable ones should know!"
It is impossible to expect that the King would develop deep faith and reverence for a śramaṇa;
it is commonly known by all that Mahārāja Prasenajit of Kauśāmbī is of a balanced nature and free from any crookedness.
"If the Gautama goes toward that city, we shall summon him to compete in supernatural powers.
Later, at another time, the World-Honored One, following his karmic conditions, departed from Rājagṛha and traveled toward Śrāvastī, eventually arriving there and staying in the Jeta Grove.
The six heretical teachers also arrived following behind them; once they had rested, they went to King Prasenajit, and after offering him blessings, they spoke these words:
"Great King, you should know!"

"We possess great supernatural powers and are endowed with great wisdom; the śramaṇa Gautama also constantly claims for himself that he possesses great supernatural powers and is endowed with great wisdom. We pray that Your Majesty will grant permission for those who possess wisdom to compete with the wise man in a contest of supernormal transformations and the dharmas of superior persons."
"If that śramaṇa manifests one miraculous transformation, I shall manifest two; and so on, up to thirty-two times as many, as extensively described before.
If he travels halfway along the road, we too shall travel halfway to compete in our supernatural powers."
Then King Prasenajit replied to the six teachers, saying, "If it is so, may you sirs stay for a while while I inform the Buddha.
The king then proceeded to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side. With palms joined in reverence, he entreated the World-Honored One, saying:

“The six heterodox teachers wish to summon the World-Honored One through their supernormal powers and superior human dharmas to compete in the measurement of their moral virtue. We only pray that, out of compassion, you will subdue these heterodox teachers to bring joy to gods and humans, causing those with faith to leap for joy, and extinguishing the source of evil for those who do not yet believe.”
Having heard this, the Great Teacher addressed King Prasenajit, saying:
"Great King, you should know!
Regarding my śrāvaka disciples, I have spoken thus:"
"O Bhikṣus! Do not manifest supernatural transformations or perform the deeds of a superior person before coming and going śramaṇas, brahmins, elders, householders, and others."
"Nevertheless, I have taught this Dharma to my disciples: 'O Bhikṣus!
Regarding the most excellent and wholesome dharmas, you should maintain concealment; as for matters of evil and transgression, you must first disclose them.'"
At that time, King Prasenajit thus entreated the World-Honored One a second and a third time, and the World-Honored One likewise replied a second and a third time.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"There are five matters for which a Buddha must certainly act."
What are these five?
First, to cause those sentient beings who have not yet resolved their minds toward awakening to give rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta;
second, to confer the empowerment and prophecy upon the crown princes of the Dharma Kings who have long planted roots of virtue.
Third, he caused his parents to perceive the True Dharma;
fourth, he manifested great supernormal powers in Śrāvastī;
fifth, all sentient beings who were transformed by the Buddha through these causes were completely liberated.
At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought:
"In what place did the Buddhas of antiquity manifest great supernormal powers?
He saw that it was in the city of Śrāvastī.
He further thought:
"When will the great assembly gather?
and saw that it would be seven days hence.
Having understood this, he said to King Prasenajit:
"Your Majesty should depart now; when the opportunity and the occasion arise, I shall perform it. The king said:
"When do you wish it to take place?
the Buddha said,
"Wait until seven days have passed."
The King paid homage at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and departed. He then went to the place where the non-Buddhist practitioners were and said to them:

“Gentlemen, you should know that seven days from now, the Tathāgata will manifest great supernormal powers for the sake of the assembly. If you have any matters to attend to, you should do as you please.”
Having heard this, the non-Buddhists deliberated among themselves:
"The śramaṇa Gautama may perhaps flee or seek out his own followers; what, then, should we do?"
They deliberated among themselves, saying, "The śramaṇa will surely seek out his own followers; we too should seek out those with whom we are acquainted.
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist ascetic in the city of Kuśinagara named Subhadra, who was advanced in years, being one hundred and twenty years old.
At that time, there were several warriors in this city who all revered, honored, and made offerings to Sudatta with deep devotion, regarding him as an Arhat.
Then, after the six heretical teachers had consulted together, they went to Sudatta’s residence and asked him: "Sudatta!..."

"Venerable sir, you are a fellow practitioner of the holy life with us. We wish to summon the śramaṇa Gautama to compete with him in supernatural powers and manifest the dharmas of a superior person; we pray that you will assist us."
He replied: "Gentlemen, it is not appropriate for you to compete with those śramaṇas in a contest of supernatural powers. Why is this?
That venerable one possesses great power and majesty. How is this known?
Because there is logical proof.
He asked, "By what reasoning? He replied:

“Before the Great Śramaṇa appeared in the world, I recall that I would often sit in meditation by the side of the great Mandākinī Lake; having gone for alms in the early morning, I would go to the edge of the Anavatapta Lake to eat in seclusion.”
At that time, the deva who resided in that lake personally took water and came to provide it for the śramaṇa Gautama.
After he had passed into parinirvāṇa, his foremost disciple, Śāriputra, had a novice named Cunda; this novice, wearing robes made of discarded rags, went to the Anavatapta Lake to wash them.

At that time, the devas by the side of the pond immediately washed [the robes] for him, took them up, and presented them to him; he used the water from washing the robes to sprinkle his own body, generating the utmost reverence.
As I reflect upon this, I do not equal those disciples of his.
"Disciples, you who are benevolent, now wish to summon that Great Master to compete with him in supernatural powers; this is truly not a good course of action.
Upon hearing this discussion, he said:
"This too is merely a faction of those śramaṇas; let us seek others to deliberate together."
Then the six heretical teachers feigned an appearance of respect and took their leave; they subsequently went to a secluded place and deliberated together, saying:
"Where else shall we seek our companions?"
One man said, "In a certain city there is one who possesses the five supernatural powers; we should go to him and devise a plan together, for he will surely assist us.
Another man replied:

"He lacks the power to manifest any supernatural transformations; however, in a secluded place within the Snowy Mountains, where dense forests and clear ponds abound with flowers and fruit, the pines release their melodic tones and beautiful birds sing in harmony."
"There are five hundred rishis dwelling there, most of whom have attained the five supernormal powers; we should go to them and deliberate together.
Having arrived at that place and exchanged greetings, they said:

"Venerable sirs, you practice the holy life alongside us. We now wish to summon that śramaṇa Gautama to compete with him in the superhuman dharmas of supernormal power; will you act as our companions and assistants?"
They all replied: "This is a virtuous undertaking; we wish to accomplish it together.
At the time of the Great Assembly, you should manifest extraordinary signs; when we see those signs, we shall immediately come to your aid."
At that time, the six heretical teachers respectfully accepted his words and departed.

Later, on another occasion, King Prasenajit had a half-brother, a prince named Kāla, who was passing by the royal palace near the city, dressed in formal attire, adorned with fragrant garlands and various necklaces.

From atop a high tower, the king’s consort saw Kāla departing; captivated by his handsome beauty, she cast a flower garland at the prince from afar. The flowers fell upon his shoulder, and this was witnessed by all the others.
Those who harbored resentment and ill will, having witnessed this matter, reported it to the high minister; the minister then addressed the king, saying:
"Prince Kāla has an illicit intimacy with a woman in Your Majesty's inner quarters."
Upon hearing this, the king acted impulsively without first examining the matter carefully; he immediately ordered a great minister to amputate the man's hands and feet.
Following the king’s command, the man was led to the marketplace, where an executioner was ordered to sever his hands and feet.
At that time, his kinsmen and the multitude of people all wept together, surrounding him in their intense grief.
Then, a non-Buddhist ascetic passed by nearby, and the prince’s relatives requested of him, saying:

"Prince Kāla has been enraged by the King and had his hands and feet cut off. Could you, by the power of truthful speech, cause this prince's severed hands and feet to be restored to their former state?"
Having heard this, the non-Buddhists remained silent and offered no reply.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was also passing by on his almsround;
the relatives informed him, saying, "Prince Kāla has had his hands and feet cut off; could the Noble One restore them so that he is as he was before?"
The Venerable replied:
"Wait for a moment! I shall inform the Buddha and return to report back to you."
Upon hearing this, the people were filled with great joy and said, "The prince has now regained his life.
Then Ānanda departed quickly; having placed the bowl and rice in the Jeta Grove, he went to the Blessed One’s presence and reported the matter in detail. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“You should now depart and have those kinsmen restore the prince’s hands and feet as they were before. Only then should you entreat him with words of truth, speaking these true words as follows:

‘Among all sentient beings—whether footless, two-footed, or many-footed; whether possessing form or formless; whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Tathāgata is the foremost.’”
Among all phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, the phenomenon that is free from defilement is the foremost.
Among all assemblies and gatherings of beings, the community of the Buddha’s śrāvakas is the foremost.
"Of all forms of ascetic observances, diligent exertion, and rigorous austerity, the cultivation of the pure and noble precepts of the holy life is the most supreme.
If this truthful word is not false, may the hands and feet of Prince Kara, which were severed, be restored to their former state."
When Ānanda had heard what the Buddha said, he addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One,
it shall be done accordingly.”
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he went immediately to Kara’s location and had his kinsmen restore the hands and feet to their former positions.
Then Ānanda, following the Buddha’s instructions, made this request with words of truth, speaking thus:
“Of all sentient beings—whether footless, two-footed, and so forth—as extensively described above, up to: ‘the pure noble precepts are the most supreme.’”
"If these holy words are not false, let the hands and feet severed from this Prince Kāla be restored to their former state.
As soon as he had spoken these words, the prince's hands and feet were immediately restored.
When the great multitude of people saw this, they all leaped for joy and raised a great cry, exclaiming in wonder:
"The Venerable Ānanda has surpassed all the non-Buddhist teachers!"
He then led the prince to the place where the Buddha was; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he stood to one side and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One, Great Virtuous One! This is Prince Kara.”
At that time, the prince also prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.

Then the World-Honored One, in accordance with his faculties, dispositions, and inclinations, expounded the essential points of the Dharma; having heard this teaching, the prince realized the fruit of non-returning and attained supernormal powers.

At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard from the Venerable Ānanda that through the power of speaking truthful words the Prince Kāla’s hands and feet had been restored as they were before, went immediately to where Kāla was and said to him: “Prince!
"Forgive me," he said. She replied,
"I forgive you."
The king said, “Kāla! You may come back home.”
He replied, "Great King!
I have already abandoned desire; I am currently staying here to attend upon the Tathāgata, and therefore I should not return."
The king said, "Excellent! Do as you wish."
At that time, the king immediately constructed a walking path (*caṅkrama*) within a forest grove, and he resided therein.
Because his limbs and joints were connected piece by piece (*aṅgapratyaṅga*), that forest was named the "Piece-by-Piece Forest" (*Aṅgapratyaṅgavana*).
At that time, King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, if the Buddha would permit it, I wish to construct a hall for manifesting supernatural powers, extending from the city gate to the Jeta Grove.”
The Buddha said, "Do as you wish.

The king immediately constructed a hall, plastering and repairing it; he set up hundreds of thousands of exquisite banners and canopies, sprinkled it with sandalwood-scented water, and scattered priceless, famous flowers. Colorful pennants were hung, fluttering in a lovely manner, while gold and pearls shone like the sun and jeweled bells chimed harmoniously. Incense from the seashore was burned, its smoke forming clouds that became parasols, resembling the Nandana Garden of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. For the sake of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he then fashioned a precious lion throne adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and agate—various decorations of such worldly rarity that they were exquisitely magnificent.

At that time, those non-Buddhist upāsakas also each constructed six seats for the six teachers according to their respective means; they were all attended by non-Buddhist followers who sat before them. They sent a messenger to inform the king:
"Great King, you should know this!"
"We have already arrived; you may summon the śramaṇa Gautama.

Having heard this report, the king immediately went with the ladies of the inner court, his chief ministers, and all the people from near and far throughout the cities and towns to the abode of the one possessed of supernatural powers. The king addressed the messenger, the young brahmin, saying:
"Go and pay homage to the Buddha, and transmit these words of mine:"
"I inquire of the World-Honored One whether you have little illness and little affliction, and whether your daily life is light and easy, and your strength is at peace.
Having made this announcement, he said:
"These various non-Buddhists have all assembled; may the Buddha know that the time has come."
Having received the king’s command, the messenger, a young brahmin (māṇava), went to where the Buddha was, inquired after his well-being, sat to one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
King Prasenajit prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and asked the World-Honored One: "Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light in your movements and well in your physical strength?
The Buddha said:
"May that Great King and you yourself be free from illness and dwell in peace and happiness."
The Māṇava said: "The Great King Śreṇika has made this announcement:
'All these followers of other paths have assembled; may the Buddha know that the time has come.'"
The Buddha said to the young brahmin,
"You may go now. At that time,

the World-Honored One empowered the young brahmin with his supernormal power, so that like a king of geese spreading its two wings, he ascended into the void and proceeded to the Abode of Supernormal Power.
At that time, when the great assembly saw him coming through the air, they all leaped for joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Seeing this wonder, the King felt deep reverence and faith, and addressed the non-Buddhist practitioners, saying:
"The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has already manifested his supernormal powers; you, sirs, should now manifest your wonders in succession."
He said: "Great King!
Now that this boundless great assembly has gathered like clouds, even if a supernatural transformation were displayed, we would not know who it was—whether it was a śramaṇa or not."

"Is this for us? Then, by means of his supernormal powers, Prince Kāla went to Mount Gandhamādana and brought back various wondrous forest trees, with abundant flowers and fruits and the harmonious warbling of beautiful birds; he followed the trees as they arrived and placed them to the north of the Hall of Supernatural Powers.
Having seen this, the King felt extraordinary wonder and addressed the non-Buddhists, saying:
"The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has already manifested his supernatural transformations; you venerable ones may likewise manifest them in succession.
They replied: "Great King!..."
"Was it not previously mentioned? Now that this boundless assembly has gathered like clouds, even if a supernatural transformation were manifested, who would know its source?
Next, the poor man, the Elder Sudatta, by means of his supernormal powers, took a wish-fulfilling tree from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and placed it to the south of the Hall of Supernatural Powers.
Having seen this, the king’s joy redoubled, and he said to the non-Buddhist practitioners:
"The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has already manifested his supernatural transformations; you may now perform yours."
The non-Buddhist replied:
"Since the assembly is so large, who can discern the victory or defeat?
Neither I nor the śramaṇa can yet distinguish between us."

At that time, hundreds of thousands of people from various distant and nearby regions gathered together; furthermore, in the sky above, hundreds of billions of great assemblies of devas also congregated like clouds, desiring to behold the divine transformations.

At that time, the World-Honored One briefly went outside his room; having washed his feet, he re-entered the room, took his seat, and entered the fire-light samādhi. Thereupon, a great flame issued forth from the hole of the door-bolt, reaching the Hall of Supernatural Powers and setting it entirely ablaze.
The various non-Buddhists said, "Great King!
This is a display of supernatural powers by the śramaṇa; his dwelling hall has been entirely consumed by fire. Summon that śramaṇa here to extinguish the flames."
Upon hearing this, the King remained silent and was unable to reply; he stayed there, harboring deep anxiety.

Likewise, Queen Śrīmālā, Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā, Prince Jīvaka Komārabhacca, Anāthapiṇḍada the Elder, Visākhā Mātā, and all other such persons of pure faith, as well as those of neutral disposition, were all utterly astonished.
The various non-Buddhist teachers and their disciples, seeing the great fire blazing, were all filled with joy.

At that time, the flames completely consumed the house of supernatural powers, cleansing it of all dust and impurities until it was pure. Its radiance became even more intense without being diminished in the slightest, and the fire naturally extinguished itself through the spiritual power of the Buddha and the power of the devas.
