When the king saw this, his joy redoubled like a dead man restored to life; he then addressed the non-Buddhist practitioners, saying:
"The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has already manifested his supernormal powers; you, sirs, should now display your own supernatural faculties."
He remained silent, with his face cast down, unable to respond.
Thereupon the World-Honored One focused his mind and, with his right foot, stepped upon that fragrant palace—the hall where the Buddha resides, known in the West as Gandhakūṭī.
*Kaṇṭha* means "fragrance," and *kuñji* means "chamber.

This is the meaning of "fragrant chamber," "fragrant terrace," or "fragrant palace. Because one may not directly touch the venerable countenance [of the Buddha], one merely calls out the name of the palace where he dwells; this is similar to how in this land one refers to the "jade steps" or the "imperial dais."
However, what is called a "Buddha hall" or "Buddha temple" does not accord with the intention of the Western [Pure Land].
At that time, the great earth shook in six ways: it quivered, trembled, and shook violently;
it quaked, trembled, and quaked violently.

It rose in the east and sank in the west; it rose in the west and sank in the east; it rose in the north and sank in the south; it rose in the south and sank in the north; it rose in the center and sank at the edges; it rose at the edges and sank in the center. Because the great earth thus shook universally, five hundred sages within the Snowy Mountains were all startled awake upon seeing these auspicious signs.
They said to one another, "A fellow practitioner of the Brahma-faring life has manifested such auspicious signs; we ought to go."

They then set out. For the sake of those beings to be converted by him, the World-Honored One emitted a subtle and wondrous golden light; from the place where the World-Honored One was until the five hundred men, there was no spot in between that was not illuminated.

At that time, the various seers saw the World-Honored One from afar; his circular halo and wondrous radiance were like the king of jewel mountains, adorned with the pure brilliance of a thousand suns. His golden body was illuminated by the thirty-two marks, while the eighty secondary characteristics shone resplendently upon his form.

At that time, when those seers beheld the marks of the Buddha, their minds became clear and settled as if they had long practiced meditation; it was like a childless man obtaining a son, a poor man finding treasure, or a king joyfully receiving the position of consecration, and like someone who has planted roots of merit in the past seeing the Buddha for the first time.
When the rishis had arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling and paid homage at his feet, they sat to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, according to their faculties and dispositions and in accordance with their individual differences, preached the Dharma to them by following the principle of the Four Noble Truths.
Having heard the Dharma, he shattered the mountain of the twentyfold view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) with the vajra-pestle of wisdom and attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti).
Having seen the truths, he immediately rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and said:
"World-Honored One!
"I pray that I may go forth under the Buddha, receive full ordination to become a bhikṣu, and practice the holy life in the presence of the Great Teacher.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata commanded: "Welcome, bhikṣu!"

"You may practice the holy life. As soon as these words fell from the Buddha’s lips, his hair and beard fell away naturally, as if he had been shaved seven days prior; dharma robes were upon his body and a water jar and alms bowl were in his hands. His majestic deportment was complete, like that of a bhikṣu of a hundred years’ standing. Thereupon, through instruction according to the Dharma, he exerted himself with unremitting diligence, shattered the wheel of suffering of the five destinies, severed all afflictions, and realized the fruit of arhatship. The full account is as elsewhere related, until it is said that he became one whom Śakra and the various devas alike venerated and respected.

At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by these five hundred seers, arhats, bhikṣus, and the rest of the assembly of bhikṣus, as well as the eight classes of devas and nāgas, proceeded to the Abode of Supernatural Powers and ascended the lion throne before the great multitude.
At that time, there was an upāsikā named Śroṇī who came to where the Buddha was and said to him:
“World-Honored One!

I pray only that the Great Master will not trouble his divine mind with anxiety. I myself shall compete in supernatural powers with those followers of external paths and manifest the dharmas of a superior person, subduing all the heterodox teachers to bring joy to gods and humans; I shall cause those who already possess respectful faith to have their hearts rejoice, and for those who do not yet believe, I shall establish the seeds of causal conditions.”
The Buddha said to the mother of the seer, “Do not trouble your mind.
Although you possess the ability to perform miraculous feats to defeat the non-Buddhists, the non-Buddhists will say:
‘It was not the Śramaṇa Gautama who manifested these supernatural transformations; rather, it was a female disciple who performed such deeds and displayed the qualities of a superior person.’”
"You should now sit down.

At that time, the householder Sudatta, the novice Cunda, the female novice Śikhaṇḍinī, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, and countless others possessing supernormal powers all approached the World-Honored One and made the same request as before; the Buddha answered them as he had previously and commanded them to sit again.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!

Please do not worry. I shall compete with these non-Buddhists in miraculous transformations and manifest the dharmas of a superior person, thereby subduing the non-Buddhists and increasing the merit of gods and humans."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"I know that you possess the power to subdue the non-Buddhists; however, those non-Buddhists say this:

'It is not the śramaṇa Gautama who can manifest supernatural transformations, but rather it is his disciple Mahāmaudgalyāyana who possesses such majesty and can manifest supernormal powers to act as my adversary.'"
"You should sit down again.
The Buddha said to King Prasenajit,
"Who invited the Tathāgata to compete in miraculous powers with the various non-Buddhists?"
Then the King immediately rose, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!

I now entreat the Buddha to manifest the supernatural transformations and the dharmas of a superior man together with the various non-Buddhists, thereby subduing the non-Buddhists and bringing joy to gods and humans. May those who already possess respectful faith see it increase twofold, and may those who have not yet believed create the causes and conditions for faith. Thus, may the great assemblies of śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, and humans in the future all receive benefit and enjoy peace and happiness for a long night."
The Buddha accepted the King’s invitation by remaining silent; knowing he had accepted, the King returned to his seat and sat down.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered such a sublime *samādhi* that he vanished from his seat and appeared in the empty space of the eastern quarter. There he manifested the four dignified postures—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—and entered the fire-light concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), emitting various rays of light: namely, blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson. Fire issued from the lower part of his body while water issued from the upper part; fire issued from the upper part of his body while water issued from the lower part. Just as he manifested these miraculous transformations in the east, so too did he do so in the south, west, and north.
Having manifested these transformations, he immediately withdrew them and sat once more upon his lion throne as before.
The Buddha addressed the King, saying:
"This is a supernatural power shared by all Buddhas and their assembly of śrāvakas. Great King, who requested that the Tathāgata appear before these non-Buddhists, humans, and devas?"
"Please manifest the unsurpassed great supernormal powers.
Rising from his seat, the king returned to his previous position and spoke thus:
"I entreat the World-Honored One to manifest the unsurpassed great supernormal powers for the sake of the great assembly to subdue the non-Buddhists," and so on, as extensively described before.
The Buddha remained silent.
Knowing that he had accepted [the invitation], the king returned to his seat.

Then the World-Honored One, with his supreme and wondrous wheel-marked hands—whose fingers were adorned with the auspicious thousand-spoked wheels and webbed membranes, and which were the marks and signs produced from immeasurable hundreds of merits—extended his hand of fearlessness to touch the ground. With a worldly mind, he formed this thought:
"How is it that these nāgas have come here, holding exquisite lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels, with a full thousand petals, stems made of jewels, and filaments of diamond?"
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they give rise to a mundane thought, even ants and insects know the Buddha’s intention;
yet when they give rise to a supramundane thought, even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot know it—how much less could birds, beasts, or nāgas know the Buddha’s thoughts?
At that time, having understood the Buddha’s intention, the Dragon King thought to himself:
"For what reason does the World-Honored One stroke the earth with his hand?

Knowing that the Great Teacher wished to manifest a supernatural transformation and required these lotuses, he immediately produced from the earth lotuses as large as chariot wheels, numbering a full thousand petals, with stalks of precious gems and filaments of diamond. They sprang forth from the ground.

Having seen this, the World-Honored One sat peacefully upon the flower. Then, to his right and behind him, immeasurable exquisite jewel lotuses—identical in shape to the one he occupied—spontaneously emerged, and upon each of those flowers sat a manifested Buddha.

To the right and behind each of those Buddhas, there likewise emerge such lotuses upon which transformation-Buddhas sit; these appear in successive layers, ascending one above the other until they reach the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, with the lotuses following one after another. At times, those Buddhas emit flames from their bodies, at times rain falls, at times they radiate light, at times they bestow predictions of enlightenment, at times they engage in questions and answers, and at times they manifest the four dignified postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, even a mere child was able to behold the image of the Tathāgata.

When the World-Honored One had thus manifested these miraculous transformations, King Prasenajit, the women of the inner palace, the princes, the ministers, and countless hundreds of thousands of people from various cities and distant lands—all gathered like clouds, gazing at the supernatural display with eyes that never for a moment wavered.

In the void of space, there were also immeasurable hundreds of thousands of assemblies of devas who, together beholding the miraculous transformations, did not alter their dignified deportment; they paid respectful offerings with undiminished devotion, and everywhere there were the sounds of drums and music, conchs and shells resounded long and loud, and songs and dances were performed in succession.

Even the birds and beasts were all filled with joy and each let out its own cry: horses neighed, elephants trumpeted, camels bleated, and oxen bellowed; peacocks and mandarin ducks each produced their plaintive melodies.
The great assembly of humans and devas, beholding the Buddha’s miraculous transformations, marveled at such an unprecedented wonder.

At that time, those devas in the midst of the sky played various celestial music and scattered many flowers—namely, *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, and *māndārava* flowers. They also scattered powdered incense of celestial agallochum and sandalwood, as well as all manner of perfumes, and rained down celestial fine garments and the finest robes of the human world in profusion.
At that time, after the Tathāgata had extensively manifested such miraculous transformations, he spoke these verses for the sake of taming and transforming sentient beings:
"You should seek renunciation And diligently practice the Buddha’s teaching;
Subdue the army of birth and death As an elephant destroys a thatched hut."
"In this Dharma and Vinaya, by always practicing heedfulness,
one can exhaust the ocean of afflictions and reach the ultimate end of suffering.
All the other numerous emanation Buddhas simultaneously proclaimed this verse:
"As long as the sun has not appeared, the firefly briefly spreads its light;
once the solar wheel rises in the great void, the torches are extinguished from that moment.
So too, while the light of the Tathāgata has not yet manifested, the non-Buddhists display their wonders."
"The Buddha’s light illuminates the world, subduing both teacher and disciple.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"All of you, remember these miraculous transformations; the great supernormal powers are now about to vanish."
When these words had been spoken, the miraculous transformations all vanished.
Then King Prasenajit said to the six teachers:
"The Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, has already manifested his miraculous powers; you masters should now likewise display your supernatural feats."

At that time, the non-Buddhist Pūraṇa Kāśyapa remained silent and gave no answer; he then touched Makkhali Gosāla with his elbow, and in this manner they passed the touch along to one another until all six had done so, yet not a single one dared to respond.

When the King repeatedly commanded them to manifest supernatural powers, those six teachers once again struck one another; as before, they remained silent with their necks retracted and heads bowed, appearing as if they had entered deep meditation, ultimately offering no response whatsoever.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Yakṣa Lord, thought to himself:

"These six foolish creatures have long tormented the World-Honored One; I must employ skillful means to cause them to reform their past ways so that they will never dare to act thus again, and shall all flee away."

Having formed this thought, he immediately unleashed a fierce wind, with rain and hail pouring down together. The heretic’s supernatural abode collapsed in various places, and the followers of the heterodox paths all scattered; some, struck with terror, entered mountain caves, while others hid among the trees and thickets of the forest. Still others entered the shrines of the heavenly deities, hugging their bellies in grief. Yet the Buddha’s supernatural abode remained entirely unmoved.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having observed this matter,
spoke these verses: "Driven by fear, many people take refuge In mountains,
gardens, groves, and forests, Or in shrines and dense thickets."
This refuge is not supreme; this refuge is not noble.
By means of this refuge, one cannot be liberated from all suffering.
Those who take refuge in the Buddha, and likewise take refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha—
Within the Four Noble Truths, one should constantly observe with wisdom:
knowing suffering, knowing the origin of suffering, knowing the eternal transcendence of all suffering,
and knowing the Eightfold Noble Path that leads to the peace of Nirvana.
"This refuge is the most excellent; this refuge is the most venerable. By means of this refuge, one will surely be able to liberate oneself from all suffering.

At that time, the World-Honored One observed the differences in the faculties and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the great assembly and preached the Dharma for them accordingly. Having heard it, the great assembly, numbering immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions, attained extraordinary understanding: some attained the first fruit, the second fruit, the third fruit, or the fruit of Arhatship; some gave rise to the mind of a Śrāvaka-bodhi, some gave rise to the mind of a Pratyekabuddha-bodhi, and some gave rise to the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. All sentient beings within the great assembly turned their hearts with utmost sincerity toward the Triple Gem.
The Blessed One taught the Dharma to that great assembly, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them; having accomplished his purpose, he rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, there were disciples such as Pūraṇa and others who were in one place with their teacher; they asked their teacher, saying: "Upādhyāya!..."
"What is the truth?
At that time, the six teachers each gave rise to deceit and, mocking one another, spoke these words:
"The world is eternal; this is the reality."
Furthermore, some say: "Impermanence is real. Others say:
"Both eternal and non-eternal.
It further says:
"Neither eternal nor non-eternal; this is called the reality."
Again he said: "It has limits; it is limitless. Again he said:
"It is both finite and infinite," and it is also said:
"It is neither finite nor infinite."
Again it says:
"There is life within the body.
And again it says:
"The body and the life-principle are distinct.
He further said:
"After death, there is a self."
Again he said: "There is no self. Again he said:
"Both self and non-self exist," he said;
furthermore, he stated:
"Neither self nor non-self exists; only this is real, and all else is false."

Although he spoke these words, his heart was filled with great shame and remorse; with his head bowed and his gaze cast downward, the fire of anxiety scorched his mind, and wishing to seek water to drink, he went toward the pond.
Halfway there, an eunuch saw him and spoke this verse:
"Where are you going now, traveling all alone?"
"His appearance is like that of a horn-broken ox;
unable to understand Śākyamuni’s sublime Dharma, he wanders about like a wild ox.
When Pūraṇa heard this verse, he also spoke a verse in reply:
"Death is always moving before my very eyes; my body possesses no strength or vigor.
Having undergone suffering and pleasure within the cycles of existence, I now seek liberation and a place of peace."
The sunlight is extremely hot, emitting blazing radiance; my body and mind are now utterly exhausted.
You should report the truth directly without guile: where can a pool of cool clarity be found?
Having heard this, the eunuch spoke again in verse:
"Nearby is a place of cool refreshment, Filled everywhere with geese, ducks, and fresh flowers;
You are an utterly evil person born blind, Failing to see the fragrant pond as we converse."
Pūraṇa spoke again in verse:
“You are now neither man nor woman, yet you do not show me the way to the pond;
I must go quickly to seek coolness, to find relief for the burning afflictions of my body and mind.”

When that eunuch had instructed him on the way, Pūraṇa went at once to the site of the pond; having arrived at the pond, he tied a sand-pitcher around his neck, entered the water, and drowned himself, whereupon he passed away.
Then those disciples asked one another,
"Venerable sirs, have any of you seen our upādhyāya?
They all replied:
"I did not see him.
They then asked one another,
"Have any of you ever seen our Upādhyāya say anything?"
One person replied:
"I have heard it said that the world is eternal; this alone is true, and all else is false.
He further said:
"I have said that all things are impermanent," and again:
"They are both permanent and impermanent."
Again it says:
"Neither permanent nor impermanent.
And again it says:
"It has limits," he said; and again,
"It is limitless."
Again he said: "It is both finite and infinite. Again he said:
"It is neither finite nor infinite," as was fully explained previously.
At that time, the disciples said to one another:
“Virtuous ones, you should know!
All these accounts are inconsistent; I ought now to seek out my preceptor and inquire about the actual facts.
He then immediately went in search of him.
On the way, he saw a young girl coming and asked her in verse:
"O fair-faced one, have you seen the great teacher Pūraṇa,
who stands upon the ground with food in his hands, without covering his body with a robe?"
Having heard these words, the young girl replied with a verse:
"He is a person from hell, Stretching out his hands to beg from others;
His hands and feet are entirely white, And he is seen sinking within the water."
The disciple also replied in verse:
"Do not speak such words; this is an unskillful saying.
One makes the Dharma one's garment; the Muni dwells in accordance with the Dharma."
The young girl replied again:
"To walk among people with one's body exposed—who would consider this wisdom?
To let the entire multitude see [one's nakedness] while possessing a heart utterly devoid of shame."
"Shamelessly exposing his body and taking this to be the Dharma—if King Vaiśravaṇa were to see him, he would surely cut him with a blade without hesitation.
When the disciples heard these words, they departed in silence; they went to the pond and saw their master, who had drowned after tying a sand-pitcher around his neck.
Among the disciples, those who delighted in the precepts made this declaration together:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false.
They also tied sand-pots around their necks and drowned themselves. The remaining assembly all dispersed in every direction and took refuge in the border regions.
After the Buddha had manifested such a great supernatural transformation, the great assembly of humans and devas were all filled with joy.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudrakavastu*, Fascicle 26. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudrakavastu*.
Fascicle Twenty-Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.

The Fourth Section of the Sixth Gate: The Remaining Verses of Summary; Explaining the Matter of Mahābhaiṣajya. At that time, the World-Honored One, through his unsurpassed supernatural powers and the methods of transformative benefit, subdued all the non-Buddhists, causing them to retreat and disperse. They remained silent and said nothing, fleeing instead to the borderlands.
When the bhikṣus saw this event, they were all filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:

"The Great Master, the Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, has kindled the torch of the True Dharma and toppled the banner of false views; his subduing of the heterodox followers is truly marvelous."
"Excellent! The Great Sage is inconceivable; you are able to perform such deeds of great benefit.
The World-Honored One said: "You should know this!"

As for me, having now abandoned the three poisons, possessed all-knowledge, attained great mastery, reached the other shore, and obtained the unsurpassed fruit; as a Great Charioteer of Men and Teacher of Gods and Humans, it is not at all rare that I cause those [enemies] to retreat and disperse who have not yet achieved their aims.

Why is this? I recall that in the past, when I was not yet free from defiled desires and was still bound by the fetters of anger, ignorance, birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction, I was nevertheless able to subdue those six heretical teachers and their followers so that they did not dare to respond, fleeing instead to remote regions or even perishing there.
"O bhikṣus, you should listen attentively.
In the distant past, there was a king of Videha named Sujāta, who ruled the world according to the Dharma, as described at length elsewhere."
At that time, the King’s consort was of dignified and handsome appearance; the King cherished her exceedingly, and when she gave birth to a son, all people delighted in seeing him.
By the power of this child’s merit, the winds and rains in his kingdom were timely, the harvests were abundant, and food and drink were easily obtained.
After twenty-one days had passed, he summoned his kinsmen to bestow a name upon the child. The king thought to himself:
"Since this child was born, food and drink have been easily obtained; therefore, I shall give this child the name 'Adequate Food' (Pūrṇabhadra)."

He then entrusted this son to eight foster mothers to provide for him according to the Dharma; when he reached adulthood, he had mastered all worldly arts and crafts, becoming courageous, robust, loyal, and virtuous, such that no one could surpass him.

That chief queen, relying on the power of her son, became somewhat arrogant and often failed to comply with the King’s commands; because of this matter, the King frequently wore an expression of sorrow.
At that time, the ministers, seeing that the king was displeased, addressed him, saying: "Great King!
For what reason do you appear to harbor such sorrow and dejection?"
The king then recounted the matter in detail to his minister.
The minister said,
"If this is the case, why not take another wife who is gentle and endowed with virtuous qualities, so that the chief queen may gradually become harmonious and compliant as well?"
The king asked,
"From where shall they be taken?
The minister replied:
"It would be appropriate to marry the princess of the neighboring kingdom.
The king said, "That country harbors long-standing enmity toward us; how can we enter into marriage with them?"
The minister said, "I shall employ skillful means to bring them together; Your Majesty, please set your mind at ease while I go to observe the situation.
The great minister then departed to see the neighboring king. Upon arriving there, he inquired about the matter of marriage. Having heard this, that king replied to the minister:

"If we are to arrange a marriage, we should first establish an agreement: 'If my daughter bears a son, he shall be established as the crown prince; provided you do not go back on this, I shall give her to you in marriage.
The minister replied, "I submit to Your Majesty's command."
The king said, "You may return to your country and inform that king; if he agrees to these terms, we shall meet again. He replied:
"The enthronement of a crown prince is always conducted by the great ministers; since I have already given my sincere word, I dare not deviate from it by even a hair's breadth.
He dispatched a messenger to inform the king, who, upon hearing this, prepared the rites to welcome him back, and they were deeply harmonious in spirit.
The king said,
"This girl is gentle and exceedingly respectful.
He then asked:
"What do you desire now? he asked.
Thereupon, [the woman] joined her palms and said:
"Great King, if you would grant me a boon, I pray that if I bear a son, he shall be made the crown prince."
Upon hearing these words, the king was overcome with grief and anxiety, and he thought to himself:

"If I grant this request now, what shall I do? Prince Pūrṇabhadra is valiant, loyal, and upright; he is highly skilled in many arts, his appearance is peerless, and he is without equal in all the world. How can I abandon him and establish another?"
"At this time, it is truly difficult for me to decide what to accept or reject.
He did not immediately answer.
At that moment, the minister observed the king's countenance and, knowing he was troubled by anxious thoughts, addressed him, saying:
"Great King! Why do you have such a sorrowful countenance?
The king then related the matter in detail to his minister, who said:
"There is no need for concern. Previously, when I sought her hand in marriage, we established an agreement together: 'Now, follow whatever she desires and do not obstruct her feelings.
I have not yet ascertained whether the lady is not a barren woman?"
"Even if a child is born, we do not yet know whether it will be a boy or a girl.
Your Majesty should now fulfill whatever wish she has requested.
The King said to the Queen:
"May it be according to your wish.

Not long thereafter, the wife gave birth to a son of extraordinary and handsome appearance. After twenty-one days had passed, they were about to bestow a name upon him, and his relatives asked together:
"What name shall we give to this child?"
The king said, "This child sought the royal throne even before he was born; he should be given the name 'Seeker-of-the-King' (Yauvarājā).
He entrusted him to eight nurses to provide for his care and service. As the years passed and he gradually grew up, he had still not been formally installed as heir apparent.
The queen’s home country, marveling at the king’s breach of faith, immediately dispatched an envoy to inform the king, saying:
"There was a prior agreement that when my daughter bore a son, he should be established as the crown prince; now is precisely the time."
"I request that you maintain your word and your faith; if you do not, I shall mobilize my fourfold army and surely march against you to wage war.
Upon hearing this, the king was struck with terror and found no way to devise a plan, falling into great sorrow. A minister asked, "Why does Your Majesty have such a look of grief?"
The king immediately informed his ministers in detail, and the ministers said: "Great King!
There is no other plan; you should instead seek out a king to establish as the crown prince, and Prince Zu-shi (Aśoka) may then be eliminated."
The king said:
"One should not speak such unlawful words; I have heard of sons who killed their fathers, but I have never heard it said that a father killed his son."
"This act of unrighteousness was not committed by me.
The minister said,
"It is the cruel deeds of one who cannot kill [himself]."
The king said,
"How does this differ from the act of taking a life?
The minister replied:
"If this is not the case, we request that you be banished far away.
The king said, "This good man is innocent; why should he be exiled?"
The minister said, "If one wishes to seek out his faults, would it not be easy to find them?
However, this prince has been established as the heir apparent; once the Crown Prince is provided with sufficient food, he will surely know for himself."
At that time, the king immediately selected an auspicious day and installed that seeker of kingship as the crown prince.
Knowing this, Pindola (Zushi) thought to himself:
"The king has abandoned me; if I remain here, I will surely be executed."
He then went to see his mother and explained his intention in detail:
"I now wish to go to the kingdom of Pañcāla, hoping thereby to prolong my life.
Upon hearing these words, the mother felt as if her heart were pierced by an arrow; she came forward, embraced her son’s neck, and wept in agitation and grief, addressing her son with this verse:
"You formerly sat and slept upon high beds and cushions, And the garments you wore were all fresh and bright;
How can you go alone to another land, Living by wearing coarse clothes and sleeping on the ground?"
Compared to you, we have always been at peace while sleeping or awake, freely roaming through cool palaces and ornate pavilions;
why then do you suffer from the pricking of cold and heat against your skin, wandering alone and piteously in the wilds?
In the royal palace, elephants and horses were at your disposal for riding; you ate rare delicacies and fine meals according to the season;
you wore exquisite garments to ward off cold and heat—why do you abandon these to go to the desolate forest?
Drums, music, strings, and song are constantly performed in succession, able to delight the minds and spirits of those who hear them.
The multitude reveres you and follows you at all times; why do you alone harbor sorrow and wish to depart?
The prince replied: "Who always experiences peace and happiness?
And who, again, constantly endures hardship?"
Calamity and misfortune are common to all; fortune and adversity must follow one another.
Suffering and joy alternate and shift, ever like the turning of the stars and the Milky Way.
From meeting comes sorrow and pain; such is the nature of worldly phenomena.
At that time, having addressed his mother with such words of sorrow and suffering, the prince took his leave and departed for Vaṃśā.
Upon reaching that country, he became distressed by hunger and thirst; he then went to rest beneath a tree by the roadside, where he lay down and fell asleep, looking about in bewilderment.

At that time, the minister Tiṣya, while on his rounds, came to the place where the prince was; observing that the prince’s deportment was extraordinary compared to ordinary men, he stood for a long while before touching him to wake him, and asked: "Who are you?"
"Whose son are you? He replied,
"I am the son of the King of Videha, named Pādapīṭhika."
He replied, "For what reason have you come here?
The prince then answered him in full detail regarding the matter.
The attendants, having learned of this, led him to the king’s presence and said: "Great King!
This is Prince Sujāta, named Pādapīṭha; his father has set aside the elder for the younger, and he has fled here."
The king then summoned his son to question him, and the prince related the circumstances in full.

Upon hearing this, the king was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy; he comforted him with great kindness and bestowed upon him vast lands and fiefs, giving him his daughter as a wife. Not long after, a son was born, whose appearance was so lovely that the multitude marveled at his extraordinary rarity.
On the day of his birth, food and drink became easily obtained throughout the kingdom; therefore, he commanded his kinsmen to bestow a name upon him:
"Since this is the offspring of Prince Pūrṇabhadra, and since food and drink have become abundant as soon as he was born, this child should be named Pūrṇabhadra."

The king entrusted her to eight nurses to care for her; later, when she had grown up and was fully proficient in all arts and skills, Prince Zu-shi (Sujāta) suddenly passed away, and the queen constantly mourned him, her grief beyond measure.
When the king saw this, he thought to himself:
"It is the nature of women to always think of men; I should now remarry my great minister and put an end to her following him."
Having arrived at that house, he felt joyful and fulfilled.
Nearby, a rooster was roosting in the house of a high minister; a physiognomist saw this and spoke these words:
"If there is anyone who eats this rooster, he shall become king."
Having heard this, the minister did not consult the physiognomist but immediately killed the rooster and said to his wife, "You may prepare a meal for me when I return from court.
The lady then ordered it to be cooked. At that time, Bahuputra returned from the schoolhouse; not seeing his mother and driven by hunger, he saw a boiling cauldron and thought to himself:
"My mother will return soon; let me briefly check the cauldron to see if there is anything edible inside.
Upon seeing a chicken head, he immediately cut it off to serve as a light meal.
When the mother had arrived, she asked,
"Have you eaten yet? He replied:
"Eat some lotus seeds," his mother said,
and she gave them to him to eat before sending him back to his place of study.
When the minister arrived, he said:
"I must eat. The lady gave him some meat, but seeing no head of the fowl, she immediately asked for the reason.
He replied, "The child came and finished eating it."
The minister thought to himself:
"Must one eat meat entirely to become king,
or will it suffice to eat only a small amount?"
Having conceived this doubt, he went along the road to consult a physiognomist. Upon seeing him, the prince said:
"Virtuous sir, previously you made such a prediction:
'If one eats chicken meat, he shall become a king.'"
"Should one eat a full meal,
or is it permissible to eat only a little? He replied:
"Even if one does not eat the whole [chicken], eating the head alone suffices.
Furthermore, if there is someone who has already eaten the chicken's head, one may kill that person and take the head to eat it as well, and thus become king."
Having heard this, the minister thought to himself:
"I should kill this child and take its head for food.
However, if the mother is unaware of this, the task will be difficult to accomplish; first, I must ask her what her intention is."
Later, during the course of conversation, he jokingly asked his wife,
"Between my husband and my son, whom do you wish to be king?
Upon hearing this, the wife became suspicious and reflected thus:
"If I were to say now that I shall make my son king, this man would immediately cast me aside.
It is best at this time to speak in accordance with his wishes. He replied:
"Let it be that my husband becomes king.
This woman, being clever, wise, and discerning, foresaw the impending crisis and said:
"This minister wishes to kill my son for the sake of the rooster; now is precisely the time to provide protection. We must deliberate together so that his life is not endangered."
Then, in a secluded place, he said to his son:

"While you were eating lotus seeds, your father intended to kill you. You should abandon this kingdom and go toward Videha; that is the ancestral home of your forefathers where all your kinsmen and relatives still reside. If you go there, you will surely find peace and happiness."
Having heard these words, the son bowed respectfully to his mother and took his leave, departing for Vaiśālī.
As he was about to reach that city, he grew weary beneath a tree and fell asleep.

At that time, King Yauśa was afflicted by a grave illness and passed away. According to the ancient law of that kingdom, the funeral carriage was not to be brought forth until a successor had been established.
Since the king left no heir, it was unknown whom they should appoint.
At that time, all the ministers inquired among themselves: "Who is capable of being our lord?
We now wish to establish one.

Then, beneath the shade of a tree, the ministers beheld that man, whose magnificent appearance was extraordinary and rarely matched among men; though the sun had passed on, the shadow of the tree did not shift. As the multitude gazed upon him together, they all sighed in admiration at such a rare wonder.

"This son of good family possesses such wondrous and upright features that none can surpass him; that the tree’s shadow remains fixed over him to shelter him is surely a sign he is no ordinary man—let us touch him to awaken him.
Once he had awakened, he asked the people, "Why have you all startled me?"
He replied, "It was because you were worthy to be king that I merely wished to inform you.
He reported this, saying:
"How could the Dharma of the Awakened King be such as this? The people asked,
"What is that Dharma like?"
He replied, "First play beautiful music to gradually awaken him.
Having heard this, the ministers thought to themselves:
"This is no poor man; he must surely come from a noble lineage.
They then asked him together:
"In what place do you reside, sir?"
"Whose son are you?

At that time, although the prince was barely past his teens, his heroic spirit was already fully formed like that of a lion king. With a loud and clear voice, he recounted his lineage and addressed the people, saying:
"My former sovereign was named Sujāta; his son was called Pūrṇabhadra, and I am his son, named Bahubhadra."
When the six great ministers heard these words, they were all filled with joy and exclaimed, "We have now recovered our original king!
They prepared magnificent regalia and arranged extensive musical performances;

followed by thousands of troops and myriads of people, he entered the city. He was consecrated as king, and his governance brought harmony to the common people. Because the former King Much-Food (Prabhūtabhakta) had long since faded from memory, his name was eclipsed, and as the royal lineage was restored, he was known as King Re-established (Punarvasu).
"Being young when he became king, the ministers treated him with contempt, and most of his edicts were not carried out.
On an occasion when the king went out of the city for a stroll, he inquired of the inhabitants of the villages:
'To whom do these belong as fiefdoms?'"
He replied, "They all belong to a certain high minister.
Thereupon, he thought to himself:

"The cities and villages all belong to the Great Minister; although I am the king, I possess nothing but the palace and food. As for the rest of the national produce, I have no share at all. Since this violates the laws of the state, what shall we do?"
At that time, a celestial deity, knowing the king’s thoughts, announced from the air:

"O King, you need not worry. In this kingdom there is a capital city named Pūrṇabhadda; within that city there is a man named Pūrṇabhadra who shall father a son named Mahauṣadha. Once he has grown up, he shall govern alongside the king, making decisive judgments according to the exigencies of the moment so that none remain unsubdued. The king will then enjoy supreme happiness, ruling with ease while his spirit remains at peace."
At that time, the king dispatched a messenger to the city of Pūrṇa to inquire whether Pūrṇa was there or not;
if he were there, the messenger was to observe whether his wife was pregnant or not.
The messenger, having received his orders, went immediately to search for them; seeing her husband, he asked the wife whether she was pregnant.
The messenger returned and reported:
"This matter is not false; that woman is indeed pregnant."
Having heard this, the king immediately dispatched a messenger to summon Pūrṇa, greeting him with kind words of consolation and bestowing this city upon him as a fief. He then told him:
"Your wife is pregnant; you must provide her with excellent care and protection so that she is not harmed."

When the moon had become full, she gave birth to a son whose appearance was so upright and majestic that he was peerless in the world. After twenty-one days had passed, they wished to bestow a name upon him.
His relatives deliberated, saying, "We do not yet know what name we should give this child?"
The mother then said, "I have suffered from a chronic ailment for years; though I consulted many physicians and took various decoctions and medicines, there was no improvement at all.
Yet, as soon as I conceived this child, my suffering has vanished. It is fitting that we name this child Mahābhaiṣajya (Great Medicine)."
The mother spoke in verse:
"Among all ailments and sufferings, Great Medicine is the most supreme;
This is the wondrous among medicines, And may thus be named 'Great Medicine.'"
"Later, his father was carrying Mahābhaiṣajya on his shoulder to bathe in a pond; seeing some fish bones on the road, he thought they were precious jewels and kicked them out."
Mahābhaiṣajya replied:
"Seeing fish bones upon the ground, One kicks them with one's foot, thinking them pearls;
Refusing to cultivate one's own karma, One forcibly seeks the treasures left by others."
"A fish bone discarded by another is certainly not a precious jewel;
how could Vaiśravaṇa have cast his jewels upon the road?
Having reached the pond with Mahābhaiṣajya, the father set him on the bank, removed his clothes, and entered the water. Seeing a white crane perched upon a lotus leaf, he thought to himself:
"I shall catch this bird.
As he immediately stepped forward toward it, the bird flew high into the air.
Mahābhaiṣajya replied:
"A bird perches upon a lotus leaf; seeing its father, it has already flown high away.
It is not fitting to draw any closer, lest you take the life of another."
On another day, carrying Mahauṣadha on his shoulder, he went toward the Gaṅgā River to bathe.
Having reached the riverbank, he set the child upon the shore, removed his clothes, and entered the water; there, a large copper bowl was coming down with the current toward the east.
At that time, a white goose was perched upon it; seeing this, the father became suspicious and, not knowing what it was, questioned his son. Mahābhaiṣajya replied:
“The Gaṅgā flows eastward below, A copper bowl drifts along with the current.”
"The white goose dwells upon it; this is no other thing.
On another day, as before, they bathed together, and Mahābhaiṣajya took [the vessel] and placed it on the bank.
At that time, a water-pot and some grass were floating downstream, with a bird perched upon them; Mahauṣadha, as before, addressed his father in verse.
By this time, Mahauṣadha had gradually reached the age of childhood and was playing together with other boys, when they all deliberated together, saying:
"We have no lord; we should honor Mahauṣadha as our king."
After Mahābhaiṣajya had established himself, he selected various youths to serve as his assistants; from that time on, his faction grew daily larger.
At that time, there was an old Brahmin who married a young wife and set out for another land, traveling along the road.
At that time, the brahmin went toward a thicket to relieve himself, when a coarse man came and asked the girl,
"Is that your father? Or your grandfather?"
The woman said, "Neither my father nor my grandfather is my husband;
he is my husband. The coarse man replied:
"You have neither shame nor modesty toward your friends; amidst these magnificent men who fill this earth, do you not see them?
For what reason do you pursue this old Brahmin?"
"This beauty of yours is being wasted in vain; you ought to abandon him and become my wife.
If that old man comes to dispute with me, you shall cite me as your husband before the great assembly."
The woman accepted his words and immediately went with the coarse man along the road.

At that time, the brahmin, having finished washing at the pond, could not find his wife; he climbed to a high place and looked in all directions. Seeing someone leading her away, he ran in haste to where his wife was, seized one of her hands, and pulled her back.
Then that coarse man also pulled at one hand, and the brahmin said,
"You are stealing my wife!
The coarse man replied:
"I can take an oath: 'This is my wife; she was never your spouse.
Because of this, a quarrel broke out and they began to pull each other by force; the young man, being stronger, carried the woman away.
At that time, the brahmin, realizing he was powerless, hoped for assistance as he traveled through the wilderness; he cried out at the top of his voice, "Thieves are plundering my wife!
Meanwhile, Mahauṣadha was playing with several youths in a forest grove when he heard that loud cry of one who had lost his wife.
Then the youths replied to Mahauṣadha, "Since you, sir,
have assumed the title of King, such an irrational act as this is unworthy; you should cry out,
'I have lost my wife!'"
"Why did you not come to each other's rescue?
Having heard this, Mahauṣadha immediately ordered the youths to seize the three men and asked them:
"What were you disputing just now?"
The brāhmaṇa said, "I am old and without strength; I have been robbed of my wife by bandits.
The bandits said:
"This man speaks falsely; she is truly my wife.
Mahābhaiṣajya asked the woman, "Who is your husband?"
She then pointed to the thief and said,
"This is my husband. At that moment,
seeing the Brahmin beating his breast in anguish and throwing himself to the ground, Mahābhaiṣajya immediately investigated to verify the truth or falsehood of the matter and asked the youth:
"From where did you bring this woman?
He replied, "I brought her from my wife's house."
He asked, "What food and drink do you have? He replied:
"Meat broth and rice, served with clear wine.
Mahābhaiṣajya said, "If it is so,
I shall observe his eating to distinguish the truth from the falsehood."
He immediately ordered his finger to probe the man's mouth, but not a single thing was found; it was merely seen that he was drooling saliva.
He asked the brāhmaṇa, "From where have you come?"
He replied, "I have come from my wife's family.
[The king asked,] "What did you eat?"
He replied, “Curd-milk, cakes, and radishes. He then said:
"Spit it out! he commanded.
It was immediately extracted, exactly as he had said.

Seeing this, Mahābhaiṣajya realized that the man was a thief who had robbed his old wife; he then gave him a severe beating, dug a pit in the ground, and buried him up to the neck. He then used peacock bile to write these words upon the man's forehead: [text omitted].
"Those who steal women shall be punished according to this same statute.
Thus, there were those who stole oxen, sheep, and so forth—numbering five hundred in total—all of whom were treated and penalized in this identical manner.
At that time, King Chongheung possessed villages and cities, all of which were controlled by the six ministers. The king thought to himself:
"My power is now weak; what shall I do?"
He then remembered Mahābhaiṣajya and longed to meet him; without informing his ministers, he mobilized his army and set out for the city of Pūrṇabhadda, wishing to see Mahābhaiṣajya.

On his way, as he passed through a perilous and obstructed region, he heard a loud cry. He searched everywhere but saw no one. The king’s attendants looked around and observed five hundred bandits with their bodies buried and only their heads protruding. They immediately informed the king and read the characters on their foreheads, which stated: "These are all bandits."
When the king saw this, he asked,
"Who has tormented you? and the people replied:
"This was performed by the youth Mahauṣadha according to the ritual; the innocent shall not be punished.
Upon hearing this, the king praised it as excellent, gave rise to a heart of compassion, and immediately released him.
At that time, Mahauṣadha and the other youths heard that the king’s army had arrived and halted at various locations.

When all the people of the city of Pūrṇadhana heard that the king was about to arrive, they prepared all manner of auspicious items; carrying golden vases filled with water, banners, parasols, and flags, they went out of the city to welcome him.
After the King had comforted him, he asked:
"The son of Pūrṇa is named Mahauṣadha; let him come here at once.
The father replied to the King:
"The boy is young and small; he is not yet fit to receive this command.
The King said, "Let him be sent forward."
The father then led him for an audience.

When the king saw the youth, he admired his elegant and refined appearance as well as his talent for valor and strategy; yet, because the boy was still too young to be entrusted with responsibilities, he left him in his father's care and returned the army to the capital.
Having arrived at his own city, he thought to himself:
"I should now test the wisdom, strategy, and skill of the youth Mahābhaiṣajya.
He then dispatched a messenger to say to Pūrṇa:
"You may take sand and twist it into a rope one hundred cubits long; send it here quickly.
Upon hearing this command, Pūrṇa was struck with great terror and, filled with deep distress, thought to himself:
"Since my birth, I have never heard of or seen such a thing as making a rope out of sand."
He remained there in a state of grief and distress.
When Mahauṣadha saw his father, he asked,
"Father, why do you have such a look of sorrow?"
He replied, "I have never heard of such a thing; the King demands from me a hundred-cubit sand-rope as a pretext to bring charges against me."
Mahābhaiṣajya replied, "Where is the messenger?
Let me see him so that I may deliver a message to the King."
The father sent a messenger to see him, and Mahābhaiṣajya replied:
"Your Honor should report to the Great King on my behalf:

'I am a humble and lowly subject of little learning and limited vision; furthermore, lacking any wisdom or strategy, I cannot fathom the mind of Your Majesty. I do not know what color of cord Your Majesty requires.'"

"Your Majesty resides in the imperial capital where the court is filled with many eminent and capable men; I request that you deign to provide a single cubit as a model for others. It would not be merely a short rope of a hundred cubits, but even one of a thousand fathoms could surely be produced."
The messenger went and reported the matter in detail to the king, who said,
"Was this spoken by the father,
or was it the son's words?"
He replied, "These are the words of Mahauṣadha.
Once the king had heard this, he was struck with wonder; remembering that what the celestial deity had said was true, he thought, "My kingdom shall surely see the end of its calamities."
“Later, at another time, the king again sent a messenger to that city, ordering them to prepare cooked rice and bring it back.

He further instructed: ‘The grain must not be pounded in a mortar, nor shall even a single grain of rice be broken. It must not be kept indoors, nor outside. When steaming and boiling it, there must be neither fire nor absence of fire. When bringing the rice, one must travel neither on the path nor off the path; one must neither walk nor ride. Let the rice not be seen by the sun, yet it must not be in the shade. The person carrying the rice must be neither male nor female.’”

The messenger, carrying the king’s command, arrived at the city of Pūrṇa and immediately summoned Pūrṇa to exchange greetings; he then delivered the king’s instructions in full so that he might know them. Upon hearing this, Pūrṇa remained in a state of even greater alarm, anxiety, and distress.
Seeing his father’s distress, Mahauṣadha approached him and said,
"Why do you have such a sorrowful countenance?
His father then related the matter in detail, and Mahauṣadha said:
"This is not worth worrying about; I shall manage it entirely.
He then took the rice and gathered many people together, instructing each one to rub the husks from every grain with their fingers, yet not a single grain of rice was broken.

Having obtained the rice, he sought a place to cook it; he immediately set up a cauldron beneath the eaves outside the gate and boiled it there. With the scorching sun overhead and fire blazing at its sides, the rice was soon cooked.
As he departed carrying the rice, he instructed the messenger, saying:
"You should place one foot on the path and the other on the wasteland; set the vessel of rice upon the crown of your head, covered by a coarse cloth parasol—neither in full sun nor in shade.
Wear shoes on one foot while the other is barefoot; thus you shall be neither walking nor riding. By employing a eunuch, you shall be neither male nor female."

Having brought the rice, he entered and presented it to the king. The king questioned the messenger, who answered him in full detail. Hearing this, the king was greatly delighted and asked: "By whom was this done?"
He replied, "It is Mahauṣadha.
The king was struck with extreme amazement and said to the messenger:
"Mahābhaiṣajya’s stratagems are profound and far-reaching; he possesses great wisdom and is well-versed in ritual protocols. Observing his plans, he is truly a talent capable of assisting a king.
Later, at another time, the king again dispatched a messenger to inform Pūrṇa, saying:
"I require a garden park, complete with groves and ponds and abounding in flowers and fruits; you must bring it here quickly."
When the messenger arrived there and related the matter in full, Pūrṇa was filled with distress and said:
"This is difficult to accomplish; the park is devoid of feeling and cannot be moved. How could one possibly wish to take it away?"
Seeing that [the father] was distressed, Mahauṣadha questioned him as before, and the father said:
"How could I not be distressed?
The King demands my garden and pond; how can they be taken away?"
Mahauṣadha said, "Father, you need not worry; I shall arrange everything so that the king is filled with joy.
He then replied to the messenger:

"Having received Your Majesty’s command, how could I dare not comply? However, as the gardens and ponds of this place have long been situated in the wilderness, I am unacquainted with the proper protocols for conduct and movement; should I arrive at the capital, I fear I might inadvertently commit some offense."
"I humbly pray that Your Majesty will deign to grant a small garden; if you would come for a moment to lead me there, I may follow after you and this matter can be accomplished.
The messenger returned and reported this in full.
The King said:
"Whose words are these?
He replied, "They are Great Medicine's."
The King was doubly amazed and marveled that this was truly rare.

Later, at another time, he again sent a messenger to deliver five hundred choice bulls to him, instructing him to feed and care for them exclusively for the purpose of providing milk and curd, ensuring there was no deficiency in their supply.
When the messenger arrived and reported the situation in full, Parṇāda was filled with grief and alarm. Mahauṣadha saw his father and questioned him as before;
his father said, "How can I not be distressed?
The King has sent a bull specifically to provide milk and curd, yet he demands what is not available, and there is no way to obtain it."
"If we do not obey the king's command, we shall incur severe punishment.
Mahābhiṣak said, "Please do not worry, father; I have devised a plan that will cause the king to hear it and cease demanding the milk and curd."
He immediately summoned the father and son and instructed them thoroughly on the matter:

"Go toward the royal city and wait for the king to go out. When you are not far from him, tie a large wooden bowl to your father’s belly and cover it with his lower garment; then, writhing on the ground, weep and groan. You, meanwhile, shall offer incense and flowers to the assembly of devas, saying:
'I pray that you protect and sustain us in all ten directions; may my father give birth in safety and peace.'"

Having received these instructions, the father and son followed one another to the royal capital. Seeing the king about to depart, they went not far from him and performed everything in succession exactly as instructed.
The child cried out and addressed the Four Heavenly Kings, saying:
"I pray that you will bestow your compassion, so that my father may experience a safe and peaceful delivery.
When the kings heard his voice, they sent a messenger to inquire about him.
"Why are you making this sound?

The messenger saw a man rolling on the ground; his belly was very large, and he was crying out. The son offered incense and flowers to the assembly of devas, and the messenger asked the man: "What are you doing?"
She replied, "My father is about to give birth but cannot do so in peace; for this reason, he weeps and implores the heavens for protection.
The messenger returned and informed the king.
The king summoned the father and son and asked,
"What were you doing? They then reported everything to the king in detail.
"My father wishes to give birth but cannot bring forth; for this reason he weeps.
When the king heard this, he laughed and said, "I have never heard of a man giving birth to a child."
The son replied, "It is indeed as the King says;
Your Majesty knows that it is not fitting for a man to give birth. Why then have you assigned five hundred oxen to Puṇyavanta, ordering him to provide curds and milk?"
"Have you ever heard of a bull giving birth to offspring?
Since it has no sons, from where could milk and curd come?
The king laughed and said:
"Whose plan is this?
The messenger replied,
"It is all Mahābhaiṣajya's."
The king marveled at his wisdom.
Later, on another occasion, the king consulted with his ministers, saying:
"Mahābhaiṣajya is possessed of vast knowledge; few can equal him."
"I shall further test and examine his spirit through another matter.
He then sent a mule to Pūrṇa with these instructions:
"Do not tether it with a halter; do not keep it indoors; do not feed it cut grass; let it loose wherever it pleases."
The messenger arrived at that city and handed the mule over to Pūrṇa, informing him of the matter in full:
"You must care for it well and not allow it to be lost; if you do not follow these instructions, you shall be punished."
Upon hearing this, Pūrṇa felt as if an arrow of grief had pierced his heart, and he thought to himself:
"This is a calamity for which even the gods can do nothing; how much less so for a mere human!"
When Mahauṣadha saw his father, he answered as before and replied, "Father, you need not worry; I shall do it all.

During the day, he let the cattle graze in the fields, and at night, he brought them home. Since it was difficult to manage them in the open air without tethering ropes, he strictly assigned twenty-one men to keep watch during the night. Five men were stationed under each foot of the cattle, with one man riding atop them, taking turns to hold and guard them in a continuous cycle that began and ended again.
The king had people secretly observe how they were guarding him;
when the messengers reported the matter, the king said, "If this is the case, the mule has no way to escape. How can I inflict punishment?"
The minister said,
"You should command those who ride with you to mount the mules and escape secretly during the night while they are asleep,
ensuring that no one knows. They all did as instructed.
When the guards reached the break of dawn, they reported to Pūrṇa:
"The mule has been lost.
Having heard this report, he feared for his life and was consumed by the fire of anxiety.
Having understood this, Mahauṣadha thought to himself:
"If I act with some degree of leniency, my plan may succeed; however, if I press him too urgently at the last moment, he will be overcome by fear.
He then said to his father:
“There is a brief plan that would be somewhat difficult to carry out; if you, father, do not shrink from shame, we may yet hope to avoid punishment.
The father said, “As long as death is avoided, what more need be said?”

Thereupon, Mahauṣadha shaved his father’s hair into seven tufts, smeared his body with blue, yellow, red, and white pigments, and had him mount a donkey to travel to the capital city. There, he raised his voice in a loud proclamation, saying:
"Mahauṣadha has now arrived, bringing his father along; this shaven and decorated appearance is truly extraordinary!"
When the king’s ministers heard these words, they spoke thus together:
“It is a good thing that Mahābhaiṣajya has come from afar; however, he has brought dishonor upon his father and stained the legal statutes.”
The king and all the people went outside the city together to welcome Mahauṣadha, wishing to observe whether his actions were real or false.
When the king and the citizens observed and realized they were indeed real, the minister then addressed the king, saying:
"How is it, Great King, that you previously spoke these words:
'Mahābhaiṣajya is wise and his strategic insight surpasses that of men,' yet when observing this deed of his, how base and contemptible it is!"
The king asked Mahauṣadha,
"For what reason have you now caused your father to suffer such humiliation? He replied:
"Great King! You now regard this as an honor, unaware of its disgrace.
Your servant possesses manifold skillful wisdom; I shall now use it to offer service to my father."
The king asked,
"Between your wisdom and that of your father, which is superior? He replied:
"I am superior. The king said,
"I have never heard of a son being superior to his father."
"A son is born from a father; the father undergoes the toil and exhaustion of nurturing and raising him. Speaking from this perspective, the father excels the son.
Mahābhaiṣajya said, "May Your Majesty examine and discern which of the two, father or son, is more virtuous?"
The king and his ministers both said,
"The father is superior.
Mahābhaiṣajya stepped forward, prostrated himself, and said:

“Great King, previously you ordered a mule to be raised, which subsequently escaped and was lost; this donkey is the father of that mule, and by principle, the sire is superior to the offspring. We pray that Your Majesty will accept him and not impose heavy punishment.”
When the king and his ministers heard these words, they marveled at his extraordinary wisdom and strategy, which was rare indeed for this age.

The king was filled with extreme joy and immediately bestowed upon him grand honors, appointing him as a high minister. He entrusted all matters of state to his judgment; his reputation spread daily, and he investigated all affairs with such clarity that those far and near placed their trust in him, all praising and honoring him.
At that time, there was a brahmin who was well-versed in the scriptures and treatises from an early age. For the sake of taking a wife, he had spent a great deal of wealth;
not long after, he thought to himself: "I have expended much for the sake of taking a wife, leaving my household with its wealth depleted. How can I survive while living alone in poverty?"
He then went elsewhere to display his own skills and seek out precious wealth; having obtained five hundred coins, he took them and returned home.
Upon reaching the outskirts of the village, he thought to himself:

"My wife is young and her countenance is beautiful. It has been a long time since we were separated, and as there is no man in the house, she may act according to her own whims. How can I know if her intentions are trustworthy?"
"It is not appropriate for me to carry these gold coins inside.
After dusk, he went to a deserted grove, dug into the ground beneath a multi-rooted tree to bury them, and then returned to his former residence.
His wife had previously been having an illicit affair with a man named Śrutavān;
that night, after preparing a sumptuous meal and eating together, the Brahmin arrived at the house and knocked on the door, calling out.
From afar, his wife asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, "I am so-and-so.

Upon hearing his name, the wife hid Shan-ti beneath the bed; she then went out, opened the door, and feigned an expression of joy, leading him inside to the bedroom. She prepared a meal for him and let him eat his fill. Having finished eating, he thought to himself:
"Is it not that this wife has been having an illicit affair with another?
For what reason is there such fine food in the middle of the night?
Her husband, being straightforward by nature, asked:
"O Worthy One! Today is not an auspicious day, nor is there any festival; by what cause has such superior food been obtained? He replied:
"Recently, in a dream, a deity told me:
'Your husband is about to arrive.
For this reason, I knew to prepare food and wait for him."
The husband said,
"I am truly fortunate that Heaven has informed me just as I was about to arrive home.
After they had finished eating, they slept together, each asking the other whether they were at peace.
The wife said, "It has been many months since you left me; have you obtained any wealth or money? He replied:
"I have gained a little.
The wife then spoke secretly, signaling to the space beneath the bed, saying:
"I shall listen well and must know their number."
He asked, "How long has it been since you obtained it? He replied:
"I have obtained five hundred coins.
His wife said,
"Where did you place them without telling me?"
He replied, "Be at ease for now; I shall bring it tomorrow.
His wife said:
"I and you are of one body; why must you hide and not inform me?
Being by nature simple and straightforward, he replied, "It is located outside the city."
He said, "I shall listen well; you must know the location. He asked:
"Where is he? He replied, "He is in a certain grove, beneath a many-rooted tree."
The wife said, "Noble son, you have traveled a long way; you should rest in peace.
Once she knew he was asleep, she spoke these words:
"Listen well; you may proceed with it quickly.
He immediately rose from his bed, went beneath the banyan tree, obtained the gold coins, and returned to his own home.

When the brahmin reached daybreak, he went to the place where the money was hidden; seeing only an empty pit with nothing to be seen, he beat his head, struck his breast, and wailed aloud as he returned to his home.
His relatives and other acquaintances came together and asked him,
"Why are you so sorrowful and grieving? He replied:

"I have long endured great hardship in my search to obtain these five hundred gold coins. Yesterday, after the sun had set and all traffic had ceased, I hid them beneath a certain tree and returned home to stay. I came here today intending to retrieve them, but they have been taken away by thieves."
The people replied,
"We cannot know the details of this matter;
you should now ask Mahābhaiṣajya, for his wisdom and strategy surpass those of all others."
"If you surrender yourself, you will surely recover your money; as for other expedients, they are not within our knowledge.
At that time, the brahmin went weeping with tears streaming down to Mahābhaiṣajya, exchanged greetings with him, and immediately informed Mahābhaiṣajya of the preceding matter.
He then asked, "Have you perhaps spoken of this to others?
At that time, the brahmin told him everything in detail, and Mahābhaiṣajya thought to himself:
"His wife must have consorted with another man and committed this irrational act.
He then comforted the Brahmin, saying, "Please restrain yourself and do not give way to grief; we shall search for the lost items on your behalf."
He asked, "Does your honorable family have any dogs? He replied:
“There is. “You may now return home and report to your wife, saying:
‘Previously, before the image of Maheśvara, I made such a vow:’”
"I thought, 'If I return safely to my former home, I shall invite eight brahmins and provide them with offerings.
Thus, you invited four, and I invited four."
After the brahmin had replied to his wife, he returned to Mahābhaiṣajya and reported,
"It has been done. Mahābhaiṣajya said:
"When eight men come, you may take one of them to my house and have him stay before the gate; when the others enter, have him observe them closely.
He then said to that man, "You should watch those eight brahmins and see which one, upon seeing the dog, turns his face away and barks at it."
What is it that causes him to lower his ears and wag his tail as he moves forward?
When you observe these signs, you must keep them in mind.
You should have your wife serve the food and drink herself, and observe toward whom he casts a wistful glance or engages in conversation.

Having received these instructions, the messenger went at once to the man’s house and stood at the gate. He called for the eight men one after another to enter; when the dog saw them, it barked at all of them, but toward Śrutasoma alone it lowered its ears, went forward to meet him, made a soft "ou-ou" sound, wagged its tail, and showed its joy.
At that time, the messenger took note and listened attentively.
Later, during the mealtime, when his wife served the food, she raised her eyebrows and smiled at the place where Śravaṇa was seated, treating him differently than the others.
The messenger returned and reported the matter in full to Mahābhaiṣajya.
Upon hearing this, Mahābhaiṣajya immediately snapped his fingers and said, "How marvelous!"
"This man has indeed stolen another's property.
He then ordered a messenger to summon Śravaṇa and rebuked him, saying:
"How can a brāhmaṇa follow such a practice as this, taking the property of others and making it his own wealth? That which you have taken must be returned to its owner immediately."
He replied, "I dare swear a solemn oath that I shall not take the wealth of others.
At that time, Mahābhaiṣajya said to the messenger:
"This is an evil man who should be confined in prison; according to the laws of the kingdom, he shall be subjected to severe punishment.
Upon hearing these harsh words, he was struck with great terror and said:
"Great Minister, please grant me protection; I shall return the goods."
He immediately took the gold coins, which remained unopened as before, and gave them to Mahābhaiṣajya; he then returned the original goods to the Brahmin.
The Brahmin, filled with joy, thought to himself:
"That I, in my old age, have recovered my principal capital is entirely due to the power of Mahābhaiṣajya; I should now repay his kindness in a significant way."
He immediately reduced the amount by half and offered it to Mahābhaiṣajya; having accepted it, Mahābhaiṣajya returned it to him and said, "My purpose is to relieve others;
how could I seek my own self-interest?"
At that time, his good reputation spread throughout the kingdom; when the king, his ministers, and the common people heard of it, they spoke thus:
"We are fortunate to have such a superior person come to protect us together, so that we shall not be subject to wrongful violence or sudden encroachment."

At that time, there was a man who, having traveled to another region and returned to his former place, rested by the side of a pond outside the city. He took some parched grain from his leather bag and ate it, then forgot to tie the opening shut as he wandered off elsewhere.

At that time, a venomous snake had entered into the flour; once the man arrived, he did not examine it carefully but tied the bag and carried it back. Outside the city gate, he encountered a physiognomist on the road, who said to him: "O man!..."
"I observe your countenance and see that your life is but a matter of moments.
Although the man heard this, he did not take it as a cause for concern; yet as he moved further away, he regretted not having sought him out immediately and thought to himself:
"I should now go first to consult Mahābhaiṣajya, and only then return home; he possesses great wisdom and skillful means, and will be able to resolve my dilemma."
Taking the bag of parched grain with him, he went to Mahauṣadha and related the matter in detail.
Mahauṣadha thought to himself:
"Could it not be that there is a venomous snake inside the bag, which is why that fortune-teller spoke those words?"

In front of the multitude, he immediately ordered the bag to be placed on the ground and pried it open with a staff; a large venomous snake emerged from within, baring its scales and spitting venom as it slithered away.
When the people saw this, they all marveled at such a rare wonder.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 27. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.

The Fourth Section of the Sixth Gate: A Summary Verse on the Remainder of Mahābhaiṣajya. "At that time, having taken charge of the affairs of state, Mahābhaiṣajya led the fourfold army and traveled throughout the realm. Whenever he reached a city or village, he would ask the people: "
"Whom do these villages belong to?
The people replied, "This belongs to such-and-such a high minister, and that belongs to such-and-such a high minister; they have taken them under their own control and made them their fiefdoms."

Upon hearing this, Mahauṣadha learned that all the villages and cities were under the jurisdiction of the six great ministers, while the sovereign possessed nothing but the inner palace and his provisions.
Having completed his thorough inspection, he returned and addressed the king, saying:
"In which cities, moats, or villages does the king hold ownership?
The king replied:
"I am now powerless; what shall I do? Fortunately, the High Heaven has granted me a premonition, saying:

'In the city of Pūrṇa, within the household of Pūrṇaka, a son shall be born named Mahābhaiṣajya. Once he has grown to maturity, he shall be appointed as a great minister, and while the sovereign remains with hands folded and robes trailing, his transformation of the people will bring harmony to all.'"
"For this reason, while you were still in the womb, I provided for all your needs by virtue of my divine mandate.

Now that you have reached adulthood and drawn near to me, having already attained the rank of high minister, you ought to follow the words recorded by that deity. You should extensively formulate wise counsels to propagate the state's governance together with me, so that I may rule as a sovereign in sovereignty, peace, and security."
At that time, Mahauṣadha bowed his head in salutation and addressed him, saying:
"Great King! Please have no anxiety; I shall assist Your Majesty so that you may attain peace and happiness."
"Mahābhaiṣajya then sent messengers throughout his own realm to all the cities and towns belonging to the six ministers, commanding them to say:
'Gentlemen, you should know this!'"

These ministers have failed to obey the national decrees, causing the burden of taxes and labor to become extraordinary and exhausting, while they themselves remain greedy, wicked, and indifferent to one another’s welfare.

I now inform you with the truth: if you follow my words, you shall enjoy lasting peace and happiness without further hardship; the taxes and levies assigned to you shall be according to your actual means, and your kinsmen and wives shall never again suffer from toil and distress.
"You six cities must each hold your positions firmly; even if the King’s command or the six ministers should pursue you, you must not heed their words.
Should they arrive in person, do not open your gates."
He replied,
"When the minister Mahābhaiṣajya arrives, I shall submit as his guest.
Having heard this instruction within their kingdom, all followed it accordingly and no longer observed the old decree.
Then those ministers addressed the king together, saying:
"The various cities have rebelled; what do you intend to do about this?
The king said:
"You all must prepare the fourfold army and go forth to suppress [the rebels] wherever they may be.
The ministers each arrived at their respective locations, but he was nowhere to be found. The ministers reported to the king, saying:
"We have no power; Your Majesty should come in person."
The King then went there in person, but they likewise did not submit; he labored in vain on the battlefield for a long time.
The various cities reported:
"We have no intention of rebelling against Your Majesty; it is because the six ministers are tyrannical that we do not follow them."
"If you cause the minister Mahābhaiṣajya to come, I shall subdue them all.
The king immediately dispatched a messenger to summon Mahābhaiṣajya; upon hearing the royal command, he hurried to the king's presence.

When the common people of all the cities heard that Mahābhaiṣajya had arrived, they all opened their gates without opposition to let him enter. Mahābhaiṣajya immediately abolished the tyrannical administration and established lighter penalties; the social order was restored, and from the smallest to the greatest, none harbored resentment. All sang of a second birth and rejoiced in their renewed salvation. He relieved the poor and destitute and showed compassion to the orphaned and widowed, treating them with the same loving care as parents would for their own children.
The people of the kingdom all gathered like clouds, and the retinue accompanied the Great King to the city; his fame was heard by neighboring states and praised far and wide.
The King then gave his daughter in marriage to Mahābhaiṣajya; though he received her favor and affection, he harbored no heart of arrogance or self-indulgence.
At that time, a poor man from another region came to seek refuge with this king, hoping to obtain honor and emolument; however, the king did not grant his request.
He then sought out Mahābhaiṣajya, who took pity on him and consequently welcomed him, providing him with food and clothing so that he lacked for nothing.
At that time, a brahmin came to Mahauṣadha to beg for bran and barley; he immediately sent it to be given to him.
