However, the keeper of the storehouse procrastinated with the matter and did not deliver it at once.
Later, on another occasion, when the king was assembled in one place with his ministers and various officials, he addressed the multitude, saying:
"In matters of private secrecy, who is it that may be informed?"
Some said: "Secret matters should be told to one's spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). Others said:
"Parents. Some say: "Wife and children."
However, Mahauṣadha remained silent and said nothing.
The king asked, "Mahauṣadha! Why do you not speak?"
He replied: "How easy it is to speak!
As I see it, one should not disclose secret matters to any man, let alone to a woman!"
The King said, "Is it truly as you say? Mahābhaiṣajya replied:
"Whether this is true or false, Your Majesty shall verify it with your own eyes.
Later, when the royal household lost a peacock, Mahābhaiṣajya captured one and hid it elsewhere; he then slaughtered another peacock before his wife and informed her, saying:
"Have you not heard that the King has lost a peacock?"
He replied, "I have heard it. Mahābhaiṣajya said:
"This bird is it; prepare it quickly, for I wish to eat it. You must not discuss this matter with anyone.
Upon hearing this, the wife thought to herself:
"My father has placed his extraordinary trust in me regarding this bird; how can I now kill and eat it?"
"Truly, my humble affairs need not fear the established codes.
He then took another woman of beautiful countenance, adorned her exquisitely, and brought her into his residence, saying to his wife:
"This young woman is a person from the royal palace whom I have loved and brought here; do not spread word of this matter."
Upon hearing these words, the wife was deeply incensed and said:

"How could my father fail to exercise careful deliberation, appointing such a lowly man of no noble lineage as a minister and entrusting him with the affairs of state? Could he truly intend to take a woman from the royal palace for his own chamber, and kill the pet bird he cherished to make a stew?"
Furthermore, foreign guests were received together with him, provided with food and clothing, and supported as honorable men; his wife reported this matter in detail to the king, saying:
"My father places deep trust in that man, yet I observe that his evil conduct is truly beyond measure; he should now be ordered to return to his home village."
Upon hearing these words, the king conceived a different view and ordered an executioner to take Mahābhaiṣajya away to be executed according to the law.

Then, the Caṇḍāla tied red *śirīṣa* flowers beneath his neck, struck a drum of ill omen, and was followed by wicked men; raising his sword, he sent him toward the charnel ground like a terrifying emissary of Yama.

As he was about to undergo execution, no one would be willing to kill him; the onlookers wept with grief, regarding him as if he were their own kin, each uttering words of lamentation and praying to the gods and Buddhas for his sake.
At that time, a foreign guest who provided them with food and clothing said to the people, "I can kill this man."
As they were about to leave the city, that brahmin seized the hem of Mahābhaiṣajya’s garment and demanded one *śīrṣa* of husked barley.
Seeing this, Mahābhaiṣajya spoke these verses:
“A king should not be befriended; An evil person is difficult to associate with.”
However, these are secret matters, not spoken of even to women to know.
I do not eat raw birds; I do not entice those within the inner palace;
I do not recall having a deceitful mind, nor do I owe others a debt of husks and barley.
At that time, as Mahābhaiṣajya was about to undergo execution, he spoke these words. Having heard them, the executioner said to Mahābhaiṣajya:
"Your wisdom surpasses that of men, yet you utter such meaningless speech."
He replied, "These words are meaningless and beyond your comprehension; you should take my message to the Great King.

The messenger went and informed the king of these words. Although the king listened to what was said, he could not yet understand it, so he ordered the messenger to go and summon Mahābhaiṣajya, asking him:
"What do you mean by 'it is meaningless'? He replied,
"The words are profound and possess principle."
The King asked,
"What is the matter? Mahābhaiṣajya replied:
"May Your Majesty listen well as I briefly set forth the meaning of my verses. Regarding the statement that a king is not to be relied upon:

previously, all the cities and towns within Your Majesty’s realm were not subject to you; they were concerned solely with food and drink within the inner palace. I devised strategies to suppress those powerful ministers, bringing peace to the state and security to the people so that all might return to their vocations. That the imperial foundation flourished and the entire land rejoiced in song, and that the treasuries became abundant—all was through my efforts.
Now, You wish to kill me to repay a past kindness; therefore, it is said that a king is not to be relied upon."

Regarding the saying that "evil people are difficult to associate with": long ago, there was a poor man traveling from another land who came to seek refuge at the King’s court to beg for his life. The King would not accept him, so he came to me. Seeing his poverty and suffering, I provided him with food and clothing so that he might survive.
Yet, instead of reflecting on my kindness, he has now come to kill me.
Regarding the statement that one should not speak of secret matters to women: in the past, while on state affairs, the King asked his people, "If there is a secret matter, who may be told?
Someone replied:
"Parents, wife, children, and so forth," as explained in detail previously. I said:
"None of these are to be trusted; you must examine them closely and verify them for yourself.
As for the peacock from the royal household, I truly did not eat it; I had another bird brought and ordered my wife to cook it as a stew.
Regarding the women of the palace, I have no connection with them; I merely borrowed their necklace temporarily and lent a woman who resides in my house [the ornaments] for a short time."
"If you do not believe me, you may summon her here.
The king summoned a palace woman; upon comparing them, they were indistinguishable.

Regarding the statement, "I have not wronged another regarding the grain and barley," the king ordered an executioner to put me to death. That man then approached and urgently seized the hem of my garment, saying:
"Return me my one *droṇa* of parched barley," he said, meaning:
"He has no compassion and does not understand the shifts of circumstance; having previously begged for barley, he now comes to demand it upon seeing me dead.

When the king heard the meaning of the verse and investigated the matter, he realized that Mahābhiṣak was without fault. Delighted, he released him and prepared a grand reception, appointing him as a high minister.
At that time, Mahauṣadha bowed his head and said to the king:
"May I observe whether it is appropriate for women to share secret counsel?
The woman you have bestowed upon me is of no use to me; please accept her back immediately."
"I shall now seek for myself a woman of equal lineage, whose speech, conduct, virtue, and character are fitting, and who is wise and intelligent, to serve as my wife.

Having thus spoken, he took leave of the king and departed in the guise of a Brahmin; carrying a pure water-jar in his hand, wearing the auspicious thread, clad in deerskin, and with three lines painted upon his face, he went toward the capital city to seek a bride.
"While traveling on the road at dusk, he encountered a brahmin, who asked him,
'Virtuous one, from where have you come?
Mahābhaiṣajya replied:"
"I have come from the city of Videha.
"Where do you wish to go? He replied:
"Head toward the city of Pūrṇavasu. He asked,
"Do you have any acquaintances here where you might seek lodging for the night?"
He replied, "There was none before.
He then took it back to his house and installed it according to the ritual.
Mahābhaiṣajya saw that the Brahmin’s wife was not chaste; having stayed the night, he wished to depart at dawn.
The Brahmin said, "This poor dwelling of mine is your home as well; please do not hesitate to come and stay whenever you wish."
Mahābhaiṣajya consented, took his hand, and they parted.

Then, along the road, he saw a young girl in a wheat field; her appearance was upright and refined, as if she were from a noble family, and he immediately conceived a feeling of affection for her and asked:
"O fair-faced one!"
"What is your name? He replied, "My name is Viśākhā."
"Whose daughter are you? She replied, "The village elder is my father."
The Great Medicine thought to himself, "Though he possesses a dignified appearance, I do not yet know his wisdom; I shall test him now.
The Great Medicine then went into a wheat field and, raising both hands high, trampled the wheat with his feet. Viśākhā said:
"I already know how to protect my hands; it is likewise appropriate for my feet.
Mahābhaiṣajya thought to himself, "This woman possesses wisdom."
He then said to her, "Maiden,
your earrings are lovely and their radiance is extraordinary. She replied:
"What good is there in covering this foul body?
He replied again,
"It is a most excellent appearance!"
He replied, "That which is born of one's parents has nothing to do with outward adornment. He asked:
"Where has my father gone? He replied,
"One body performing two tasks."
He asked: "What is the meaning of these words? He replied:
"He has taken up thorns with his body, severed his old path, and opened a new road.
[The king asked: "Where is his mother? He replied:
"Go home and fetch some seeds; I wish to plant them in the late-ripening fields.
He asked, "Can you become my wife?"
He replied: "This is due to my parents; it is not something I know. He was asked:
"Where lies the road to the city of Pūrṇabhadda?
It should be level, straight, soft, and free of thorns; you should point it out so that I may travel there in safety.
The woman pointed toward a winding path.
He immediately went forward on his own, approached the edge of the pond, changed his clothes, and sat down. He squinted one eye and thought, "I shall test whether Mahābhaiṣajya recognizes me.
After a short while, Mahābhaiṣajya arrived at the edge of the pond; seeing him from afar, he recognized him and spoke this verse:
"Your body wears a garment without thread or weave, Not originally produced from cotton or silk; [...]"
"Please, with a single glance, point out to me: which path should I take to go to the City of Wondrous Flowers?
Having heard these words, the young maiden smiled and said:
"One should travel by the smooth road; one need not proceed by the rough path."
Seeing from afar a great forest, one may pass by its edge;
seeing further a place where flour is ground, with a tree bearing red flowers,
one should leave it to the left or right and follow this path away.

"Mahābhaiṣajya followed these words and set out on the road. Upon reaching the city of Puṣpapura, not far from the city, he went to the residence of Viśākhā but did not see her parents. He then asked the city lord, saying:
'If you could grant me Viśākhā, it would be a profound act of kindness.'"
When those people heard these words, they were all filled with indignation and replied:
"Brāhmaṇa! You who live by begging truly have no sense of shame; why do you so recklessly seek Viśākhā?"
"This girl’s appearance is like that of a celestial nymph; you should depart immediately and leave the corner of my city. If you come back again, I will have the dogs devour you.
When the brahmin found his hopes frustrated, he returned to Viśākhā's place. Seeing him from afar, the girl cried out, "Welcome!"
At that time, Mahauṣadha related the preceding events in detail:
"When I questioned the people just now, how many were not beaten?
The woman said:
"What you have done is irrational and a mark of lack of wisdom; this is not the proper way to seek a marriage alliance.
Mahābhaiṣajya asked, "How, then, should it be done?"
The woman said:
"First, let us become acquainted; next, let us grow close; afterwards, you may invite me to partake of various fine foods, and only then shall I fully explain what I have to say."
Having heard this announcement, they proceeded to prepare the meal in its proper sequence; afterwards, when they sought Viśākhā, the people said to her, "We shall do as you wish."
While they were discussing this matter, his parents arrived; Mahābhaiṣajya then went with the city lord to their home and informed his parents of the marriage arrangements.
He replied,
"Gentlemen, please wait a moment while I reflect.
The men said to him:

"You need not deliberate further. This young Brahmin is handsome and has mastered the scriptures; he is thoroughly proficient in the Four Vedas and the Five Treatises. It would be a waste of time to delay, for such individuals are difficult to encounter. You should betroth her to him without further hesitation."

At that time, once the people had formally promised their daughter to Mahābhaiṣajya with sincere words, the matter was settled; they presented him with fine garments for his parents, and Viśākhā also left behind gifts as a token of respect. He then returned toward the city of Vaiśālī, intending to go to the presence of King Udayana.

On the way, he encountered another who was holding a festival; having obtained one *śīrṣa* of husked barley wrapped in the hem of his garment, he went to the place where the Brahmin had previously stayed and knocked on the door, calling out. The Brahmin’s wife came out and asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, "This is your husband’s friend.
The wife said:
"My husband is away; I do not admit outsiders. You may go to another house to seek a place to stay.
Then Mahābhaiṣajya thought:
"What could be the reason that she will not allow me to stay the night?"
Before he had gone far, he saw another person enter the house.
Bhaiṣajyarāja thought again:
"It is because of this outsider that they will not let me in."
While she was thus hesitating, her husband arrived and called for the door to be opened; hearing her husband's voice, the wife’s soul was struck with terror and she knew not what to do.
She then placed the paramour inside a small grain-bin.
The husband entered the door at the same time as Mahābhaiṣajya.
Mahābhaiṣajya asked, "Where shall I place this husked barley of mine?
His wife replied:
"You may pour it onto the ground. He replied,
"I fear the mice might eat it."
He then looked at the corner of the room and beneath the bed, but saw nothing; nearby was a small granary, and Mahābhaiṣajya reflected:
"The person must certainly be here."
He said to his wife,
"Place the wheat in the granary.
His wife replied:
"All that belongs to my household is kept here; what would you do with it if it were grain?
Her husband said, "You wretched woman!"
"Why do you not take out the goods and place the barley inside the granary?
He then resisted and refused to let her approach. The wife, realizing his intent and feeling helpless, became terrified and, having no other recourse, replied:
"The granary is damp; I fear it will damage the barley."
The Great Medicine said, "You need not worry; I shall not let it be damaged.

He then took firewood, grass, and dried cow dung, intending to heat the sides of the granary with fire. His wife, in a state of panic, feared the fire would burn it, and immediately sent another person to inform her father, saying:
"Your son has met with misfortune; you must come at once.
Upon hearing this, the father ran there and, finding his son inside the granary, said to Mahābhaiṣajya, "If you require the granary, I shall pay its price; how much do you ask?"
He replied, "Five hundred gold coins.
While they were thus discussing, fires were lit on all four sides; then the father said:
"My son has now died; what use would I have for money?
she said, and so she gave him a gold coin and took away the basket.
The next day, Mahābhaiṣajya divided one hundred [coins], leaving them with the host, and informed him of all the circumstances of the matter.
"Your wife’s conduct is wicked; you must guard against it closely.

He then immediately drafted a letter for the Brahmin, instructing him to go to the city of Puṣpapurī and deliver four hundred gold coins to Viśākhā, while also conveying this message to the city lord:
"I am not a traveler, but a high minister of the king. I previously went there for the sake of seeking a marriage; you should properly care for and protect Viśākhā."
Bhaiṣajyarāja then immediately went to Videha.
That brahmin took the letter and the money to Viśākhā’s place, where he handed over the letter and the three hundred gold coins he had brought.
Viśākhā received a letter that said:
"Four stakes can produce a robe; with one missing, it cannot be woven.
If there is a deficiency in your pegs, you shall be bound at the feet and made to deliver them."
Having finished reading the document, he next received the money, but obtained only three hundred coins; he then searched beneath the bed for the remaining shackles.
The messenger asked, "What do you seek?"
He replied, "At present,
there is a criminal from the royal household whose feet must be shackled.
Having obtained the shackles, he informed the messenger, saying:
"I do not know how to secure it;
you may extend your foot so that I may try it for a moment.
That Brahmin was by nature simple and straightforward, so he immediately extended his foot into the shackle. Viśākhā then struck it with a wedge from behind to make it firm. The messenger said:
"Why have you forbidden me? He replied,
"He entrusted four hundred [coins], and you stole one hundred."
The messenger thought to himself:
"This is truly extraordinary; both are wise, and their matter is difficult to deceive.
He then returned the hundred coins exactly as counted.
When his parents arrived, he presented them with the money and informed them, saying,
"The one who previously sought me was not a poor brahmin, but rather the king’s minister of Videha named Mahābhiṣak."
When the parents and their kinsmen heard these words, they were all greatly rejoiced, saying:
"We are fortunate to have the opportunity to form a marriage alliance with such a preeminent minister; we hope that this person will bring prosperity to our family."

From that time forward, Viśākhā was provided with bathing facilities, clothing, food, and bedding, all of which were exquisite and abundant; as her nourishment became plentiful, her appearance became twice as usual, dignified and lovely.
At that time, Mahauṣadha arrived at his native city; when the king and his ministers heard that Mahauṣadha had arrived, they were all filled with joy.
Upon meeting the king, the king asked Mahauṣadha:
"Did you succeed in finding a wife?"
He replied, "I have obtained it. The king said:
"How is she? he asked.

He replied, "This young woman’s beauty and countenance are peerless; she is intelligent, wise, and possesses extraordinary eloquence and discernment. She is a match for me as a wife; shall I now petition the King to take her as my future consort?"
The King said:
"You are a great minister beyond reproach; as for the necessary rites and ceremonies, they must be exquisite and extraordinary. Adorn them as you see fit to bring joy to the multitude."

Having received this command, Mahauṣadha immediately joined other ministers, brahmins, householders, and the various multitudes—leading the fourfold army of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—to the city of Puṣpapurī. Upon arriving at the residence of Viśākhā, they performed the marriage rites; once the ceremonies were completed, he returned to Vaiśālī and dwelt there in joy.
"At that time, there were five hundred merchants from the north who came to Vaiśālī for the purpose of trading horses.

In this city, there were five hundred courtesans whose appearance was upright and elegant, and whose singing, dancing, and speech were all preeminent; whatever merchants arrived there, they caused their entire wealth to be exhausted."

The five hundred courtesans approached the five hundred men, each engaging in amorous play; however, the merchant leader alone remained unswayed by their allure. The foremost among those courtesans went to the merchant leader’s side and sought to form an intimate bond with him.

Not being permitted by him, the others came again day after day; yet that merchant leader remained steadfast and unyielding, and they continued to come frequently to engage in conversation and laughter with him.
The merchant leader said, "I have no improper thoughts; my coming and going has been in vain.
The courtesan said:
"If you diminish your resolve, what will you give me? He replied,
"I shall give you five fine horses."
"If you have no private faults, you shall give me five hundred gold coins.
Having made this agreement, she redoubled her efforts at artifice and came to flatter and cajole him; yet she could not cause the merchant leader to change his mind.
The merchants said, "In this city,
it is absolutely forbidden to go against one's feelings.
The caravan leader replied:
"I had an intimate encounter with him in a dream last night; why trouble yourself to see him in person?
When the people heard this, they reported it together to the courtesan.
She immediately brought her men-at-arms to demand payment from the merchant leader.
"You should fulfill your previous word by giving me five horses; you have already failed in your resolve and committed an unrighteous act with me.
The merchant leader said, "You are shameless to falsely accuse an honest man."
He then went to the royal court of justice, where they deliberated until evening without reaching a verdict on who was right or wrong,
saying, "You may come tomorrow for further examination. Mahābhaiṣajya returned home later than usual, and Viśākhā asked, "Why have you returned so late?"
He then related everything in detail, saying,
"The case has not yet been settled.
His wife said:
"You all are well-versed in the principles of logic, yet you do not even understand this; how can you be considered wise?
Mahābhaiṣajya replied, "We are not yet proficient; are you able to resolve it?"
The wife said, "I shall try to resolve this; let us observe what your wisdom is like.

First, report to the King and summon the assembly of ministers, and lead the five horses together to the edge of the pond. There, in the midst of the assembly, you may call that courtesan and ask her:"
"The caravan leader has committed an act of unrighteousness against you; you may take the real horse.
Just as in your dream, you may lead away the reflected horse from the pond as you please. If he says:
"The shadow-horse has no substance that can be grasped. "The acts of desire committed in a dream are likewise so.

Upon hearing this, Mahābhaiṣajya was deeply moved with admiration. The very next day, he petitioned the King to summon his ministers; they gathered a great multitude along with courtesans and went together to the edge of the pond. The five horses were led out and stood upon the bank. Following the plan devised by Viśākhā, Mahābhaiṣajya questioned them one by one. When the King and the assembly heard this, they all felt a sense of wonder. The King then said to Mahābhaiṣajya:
"Since you all made this decision yesterday morning, there is no need for the trouble of assembling again today.
Whose plan was this? They replied:
"This is Viśākhā; last night when I returned, she related the matter in full.
The king and his retinue marveled at this, saying, "Viśākhā possesses great wisdom and strategic insight."
His fame spread far and wide, and everyone, both near and distant, came to know of it.
At that time, two mares were presented from the north:
one was a mother and the other was her daughter.

Their physical dimensions and fur color were indistinguishable; neither the mother nor the daughter could tell them apart, and when the king and his retinue observed them together, no one could identify them.
Having heard this, Viśākhā said:
"The one with coarse fur is the mother; the one with soft fur is the daughter."
The assembly marveled at this rare occurrence.

At another time, a snake-charmer brought two venomous snakes to the King’s presence; they were so similar in appearance that it was impossible to distinguish male from female, and no one could identify them.
Mahābhaiṣajya informed Viśākhā of these matters; upon hearing this, she smiled and replied:
"If you are thus deluded regarding this matter, how can you be called wise men?
How can you be known by the King?"
"You eat in vain upon the merit of your fief and emolument.
Mahābhaiṣajya said, "Do you know this?"
He replied: "I understand well.
One should tie a soft object to the tip of a staff and rub it against the snake's back; if the back curves and moves, it is male, and if it does not move, it is female."
He immediately acted according to the words, and his visual verification proved them not false; everyone marveled at his skill.

At that time, a merchant from the southern country brought a sandalwood staff to the King’s presence. As its two ends were identical, it was difficult to distinguish the base from the tip. When he questioned Viśākhā, she laughed as before and said:
"Place this staff in the water of the pond; the base will sink down, while the tip will float up."
The trial proved exactly as he had said, and everyone marveled at his excellence.
The king then thought to himself:
"I now wish to test which among my ministers possesses the greatest wisdom."

He immediately erected another banner-pole upon the upper story of the pavilion and placed a luminous jewel at its tip; when the sunlight shone upon it, its reflection fell into the pond, indistinguishable from the actual jewel itself.
He addressed the people, saying:
"If you enter the pond and obtain this pearl, I shall grant it to you.
Everyone entered the pond to seek it, but none could find it.
Mahābhaiṣajya returned and reported this to Viśākhā, who replied:
"Look upward and you shall find the origin of the pearl.
Following her words, he retrieved it, whereupon the King said:
"Who is this person of supreme wisdom? He replied, "It is Viśākhā."
The King then gave him the jewel, praising him all the more.

At that time, the various ministers, seeing that Viśākhā’s appearance was so exceptionally distinguished as to be peerless in the world, all conceived a desire for her in private love and sent back and forth messengers with exquisite jewels.
However, Viśākhā had never entertained such thoughts; seeing that [the man] continued to beg for her without ceasing, she said to Mahābhaiṣajya:
"In your kingdom there are those who, upon seeing another's beautiful wife, immediately seek her in secret—this is truly base and loathsome."
He replied, "This is a worldly custom that everyone transmits; however, if that woman is one of virtuous integrity, she will not comply.
The wife said:
"I wish to humiliate him; do not hold me accountable for this. He replied, "As you wish."
The wife said, "You may claim to be ill; I myself will know the right time.
Mahābhaiṣajya did as he was told and excused himself on the grounds of illness. The ministers sent a messenger to inquire after Viśākha, who replied:
"Indeed, my intention is not to cause harm.
He then fashioned a wooden figure identical in appearance to Mahābhaiṣajya, laid it upon a bed, and covered it with a thin garment.
He then informed the people, saying:
"My husband is gravely ill and his life is at its end; you may come to me as you wish according to your own strength, but do not let anyone see you.
She then constructed six large chests and placed them within six rooms, telling the ministers who arrived:
"Hide yourselves here for now, lest someone discover you."
Once they had entered, he immediately locked them securely inside; thus, all six ministers were placed within the chest.
He then announced to the people:
"Mahābhaiṣajya has died."
The king, his ministers, the ladies of the inner court, and the commoners all thought to themselves:
"Such a superior man has perished in a single day.
Each gave rise to grief and suffering, wailing and crying out until their voices failed.
Then Viśākhā carried six chests and went to the king’s presence, saying: "Great King!
Mahābhiṣak has passed away; all his precious goods are within these chests, and you should personally receive them."
He then recited two verses.
Seeing his pitiful state, the king thought, "Today he has died and has already brought these goods here.
At that moment, Mahābhaiṣajya entered through a side gate, his body adorned with flower garlands, and approaching the king, he spoke with a smile: "Your Majesty," he said.
"He cherished me with such profound affection that he did not wait even until death before immediately seizing my wealth.
The King said, "It was not I who demanded the wealth; rather, Viśākhā herself brought it here and spoke these words:"
“‘O Great King, you should now know!
Mahābhaiṣajya’s body has already passed away; these are his precious treasures. Open the chest and behold them for yourself.’”
"My husband’s form and shadow have vanished; I am solitary and widowed with no one to rely upon.
Fearing that some outsider might deceive me and cause me to lose this property of the royal house," said Mahābhaiṣajya. He replied:
"If that is so, Your Majesty, you may open it and see what precious treasures are within.
Once the chest was opened, the six great ministers each emerged from inside.
The king asked for the reason, and the six ministers replied:
"By our own passions, we have been deceived by women;
we pray for the Great King’s grace that we shall never again act in such a manner."
The King said: "The cycle of rebirth in this world arises entirely from form and desire; having suffered such humiliation, he deserves to receive a heavy penalty.
You may return for now; I shall deliberate further on this matter later."
The King then sighed and said:

"Alas, woman! To possess such pure and extraordinary integrity, and a strategy that transcends all others, never before seen; though the ministers and counselors have been brought to such humiliation, you are thereby able to restrain those who are addicted to desire."
The King was filled with joy and increased Viśākhā’s fief and emoluments twofold; this news spread throughout all the kingdoms.
At that time, the Great King thought to himself:
"Mahauṣadha possesses such merit that he has won over a wife of such wisdom."
He then said to Mahābhaiṣajya:

"You must seek for me a lady who possesses both wisdom and talent, one capable of ensuring that the internal and external affairs of state remain peaceful and secure, so that I may dwell in ease with my hands folded in idleness."
Mahābhaiṣajya replied, "Where may it be sought?
The king said:

"I have heard that the King of Pañcāla has a daughter named Bhaiṣajyā, whose beauty is peerless and whose refined intellect surpasses all others; it would be fitting to go and seek her hand in marriage, for it stands to reason that we should obtain her."
Mahābhaiṣajya replied, "That is a neighboring kingdom, and our relationship is like that of enemies; one must first employ skillful means before seeking to reach them.
The King ordered the minister to go in person to propose the marriage. When the king’s ministers there saw the envoy arrive, they deliberated together, saying:
"King Videha possesses great military power; if one forms a marriage alliance with him, their relationship will be harmonious.
Should he come here of his own accord, matters of both auspicious and inauspicious concern may be handled as you wish."

Having deliberated thus, they immediately gave their consent; having selected an auspicious morning by divination, it was decided that on such-and-such a day, one should come here to perform the marriage ceremony together.
The envoy returned and reported to the king:
"I have found that woman; we shall complete the marriage ceremony with due rites on such-and-such a date.
On that day, the king prepared an extensive array of delicacies, mixing all the food and drink with poison.
At that time, King Semicara sent a messenger to report to Vidarbha, saying:
"I have already made all preparations; you should come quickly.
When the messenger arrived, Mahauṣadha said to the king:
"One must not act precipitously; one should deliberate well.
It has been a constant occurrence since antiquity that neighboring states become enemies, and whenever there are disputes or battles, it is difficult for them to remain on friendly terms.
The King said:
"With whom did you deliberate?
He replied, "Great King!"
"Do not worry; I have a parrot named Kalinga who possesses great wisdom and is well-versed in human affairs. Send him to that city to observe the situation and return with a report."
The king said, "As you wish.

Having received these words, the parrot took flight with a warbling cry, soaring toward that city. Perching upon the tip of a tree, he looked around in all directions to observe who might be consulted for the purpose of conveying messages back and forth.
"Who is capable of being entrusted with this task?
Ultimately, not a single bird came to consult with him.
He then entered the royal palace and, seeing a sārika bird's nest within a bamboo grove, went directly to the side of the nest and exchanged greetings with them.
"From where have you come? Viśākha replied, "I have come from the presence of King Śrī in the north.

Previously, I was a superintendent of the gardens and took a śarī as my wife; she was young, of incomparable beauty and grace, diligent, wise, and skilled in speech. Having gone out for a brief excursion, she was seized by a hawk. Because of this, the arrow of grief has pierced my heart, and I have wandered here and there in search of her until I arrived at this place. I have no companion; I wish for you to be my wife."
He replied, "I have never heard of nor have I ever seen a parrot taking a śarī as his wife; I have only heard of parrots taking other parrots as their wives."
At that time, Lakṣmaṇā further exhorted him with various skillful means and words, speaking in verse:
"I am the king of the northern region; Śrī is my gardener.
Śāri is my wife; she possesses wisdom and eloquence."
"Having briefly gone out for sport, I was carried away by an owl;
because I sought him out, I have drifted here. Śāriputra replied:
“The wife of the Śāri parrot has never heard of such a thing;
yet she brings back a parrot in response—this is what the wise know together.”

After each had spoken their verses, they further deliberated; when their minds reached mutual understanding, they became spouses, and having thus formed a close bond, their affection remained without interval.

At that time, Lakṣmaṇa saw that the royal household was preparing various kinds of exquisite cakes and foods; they were of many varieties and all were rare. Having seen this, Lakṣmaṇa said to Śāriputra:
"For what purpose are these sumptuous delicacies being prepared in the palace? May I now taste their flavor?"
He replied, "Although there are such exquisite and wonderful cakes and foods, they are all infused with poison. He asked:
"Why is that? He replied, "This food and drink are prepared because King Videha wishes to come and perform the rites of hospitality; however, there is a hidden intent to destroy that king's army."
Having questioned him in detail and examined the matter thoroughly, he spoke in verse:
"It is said by all that this king’s daughter Has been betrothed to the King of Videha;
Though such a report exists, We do not yet know whether it is false or true."
Śāriputra replied: “The King will not give her to him; the fool recklessly overestimates his own worth.
Using this as a pretext, he intends to carry out a massacre.”
At that time, having learned of this matter, the parrot was as joyful and exultant as a great merchant chief who had obtained a rare and wondrous treasure.
He said to Śāri: "I shall now return to the north To inform King Śrī;
I have found a clever and wise wife Who understands speech just like me."
Śāri replied: "Noble son, as you depart now, go to see King Śrī;
you must return after seven nights, and it is not fitting for you to delay any longer."

At that time, the parrot flew up into the air and before long arrived at the place where Mahauṣadha was. It reported the matter in full detail, and Mahauṣadha related everything in sequence to the king, advising him that he need not go.
At that time, the king, realizing that he could not leave, marshaled his fourfold army and marched toward Vitihotra; they surrounded it on all sides, leaving him no way to advance or retreat.
The king consulted with Mahābhiṣak, asking, "What plan do you propose?"
Mahābhaiṣajya said, "It is not possible to engage in battle; we should instead sow dissension.
At that time, there were five hundred ministers within that camp, all of whom he presented with gifts of the state's most precious treasures.
Once the ministers had received [the message], they all conceived doubts and refused to follow the King’s words.
After Mahāyāsa had performed this deed for the King, he sent a messenger to report:

"It is not that I am incapable of fighting against you; however, since you are my wife's father, you are my close kinsman. You should carefully consider that the preservation of one's life is the fundamental priority."
"Now that I have come to my own place, my livelihood is no longer independent; if you do not believe my words, you must verify them for yourself.
I gave a certain object to a certain great minister, and all five hundred men received that gift. You may immediately search and question them to determine the truth of the matter."

He then investigated and found that everything was indeed as reported. Knowing the situation had changed, he withdrew his army at midnight; having reached the city, he subsequently executed all five hundred ministers and ordered the sons of those ministers to succeed to their fathers' positions.
Mahābhaiṣajya said to the king:

"Since matters have come to this, and there are no other obstacles, I wish to go for a moment to seek her hand in marriage; whether I shall succeed or not remains unknown, and I must observe her intention."
The king said, "Go as you please.
Mahābhaiṣajya led his troops to the park of the kingdom of Pañcāla and took up residence there; the king of that land then summoned him, saying, "Please enter the city."
He replied, "I shall not enter the city; for now, it would be best to go to the house of that minister.
The king said:
"As you wish. At that time, the sons of the ministers deliberated together, saying:
"The fact that our fathers were killed was entirely due to Mahābhaiṣajya; since he is our enemy, we must not release him so easily."
The minister said to the king: "King Videha possesses no strategy of his own;

the flourishing of his royal enterprise is entirely due to the merit of Mahābhaiṣajya. Because of this, we have been unable to carry out any incursions or plunder. Let him remain here for now and do not allow him to go forth in the four directions; I shall lead my troops to go and destroy that city."
The King then praised this as excellent and immediately led his fourfold army to the kingdom of Videha, surrounding its city.

At that time, Mahābhaiṣajya learned that King Parantapa had departed by a certain road toward Videha; he further discovered that the king’s treasures were all located at a particular spot, where they were kept together with the maiden Bhaiṣajyasundarī.
Mahābhaiṣajya then forcibly entered the palace, took the maiden Bhaiṣajyasundarī along with various precious jewels, and led his troops back by a different route.
Upon seeing the king, he assembled all the court officials, who were filled with immeasurable joy.
At that time, an envoy from the kingdom of Tiṣya arrived and reported to the king:
"The precious treasures and the maiden have been taken away by another.
Having received this news, the king then ordered the army to turn back.
At that time, the King performed extensive and grand ceremonies, and once the marriage was concluded, he immediately installed Mṛgāvatī as his chief consort.
Then, King Śibī dispatched a messenger with a letter to Mṛgāvatī, saying:
"I am filled with grief and distress; do you not know this? Investigate thoroughly who spread this rumor that food mixed with poison was intended to harm the King."
Having received the letter, the woman investigated the matter and realized it was a secret message transmitted by Mahābhaiṣajya’s parrot; she sent a messenger to inform her father.
Upon receiving the letter, the father again dispatched a messenger to convey this news:

"All this has resulted from the parrot observing matters and traveling back and forth to report them, thereby causing widespread turmoil and the ruin of our family and state. That parrot should be brought here."
The woman placed the parrot in a cage and sent it to her father, the King. Upon seeing the parrot, the King’s anger redoubled:
"It was because of this wretched bird that the kingdom was lost and my kin perished; do not debate the matter further, but kill it immediately."

The bird then bowed its head and said to the king, "I would be most fortunate if you would allow me to end my life according to the dying custom of my ancestors; even in death, I shall have no regrets.
The king said:
"Kill him according to his method of death.
The butcher asked, "What is his method of death?"
The parrot replied, "Wrap my tail in hemp, drench it with oil, set it on fire, and let me die naturally. The butcher did as he was told and released him;

the parrot then flew up into the air, ruffled his feathers, and the fire spread through the entire house, burning it to the ground without remainder. He then entered a pond to bathe and depart, rising into the clouds and shaking his wings as he flew toward Bhṛtikā.
Mahābhaiṣajya asked,
"Have you returned from the dead?
The parrot answered in full detail, and Mahābhaiṣajya was filled with joy.
King Cañcā, his anger blazing fiercely, again wrote to his daughter:
"Because of this parrot, my palace has been burned.
You must bind it securely and send it here immediately."
The woman immediately returned the parrot as she had been told.
When the king saw this, he was greatly incensed and ordered that its feathers be plucked and it be boiled in boiling water.
The executioner removed the feathers and threw it outside the eaves, reporting back:
"Go! she said. The flying owl descended to look, seized her, and soared through the air to a shrine.
Just as the owl was about to eat her, she addressed the owl, saying:
"Brother, you have eaten the flesh of my body for but a single day; if you were released, I would ensure that you were always satiated with the finest meat every single day.
The owl said, "Who would believe you?"
He replied: "I have made a solemn oath; moreover, as I lack wings and feathers, I cannot fly through the air, so I shall observe the truth or falsehood with my own eyes for one or two days."
He spoke again to the owl, saying:
"Although you are kind, you have not yet found the proper place. Carry me to the vicinity of that king’s temple and release me gently upon the ground.

Following these words, the owl carried him to the location of the shrine; he entered the hall and crawled into a small hole behind the deity, where the guardian of the temple was making offerings of various fragrant flowers before the god.

The parrot said: "Go and inform the king: 'The king has committed evil deeds, and all the gods are incensed together. All the calamities you have recently encountered were caused by me; if you do not make offerings, the cruel misfortunes will not cease. You should offer much raw meat every day, along with one *śī* of sesame seeds and beans each; if you maintain such sincerity, I shall deliberate upon your behalf.'"
Then the guardian reported these words to the Great King, who said:
"If it is so, I shall perform this sacrifice for the deity exactly according to your instructions."

After a long period of time had passed, the crow had grown accustomed to eating raw flesh, while the parrot’s feathers gradually grew back from feeding on hemp. Once the parrot was capable of flight and intended to depart, it said to its guardian:
"You should inform the King: 'You have provided for me for a great length of time; furthermore, there is one matter you must not disregard.'"

"The King, the ladies of the inner palace, the city officials, and the common people shall all shave their hair and beards and come together to me; I shall bestow upon them inexhaustible wealth and happiness.

The messenger reported this to the King, who immediately acted accordingly. Having completely shaved off his hair and beard, he went to the temple of the gods, where he prostrated at the feet of the deity and sought mercy through repentance.
The parrot flew out and spoke a verse in mid-air, saying:
"All things involve a reciprocal response; there is none that does not respond.
You have plucked the feathers from my body; I shall now shave yours in return."
Having spoken these words, he soared into the sky and departed.
Arriving at the place where Mahauṣadha was, he asked,
"For what reason have you been so late as to cause me such concern?"

He then recounted in detail all that had transpired; upon hearing this, Mahābhaiṣajya was filled with great joy and reported it fully to the king. The king marveled at its rarity and replied, "Mahābhaiṣajya!..."
"You truly possess great merit, for the attendants you have attracted are all exceptionally intelligent.
Viśākhā’s divine wisdom surpasses that of ordinary men, and the parrot’s understanding is beyond the reach of the world."
Later, at another time, the king thought to himself:
"Among all my ministers, who is the most intelligent?
He then gave a dog to each of his great ministers and commanded them to feed and raise it, teaching it to speak human speech within a fixed period of time.

The ministers each took their dogs back to their respective homes and provided them with double the usual care and nourishment; yet, they possessed no method by which they could cause the dogs to speak.
When Mahābhaiṣajya obtained his dog, he also brought it home and tied it up not far from his usual dining table.
Whenever the dog saw Mahābhaiṣajya eating, the fragrant aroma was intense and the food—cakes and fruits—was piled before him; yet, despite the dog’s longing, not even a single morsel was given.
He was fed only coarse food, just enough to sustain his life and prevent death, until his form became emaciated and he barely maintained his physical existence.
The King issued a general command that all dogs maintained by his ministers should be brought together to test once more whether they could understand human speech.
When the dogs arrived, they were all plump and well-fed, yet none understood speech; only the dog of Mahābhaiṣajya was exceptionally emaciated.
The King asked, "Why is your dog so thin?"
He replied: "Great King!
That which I eat always shares the same flavor as yours."
The dog then said, "This man speaks falsely;
I have constantly suffered from hunger until I was nearly at the point of death.
Great Medicine said:
"This interpretation of human speech was personally witnessed by the King.
The King then rejoiced greatly and marveled at the various men.
Later, on another occasion, the King tested his ministers to see who possessed wisdom.
He then gave one mouthful of food to each of the sheep-men and instructed them, saying:
"Raise them until they are plump and flourishing, but do not allow their flesh to become greasy.
Being ignorant, the men all raised them until they were fat.

Mahābhaiṣajya provided the sheep with constant food and drink, ensuring they were satiated and their bodies became plump and robust; however, he carved wooden jackals that would occasionally appear to terrify them, so that although the sheep ate their fill, no fat or grease was produced.
Having slaughtered them, they examined the results together as they were.
The King asked,
"For what reason do the other sheep have fat while your sheep has none?"
He answered in full detail regarding the matter.
The King said,
"You possess truly profound and extraordinary wisdom."
"Later, at another time, about five hundred sons of the ministers gathered together in the Fragrant Garden for a social gathering. In the course of their conversation, they asked one another:
'In whose house is there some extraordinary occurrence?'"
"Or have you seen it elsewhere?
Each of you should speak.
At that time, when all the others had finished speaking, he next questioned the son of Mahauṣadha:
"What wonders are there within your house?
He replied, "In my home,
there is a stone which, sustained by the power of incantations, is placed in water and floats without sinking."
The people replied, "We have never heard of or seen a stone floating upon water.
They then made a mutual agreement to wager five hundred gold coins. The son returned and reported this to his father.
I said, "Fushí, I bet five hundred coins. His father said:
"One should not display the stone; instead, give five hundred coins to those people.
At his home, Mahauṣadha had trained a monkey well in music and instructed his son:
"When you attend the assembly, you should ask the people:"
When they have all said, "Who else has seen such a marvelous thing?", you should reply:
"I have a monkey who is well-versed in music; there is no singing, dancing, lute-playing, or *si-zhu* playing that he does not fully understand."
The people replied: "Previously, when there was no floating stone, you were already fined five hundred gold coins.
If you are now again false, you must pay double, a total of one thousand."
"If this is indeed true, I shall pay a thousand coins.
He then took the monkey with him to the king's presence and had it perform music; when all these things were accomplished, he paid out the thousand coins as the stake for the wager.
The king said,
"I have never before seen such a thing.
Overwhelmed with great joy, he bestowed abundant treasures upon him and exclaimed:
“‘The wisdom of Mahauṣadha is the foremost among all beings.

At that time, there was a Brahmin in this city who was intelligent, sagacious, and well-versed in the four Vedas. Not long after he married, a daughter was born to him; she was of upright and beautiful countenance, and her name was Udumbarā.”
The Brahmin established a condition himself, saying:
"If there is a man who studies under me and becomes my equal, I shall give this excellent daughter of mine in marriage to him."

As the girl gradually grew up, there was a Brahmin in this country who fathered a son whose appearance was loathsome and possessed eighteen kinds of ugly traits. When his parents saw him, they felt extreme displeasure and named him "Ugly Features" (Dauḥśīlya). Although he gradually reached the age of childhood, they did not teach him to study, thinking, "This child’s ugliness brings shame upon us."
As the boy grew up, he regretted his own lack of knowledge and entered the city to seek learning.
Upon reaching the abode of that wise Brahmin, he paid his respects and said:
"I have come to request instruction; I pray you will deign to show me compassion."
He accepted [the challenge], and before long, he had mastered all the books and treatises.
The brahmin then thought to himself:
"I previously made a vow that if anyone were to master my craft, I would give my daughter to him in marriage."
"Although this child’s appearance and demeanor are indeed ugly and repulsive, it would be difficult to violate our original agreement;
one who betrays their heart shall not be reborn in heaven.
Even if all people should laugh at me, I shall not break my vow."
He immediately performed the proper rites and betrothed his daughter to him.
The girl’s majestic radiance was so solemn and awe-inspiring that Duḥśākha did not dare to approach her.
Duḥśākha thought to himself:
"I am now a guest and feel timid and apprehensive; it would be best to return home and do as I please.
At that time, having seen these ill omens, Udāyin felt displeasure in his heart and thought to himself:
"I possess a handsome appearance while my husband is so ugly; I am ridiculed by others—what face could I have for living?"
Durmukha then led him back to his original location; however, by the time they reached a pond on the way, their provisions were completely exhausted, and they were driven by hunger.

At that moment, a traveler was mixing flour with water to drink, so Udumbara begged some from him, and the traveler reduced his portion to give it to him. Durmukha took the remainder and ate it himself, whereupon Udumbara said to him:
"You should divide some of it with me to at least stave off our hunger."
The man of evil appearance said to her:
"There is a rule established by the ancient seers that women do not drink gruel;
it is for this reason that I will not give you any."
Next, while in the wilderness, they suddenly encountered some discarded meat; the one with the evil appearance took it and ate it without giving any to Uttamā, saying:
"The ancient seers did not permit women to eat this either."
Utpalavarṇā thought to herself, "I have no merit; my parents have married me off to this wicked man.
She felt deep regret and resentment.
Next, they arrived at an udumbara tree; the man with the evil appearance climbed the tree to gather and eat its fruit.
His wife said, "You should strike it down so we may eat together; it is not right that you eat alone."
He then dropped the unripe fruit and ate the ripe ones himself.
[The other] replied,
"You may pluck the ripe ones."
He said, "If you wish for them to ripen, climb the tree and take them yourself.
Driven by hunger, he immediately climbed the tree, plucked the fruits, and ate them.
Having seen this evil omen, he thought to himself:
"I am devoid of merit; it is because of my lack of fortune that I have brought such a frivolous woman as this, who climbs high trees to pluck fruit for her own eating."
"Furthermore, my own body cannot even save itself; who could possibly support this useless wife?
Having conceived such contempt and disdain, he immediately went down, gathered thorns, and surrounded the tree before departing.
At that time, King Chungseong went out on a hunting excursion and arrived at the edge of that forest. The woman, having lost her husband, was overcome with grief and wailed aloud in lamentation.
Hearing her voice, the king commanded, "Since this is a deserted forest, who is it that is weeping?"
Following the sound, he went to the side of the woman Uttamā; observing her appearance and demeanor, he suspected she might be a celestial maiden or perhaps a deity, and asked:
"O immortal, for what reason have you come here?"
The woman replied in verse:
"Great King, you should now know:
I am not a celestial maiden, nor am I of the class of spirits; I am without a husband and suffer bitter hardship."

Then the king sent men to support him down from the tree; they greeted one another with such unreserved joy that it was as if they had been together all their lives, and he was finally taken in the same carriage into the palace.
At that time, as they traveled along the road, Aśubharūpa felt remorse, thinking:
"I have acted unlawfully; why have I abandoned my young wife alone in the wilderness!"
"You may take them back and return home together.
When they arrived beneath that tree, they did not see the udumbara;
the others told them, "The king has taken it away; he mounted it and entered the palace together with it."
Upon hearing this, Pāpaka became even more filled with grief and distress; he went to the king’s gate but had no means of entry.
Seeing brick-carriers, he followed them inside. From a distance, he beheld his wife sporting joyfully with the king and thought to himself:
"By what means might I briefly obtain the opportunity to speak with her?"
Thereupon, under the pretext of another matter, she spoke a verse in a loud voice, saying:
"You recline upon a golden bed, Adorning yourself with floral cosmetics;
Yet you do not share your pleasures with me— A skilled craftsman now holds his axe and chisel."
The woman heard this and replied:
"Starving and thirsty, I came to the edge of the pond To seek flour and drink from you;
You replied that it was improper for a woman, A long-standing grievance, like the beating of a war-drum."
Traveling together through the wilderness, they ate meat without sharing;
thinking of this until their bodies withered away, one must observe the proper measure when dancing.
Climbing up the udumbara tree, they did not bestow ripe fruit upon one another.
"Recalling this, my body and mind are withered, and my two breasts hang down before me.
The woman of evil appearance replied:
"You do not remember me, who was learned, possessed of great talent and wisdom."
Because human affairs were slightly deficient, you abandoned me for a long separation.
You climbed the mountain and threw yourself down to die; you took poison to end your life.
The sin of killing shall fall upon your own person; you crafty fellow, hold fast to your chisel!
The woman replied: "I would rather die on the mountain peak at my own will, or perish by eating poison as I please;
since you hold me in such low regard, how could I possibly strike the drum?"

"In this regard, the fourth line of each verse was composed at that time by taking up events from the preceding day; the phrasing and intent were designed to confuse others and possess no further meaning. At that time, the two individuals responded to one another using indirect speech, whereupon the King asked:
"What is the meaning of what the lady says?"
"I have heard this but do not understand; please explain it to me.
Udumbara then spoke in detail to the king:
"This is my husband, whom my parents gave me in marriage. He possesses great wisdom and has a profound mastery of the four Vedas; he has come here now seeking you."
The King said:
"You may remain silent; there is no need for further conversation.
Furthermore, what is your intention today?"
"Furthermore, do you still harbor feelings of former affection for that person? He replied,
"How could such a thing be possible?"
"I shall naturally cause him to feel aversion toward me.
However, this brahmin is highly skilled in incantations; one should not hastily or harshly reproach him.
The King then informed Mahābhaiṣajya of these circumstances, and Mahābhaiṣajya said:

"May Your Majesty not worry; I shall cause her to hold you in deep affection. That Brahmin’s physical form is coarse and inferior, whereas the Lady’s radiance surpasses all others, so she will not dare to draw near him."
At that time, Mahauṣadha replied to the brahmin,
"Noble sir, having come into the palace, what do you seek? He answered:
"My wife, Great King, is about to enter the palace. He asked,
"Do you recognize your wife?"
He replied, "I recognize them. Mahābhaiṣajya said:
"Bring all five hundred palace women before me; if one among them is your wife, you shall take her by the hand.
If you are mistaken, I will have your head severed with a sword. He said:
“As you command,” they replied.

The king commanded his palace women to all adorn themselves and come to my location; they immediately assembled together like the five hundred celestial maidens in the palace of Śakra, and followed Udāyin to the place where the king was.
Mahābhaiṣajya then asked the brāhmaṇa,
"Do you recognize your wife?

Upon seeing her adorned with such extraordinary finery, the one of evil appearance remained as silent as a dragon or snake bound by a mantra, and dared not look upon her, as if facing the blazing sun.

At that time, the brahmin stood watching from afar as all the women passed by; there was a maidservant, whose appearance was like that of a hungry ghost, walking behind them. With his evil countenance, he seized her and said, "She is my wife."
The Great Medicine said,
"If she is indeed your wife, take her as you please.
He then took her and spoke this verse:
"The superior person still loves the superior; the mediocre person loves the mediocre themselves.
I am in the form of a hungry ghost, yet I still pity you who are hungry ghosts."
"Abandoning this celestial palace, we follow one another toward the abode of ghosts;
our natures are perfectly suited, and no other companion can be found.
At another time, because Great Medicine had committed a minor transgression, the King’s mind was displeased, and he consequently ceased to speak with him.

The king and his palace ladies spent the entire day sporting in the garden. At that time, the lady removed a necklace of pearls from her neck, worth hundreds of thousands of taels of gold, and hung it upon a tree branch; she forgot it and did not retrieve it. When evening came and they were about to return home, she fell asleep until midnight before she finally remembered it.
At that time, the pearl-carrying monkey saw him and took it up into a high tree. The king ordered a messenger to go and fetch the pearls immediately, but the messenger went and did not obtain them.
Then there was a beggar who, having gathered leftover food, was about to leave the garden when the messenger seized him, saying:
"No one else has entered here; return my pearl necklace!"
He replied, "I am a beggar;
I saw no necklace. He was then immediately beaten and tortured, and handed over to the official in charge of prisoners.
The beggar thought to himself:
"I must now employ a skillful means; if I remain here any longer, I shall die of hunger.
He said to the messenger:
"I have obtained this pearl necklace; I shall take it and give it to the son of such-and-such a householder.
The messenger immediately seized the householder’s son and bound his feet with the same wooden stocks as [the messenger's].
Whenever it was time for a meal, the elder’s son would bring many choice delicacies; when beggars came seeking them, the son would scold them, saying:
"It was for this very reason that you led me here; I cannot give them to you."
When the son had finished eating and was about to turn back and leave, he replied:
"My time has not yet come; I cannot go with you.
He then spoke to him with affectionate words:
"You may accompany me on my journey, and I shall ensure that you are at peace and happy. He replied,
"If you will make a solemn vow, I shall follow your word."
Having made this vow, they set out together.
The son informed his family, saying,
"From tomorrow onwards, bring food for two people every day."
Because of this, the beggar felt joy in his heart and thought to himself:
"In the past, though I wandered through the city and its suburbs, I could not even obtain coarse food to sustain my body; now that I am eating such fine delicacies, what more could I possibly lack!"
"However, I cannot lie down alone.
He then brought forth the foremost courtesan of the city and said,
"She, too, shall share the jeweled necklace with me."
Once the woman had arrived, they stayed together in seclusion and indulged in pleasure to their hearts' content.
The beggar thought to himself:
"Even if my body remains confined for twelve years, I shall not seek release; yet, as the five desires are not yet fully satisfied, I must at least have beautiful sounds to delight my ears."

He further invited musicians to go together and retrieve the necklace; although they protested their innocence, they could not avoid being detained. Music was provided according to their wishes so that they lacked for nothing, and in this manner they remained there for many months.
The people, exhausted and weary, said together to the beggar:
"Release us, and we shall let you be at ease.
The beggar thought to himself:
"Now that these have departed, why should we worry further?
As I reflect upon it, were it not for the brilliant strategic insight of Mahābhaiṣajya, my life would not have been spared from this dark prison."
He then led forth the son of Mahauṣadha and likewise shared out the pearls among them.
Once his son was imprisoned, Mahauṣadha thought to himself:
"My son has been cast into confinement; how can I remain idle?"
He immediately went in and informed the king:
"Although I have committed an offense, my son is without fault; for what reason has my son’s person been suddenly detained?
The king said:
"A necklace of pearls worth hundreds of thousands of taels of gold has been taken by a beggar and divided among others outside.
He related the circumstances in detail to Mahābhaiṣajya,
who then addressed the King, saying:
"Please do not worry; no one has taken this exquisite neck-jewel. By my plan, I am certain we shall recover it; therefore, I request that all those who have been detained be released."
The King ordered his release.
Mahābhaiṣajya entered the garden to search for the place where the lost pearl was lost; looking up at a tall tree, he saw a monkey and thought:
"That pearl necklace must have been taken by this creature, yet it requires a skillful means before it can be recovered."
He then addressed the king, saying:
"Let the palace women come forth as before, all adorned with necklaces beneath their throats.
Seeing them from afar, the monkey took the pearls and hung them around his own neck.
Mahābhaiṣajya said,
"The palace women are dancing.
When the monkey saw this, it also began to dance, whereupon Mahābhaiṣajya said:
"Everyone, lower your heads.
The monkey also lowered its head, and the pearl immediately fell to the ground.
Seeing this, the king was greatly delighted; he marveled at its extraordinary wisdom, pardoned its offense, rewarded its merit, and significantly increased its fief and stipend.
At that time, those six ministers gathered in one place and deliberated together, saying:

"In the past, we were all cherished and esteemed by the King; we divided the strongholds and demarcated the territories, each of us dwelling in peace. Today, because of this poor, lowly, and vulgar man who has presented a few meager skills, he has come to hold power at court. This has caused us to lose our emoluments and positions, as he encroaches upon our cities and seizes our districts—what do you intend to do about this?"
One minister said:

"We six shall make a solemn covenant together that we will never betray one another's word; with one heart and united strength, we shall eliminate our enemies. Great Medicine and the King hold no grudge against us; let our rank and emoluments be restored to what they were before."
Having deliberated thus, on the following day the six ministers went together to the park.
Seeing that the six ministers had gathered in one place, Mahābhaiṣajya realized there must surely be some extraordinary counsel being discussed; he then said to his parrot, Viśeṣacintin:
"Go to the park and observe their assembly: what kind of consultation are they holding?"
"Return and report back to me.
The parrot immediately departed, concealing itself in the forest to listen to their conversation.
When the six ministers arrived at the garden, they each had their sons and daughters marry one another, saying these words:
"Since we are now close and free from suspicion, do not let our plans leak out to others; tell me the truth.
The other replied, "I have previously eaten peacocks from the royal household."
One said, "I have had illicit relations with the women of the inner palace.
The others each likewise recounted their own circumstances, and together they plotted their course of action.
Thus these six men informed one another and proceeded to eat together at a single table.
When Śuka heard this, he informed Mahābhaiṣajya, who entered the inner quarters and reported the matter in detail to the King, saying:
"Your Majesty’s ministers are so loyal and upright; I humbly pray that you will consider and examine how this matter should be handled."
The king questioned him thoroughly and, knowing that everything was indeed true, immediately banished and expelled him to the borderlands.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Do not harbor doubts;
the Great Physician of that time was none other than myself, the Restorer of the Kingdom was Śāriputra, and those six great ministers were the six heretical teachers."
"In the past, I banished those six ministers; now, as the most honored one in the three realms, I manifest great supernormal powers and once again drive away the six heretical teachers.

You bhikṣus, you should draw near to virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra). For it is through association with wise and intelligent friends who are thoroughly proficient in all internal and external scriptures that one can ultimately achieve such magnificent virtue; you should practice and learn accordingly."
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 28; *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 29.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. Section Six, Part Four, the Remainder of the Compendium:

Clarifying Matters such as the Buddha’s Descent from Heaven. At that time, the Buddha was in Śrāvastī. Having manifested great supernormal powers and subdued the various non-Buddhist teachers, he brought immeasurable multitudes to benefit, causing all to take refuge according to their respective natures. He caused all humans and devas to rejoice; Brahmins from distant and nearby cities and towns, as well as artisans, all gathered in Śrāvastī and went forth into homelessness under the World-Honored One.
Then all the kinsmen of those people came searching for them and arrived at this city; having seen them, they said:
"You have abandoned the secular life to come forth as renunciants; how then shall we, your kin, survive?"
He replied, "If you desire it, you may remain here and receive the Dharma. He said:
"Excellent! We shall practice and learn accordingly.
Thereupon, they all went forth into homelessness.
When the brahmins and others saw this, they spoke with derision and contempt:
"These craftsmen have left the household life to become renunciants; when I have work to be done, whom shall I employ?
The bhikṣus then reported these circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
“After those skilled in crafts have gone forth as renunciants, they still keep their former tools; because of this, they become objects of reproach and censure.
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Once you have gone forth, you should not keep tools for crafts anymore. If you continue to keep them, you commit an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).”
After the Buddha had established the precepts, there was a physician who, having gone forth into the religious life, traveled from place to place until he arrived at Śrāvastī.
There, an elder bhikṣu who was afflicted with a painful illness saw the visiting bhikṣu coming and addressed him, saying:
"Venerable one!..."
"You may treat me.
He replied, "The Buddha does not permit those who were previously physicians to keep medical instruments; with what, then, shall I treat your illness?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I now permit the bhikṣus: those who were previously physicians may carry needles and lancets; those who were clerks may carry pens and ink; and those who were barbers may keep scissors."
The setting was as before. After the Buddha had displayed his supernormal powers, humans and devas were filled with joy, and the Buddha and the bhikṣus received abundant offerings.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to sever the faults associated with such gains, ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and entered the three-month rains retreat in the Palace of Jasper. There, near the Pārijāta tree, he taught the Dharma to his mother and the other hosts of devas.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was observing the rains retreat at Jetavana.

At that time, as the fourfold assembly no longer had the Blessed One with them, they all went together to the place where Mahāmaudgalyāyana was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat down to one side.
Upon seeing them approach, the Venerable One preached the Dharma for them, expounding it according to their individual capacities to instruct, benefit, and gladden them; he then remained silent.
At that time, the fourfold assembly rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Venerable One, saying:
"Virtuous One, have you perhaps heard where the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, is currently observing the rains retreat?"
The Venerable replied,
"I have heard that the Buddha has gone to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to observe the rains retreat in the Palace of Jasper and Crystal, where he teaches the Dharma to his mother near the Pārijāta tree."
At that time, having heard the Dharma, the fourfold assembly learned where the World-Honored One was staying; they felt profound joy, prostrated at his feet, and departed.
When the summer retreat concluded, the fourfold assembly returned, prostrated at the Venerable’s feet, and sat to one side.
After the Venerable One had preached the Dharma, the great assembly each rose, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Virtuous One! For a long time the people have not seen the Buddha, and all have conceived a deep longing for him. We wish to pay our respects to the World-Honored One."
"Excellent, O Great Virtuous One!

If you do not disdain this labor, we pray that you will go to the presence of the World-Honored One on our behalf and prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, saying: 'We humbly inquire whether the Great Master has been living in lightness and ease, free from illness and with few afflictions, dwelling in peace and happiness since the beginning of this summer retreat.'"
He spoke again to Śakra:
"All the fourfold assemblies within this continent have long been separated from the holy countenance of the World-Honored One and all yearn to pay him homage in person.

We members of the fourfold assemblies possess no supernormal powers by which we might reach the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to prostrate at the feet of the World-Honored One, to behold him, and to make offerings."
"Yet these celestial hosts have been able to come here;
we pray that the Buddha, out of his compassion, will take pity on us.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana silently granted their request. Knowing he had consented, the assembly paid their respects, took their leave, and departed.

When the Venerable One perceived that the great assembly had departed, he immediately entered a supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*). In the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, he vanished from this place and appeared in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. From afar, he saw the World-Honored One in the Jades-and-Stone Palace, preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for an immeasurable and boundless multitude of devas.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana could not help but smile and thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has arrived here surrounded by these devas, like the boundless fourfold assembly of Jambudvīpa."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s mind, addressed him, saying: “Maudgalyāyana!
This great assembly did not come of its own accord; their coming and going is entirely due to my power.”
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling and prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side; surveying the great assembly, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
He reflected that this great assembly was most marvelous and rare, having all gathered like clouds.

Because they had, in their previous lives, accomplished a profound mind of indestructible faith toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the pure, noble precepts, they passed away from those lives and were reborn here.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"So it is, so it is! This great assembly, because in their previous lives they had accomplished a profound mind of indestructible faith toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the pure, noble precepts, have passed away from there and been reborn here."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, engaged in discourse with Mahāmaudgalyāyana, immediately addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana before the Buddha:

"Relate this matter once more; it is because of his reverent faith in the Triple Gem and his pure, noble precepts—expounding at length until one arrives at the point that he has attained rebirth here."
Furthermore, another devaputra addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"I shall recount the matter once more, explaining it in detail until [the point where he] was reborn here.
Then, yet another devaputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Because I had deep faith in the Buddha in my previous life, I have passed away from there and been reborn here.
Furthermore, other devas spoke these words:

"Due to my having, in a previous life, deeply conceived pure faith in the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the pure noble precepts, and having fully undertaken and maintained them, I have passed away from that life and been reborn here."

At that time, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas who, in the very presence of the Buddha, all realized the fruit of stream-entry; they each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and then vanished from sight.
At that time, after Maudgalyāyana had seen the assembly depart, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
All the fourfold assemblies in Jambudvīpa have come to my place with great devotion and spoken these words:”
"Venerable One!
We have not seen the Buddha for a long time and all feel a deep longing for him. We wish to pay our respects to the World-Honored One.
It would be well, Venerable One!"

"O you who do not shrink from toil, we pray that you go to the presence of the World-Honored One on our behalf and convey these words: 'We prostrate ourselves at the Buddha's feet. We humbly inquire whether the Great Master has been dwelling in ease, free from illness and few afflictions, and living in peace since the beginning of this summer retreat.'"

"We of the fourfold assembly lack the supernormal powers to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One, to behold him in person, and to make offerings; yet those devas are able to come here."
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
Out of compassion and pity, please descend from that celestial realm to Jambudvīpa.
Having made this request, the World-Honored One then addressed Maudgalyāyana:

“You should now go to Jambudvīpa and inform the fourfold assembly: ‘When these seven days have passed, the Buddha will descend from the celestial realm toward Jambudvīpa, landing at the side of an udumbara tree in the pure wilderness of Saṃkāśya City.’”

When Mahāmaudgalyāyana had heard the Buddha’s words, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately entered meditative concentration. In the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he vanished from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and reappeared in Jambudvīpa. He addressed the fourfold assembly:
“When these seven days have passed, the Buddha will come from the celestial realm and descend beside the Udumbara tree in Jambudvīpa.”
At that time, the fourfold assembly each took fragrant flowers and proceeded toward the city of Saṃkāśya.

All the people within that city, hearing that the Buddha was about to arrive, were filled with great joy.
