They cleared away all impurities and swept and adorned the streets, sprinkling them with scented water and scattering famous flowers everywhere. Banners, flags, silken canopies, and parasols decorated every place, making it as delightful as the Garden of Joy (Nandana-vana). At a preeminent spot, they prepared a magnificent high seat, awaiting the Tathāgata with longing thoughts.
At that time, after the Tathāgata had taught the Dharma appropriate to the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas— showing, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them— he vanished from that place and,
taking the host of devas with him, went to the Yāma heaven; having taught the Dharma there as well,
he vanished from that place and again took the host of devas to the Tuṣita heaven to teach them the Dharma, and so on.
As for the gods of Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita,
Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha,
Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, and Sudarśana.
Having taught the Dharma to all beings as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven—instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them—he vanished from that place and appeared in the Sudarśana Heaven;
in this manner, he proceeded downward through the heavens until reaching the Trayastriṃśa Heaven.
At that time, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Do you now wish to go to Jambudvīpa?"
He replied, "I am going. He then addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"Did you travel by means of supernatural powers, or did you go on foot? He replied:
"Take a step! Śakra then commanded the artisan devaputra, saying:
"You should create three jeweled staircases—of gold, vaidūrya, and sphaṭika."
He replied, "Very well!
and immediately manifested three staircases made of the seven precious substances.

The World-Honored One proceeded through the center, treading upon a path of lapis lazuli; to his right, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, trod upon a path of gold, holding a subtle white fly-whisk worth hundreds of thousands of taels of gold, accompanied by the various devas of the Form Realm as his attendants.

Śakra, Lord of the Devas, walked upon a crystal path to the left, holding aloft with his hand a hundred-ribbed parasol worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold to shade the Blessed One, while being attended by the various devas of the desire realm.
The Buddha had this thought:
"If I were to go there on foot alone, I fear the non-Buddhists would criticize me, saying:

'The śramaṇa Gautama went to the Heaven of the Thirty-three by means of his supernormal powers; seeing their exquisite forms, his mind became attached, and he lost his supernormal powers and returned on foot.'"
"If I were to use my supernatural powers, it would merely trouble the celestial artisans.
It would be better for me now to go to Jambudvīpa by using half my supernatural power and half by walking.

At that time, the World-Honored One descended the jeweled staircase; at a distance of twelve yojanas from here, the human breath wafted upward like the stench of a corpse, such that those devas were unable to smell it.
The World-Honored One, having known this, manifested a grove of ox-head sandalwood whose fragrance was so pervasive that all who smelled it were filled with joy.
The Buddha then thought:

"If the men of Jambudvīpa were to see celestial women, or the women were to see celestial men, their minds would become stained with passion; because their lustful desires are so extremely intense, they would vomit hot blood, fall into a swoon, and die."
"I should now employ my supernormal powers so that the men see celestial males and the women behold celestial females;
having done this, I shall not allow them to be disturbed in their minds by defiled passion."

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti was dwelling in seclusion during the day beneath a tree. From afar, he saw the World-Honored One surrounded by a great assembly of devas, his majestic virtue and dignity venerable as he descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to this place.

He then thought to himself: "All these highly virtuous devas will take their leave of the Buddha and return to their celestial abodes; and within a hundred years, all these people in the assembly shall likewise pass away."
When the Buddha’s conditions for transformation are exhausted, he likewise enters parinirvāṇa; such majestic splendors as these are all subject to extinction.
How excellent, World-Honored One!
In every place, you have earnestly spoken these words:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; their nature is one of constant change.
The law of arising and ceasing is a thing to be loathed.
Now, I have given rise to a profound sense of revulsion toward this, and I contemplate the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.

Having understood this, he shattered the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of a self-identity with the vajra-thunderbolt of wisdom. Attaining the fruit of stream-entry and obtaining indestructible faith, he immediately and swiftly rose from his cross-legged posture, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and stood gazing up at the World-Honored One from afar while paying him homage.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalā had this thought:
"The Buddha is descending from the heavens to Jambudvīpa; by what means may I be the first to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One?"

"The great assembly has gathered so densely that there is no room to turn one's heel; if I were to simply assume the form of a bhikṣuṇī, everyone would look down upon me and I would have no way to proceed. I should now manifest great supernatural powers."

He immediately transformed his own body into that of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), preceded by the seven treasures and surrounded by an army of ninety-nine billion followers. Accompanied by a full thousand sons, he was exquisitely adorned in the shape of a half-moon as he approached the place where the World-Honored One resided.

At that time, there were immeasurable billions of śramaṇas, brahmins, followers of external paths, and followers of internal paths—the four boundless assemblies—all of whom followed him like shadows, exclaiming in wonder at such an unprecedented marvel.

Carrying a white parasol above him, his retinue followed like rushing clouds; he was like the sun emitting a thousand rays of light, or like the clear radiance of the full moon emerging from the Milky Way.

Thus adorned and magnificent beyond thought, he approached the World-Honored One. Upon seeing him, the great assembly was filled with wonder; gazing at him, they forgot their fatigue and each gave rise to this thought:
"Where could there be such a king whose military array is so lovely? He must surely be a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) or a sovereign lord from another realm."
Having seen this, each of them conceived a wish,
thinking, "How may we obtain such pleasure?
The great assembly opened a path for them to draw near.
At that time, the bhikṣu Udāyin was present in this assembly and said to the people:
"This is not a wheel-turning monarch; it is the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, who has manifested her own supernatural powers to come and pay homage at the Buddha’s feet."
Then the assembly asked:
"Venerable One!
How do you know that she is an *utpala* nun?"

He replied, “The fragrance of the utpala flowers is most exquisite, and their utpala color is uniform throughout the entire assembly; therefore, we know it is he who has manifested this supernatural transformation.”
When the bhikṣuṇī had arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, she withdrew her supernormal powers, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, once the World-Honored One was seated comfortably, he addressed the Bhikṣuṇī Utpalā, saying: “You may go now!”
"A bhikṣuṇī must not stand before me.
It is improper for a nun to manifest supernatural powers in the presence of the Great Teacher.
Having been rebuked by the Buddha, she then went to one side.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"For a bhikṣuṇī to manifest supernatural powers in the presence of the Buddha carries such faults as these.
I shall prohibit all bhikṣuṇīs from manifesting spiritual powers before the Great Teacher."
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"From this day forward, no bhikṣuṇīs shall manifest supernatural powers (ṛddhi) in the presence of the Great Teacher; whoever does so shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
At that time, the great assembly, seeing the great majesty and power of this Wheel-Turning King, conceived a longing desire to be reborn in the human realm;
others, seeing the lovely radiance of the various devas, all conceived a longing desire to go among the heavenly hosts.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having witnessed these events, in order to prevent those humans and devas from harboring worldly aspirations, preached the sublime Dharma according to their individual capacities and conditions. Having heard the Dharma, some attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), some the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and some the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*). Some left the household life, severed all afflictions, and attained the fruit of arhatship; some resolved upon the bodhicitta of a śrāvaka, some resolved upon the bodhicitta of a pratyekabuddha, and some resolved upon the unsurpassed great bodhicitta. Others generated roots of goodness such as *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, or developed the levels of medium and lower patience (*kṣānti*). Thus, he caused the entire assembly to take refuge in and place faith in the Triple Gem.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses on this occasion:
"Even if one becomes a Wheel-Turning King, Or is reborn in the heavens,
And though one attains supreme meditative concentration, It is not equal to the fruit of Stream-entry."

At that time, after the Blessed One had taught, instructed, benefited, and gladdened the great assembly by preaching the sublime Dharma, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested of the Blessed One:
"For what reason did the venerable Udāyin know it was that nun upon hearing the fragrance of the utpala?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only today that I have known a matter by smelling its fragrance; in the past as well, I have known such matters by smelling their fragrance."
"You all should listen.
In a past age, there was a merchant leader in the city of Vārāṇasī who, not long after marrying his wife, found her pregnant.
At that time, the merchant leader wished to enter the great ocean to seek precious jewels and said to his wife:"
"O Worthy One! I am going to other directions to seek exquisite treasures; you should look after our household with diligent care. He replied:
"Noble son! If it is so, I too shall go with you. He replied:
"Who will provide for you? he asked, and the man immediately wept.
Seeing his distress, his companions asked him:
"Why? He replied, "I wished for you to travel together with me in one place; seeing that you would not follow me, I shed these tears."
The companion said, "He intends to leave; why do you not follow him? He replied:
"Who will provide for you?
His companion replied, "Simply let us go together; I shall provide for you."
She was then taken away.
Once they had entered the great ocean, their ship was wrecked by a makara fish.

At that time, the merchant leader died because of this, and the others also perished. His wife, left all alone and destitute, happened upon a plank and, fortunately aided by a favorable wind, was drifted to a sea-island.
There was a king of the garuḍas who resided there; he subsequently took this woman as his wife.
Before long, she gave birth to a son from her former pregnancy, whose countenance was upright and handsome.
At a later time, another chick was born, its form resembling that of a *garuḍa*, and its father subsequently passed away.
At that time, the flock of birds established the son as their king. The mother said to her son:
"By inheriting your father's lineage, you have attained the status of king."
"This is your elder brother; you may now take him to Vārāṇasī and establish him as the sovereign of the nation among the people.
He replied, "O Queen Mother!"
"I shall establish him.
At that time, there was a king in the city of Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta, who ruled the world with the Dharma, bringing peace, security, and abundance, as described at length elsewhere.

While the king was seated among the assembly at a court gathering, the King of the Garuḍas seized his two arms with his twin talons and cast him into the great ocean. He then took his elder brother, who was adorned with exquisite necklaces and ornaments, and brought him to the royal city, placing him upon a lion throne.
He addressed his ministers, saying:
"This is your king; you must serve him with devotion. Should you act in opposition, I shall cause you all to sink together into the great ocean."
Everyone was filled with fear and acted according to his instructions; the minister also did not dare to inform anyone of this matter, and everyone believed it was King Brahmadatta.
Then the king replied to the garuḍa, saying: "From time to time, let us meet."
He replied, "I am coming!
Later, at another time, the king's female elephant gave birth after her term was full; however, only its head emerged while the body could not follow. The ministers informed the king, who said:
"Lead him into the inner palace and command all the palace attendants to swear an oath of truth, pledging that he shall emerge quickly;
they must recite this incantation: 'If there is no man present other than the King, may the young elephant safely emerge.'"
He then led him inside. At that time, all the women of the inner apartments made this oath:
"If there is no one other than the King within these walls, then let the elephant calf come forth."
Although she made this vow, the elephant suffered extreme distress and the child could not be born; everyone cried out loudly, not knowing what to do.
At that time, there was a cowherd girl whose house was not far from there; hearing the sound of the people's cries, she asked why they were doing so:
"For what reason is there such a great outcry within the palace?"
The people related the matter in full, and the cowherd girl said, "I shall make a solemn vow that will enable the elephant calf to emerge safely.

Having heard this, the people informed the minister in detail, and the minister addressed the King, who then summoned her into the inner quarters. The woman immediately made a vow before the elephant using words of truth:
"From the time of my birth until now, I have had no other man besides this one husband; if this is true, may the elephant cub be born safely.
Having spoken these words, the elephant gave birth to the cub, yet its tail would not emerge. Seeing this, the woman smiled and said:
"Even this small transgression you cannot tolerate!"
The palace attendants asked,
"What transgression have you committed? He replied:

"In a former time, I was holding another's child; the child urinated, and the urine flowed into my vulva. At that moment, it felt as though I were experiencing pleasure. Because of this minor transgression, my tail does not follow my body."
Because of these truthful words, the tail also emerged accordingly.
The minister reported to the king, saying,
"The elephant calf has been born."
The king asked,
"Who can cause her to come out?
At that time, the great minister reported the matter in detail.
The king then lamented, saying:
"All my palace women are devoid of integrity and virtue; only this cowherd remains pure and undefiled.
The king said:
"Call the cowherd woman here; I must question her myself.
When the woman arrived, the king asked:
"Did you cause the elephant to give birth to offspring by speaking the truth?"
He replied, “It is so. The king then had this thought:
"Since the mother is so virtuous and good, the daughter must be as well.
Let me test her by asking.
[He asked: "Do you have a daughter?"
He replied to the king, “There is. “What is his name?”
He asked, "What is your name? She replied, "My name is Miaorong (Wonderful Countenance).
He asked again, "Have you ever been with another man?"
He replied, "I have never given it.
[The mother said,] "Mother!"
"If it is so, you may give it to me.
He replied, "As Your Majesty wishes."
He immediately prepared the ceremonial rites and took her into the palace.
The King thought again:
"The palace women are not chaste and have already violated their oaths; if she is made to dwell here, she will surely commit unrighteous acts."
Later, when a garuḍa arrived, the king informed him of the matter in full:
"Brother, you should take my wife away during the day and place her on the island in the sea, and bring her back at night."
He replied, "Very well.
He then entrusted his wife to the garuḍa, who, according to their agreement, would depart during the day and return at night.
"At that time, on that island in the ocean, there was a fragrant flower called 'Healer' (*Gami*). The wife would daily bind these flowers into garlands and send them to Brahmadatta.

Now, in Vārāṇasī, there was the son of a brahmin who, needing to go into the mountain forest to gather firewood, encountered a *kiṃnara* goddess. She then led the brahmin’s son into a stone grotto, where they engaged in sexual intercourse and became intimate with one another."
Whenever the girl went out to seek flowers and fruit, once she had departed, she would close the door with a large stone that no one could move.
After a long time had passed, she gave birth to a son; as the boy walked, his physical form was extremely swift, so they gave him the name "Swift" (Kṣipra).
The father would constantly sigh and say before his son:
"Vārāṇasī is a pleasant place to dwell; you should know this now.
The son asked his father:
"Where was my father born? He replied, "Vārāṇasī was his place of birth."
He replied, "If that is so,
why do you not return to your home?
His father said:
"When your mother goes out to seek flowers and fruit, she will surely cover the mouth of the hole with a large stone; I cannot move it, and there is no way for me to escape.
He replied, "I shall open it for you."
The father said, "Very well!
The son then repeatedly took up stones to test them, until his strength had developed such that he was able to push aside large rocks; he then reported this to his father, saying:
"The door has been opened; let us flee together with your father.
The father said, "Your mother has gone out for a moment to fetch flowers and fruit; she will return immediately, so there is no way you can escape."
"If he should encounter me on the road, he will certainly harm me.
He replied, "I shall employ a skillful means to cause him to arrive late."
The father said, "A fine thing.
When the mother brought the fruit, the son took it, chewed it, and spat it out; the mother said:
"What do you mean by this? Is it not beautiful?
He replied, "My mother was too lazy to go far; she sought bitter fruit nearby. Who else could have eaten them?"
"Therefore, you must discard it.
The mother said, "If that is so,
I shall go far away to seek out fine fruit and bring it back."
He replied, "Excellent!
In order to seek out someone suitable, the mother departed that very night; the son then reported to his father:
"Now is the time to flee; it would not be right to delay further.
Thereupon, they removed the stone and both father and son fled together, arriving at Vārāṇasī, the place where the father was born.
His mother came there and, seeing that the stone chamber was empty, beat her breast and wept bitterly.
A neighbor asked her,
"For what reason do you weep?"
He then answered in full detail regarding the matter.
The neighbor said,
"Since he is a human being who has come among humans, why should you worry or suffer over him?"
The mother said, "I do not grieve over this separation from you; I only regret that I have never taught you a single craft by which you might earn a livelihood. He then replied:
"I also frequently travel toward Vārāṇasī; if there is any means for you to survive, you may give it to me, and when I see him, I shall pass it on to my son.
Her mother then gave her the lute and said, "Sister!..."
If you see my son, hand him over to me personally and say to him:
"You may play this *vīṇā* to earn your livelihood, but you must not touch the first string; if you touch it, harm will surely come to you."
He then took him away. At that time, the Brahmin quickly entrusted his son to a teacher for instruction, and the teacher immediately began to teach him.
On a day of leisure, the boy went quickly into the mountains to gather firewood and encountered a neighbor, who asked Sūjāta:
"How have you been lately?
he asked. He replied, "I am constantly suffering from hunger; what else could I know?"
He replied, "Your mother remembers you and her tears flow constantly; why do you not go to her? He answered:
"He is a yakṣa; who could live with him?
He replied, "If you cannot leave, I shall now give you the means for your livelihood, but you must not give it to anyone else."
He replied, "I will not give it.
[The other] then handed over the lute and said:
"If you wish to make a living by playing this [lute], the finger must not touch the first string; if it touches it, there will surely be harm.
He replied, "Excellent!"
"I have done so. He then took his lute and went to the place of study, where he saw his companions.
They asked him, "Why have you arrived so late?"
He replied, "I saw my mother’s friend give me this lute. The people asked:
"Can you play? He replied, "I can."
"You may play it for us, and we shall listen together.
He then played for them; however, he did not touch the first string, whereupon they asked, "Why do you not touch the first string?"
He replied, "One who touches will inevitably give rise to faults and calamities.
[The other] said, "If you merely touch now, what fault could there be?"
He then touched them with his finger, whereupon the students could not contain themselves and all began to dance. Because of this, they arrived at their teacher's place late in the day.
He asked, "Why are you so late?"
He then answered in full detail. His elder brother asked, "Are you able to play the lute? He replied:
“I can. “If that is so, then play a melody for me.
He immediately began to play; however, he did not touch the first string, whereupon the elder said:
"For what reason is the first string not touched by the finger?
He replied, "If it were touched, I fear that some fault would arise."
"You need only touch it with your finger; what fault could there be in that?

He then plucked and touched it, whereupon both the elder man and his wife began to dance, unable to restrain themselves. The house they inhabited collapsed entirely, and all the jars and vessels were shattered without exception.
The Master became greatly incensed and immediately seized him by the neck, driving him out of the village.
Once cast out and wandering alone wherever he went, he sustained his life solely by playing the *vīṇā*.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants carrying their wares who wished to enter the great ocean. They deliberated among themselves, saying:
"We have all necessary things, yet we lack music; how shall we amuse ourselves?"
"Who in the great ocean can dispel our grief and distress?
One man replied, "The son of the Brahmin Sūcī is skilled at playing the *vīṇā*; we should go along with him."
They immediately took him quickly to the ship.
Once they were in the midst of the great ocean, the people said to him:
"Play the *konghou* lute for us; let us all enjoy ourselves together."
He then plucked the first string without even touching it. The people asked, "Why do you not touch the strings? He replied:
"If there is a fault in contact," he said,
"what fault could mere contact possibly cause?"

He immediately plucked and struck it; at that moment, the ship leaped and reeled upon the sea until it was shattered into pieces, and all the merchants were swept away and drowned, their lives ending simultaneously.

Only one person, Suji, survived; having encountered a plank and met with favorable winds, his life was sustained by these celestial conditions, and he was eventually blown to the island of the Garuḍas.

In a certain grove there were no other men, and he saw only the woman Varadattā, the wife of King Brahmadatta, who was of exquisite beauty; he engaged her in conversation and they became intimate with one another.
"We see each other by day, yet we part at night.
He asked, "Where do you go and from where do you come every night?"
Having opened his heart, he told him everything, and the other replied:
"O worthy one! If that is so, why do you not take me with you to Vārāṇasī?"
The woman replied, "Very well!
I shall go with you."
He asked the man,
"What is your name?
[The man replied,] "My name is Swift."
"What is your name? "My name is Miaorong (Wonderful Beauty).

The girl then gradually gathered small stones until they were equal in weight to a human being; once she had measured them out, she called for Speedy, and together they mounted the golden-winged bird and flew toward Vārāṇasī.
The woman said, "You may close your eyes; if you open them, they will be damaged.
As she approached the edge of the city, she heard people shouting and calling out, whereupon she had this thought:
"He seems to be approaching.
As she opened her eyes to look out, the bird suddenly swooped down with a fierce wind, and her two eyes were instantly blinded.
At that time, Miaorong placed him within the garden and went herself to the King's side.
Later, when spring arrived and the famous flowers were in full bloom while the various birds sang their plaintive songs, the King entered the garden with his court ladies to enjoy the sights.
At that time, the maiden Sucitrasundarī was also among them; as soon as she smelled the fragrance of the *utpala* flower, she immediately spoke in verse:
"The wind blows upon the *utpala* flower, Its sweet fragrance is truly lovely."
"Just as on a sea-island, one dwells together with a woman of exquisite beauty.
When King Brahmadatta heard this sound of verse, he commanded his inner women, saying:
"Examine everywhere to see who has made this sound!"
The people replied, "There is a man afflicted with eye disease who makes this sound.
The king then summoned him and asked:
"Did you compose this verse? He replied, "I did."
"You should perform it again; I shall listen to it. He then thought to himself:
"Perhaps the King enjoys hearing refined songs and odes; if I perform them for him, he might perhaps grant me a reward."
He then spoke this verse: “The *vāyujātī* flower, wafted by the wind, Its fragrance is truly lovely;
It is like dwelling together with one of exquisite beauty Upon an island in the ocean.”
Then the king asked: "As for what you call the Sea Isle, how far is it from here?
He replied with a verse:
“The dwelling place of Subhadrā is a hundred *yojana* from here;
beyond the great ocean lies a most lovely island.”
Having heard this, the king replied in verse:
"Have you ever heard of or seen anyone like those whom I love and cherish?
If it be one with such a wondrous form and body, you may describe their characteristics."
At that time, the blind man replied in verse:
“On his waist there is the figure of ten thousand; Upon his chest there is a single curl.
He constantly wears the *gokṣura* flower; It has been sent here for the lord of men.”
Having heard these words, the king thought to himself: "This man’s conduct is wicked;
even though he has been settled on a sea-island, he still commits illicit affairs. Since there is no further use for him, it is fitting that I harbor this resentment within my heart."
Then he spoke in verse:
“Take this woman of exquisite beauty, adorned with her jeweled necklaces, and deliver her to this blind man.
It would be well to have her mount a donkey and drive her out of the city walls.”

At that time, the two were banished by the king; the blind man, taking his wife with him, wandered aimlessly until evening, when they sought refuge in a large village and stayed temporarily in an empty temple.

At that time, a band of five hundred thieves entered this village at night; when the villagers discovered them, they slaughtered them all, with the exception of the sole leader of the band, who fled into a celestial temple and barred its door from within.
A villager came and asked,
"Who is that in the temple?
The blind man replied:
"I am a guest and not of the thief's kind," he said. The people replied,
"If there is a thief, you should be sent out immediately."
At that time, the bandit leader replied to Miaorong,
"What use have you for this blind man?
You should cast him out so that we may live together."
Miaorong consented and sent the blind man out.
When the villagers saw him, they cut off his head.
At daybreak, the bandit leader took Miaorong away; they reached a riverbank where there were no boats or rafts, and they could not cross.
The bandit said to his wife,
"O virtuous lady! Since the river has overflowed its banks, there is no way for us to cross together."
"You stay here for a moment and bathe your body; I shall first take all your ornaments across to the other shore, and once they are placed there, I will return to collect them.
The wife said, "As you wish."
He then took off his garments and various ornaments and gave them to the leader of the bandits; he entered the water and sat down, thinking to himself:
"Could it be that this man is fleeing with my belongings?"
He called out to her from afar, saying:
"The great river now overflows; take these necklaces with you.
Such thoughts have arisen in me, for I fear you might steal them away."
Having heard this, the bandit leader replied from afar in verse: "Your husband was innocent, yet you caused him to be killed; who would believe that I have any affection for you?"
"I shall take all these ornaments and go, for I fear you might find an opportunity to harm me.
At that moment, the bandit leader immediately took the goods and departed with the woman; the girl, however, then emerged from the river in her naked body and stayed hidden in the grass.
Not far from this place, there was an old jackal walking along the riverbank with a piece of meat held in its mouth.

At that time, a fish leaped from the water and threw itself onto the shore; seeing this, the jackal dropped the meat it was carrying and attempted to seize the fish. However, the fish plunged back into the water while the meat was snatched away by a hawk. Having lost both things, the jackal hung its ears and fell into grief.
At that time, from within the thicket of grass, Surūpā saw the jackal from afar and spoke this verse:
"The meat has been carried off by the owl, And the fish has entered the river;
Both things have perished together— What benefit is there in knowing this grief?"
At that time, having heard the sound of the verse, the jackal looked around in all directions but saw no one. He then spoke this verse:
"I did not laugh for joy, nor did I perform songs or dances;
who is it within the thicket of grass, jesting with me in speech?"
Having heard this, Miāoróng replied from within the thicket of grass to the jackal, saying,
"I am Miāoróng. Upon hearing her voice,
the jackal immediately spoke with anger and abuse:
"You, a transgressor, feel no shame for your own faults, yet you come back to mock me.
She replied with a verse:
"The former husband has already been killed; The new husband is taking the goods away."
"Neither of us has anyone to turn to for refuge; we lament and cry out amidst the grass.
Having heard this, Miaorong replied in verse:
"I shall now return to my own home, remaining chaste and devoted to one man alone."
"Fearing harm to my clan, I shall no longer act with such madness and folly.
At that time, the jackal also replied in verse:
"Even if the waters of the Gaṅgā were to flow upstream, and even if crows and birds were to turn white,"
Jambū and Jātī, you are able to remain devoted to one.
The crow and the owl dwell together in a single tree;
they are harmonious with one another, and you are able to remain devoted to one.
Even if a snake, a rat, and a wildcat were to roam together in a single burrow;
even if these two creatures were to feel mutual affection, you would still be able to remain steadfastly faithful to one alone.
Even if one were to use tortoise hair to weave a garment of the most exquisite quality—
In cold weather one may wear it; you indeed possess such integrity and singleness of purpose.
Even if one were to build a multi-storied pavilion from the legs of mosquitoes, making it firm and unshakable, you are able to maintain such single-minded devotion.
Even if one were to construct a bridge from lotus stalks for the multitude to cross,
such that even a great elephant could pass over it— you alone are capable of maintaining single-minded concentration.
Even if a mass of fire were to arise within the waters of the great ocean;
"All people turn toward [the many], yet you alone are able to remain steadfast in one.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the jackal said to Surūpā:
"I have merely uttered these words of playful jest; if I can cause you to regain your former status as the Queen of the State, what recompense will you offer me?"
He replied, "Friend,
if you can restore me to how I was before, I shall provide you with meat every day so that you never lack for it.
The jackal said:

"If it be so, you should follow my words: enter the Ganges River and let the water rise to your throat; then, with palms joined toward the sun, remain there while recollecting the deity, and I shall report this to the king."
The jackal then departed and went to where the king could hear him, letting out a great cry and speaking these words:
"Miaorong is now bathing her heart and refining her conduct in the Ganges River; you should quickly summon her back to enter the inner palace."
The King, having previously learned the language of jackals, heard of this matter and said to his ministers:
"You should now go to the banks of the Ganges; I have heard that Miaorong is there undergoing arduous penance to reform her heart and change her ways, so bring her here to meet me."
When the ministers saw that her appearance was exquisite, they immediately adorned her body with necklaces and fine garments and brought her to the king’s presence.

Upon seeing her, the king was filled with joy and reinstated her as his chief consort, just as she had been in former times. Consequently, he began to provide the jackal with fine meat every day, but later he suddenly ceased doing so.
At that time, the jackal returned to a place near the royal palace and called out, saying:
"O Lady of Exquisite Beauty!
If you do not provide me with meat, I shall have the King beat you severely until it is no different than before."
Upon hearing this, the lady was terrified and immediately returned the jackal’s meat.
You bhikṣus, do not harbor other thoughts.
She who was Suvarṇapuṣpā in the past is none other than this Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā; he who was Javila at that time is none other than Udāyin.
Just as in the past she recognized Suvarṇapuṣpā by smelling the fragrance of the *yāti-ghoṣa* flower, so now she recognizes that Bhikṣuṇī by smelling the fragrance of the *utpala* flower.
"O bhikṣus, you should know this: all undertakings have habitual practice as their causal condition.
Having heard this, the great assembly rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The fifth sub-section of the sixth chapter is summarized in verse as follows:
The ordination of nuns and the eight weighty rules; Nuns should sit according to seniority;
The affairs of the two assemblies differ; A nun who has returned to lay life shall not be ordained again.
The Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in the city of Kapilavastu.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred Śākya women, went to the place where the Buddha was. Having prostrated at his feet, they withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha then taught them various sublime dharmas, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them.
At that time, having heard the Dharma, Mahāprajāpatī arose from her seat with a heart of profound joy and, joining her palms toward the Buddha, addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Is it possible for a woman to go forth from home within the Buddha’s Dharma, receive full ordination, attain the status of a bhikṣuṇī, and by steadfastly practicing the holy life, realize the fourth fruit of śrāmaṇya?
The Buddha said, “Mahāprajāpatī!

You should remain at home wearing white garments and practice the various holy life (brahmacarya) in its entirety, perfection, purity, and stainlessness; by doing so, you will obtain peace, benefit, and happiness for a long night.”
Thus he requested three times, but the Buddha did not grant permission; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and left the city of Kapilavastu for the village of Veṇugrāma.

When Mahāprajāpatī heard that the Buddha had departed, she and five hundred Śākya women shaved their own heads, all donned saffron-colored saṃghāṭī robes, and followed behind the Buddha, traveling one night's journey at a time.

When the Blessed One arrived there, he stayed in the Śiṃśapā Grove. At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, exhausted from the journey and her body covered in dust, went to where the Buddha was; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, she withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the sublime Dharma for her, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening her.
Having heard the Dharma, Mahāprajāpatī rose from her seat, joined her palms, and said to him:
"World-Honored One!"

Is it possible for a woman, within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha, to go forth, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣuṇī, and by firmly practicing the holy life, realize the fourth fruit of śrāmaṇya?
The Buddha said: “Mahāprajāpatī!

You should shave your hair and don the saffron robes; then, for as long as life lasts, you must firmly cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya), which is singular, perfect, pure, and untainted. By doing so, you will obtain peace, benefit, and happiness for a long night.”
Thus she requested three times, but the Buddha did not grant her permission on any occasion.
When Mahāprajāpatī realized that the Blessed One repeatedly refused her request, she stood outside the gate weeping with tears.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having seen her, asked: "Gautamī,
for what reason do you stand here weeping?"
She replied, "Venerable Sir!
We women are not permitted by the Blessed One to go forth and become bhikṣuṇīs; for this reason, we weep."
Ānanda replied, “Gautamī, you may stay here; I shall inquire of the Tathāgata.”
At that time, Ānanda went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at his feet, and standing to one side, addressed the Buddha, saying: "Blessed One,

is it possible for a woman to go forth in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha, receive full ordination to become a bhikṣuṇī, and by firmly practicing the holy life, realize the fourth fruit of śrāmaṇya?"
The Buddha said,
"It is possible.
[She replied,] "If that is so, I pray you grant permission for women to go forth."
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!
You must not now request that women go forth from home within my well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and become bhikṣuṇīs."
Why is this? If one permits women to go forth [into homelessness], the Buddha-dharma will not endure for long.
It is like a household where the men are few and the women many; it will then be destroyed by wicked thieves.
The destruction of the True Dharma by women entering the monastic order is likewise so.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
It is like a farmer’s field whose crops have ripened, only to be suddenly ruined by wind, rain, frost, and hail.
The ruin of the True Dharma by women entering the monastic order is likewise so.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
Just as when a field of sugarcane has reached maturity, if it is struck by the *rakta-parvan* disease, it is utterly destroyed with nothing remaining.
"If women were permitted to go forth, it would likewise cause the True Dharma to be damaged, so that it could not remain for long and would quickly perish.
The Venerable Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The Great Lady of the World has indeed rendered great kindness to the World-Honored One; since she was the Buddha’s mother who nurtured him with her milk until he reached adulthood, would the World-Honored One not compassionately accept her?"
The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is indeed so.

She has been of great benefit to me, and I have already repaid her kindness. Because of me, she came to know the Three Jewels; she took refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, received the five precepts, and became free from all doubt regarding the principle of the Four Noble Truths. Having attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), she shall reach the end of suffering and realize the state of non-arising."
“Such a debt of gratitude is even more difficult to repay; it cannot be compared to things such as food or clothing.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

“Since you, for the sake of women, have requested their ordination to become bhikṣuṇīs, I shall now establish eight rules of respect which must be practiced for the duration of one’s life and not transgressed.”

These rules I have established are like a farmer who, at the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, firmly repairs the embankments and dykes at the river channels to prevent the water from flowing away; thus, the irrigation of the young crops is made sufficient everywhere. The Eight Rules of Respect are also like this.
What are the eight? Ānanda!
Bhikṣuṇīs should seek ordination from the bhikṣus, receive full admission (upasaṃpadā), and attain the status of bhikṣuṇīs; this is the first law of respect.
This matter must not be contravened; for as long as life lasts, all bhikṣuṇīs should diligently train in this. “Ānanda!
Every half-month, one should request instruction from the bhikṣus; this is the second rule of respect.”
This matter must not be contravened; you should diligently practice and study it for as long as you live. "Ānanda!
One must not enter the rains retreat in a place where there are no bhikṣus. This is the third rule of reverence."
This matter must not be contravened; you should diligently practice and study it for as long as you live. "Ānanda!
A bhikṣuṇī must not interrogate a bhikṣu, nor should she bear in mind any faults of a bhikṣu, namely: violations of the precepts, views, conduct, or right livelihood."

Ānanda! If a bhikṣuṇī sees that a bhikṣu has committed a transgression regarding his precepts, views, conduct, or livelihood, she should not reprimand him; however, if a bhikṣu sees that a bhikṣuṇī has committed a transgression, he should reprimand her.
Ānanda! This is the fourth rule of respect. It must not be transgressed;
you should diligently practice and study it for as long as life lasts.
“Ānanda! A bhikṣuṇī must not revile, become angry with, or rebuke a bhikṣu; whereas a bhikṣu may do these things to a bhikṣuṇī. This is the fifth rule of respect.”
This matter must not be contravened; you should diligently practice and study it for as long as you live. "Ānanda!

Even if a bhikṣuṇī has been fully ordained for a hundred years, upon seeing a bhikṣu who has only recently been ordained, she should show respect by joining her palms in greeting, welcoming him, and prostrating with reverence. This is the sixth rule of respect."
This matter must not be contravened; you should diligently practice and study it for as long as life lasts. "Ānanda!
If a bhikṣuṇī violates any of the rules of the communal teaching, she must perform the *mānatva* penance before both assemblies for half a month. This is the seventh rule of reverence."
This matter must not be contravened; one should diligently practice and study it for as long as life lasts. "Ānanda!

If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the summer retreat, performs the *pravāraṇā* ceremony before both assemblies by means of the three matters—what has been seen, heard, or suspected—this is the eighth rule of respect."
This matter must not be contravened; one should diligently practice and study it for as long as one lives.
