Fascicle Thirty-Three.
Translated by the Dharma Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The internal summary verse says:
Full ordination is received from bhikṣus; every half-month, one requests instruction;
one observes the rains retreat in dependence upon bhikṣus; one should not speak of faults seen [in them]; one should not scold with anger;
one should pay homage to those junior [to oneself]; and with a joyful mind, one should attend within the two assemblies.
"According to one's wish, one should address the bhikṣus; these are called the Eight Rules of Reverence. Ānanda!
I have now established these Eight Rules of Respect for the Bhikṣuṇīs, which must not be transgressed."
"If Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī can uphold these eight rules of respect, she shall thereby go forth, receive full ordination, and attain the status of a bhikṣuṇī.
When the Venerable Ānanda heard the Buddha’s teaching on the eight rules of reverence, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet, took his leave, and went to Mahāprajāpatī, where he spoke to her as follows:
"Mahāprajāpatī, you should know this!"

The Blessed One has already granted permission for women to go forth from the household life into homelessness within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha, to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), and to attain the status of a bhikṣuṇī.

However, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has established eight rules of respect (*gurudharma*) that all bhikṣuṇīs must practice without violation; they should diligently train in them throughout their entire lives.
"I shall now explain for you the Eight Rules of Respect established by the Blessed One; listen now attentively and reflect upon them well!
Then Mahāprajāpatī said, "I pray that you will speak for me; I shall listen with a single-minded focus."
The Venerable One replied:
"As the Blessed One has said, 'Noble bhikṣuṇīs should seek ordination and full admission from the bhikṣus to become bhikṣuṇīs'; this is the first rule of respect."
"This matter must not be contravened; for as long as life lasts, all bhikṣuṇīs should diligently practice and study it.
Thus he informed her of each point in detail until the end.
When Mahāprajāpatī heard Venerable Ānanda explain these rules of respect, she was filled with deep joy and, receiving them upon the crown of her head, upheld them. She then addressed Ānanda, saying:
“Venerable Sir!
It is like a daughter from a noble family of the four castes, who bathes her body, anoints it with fragrant unguents, cleanses her hair and nails, and wears fresh, clean garments.”

At that time, another person took *campaka*, *utpala*, and other flowers, bound them into a floral garland, and presented it to the woman; when the woman saw the flowers approaching, she received them with joy and placed them upon the crown of her head.
"Venerable One!
I too shall likewise receive and uphold with my body, speech, and mind the eight rules of respect for the Tathāgata.
At that time, when Mahāprajāpatī received these rules of respect, she and the five hundred Śākya women simultaneously went forth, received full ordination, and became bhikṣuṇīs.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying:
"As the Buddha has said:
'If Mahāprajāpatī accepts the eight weighty rules, she is then ordained, she is then fully ordained, and becomes a bhikṣuṇī. I do not yet know what the case is for other groups of women."
The Buddha told Upāli:
"As for the other women, they shall be granted the going forth and the full ordination according to the proper sequence.
When the women heard this instruction, they did not know what that sequence was.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"Let Mahāprajāpatī at their head, along with the five hundred Śākya women, receive the rules of respect; this shall constitute their going forth, their full ordination, and their attainment of the status of bhikṣuṇīs."
All other women should likewise receive [the precepts] in this successive manner.

If there is a woman who seeks to go forth, she should approach a nun and perform prostrations; that nun should then inquire whether she possesses any obstructing conditions (*antarāyika-dharma*). If she is free from such obstacles, she should be accepted and granted the Three Refuges along with the Five Precepts (*pañca-śikṣāpada*). First, she should prostrate to the sacred image, then prostrate to her teacher, and be instructed to join her palms and speak these words:
"Venerable Ācārya, please attend to me."

I, [Name], from this day forth until the end of my life, take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the most honored among all assemblies.
Thus he spoke three times.
The Master said:
"Excellent."
He replies, "Very well.
Next, the five precepts are conferred, and he is instructed to say these words:
"Venerable Ācārya, please attend to me.

Just as the noble Arhats, for as long as they live, abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, and abstain from drinking intoxicants."

I, [Name], from this day forth until the end of my life, shall not kill living beings, shall not steal, shall not engage in sexual misconduct, shall not speak falsely, and likewise shall not drink intoxicants; these are my five precepts of training, which are the training rules of the noble Arhats, and I shall follow, practice, and maintain them accordingly.
Thus he says three times:
"May the Ācārya bear witness that I am an upāsikā, who has taken refuge in the Three Jewels and received the five precepts."
The Master said, "Excellent. He replied:

"Excellent. This occurred while the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the Blessed One instructed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and five hundred Śākya women to receive the Eight Rules of Respect; the Buddha declared that by doing so, they were ordained and perfected, attaining the status of bhikṣuṇīs.

Therefore, the community of nuns conferred the full ordination upon others, thereby establishing them in the status of bhikṣuṇīs; in this manner, they successively conferred it upon yet others, and the community of nuns flourished.
Later, at another time, several senior bhikṣuṇīs went to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and spoke to her thus:
"Excellent, Noble Lady! You should know this:"

"We, the community of bhikṣuṇīs, have been ordained for a long time, while these other bhikṣus were ordained as novices and received full ordination not long ago; let them respect one another according to seniority."
When she had spoken these words, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said: "Sisters,
wait a moment while I go to the place of the Venerable Ānanda to inquire about this matter."
She then went to the Venerable Ānanda and related the matter as above.
Ānanda said, "Great Lady, wait a moment; I shall go and inform the Buddha."
Then Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!

There are elder bhikṣuṇīs who have been ordained for a long time, and there are other young bhikṣus who have recently received full ordination. Is it possible to have them respect one another according to their seniority?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should not speak of this matter now.
For what reason?

If women had not gone forth into this noble Dharma and Vinaya, then the faithful elders, brahmins, and others would have seen the bhikṣus all receiving fine food and would have provided it to them together, ensuring they lacked for nothing.
Ānanda! Furthermore, there are faithful householders, brahmins, and others who spread out new, clean white cotton cloths upon the streets and speak these words:
"May you, O worthy śramaṇa, tread upon this cloth; may we obtain great benefit and long-lasting peace and happiness for a long night."
"Ānanda! Furthermore, there are faithful householders, brahmins, and others who spread their hair upon the ground and speak thus:
'May the venerable Śramaṇa tread upon my hair with his feet, so that I may obtain great benefit throughout the long night and attain lasting peace and happiness.'"
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If women had not gone forth in this well-expounded Dharma and Discipline taught by me, then even the sun and moon, despite their great radiance, would not have been able to eclipse the majesty and virtue of my disciples, let alone other dead corpses such as the followers of external paths."
Furthermore, Ānanda!
Had women not gone forth from the household life, my teaching would have endured for a full thousand years, complete and pure, free from all defilement;
because they have gone forth, it has been reduced by five hundred years.

Therefore, Ānanda! I decree that even a bhikṣuṇī who has been fully ordained for a hundred years should respectfully join her palms to welcome and reverently prostrate before a bhikṣu who has newly received full ordination.
The setting was as before.
At that time, certain bhikṣuṇīs had matters involving groups of four, groups of five, or groups of twelve arise; they then assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions.
As administrative affairs became numerous, they eventually interfered with teaching, recitation, and reflection.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:

"The two assemblies have separate duties; except for matters such as the expiation of offenses, the full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the fortnightly ritual (*poṣadha*), which must be performed together, all other matters shall be conducted separately."
At that time, there was a householder in Śrāvastī who, not long after marrying his wife, became pregnant. When the months were complete, she gave birth to a daughter.
After the girl was born, her father died; once she had grown up under her mother’s care, her mother also passed away.
Later, the nun Thullanandā entered the house while begging for alms; seeing the girl, she asked, "To whom do you belong? She replied:
"Noble one! I have no protector and have never belonged to anyone. He replied:
"If this is so, why do you not go forth [into homelessness]?
The woman replied,
"Who would allow me to go forth?"
The nun said, "I can give you [ordination]; you may follow me.
He immediately followed her, and upon reaching the nuns' residence, she granted him ordination. Later, however, being entangled by the afflictions (*kleśa*), he eventually returned to lay life.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā, while going out to beg for alms, encountered the girl and asked, "Young woman,
how do you manage to survive?"
He replied: "Noble One! I am without protection; I live my life in hardship."
He replied, "If that is so,
why have you not gone forth [into homelessness] once again? He answered:
“I have already returned to lay life;
who can ordain me? The nun said, “I can.”
She was immediately ordained and proceeded to beg for alms.
When the elders and brahmins saw this, they all criticized her together, saying:

"The women of the Śākya clan are capable of performing good deeds; at times they leave the household life to cultivate pure conduct, yet at other times they abandon the path and return to the defilements of worldly life. Acting according to their own whims—how can this not be considered a 'good deed'?"
When the nuns heard this, they informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:
"Because of such faults committed by nuns who have returned to the lay life, from this day forward, no nuns who have returned to the lay life shall be permitted to go forth again."
These elders and others mock and disparage my Dharma; therefore, once a bhikṣuṇī has abandoned her dharma-robes and returned to the lay life, she should not be permitted to go forth again.
"If one grants ordination [to such a person], the preceptor incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The sixth section, the sixth sub-section, is summarized in verse as follows:
"Because of the ordination of Gautamī, there are five benefits to becoming a renunciant."
One should understand that the matter of censure occurs within the fivefold assembly.
The setting and circumstances are as before.

At that time, there was a householder in Vārāṇasī named Ghoṭamukha, who was very wealthy and possessed great riches. Not long after he had married, he took his goods and traveled to the city of Takṣaśilā for trade. Having arrived there, he went to a certain household to seek lodging.
At that time, the host, a householder named Yaśas, saw him and cried out, "Welcome!
With a joyful heart, he invited him to sit; they immediately became acquainted and formed a close friendship.
At that time, Gautama had sold his old goods and purchased new ones, returning to his native village.

Later, on another occasion, the householder who was his former master traveled for trade to Vārāṇasī and went to stay at Gautama’s house. Seeing him, Gautama was filled with joy and cried out: "Welcome!"
They exchanged pleasantries for a long time.
Then, the householder Takṣaka said to Gautama,
"By what means can we ensure that after we have passed away, our descendants will remain close and affectionate toward one another, without becoming estranged?"
Gautama said, "Excellent are these words!
Now let us form a marriage alliance by the joining of our bellies; if a son is born to one family and a daughter to the other, the two shall be wed."
He replied, "So be it;
my mind is likewise inclined.
Thereupon, the elder sold his old goods and purchased new ones, and returned to his own home.

His wife became pregnant and, when her months were full, gave birth to a son. After twenty-one days had passed, he gathered his kinsmen and bestowed a name upon the child, calling him Youfang (Wanderer).
At that time, Gautama of Vārāṇasī, hearing that a son had been born, was filled with great joy and thought to himself:

"The householder Daśa is my close friend; now that he has fathered a son, I shall give birth to a daughter. He is the future husband for my daughter, so I shall provide him with ornaments, necklaces, and fine garments."
He sent a messenger with the following letter:
"I have heard that you have fathered a son and am filled with great joy; I now send these garments, which I hope you will graciously accept.
Upon receiving the letter and its message, the Elder Takṣa replied with a letter of his own.

At that time, Gautama received a letter conveying his intentions and requested the girl; not long thereafter, his wife became pregnant, and when the months were complete, she gave birth to a daughter. Although her features were upright and handsome, she was thinner than ordinary people. When all the relatives gathered to give her a name, they all deliberated and said:
"This girl’s form is thin, and she is the daughter of Gautama; therefore, we should give her the name Kṣemā Gautamī."
At that time, when the elder heard that a daughter had been born, he thought to himself:
"My friend has borne a daughter; how could this be in vain? I should send garments and necklaces to express my congratulations, for she is none other than my own new bride—of this there is no doubt."
He then composed a letter, saying:

"I have heard that you have given birth to a daughter, and my heart is filled with double joy. I have sent these garments and necklaces as a token of my congratulations; I trust you will accept them so that this gesture may not be in vain."
Having read the letter, he replied with a letter of his own, saying:
"The proposal for an alliance has now been fulfilled according to our wishes; let us each wait until they have reached maturity before arranging their marriage.

When Gautama had finished reading the letter, he gradually brought his daughter to the age of puberty and instructed her in learning and knowledge. The Elder Takṣaka likewise instructed his son to master all the various arts.

Previously, this elder had a mistress with whom he had an illicit affair; he entrusted his son to her to learn the "Secret Script" (*śāstra*), a treatise concerning the secret, deceptive, and difficult-to-discern matters of women's sexual relations with men. After studying for a long time, the boy reported to her, saying: "Mother!..."
"I have now mastered what I was learning and wish to return home.
His mother replied, "You may continue your studies well; do not return home yet."
He replied, "Mother! I have already learned well how to remember my home and must return."
The mother then secretly grasped a ball of purple lac cotton and said,
"If you are determined to leave and refuse to stay, I shall strike your head until it is broken and bleeding."
He replied, "Mother! You must not detain me so insistently; I shall not go yet."
The mother said, "As for those wretched, destitute people who claim to have mastered the arts of private seduction, even you do not know them.

How could I ever strike my own head until it is broken for the sake of another's child? I intended to take moist purple mineral cotton and press it against my head so that a red juice would flow down, which people would see and mistake for blood."
"You truly lack wisdom; you must not yet speak of returning.
Having heard his mother's words, he stayed for a while. Before long, he spoke again: "Mother!..."
"I wish to return home.
His mother replied, "You should stay for now!"
He replied, "I am going. His mother said:
"If you go, I shall throw myself into the well and die. She replied, "Mother!"
"If it must be so, I shall not return home.

Her mother said, "You foolish creature, who claims to be well-versed in the secrets of letters—you do not even know this! How could I, for the sake of another's son, throw myself into a well and die? I intend to place many straw mats inside the well and cast myself down; when people see me there, they will say I am dead."
"You truly lack wisdom; you may not yet speak of taking refuge.
After a short while, she spoke again: "Mother!"
"I wish to return home.
His mother said,
"You have already earnestly requested to go three times."
"If you do not stay, I shall prepare milk-gruel; only after I have finished eating it will you depart.

Once the milk-gruel was cooked, she placed it in a copper basin, added plenty of ghee and honey, and ate it all before her son's very eyes. Having finished eating, she then spat it back out into the basin.
He commanded, saying,
"Eat," and [the other] replied:
“Mother! How can you eat again food that has been spat out?
The mother then wept, and when the neighbors heard this, they all came together to inquire.
"Why are you weeping?
Her mother then informed her neighbor, who replied, "I have prepared gruel for you; for what reason do you not eat it?"
He replied, "This is vomit; how can it be eaten?
His mother then beat her breast, wept aloud, and said to the people:
"How could one possibly spit out food and give it to another?
The neighbors all gathered and forcibly compelled him to eat; when the boy was thus pressured, he was about to consume the gruel.
His mother then seized his hand and struck him across the face, saying:
"You fool! You claim to be well-versed in the books on private matters, yet you truly lack wisdom; how could you possibly look upon someone vomiting food and then eat it yourself?
He then immediately drove him out and would no longer live with him.

At that time, having been expelled, the son of the elder returned to his former residence and became a merchant leader himself; taking five hundred merchants and carrying a great quantity of goods, he traveled south toward the Central Kingdom.
He constantly spoke to people about the repulsiveness of female form, and gradually traveling on, he arrived at Vārāṇasī.
At that time, while other merchants coming and going all engaged in sexual relations with courtesans, he—having heard these virtuous words—did not enter the brothels.
The courtesans deliberated, saying:
"Sisters, you should know!
The merchants from the northern lands with whom we previously had many dealings have now all become free from desire and no longer visit us."
One woman said: "I have heard that the merchant leader is well-versed in the secret scripts and feels extreme revulsion toward women; for this reason, everyone has ceased coming and going with him."
In the assembly, there was an elderly courtesan who asked the people, "Is he a man?
They replied:
"He is a man with all his faculties complete. She replied,
"If my daughter can seduce him, she shall be established as the leader among all the women."
He replied, "If one succeeds, let him be established as the foremost; if he does not succeed, what would you have me do? He answered:
"I shall repay you all five hundred gold coins.
The crowd said, "Excellent."
The mother immediately went to the merchant leader and rented a house to live in, where she stored a great quantity of various goods so that there was never a lack.
From time to time, members of the merchant leader’s household would come to the shop to seek whatever they required.
The old woman asked,
"To whose family do you belong? He replied:
"I am a merchant leader," [he said].
His mother replied, "My son, you too have taken goods and traveled to other regions as a merchant leader; why not seek this same status from others?"
"From this day forward, you may come to my house; whatever you require, take it as you please.
Having heard these words, he came repeatedly to take things, whereupon the merchant chief became suspicious and asked his family members, "Where have you obtained these extraordinary items?"
The family members said, "Not far from here, there is the home of an old woman who stores many kinds of goods. She says of herself:
'My son took his goods and likewise went to another region as a merchant leader; why should he not seek [wealth] from others in this same way?'"
"Whatever you require, come and take it as you please.
Whenever I had need of anything, I would seek it from her.
Having heard this, the merchant leader conceived a feeling of affection for his mother and said to his family members:
"Since his mother provides for him in such a manner, he treats her as if she were his own mother.
A family member went to her and reported this to her mother, saying,
"The merchant leader has conceived a deep affection for you that is no different from what he feels for his own mother."
The old woman asked,
"When shall I be able to see my son's face? He replied:
"Excellent! I shall inform the caravan leader.
He then returned to report it, and upon hearing this, the caravan leader replied:
"Excellent! He then went at once to the old woman's shop; having met her, she welcomed him with joyful laughter, and the mother asked:
"What is your name?"
He replied, “My name is Youfang.
His mother said:
“My son, the merchant leader, also bears this same name; you are that very person, no different in essence. Come and go to my place without harboring any other thoughts.
He replied, “So be it;
there is no distinction between our hearts.”
The mother commanded her daughter:
"You may come forward and meet your brother.
The daughter immediately came out and exchanged greetings with him.

At that time, the merchant leader saw the woman approaching; her appearance was so dignified and exquisite that she was peerless in all the world. He was immediately struck with passion as if by a violent wind, such that he was unaware of where he was or what he should do.
Awakening for a moment, he said to his mother,
"Whose young daughter is she? She replied:
"Beloved child! This is your sister. He asked:
"Is she already under the care of another? He replied,
"She is not yet under anyone's care."
He replied, "Mother! If that is so,
why do you not give it to me?"
The mother said, "I wish to have you serve me; I do not intend to give you to another.
However, there is one fault that causes me to harbor doubt: though we were united for a time, you wished to depart and then abandoned me."
He replied, "Mother! If you can grant me this,
I shall certainly not cast you aside."
The mother said, "If it is so, then bring all your wealth and property into my house; only then will I believe that your heart and words are one and the same. He replied:
"Very well," he replied.

He then transported his goods into the man's house; as soon as they entered through a back door, they were immediately taken out. Once he realized the goods had been exhausted, he said, "You should choose an auspicious day, and we may then perform the marriage ceremony together."
The mother then replied to the courtesans:
"On such-and-such a day, each of you should adorn yourselves, put on your finest garments, and come together to my house for a gathering."
When the day for the wedding arrived, the merchant leader was astonished and asked,
"Mother! For what reason is there such a great assembly, yet there are no men present, only women?"
The old woman spoke falsely, saying,
"The man has not yet arrived.
At that time, a certain woman then whispered into the caravan leader's ear:
"Do you not know that we are all courtesans?
The merchant leader thought to himself,
"I have been deceived by these courtesans."
After they had been in amorous union for many days, the woman said to the merchant leader,
"Give me some gold coins. He replied:
"All my wealth has been placed within your house; what further thing do you seek from me that I might give it to you? The woman remained silent.

Later, the merchant leader fell asleep from wine, whereupon she wrapped him in a straw mat and cast him onto the street. At dawn, as people were passing by, he woke up; seeing his body in such a state, he was deeply overcome with remorse and distress. With tears streaming down his face and tormented by the fire of hunger, he went to the laborers to seek employment.
At that time, the elder Ghoṣila built a new residence and hired many laborers, instructing them to go throughout the marketplace to search for and summon the son of the elder.
At that time, Gautama, seeing that the man’s demeanor was extremely timid, said to the messenger:
“In my view, this person seems to have never performed such work before; seek another.”
Upon hearing these words, he was further overcome with grief and distress; with tears streaming down his face, he gazed at the elder’s countenance.
The elder, surprised, asked him: "Whose son are you?"
"From where have you come?
What is your name? He then replied with a choked and hoarse voice:
"O Father, you should know!
I am from the northern city of Takṣaśilā, and my name is Youfang (Wandering). I have come here due to celestial circumstances.
I do not know where I should go now."
"Now that I have encountered this hardship, whether I live or die is uncertain.
At that time, Gautama, seeing his words and moved by compassion, asked:
"Do you know the person named the Elder from the city of Takṣaśilā?"
He replied, "O father! I am a man of meager merit; he is my father."
When Gautama heard that he was being addressed as "father," he realized they were long-standing relatives; his affection for them deepened further, and he spoke these kind words:
"Have no fear and do not give way to grief; you shall be my son-in-law, and this home is yours."

Having received this consolation, his sorrowful heart was at last stilled. The elder then bestowed upon him clothing and articles for adorning the body, as well as bathing facilities, scented ointments, food, drink, and a dwelling; indeed, he provided everything necessary so that nothing was lacking.
He spoke again to his wife, saying, "You should prepare necklaces and ornaments for the girl; once the son-in-law has arrived, we shall perform the marriage ceremony.
He then addressed the wandering monk (Youfang) in the presence of his kinsmen:
"This is now an auspicious hour; let us together perform the marriage rites. Youfang replied, "Father!..."
"I have not yet entered into marriage; let me first seek wealth and goods.
The elder replied, "Whatever wealth you require within this house is at your disposal. Since there is nothing lacking, what further use would there be in seeking more?"
However, the original intention of this traveler was to go to the courtesan’s quarters to take private revenge;
he replied, "Father!
On the day I entered into marriage, I prepared the full array of ceremonial rites; how could I be like ordinary folk who marry as circumstances permit?"
The householder remained silent.

At that time, the Wanderer went out of the city to sightsee and saw a corpse in the great river being carried away by the current. Crows on the bank wished to eat its flesh, but as they extended their beaks they could not reach it; looking toward the riverbank, they then used their claws to grasp a bamboo chopstick and wipe their beaks with it, whereupon their beaks grew long and they were able to eat the dead flesh.
After he had finished eating his fill, he took another chopstick and rubbed his lips so that they shrank back to their original state, no different from before.
When Youfang saw this, he took the chopsticks and returned; he then went to the house of a courtesan with five hundred coins and said, "O fair lady!"
"Previously, because you had no money, you bound me and drove me out; now that you have wealth and goods, we may rejoice together.
When the woman saw that he had money, she agreed to stay with him.
At that time, the wanderer, having found his opportunity, took a single chopstick and rubbed it against her nose; her nose then grew to a length of about ten fathoms.

At that time, the family was struck with terror and summoned all the physicians, commanding them to provide a cure; yet not a single one was able to restore her to her former state, and the doctors all abandoned her and departed.
Seeing the physicians leave, the girl became even more terrified and said to Viyāṭa:
"Noble son, out of your compassion!..."
"I pray you will forget my past transgressions and not dwell on our mutual betrayal; please treat me.
Youfang replied, "First you must make a vow: I shall treat you provided that you first restore to me all the wealth you seized from me."
He replied, "If you can be cured, you shall repay me double; in the presence of this assembly, I dare say that I would never dare deceive you.

He then took a single chopstick and rubbed it against the woman's bridge of the nose, whereupon her nose was restored to its former state. The woman then produced all the goods she had received and returned them to him.
Having acquired wealth, he returned home and prepared a grand wedding feast, summoning his kinsmen to take a wife and establish a household.
At that time, Gautama had a residence outside the city;
he informed his son-in-law, saying, "You may take your wife and reside there; I shall provide you with all the villages and estates located there."

Having arrived there, he lived in peace and comfort. Before many days had passed, his wife became pregnant; when the time for birth drew near, she said to her husband, "I wish to return home now so that my mother may care for me."
He replied, "As you wish.
Once they had arrived at the house, a son was immediately born; he then took the child back to their former residence.
Before long, she became pregnant again; as her due date approached, she once more requested to return to her mother’s home.

She then took her son and traveled with her husband by carriage. Along the way, the husband alighted from the carriage and went beneath a tree to lie down and sleep. A venomous snake came and bit him, and he died as a result.
While the wife was in the carriage, she gave birth to a son; having given birth, she descended from the carriage and went to the side of the tree, reporting to her husband:
"I have borne a son; you should rejoice."

He cried out loudly but could not speak; only when he touched him with his hand later did he realize that his life had ended. He wailed and sobbed, beating his chest in agony, overwhelmed by grief and despair.
At that moment, a bandit forcibly stole his ox and departed, leaving only the empty cart behind, which intensified his lamentation. Looking in all four directions, he saw no one else.

Carrying his two sons, he returned to his original location; as they traveled along the way, they encountered a great wind and rain, and the river swelled so high that there was no means of proceeding.
He then had this thought: "If I attempt to cross with both children at once, neither I nor my children will survive."

She then left the elder son behind, cradling the younger child in her arms; having successfully crossed the river, she placed him on the bank and turned back to fetch the elder son. As she floated toward the middle of the stream, a jackal came and seized the younger child. The child cried out, and the mother called from afar.
The prince thought his mother was calling to him, so he threw himself into the water and immediately passed away.
His mother hurriedly climbed onto the bank to pursue the jackal; having found her son and seeing that his life had ended, she wept aloud and cast him into the river.

He then saw an adult man being carried away by the current; thinking that he might still be alive, he entered the water and swam toward him. Upon observing him and realizing he was dead, he wept with bitter grief and quickly climbed back onto the bank.

Her son having departed and left her behind, she wandered alone through the vast wilderness, clad in but a single garment. Wailing and crying out in lamentation, she beat her breast in anguish, unable to restrain herself; now walking and now sitting, she rolled about upon the ground.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should know this!
When the retribution of past karma ripens, it must be experienced by the body; there is no way to escape it.

At that time, his parents at home and all his relatives were struck by lightning and all lost their lives, with only a single servant remaining alive. Wailing and weeping piteously, the servant ran swiftly toward him.
The woman saw him and asked,
"Why are you walking so hurriedly?
He then fell to the ground, wailing piteously, and said:
"All my kinsmen have been struck by lightning, yet I alone have escaped with my life.
Upon hearing this cry, the woman was overcome with grief and spoke these verses:
"What evil karma did I commit in a previous life, That I am now abandoned by all my relatives?"
My children and my parents—have my kinsmen all perished at once?
I am a person of meager merit; I must wander alone wherever fate leads me.
With my relatives all scattered and gone, with what face could I wish to live on?
"It would be better to dwell among the mountains and thickets, in the vast wilderness where no people live, than to remain in a household where sorrow increases day and night.

Having spoken these verses, he took his leave of the slave and wandered alone toward the east or west as he pleased. Upon reaching a village, he encountered a household where an old woman was spinning cotton thread; he requested temporary lodging, and the woman granted him permission. He then went to her side and joined her in spinning the thread.
There was a young weaver who would occasionally come to his mother’s place to buy cotton thread. On another occasion, the mother took some fine yarn and went to the youth’s place.
He asked her, "Mother, the thread was coarse the other day; why is it so fine and exquisite today?"
The mother said, "This was not my doing. He asked:
"Who did it? He replied, "There was a guest; he was capable of doing it skillfully."
He replied, "Mother! I am all alone;
I have no second hand to help me. Why do you not give it to me? I shall provide for you with food and clothing."
He replied, "I shall go back and ask him; once I know his intention, I will report it to you.
He then purchased thread at a high price, prepared fine food and drink, and adorned her with fragrant flowers before sending his mother back home.
Śrīmatī Gautamī saw her and asked:
"Mother! Where did you sell thread to obtain this money for scented flowers and colored powders?"
He replied, "Young woman!
Not only have you obtained money for a high price, adorned your body with flowers and colors, and further enjoyed a full meal of fine food, but you have returned in great joy."
The woman said,
"I find this most extraordinary and have questioned you about it.
She then spoke of the weaver's excellence right before her, adding further words:
“O maiden! That weaver has no wife; can you live with him and provide for his food and clothing? She replied:
“Mother! Do not speak such words.
I have developed a deep sense of weary aversion toward my family; I shall sustain my life as circumstances require and seek nothing further.
His mother said:
"A woman has no means of survival without a protector; it would be best to find a place for her to settle and live in peace.

He then recounted a hundred kinds of reasons to persuade her to remarry. The woman’s mind changed and she complied with his request. Once the weaver learned this, he welcomed her home with due ceremony.

At that time, the weaver was by nature cruel and malicious; although she had committed no offense, he constantly inflicted beatings upon her. The girl then went to her elderly mother and said, "For what reason have you handed me over to a yakṣa?"
"Constantly suffering such torment, what plan do you know to take?
He replied, "Young maiden!"
"Do not harbor grief; if there be a son or daughter born to you whom you love and cherish, all the family estate and wealth shall belong to you.

Before long, the woman became pregnant. When her husband learned of this, he ceased his harsh treatment of her. His wife, however, became arrogant and no longer behaved as she had before. The weaver, having perceived this, remained there harboring resentment.

Later, the weavers gathered together; being intoxicated with wine, they returned home and knocked on the door, calling out. At that time, their wives were in labor and sat with the doors closed; though they heard the shouting, they had no way to go out and look.

The weaver was by nature malicious; further intoxicated by liquor, he harbored resentment in his heart and his anger increased even more. Only after the woman had given birth did she open the door for him, saying to her husband, "I have borne a son; you should rejoice."
Upon hearing these words, he harbored malice in his heart and thought to himself:
"When she was pregnant, she already showed me contempt; now that she has given birth to a son, her arrogance has increased even further. If I do not kill her, she will surely become my enemy."
He then replied to his wife,
"Quickly heat the cauldron and place oil within it.
Seeing that the oil had begun to boil, he said to his wife:
"You must throw your son into the cauldron.
The wife said, "This is your own newborn son who knows nothing; what fault has he committed that you wish to kill him?"
"This is unacceptable.

He then struck his back with a heavy staff; for in this world, there is nothing more beloved than one's own body, and being unable to bear the suffering, he immediately lifted his child and placed him inside a cauldron of oil.
Once he had seen that [the meat] was cooked,
he replied, "You may now eat this meat. He answered:
"How can I eat my own son's flesh?
The husband then subjected her to twice the usual torture and oppression; unable to endure the suffering any longer, she finally ate his flesh.
As the World-Honored One said:
"Desire is a minor fault, which even the foolish can eliminate;
hatred and delusion are great calamities, which the wise should swiftly abandon.

At that time, the weaver was overcome with regret; he sat and lay restless, as if his heart were being consumed by fire. He was so filled with grief, distress, and resentment that he fell asleep. His wife then thought to herself:
“The man has killed his own son so that he may eat his flesh; as a yakṣa among humans, it would be best for me to flee.
He then took provisions for the journey and ran out of the city.
At that time, there was a merchant from the north who wished to return to his own country, and [the yakṣa] became his companion, sustaining himself as the occasion required.
When that great caravan leader saw this woman, her appearance and demeanor were so upright and graceful that he conceived a feeling of affection for her and asked:
"Young maiden, to whom do you belong?"
“Where do you intend to go?

She replied, “I previously had a husband who was bitten to death by a venomous snake; one son, newly born, was killed by a jackal; another son, two years old, drowned; and all my parents and kinsmen were struck by lightning. Having no one to rely upon, I have been wandering everywhere and am now staying with these merchants to seek a means of survival.”
The merchant leader thought to himself,
"A woman with such beauty and grace is difficult to find.
He then accepted her and took her as his wife.
Suddenly, while on the road, mad bandits broke into the camp; they seized all the property and killed the husband.
Seeing that the woman’s appearance was lovely, the bandit leader provided her with food and clothing and took her as his wife.
Later, the ruler of the northern kingdom executed the rebel leader and took this woman as his principal consort.

Before long, the king passed away; at that time, the ministers and officials performed the grand funeral rites according to the laws of that country, which required human sacrifice to accompany the deceased.

When the king and his queen were interred within the tomb, bandits broke into it and bored a hole through the wall. While Śrīmatī Gautamī was inside the grave, dust entered her nose and she immediately sneezed.
Upon hearing the sound, the bandits were all struck with terror and fled in all directions, thinking it was a *vetāla* (reanimated corpse).

At that moment, Śrī-Gautamī saw the tomb open and bright, and she emerged through the opening. Once outside, she looked about in a daze; overwhelmed by a hundred kinds of anxiety and grief, she found no way to escape her life. Furthermore, hunger and thirst pressed upon her body and mind, causing her to go mad and lose track of time. With mud smeared over her entire body and her hands and feet cracked and split, she departed naked.
Traveling alone by stages over a distance of ten thousand *li*, he arrived at Śrāvastī.
As the World-Honored One has said:

"The karmic retribution of sentient beings is inconceivable; whatever deeds one has previously committed, one must experience them all oneself. Only when evil conditions are exhausted will wholesome fruits finally arise."
Next, he proceeded forward until he reached the Jeta Grove.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the sublime Dharma. From afar, he beheld the Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, his body universally embellished and peerless in the world. His perfect brilliance was so radiant and majestic that it surpassed a thousand suns; like a king of jewel mountains, those who gazed upon him forgot all weariness.

The woman gazed up at him with utmost reverence and thereby regained her original mind; beholding her own appearance, she felt deep shame and immediately sat upon the ground, not daring to move about.
At all times, the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has nothing he does not know or see;
he constantly gives rise to great compassion to benefit all beings, being foremost among those who provide protection and rescue, most heroic and valiant, and free from any double-tongued speech.
Abiding in concentration and wisdom, they manifest the three types of clear knowledge; they skillfully cultivate the three trainings and harmonize the three karmas.
They cross over the four torrents and establish themselves in the four bases of spiritual power. Throughout the long night, they practice the four means of attraction;

they abandon the five hindrances, distance themselves from the five factors, and transcend the five paths. Their six faculties are complete, their six perfections are fulfilled, and they possess the seven riches.
Universally bestowing gifts, he causes the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment to bloom; free from the eight difficulties, he delights in the eightfold noble path;
forever severing the nine fetters, he is clear and proficient in the nine meditative absorptions; fulfilling the ten powers, his fame resounds throughout the ten directions;

among all those who possess mastery, he is most preeminent; having attained fearlessness in the Dharma, he subdues Māra and his enemies, shaking the great thunderous sound and uttering the lion’s roar.
Throughout the six periods of day and night, he constantly observes all worlds with the Buddha-eye: who is increasing?
Who is declining?
Who has encountered suffering and calamity?
Who is heading toward the evil realms?
Who is mired in the quagmire of desire?
Who is capable of being transformed through instruction?
By what skillful means shall they be rescued and brought forth? Those who lack the noble wealth shall be made to obtain it;

with the *añjana* of wisdom, the film of ignorance shall be pierced. Those who lack roots of goodness shall be made to plant them; those who possess roots of goodness shall be made to increase them. Placing them upon the path of humans and devas, secure and unimpeded, they shall be led toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
As it is said in a verse:
"Even if the tide of the great ocean Should ever miss its appointed time;
The Buddha, in regard to those he transforms, Never fails to deliver them at the proper moment."
"The Buddha, toward all sentient beings, With compassion, never abandons them;
Thinking to rescue them from their suffering and hardship, He is like a mother cow following her calf.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
“Go outside the assembly and give this upper robe to the merchant’s wife, Śrīmatī Gautamī; have her put it on and come here to listen to the Dharma.”

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, went at once to that place, covered [the body] with his robe, and brought him to the Buddha’s presence; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew and sat to one side.

The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, observed their faculties and dispositions and taught the Dharma accordingly, causing them to realize and awaken to the principle of the Four Noble Truths. With the vajra-pestle of wisdom, he shattered the twenty kinds of peaks of the mountain of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (the view of a self-existent body), whereby they attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
Having attained the fruit, she rose from her seat, joined her palms toward the Buddha, and marveled at this unprecedented occurrence, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Out of your compassion, I pray that you will grant me permission to renounce worldly life and leave the home for the sake of the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya, becoming a bhikṣuṇī and practicing the holy life."
The Blessed One, having understood this, entrusted her to Mahāprajāpatī.
Having received her, she immediately caused her to go forth and conferred full ordination upon her, instructing her in the Vinaya and teaching her according to the Dharma.

He immediately exerted himself with single-minded diligence and without weariness; observing and knowing that the five destinies revolve without ceasing, and that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and ultimately end in destruction, he severed the delusions of the three realms and shattered the wheel of the five destinies. He realized the fruit of Arhatship, becoming endowed with the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). He attained the knowledge of reality as it is:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."

The mind is free from obstruction, like a hand waving through space; whether cut by a blade or anointed with fragrance, neither love nor hatred arises. Viewing gold and earth as equal and without distinction, one completely renounces all fame and profit, such that Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas pay him homage.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my disciples, the bhikṣuṇīs, Kṣemā Gautamī is foremost in the mastery of the Vinaya.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard the Buddha’s pronouncement, a group of them went to Kṣemā Gautamī to listen to her teaching of the Dharma.

At that time, Gopikā, wishing to inspire a sense of weary detachment in the bhikṣuṇīs, proceeded to recount the karmic causes and conditions of her past lives; having heard this, the bhikṣuṇīs went and related the matter in detail to the bhikṣus.

Later, at another time, Śrīmatī Gautamī came to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet. When the bhikṣus saw her, they whispered to one another about her karmic conditions. After Śrīmatī Gautamī had paid homage at the Buddha’s feet and taken her leave, she departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the situation], intentionally asked Ānanda:
"What is it that these bhikṣus are whispering to one another?
Then Ānanda informed the Buddha of the circumstances, and the Buddha said to Ānanda:

“The karmic retribution of sentient beings is inconceivable; the entire world is created by the mind. All things arise from karma and abide in dependence upon karma; whatever actions one performs for oneself, one shall surely receive their retribution.”
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One, what karma did this Śyāmāvatī previously commit?"

Her husband died from the bite of a snake; one son was killed by a jackal, and another drowned. Her parents and kinsmen were all struck by lightning. Consuming her own sons’ flesh, she became mentally deranged and insane. Wandering gradually, she came to the presence of the Buddha, where she went forth and received full ordination within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya. Having severed all afflictions, she realized arhatship and received a prediction from the Buddha that she would be foremost among the bhikṣuṇīs in upholding the Vinaya.
The Buddha said: "O bhikṣus, you should know!

Because of the karma created by this nun in the past, when the retribution ripens, it must be experienced by her alone; it is not the external four great elements, and so forth. He then spoke a verse, as detailed elsewhere.
"Listen attentively, you bhikṣus.

Long ago, in a certain village, there lived an elder who was immensely wealthy and possessed great riches. After he had been married for a long time, he remained entirely without offspring, and his heart was filled with anxiety and distress:
'I possess vast wealth, yet I have no heir; when I pass away, it will all be confiscated by the government.'"
The wife asked,
"What is your worry?
The husband answered her with the facts of the matter, and the wife thought to herself:
"I do not yet know whether it is because my husband’s merit is meager or that I myself lack fortune that no offspring have been born.
Is it not possible that my husband has conceived a different feeling toward me and sought another wife? He stood before me with his palms against his cheeks and spoke at length of his grief."
"I ought to go myself; there is no need to trouble another to send me.
She said to her husband, "I have committed evil karma and cannot conceive a child. You should seek another wife, for then a son or daughter shall be born."
He replied, "O noble sir! Have you not heard?

When a household has two wives, there is no way to drink even cold water with their parched grain; they are constantly engaged in quarreling and strife within the house, harassing one another without ceasing."
The wife feigned affection and replied, "Noble son! You should bring her here to marry.
If her age and appearance are similar to my sister's, I shall look upon her as I do my sister; if she resembles my daughter, I shall care for her as I do my daughter."
Upon hearing these words, he then sought a wife once more.
In another village there was an elder who had a daughter and two sons; when the girl had grown up, both her parents passed away.
The man then went to his two younger brothers and requested their sister as his wife; they granted him her hand, and with great ceremony they were married.

It is the nature of things that when one obtains a new wife, one forgets the old and no longer thinks of the former spouse. The elder wife’s womb had long been afflicted by a malignant ailment such that she could not bear children. Seeing her husband cast her aside, she was overcome with extreme jealousy; consequently, her illness was cured and she immediately became pregnant.
She reported to her husband, saying, "I am now pregnant; you should rejoice.
Her husband said:
"O noble one! If you should have a son, after my death he may become the successor and take over as the master of the household.
The wife said:
"It is exactly as you have said.
If your second wife had not used medicine to cause my miscarriage, this would certainly not have happened.
The husband said:
"O Worthy One! I told you before:
'If a household has two wives, they will certainly cause each other distress.'"
"You have spoken these words prematurely for no reason," she said,
and the wife remained silent.
When the months were complete and she gave birth to a son, the mother thought to herself:
"This child has fortunately been born through a fortunate karmic connection; he will surely be harmed by his stepmother. I shall now entrust him to her to raise as her son.
Having thought this, he said to the stepmother:
"Younger sister!..."
"I shall raise this child together with you; let us both treat him as our own son without any difference in feeling.
He replied, "A most excellent thing."
Thus they raised him together, but before long, a malicious intent arose within her, and she thought to herself:
"This is not my son; how could he ever succeed our family? If he grows up, his mother will become the lady and he will be the master, while I shall undoubtedly be reduced to a servant."
"What is the use of nourishing an enemy?
You should kill me as soon as possible.

Having conceived this evil thought, it was like adding fuel to a fire, causing its flames to blaze even more fiercely; his harboring of such poisonous and wicked intent was likewise so. He then used a bamboo splinter to pierce the child's throat. The child suffered excruciating pain and cried out in extreme agony, asking his stepmother:
"Why, child, are you weeping? He replied, "I do not know."

The mother immediately took him in her arms, comforting and patting him with pity; however, the child’s suffering intensified as he wept even more. She then placed the breast at his mouth, only then noticing the bamboo splinter and hurriedly pulling it out; because of this, the child died instantly.
The mother, consumed by intense anguish, wept and wailed, beating her breast and crying out; when relatives and neighbors gathered and asked the reason for this, she replied:
"My son’s stepmother was jealous and ended his life with the bitter agony of piercing his mouth with bamboo splinters."
Upon hearing this, all the relatives and neighbors gathered in astonishment and asked,
"For what reason are you weeping with tears streaming down?
She answered them fully regarding the matter, and people from near and far assembled together, all expressing their indignation toward the stepmother and saying:
"The child has done no wrong; for what reason do you kill him so cruelly?
Having heard this, she beat her breast and made a vow:

"If I have killed this child out of a jealous heart, may my husband die from the bite of a venomous snake; may one son be harmed by a jackal and another drown; may my parents and kinsmen all be struck by lightning; and may I eat my children's flesh, my mind deranged and insane, wandering about naked with no awareness."
"O bhikṣus, what do you think?
Was that elder’s later wife anyone else?
She was none other than this Śyāmāvatī."

Due to her extremely malicious intent in the past, she made a solemn vow to kill another’s son; because of this karma, her husband was bitten by a snake, one son was killed by a jackal, and another son died by drowning. Her parents and kinsmen were all struck by lightning, and she herself, having eaten her own son’s flesh, became mentally deranged and insane, wandering away naked without any awareness.
"Furthermore, monks!

In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this Śroṇakoṭīviṃśā went forth as a nun under that Buddha’s Dharma; she practiced the holy life until the end of her life, yet she attained nothing through realization."
Relying upon a single nun as her *upādhyāyī*— who was foremost in upholding the Vinaya within that Buddha’s teaching and had also received a prophecy from that Blessed One—
the emaciated Gautamī made this aspiration at the time of her death:

"By whatever roots of virtue I have cultivated through practicing the holy life for as long as I live within the teaching of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One, may I, just as the Buddha Kāśyapa prophesied to the young brahmin, attain perfect awakening in a future age when the human lifespan is one hundred years, and be named Śākyamuni."

"I wish to go forth in the Dharma of that Tathāgata, sever all afflictions, and realize arhatship; just as Kāśyapa Buddha declared my upādhyāya to be foremost among nuns in upholding the Vinaya, may I likewise receive the Buddha’s prediction that I am foremost in upholding the Vinaya."
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Sir!
What karma did those parents previously commit that they all met with a lightning strike?”
What sin did he commit to be bitten by a venomous snake?
What fault did the two sons commit,
that one was harmed by a jackal and the other perished by drowning?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Each performs their own karma, and all reach full maturation, as explained at length previously.
You bhikṣus, listen with a single-minded focus!"

In this Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, complete with the ten titles, at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near Vārāṇasī.

At that time, there was in this city an elder who was immensely wealthy and possessed great riches. Not far from the city, he built a residence on the opposite bank of a river; monks from all quarters came and stayed there. The elder entrusted his wealth to the villagers, instructing them to engage in trade and commerce with it.
At that time, there was a man who three times took wealth and lost it each time. The elder summoned him and asked:
"You lack wisdom; you have taken wealth three times and lost it on every occasion."
"If you do not return me to him, I will not let you go back. He replied,
"O Householder!"

"Furthermore, we allow you one more opportunity to engage in trade with this wealth; if it is not returned in its entirety, both husband and wife along with our two children shall be forfeited as slaves.
Thereupon, they drew up a formal contract, and the elder brother gave him the money.
The wealth was once again lost and dissipated; the elder then took his wife, son, and himself to serve as temple attendants (*śrāmaṇera*) residing within the city.
Every day they crossed the river to provide for the monastery: he would personally cook the rice, while his wife and two sons prepared various other flavors and dishes.

At that time, there was an Arhat bhikṣu who served as the monastery’s overseer. It happened that it was raining, and the river had overflowed its banks; thus, the husband, wife, and son all failed to arrive. The Arhat, wondering why they had not come, went to them and said:
"The time for the meal is nearly upon us; for what reason have you not set out?"
"I wish to cause all the members of the Sangha to go without food.
Upon hearing these words, they all gave rise to anger. When their parents and kinsmen heard this, they cursed, saying:
"That man has done nothing to them, yet he oppresses them so harshly; why does he not meet death by a bolt of lightning?"
When he had spoken these words, "This man came along this road; why was he not bitten to death by a venomous snake?
another son replied:
"Why did you not die by drowning? Another son said,
"Why were you not killed by a jackal?"
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor other thoughts. Was the attendant of that time someone else? He was none other than this husband and wife.

Those who were their parents are the ones who died by lightning; he who was the husband at that time is the one bitten by the snake; and those two sons of that time are the one who drowned and the one killed by the jackal."
All of these have received this retribution because, in the past, they harbored malice toward arhats and uttered coarse and evil speech. You bhikṣus!
For this reason, I constantly proclaim that black karma yields black retribution, white karma yields white retribution, and mixed karma yields mixed retribution.
"You all should diligently cultivate pure deeds and abandon dark and mixed deeds.

When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they were all greatly rejoiced; with faith and acceptance, they took it to heart and practiced accordingly. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took their leave, and departed.
The setting is the same as before.

At that time, the foolish and wicked Ajātaśatru slaughtered all the Śākya sons without cause; the Śākya daughters—along with their honored relatives, brothers, sisters, and husbands—all perished. Each harboring grief and suffering, they came to the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha to seek ordination.

Having gone forth, it was as if the ringing of a bell; his anxious thoughts gradually subsided. However, later, because he was entangled by desire, his afflictions flared up again and could not be restrained.
As the World-Honored One said:
"A great black venomous snake has five faults."
What are the five?
First, being prone to anger;
second, harboring resentment.
Third, enmity; fourth, ingratitude; fifth, malice.
Women are likewise.
They harbor much resentment, bear many grudges, lack gratitude, and are maliciously poisonous.
As for the poison of women, it refers to those of a certain class whose minds are heavily stained by lustful desire.
Then the Śākya bhikṣuṇīs gathered together for discussion and went to the place where the bhikṣuṇī Pūraṇā was. Having arrived, they prostrated themselves, sat to one side, and said:
"Noble Lady!..."
"The affliction of the desire-mind is truly difficult to restrain; it constantly torments women—how can it be stopped?
She replied, "Sister!"
"What further do you intend to do?

You youths should abandon the precepts and seek out young male merchants who possess great wealth; by engaging with them, your afflictions and lustful desires will naturally cease. If I were a youth, I would go with you."
Having heard this, the nuns prostrated at her feet and returned, whereupon they deliberated further among themselves: "Sisters!
Since the Venerable Tullānanda has spoken thus, how do we intend to provide a dwelling for her?"
Some said: "Tulānandā’s words are most excellent; we should go and investigate the matter. Others said:
"Sisters! It is extremely rare for women to obtain ordination within the well-expounded Dharma of the Buddha; you should go and inquire of the noble Śrī-Gautamī."
They all replied, “So be it.
They immediately went together to him, prostrated at his feet, and said:
“Noble One! The affliction of sensual desire is truly difficult to restrain; it constantly torments women. By what skillful means can we bring it to a halt? She replied:
"Sisters! Do not speak the name of desire. Why is that?
Its flavor is extremely slight, while its faults are exceedingly many.
As the Blessed One has said:
"All wise people know that there are five disadvantages in the matter of sexual desire; therefore, they should not engage in it."
What are the five? First, one contemplates that sensual desires have little flavor and many faults, and are constantly accompanied by manifold sufferings;
second, at the time of indulging in desire, one is perpetually bound and fettered.
Third, those who indulge in sensual desires are never satisfied;
fourth, those who indulge in sensual desires commit no evil that they will not do;

fifth, regarding the objects of desire, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, the assembly of Śrāvakas, and all superior persons who have attained right view, have explained the faults of desire through immeasurable means; therefore, the wise should not practice desire.
Furthermore, the wise person knows that there are five benefits to going forth from the household life. What are these five?
First, the merit of going forth is one's own personal benefit, not shared with others; therefore, the wise person should seek to go forth.

Second, one should know for oneself that while previously a lowly person driven by others, after having left the household life, one receives offerings, prostrations, and praise from others; therefore, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
Third, when life ends here, one shall be reborn in the heavens and remain free from the three evil realms; therefore, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
Fourth, by relinquishing worldly attachments, one departs from birth and death and shall attain the secure, unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*; therefore, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
"Fifth, one will always be praised by the Buddhas, the assembly of śrāvakas, and all superior persons; for this reason, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
You all should contemplate these benefits and, with a sincere heart, cast off the worldly nets to seek great merit."
"You sisters! Do you wish to hear of the faults and afflictions associated with my indulgence in sensual desire in previous lives,
or those associated with the suffering of indulging in sensual desire in this present life?"
The nuns replied, "Let us set aside matters of past lives; we pray that you will speak of this present life.
Thereupon, Śrī-Gautamī proceeded to relate:

"From birth until now, I have lost both my parents; my husband and son have died; furthermore, I ate the flesh of my own son and entered a tomb alive; I have become insane and deluded"—thus she spoke in succession.
Upon hearing this, all the nuns were filled with sorrow and fear, their hair standing on end; they then listened attentively and gazed upon the face of Śrī-Gautamī.

At that time, Gautamī observed their faculties and dispositions and taught the Dharma accordingly, causing them to realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard the Dharma, they attained the fruit of stream-entry, as described in detail above.
Having attained the fruit, she said to Pāṇḍulohitakā Gautamī:
"I was nearly lost; I had been cast by Utpalā Nandā into the mire of desire, where I would have sunk forever into birth and death."
Śrī-Gautamī asked, “What did he do?
She then related everything as above, and [Gautamī] replied:
"Sisters! Do you know what she intends to do?
Because she engaged in evil conduct and brought ruin upon the Buddha-dharma, the nuns of few desires all felt mutual resentment and shame.
"What is it for a bhikṣuṇī to cause another to abandon the training and return to lay life?
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī should not instruct another to abandon their precepts and encourage them to return to lay life; if she so encourages them, she commits a thullaccaya offense."
The setting was as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who reviled a bhikṣu; the bhikṣu, feeling ashamed, remained silent.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī must not revile a bhikṣu; if she does so, she commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma (vinayātikrama).
Just as a bhikṣuṇī must not revile a bhikṣu, likewise she must also not revile a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī."
"In this manner, the three lower assemblies must each keep their heads bowed and must not revile the five assemblies;
all [who do so] incur an offense against the Dharma. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 30. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.

The sixth section, seventh sub-section, is summarized in a verse as follows:
A bhikṣuṇī should not walk in front [of a bhikṣu]; upon seeing a bhikṣu, she should rise in respect;
she should sit on a seat that is half-a-step lower than the bhikṣu-saṃgha; and if she returns to lay life, there is no basis for questioning her.
The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was staying at the Eastern Grove, the residence of Mṛgāramātṛ; during the morning mealtime, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
The nun Tullanandā was also begging for alms; seeing Mahākāśyapa from afar, she thought to herself:
"I should now deal with this foolish man."
When Kāśyapa arrived at the house in due order, Pūtanā entered it first and stood behind the door-panel.
When Kāśyapa approached, she said to him: "Noble One!"
"You should pass by my house, but there is no cooked food.
The Venerable One then departed.
Having spoken these words, he went to another house; when Kāśyapa arrived, he told him the same thing as before.
Thus it was passed on from one house to another until many families had heard these words and were filled with wonder and suspicion.
If an Arhat does not observe beforehand, he will not know what has occurred; he must then enter meditative concentration to observe who is troubling him.
Seeing the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, he said to her:
"Sister! You have committed no fault;
rather, it was the venerable Ānanda who committed this transgression by insistently requesting the World-Honored One to allow such women of evil conduct to go forth and receive full ordination."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:
"Because bhikṣuṇīs have many faults and dangers, a bhikṣuṇī should not walk ahead of a bhikṣu at the place where alms are being sought."
Having had this thought, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Kāśyapa has spoken well on this matter; therefore, I now decree that among the bhikṣuṇīs, a bhikṣuṇī shall not go ahead of a bhikṣu when they are begging for alms."
The bhikṣuṇīs then did not dare to go about, and because of this, it became difficult to obtain alms.
They told the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Where the bhikṣus beg for alms, the bhikṣuṇīs should avoid those places and proceed elsewhere."
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Pūraṇa-dhanadā was preaching the Dharma in the midst of an assembly of countless hundreds of thousands of people.
Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa arrived there; when the assembly saw him, they all rose, but Pūraṇa-dhanadā remained seated without moving.
The people then said to Pūrṇa Nanda: "Venerable One!
Mahākāśyapa is revered by both humans and devas; when we saw him from afar, we all rose in awe. Yet you, Venerable One, remained seated without moving—this was most improper."

She replied, "He was originally a follower of the heterodox paths, extremely foolish and dull-witted, who came to leave the household life. I am a daughter of the Śākya clan who left the household life under the Buddha; I have mastered the Tripiṭaka and am skilled in preaching the Dharma, harmonizing with the ultimate truth so that my discourse is without impediment. How could it be appropriate for me to see him rise from his seat?"
When the assembly heard this, they all expressed their censure and disapproval.
The bhikṣus reported these circumstances to the Buddha, who said:
"The faithful householders, brahmins, and others have rightly censured you. From this day forward, when a bhikṣuṇī sees a bhikṣu from a distance, she should rise from her seat."
"If anyone violates this, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

As the Blessed One had spoken thus regarding seeing a bhikṣu rise from his seat, at a later time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā was expounding the essential points of the Dharma for the great assembly at the entrance of the monastery.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, while going on his almsround, arrived at the nuns' dwelling. Seeing him from afar, the nun Utpalavarṇā rose quickly from her seat.
As soon as Ānanda arrived, she offered him her seat; he sat down and asked, "Sister!..."
"What teaching have you expounded for the great assembly?
He replied, "I have expounded such-and-such a sutra."
Then the Venerable Ānanda extensively explained its meaning to the great assembly, while the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā stood attentively, listening to his teaching.

Because Ānanda was greedy for the opportunity to preach the Dharma, he did not allow the nun to sit down. Standing for a long time, she grew weary; her body was scorched by the sun, and she fell to the ground in a faint.
At that moment, those among the assembly who lacked faith deliberated together, saying:

"I have heard that the nun Utpalavarṇā is free from all defiled desires; yet now, seeing Ānanda’s handsome appearance and graceful demeanor, she conceived improper thoughts. The fire of lust burned her heart, and she immediately fell to the ground."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus!
The householders and brahmins have rightly spoken of the fault. From this day forward, when a bhikṣuṇī comes to a bhikṣu to listen to the Dharma, she should say: "
"Sisters! Please take your seats.
If a bhikṣu, while preaching the Dharma, forgets to command them to sit, the bhikṣuṇīs should inform him, and they may then sit down as appropriate.
The setting was as before.
As the Blessed One said: "O bhikṣus!..."
Through this parable, you shall be able to understand its meaning; therefore, you should listen to my brief instruction.
That which is called "the rising of the sun" refers to the appearance of the Tathāgata in the world, which is likened to the sun rising and emitting great radiance.
"The various birds all singing" refers to the Dharma-preacher weighing and comparing the principles and meanings.
"The farmers plowing and working" refers to the various other faithful donors and patrons who cultivate the fields of merit and wisdom for my disciples.
"The multitude of thieves has all dispersed" means that the demonic armies and all the non-Buddhists have fled and scattered.

Thus, O Bhikṣus, the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has commanded his Śrāvaka disciples to perform what they ought to do; out of compassion and with a heart of great mercy, he has accomplished their benefit. The task that was to be done by me is now finished. You who are to act may now practice yourselves: you should leave behind clamor and dwell alone in seclusion. Go to the empty forest and stay beneath a tree, or in an empty room, or on a mountain cliff, or in a cave, or upon a heap of straw, or in the open air, or toward a cemetery, or in a charnel ground—using whatever bedding is suitable to sustain the body.
In such places as these, you should straighten your mind and diligently cultivate meditative concentration; do not be negligent, lest you feel regret later on.
This is my instruction to you.

When the bhikṣus had heard what the Buddha spoke, they went to mountain forests, caves, and grottoes—to places of lush woods, clear ponds, flowers, and fruits—and there, with single-minded meditative concentration, they remained far removed from negligence.

The bhikṣuṇīs also frequented the vicinity of the royal garden, whether in the Dark Forest (Andhavana) or in other locations, where they made use of bedding and requisites provided according to the season, sitting cross-legged in meditative silence and contemplation.
Consequently, insects entered her urinary tract, causing her great suffering.
Upon hearing this, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Nuns should not sit in the full lotus posture; when practicing meditative concentration, they should sit in the half-lotus posture."
At that time, the nuns followed the instruction and acted accordingly; however, small insects still entered their bodies and caused them distress. The Buddha said:
"One should first cover oneself with old, tattered clothes or soft leaves, and only then, having applied the half-casualty posture, should one cultivate meditative concentration."
The setting was as before.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One: "Bhadanta!..."
“If a bhikṣuṇī who has renounced the precepts and returned to lay life seeks to go forth again, may she be granted the going forth and full ordination?
The Buddha said, “Upāli! [She may.]”
"Once one has relinquished the precepts, one should not go forth again.
The setting of the occasion was as before.
The Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!

Previously it was established that bhikṣuṇīs are not permitted to interrogate bhikṣus regarding their faults—namely, those concerning broken precepts, broken views, broken deportment, or broken right livelihood. Is there perhaps another circumstance under which bhikṣuṇīs may inquire about the faults of bhikṣus?"
The Buddha told Upāli:
"There is certainly no cause or condition by which bhikṣuṇīs may reprimand bhikṣus for faults or transgressions of the same category as those previously mentioned."
The eighth section of the sixth chapter, summarized in verse, says:
The householder and leftover food; Leftover and touched, not avoiding one another;
Not inquiring into private matters; And the seat for full ordination—these should be known.
The setting was as before.

There was a householder who was very wealthy and possessed great riches; though he had been married for a long time, he had not fathered a son or daughter. Later, when his wealth and property were entirely exhausted, he said to his wife:
"I am now old and unable to seek further wealth; I wish to go to the Jeta Grove to undertake the life of a renunciant."
The wife said, "Noble son!
If you go forth from the home life, upon whom shall I rely? I too shall go forth."
The husband said,
"O virtuous lady!
You may go together with me."
The householder took his wife to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, prostrated at her feet, and said:
"Noble Lady, this is my wife;
she desires to go forth within the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya. I pray that you will compassionately accept her."
"I shall now also go to the Jetavana Grove to seek ordination.
He replied, "Excellent, noble sir!"
That a husband and wife can give rise to such a sublime and wondrous resolve, and both together leave the household life, is a most excellent matter.
As the World-Honored One has said:
"For those who have left the household life, there are five benefits; their merit is boundless and praised by the noble ones."
"The five benefits are as previously explained at length.
You may go now; I shall grant you the going-forth.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī shaved her head.
The elder immediately went to the Jetavana Grove and sought out a bhikṣu to ordain him as a renunciant.
At that time, everyone throughout the city, both far and near, heard of it and said:
