"This elder is truly fortunate to have now gone forth; he shall receive abundant offerings of the four requisites of superior quality."

Later, at another time, he entered the city to beg for alms; his wife, who was also a bhikṣuṇī, came along to beg as well. At that time, there was a famine and it was difficult to obtain anything through begging. He encountered his wife and asked her, "O virtuous one!..."
"How can we survive?
His wife said, "In these times of famine, it is difficult to obtain anything through begging; we struggle painfully to keep ourselves alive."
She then said, "I have now received a great abundance of food and drink offerings; if the Buddha permits, I shall give you half.
The bhikṣuṇī returned to her own quarters and related the matter in detail to the assembly of nuns.
When the nun had heard this, she told the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"If there are bhikṣus who have such bhikṣuṇīs, and the times are such that famine prevails and alms are difficult to obtain, those bhikṣus should give their food to them; do not harbor any doubt about this."

As the Blessed One has said: "If a bhikṣu has such a bhikṣuṇī, and during a time of famine when alms are difficult to obtain, he should give her food without harboring any doubt. Thus, once the bhikṣu had obtained alms-food, he would immediately set aside half for her, and the bhikṣuṇī would constantly come to him to eat.
Then on another day, that bhikṣuṇī obtained food elsewhere and did not come to join them; the bhikṣu thought:
"The bhikṣuṇī must have obtained food elsewhere, which is why she has not come; what is the use of setting aside a portion for her?"
Having reflected thus, she did not distribute any portion.
The next day, the nun came to seek food, and [the other] replied:
"O virtuous one!..."
"Yesterday, because I did not see you coming, I did not prepare food; though there is some now, it has become leftover from the previous night and is defiled by contact, making it unfit for use.
Having heard these words, the nun prostrated at her feet and returned to the nuns' quarters, where she recounted the matter in detail.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, bhikṣus may eat what has been left over by bhikṣuṇīs, and bhikṣuṇīs may eat what has been left over by bhikṣus."
The setting was as before.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, in the midst of the saṃgha, asked a bhikṣuṇī about matters concerning her private parts that were not shared with the monks. Upon hearing this, the nun felt ashamed and stood with her head bowed.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not inquire about the private or intimate matters of a bhikṣuṇī; however, bhikṣuṇīs may certainly inquire among one another."
"If a bhikṣu asks [about this], he commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The bhikṣu then asked about a secret matter concerning their shared precepts; she again felt ashamed. The Buddha said:

"One should have a bhikṣuṇī stand between them before questioning that bhikṣuṇī. She should report the matter to the intermediary bhikṣuṇī, and once the intermediary bhikṣuṇī has heard it, she shall then inform the bhikṣu."
"Because she did not respond to his words out of a slight sense of shame.
The setting was as before.
After the Venerable Śāriputra and others had conferred full ordination upon a bhikṣuṇī, they addressed her with a verse, saying:
“You have fully received the precepts within the most excellent teaching;
you should uphold them with a sincere heart. A body free from obstacles is difficult to obtain.
Those who are upright leave the household life; those who are pure receive full ordination.”
"This is what is spoken by those who speak the truth, that which is known by the Perfectly Awakened One.
When he had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣuṇī’s menses suddenly began to flow. Śāriputra said to her: "Sister!"
"You may rise and depart.
The nun, out of shame, refused to rise; Śāriputra, perceiving the reason for her hesitation, immediately rose and left.
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"Sisters! Having just received full ordination and not yet left the ordination platform, how could it be appropriate to disturb the ācārya, causing him to rise when he should not?
They replied:
"Sisters! He is a great man;

he would not tolerate seeing my vulgar and lowly affairs. You yourselves should know better than to reproach me further. I was sitting crouched before him when my menses suddenly began; how could I have risen and departed?"
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"From now on, when conferring full ordination upon women, do not have them squat; rather, let them sit upon bricks, or upon a seat of grass, or upon a small cushion, because the bodies of women are naturally supple."
The ninth sub-section of the sixth chapter, summarized in verse, says:
A bhikṣu’s surplus bedding and requisites Should be given to a bhikṣuṇī;
A bhikṣuṇī must not step on bridge planks, Nor wear articles intended for personal adornment.
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī was traveling through the countryside with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs. As the sun was about to set, they arrived at the Jeta Grove and had this thought:
"The proper time has already passed and the day is now drawing to a close; there is no leisure to enter the city. We should stay here for the time being and wait until dawn before entering the city."
He then slept on the open ground within the monastery, and his robes were soiled by dust and dirt.
When dawn broke, he thought to himself:
"If I do not pay homage to the Great Master, I will have to return to the city once more."
She immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
Seeing that her robes were stained with dust and dirt, the Buddha, though already knowing the reason, intentionally asked Gautamī:
"For what reason have your robes been stained with dust and dirt?"
He then reported the matter in detail.
At that time, the Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Did you not give the bhikṣus' surplus bedding to the bhikṣuṇīs?"
He replied, "I will not give it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“From this day forward, when bhikṣus make use of leftover bedding and requisites, they should give them to the bhikṣuṇīs; do not harbor any doubt regarding this.

As the Blessed One had said that the bedding should be given to the bhikṣuṇīs, at the time when the bhikṣus were distributing the bedding, they all took the inferior items for themselves and kept the superior ones to give to the bhikṣuṇīs. The Buddha said:
"One should not keep the superior items for the bhikṣuṇīs; rather, one should give them the coarse items. One should provide them with supplies as needed at all times so that they lack nothing.
When food is required, it should be given."
The setting is as before.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having dressed and taken his bowl at the time for the morning meal, entered the city to beg for food.
Then the bhikṣuṇī Pūtanā, coming from outside and wishing to enter her residence, encountered a river in flood. Seeing Kāśyapa upon a wooden bridge, Pūtanā thought to herself:
"This dull-witted fellow may now be disciplined.

He quickly went to the edge of the bridge and stepped firmly upon it; at that moment, Kāśyapa immediately fell into the river, his robes became soaked, his bowl sank to the bottom, and his mendicant’s staff was carried away by the current.
Kāśyapa said, "Sister! You have committed no transgression;

rather, it was the Venerable Ānanda who committed this fault by insistently requesting the World-Honored One to ordain a woman of such evil conduct as you, allowing her to leave the household life and become a bhikṣuṇī within the Buddha-dharma."
Having heard this, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself,
"These faults have arisen because of the bhikṣuṇīs," and he said:
"From this day forward, a bhikṣuṇī should not walk upon a bridge together with a bhikṣu; if she does so, she commits an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

As the Blessed One had thus spoken—that a bhikṣuṇī must not walk upon a bridge together with a bhikṣu—there was at that time a great bridge, secure and vast, yet the bhikṣuṇīs did not dare to walk upon it together [with the bhikṣus]. The Buddha said:
"In this way, one may cross this broad and great bridge together without fault.
The setting is the same as before.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Pūtanā, having dressed and taken her bowl at the time of the morning meal, entered the city to beg for food, and proceeded in order until she reached the residence of Queen Vaidehī.
Upon seeing him, the lady exclaimed,
"Welcome! She immediately prepared a seat for him to sit upon and engaged him in conversation.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā asked Śrīmālā:
"Sister! Why are your hips so broad and your waist so slender?"
He replied, "Noble One! Why must you ask this?"
"I merely bound it with materials to please the King's mind.
The nun said, "I shall now ask you this as a casual inquiry."
He replied, "Noble One, it is coarse because I have wrapped it with material."
The nun said, "Because of this,
all who see these people love one another.
Śrīmālā remained silent.
When the nuns arrived at their residence, they also wore these garments. The other nuns asked, "These are not robes permitted by the Dharma;
how can it be appropriate for nuns to possess them?
They informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"This is not a robe permitted by the Dharma; whoever wears it shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Pūraṇa-dhanadā again saw the lady’s breasts were round and well-proportioned; the dialogue was the same as before, and the lady said:
"I wear a breast-covering garment.

She also saw the lady wearing a breast-supporting garment and a waist-binding garment; whenever Tullānandā saw them, she inquired about them, and each time she was answered in full as above. The nun then learned how to make and wear these garments herself.
The Buddha said:
"None of these are permissible; whoever wears them shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The summary verse for the tenth section of the sixth chapter states:
One should not splash water so as to soil one's clothes; one should not carry a dead fetus;
one should not swallow impurities; and when touching one’s own child, it is not the same as touching another’s.
The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Pūtanā entered the city to beg for alms.
Then Mahākāśyapa was also begging for alms in the city, walking along a canal embankment. Seeing him, Pūtanā thought to herself:
"I should now deal with this foolish man."
He then took a large brick, went quickly to the side, and hurled it from afar into the trench; foul-smelling, filthy water splashed onto his robes.
Kāśyapa said, "You have committed no offense; rather, it was Ānanda who committed this transgression."
He related the matter as above.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the circumstances to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī must not defile a bhikṣu’s robes with foul water; whoever violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
The setting was as before.
At that time, there was a householder who was very wealthy and possessed great riches; not long after he had married his wife, he took his various goods and wealth to travel abroad for trade.
The wife ate fine food and wore exquisite garments; her lustful desire became intense, and she subsequently engaged in secret intercourse with a man, whereby she became pregnant.
After several months had passed, she thought to herself:
"I ought to induce an abortion; if I do not, when my husband arrives, he will surely harm me."
She then miscarried the fetus.
Filled with anxiety and worry, she thought:
"Now that it has been lost, where shall I place it?"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Dhanika entered the house while begging for alms and said,
"O Lady of Excellent Features!
You may give me food from your bowl."
He replied, "Noble one,
you may go; there is no one to give you food, and I am filled with distress."
He replied, "Miaoxiang! Has anyone passed away?"
He replied, “No one has died;
however, I have had a miscarriage and do not know where I should discard it.
He reported this, saying:
“O Subhūṣaṇā! If I were to abandon you, would you be able to constantly provide me with food from alms bowls? She replied:
"I shall give it.
[The other asked: "Can you also give it to my attendant and the administrative official? He replied:
"So be it. He then took the dead fetus in his large alms-bowl and cast it away toward an empty house.
At that time, many profligate men were already gathered inside that house, standing together when they saw him and asked:
“What do you intend to do, you shaven-headed daughter of the Śākyas? She replied,
“It was solely because of you shameless, mad men who consorted with another’s wife that this transgression was committed, causing me to lose my fetus.”
Having heard this, the man reviled them and departed.
On the way, he encountered some bhikṣuṇīs and said to them:
"You sinful creatures!"
"You, the nun Tullānandā, have committed such an evil deed as this—abandoning an embryo.
The nuns remained silent.
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha then reflected thus:
“There are such faults as these in a nun possessing a large alms-bowl; therefore, nuns should not carry a large bowl.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
“Tulānandā has acted contrary to the conduct of a śramaṇa. You should know that nuns must not perform such unlawful acts, and must not carry a large bowl.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī carries a large bowl and performs such an act, she incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
Since the Buddha had thus prescribed that bhikṣuṇīs should not carry large bowls, the bhikṣuṇīs did not know what kind of bowl they should carry.
The Buddha said:
"The small bowl of a bhikṣu is the large bowl of a bhikṣuṇī.
The setting of the occasion was the same as before.

At that time, the nun Gopā placed one drop of the impurity in her mouth and another drop within her private organ; the karmic retribution of sentient beings is inconceivable, and she immediately became pregnant and gave birth to the youth Kāśyapa.
At that time, the nun Guptā did not dare to touch him with her hand,
so the child began to cry. His relatives asked, "Why is the child crying?"
Upon hearing this, the nun remained silent.
The other nuns replied, "The World-Honored One has established a precept forbidding us from touching men; therefore, we did not dare approach him, and for this reason we were weeping."
He replied: "The World-Honored One possesses great compassion; why would he not allow his own son to touch him with his hand?
If the mother does not touch him, how could his life be sustained?"
Upon hearing this, the nun praised it as excellent and went to inform the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who said:
"One may touch one's own child; there is no fault in nursing, holding, or embracing them."
The setting is the same as before.
The Buddha said:

"One's own child should be touched, nurtured, and held," yet women, out of excessive affection, would seize this child and pass him from shoulder to shoulder, competing to hold him; consequently, the child became emaciated.
When his relatives saw this, they asked,
"What is the meaning of such behavior?
He then explained it in detail, whereupon they all joined in censuring him.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Nuns must not touch others' children; if they do so, they commit an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The summary verse for the seventh section says:
Guptā the nun not remaining, saṃkakṣikā, hermaphrodites,
when the *karmavācanā* for a narrow path, a nun selling liquor, the transformation of the faculties,
and not using bone outside the monastery— these should be known as the seventh summary.
The first sub-section of the seventh chapter, summarized in verse, says:
Guptā stayed overnight with her child; the yakṣa deity of Rājagṛha;
giving a garment for the child to tie around its neck; and calling out the name while offering sacrificial food.
The setting is the same as before.
As the Blessed One has said:
"A bhikṣuṇī must not sleep in the same room as a man."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Guptā sent the boy Kāśyapa outside to stay overnight; the child immediately began to cry.
When his relatives heard this, they asked Guptā, "Why did the young boy Kāśyapa cry out in the night?"
The nun remained silent and did not respond.

The other nuns said to her, "The Blessed One has not permitted bhikṣuṇīs to sleep in the same room as a man; it was for this reason that he ordered you to leave, and because of this, you wept through the night."
The relatives said, "The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate; if this young boy does not sleep with his mother, he will surely encounter misfortune.
You should inform the World-Honored One."
The nuns reported this to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"The nun Guptā should request from the Saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) for sleeping in the same room as her son."

One should beg in this manner: after the seat has been spread, the *gandī* struck, and the community of nuns has assembled, Guptā should join her palms and pay homage as appropriate; then, sitting before the senior nun—either upon a grass mat, a brick, or a cushion—she should remain with palms joined and make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha of nuns, listen!
I, the bhikṣuṇī Guptā, have given birth to a son and wish to sleep in the same room as my child.
I now request from the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) for sleeping in the same room as my child.
"I pray that the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha will grant me the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for sleeping in the same room as my son, out of compassion.
Having said this three times, she should then have the nun Gupitā move to a place where she can see but not hear, and one Bhikṣuṇī should perform the *jñapti-karman* as follows:
"Listen, Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha!
This bhikṣuṇī Gupta has given birth to a son.
This Gupta now requests from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of being permitted to sleep in the same room as her son.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha consent; the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha shall now grant Gupta the formal act of being permitted to sleep in the same room as her son.
"Thus it is announced.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī Guptā has given birth to a son of her own.
This Guptā now requests from the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of being permitted to sleep in the same room as her son.
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for Gupitā to sleep in the same room as her son.
If the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha permits Gupitā to sleep in the same room as her son, you should remain silent; if you do not permit it, speak.

"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has completed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of permitting Guptā to sleep in the same room as her son; the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence. Thus do I now uphold this."

"If a bhikṣuṇī has already received the formal act (karmavācanā) from the Saṃgha authorizing her to sleep in the same room as her son, she should indeed sleep in the same room with him; let there be no doubt about this."
Guptā’s fellow nun also stayed with her overnight. The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"A nun who has a son should stay with her son, and not with anyone else."
"If one sleeps together with others, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, Guptā’s son had grown up, yet she still slept together with him. A nun reported this to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If a nun's son has grown up, she should not sleep together with him."
The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.

At that time, on the side of a mountain within this city, there lived a yakṣa deity named Sata, who constantly protected King Bimbisāra, the ladies of the inner palace, the king’s ministers, the high officials, and all the people.

By the power of that merit, the king and all his subjects were entirely at peace and happy; timely and sweet rains fell, causing the crops to flourish; flowers, fruits, springs, and ponds abounded everywhere; and there was never any famine, for food and necessities were easily obtained even by those who begged.
All those śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the solitary, and merchants who came to the kingdom of Magadha were all protected by this yakṣa.
Saudāsa then took a wife from among his own kind and lived with her.

At that time, in the northern kingdom of Gandhāra, there was another yakṣa named Pañcāla who resided there constantly and always provided protection, causing that country to be peaceful, secure, and prosperous, no different in its affairs from the realm of Magadha; at that time, this yakṣa also took a wife from his own kind and lived together with her.

Later, at another time, the yakṣas from various regions gathered together; these two yakṣas were able to express their mutual affection and became close friends, and after taking their leave, each returned to his own dwelling place.

The yakṣa Sata took exquisite flowers and fruits from Magadha and sent them to Pañcāla; he, in turn, sent flowers and fruits produced in the north to Sata. In this manner, they maintained a friendly rapport for a long time.
Furthermore, as they met again through a gathering and rejoiced in their renewed fellowship, Sata said to Pañcāla:
"By what means may we ensure that after our deaths, our descendants shall remain dear to one another and not become estranged?"
The Pañcāla said: "Excellent are these words!
My own intention is the same as yours."
Sāta said, "Now we may form a marriage alliance by mutual exchange of children; if a son or daughter is born to either of our two families, they shall be joined in marriage. He replied:

"So be it. Not long after, Satā’s wife became pregnant; when her months were full, she gave birth to a daughter whose countenance was so upright and dignified that all who saw her loved her. At the time of her birth, the host of yakṣas all rejoiced, and her kinsmen bestowed upon her the name Priyadarśanā (Joyful).
At that time, when Svacchanda heard that a daughter had been born to him, he was filled with great joy and thought to himself:
"Sata Yakṣa is my dear friend; now that he has fathered a daughter, I shall father a son. She will then be my beloved new bride, for whom I can fashion ornaments, necklaces, and garments."
He sent a messenger to deliver it along with a letter that read:
"I have heard that you have given birth to a daughter and am greatly delighted; I now send these garments, which I hope you will graciously accept.
At that time, Sāḍha received the letter and its message, and replied with a letter of his own.

However, since Pañcāla’s intention was solely to obtain a son, before long his wife became pregnant; when the months were complete and she gave birth to a boy, they conferred a name upon him, and as he was the son of Pañcāla, he should be named Pañcika.
At that time, when the yakṣa Sata heard that Pañcāla had fathered a son, he thought to himself: "My friend has fathered a son;
how could this be in vain? I should send him garments and necklaces to express my congratulations. He is surely the husband of my daughter—why should there be any doubt?"
He then composed a letter, saying:

"Hearing that you have given birth to a son, joy and delight fill my heart. I have sent these garments and necklaces as a token of my congratulations; I hope you will accept them so that my good wishes may not be in vain."
Having read the letter, he replied with a letter of his own, saying:
"Our agreement to form a kinship has now been fulfilled; let us each wait until our children have reached maturity before we arrange the marriage."

At that time, the yakṣī Satā became pregnant again. Then, all the mountains let out sounds like the trumpeting of great elephants; when the full moon arrived and she gave birth, the mountains roared once more. Her kinsmen deliberated, saying:
"On the day this child was conceived and on the day he was born, the mountains all resounded with roars. Since he is the son of Satā, he should be named Satagiri."
Once he had grown up, his father passed away, and he became the head of the household. At that time, when Nandika had reached adulthood, he said to his younger brother:
"I now wish to travel to Rājagṛha; there are currently many people who have given birth to sons and daughters, all of whom I intend to take and eat."
The younger brother said, "Sister!

I have heard that my father always protected the lord of this city and the multitude of people, enabling them to dwell in peace and happiness, free from all distress and affliction. I should now increase my own guard; for this is the domain I am charged with defending, and if there are others who would cause harm, I must shield and protect it."
"How can you now give rise to such an evil thought?
You ought to eliminate this intention.

Nevertheless, because the yakṣī was driven by the force of habitual tendencies from having made evil and perverse vows in her previous life, she again spoke to her younger brother about the matter as before.
The younger brother, knowing that his sister’s intent was difficult to change or turn back, thought to himself:

"I am not able by my own power to ward off her evil intention; however, while our father was still alive, she was promised in marriage to another. Therefore, I should now proceed with the marriage rites."
He then immediately drafted a letter for the yakṣa Pañcāla, saying:
"My sister Praharṣiṇī has reached full maturity; you should take her as your kin and come here at once."
Having received the letter, he performed the grand ceremonies and went to Rājagṛha to take a wife and return home.
After he had been in his native city for some time, he became harmonious with his husband in both affection and purpose, and spoke these words:
"Virtuous one, you should know!..."
"I intend to seize and eat all the sons and daughters currently born among the people within the city of Rājagṛha.
He replied, "O worthy one!"

All those places are the residences of your own kin; since you would even wish to prevent others from coming and causing them harm, how can you now suddenly harbor such cruel intentions and give rise to these evil thoughts?
"Do not speak of this again.
Due to the power of the habitual tendencies from a wrong vow made in his previous life, he uttered a sound of resentment and remained silent out of anger.
Later, at another time, he begot a son; in this manner, he successively fathered five hundred more, the youngest of whom was named Priyaputra (Beloved Son).

At that time, the five hundred sons had attained full maturity and influence; relying on their power and strength, the mother wished to commit unrighteous acts. Although her husband repeatedly exhorted and instructed her, she ultimately refused to accept his words. Knowing her mind, the husband remained silent.
At that time, Nandika would follow the comings and goings within the city of Rājagṛha, devouring the sons and daughters born to the people present there.
When the city had thus lost its children, all the inhabitants together addressed the king:
"Our sons and daughters have all been stolen away; we do not know who is committing this great harm."
"In the midst of such extreme agony and distress, how can it be dispelled?
We pray that Your Majesty, out of compassion, will graciously investigate this.
The King immediately issued an edict for all streets and thoroughfares and commanded soldiers to guard and patrol the four city gates.
At that time, the soldiers were also stolen away; though they noticed fewer men each day, they did not know where they had gone.
Those women who were pregnant were likewise all stolen and taken to other places.
At that time, a great calamity broke out in the city of Rājagṛha, and the king’s ministers and officials addressed the Great King again, saying:
"A great disaster has now arisen within this kingdom," and they related the aforementioned matters in detail.
Upon hearing this, the king was struck with alarm and wonder; he immediately summoned a diviner and asked him the reason for it.
The diviner replied, "This calamity is entirely the work of yakṣas. You should quickly prepare various exquisite foods and drinks to perform a sacrificial offering."
The king issued a clear decree and beat the drums to proclaim it to all people, saying:

"Whether host or guest, everyone within my realm must prepare food, drink, incense, and flowers; sweep and sprinkle the streets, roads, city walls, and villages; and provide various adornments such as musical instruments, sounds of drums, bells, and banners."

At that time, the people of Rājagṛha, having received the king’s decree, each with a devoted mind prepared food, drink, incense, flowers, and other offerings; they adorned the streets like the Garden of Joy (Nandana), performing sacrifices everywhere.
Although they prepared defenses with great effort, calamities were not averted; they remained in a state of suffering, distress, and anxiety, not knowing what to do.
At that time, the deity who protected the city of Rājagṛha appeared in their dreams and said to them:
"All of you, men and women alike, are being devoured by the yakṣa Nandika. You should go to the place of the World-Honored One; the Buddha shall subdue all these misfortunes and sufferings."
The people replied to the goddess, "Since she has taken our sons and daughters to serve as food, she is a wicked yakṣa; why should she be named 'Joyful'?
For this reason, all the people called her the Yakṣī Hārītī.
When the people of Rājagṛha heard of this matter, they all went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"World-Honored One!
This yakṣī Hārītī has long been causing harm to the multitude of people residing in Rājagṛha."

"We harbored no ill intentions toward them previously; however, they conceived a heart of malice and harm toward us, stealing away all the sons and daughters born to us to serve as their food and drink."
"We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for us, will act as our subduer.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted their request by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted their request, they prostrated at his feet, took their leave, and departed.

When the following morning arrived, the Buddha dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for alms. Having completed his sequential begging round, he returned to his original location; when he had finished his meal, he proceeded to the dwelling place of the yakṣa Hārītī.
At that time, the yakṣī had gone out and was away, leaving her youngest son, Priyaputra, at home; the World-Honored One then covered him with his alms-bowl.
Through the Tathāgata’s majestic power, the elder brothers could not see the younger brother, while the younger brother saw all the elder brothers.
At that time, the yakṣī returned to her dwelling and, not seeing the young child, was seized with great alarm and began searching everywhere; she also asked her other sons, "Where is my beloved son?"
They replied, "We have not seen them at all.

Thereupon, they beat their breasts and wept with tears streaming down; their lips and mouths grew parched and their spirits became disoriented. With hearts pierced by intense grief, they hurried toward the royal city, searching everywhere through the various wards, main thoroughfares, gardens, ponds, celestial shrines, spirit halls, guesthouses, and empty rooms, yet they could not find them anywhere.
The pain became even more excruciating, and he immediately fell into a state of madness; stripping off his clothes, he wailed aloud, crying out:
"My beloved son! Where are you now?"

He then went outside the city and traveled through the villages and great settlements, searching everywhere but failing to find him. He went to the four quarters and even to the four oceans, yet he was nowhere to be seen. With his hair disheveled and body naked, he rolled upon the ground, crawling on his elbows and knees, and sitting in a crouching posture. In this manner, he gradually traveled to Jambudvīpa, the seven Great Black Mountains, the seven Great Golden Mountains, the seven Great Snow Mountains, Lake Anavatapta, and Mount Gandhamādana, searching everywhere but finding him not; his heart was filled with such bitter anguish that his breath was choked and could not pass.
He then went to the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha, the western continent of Aparagodānīya, and the northern continent of Uttarakuru, yet he did not see them there either.

He proceeded to the Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma—thus, in all sixteen great hells, he likewise did not see them.

Again, he went to Mount Sumeru, first ascending the lowest terrace, then the second and third; passing directly through the palace of the Muchilinda Heaven, he reached the summit of Mount Sumeru. He first entered the Caitraratha Grove, then the Miśrakāvana, the Pāruṣyaka, and the Nandana groves, but could not find him anywhere. He then proceeded to the foot of the Pārijāta tree and even into the Sudharmā Hall.
As he was entering the city of Sudarśana, intending to enter Śakra’s most excellent palace, there was the great deity Vajrapāṇi, who stood guarding the gate together with immeasurable yakṣas.
Upon seeing him enter, he was immediately driven out beyond the city of Sudarśana; his grief became even more intense.
Reaching the realm of the Tuṣita devas, he threw himself down from a great rock onto the ground, wailing and weeping in lamentation.
He addressed him, saying: "Great General!
My young son, my beloved child, has been stolen away by another; I know not where he may be."
"I pray that you will grant me this.
The deity Bahudhātī said, "Sister!"
"You need not worry or distress yourself to the point of going mad. For now, observe those who frequent your household; who comes to dwell there during the daytime?
He replied, "Great General!"
"The śramaṇa Gautama resides there.
He replied, "If that is so, you should go quickly to the presence of that Blessed One and take refuge in him; he will cause you to see your beloved son."
Upon hearing these words, his heart was filled with joy; it was as if he had been reborn after death and returned to his original place.

From afar, he beheld the World-Honored One, whose body was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, radiant and brilliant, surpassing the thousandfold light of the sun like a mountain of exquisite jewels. Deep longing arose within him and all his distress was dispelled, his heart feeling as if he had finally obtained a son.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
I have been separated from my young son for a long time; I only pray that, out of your compassion, you will allow me to see him.”
The Buddha asked the yakṣiṇī Hāritī,
"How many sons do you have? She replied:
"I have five hundred sons. The Buddha said, "Hāritī!"
"If one among these five hundred sons were missing, what would be the cause for suffering? He replied,
"World-Honored One!
"If I do not see my beloved child today, I shall surely vomit hot blood and meet my end.
The Buddha said, "Hāritī!"
"Among five hundred sons, not even one was seen to undergo such suffering; how much less so for another's only son whom you stole and ate—how could this not be suffering?
He replied, "This suffering is many times greater than mine."
The Buddha said, "Hāritī!
Since you clearly understand the suffering of being separated from those one loves, why do you eat the children of others?"
He replied, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will instruct me.
The Buddha said:
“Hārītī! You may accept my precepts;
I grant fearlessness to all the people currently present in the city of Rājagṛha.
If you can do this, you shall rise from this seat and see your beloved child.”
He replied: "World-Honored One!
From this day forward, in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions, I shall grant fearlessness to all people currently residing within the city of Rājagṛha."

After these words were spoken, the Buddha caused her to see her beloved child. At that time, Hāritī took refuge in the Tathāgata and requested to receive the precepts; consequently, the multitude of people within the city all attained peace and happiness, being freed from all sorrows and afflictions.
Then Hāritī Mātṛkā received the three refuges and the five precepts from the Buddha—ranging from not killing to not drinking alcohol—and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
“From this day forward, when I and my children have departed, what shall we eat?
The Buddha said,
“O virtuous woman!”

"You need not worry. Among all my śrāvaka disciples in Jambudvīpa, whenever they partake of their meals, they shall set aside food for sentient beings and provide a single dish at the end of the meal; they will call out your name and those of your sons, ensuring that you all eat your fill and never suffer from hunger."

Furthermore, if there are other sentient beings currently existing, as well as various ghosts and spirits dwelling in the mountains, rivers, and seas who ought to eat, he directs his mind toward them all so that they are completely satisfied.
The Buddha said to Hāritī:

"Furthermore, I now entrust you with this: within my Dharma, in all monasteries and dwelling places of monks and nuns, you and your children must always, day and night, diligently protect them with a focused mind, ensuring they do not suffer decline and that they may attain peace and happiness."
"Until my Dharma has ceased to exist, you should act in this manner within Jambudvīpa.

When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, the five hundred sons of Hāritī, along with the assembly of yakṣas who had gathered there, were all greatly rejoiced; they prostrated themselves in worship and respectfully set out to practice his instructions.
When the bhikṣus had heard the Buddha’s teaching, they were all filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
“What karma did Hāritī commit in the past that she gave birth to five hundred sons who suck the vital energy of humans and devour the children born of those in Rājagṛha?”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
This yakṣiṇī and the people of this city must themselves experience the results of the karma they previously created.”

“O Bhikṣus! In the distant past, there was a cowherd in the city of Rājagṛha who, shortly after marrying his wife, became pregnant. At that time, no Buddha had appeared; rather, a Pratyekabuddha had manifested in the world. Delighting in solitary seclusion, he made use of simple and modest bedding and requisites, being the sole field of merit in the world.

At that time, this Pratyekabuddha was traveling through the human world and arrived at Rājagṛha. A great assembly was being prepared; five hundred people, each having adorned themselves, all carrying food and drink and bringing musical instruments, went together to the Fragrant Garden.
Along the way, they encountered a pregnant cowherd girl carrying jars of curd and whey, and the men said to her: "Sister!
Come dance with us and enjoy our merriment."
Upon seeing them calling out to one another, the woman immediately conceived a lustful desire; she raised her eyes and arched her brows, and they danced together.
Because of her exhaustion, she subsequently miscarried.

All the people of the city went toward the garden, while the woman, filled with grief and distress, stood with her cheek pressed against her palm; she then purchased five hundred mangoes for a portion of curdled milk.

At that time, the Pratyekabuddha came to the woman's side; seeing from afar his body and mind in tranquil composure and his dignified, orderly gait as he walked along the road, she felt a sense of veneration and respect. She immediately approached him, prostrated at his feet, and offered fragrant, delicious fruits to the Noble One.

The Pratyekabuddhas, who convert others solely through their physical presence and do not preach with their speech, desired to benefit that woman; thus, like a great king of geese spreading its two wings, they ascended into the void and manifested various supernatural transformations.
When ordinary people witness such supernatural powers, their hearts turn toward them like a great tree collapsing; they throw themselves to the ground, join their palms, and make this vow:

"By the merit of the offerings I have now made to this true field of merit, may I be reborn in the city of Rājagṛha in the future; and among the men and women currently born within that city, I shall devour them all."
"O bhikṣus, what do you think? Was that cowherd girl anyone else? She was none other than the yakṣiṇī Hārītī.

Because she formerly offered five hundred āmra fruits to a pratyekabuddha while making an evil vow, she has now been born as a yakṣiṇī in Rājagṛha, giving birth to five hundred sons who suck the vital essence of humans and devour all the boys and girls within the city."
"O bhikṣus! I have always proclaimed:
black karma has black retribution; mixed karma has mixed retribution; white karma has white retribution."
"You all should diligently cultivate white karma and remain free from black and mixed karma; even unto its fruition, it shall be experienced by each person for themselves.
When the bhikṣus had heard the Buddha’s teaching, their hearts were filled with great joy; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took their leave, and departed.
The setting is the same as before.

At that time, after Hāritī had received the three refuges and the five precepts from the Tathāgata, she was subsequently afflicted by various other yakṣas who caused her misfortune; she therefore offered her children to the community of monks.
Whenever they saw a bhikṣu going out for alms, they would all transform themselves into small children and follow behind him.
When the women of Rājagṛha saw them, they mostly felt pity and affection, coming forward to embrace them; at that moment, the children would vanish.
Then the women asked the bhikṣu, "Whose son is this? He replied:
“Hāritī’s son! The woman replied,
“Is this the son born of that Yakṣa who is a hateful enemy and a poisoner?”
The bhikṣus replied, "They have all already abandoned their malicious intent; they are giving these to us as an offering because the yakṣas were causing us calamities."
The women thought: "If even a yakṣī can abandon her evil intent and offer up her son as a gift, why should we, who have many sons, not do the same?"
She then offered her son and daughter to the Saṃgha, but the Saṃgha would not accept them.
The woman said, "Noble ones!..."
"If he was even able to accept the daughter of a yakṣa who had brought him poison and harm, why does he not accept our sons and daughters?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"He should accept them."
Although the bhikṣus received [the boy] in accordance with the instruction, they did not guard him, allowing him to wander about at will according to his own inclination.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a male child is offered to the Saṃgha, one bhikṣu shall receive him and, using a fragment of an old *kāṣāya* robe, tie it upon his head to guard him."
"If they offer much, you may accept it as you wish from those of superior, middling, or inferior rank; guard it as before and do not harbor any doubt.
At that time, the parents brought the goods back to redeem them, but the bhikṣus would not accept them. The Buddha said, "You should accept them."

Later, she felt a sense of affection and attachment, and wishing to repay his kindness, she offered clothing and other items to the bhikṣu. Knowing her intention, the bhikṣu did not accept them. The Buddha said:
"You should accept them."

Regarding the Blessed One’s instruction that one should accept the wealth and goods offered as ransom for a child, the group of six bhikṣus then demanded the full price from the parents. The Buddha said:
“One should not demand a price; rather, one should accept it according to their intention, being content with what is received.”
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, the yakṣiṇī Hārītī, having already offered her sons to the Saṃgha, lay down at night and suffered from hunger, weeping until dawn.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"In the early morning, one should take food and drink and offer them as a sacrifice while calling out their names.
Some wished to eat during the time of the fast; the Buddha said:
"One should give.
Or, if there are those who wish to obtain food and drink at an improper time, the Buddha said:
"One should give."
There were some who wished to eat the remnants of food remaining in the bowl of a bhikṣu;
the Buddha said, "One should give it to them. There were some who wished to eat various impure things; the Buddha said:
"It should be granted.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 31. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.
Volume Thirty-Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The second subsection of the seventh section; the summary verse says:
A bhikṣuṇī should not dwell in an araṇya, nor reside in a monastery outside the city;
she is not permitted to look out from before the gate, nor gaze through a window.
This was when the Buddha was at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.
In this city there was a courtesan named Utpalavarṇā, who made her living by the profession of displaying her beauty.
At that time, a brahmin came and said to her,
"Maiden, are you not well?"
"You may engage in amorous acts with me.
She replied, "Do you have any money?"
He replied, "I have none. The woman said:
"You may go seek some money and come back to see me later.
He replied, "I shall seek it."
She then traveled south, engaging in business as she went, and having obtained five hundred coins, she returned to the woman’s residence.

At that time, because of her reliance on the Venerable Maudgalyāyana as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), Utpalavarṇā subsequently went forth, received full ordination (upasampadā), and attained the fruit of Arhatship; then, according to her inclination, she departed from Rājagṛha for Śrāvastī.

At that time, as the Blessed One had not yet prohibited bhikṣuṇīs from dwelling in araṇyas, Utpalavarṇā went to the Dark Forest and, sitting in meditation in a secluded place, entered into samādhi to experience the bliss of liberation.
At that time, a brahmin took five hundred gold coins and went to the city of Rājagṛha, asking the people,
"Where has the woman Utpalavarṇā gone now? They replied:
"He has already gone forth within the Dharma of the Śākya son and is heading for Śrāvastī.
Having heard this report, he immediately went to the Jetavana and asked the bhikṣus:
"Venerable ones!..."
"The woman of Rājagṛha named Utpalavarṇā has traveled here; where is she now?
He replied, "That woman has already abandoned unrighteousness and gone forth as a renunciant; she is in the Dark Forest, single-mindedly practicing sublime contemplation."
He then went to her and said, "Young woman!
As we previously made an agreement, I have now brought the money; you may now enjoy pleasure with me."
He replied, "Brahmin!
I have already abandoned sinful deeds; you should now depart."
He replied, "Young woman!
Though you may abandon me, I shall not abandon you."
"You ought to rise; I certainly will not let you go.
She replied, "In which part of my body do you take particular pleasure?"
He replied, "I love your eyes. Thereupon,
by means of his supernormal power, he gouged out both of his own eyes and gave them to him.
Then the brahmin thought to himself,
"This shaven-headed female śramaṇa can perform such sorcery.
He struck the nun on the head with his fist and abandoned her, departing.
He then informed the community of nuns of these circumstances.
The nuns reported this to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:
"Because bhikṣuṇīs dwell in forest hermitages (āraṇya), such faults arise. From this day forward, bhikṣuṇīs must not seek solitude by staying in dark groves or in empty wilderness areas."
"If anyone should remain [in such a state], they shall incur an offense against the Dharma. This occurred in Śrāvastī.
As the Blessed One said:
“Bhikṣuṇīs should not dwell in forest hermitages (āraṇya).

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs sat in meditation and practiced tranquility in the streets and alleys, which again invited the same faults as before. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Bhikṣuṇīs should practice while residing within the monastery.”

At that time, lay followers with faith, having heard that the Buddha had instructed the bhikṣuṇīs to practice meditative concentration within a monastery, subsequently constructed a nunnery outside the city walls for them to reside in. However, they were once again harassed and disturbed by various thieves and wicked men who came there together.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Nunneries should not be established outside the city; they should be located within the city.
The circumstances were the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Tullānandā stood waiting at the entrance of the nunnery; whenever she saw someone approaching, she would immediately flirt with them.
The lay travelers all joined in mocking and disparaging her. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who thought to himself:
"For a bhikṣuṇī to stand at the gate has such faults; therefore, a bhikṣuṇī should not remain standing beneath a gate."
"If a bhikṣuṇī stands at the entrance of a door, she commits an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The setting of this account is the same as before.

Since the Buddha had prescribed that bhikṣuṇīs should not stand at the head of a doorway, they instead peered through the windows and teased one another from afar, giving rise to faults just as before. The Buddha said:
"This also constitutes an offense of transgression of the Dharma, as previously established.
The third sub-section of the seventh chapter contains this summary verse:
"It is permitted to wear the *saṃkakṣikā*; one should not bathe in a pool where there are men."
"One should not cross at a crossroads; one ought to walk along one side.
The circumstances were as before.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs, while performing various tasks within the monastery, wore the five robes (pañcaka-cīvara); consequently, they became distressed by the heat, grew fatigued, and thereby became physically weak. They then informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"When nuns perform various tasks within the monastery, they should wear the saṃkakṣikā.
When laypeople see them, they may give rise to lustful thoughts; those with faith will see this and join in their derision."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If laypeople find this matter offensive, from now on, when bhikṣuṇīs are in the presence of householders or brahmins, they should not wear the saṃkakṣikā while performing their duties."
If one wears it [in such a manner], one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (dharma-āpatti).
If performing work in the presence of laypeople, one may use a saṃkakṣikā to cover both shoulders and arms, and then don the five-strip robe (pañcakaṭika) before undertaking the task.
The setting was as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Dhanika went to a place where men were bathing to bathe herself.
Several young men also came there to bathe; seeing the nun enter the water, they consulted one another, saying:
"Look at this shaven-headed śramaṇī; her body is like that of a wild water buffalo.
The nun informed the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu informed the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:
"This fault has arisen because the bhikṣuṇī went to the bathing place of men."
"From this time forward, bhikṣuṇīs must not go to places where men bathe to wash their bodies.
Should any go there, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The setting of the occasion is the same as before.
The bhikṣuṇī Tullānandā stood in the middle of a crossroads; whenever she saw a layperson approaching, she would immediately flirt with them.
The people replied, "Shaven-headed daughter of a śramaṇa!"
"How could it be appropriate to flirt with us in the middle of a crossroads?
The nun reported this to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, a bhikṣuṇī should not pass through the middle of a crossroads; she should stay near one side and proceed as is convenient."
"If one passes directly through [the door], one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The fourth section of the seventh chapter, summarized in verse, says:
"If she is a hermaphrodite, or if she belongs to the class of those whose paths are joined,"
Some constantly had blood flow from them, while others were persons without blood.
The setting was as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who ordained a person with both sexual organs; when she saw another bhikṣuṇī approaching, she would manifest strange signs.
He asked, "Sister! Who are you?"
He replied, "Sister! I am a person of both sexes."
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"This person is neither male nor female and should not be ordained. Even if they were to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), they would not generate the protective restraint (*saṃvara*); they should be expelled immediately."
From this time forward, if there is a woman who comes seeking to go forth, one must first ask her:
"Are you not of dual gender?
If one grants the going forth without asking, the preceptor incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who had ordained a woman with a double vaginal opening; whenever she urinated, excrement would come out as well, defiling the place.
Other nuns came in, and upon seeing this, they asked:
"Who has defiled this place? They replied:
"Sister! It was not my intention to defile that place; it was because my two channels were joined that when I wished to urinate slightly, both urine and feces came out together.
The nun informed the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"This person is neither male nor female and should not go forth; even if they were to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), they would not generate the vows of restraint (*saṃvara*).
They should be expelled immediately. From this day forward, if a woman comes seeking to go forth, she must first be asked:
'Are you not a hermaphrodite (*ubhayavyañjana*)?'"
"If one ordains a woman without first inquiring [about her condition], the preceptor incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The setting of this account is the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who ordained a woman whose blood flowed constantly; her lower garment became stained and soiled, attracting many flies.
The nuns asked, "Sister!
Does your body constantly bleed?"
She replied, "I am a woman who constantly bleeds.
The nun reported this to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"This too is the same as before: she is unfit for communal residence.
The setting and circumstances are the same as previously described.

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who had ordained a woman who had never menstruated. Seeing other bhikṣuṇīs from time to time exhibiting menstrual flow, she felt aversion and shame, and said to them:
"Little sister!
Because you harbor improper thoughts and cannot remain free from desire, your menses appear from time to time. She replied:
"Sister! Why do you show me such disdain?
Is this not the constant nature of women; could you possibly be without it?"
She replied, "I am not a woman who menstruates; how could such a thing be possible?
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"This is a woman of the *ṣaṇḍha* (eunuch) class; she should be expelled so that wholesome dharmas do not arise [in her].
If one sees a woman seeking to go forth, one should ask:
'Are you not without blood?'"
"If one does not inquire, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The fifth sub-section of the seventh chapter, summarized in verse, says:
"The path is narrow; wearing the inner robe; not spitting near a bhikṣu."
If a monk or nun does not speak face-to-face, it should be done in the presence of their own assembly.
The setting and circumstances were as before.

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who had ordained a young girl as a novice; the woman then went to the place for relieving herself and remained there for a long time before emerging. Another nun asked her:
"Why have you come out so late?
He replied, "Knowing what could I do?"
"My body is of inferior capacity and my faculties are incomplete; for this reason, I am slow!
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "This is a female *paṇḍaka*; she should be expelled immediately."
The setting is the same as before.

At that time, there were several nuns who, during their menstrual periods, soiled their robes and bedding such that many flies would cluster upon them; even after washing and dyeing them, they remained as dirty as before.
The Buddha, knowing this, told them:
"Nuns of such a class should wear an inner garment.
The nuns then put one on.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Gulmavilāsinī was also wearing this garment when she entered the city to beg for food; it fell off in the middle of the street.
People saw it and asked, "What is this object left upon the ground?"
The nun replied with anger:
"You of evil birth!
You should quickly ask your mother or sisters at home; they shall explain it to you."
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣuṇī wears the inner robe, she must fasten a band around her waist so that this fault does not arise.
If she does not fasten a band around her waist, she commits an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
The setting was as before.

At the time of the morning meal, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. Seeing him, the nun Utpalavarṇā quickly went up to his side, spat on the ground, and cried out:
"What an utterly foolish and dull-witted thing!"
Kāśyapa said: "This is not your fault, but rather the error of Ānanda, who allowed this woman of evil conduct to forcibly request ordination within the sublime Dharma and Vinaya."
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"What the Tāpanī has done is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; even lustful women would not utter such base and evil words toward a bhikṣu."
From this time forward, when a bhikṣuṇī sees a bhikṣu, she must not spit on the ground and cry out, "You are utterly foolish! You are utterly dull-witted!
Should she do so, she commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had committed an offense; seeing a bhikṣuṇī approaching, he called out to her and invited her to sit. She asked:
"Noble one! What do you wish to do? He replied:
"I have committed an offense and now wish to confess it.
The nun sat down facing him, and the bhikṣu said:
"Āryā, be mindful! I [name]..."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense. I now confess this offense before Āryāyika and do not conceal it; by means of this confession, I shall abide in peace and happiness.
The nun said, "Venerable one,
have you also committed such a transgression?
This is not a virtuous deed."
The bhikṣu remained silent with shame.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"A bhikṣu should not confess his offense before a bhikṣuṇī; he should instead disclose and confess his offense before a pure bhikṣu whose views are identical to his own."
"If one acts thus, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The setting for this account is the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who had committed an offense. Seeing a bhikṣu approaching with sincere reverence, she prostrated at his feet, joined her palms, and requested:
"Noble One! Out of compassion for me, please deign to sit for a short while. The bhikṣu asked:
"What do you wish to do? He replied, "Noble One!"
"I have committed an offense and now wish to confess it.
The bhikṣu sat facing her, and the bhikṣuṇī joined her palms and said:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me!"
"I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense.
[The details] are as explained above. The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī should not confess her offense before a bhikṣu; she should instead declare her offense before a pure bhikṣuṇī."
If one acts as the officiant [without authorization], one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The sixth sub-section of the seventh chapter, summarized in verse, says:
When a bhikṣu performs a formal ritual (karmavācanā), a bhikṣuṇī should listen with careful attention.
Spread out the seats and have the people sit; the seats for the nuns should be distinguished.
The setting and circumstances are as before.
As the Blessed One said:

The formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) for bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs differ; with the exception of those procedures common to both, when a bhikṣuṇī performs a formal procedure within the assembly of monks, she cannot act without fear, and thus the procedure is not validly accomplished.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"The bhikṣus should perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), and the bhikṣuṇīs should listen.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know how they were to listen attentively.
The Buddha said:
"Reflect upon this with a sincere and virtuous mind, and say:
'This is the conclusion of the first karmavācanā.'"
"The second and third [recitations] should be performed in this same manner; this refers to the two assemblies receiving the *bhikṣuṇī* precepts.
The setting of the narrative is the same as before.
Regarding what the World-Honored One had said—that those capable of reciting the sūtras should do so—at that time, the *bhikṣus* did not spread out seats. The Buddha said:

"It should be spread. Later, on another occasion, when nuns came to listen to the Dharma, they sat upon fine seats. At that time, one nun suddenly began her menstrual period and soiled the seat-cloth; having finished listening, she departed. When the administrator arrived intending to collect and put it away, he saw many flies clinging to it. He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When nuns come to listen to the Dharma, you should not allow them to sit upon fine seats."
As the Blessed One had said, "A bhikṣuṇī must not sit on a fine seat to listen to the Dharma," whenever a nun arrived, she was given only a small seat.
On one occasion, when Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī came to listen to the Dharma, she was likewise made to sit on a small seat.
Mahāprajāpatī said, "Even when I was still a laywoman, I never sat upon such a small seat; how much less can I sit upon it now? The bhikṣus said:
“Mahāprajāpatī! This is the instruction of the Blessed One: he does not permit bhikṣuṇīs to sit on fine seats while listening to the Dharma. Mahāprajāpatī said:
"How could I possibly share that same blameworthy fault? That fault arose because the previous nun lacked mindfulness.
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I now grant permission."
"If a bhikṣuṇī comes to listen to the Dharma with mindfulness, you should provide her with a good seat and harbor no doubts.
The summary verse for the seventh section, seventh subsection, says:
Selling liquor, the house of a courtesan, not touching a woman on the road.
"Exposing one's undergarments at any time, and performing songs and dances, should not be done.
The setting and circumstances were as before.

At the time for the morning meal, the bhikṣuṇī Khujjuttarā put on her robes, took her bowl, and went on her alms-round in due order. Seeing a laywoman wearing exquisite garments and jewelry, she asked:
“Maiden, by what means did you obtain these exquisite garments and necklaces? She replied:
“Noble one! I obtained this robe and necklace by selling liquor.
The nun then thought to herself:
"This is a skillful means," he thought,
and without letting his mind stray from this thought, he continued on his almsround. Again,
he encountered a woman wearing tattered, old clothes who was walking away, emaciated and weak.
He asked, "To whose family do you belong? She replied:
"Noble one! I have no master;
as long as I receive food and clothing, I shall serve you.
The nun said:
"If that is so, why do you not sell wine? He replied, "Noble one!"

"How could someone like me possibly sell wine? To sell wine, one must have a spacious residence, beds, couches, seats, mats, cups, ladles, platters, and jars; one must have ample capital on hand and provide service according to the proper method. Only when there is no lack for arriving guests will there be profit."
The nun said, "If that is so, I shall provide for you whatever things you require; will you give me a share of the wealth you obtain? She replied:
"I shall give it to you.
He then built a large residence near the nunnery and provided him with all the necessary furnishings; he also gave him a large capital sum to enable him to sell wine.
Many who wished to drink came to this place, and the other taverns all became envious.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Gulavānanda obtained great wealth and profit. Later, when the king held a great assembly, he summoned all the tavern keepers.

They replied, "Next to the monastery of the bhikṣuṇī Gulavānanda, there is a large shop where fine wine is sold in abundance; many people drink there and she collects much profit. Why do you not summon her instead? Why do you single us out with such hardship?"
Having heard this, the messenger went to seize the girl, who immediately cried out in alarm, saying:
"Venerable Tullānanda! A royal messenger has unjustly come to drag me away; please come out!"
Upon hearing this, the nun came out quickly and immediately reviled her, saying:
"You wretched, evil creature!
What are you doing, dragging away my daughter?"
The messenger replied,
"Noble One! How could it be appropriate to set up a shop to sell wine?"
He replied, "I am treading on the necks of my enemies with my feet; what business of yours is it that I am engaged in the trade of selling liquor? He asked:
"Noble One! Do you also have enemies? He replied:
"You are the enemy! You have taken my daughter away!
Because of this, they fell into a quarrel.
When the householders and brahmins saw it, they asked:
"Why is this? they asked, and after recounting the matter in detail, they all spoke with derision:
"The daughters of the Śākyas have acted out of their own restlessness and committed unrighteous deeds; these shaven-headed śramaṇī women do not follow pure conduct, but instead sell liquor."
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"The conduct of the bhikṣuṇī Toraṇadā is not the dharma of a daughter of the Śākya clan. From this day forward, bhikṣuṇīs must not sell liquor."
"If one sells [it], they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The setting of this episode is the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Tullānandā, having put on her robes and taken up her bowl, went on her almsround in due order.
Seeing a courtesan wearing fine garments and necklaces, he asked,
"Young woman! Where did you obtain these exquisite garments and necklaces?"
He replied, "Venerable One!
I obtained this robe by selling my own beauty."
The nun thought to herself:
"This is an excellent expedient; I shall now test whether it can lead to deliverance.

With her mind focused on this matter, she went out for alms and, at a certain place, saw a young woman whose clothes were soiled and greasy, whose appearance bore the marks of hunger, and who walked with a frail gait yet possessed well-proportioned limbs. She asked her:
“Maiden! To whose family do you belong? She replied:
"I have no master; I belong only to those who provide me with food and clothing.
He replied, "If that is so, for what reason do you not engage in the profession of a courtesan?"
He immediately covered his ears with both hands and replied,
"Noble One! Within my family,
such an evil deed has never been heard of."
The nun said, "Young woman!
For the most part, all women engage in this occupation; you are neither a princess nor born of a noble family such as a householder or a brahmin."
"However, all women love men; even if I do not go forth, I shall surely do so myself.
Upon hearing this seductive enticement, she replied to the nun: "Noble Lady!"
"If one were to become a courtesan, could it be accomplished immediately?

"Only when all conditions are fully prepared can that matter be accomplished; first, one must have a spacious residence, clothing of fresh and brilliant colors, and be adorned with necklaces so that those who see one feel affection and longing."
"If any man comes to enter this house, you must provide him with food, drink, incense, and garlands according to his status,
whether he be noble or lowly. The nun said, "Young girl!"
"Whatever you require, I shall provide for you; I will give you food and clothing.
Can you give me whatever wealth you have acquired? He replied:
“Give it all to her.

The nun built a large residence near the monastery and prepared everything she required; she provided her with baths, incense, flowers, clothing, and necklaces. She allowed her to eat whatever she desired until her appearance became robust and flourishing, making her the foremost among all the courtesans, so that people from all quarters flocked to her.
When those courtesans saw this, they were filled with jealousy, for the nun Tullānandā had obtained much wealth.
Later, when the King held a great assembly and used a large quantity of fragrant ointments, the messenger gathered the courtesans together to prepare them.
The women slandered her by telling the messenger, "There is also a courtesan near the convent of the nun Tullānandā; she should be summoned as well."
Once the messenger had departed, he summoned the girl and seized her; she then cried out loudly, saying, "Noble One!
There is now a royal minister who has grabbed me and is taking me away!"
The nun then quickly came out and said to the messenger,
"You wretched man, you are taking my daughter away! He replied:
“Noble one, you also frequent houses of prostitution. He replied:
"I have already trampled the enemy's neck with my feet; what business is it of yours whether I engage in the profession of a courtesan?
She spoke at length as before, until the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, no bhikṣuṇīs shall engage in the profession of a courtesan."
"Whoever violates this shall incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The setting and circumstances were as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā took a young girl and, along a major road in a forested wilderness, made her livelihood by plying the trade of prostitution in order to seek wealth.
When she was seized by others, the nun reviled them with harsh words as extensively described above.
[The Buddha declared: "If anyone should do so, they shall incur a thullaccaya offense.
This occurred in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus frequently engaged in singing and dancing together with musicians. They deliberated among themselves, saying: "Venerable sirs!
The reason we are constantly compelled by these musicians to perform songs and dances is entirely due to the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs."
If he does not privately give his robes, bowl, and other belongings to the musician to cause me distress, he will be unable to make me perform music.
He ought to be punished; now is the very time to devise a plan.
Upānanda said, "We should beat him together. They all agreed, saying:
"So be it," they said, and proceeded together. From a distance, they saw the bhikṣuṇī Pūrṇa-nanda and said to one another, "This nun is a leader; she ought to be severely punished."

They immediately went forward and seized him together; some struck him on the head with their fists, others trampled his waist with their feet, or used their mendicant staffs to beat him. His entire body became swollen and bruised blue, and he was no longer able to walk; they rubbed oil onto his body, and he lay upon his bed.
The bhikṣuṇīs saw her and asked,
"Why is it like this? She replied:
"I have been struck. He asked, "By whom?"
He replied, "Venerable ones, the group of six.
[The others asked,] "What offense have you committed?"
He replied, "He is my Dharma elder brother and I am his Dharma younger sister; it is our constant custom to instruct one another.
How can this be compared to others? Why trouble yourself to inquire about our faults?"
When the nuns heard this, they all spoke with reproach and disdain:
"How can a bhikṣu strike the community of nuns?
They informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha then reflected thus:
"When a bhikṣu strikes a bhikṣuṇī and touches her body," he told the bhikṣus:
"If one strikes a bhikṣuṇī, it is improper to do so; one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma."

The setting was in Śrāvastī. As the Blessed One had taught regarding nuns wearing the inner robe (*antarvāsaka*), although they wore this garment, blood still stained it, defiling their bedding and attracting many flies and insects. Consequently, feelings of revulsion and contempt arose, and they harbored distress in their hearts.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I now permit the bhikṣuṇīs to wear a skirt over their inner garments.
The bhikṣuṇīs then followed the instruction and wore them, yet the garments remained stained and soiled. The Buddha said:
"At appropriate times, you must wash and dye [the robes], and while sleeping or resting, you must always maintain mindfulness.
Should you fail to do so, you shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
This was the occasion at Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Pūrṇa; after his death, his body was carried to the charnel ground and cremated.
Then, twelve bhikṣuṇīs immediately began to sing and dance right beside him.
The nuns felt ashamed and reproachful, and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It is not in accordance with the dharma for a nun to perform songs or dances herself.
One who does so commits a *vyatikrama* offense."
The eighth sub-section of the seventh chapter contains this summary verse:
“If the faculties of a monk or nun should change, And it occurs up to three times, they shall all be expelled.
The Dharma and the circumstances are explained in detail; Utpalavarṇā acted as the messenger.”
The setting was as before.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying: "Bhadanta!..."
“If a nun undergoes a change of gender, what should be done?
The Buddha said:
“She shall be considered as having received full ordination according to her original status, and she shall move to the monastery of the monks in accordance with the sequence of her seniority.”
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
When a nun undergoes a change of gender, she shall immediately be sent to the monastery for monks based on her original seniority."
“If a monk undergoes a change of gender, should he still return to the nunnery based on his original summer retreat?
The Buddha said,
“In this case as well, he should be sent to the nunnery.”
“Venerable One! Once these two persons have reached that place, their faculties revert once more; what is the nature of this matter?
The Buddha said:
"Return each to its respective original place as appropriate. "Venerable Sir!
This was repeated three times in this manner; what does it mean?"
The Buddha said:
"If they reach the third turning [of the wheel], they are no longer monks or nuns; they must be expelled. Do not harbor any doubt.
The setting of this episode is the same as before.
At that time, there was an elder named Devadatta, who was immensely wealthy and possessed great riches; he lived with his wife.
Furthermore, in another place, there was an elder named Mṛgāra, who was also immensely wealthy and lived with his wife.

These two families vied with one another in boasting of their wealth, each claiming superiority; later, they became close friends who frequented each other's company, and whenever they possessed any unusual object, they invariably presented it as a gift to one another.
At that time, when there was business for the people of this city, they all gathered at the Fragrant Garden; once their deliberations were concluded, they each returned home.
At that moment, the two elders Devadatta and Mṛgāra were staying in the garden, conversing together, when Devadatta said:
"By what means can we ensure that after we have passed away, our descendants shall remain affectionate toward one another and not become estranged?"
Mṛgāra said, "Excellent are these words!
Now let us form a marriage alliance between our wombs; if children of either sex are born to our two families, they shall be joined in matrimony."
He said, "So be it! My mind is likewise."
Having made this deliberation, they each returned to their respective abodes.
Later, Devadatta’s wife gave birth to a daughter whose appearance and demeanor were so exceptionally beautiful that she surpassed all her peers, yet her disposition was such that she wept frequently.
If a bhikṣu came to the house to preach the Dharma for her father, the child would stop crying and listen attentively with rapt attention.
After twenty-one days, when the relatives gathered in celebration to name the girl, they deliberated together, saying:
"This girl loves the Dharma and listens attentively with rapt attention; since she is the daughter of Devadatta, she shall be named Dharmadinnā."
Entrusted to eight foster mothers who nurtured her with kindness and compassion, she grew up quickly, like a lotus emerging from the water.
When the householder Mṛgāra heard that a daughter had been born to his friend, he thought to himself:
"How could the birth of a daughter to my friend be in vain? I should send garments and necklaces to express my congratulations; she shall be my new bride—of this there is no doubt."
He also delivered this message:
