"I have heard that you have given birth to a daughter, and my heart is filled with double joy. I have sent these garments and necklaces as a token of my congratulations; I trust you will accept them so that my gesture may not be in vain."
Devadatta took the message and replied accordingly:
"If she gives birth to a son, he shall certainly become my son-in-law.

At that time, Mṛgāra, having received this news, felt his heart’s desire for a male child; before long, his wife became pregnant, and when the months were complete, she gave birth to a son. After twenty-one days had passed, the relatives gathered in a joyful assembly, and while deliberating on a name for the boy, they said:
"Since this child’s birth was under the constellation Viśākhā, he should be named Viśākhā.
She was then entrusted to eight nurses to be held and nurtured.
At that time, when the elder Devadatta heard that Mṛgāra had fathered a son, he thought to himself:

“The householder Mṛgāra is my close friend; since he has now fathered a son and I have fathered a daughter, he is the groom for my daughter. You should prepare ornaments, necklaces, and garments, and send them there by messenger.”
He also delivered this message:
"I have heard that you have fathered a son and am deeply delighted; I now send these garments, which I hope you will graciously accept.
Having received the letter, he sent back a reply with this message:
"For a long time we have been close friends, and now our wishes have all been fulfilled; let us each wait until we are grown and then enter into marriage.

Dharmadatta grew up and, finding his heart’s delight in leaving the household life, knelt and said to his father, "I now desire to leave the household life to follow the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya."
The father said,
"My daughter! I have a prior statement:..."
"I have given you in marriage to Viśākhā, the daughter of the householder Mṛgāra.
She is your husband; it is truly not permissible [to refuse].
When the nun Utpalavarṇā, who was her preceptor at that time, came to inquire after her, Dharmadinnā said to her:

“Noble One! I take delight in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya and wish to go forth, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣuṇī; I pray that you will come here and grant me the going-forth in secret.”
"Why is this? My father has forbidden me, so there is no way for me to go out.
The nun said:

“Excellent! Young woman, you are able to give rise to this mind and delight in going forth into homelessness. The flavors of sensual desires are few, while their faults and calamities are exceedingly many.
As the World-Honored One has said:”
"Those who possess wisdom know that there are five faults regarding the matter of sexual desire;
therefore, one should not engage in it. What are these five? "
First, one contemplates that sensual desires have little flavor and many faults, and are constantly accompanied by manifold sufferings;
second, those who indulge in sensual desires are perpetually bound and fettered;
third, those who indulge in sensual desires never reach satiety.
Fourth, those who indulge in sensual desires commit no evil that they do not;

fifth, regarding the objects of desire, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, the assembly of Śrāvakas, and all superior persons who have attained right view, have explained the faults of desire through immeasurable means; therefore, the wise should not practice desire.
Furthermore, the wise person knows that there are five benefits to going forth from the household life. What are these five?
First, the merit of going forth is one's own personal benefit and is not shared with others; therefore, the wise should seek to go forth.

Second, one should know for oneself that while previously a lowly person driven by others, after having left the household life, one receives offerings, prostrations, and praise from others; therefore, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
Third, when one’s life here ends, one shall be reborn in the heavens and remain free from the two evil realms; therefore, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
Fourth, by renouncing the secular world, one departs from birth and death and shall attain the secure, unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*; therefore, the wise should seek to leave the household life.
"Fifth, one will always be praised by all Buddhas, the assembly of śrāvakas, and all superior persons; therefore, the wise should seek to go forth from the household life.
You should now contemplate these benefits and, with a sincere and earnest mind, cast off the worldly nets to seek great merit. For this reason, I shall now ordain you and allow you to go forth.
"You should remain here for now; I shall go and inform the Buddha.
Then, the nun Utpalavarṇā went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and with palms joined, addressed him, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!"

The daughter of the householder Devadatta, named Dharmadinnā, felt a deep aspiration to go forth and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha, thereby attaining the status of a bhikṣuṇī; however, because her father had previously intended to marry her to Viśākha, the son of Mṛgāra, her parents shielded her and would not permit her to go forth.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Go and inform the community of nuns that the daughter of the householder Devadatta, Dharmadinnā, desires to go forth. You should send the nun Utpalavarṇā to Dharmadinnā’s place and say to her:
'In accordance with the instruction of the Blessed One, I shall confer upon you the three refuges and the five precepts.'"
"Immediately, she shaved her head at home, left the household life, and received the ten precepts.
Then Ānanda, having received the World-Honored One’s instruction, informed the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs; they gathered together and sent the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā to her, saying:
"Young woman!..."

Now the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, following the instruction of the World-Honored One, has sent me here to grant you the going forth. First, receive the Three Refuges along with the Five Precepts; you should receive them with a focused mind.
Having thus received [the precepts], he said to her:
"You are now a female lay follower (upāsikā); next, the ten training rules shall be conferred.
He spoke as follows:
“You have now completed your renunciation; you should diligently practice and train, upholding the Dharma according to the World-Honored One’s instructions.

At that time, the woman was filled with joy and gave rise to deep yearning, listening attentively. The nun Utpalavarṇā observed her faculties and delivered a teaching suited to her capacity, causing her to awaken to the principles of the Four Noble Truths. With the vajra-thunderbolt of wisdom, she shattered the twenty-fold mountain of the view of a self-existent body and attained the fruit of Stream-entry.
Then the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā came and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have completed what was to be done according to the Great Teacher’s instructions.
The Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Go and inform the community of nuns that the nun Utpalavarṇā should go to that household to bestow the six rules and the six secondary rules upon her for two years of formal training.”
Then Ānanda, following the instructions of the Blessed One, addressed the community of nuns:
"Send the nun Utpalavarṇā to Dharmadinnā’s place and, in accordance with the Buddha’s command, bestow upon her the six rules and the six secondary rules."
He said to her:
"You are now a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā); for two years you should receive instruction and practice training, upholding the Dharma according to the World-Honored One’s teaching."
Furthermore, he preached the sublime Dharma to him according to his capacity; having heard the Dharma, the youth attained the fruit of a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).

During those two years, Dharmadatta studied the six rules and the six secondary rules. As the years passed and he grew older, his appearance became exceptionally refined and outstanding, surpassing all his peers, so that his kinsmen all came together to behold him.
When the householder Mṛgāra knew that his daughter had reached maturity, he sent a messenger to inform the householder Devadatta, saying:
"Since our children have grown up, it is fitting for them to be united in marriage; please select an auspicious day so that we may perform the grand ceremony."
Devadatta replied: "Excellent!
This matter should be handled in this way."
He immediately summoned various masters of yin and yang to determine an auspicious day and instructed his distant and near relatives:
"My daughter Dharmā will be married on such-and-such a day; whether you are old or young, all must assemble together to celebrate, and you may bring all manner of ornaments."
At that time, the householder Mṛgāra also informed his kinsmen; since his relatives and family were so numerous, they all gathered together until Śrāvastī was filled with them.

At that time, King Prasenajit, Lord of Kośala, as well as those within the inner palace and all the commoners, heard that the daughter of the householder Devadatta, Dharmadinnā, was to be married to the son of the householder Mṛgāra on an auspicious day; consequently, their kinsmen gathered in great numbers, filling the city to its brim.
The king addressed his ministers, saying:
"You, too, should join him in providing assistance.

Thereupon, the ministers proclaimed the king’s decree, ordering all the noble and wealthy clans within their respective districts, villages, and hamlets to bring forth all their finely adorned and extraordinary articles to assist the elder in his wedding ceremony.
When the various nobles heard the king’s command, they all brought diverse and extraordinary objects and came to offer their assistance.

At that time, the city walls, main thoroughfares, and alleys were filled with crowds of people; they were swept and sprinkled, adorned and made free of all impurities, perfumed everywhere with burning incense and strewn with famous flowers, so that it was as delightful as the Garden of Joy (Nandana).
Fayü saw from afar and, marveling at its extraordinary nature, asked his family members,
"Are you intending to hold an untimely White Flower Assembly?
His family replied:
"By virtue of your merit, we shall hold an untimely White Flower Assembly for you to perform the marriage rites.
Upon hearing these words, the girl was filled with grief and distress; she went quickly to her father’s side, knelt, and said to him:
"I have no desire or pleasure for the five objects of sensory enjoyment; I pray that my father will permit me to go to the nuns' quarters at the Rājārāma monastery."
The father said,
"Before you were born, I made a solemn vow:
'I shall give her in marriage to Viśākha, the son of the householder Mṛgāra.'"
"He is your husband now; you no longer depend on me.

Furthermore, the King of Kośala, the Great King Prasenajit, along with his officials, commoners, nobles, and lowly subjects, all know and hear that you have been married to Viśākhā, the son of Mṛgāra. How could he ever permit you to enter the royal park monastery?"
"Do you wish to have me and my kinsmen imprisoned?
Tomorrow is our wedding; do not act so rashly.
Furthermore, all the relatives came and said to him:
“Maiden! You should not act with such haste; since you are in the prime of youth, it is difficult to establish the holy life.

Having heard this admonition, she immediately exerted herself, applying her mind to diligent cultivation and seeking the Noble Path with single-minded devotion, yet in the end she was unable to attain the means for detachment from desire.
At that time, there was nothing the World-Honored One, the Great Teacher, did not know or see.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas to always give rise to great compassion for the benefit of all beings;
they are foremost in providing protection, most heroic and valiant, free from double-tongued speech, and abide in concentration and wisdom, manifesting the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
Skillfully cultivating the three trainings and skillfully disciplining the three karmas; crossing over the four torrents and establishing oneself in the four bases of spiritual power;
practicing the four means of attraction throughout the long night; abandoning the five hindrances, distancing oneself from the five factors, and transcending the five paths;
possessing the six sense faculties and perfecting the six perfections; universally bestowing the seven riches and opening the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment; free from...
Delighting in the Eightfold Noble Path amidst the eight difficulties, forever severing the nine fetters and being proficient in the nine meditative absorptions;
fulfilling the ten powers with a reputation that reaches the ten directions, he is the most preeminent among all those who possess mastery;

having attained fearlessness in the Dharma, he subdues Māra and his enemies, thundering with the great sound of a lion’s roar, constantly throughout the six periods of day and night, [acting] as a Buddha.
Observing all the worlds with his eyes, he considers: who is increasing?
Who is decreasing?
Who has encountered suffering and calamity?
Who is heading toward the evil realms?
Who is mired in the quagmire of desire?
Who is capable of receiving transformation through instruction?
By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver them so that they may emerge?
To those who lack the noble wealth, I shall cause them to obtain the noble wealth; with the *añjana* of wisdom, I shall break the film of ignorance.

To those without roots of goodness, I shall cause them to plant roots of goodness; to those who possess roots of goodness, I shall cause them to increase. I shall lead them along the path of humans and devas, safely and without obstruction, toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
As it is said: "Even if the tides of the great ocean should ever miss their appointed time,
the Buddha never fails his appointed hour when delivering those he transforms."
"The Buddha, toward all sentient beings, With compassion never abandons them;
Thinking to rescue them from their suffering and hardship, Like a mother cow following her calf.
At that time, while walking in meditation, the World-Honored One smiled, and from his mouth issued subtle light of five colors, which at times shone downward and at others ascended upward.
The light that shone downward reached the Avīci Hell and the other hells; those experiencing the heat of the fires everywhere obtained coolness, while those dwelling in the icy cold attained warmth.
Those sentient beings each found peace and happiness, and all thought to themselves: "Have you and I died in hell to be reborn elsewhere?"
At that time, after the World-Honored One had caused those sentient beings to give rise to faith, he further manifested other signs.
Upon seeing these signs, they all thought:
"We have not died here to be reborn elsewhere; rather, it is certainly through the power of the majesty of the Unsurpassed Great Sage that our bodies and minds now experience peace and happiness."

Having thus given rise to reverence and faith, they are able to extinguish all sufferings and receive superior and wondrous bodies within the realms of humans and devas; they shall become vessels for the Dharma and perceive the principles of the True Truths.
Those who ascend reach the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, where, amidst the light, they proclaim the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and further recite two gāthās:
"You should seek renunciation, And diligently practice the Buddha’s teaching."
Subdue the army of birth and death, as an elephant destroys a thatched hut.
Within this Dharma and Vinaya, always remain heedful;
you shall dry up the ocean of afflictions and reach the ultimate end of suffering.
Then that radiance, having illuminated the trichiliocosm, returned to the place where the Buddha was.

If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, speaks of past events, light enters through his back; if he speaks of future events, light enters through his chest; if he speaks of matters concerning hell-beings, light enters through the soles of his feet; if he speaks of matters concerning animals, light enters through his heels; if he speaks of matters concerning hungry ghosts, light enters through his toes; if he speaks of matters concerning humans, light enters through his knees; if he speaks of matters concerning a Cakravartin King of Power, light enters through the palm of his left hand; if he speaks of matters concerning a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), light enters through the palm of his right hand; if he speaks of matters concerning devas, light enters through his navel; if he speaks of matters concerning Śrāvakas, light enters through his mouth; if he speaks of matters concerning Pratyekabuddhas, light enters between his eyebrows; and if he speaks of matters concerning Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, light enters through the crown of his head.
At that time, the light circled the Buddha three times and entered through his mouth.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha smiles with a joyful countenance; it is not without cause or condition.
He then spoke these verses to request the Buddha's teaching:
"From his mouth issue various wondrous rays of light, Flowing and filling the great trichiliocosm in manifold forms."
Pervading all lands throughout the ten directions, like the sun’s light illuminating the entirety of space;
the Buddha is the most supreme cause for sentient beings, able to remove arrogance as well as grief and sorrow.
Without a specific cause, his golden mouth does not open; when he smiles, he will surely proclaim something rare and marvelous.
The serene and discerning Honored Sage, who delights in speaking for those who wish to hear, roars with a great lion’s roar; we pray that you will resolve our doubts.
Like the King of Mountains within the great ocean, which does not shake without cause or condition;
you, out of sovereign compassion, manifest a smile, and for those who look up with longing, explain the causes and conditions.
At that time, the Blessed One said to Ānanda: "So it is, so it is! Ānanda!"
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not manifest a smile without cause or condition. Ānanda!

Did you not see how I entrusted the maiden Dharmadinnā to the community of bhikṣuṇīs, so that she might be granted the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten precepts in succession, and become a śikṣamāṇā training for two years in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas?
"Tomorrow she will depart for her marriage;
why have all her kinsmen assembled? Ānanda replied, "I have already seen them all."
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!
It is impossible for one who stays in his house to eat leftover food kept overnight; before long, he shall realize the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of arhatship."
"You should now go and inform the nuns, saying:

'Dharmadinnā has already completed two years of training in the six rules and the six secondary rules; the community of nuns should dispatch the nun Utpalavarṇā as a messenger to her family home to perform the formal rite for the holy life.'"
When Ānanda had finished speaking to the bhikṣuṇīs, the community gathered together and sent Utpalavarṇā to the woman’s home to perform the fundamental rite for her.
Having done so, they said to Dharmadinnā, “It will not be long before you receive full ordination.”
Furthermore, he again preached the Dharma to her according to her capacity, whereby she attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) and manifested supernormal powers (ṛddhi).
Then, the nun Utpalavarṇā went to inform the Blessed One, who said to Ānanda:
"Go to the place of the bhikṣuṇīs and, transmitting my instructions, speak these words:"
"The two assemblies of monks and nuns should confer the *dharmadeśanā* and the full ordination (*upasampadā*), using the nun Utpalavarṇā as the messenger.

Having received the Buddha's instruction, Ānanda went to inform the assembly of nuns and convened the Saṃgha; with the nun Utpalavarṇā serving as the messenger between the two assemblies, he conferred the *dharmadeśanā* and the full ordination right there.
When the formal ritual had been completed, Utpalavarṇā went to her and said:
"Young woman! The Saṃgha of both divisions has already conferred full ordination upon you; you should practice well that which the Buddha has permitted."

He further preached the Dharma for him, and having heard the Dharma, he gave rise to a profound sense of renunciation, contemplating the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.

Having understood this, with the vajra-pestle of wisdom he shattered all afflictions and attained the fruit of Arhatship, endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations. He attained knowledge in accordance with reality:
"Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further existence."

The mind is without obstruction, like a hand waving through space; whether cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance, neither love nor hatred arises; viewing gold and earth as equal and without distinction, one relinquishes all fame and profit, and even Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas all pay him reverence.
"It would not be possible for an Arhatī whose outflows are exhausted to remain in the home of a layperson, eat leftover food from the previous night, or practice the customs of the laity.
At that time, once Dharmadinnā had attained the fruit, she said to her parents:
"O parents, you should know this!"
"I have already attained the fruit of Arhatship and now wish to go to the Rājakārāma nunnery.
Her parents replied, "If it is so, we fear that the king's law will bring punishment upon us; you should devise a plan to go with the Buddha."
He replied, "Excellent! I pray that you will act as our expedient means."
Then the householder Devadatta immediately invited the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus, and sent a messenger to inform the householder Mṛgāra, saying:
"Good friend! You should know that my daughter Dharmadinnā has no desire for secular life and will certainly renounce the world; you ought to come soon and insist upon her marriage."
Then Mṛgāra addressed the Great King Prasenajit, Lord of Kośala, saying:

"Your servant previously entered into a covenant with Devadatta, pledging our families as close kin by the joining of our bellies. Now that his daughter desires to renounce the world and enter the homeless life, I have brought her relatives here to compel this marriage."
The king said, "As you wish. Thereupon,
the elder immediately summoned his kinsmen to arrange the marriage.
The householder Devadatta prepared various foods and drinks and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The offerings have been prepared; may the Buddha know that the time has come.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and, leading the assembly of bhikṣus, proceeded to Devadatta’s residence and sat upon the seat. The rest of the saṃgha each sat down according to their rank.
The householder Devadatta, together with his kinsmen and relatives, all brought various kinds of exquisite food and drink to provide for the Buddha and the Sangha, ensuring they were fully satisfied.

At that time, the householder Mṛgāra and his retinue, along with princes, ministers, and the general populace, escorted Viśākhā and prepared the full ceremonial rites, arriving at the gate intending to perform the wedding.

At that time, the householder Devadatta, knowing that the Buddha and the great assembly had finished their meal, completed their rinsing, and put away their bowls, sat upon a low seat together with his kinsmen to listen to the essential teachings of the Dharma before the Great Master.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the sublime Dharma to them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them, before rising from his seat and departing.

Then, the nun Dharmadinnā had severed the afflictions of the three realms and attained fearlessness; yet the matters of marriage were once again before her eyes, as the prince, the ministers, and the multitude of people, along with Viśākhā and her kinsmen, had prepared music and stood waiting for her.

At that time, the nun Dharmadinnā followed behind the World-Honored One and emerged to the front of the gate. When Viśākhā saw Dharmadinnā, she immediately reached out her hand and grasped Dharmadinnā’s arm; this was witnessed by a great assembly of countless hundreds of thousands.
At that moment, Dharmadinnā immediately manifested her supernormal powers; like a great king of geese spreading its two wings, she ascended into the air to perform a miraculous feat.

When the king, his ministers, Viśākhā, all their retinues, and the gathered multitude saw this miracle, they were filled with wonder. They threw themselves to the ground like falling great trees, prostrated from afar at her feet to offer their apologies, and cried out:
"O Noble Lady!..."
"Having realized such sublime and supreme virtues, it is not reasonable for one who desires to enjoy worldly pleasures and consume leftover food from the previous night to remain a householder.

At that time, Dharmadinnā descended from her position and proclaimed the sublime Dharma to the great assembly. Among those who heard the teaching, immeasurable hundreds of thousands attained superior understanding; some attained the fruits of Stream-enterer, Once-returner, or Non-returner; some went forth in the Buddha’s Dharma, severed all afflictions, and attained the fruit of Arhatship; others gave rise to the mind of enlightenment as Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Great Bodhisattvas; and she further led the great assembly to take refuge in the Triple Gem and seek liberation from birth and death.
At that time, the nun Dharmadinnā, having obtained great benefit, went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and departed.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among the śrāvikā community in my Dharma, the one who is foremost in skillfully preaching the Dharma is the nun Dharmadinnā."
When the bhikṣus had heard what the Buddha said, they were all filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"What karma did this Dharma once perform for the sake of the nun?"

He went forth into the homeless life within his own home; having received the Buddha’s permission and been ordained by a messenger, he attained the fruit of arhatship at that very spot and became the foremost among those who preach the Dharma.
"I only pray that, out of compassion, you will explain his past karma.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Regarding the karma performed by Dharmadatta in his previous life, when its retribution ripens, he must experience it himself; it does not fall upon anyone else."
The detailed explanation is as in other [texts], up to the verse which says:
"Even if a hundred eons were to pass, The karma one has created does not perish;
When the causes and conditions meet, One must experience the retribution oneself."

“O bhikṣus! During this Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of humans was twenty thousand years, there was a Buddha in the world named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with the ten titles, who dwelt at Ṛṣipatana in the Mṛgadāva forest.”

At that time, there was a householder in Vārāṇasī who was immensely wealthy and possessed great riches. Not long after he had married, his wife became pregnant; when her months were complete, she gave birth to a daughter.
As the girl grew up, she felt a desire to leave the household life, but her parents would not permit it.
At that time, there was an elderly nun who was her preceptor; the girl immediately said to her, "Noble Lady!
Would you be able to grant me ordination here, so that I may receive full admission and become a bhikṣuṇī?"
The nun said, "I shall go and inform the Buddha; you should remain here at ease for now.
She then went to where the Buddha was and reported the matter to him.

The Buddha then dispatched a nun to the woman's home to grant her the going forth; she conferred upon her the three refuges, the five precepts, and the rules for female trainees (śikṣamāṇā), and the Saṃgha of both divisions likewise dispatched a nun to confer full ordination (upasampadā) upon her.

At that time, the old nun observed their faculties and dispositions and taught the Dharma according to their capacities; they immediately realized the fruit of Arhatship within their own home. That Buddha praised her as the foremost among nuns who preach the Dharma.
At that time, the old nun thought to herself:

"That this girl has gone forth and received full ordination, heard the Dharma and attained realization, and achieved the fruit of Arhatship—all these benefits have come about solely through my support."
Having formed this thought, he immediately made this aspiration:

"By all the roots of virtue from my cultivation of the holy life for as long as I live within the teaching of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa—just as the Buddha Kāśyapa prophesied for the young brahmin—that in a future age when the human lifespan is one hundred years, I shall attain perfect enlightenment under the name Śākyamuni."

I vow that within the Dharma of that Tathāgata, this woman shall not leave her own home, yet attain renunciation and receive the various precepts; hearing the Dharma, she shall realize its meaning, sever all afflictions, and attain arhatship.
"Just as Kāśyapa Buddha praised this nun, declaring her to be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma, may I also be so in the future. O bhikṣus!
"What do you think?
Is that old nun anyone else?
She is this very Dharma."

In the past, during the teaching of Kāśyapa Buddha, she practiced the holy life until the end of her life; by dedicating all those roots of virtue and making aspirations, she was enabled to leave the household life from being a laywoman, received the various precepts, became a bhikṣuṇī, severed all afflictions, realized the fruit of arhatship, and was granted a prophecy by the Buddha as the foremost in preaching the Dharma.
"O bhikṣus! For this reason, I say:
black karma yields black retribution; mixed karma yields mixed retribution; and white karma yields white retribution."
"You all should diligently cultivate white karma and remain free from black and mixed karma.
[The Buddha] even spoke in verse.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, all the bhikṣus were filled with great joy; they accepted it with faith and put it into practice, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took their leave, and departed.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudrakavastu, Scroll Thirty-two.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudrakavastu, Scroll Thirty-three.
The Seventh Section, Ninth Sub-section: A Summary Verse states: One shall not perform repentance outside the monastery;
One shall not allow a person to shave their hair alone.
Do not rent rooms in a *ni* temple; do not scrub the body with bricks or similar materials.
The setting of the occasion is the same as before.

A certain *bhikṣuṇī* went to the place of a *bhikṣu* to receive instruction from him. When the *bhikṣuṇī* committed a transgression, he rebuked her and sent her away; she then went back to the temple and lay down on her side.
His preceptor saw him and asked,
"For what reason are you lying prostrate? He replied:
"The Ācārya has rebuked me; what do you think should be done?
The teacher said, "Young girl!..."
"What more is there to do?
That preceptor rebuked you for the sake of causing the Dharma to endure; you ought to go quickly and beg his forgiveness. He replied:
"Excellent! I shall go to offer my apologies.

However, he did not see him in his cell at Jetavana; so he searched for him and found him walking back and forth in various places outside the monastery, whereupon he approached and prostrated at his feet.
He did not accept her and departed.
When the men and women saw this, they thought his mind was entangled by lustful passion and said to the nun:
"We understand the meaning of the Noble One’s apology; if he will not accept you, you may come to us. Whatever you require, we shall seek for you."
The nun, filled with shame, returned silently to the monastery.
She informed the bhikṣus, who in turn reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:
"Because the bhikṣus do not accept the confession of the nuns, men and women have become infatuated with desire and deluded, giving rise to evil discriminations."
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"A bhikṣuṇī must not seek *ānanda* from a bhikṣu outside the monastery; the bhikṣu should accept her apology and must not depart."
"If you do not comply, both shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The setting of the occasion was as before.
Some bhikṣuṇīs had a barber shave their hair; upon seeing a youth, the bhikṣuṇīs felt lustful desire arise in their hearts.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You bhikṣuṇīs, your minds are constantly restless; if you do not fix your thoughts, you will always be deceived and deluded. The sexual desire of women is fierce and sharp."
From this time forward, a bhikṣuṇī should not allow another person to shave her hair alone.

When shaving hair, she should have another bhikṣuṇī sit nearby. If the person shaving the hair should give rise to lustful thoughts and manifest strange signs, that bhikṣuṇī should say to him: "O worthy one!"
"You should know that this female body is a mere assemblage of flesh and bone, false and unreal; do not harbor improper thoughts toward a bhikṣuṇī, lest you invite the suffering of hell.
If a bhikṣuṇī should entertain such perverse thoughts, one should say to her: "Sister!..."

You have already renounced the household life and abandoned worldly concerns; you should now recollect what solemn vow you made when receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) amidst the two assemblies.
As the Blessed One has said, those defiled by sensual desires possess little flavor but many faults.
"You should now abandon these evil thoughts and maintain the mind of one who has gone forth.
It is well if she speaks thus; if she does not so inform her, the accompanying nun incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (dharma-āpatti).
The setting was as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Gulatānandā exhorted a certain householder to construct a nunnery for her, and many bhikṣuṇīs came to reside there.
Later, at another time, five hundred merchants came from the south toward Śrāvastī; seeking a place to stay, they were unable to find one, so they took temporary rest by the roadside.
As the sun was about to set and rain began to fall again, they each sat with their cheeks in their palms, filled with sorrow.
At that time, the nun Khuddā (Tulā) saw them and asked, "O noble ladies!
Why do you sit thus?"
"The heavens have already sent down rain; why do you not quickly gather up the goods you are carrying and seek a place to store them?
He replied, "Noble One!"
"We guests have searched everywhere for a place to stay, yet now the people of this city lack benevolence and righteousness; they refuse to rent out rooms.
Knowing this, what shall we do? The nun said, "Sons!..."
"The night has already advanced with the stars appearing and it is now raining; why do you not say that a higher price should be given?
If all these goods are not collected and secured, they will all be ruined—who would then be willing to take them?"
He replied, "Noble One!
Observe that the sentiments of these people are difficult to fathom; even if one were to offer double the price, they would not accept it."
"This is my own evil karma; what more can I say?
Be patient until daybreak, and only then may we move on to seek another place. The nun said:
"O sons! If you can indeed double [the amount], you may enter the temple.
They replied:
“Excellent! It shall be as the Noble One has said.
They then immediately moved into the monastery.

At that time, the nun Thullanandā also entered the monastery and expelled all the resident nuns, leasing the quarters to merchants. As the nuns dispersed in the mud and rain under the darkness of night, they headed for other monasteries with their robes completely soaked through.
Having arrived at the monastery, that nun asked:
"Sisters! For what reason have you come through the rain at such a late hour?"
They all then recounted the matter in detail.
Upon hearing these words, the nuns who possessed few desires all censured her together, saying:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī cause a donor to build a monastery, only to drive the nuns out and rent it to laypeople?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not rent a monastery to laypeople; whoever rents it shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The circumstances were the same as those previously described.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Tullānandā entered the place where men wash, scrubbing her body with bricks to bathe.
When the men saw her, desire arose within them, and they said to one another,
"Look at this shaven-headed nun, imitating us by bathing!"
Because of this, they gave rise to derision and laughter.
When the matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should not scrub one's body for bathing among those who are foolish and dark-minded, whose hearts are disordered by lust."
"A bhikṣuṇī who rubs her body with a brick incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The summary verse for the tenth section of the seventh chapter says:
"One must not rub [the body] with bone or stone, nor with wood or the fist;"
"One may only rub the body with the hand; other objects are entirely improper.
The setting and circumstances were as before.

Since the Buddha did not permit nuns to scrub their bodies with bricks, the nuns instead used bone, stone, wood, or even their fists to scrub their bodies, which resulted in the same fault as before. The Buddha said:
"One should rub with the hands.
If, after removing [the dirt] from the hands, one uses another object to rub the body, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The summary verse for the eighth section says:
The section on the confession before the stūpa; One who has been assigned [to a task] should not keep [extra items];
Not sharing with a woman due to her being a wife; Writing medicine, the three robes, and snakes.
The first sub-section of the eighth door is summarized in this verse:
Except for repairing damage to a stūpa, Upāli, one must not transgress the regulations of the Saṃgha.
Nuns may enter when there is no obstacle; instructions and admonitions should be given according to the occasion.
The setting and circumstances are as before.

After the body of the bhikṣu Mahānāman had been cremated, the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs collected his remaining bones and constructed a stūpa in a spacious location. They placed exquisite silk banners, canopies, and flower garlands atop the stūpa and made offerings with sandalwood-scented water.

Furthermore, two nuns skilled in chanting were appointed to carry powdered earth and pure water daily. Whenever they saw visiting bhikṣus from other regions arriving, they would provide them with earth and water to wash their hands and feet, offer them incense and flowers, lead them forward while chanting praises, and circumambulate the stūpa.

Later, at another time, there was an arhat bhikṣu named Kapphiṇa who, traveling through the countryside with five hundred disciples, arrived at the road leading to Śrāvastī and stayed by the side of a stūpa.
If an Arhat does not reflect when he is unaware of past events, and sees that stupa from afar, he thinks to himself:
"Who has newly constructed this stupa for the fingernails and hair of the Tathāgata?"
"I shall pay my respects.
He then went there at once.

When the two nuns saw that he had arrived, they gave him earth and water for him to wash his hands and feet; they presented him with incense and flowers, led the way while chanting praises, and escorted the five hundred people as they circumambulated the stupa. Having paid their respects, they departed.
Not far from the stūpa, the Venerable Upāli was sitting in meditative seclusion beneath a tree;
seeing him, he asked: "Venerable Kapphiṇa!"
"One should examine whose stūpa one ought to pay homage to.
Then he had this thought: "Venerable Upāli!"
"Why does he cause me to focus my mindfulness? Whose stūpa should I contemplate?

He then observed and saw the skeletal remains of the bhikṣu Mahānāman within the stūpa. Because that monk still possessed the habitual tendencies of anger, [Upāli] felt resentment and turned back to reply, "Venerable Upāli!..."
“Venerable sir, you dwell here while the Buddha-dharma is like a swelling; why do you neglect it and fail to inquire?
When Upāli heard this, he remained silent and did not respond.
At that time, the Arhat said to his disciples:
"Venerable ones!
If you are able to respectfully receive the Great Master’s teaching, you should go together to the place where the bricks are piled; each person should take a brick and destroy that stūpa."
At that time, the assembly of disciples, having received their teacher’s instruction, each took a brick and in a short while had them all destroyed.
When the two bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they broke out into loud wailing and quickly went to inform the rest of the bhikṣuṇī community.
At that time, the group of twelve nuns and other nuns who had not yet abandoned desire heard of the destruction of the stupa and wept aloud, crying:
"Today our elder brother has finally passed away!"
Then the bhikṣuṇī Dhanika asked the two nuns: "Sisters!
Who told them that?"
She replied, "Sister!
He is a visiting monk and there is no way for me to know; the Venerable Upāli is staying nearby and spoke to the guest."
Then the nun Tullānandā replied, "Little sister!

As soon as I heard this, I knew that this man who previously shaved my head had committed such an evil deed; though he has left the household life, his innate nature has not changed, and he ought to be severely punished until he is ruined."
As the World-Honored One has said:
"One who ruins the assembly should not be retained.
I should now depart; how could I abandon them?
Filled with great rage, she took a sharp blade, an iron awl, and a wooden drill, and went to where the Venerable One was staying, intending to take his life.
At that time, Upāli saw the nuns approaching in haste from afar and thought to himself:
"Judging by the urgency of these nuns' movements, they must surely have some ulterior motive to harm me; I should observe them closely."
He immediately entered meditative concentration and perceived that the nuns, each harboring malice, were about to come and harm him.

At that moment, the Venerable One felt a sense of urgency; without employing his supernormal powers to empower his great robe, he simply withdrew his mind and entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
When the nuns arrived, they hacked at him indiscriminately with knives and pierced his entire body with iron awls and wooden drills.
At that time, by the power of his meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the Venerable One ceased all breathing, becoming no different from one who was dead.
The bhikṣuṇīs deliberated, saying:
"We have already slain our evil-doing enemy; since our vengeance is accomplished, we should return to the monastery.
Having said this, they abandoned him and departed.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli emerged from meditative concentration; seeing that his robe had been damaged, he returned to his dwelling.
When the bhikṣus saw him, they asked:
"Venerable one!"
"Why is this so? He replied, "Venerable sir!"
"The bhikṣuṇīs have nearly killed me. He asked,
"For what reason?"
The Venerable One then recounted the matter in detail.
Upon hearing this account, all the bhikṣus of few desires collectively censured him and deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Venerable sir, you should know!..."

If a bhikṣuṇī harbors resentment toward a bhikṣu, she should merely refrain from paying him homage, showing respect, or greeting him; how could it be appropriate for her to impulsively take a sharp blade, an iron awl, or a wooden drill in her hand and go to kill the venerable Upāli, nearly depriving him of his life? How could such a thing be possible?
One person said: "Venerable sirs!
This matter has already passed and cannot be pursued further; what do you intend to do from this point forward?"
He said, "What do you wish to do with this?
It would be appropriate to go and inform the Buddha."
He further said:
"There is no need to inform the Buddha; let us simply establish a regulation that none of the bhikṣuṇīs shall enter the Jeta Grove.
Once the people had collectively established this clear rule, when the bhikṣuṇīs heard of it, they all refused to enter and showed no respect.

At that time, it was the constant custom of Mahāprajāpatī to come daily to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet before departing as she pleased; when she entered the monastery, a bhikṣu said to her, “Gautamī!”
"The community of monks has established a regulation not permitting nuns to enter the monastery,
and they have barred me from entering. She replied, "Noble One!"
"How could I possibly commit such a great transgression as they do?
He replied, "The community of monks has established a regulation; what can I do about it?"
The nun then turned back and returned to her residence.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the reason] yet asking deliberately, said to Ānanda:
"Is it that Mahāprajāpatī has fallen ill?"
He replied, "I am free from illness.
[The other asked,] "If that is so, why have you not come?"
Then Ānanda reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
“Ānanda! These bhikṣus have unilaterally established this regulation.”
However, since the bhikṣuṇīs are dependent upon the bhikṣus, if they do not enter the monastery, they will fail to show respect.

From this day forward, whenever bhikṣuṇīs enter a monastic residence, they must first inform the bhikṣu guarding the gate before they may enter; furthermore, they should not provide instruction to the bhikṣuṇīs.
As the Blessed One said:
"One should enter only after making a formal announcement (*jñapti*)," yet the nuns did not know how to perform this announcement.
The Buddha said:
"When a bhikṣuṇī enters a monastery, she should announce as follows:
'Venerable ones, please observe; I wish to enter the monastery.
The gate-keeping bhikṣu should then ask the bhikṣuṇī:"
"Sisters! You who do not harbor obstacles and do not carry knives or awls may enter.
If one enters a monastic temple without having made such an announcement, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (vayattika).
If a bhikṣu sees a bhikṣuṇī entering a monastery and does not inquire [about her], he incurs the same offense as before.
As the Blessed One said:
"A bhikṣu should not instruct bhikṣuṇīs," yet at that time the group of six bhikṣus continued to instruct them without ceasing. The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣuṇī has committed an offense, and the bhikṣu-saṃgha has not yet granted her leave, should one nonetheless proceed to instruct her, one incurs a *vyatikrama* (transgression of the Dharma).
As it is with the rules for instruction, the same applies to the *poṣadha* and the *pravāraṇā*."
The second sub-section of the eighth chapter, summarized in verse, says:
A nun’s confession must not be treated lightly; In the *pravāraṇā*, one does not perform the *poṣadha*;
One should mutually offer apologies; And one should know the proper seating for the assembly of nuns.
The setting is the same as before.

At that time, there was a nun who received instruction from a bhikṣu. Because she was dissatisfied with him, he rebuked her and told her to leave. Once she had returned to the monastery, her teacher asked her to perform an act of repentance. She went to his room to offer her apologies; the details are as extensively described above.
At that time, when the bhikṣu saw her coming to pay his respects and repent, he stepped over her head with his foot and departed; the nun then returned silently to the nunnery.
When the other nuns saw her and asked, "Sister!..."
"Have you already finished paying your respects to the preceptor? He replied,
"May I never again encounter such a teacher."
He asked, "For what reason? and she answered him fully with the details of the matter.
When the nuns heard this, they all spoke in reproach: "Sisters!
Observe how he treats women with such contempt; when asked for alms out of joy, he did not accept them, and moreover, he walked away trampling her head with his foot."
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"It is indeed appropriate that the community of nuns should be subject to such reproach. From this day forward, when a nun comes to perform repentance, you must not cast her head over and walk away; whoever acts in this manner shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
"When a bhikṣuṇī is being reprimanded, she should not hastily seek to offer an apology; rather, she must follow the proper sequence before seeking *kṣamāpanā* (expiation).
They all did not know what that sequence was.

"You should first dispatch a bhikṣu, or a bhikṣuṇī, or an upāsaka, or an upāsikā, to the teacher's presence to skillfully employ expedient means so as to gladden his heart, and only then perform the confession."
The setting is the same as before.

As the Buddha has taught, one should perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony based on three grounds: what has been seen, heard, or suspected. When the monks had finished the summer retreat and completed the *pravāraṇā*, they then performed the *poṣadha*.
A certain monk said: "I observe that both the *poṣadha* and the *pravāraṇā* serve the purpose of purification; therefore, I know that the *poṣadha* is itself the *pravāraṇā*."
Some said, "The *pravāraṇā* and the *poṣadha* are two distinct matters.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Although these two matters differ, both serve the purpose of purification; therefore, you should know that once the *pravāraṇā* has been performed, there is no need for further *poṣadha*.
The setting of the occasion is the same as before.

At that time, some bhikṣus who already harbored mutual animosities and could not bear one another began to seek out each other's faults. During the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, amidst the great assembly, they recalled their grievances and cross-examined one another, each proclaiming violations regarding precepts, views, conduct, and livelihood.

At that time, all those who were close friends, as well as the two teachers and their fellow students, each formed factions and, because of this, engaged in strife and contention; they caused a great schism in the Saṃgha and gave rise to divergent views.
There were some neutral persons who restrained one another, saying:
"Venerable ones! Do not engage in quarreling; abide in the mind of one who has gone forth."
As the Blessed One has said:

"If there are bhikṣus in a certain place who are engaged in mutual strife and contention, dwelling in mutual recrimination, I would not even wish to hear of it, much less go there; however, if the matter should be settled, I shall certainly go."
If that bhikṣu abandons three dharmas and frequently practices three other dharmas,
what are the three dharmas he abandons?
They are the abandonment of the wholesome root of non-attachment, the wholesome root of non-hatred, and the wholesome root of non-delusion.
What are the three things that are frequently practiced?
They are the frequent practice of the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion.
Those bhikṣus will then become angry and contentious, engaging in mutual strife and dispute, and they will dwell harboring resentment as they engage in further mutual recrimination.
If that bhikṣu abandons three things and frequently practices three things, what are the three things he abandons?
They are the abandonment of the three unwholesome roots: namely, greed, hatred, and delusion.
What are the three dharmas that should be practiced frequently?
They are the frequent cultivation of the three roots of goodness: non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
Monks who practice these will not be angry or contentious, nor will they engage in mutual strife, dispute, or malicious recrimination.
"Therefore, O bhikṣus! You should abandon unwholesome dharmas and practice wholesome deeds.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not cease their quarreling; some neutral persons among them attempted to restrain them, saying:
"Venerable ones!
Do not engage in strife; abide in the mind of one who has gone forth.
Yet those bhikṣus, harboring anger that did not subside, continued to quarrel with one another.
When the lay travelers saw this, they all felt contempt and shame, saying:
"When these shaven-headed śramaṇas perform the *pravāraṇā*, they lack the mind of renunciation and constantly harbor strife.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Monks, it is only right that householders and brahmins should find this censurable.

From this day forward, if a monk knows that another monk has a grievance against him, he must not perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony together with him in one place; he must first offer an apology before they may do so together.”

At that time, when the monks were performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, they offered their apologies [to one another], yet their hearts of resentment and contention increased further and they could not let go of them. The Buddha said:
"On the day of the *pravāraṇā*, one should not offer apologies; rather, one ought to offer them in advance seven or eight days prior."
As the Blessed One has said:
"One should proactively perform confession seven or eight days in advance. At that time, all the bhikṣus collectively performed confessions and apologies. The Buddha said:
"No bhikṣu should perform a formal confession; rather, those who have harbored resentment or whose minds are at odds should offer apologies and together request one another's reconciliation."
The setting is as before.
As the Blessed One has said:
"Every five years, one should hold the Uṣṇīṣa Great Assembly."

At that time, the various brahmins, elders, and householders each vied for preeminence and held an unrestricted great assembly (*anavadya-mahā-pariṣad*), where both divisions of the Saṃgha gathered like clouds.
As the Blessed One said:
"Each shall sit according to the order of seniority by years of ordination.
At that time, when the nuns sat according to their seniority, there was great clamor; the Buddha said:

"Women are by nature covetous; therefore, during a large assembly, two, three, or four should sit in succession according to order, while the remaining nuns may sit as they please in places where they know one another."
The third sub-section of the eighth chapter, summarized in verse, says:
One should not perform the *poṣadha* in front of the gate; Two nuns must necessarily be appointed.
When the time for the *poṣadha* arrives, Appoint a person to wait for the nuns' announcement.
The setting is the same as before.
As the Blessed One has said:

"The formal acts (*karmas*) of the bhikṣus are distinct, and the formal acts of the bhikṣuṇīs are distinct, except for those formal acts performed in common. At the time of the *poṣadha*, all the bhikṣuṇīs came to the Jetavana grove to perform the *poṣadha*; the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs then performed the *poṣadha* together at the main gate.
When the various householders, brahmins, and others saw the commotion, they all came together to watch and stood there.
Having asked about this matter, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not perform the poṣadha ceremony at the entrance of a gate."

At that time, the bhikṣus performed the *poṣadha* ceremony with the bhikṣuṇīs inside the nunnery; because they gathered together, much idle chatter ensued. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"For this reason, a bhikṣu should not perform the *poṣadha* ceremony with bhikṣuṇīs within a nunnery."
The nuns did not know [the time] and returned to the monastery. The Buddha said:
"When the nuns have come halfway, the bhikṣus should go there and perform the Poṣadha together with them.
At that time, the bhikṣus followed the instruction and acted accordingly.

At that time, there was an elder brahmin traveling along the road who encountered a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī performing the poṣadha ceremony midway. He conceived a strange thought and gave rise to a false discrimination, saying to himself in consultation with others:
"What are these shaven-headed śramaṇas, male and female, discussing?"
One person said: "Observe this situation; what more is there to discuss?
While we were speaking privately at home, the nun overheard our words and now speaks of them here in this secluded place to the bhikṣus."

Having heard this, the bhikṣus reported it to the royal household, saying, "Whatever fines and punishments the King imposes upon us are all due to the slanders of these shaven-headed men and shaven-headed women.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:

"One should not perform the *poṣadha* ceremony midway. On the day of the *poṣadha*, two nuns should be appointed to go to the community of monks every half-month to announce their purity and request instruction."
The nuns then sent those who were powerless; when they went before the Saṃgha, they were unwilling to declare their state of purity. The Buddha said:
"One who is capable should be sent."
"Two people are difficult to find," the Buddha said.
"One person who possesses sufficient strength may go among the Saṃgha.
Although he arrived at the monastery and beheld the majestic and solemn presence of the Buddha and the great assembly of monks, toward whom should he direct his declaration of purity (*poṣadha*)?
She returned immediately, at which time the community of nuns had not yet performed the *poṣadha*.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One nun should be appointed to come and inform [the monks]. Although the community appointed one nun, she likewise did not know how to proceed, and thus the same fault occurred as before.
The Buddha said:
"The appointed bhikṣu should stand at the gate; when he arrives, [the candidate] should announce it.
Having first received this announcement, he should inform the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha should then appoint an instructor by means of the formal motion and proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman)."
The fourth sub-section of the eighth chapter, summarized in verse, says:
Being dispatched, one should not avoid going; One must inquire after the teacher’s name;
Wearing a cap as a bowl-bag; And for a nun, it is improper to tie flower garlands.
The setting is the same as before.
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu has been appointed to wait for a bhikṣuṇī to announce that she has purified herself, even though he is at the doorway, when the bhikṣuṇī arrives, he shall inform her, saying:"
"Do not come near me!
Do not touch me!
she cried, and immediately she ran away.
The nun waited but was unable to return to her own monastery; consequently, the community of nuns was unable to perform the *poṣadha* ceremony.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu who has been appointed [as a messenger] should not run away."
One should receive it as follows, speaking these words:
"Sister! Please sit; do not touch me closely; you may declare your purity."
"If one does not accept the invitation and instead runs away, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
As the World-Honored One said:
"A person should be appointed to stay at the gate to await the instruction for the bhikṣuṇīs," yet the appointed person arrived late at the gateway.
At that time, there was a naked ascetic wearing a woolen shawl who was contemplating the wheel of birth and death beneath her door;
seeing him, the nun thought to herself, "I should approach him and inform him of my purity."
He immediately prostrated at his feet, joined his palms, and crouched down, saying:
"Venerable One, please attend to me!
He then thought silently:
"I shall now observe what this shaven-headed female śramaṇa has to say. [She replied:

"The nun of Rājakārāma sent me here specifically to inquire after and pay homage at the feet of the noble assembly in Jeta’s Grove, asking whether you are free from illness and affliction, whether your daily life is light and easy, and whether your strength is superior to usual and you are dwelling in peace and happiness?"
"On the day of the *poṣadha*, the community of bhikṣuṇīs shall all declare their purity.
Having heard this, the non-Buddhists did not understand the words and remained silent.
The bhikṣuṇīs then instructed them, saying:
"Noble one! You should say: 'So be it.'"
Hearing this, she did not understand and, feigning a grunt, nodded her head and departed.
Then those two nuns returned to their own monastery. Later, when the preceptor of the nuns arrived at the gate and waited for a short while, seeing that no nuns had come, he returned to his quarters.
When the one who recites the precepts has performed the single formal motion (*jñapti*), the official in charge addresses the assembly, saying:
"Who will bring the nuns' report on purity?
No one in the assembly answers.
"This is me. Everyone thought to themselves:
"Is it not that the community of nuns has failed to come and announce their purity?"
"Did you not send anyone else to inquire whether she had arrived?

After the Elder had recited the precepts and completed the *poṣadha*, when it came time for the subsequent recitation of the precepts, he informed the nuns of his purity (*śuci*). However, the nun who had previously come to the gate did not return to her own monastery, as no one was seen there; thus, the formal purification (*pravāraṇā*) of the community of bhikṣuṇīs was not accomplished.
The next day, all the bhikṣuṇīs came to the place where the monks were and asked,
"Venerable Saṃgha!
For what reason do you not accept the declaration of purity from the community of bhikṣuṇīs?"
The bhikṣus said, "Sisters!
On the previous day of the poṣadha, which nun was appointed to come and announce the purity?"

The two nuns who were there previously stepped forward and replied, "We arrived at the entrance of the gate and saw this venerable one in such a form and demeanor, contemplating the wheel of birth and death; we then informed him that we were pure and subsequently returned to our own monastery."

When the bhikṣus heard it said that the person’s physical appearance was consistent with his declaration of purity, they immediately recognized him as a naked ascetic (nirgrantha) and discussed among themselves:
"This bhikṣuṇī has declared her state of purity before a non-Buddhist."
They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:
"Because the bhikṣuṇīs came to announce their purity without being asked for the name of the instructor, this fault has arisen; however, there is no offense for the two bhikṣuṇīs who announced it."
From this time forward, when a bhikṣuṇī comes to announce her purity (*poṣadha*), you should ask for the name of the instructor bhikṣu,
saying: "Venerable one, what is your name?"
"If one does not inquire in this manner when another has declared their purity (*pārisuddhi*), one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).

As the Blessed One had stated that when a nun declares her purity, she must state her name, when a nun came to declare it, those who were already acquainted with her also asked for her name. The Buddha said:
"In the case of a bhikṣu whom you already know, there is no need to ask again."
The setting was as before.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī was afflicted by the suffering of illness, and a nun came to visit and inquire after her: "Noble Lady!"
"Why do you not leave the room?
She replied, "Young maiden!"
"My body is afflicted with illness.
He asked, "What did you previously hold that caused the illness to be immediately eliminated?"
He replied, "When I was a layman, I wore a cap on my head.
[The Buddha asked,] "If that is so, why do you not wear one now?"
He replied: "I have now gone forth as a renunciant; since the World-Honored One has not permitted it, how could I possibly carry one?
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“A bhikṣuṇī staying within a monastery should wear a head-covering.
This occurred in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a brahmin in this city who went about begging for alms; he entered a certain house and said:
"I beg for alms.
The host replied, "I have nothing; you should depart."
As this person was leaving, Mahāprajāpatī entered from the opposite direction to beg for alms.
He thought to himself: "Did she not give to me alone?"
Seeking a flaw or opening, he stood waiting and did not depart.
The host thought to himself:
"It is my good fortune that the Mother of Buddhas has come to enter my home."
She immediately quickly spread out a seat and invited him to sit; they exchanged greetings and laughter, and she took the finest food, filled a bowl, and offered it to him.
When the brahmin saw this, jealousy arose in his heart, and he said to the nun:
"Let me see what kind of delicious food you have obtained in your bowl."
The nun showed him her bowl and immediately spat into it.
Mahāprajāpatī said, "Child,
why have you now defiled the food in the bowl?"
"If you request it, I shall give it to you.
At that time, the brāhmaṇa remained silent and did not respond.
The bhikṣuṇī informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha then thought to himself:
"The nature of women is that they possess little majesty; having caused foolish men to commit evil deeds, they bring about much suffering as retribution.
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"From this day forward, when a bhikṣuṇī goes out for alms, she should carry a bowl-bag to cover [the bowl] as she departs."
The nuns did not understand what a "bowl-sack" (*pātraka*) was.
The Buddha said:

"One should make a square布袋 (*pūta*) one cubit on each side. Attach two handles to the top corners and place the bowl inside. Short loops should be provided for the corners; when taking it out to go begging for food, this will prevent dust from settling upon it and make it easy to carry."

"In the land of China, such alms-bowl bags have not existed until now; because of their downward-pointing corners, the bowl remains steady and does not sway, unlike flat head-cloths which shift and cause the contents to spill."

When making it, one should take a piece of cloth measuring two small cubits and fold it so that it is square; trim the sides and use them to form the horizontal straps. When used, this is extremely practical and secure. This occurred while [the Buddha] was in Śrāvastī.

The people of this eastern land are fond of garden flowers; once, on a certain occasion, the people within the city held a great festival, each bringing various kinds of exquisite food and drink as well as musical instruments, and together they proceeded to a fragrant garden.
At that time, a certain man sent a messenger to inform his wife that she should prepare a flower garland and have it delivered immediately.

His household possessed a grove of exquisite flowers; following these instructions, the wife entered the garden to gather them, but as she did not know how to weave them herself, she immediately summoned a garland-maker.

At that time, it happened to be a festival in the city where all the garland-makers were occupied with work for others; she searched everywhere but could not find anyone, and her heart was filled with anxiety and worry:
"My husband has ordered me to weave exquisite flower garlands, yet I do not know how to do it myself. Having sought help in vain, what am I to do?"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Dhanika entered the house while begging for alms and said,
"Young girl, give me some cakes from your bowl. She replied:
"Noble one! Please depart;
I am currently burdened by grief and have no one to bestow [this] upon.
The nun said:
“Maiden! What business do you have?
She then related everything in detail, and the nun said:
"Why do you not tie it? He replied,
"I did not know how before."
He then asked the nun:
"Noble lady! Do you understand?"
He replied, "Young woman!
I am now advanced in years; when I was young in the past, what was there that I did not understand?"
“Noble One! If that is so, out of compassion for me, please deign to weave this garland. He replied:
“Maiden! If you can provide me with various kinds of food and drink, I shall form a bond with you. She replied:
"I will give it to you.
The nun then set her bowl aside, sat down with her legs extended, and began intently weaving the garland.
When the woman saw this, she marveled at her skill; her heart was filled with great joy, and she gave much food from her bowl.
The nun went to another house and again helped them string garlands;
having obtained much food and drink, she was returning to her own monastery when the garland-makers arrived at their daughter's place and said, "Give us the flowers; we shall string them now."
He replied, "Why have you arrived so late?
The flowers have already been gathered and are being taken toward the garden."
He asked, "Who has bound it? He replied:
“Venerable Uppalavaṇṇā! he then reviled her, saying:
“A daughter of the śramaṇas performs such unrighteous deeds; how can you deprive me of my means of livelihood?”
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"It is not the dharma of a śramaṇī and is rightly subject to reproach. Therefore, the community of nuns should not tie garlands; whoever does so commits an offense of transgression against the dharma."
The Buddha had prohibited nuns from weaving flower garlands. At that time, it was the occasion of the *Cūḍā-pañcavārṣika* assembly and the five- and six-year assemblies.

King Prasenajit, Queen Vaidehī, Queen Vāsabhakhattiyā, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, Visākhā Mṛgāramātā, the former minister Yaśas, Mahānāman, and other laymen and laywomen each sought the most excellent offerings, vying with one another to present fragrant flowers. Furthermore, monks and nuns from all directions had all gathered there; while the flowers and garlands were in great abundance, there were very few people to weave them into garlands.
At that time, those with faith who could be found to weave flowers were few; they therefore addressed the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"We are now making offerings to the Great Master; would you be able to assist us in weaving these flower garlands?"
The nuns replied, "Do you not know that the Great Teacher has given instruction forbidding us nuns from binding ourselves with flower garlands?
How then can we wish to assist you in making merit?"
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣuṇīs may tie flower garlands for the sake of the Three Jewels.

However, some bhikṣuṇīs stood at the main gate or in the corridors with their legs stretched out wide while tying flower garlands; when lay travelers saw this, they mocked them, saying: [text continues]
"Noble ladies! You are all daughters of garland-makers who have come forth to renounce the world.
The nuns were ashamed and remained silent.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"Since worldly people have criticized them as being unreasonable, the bhikṣuṇīs should not tie flower garlands at the main gate, along the corridors, or under the eaves. Those who do so shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
"One who unties a garland of knots should do so in a secluded place and not allow it to be ridiculed by the laity.
The summary verse for the fifth section of the eighth chapter says:
"One should not keep copper vessels; one should restore wine that has turned sour."
Renting rooms to lay travelers; deceiving others by practicing as physicians or shamans.
The circumstances were as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Tullānandā went to a household of copperware makers and said:
“O worthy one! Could you perhaps fashion for me a large copper bowl? He replied:
“Noble One! Why is it that my past karma cannot [accomplish this]? He asked.
"Do you wish to make it large or small?
He replied, "It must be made very large."
He asked, "Venerable One!
What use have you for such a large alms bowl?"
The nun said, "You poor thing!
Will you not take payment for making it for me?"
"I shall give you a good price; you ought to make it large.
The artisan thought to himself, "What harm is there to him making it large as he wishes?"
Mahāpātra saw this and said,
"Make another smaller one for me that will fit inside this bowl.
They made another for him, and in this manner they gradually produced seven layers, all of which fit inside the bowl.

Tulānanda had the female novices scrub and polish [the bowls] until they were clean, then strung them together in sequence with threads of five colors and placed them inside. Whenever there was an invitation or summons, she would have a junior nun carry them on her head; having arrived, she would open the container and set them out beside her as she sat down.
A lay traveler saw him and asked,
"Venerable sir, have you opened a copperware shop today? He replied:
"Fool! How could you possibly know the vessels I require?
The largest is for holding rice; the next is for soups and stews; the next is for receiving fine morsels; and the remaining one is for miscellaneous flavors."
He replied, "If that were so, we would require even more; when other items arrive, there will be no place to put them.
The other then remained silent.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:

"The bhikṣuṇīs keeping copper bowls have such faults as these. From this day forward, no bhikṣuṇīs shall keep copper bowls for themselves; if any do so, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
"Except for the copper spoon, the salt dish, and the copper bowl for drinking water.
The setting is as before.

At that time, there was a householder’s wife who gave birth to a daughter; her right eye was crossed, which was considered an inauspicious sign, so no one would marry her. There was another householder who had recently married a wife, but she died shortly thereafter. This happened seven times in succession, and people at the time called him "the Householder Who Kills His Wives."
He further asked another woman, seeking her to be his wife, but she replied,
"How could I possibly wish to kill this girl?
He then sought a widow, but she said:
"How could I ever wish to take my own life?
Since he had no wife, he managed the household affairs himself.
At that time, a friend came to visit him and asked:
"Why do you manage your own household affairs?
Is it not possible for you to seek a wife? He replied:

"I am of little merit; not long after I married a wife, she passed away. In this manner, I took another and so on up to seven times, yet they all died. Consequently, the people of the time called me 'the husband-killer'."
He replied, "Why do you not seek further?
He then explained the matter in detail, just as described above.
"If that is so, why not ask for the daughter with the piercing eyes?
He replied, "She will not give her up either."
He replied, "I know that the daughter in that household has been raised for a long time; she must surely be ready for marriage, so I shall go there to seek her.
When he saw him, the man asked:
"What do you require for coming here? He replied,
"I wish to seek a daughter in marriage."
“Who is this girl? “She is one whose eyes have a piercing gaze.
The father said:
"It shall be as you wish; we should arrange the wedding together on such-and-such a day.
Consequently, they sought out fine wine from neighboring households, and all the taverns immediately prepared it for them.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā entered the house of Tongjing to beg for alms. A member of the family replied, "I am busy preparing wine;
there is no opportunity to give you food.
The nun asked for the reason, and he then informed her in detail:
"My wine has soured," he said. The nun asked,
"Why did you not cause it to turn into good wine?"
He replied, "Noble One! I do not understand this;
if you possess a method, I would be grateful if you would kindly bestow it upon me."
The nun said, "Young woman!
I am now advanced in years and no longer engage in such things; when I was young, what was there that I did not know?"
He replied, "Noble One! Out of compassion for me,
please transform this wine so that it becomes good."
The nun said, "Young woman!
If you can provide me with the price for fine food, I will ensure your wine is excellent."
She replied, “Give much. The nun said:
"Bring out the wine jar; I shall examine it.
It was immediately carried out, and at that time, the nun Thullanandā looked up and down at the jar to see for what reason the wine had spoiled.
He then realized it was due to heat;

he immediately opened the windows and doors, had damp sand placed beneath the jars, and further took green moss to wrap around them. He fanned away the hot air, and because of the resulting coolness, the wine became good once again.
All his kinsmen gathered together, and all the taverns made preparations for him; wondering why he did not come to fetch any, they sent people to inquire:
"Why do you not take some wine?"
He replied, "My wine has turned excellent; there is no need to trouble yourself to fetch another. He asked:
“Who taught you how to restore spoiled wine to its original quality?
He replied, “Noble One!”
“Tūlanandā has been kind to me; she is capable of doing this.
She then spoke with derision:
“The Śramaṇī daughter of the Śākyas performs an unrighteous act.”
"How can you deprive me of my means of livelihood?
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This is not the way of a śramaṇī or a daughter of the Śākyas; it is rightly subject to reproach."
Therefore, nuns should not instruct others on how to transform already spoiled wine;
whoever does so commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The setting of the occasion is the same as before.

At that time, there was an elder who delighted in giving alms. Suddenly he fell ill, and his condition gradually grew grave and critical. Knowing that his life would soon come to an end, he bestowed all his wealth and possessions upon śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the solitary, beggars, virtuous friends, and his own kinsmen; yet there remained only one house that he had not yet given away to others.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Gulmavilāsinī heard of this and came to the house, saying: "Householder!
Generally, the gains of women are meager; when you are inclined to give, please grant us a small or large share."
He replied: "Noble One! You have arrived late;
my wealth and possessions have all been given away in charity, and this house alone remains."
The nun said: "Householder!
I originally intended to come with my face raised in hope; now that you have sent me back empty-handed, it does not accord with my original purpose."
He replied, "Noble One! This is the only room I have;
