if you wish to take it, I will not begrudge it to you for the rest of my life."
The nun said, “If that is so, I shall accept it now; may you be relieved of your illness.
Later, the elder passed away. His relatives gathered and, with a funeral bier adorned with blue, yellow, red, and white silks, escorted him to the charnel ground.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Tullānandā, hearing that the elder had passed away, went there in haste, sealed the room, and stood to one side.
When his kinsmen had finished cremating him and all returned home, they saw the house was sealed and asked, "Who closed it?"
The nun said, "The recipient has come herself to seal it. She replied:
"Noble one! To whom shall it be given?
The nun replied:
“Give it to me. “Noble one! If that is so, then let me hire it from you for now; I shall pay the price later.”
The nun asked, "Is it true or false? He replied:
"I truly will give it.
The nun then opened the door and let him enter.
At that time, some householders and brahmins came to her house and, hearing of these matters, all spoke in common reproach and disdain:
"A female ascetic of the Śākya clan has committed such an unrighteous act; how can she rent out her house to others?
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "This is not the way of a female ascetic; it is rightly subject to reproach."
"From this day forward, no bhikṣuṇīs shall rent out dwellings to others; those who do so shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The setting of the occasion is the same as before.
A certain elder was fond of giving; knowing he was about to die, he had given away everything except for one shop.
When the nun heard that they had come to beg for the items, the circumstances were identical to those previously described, until her death, after which the nun sealed them up.
People felt resentment and shame, and the bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If one rents out a shop [in such a manner], one commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
Fearing that it would be too cumbersome, the setting is abbreviated as before.

The nun Tullānandā entered the city to beg for alms and saw a female sorceress ringing a bell and wandering from house to house discussing omens of good and ill fortune; she obtained many material offerings, which were sufficient to support herself.
Thereupon, she thought to herself: "This is an excellent method; I shall do the same."

Having obtained the bell, he entered the city the following morning and went from house to house shaking it to produce a ringing sound. He bathed the bodies of men and women for them, falsely proclaiming good and bad fortune and speaking deceptively of future omens; thus, those suffering from illness were all cured through his "divine intervention."

Consequently, this became known throughout the royal city; there was no prayer or petition that was not brought forth with full sincerity, while other practitioners of sorcery and divination were no longer consulted.
At that time, the former physicians and sorcerers went to various people's homes and asked, "If you have any matters, I shall perform divinations and physiognomies for you."
The people replied, "Do not trouble yourself further;
we have a holy teacher who is well-versed in all matters. His divinations and medical treatments are entirely to our satisfaction."
He asked, "Who is this? and [the other] replied:
“Venerable Uppalavaṇṇā! Hearing this reproach, she spoke these words:
“An unrighteous daughter of the Śākyas, falsely practicing divination, you have robbed me of my livelihood.”
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"Nuns who practice as physicians or sorcerers commit such faults; by making false and deceptive claims, they invite the derision and reproach of the laity."
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now forbid nuns from practicing as physicians or shamans; should any do so, they shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 33.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu,
Fascicle Thirty-Four,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
The sixth sub-section of the eighth chapter, summarized in verse, says:
One should not bathe together with women, Nor should one wash against the current.
A base for the bowl should be provided, And one must not keep a lapis lazuli cup.
The setting is as before.
A certain woman went into the river to bathe her body; having finished bathing, she stepped onto the bank and stood there combing her hair.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Pūraṇā took some soap powder and went to bathe there. Seeing the woman combing her hair, she felt resentment and jealousy, and thought to herself:
"Stupid woman! You have combed your hair only because you wish to compete with me, as if I had originally been hairless all along?
You should be severely punished to deter future transgressions, so that even if you see me again, you will not dare to compete."
He then silently took powdered *āmala* fruit, sprinkled it upon her head, and rubbed it with his hand.
The woman asked, "Noble One!
What fault have I committed?"
"As soon as you have washed your hair, you sprinkle *āmra* powder upon my head.
The nun said, "You interpret it thus: [that I am your mother]."
“Tulanandā previously came here with no hair on her head;
since her head was not clean, she should have come back to wash it again.
The woman then spoke words of reproach and disdain.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"The bhikṣuṇīs have acted improperly; their conduct is rightly subject to reproach.
From this day forward, no bhikṣuṇīs shall apply mixed powders or similar substances to the clean-shaven hair of others. Whoever does so shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Udāyinī went with a group of nuns to bathe in a river. Thereupon, Udāyinī stood against the current in a place where the flow was swift, experiencing the pleasure of its touch.
The nuns asked, "Venerable One, what are you doing?"
He replied, "Little sister! I am experiencing the pleasure of touch."
The nuns replied, "Venerable One!
This is not a pure practice; it is improper to stand in a swift current and experience the pleasure of touch."
He replied:
"This is utterly pure; what irrationality is there?
If it were impure, who would have established the rules for it?"
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It is only natural that the nuns would incur such reproach.
From this day forward, the nuns must not stand against the current in swift-flowing waters to experience the pleasure of physical contact."
"If one accepts [the bowl] for pleasure, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The setting of the narrative is the same as before.
As the bhikṣuṇīs placed their bowls in various locations, rust eventually formed on the iron; furthermore, due to being tossed about or struck, many were damaged.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣuṇīs should not place their bowls anywhere at random; they should use a thin tin cover to protect the bowls."
Regarding what the Blessed One said concerning "enclosing the bowl with tin," the nuns wrapped their bowls entirely with tin. When lay travelers saw them, they asked:
"Noble ladies! What is this?"
He replied, "Venerable sir,
the Blessed One has prescribed that one should use a mendicant’s staff as a substitute for an alms bowl.
He reported this, saying:
"Noble one! Could it be that the Buddha has commanded us to wrap our alms bowls completely?
You are speaking falsely now; this is not a task to be performed by a śramaṇī of the Śākya clan."
Upon hearing this, the nun felt ashamed and remained silent, offering no reply.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, who said:

"It is only natural that lay travelers would find this offensive; therefore, nuns should not wrap their bowls entirely with tin. Instead, they may use a small pad just large enough to support the bottom of the bowl."
He performed various strange and extraordinary gestures, whereupon the Buddha said:
"This is not permissible. There are two kinds of substitutes: [text continues]."
"First, like the leaves of a Bodhi tree or a many-rooted tree;
second, like the palm of a hand.
The setting was as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā obtained a lapis lazuli cup. Then, a certain woman, having guests arrive, went to the nun's place and said:
"Noble Lady!..."
"I would be fortunate to borrow your lapis lazuli cup. The nun then asked,
"What do you intend to use it for?"
He replied, "Noble One!
My son-in-law has come; I have no cup with which to drink."
The nun took it and departed; however, he was not careful, and his hand slipped, causing it to break.
He said, "Noble lady!
I shall pay you its price."
The nun said, "Little sister!
There is no need for payment; just return my old cup to me."
He replied, "Noble One!
Please purchase another cup as a replacement."
The nun said, "I must have the old cup.
Thus they quarreled and contended.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"This fault has arisen because these bhikṣuṇīs keep lapis lazuli cups.
He then addressed the bhikṣus:
“Nuns must not keep lapis lazuli cups; if they do keep them, they commit an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The seventh sub-section of the eighth chapter, summarized in verse, says:
“The staff was established because of a woman; dancing while performing gave rise to an offense.”
"Eating moist cakes after having accepted an invitation; announcing the preaching of the Dharma to one's companions.
The setting for this account is the same as before.

There was a householder of great wealth and many possessions whose wife gave birth to a son; he was filled with great joy and invited his kinsmen to celebrate together. The husband and wife fell asleep in separate rooms and did not rise until daybreak.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu seeking alms who, seeing many doors, entered the house and became confused as to the way out; he proceeded deep inside until he reached the front of the elder’s chamber, whereupon the elder was startled awake.
The bhikṣu then passed by his wife, whereupon the elder saw him and said,
"He has committed an unrighteous act with my wife!
He immediately struck the bhikṣu until his head was split open and blood flowed, and his alms bowl was also broken.
The woman woke up and informed him, saying, "The bhikṣu has done no wrong; you may release him and let him go.
Then that bhikṣu, maintaining this same dignified demeanor, arrived at the Jetavana Grove, where the other bhikṣus asked him:
"Why is this so? he asked, and the matter was explained in full.
The bhikṣus reported these circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu begging for alms should not enter a multi-door household in haste; he should first mark the door with a cake or flour, and only then enter.
When a bhikṣu entered silently and a woman was seen fleeing naked, the laypeople felt disdain and shame. The Buddha said:
"When wishing to enter a house, one should make a sound to alert them."
He entered making a clamorous sound by "ha-ha"ing; the family members reported, "Sir, do you enter our home with the 'ha-ha' sound of a small child?"
He replied, "The Buddha commanded that one should enter making a sound; for this reason, I am laughing 'ha-ha'. He answered:
"There is no other expedient by which sound can be produced; is this 'ha-ha' the only thing capable of providing an alert?
The bhikṣu remained silent.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not enter another's house making the sound 'ha-ha'.
When the Buddha had prohibited this, [the monk] nevertheless entered while striking the door panels with his fist to make a noise. The family members, wondering at this, asked:
"Why have you broken our door?"
They remained silent and offered no reply.
The Buddha said, "One should not knock on the door; rather, one should make a *khakkhara* (monk’s staff).
The bhikṣus did not understand, so the Buddha said:

"A ring should be attached to the tip of the staff, circular like the rim of a cup; by shaking this small ring to make a sound as a warning, the dog will come out and bark, at which point one may strike it with the *khakkhara*. The Buddha said:
"One should not strike the dog with the staff; one should only raise it to frighten it."
At that time, there was a vicious dog whose anger intensified when it was frightened;
the Buddha said, "Take a handful of rice and throw it on the ground for it to eat.
When he went to the house of a person who lacked faith and shook his staff for a long time, he eventually became weary, yet the family members did not come out to inquire; the Buddha said:
"One should not shake [the bowl] for a long time; one may shake it two or three times. When no one asks for it, one must depart.
The setting of the occasion was as before.

At that time, a householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to a meal at his home. The community of bhikṣus all went to attend the offering, while the Buddha remained in the monastery, having someone fetch food for him.
For five reasons the Buddha permitted the taking of food. What are these five?
First, because he desired seclusion and tranquility.
Second, preaching the Dharma for the sake of gods and humans;
third, visiting those who are ill;
fourth, inspecting the bedding and furniture.
Fifth, the training rules were established for the sake of the śrāvakas.
Now, for the purpose of establishing these precepts, he remained within the monastery.
At that time, the elder temporarily provided leaf-shelters and directed the assembly to sit; it happened to be a time of cold rain.
The elder served rice gruel, followed by dry cakes, and then distributed *apūpa* cakes along with radishes.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who made a "hu-hu" sound while gulping down the gruel; another made a "ba-ba" sound while chewing the dry cakes; and another made a "lie-lie" sound while eating the *apūpa*.
The rain falling from the roof made a "suo-suo" sound, and the water being drunk from a jar made a "gu-gu" sound; these various sounds all blended together in a cacophony.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had previously been skilled in singing and dancing; upon hearing the melody, he was reminded of his former mastery of stringed instruments and could not restrain himself. He rose from his seat and, following the tune of the music, began to dance with his hands, saying to the great assembly:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Venerable sir, this is the sound 'hu-hu'; venerable sir, this is the sound 'ba-ba'; venerable sir, this is the sound 'la-la', this is the sound 'sa-so', and this is the sound 'ku-ku'."

Their snapping of fingers harmonized with one another so perfectly that it was never out of rhythm; those in the great assembly who lacked concentration immediately smiled, while those who were attentive were all struck with astonishment. Those serving the food could not help but laugh aloud, some even feeling contemptuous, and the donors were deeply perplexed.
The bhikṣu who had been invited to eat felt great shame; he took the food to the monastery, set it aside, and prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.
It is the natural custom of the World-Honored One to exchange friendly greetings with those who bring him food, asking:
"Has the assembly received sufficient fine food and eaten their fill?"
He said, "Venerable Sir!
Although the fine food is sufficient, the donor will surely find it strange."
He asked, "For what reason?
and related the circumstances in detail.

When the Blessed One had finished his meal, he went outside to wash his feet, then returned to his chamber and sat in meditative seclusion. When the time for the afternoon meal arrived, he arose from concentration, took a seat among the assembly of bhikṣus, and addressed the dancing bhikṣu, saying:
"With what intention did you perform a dance in the house of a donor?"
He replied: "Venerable sir,
I performed the dance with the intention of deriding him and with a mind of agitation."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu dances out of a state of agitation, he incurs an offense against the Dharma; if he does so with the intention of mocking another, there is no offense."
"O bhikṣus! All these faults arise from eating while making noise. Therefore, bhikṣus, you must not eat while making noise; whoever does so commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma."

After the Buddha had thus prohibited it, there were at that time some lay devotees who brought various dried cakes, radishes, and sugarcane to offer to the bhikṣus, yet none of them dared to accept them.
They asked: "Venerable One!
Before the Buddha appeared in the world, we all took non-Buddhist practitioners as our field of merit; [how is it now that we have come to rely on you?]"
“World-Honored One, since you have appeared in the world, you have been the most supreme among our fields of merit, such as ourselves.
We brought whatever meager offerings we had to present to you, yet you accepted none of them. Will this leave us without provisions for our journey when we reach future lives?”

Furthermore, as the Buddha taught regarding giving at the proper time: when new grain and various fruits have first ripened, if one first takes them to offer to those who possess the precepts and virtuous qualities, and only afterwards eats them oneself, one will obtain immeasurable merit.
“I only pray that, out of compassion, you will accept them for me.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

“These offerings should indeed be accepted. As for the dry cakes, they should be eaten mixed with the soup; as for the radishes and sugarcane, cut them into small pieces and eat them without making noise.”
The setting was as before.

At that time, a householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his home for a meal. The bhikṣus did not depart all at once but traveled in separate groups; having arrived at the house, they waited for the others, and until everyone had assembled, they informed the householder, saying, "You may serve the food now; we shall eat first."
Having finished eating, he departed.
When others arrived and were again served food, this process continued until the host became exhausted and said,
"Venerable ones!..."
"Wait until we are all seated; I shall eat at the same time.
Because this caused disturbance and vexation, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"When accepting an invitation from others, one should not go about in a disorderly manner. Those who arrive first should wait at the door until everyone has gathered, and only then enter together."
"If one goes away distractedly, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

As the Blessed One has said regarding not going distractedly, there was a sick bhikṣu whose attendant, having finished eating, took the food away only after [the patient] had eaten; thus, the patient remained waiting for the food and became emaciated by hunger.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There are five causes and conditions for which one may accept an invitation for a meal early and eat it in one's own room. What are these five?
First, those who are guests newly arrived;
second, those who are about to depart;
third, those whose bodies are afflicted by the suffering of illness.
"Fourth is the one who attends to the sick;
fifth is the one who serves as the administrator.
The setting for this account is the same as before.
At that time, there was an elder of great wealth and many possessions who, with a heart of faith and reverence, invited the Buddha and the community of monks to his home for a meal.
The World-Honored One did not go himself, but sent someone to take the food on account of five causes and conditions, as explained in detail above; now, a precept is established for this purpose.

Once the bhikṣus had finished eating, they immediately returned to the monastery; since the donor’s original intention was to hear the Dharma and not a single bhikṣu preached the Dharma for him, he consequently felt resentment and shame.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is indeed reasonable that they should be subject to reproach; therefore, the bhikṣus should not all return to the monastery immediately after finishing their meal.
If they depart at once, they commit an offense of transgression against the Dharma (vayadharmika-āpatti); they ought to preach the Dharma for them."
When the Buddha commanded that someone should preach the Dharma, the bhikṣus did not know who should do so.
The Buddha said:

"The elder (sthavira) should be requested to preach for them; if he is unable, the second in rank should be requested; if he also is unable, the third should be requested. If there is no one capable, they should be assigned by turn, or whoever is able should be invited in advance."
The setting was as before.

There was a certain householder who possessed faith; from time to time he would go to the Jeta Grove to hear the True Dharma. On one occasion, he invited the Buddha and the community of monks to his home to receive a meal.

The bhikṣus all departed; the World-Honored One remained as before. There are five causes and conditions, as explained in detail above, for which this rule was established: the Buddha does not go in person to receive food, but sends others to fetch it.

As the Blessed One has said, "If the meal is finished and the donor desires the Dharma, one who is capable of preaching should be appointed to remain and teach the Dharma while the rest of the assembly departs. Thus, they dispatched one person to remain and preach the Dharma, and the entire community departed.
At that time, the donor and his entire retinue gathered together in one place; possessing great majesty, they listened to the essential points of the Dharma and requested, saying:
"Noble One! Please teach us the Dharma."
Because the bhikṣu perceived the great power of that [layman], he felt fear and was unable to preach the Dharma. The householder thought to himself:
"I have many followers; because the bhikṣu is afraid, he does not proclaim it for me. I should preach it myself."
He replied: "O Noble One! As the Blessed One has said: "
"Giving brings great wealth; observing precepts leads to rebirth in heaven;
by single-minded cultivation one severs afflictions—this is the Dharma you should follow."
When that bhikṣu had heard these words, he remained silent and returned by the same way he had come.
Once he arrived at the monastery, the other bhikṣus asked him,
"Venerable one!..."
"Does he dwell there and preach the Dharma for them? They replied,
"O Venerable Ones!"
"I am left all alone with no companions or assistants; the donors and kinsmen are of great majesty and have all gathered together. I feel such fear that I am unable to preach the Dharma."
"The donor, seeing my state of mind filled with fear and trepidation, has instead proclaimed the sublime Dharma for me.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "What this bhikṣu says is reasonable; therefore, one should not cause [a single person] to preach the Dharma alone."
"From this day forward, four bhikṣus shall be appointed to accompany the Dharma-preacher.
The occasion for this occurred in Rājagṛha.
As the Blessed One had prescribed:
Regarding the rule that a bhikṣu preaching the Dharma should be accompanied by four companions: when there is a place where he is summoned to preach, a preacher and four companions are assigned.
However, at times these companion bhikṣus would go toward their own families or go out on errands without informing him at all; consequently, they were absent when needed for the occasion.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When accompanying a bhikṣu who is preaching the Dharma to another location, one should inform him before departing.
If one does not inform him, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
The eighth section, the eighth sub-chapter, is summarized in verse:
Purgative medicine, teeth with poison, The tongue-scraper should be washed;
Through the exhaustion of his karmic offenses, He realized arhatship.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
There was a brahmin who, not long after marrying his wife, fathered a son. When the boy had grown up, he went forth into homelessness within the True Dharma.
Later, at another time, his body suddenly became afflicted with illness. He went to a physician and said:
"Worthy sir! My body is diseased; please provide me with medical treatment."
He replied, "Noble one!
You may now take such a purgative as this, and your illness will be cured."
The bhikṣu took the medicine immediately; as soon as he had passed stool once, he rinsed himself clean with cold water, and the medicine did not descend.
When the physician came and asked, "Venerable One!..."
"Is this purgative effective? He replied,
"O worthy one!"
"The medicine has no potency; it causes only diarrhea.
The physician said, "Venerable One!"
"Was it washed clean with cold water? He replied, "It was."
The physician said,
"Venerable One!
How can you cause diarrhea by washing with cold water?"
"Virtuous one, you may now take the aforementioned purgative again, but do not wash yourself; only when the diarrhea has nearly ceased should you wash.
He replied, "Virtuous one!"
"The Buddha has not yet granted permission.
The physician said,
"Venerable One!"
"The rules for medicine should be followed thus; they must not be contravened.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If this is the case, I now grant permission: while the diarrhea has not yet ceased, one should properly wipe clean."
The bhikṣus did not know with what object to wipe themselves.
The Buddha said:
"One should use a clod of earth, or a tree leaf, or a piece of torn cloth or old paper to wipe oneself clean; once the diarrhea has ceased, one should wash thoroughly with warm water."
The setting was as before.

In a certain forest there lived a venomous snake. Some shepherds set fire to the forest, and as flames approached from all four directions, the snake became terrified; it writhed and crawled on its belly, forcing its way out through the fire and barely escaping with its life. It then sought refuge at the foot of a tree, coiling its body there to remain.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, while traveling through the human realm, arrived at the foot of a tree. Seeing this venomous snake scorched by fire, its body mangled and suffering various agonies, he then observed whether it possessed any roots of goodness from past lives.
The Venerable One perceived that he possessed roots of goodness; furthermore, he observed with whom he was karmically connected.
Seeing that his own body shared a causal affinity with him from a former life, he sprinkled water upon him and taught the Dharma in three phrases, saying:
“O noble one, you should know:

all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all dharmas are without self, and nirvāṇa is tranquil extinction. You should give rise to a profound and pure mind toward me; by casting off this body of an animal, you shall be reborn in a happy realm.”
When the Venerable One had spoken these words, he departed immediately. At that time, a crow came and carried him off to eat him.

Because this venomous snake had conceived a virtuous mind toward the Venerable One, after his life ended, he was reborn in the house of a Brāhmaṇa in Śrāvastī as one who was well-versed in six matters: first, knowing how to personally arrange a religious assembly; second, teaching others how to arrange an assembly; third, being skilled in recitation; fourth, knowing the rules for giving alms; fifth, knowing the rules for receiving offerings; and sixth, being skilled in discerning what is pure and what is defiled.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, knowing that he had passed away, immediately observed where he had been reborn.
He saw that he had taken birth in the house of a brahmin in this city who was well-versed in the six branches of knowledge.
In order to discipline them, the Venerable One frequently visited the house of the brahmin and bestowed upon the husband and wife the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
Later, at another time, he went to their house alone; seeing him, the brahmin said: "Noble One!"
"Do you have no attendant?
The Venerable replied, "My attendant was not born from grass; I obtained him from your honorable presence."
The brahmin said, "I have no son capable of serving as an attendant; my wife is pregnant, and if she gives birth to a boy, I shall offer him to you as an attendant."
He replied, "May you be free from illness; I have already accepted it," and then he departed.
When her pregnancy reached full term, that wife gave birth to a son. While nursing at the breast, his claws and teeth would wound it, causing the breast to swell.
Once, while playing together with other children, if he were to become angry and wound them with his claws or teeth, the resulting sores and swellings would take a long time to heal.

At that time, Śāriputra, knowing that the moment had come for the young boy to go forth, went to his home and preached the Dharma to his parents. When the boy saw the Venerable One coming out, he thought to himself: "Is this my attendant?"
The father said to his son, "Before you were born, I promised to offer you as an attendant to the Noble One; you should now go with him and not harbor any lingering attachment."
"This person is one in their final birth. Having stood for a long while gazing at the Venerable’s face, he followed after him.
Upon arriving at the monastery, the Venerable granted him the going-forth (*pravrajyā*) and the full ordination (*upasampadā*); he then instructed him according to the teachings to train.

Later, after chewing his tooth-stick and scraping his tongue, he discarded it without rinsing it. A fly came and alighted upon it, and it died there. Next, a lizard came to eat the fly and consequently died; next, a mongoose came to devour the lizard and likewise lost its life; next, a puppy ate the mongoose and also met its end; and finally, the remaining scraps were nibbled by ants, all of whom perished.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu standing nearby who witnessed these events.

When morning came the following day, the bhikṣus came to that place to chew their tooth-sticks (dantakāṣṭha). Seeing that the dog and the swarm of ants had both died together in one spot, they marveled at the cause and said to one another:
"For what reason have the dog and the ants died together in this one place?"
Some said, "I do not know. Others said:
"Let us investigate together who committed this transgression.
Then that bhikṣu said to the people:

"Yesterday, the son of a brahmin—who was a disciple of the Venerable Śāriputra—was seen by me here chewing his tooth-stick; he discarded the tongue-scraper without washing it. It must have been because of this that his life came to an end."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "Bhikṣus,
you should know that among human beings there are those who carry poison, no different from snakes."

From now on, when chewing a tooth-stick, once you have finished scraping the tongue, you must rinse it with water before discarding it; to discard it without rinsing constitutes an offense against the rules.
As the Blessed One has said:
"Having chewed the tooth-stick, one should wash it before discarding it. Some bhikṣus, however, finding water scarce, did not know what to do.
The Buddha said:
"Rub it on ashes and soil, then discard it.

Later, at another time, the monk who possessed the poison was dyeing his own robes, spreading them out in the sun to dry and turning them over. At that moment, the Venerable Upānanda came along, saw him dyeing the robes, and said:
"Venerable one!..."
"I would be happy to assist you. He replied, "Excellent!"
"As you wish, Venerable Sir.

At that time, Upānanda, whose nature was inclined toward evil conduct, took the new robes and dried them in the shade, while exposing the old ones to the sun; furthermore, he turned the dry robes to the sun and dried the damp ones in the shade.
He said, "Venerable sir,
do not do such a thing."
Then Upānanda acted as before; thus he did so a second and a third time, refusing to desist despite being restrained. Thereupon, that bhikṣu became enraged and intended to seize him.
Upānanda immediately ran away, and he pursued him from behind.
At that time, Śāriputra came along and saw them chasing one another, and said:
"Venerable One!..."
"What do you intend to do?
Because his anger was so intense, he continued to pursue him without ceasing.
Being thus urgently pursued, Upānanda took a tree branch and struck him from a distance, yet he still did not stop.
At that time, Śāriputra immediately comforted him with gentle words so as not to let him catch up, and Upānanda fled far away.
With his anger still intense, he bit the tree; as his teeth bit the tree, all its leaves fell off.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not cause such a person to be troubled or to give rise to anger.
As the World-Honored One has taught:

"One should not cause annoyance that gives rise to anger. Later, at another time, it was Upānanda’s turn to take charge of the monastery affairs; he went to the poisonous bhikṣu and said, "Venerable One!"
"Act in this manner.
Upon seeing him come to inform [him] of this, he gave rise to great anger.
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If this person harbors malice or has previously held ill intentions, one should not go there oneself to have them perform tasks; rather, one may have another person inform them of what needs to be done. Upon hearing this, they should carry out the work without omission."

That poisonous bhikṣu practiced diligently without weariness; he shattered the wheel of the five destinies, severed all afflictions, and realized arhatship. As described at length elsewhere, there were none among gods or humans who did not revere him.
The bhikṣus said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"The disciple of the Venerable One harbors such intense malice; that such a person as this can still realize the fruit of arhatship is truly most rare."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra related the preceding circumstances in detail to the bhikṣus.
Then, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying: "Bhadanta!..."
"What karma did that bhikṣu previously perform such that he cast off his body as a venomous snake and was reborn in the human realm?
The Buddha said, "O bhikṣus!..."
Having performed those actions oneself, when they reach maturity, one must experience their results oneself.
As explained at length elsewhere, it is said in verse:
"Even if a hundred eons pass, The karma one has created does not perish;..."
"When causes and conditions meet, one receives the retribution for oneself. "O bhikṣus,
listen with a single mind!"

In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, endowed with the ten titles, who dwelt at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near Vārāṇasī.
This poisonous bhikṣu lived as a renunciant within that Buddha’s Dharma and practiced the meditation on loving-kindness (maitrī-vipaśyanā).
When the other bhikṣus saw him, they all addressed him, saying, “Meditator on Loving-Kindness! (Maitrī-vipaśyaka!)
“Maitreya! They replied,
“Virtuous ones, do not call me Maitreya anymore!”
"Compassionate One!
He called out thus a second and a third time, yet [the monk] still did not stop. Consequently, he conceived hatred toward the bhikṣus and uttered these evil words:
"I am Compassionate One; you are poisonous snakes among men."
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus, what do you think?
Is the one who went forth in the True Dharma of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa and practiced the meditation on loving-kindness anyone else?"
"This is that bhikṣu.

Because in the past he gave rise to a mind of malice and uttered harsh words toward a disciple of the Buddha, he was constantly reborn as a venomous snake for five hundred lifetimes; through the remaining force of that karma, he now experiences the retribution of virulent poison within this human life."

Because he had in the past performed the work of recitation and cultivated the various categories of precepts, and because he attained skillfulness regarding the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and the possible and impossible, through those roots of goodness he went forth in my Dharma, severed all afflictions, and realized arhatship.
"O bhikṣus! For this reason, I have always proclaimed that black karma yields black retribution, mixed karma yields mixed retribution, and white karma yields white retribution."
"You all should diligently cultivate white karma and remain free from black and mixed karma.
When the bhikṣus had heard the Buddha’s teaching, their hearts were filled with great joy; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took their leave, and departed.
The ninth sub-section of the eighth chapter, summarized in verse, says:

Wearing the three robes according to the occasion, One should know the rules for forest hermitages (araṇya), Bathing, guarding the gate, and exquisite flowers; One should not dwell in improper places.
The setting was as before.

At that time, the bhikṣus would regularly wear their saṃghāṭī robes while inside the monastery; they swept and prepared altars, smeared the ground with cow dung, entered the latrines, moved about, dyed their robes, and washed their garments.
Just as with the *saṃghāṭī*, the seven- and five-panel robes (*saptaka* and *pañcaka*) are all used in the same manner for various activities.
When the bhikṣus saw one person doing this, they said to him:
"It is not reasonable to wear these various robes without distinction, using them interchangeably in any place."
As the World-Honored One has said:
"The *saṃghāṭī* is the great outer robe.
How could it be appropriate to use it without making such a distinction?
They all said, "Venerable one!
These words are well spoken; let us go together and inform the Buddha."
The Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus! It is indeed proper that you should thus admonish one another."
"The saṃghāṭī is the king among robes; therefore, one should not wear it for various activities in any place whatsoever.
Regarding what the Blessed One said—that the saṃghāṭī robe should not be worn in any place whatsoever—the bhikṣus did not know where it should be worn.
The Buddha said:

"When entering a village, when going on almsround, when eating according to one's meal-time, when eating in a communal assembly, when paying homage to caityas, when listening to the Buddha-dharma, when listening to the Dharma day and night, and when prostrating before the two teachers and fellow practitioners of the holy life—in such circumstances as these, one may wear the great robe (saṃghāṭī)."
The *uttarāsaṅga* should be worn in clean places and used for activities such as eating;
however, the *antarvāsa* may be worn at will in any location whatsoever, and in all such cases there is no transgression.
The setting is as before.
As the Blessed One has said:

"Once the sun has risen, all the birds cry out and the farmers begin their plowing," as described at length previously, up until: "One should leave behind clamor and dwell alone in seclusion; one ought to straighten the mind and diligently cultivate meditative concentration."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu of little learning and shallow understanding who went to a secluded place and built a grass hut. With the exception of going for alms, he spent his days and nights diligently engaged in contemplation; this became known to everyone, including the cowherds.

At that time, there was a band of thieves who had been attacked by others; many were wounded and they were oppressed by hunger and thirst. The group deliberated together, not knowing where to go. One man said:
"In that forest hermitage (āraṇya) there is a son of the Śākya clan; generally, all śramaṇas are accustomed to storing provisions, and he possesses a compassionate heart and is free from fear."
"You virtuous ones may go; you should all go together to seek refuge, and you will surely obtain something.
The bandits all said, "Excellent indeed are these words!"
"It would be fitting for us to go together.
They all looked up with hope and proceeded together to the araṇya.
Upon seeing them, the bhikṣu exclaimed:
"Welcome! At that time, the bandits felt fearless in their hearts; after staying for a short while, they said, "Noble ones!..."
"I am cold and need fire.
The bhikṣu replied, "I dwell in an araṇya; there is no fire to be found here."
He spoke again, saying:
"Noble One! I am parched with thirst and have need of water."
The bhikṣu replied, "No. The thief spoke again:
"Noble one! Please give me a small amount of flour to apply to my wound.
The bhikṣu replied:
"No. The thief spoke again, saying,
"Venerable One!..."
"I need an old cloth to bandage my sore.
The bhikṣu replied,
"I have none."
Next, he requested ghee and oil to apply to the wound.
The bhikṣu replied,
"I have none."
He spoke again, saying:
"Noble One! I am famished and in need of food."
The bhikṣu replied, "No. The thief asked again:
“Noble One! What time is it now, and under which constellation does it fall?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I dwell in an araṇya and am unacquainted with this matter.
Among them was one who previously knew the monastic rules; he then became angry and said, "Venerable One!..."
"The previous matter has already passed; let me ask you further: have you, Venerable One, attained the fruit of Arhatship, Non-returning, Once-returning, or Stream-entry?
The bhikṣu replied, "I dwell in an araṇya."

The bandits said, "Set that matter aside for now; we ask further, O Noble One: have you attained the meditative concentrations of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of infinite space, and the four dhyānas?"
The bhikṣu replied, "I dwell in an araṇya.
The bandit said:
"Noble one! Are you a master of the Tripitaka, upholding the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma?
The bhikṣu answered as before, and the bandit said:
"Noble one! What is your name?
He replied as before, and the thief said:
"In which direction is this?
The bhikṣu replied as he had before.
Whatever the bandits asked, the bhikṣu answered them all.
"I dwell in an araṇya," [the monk replied].
The bandits then became greatly incensed and said to the people:
"Though we are bandits, this bhikṣu is a great bandit indeed."
"Why is this? They do not even know their own names and titles, yet they falsely assume an air of dignity to deceive and delude the world.

At that time, the bandits harbored resentment toward the bhikṣu; they beat him severely together until his body was broken, his robes, bowl, and staff were all shattered to pieces, and he barely survived with his life. The bandits abandoned him in the night and departed.
At that time, having suffered such humiliation, the bhikṣu went to the Jeta Grove when dawn broke. When the other bhikṣus saw him,
they asked, "Venerable one,
why is your appearance so exhausted?"
He then related the matter in full.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "O bhikṣus!..."

I have prescribed this code of conduct for bhikṣus dwelling in araṇyas: those living in an araṇya must store water and fire, as well as keep ghee, oil, parched grain, and old cloth; they should leave a small portion of food behind; they must recognize the stars and know the seasons, the times, and the cardinal directions; they must be well-versed in the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, even to the point of knowing their own names.
"If a forest-dwelling bhikṣu does not abide by these regulations, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The setting of this account is the same as before.
At that time, a heterodox practitioner of wrong livelihood suddenly fell ill; he went to a physician and requested medical treatment, to which the physician replied:
"One should construct a bathhouse to wash and bathe the body,
so that the illness may be cured. He replied, "Worthy sir!"
"Where could I possibly have a bathhouse?
I merely sustain my life by begging for food at the appropriate times. He replied:
"Noble one! The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, bathe in the bathhouse every half-month; you may go there to wash your body.
When the bhikṣu was washing, he entered the interior wearing saffron robes; [the others], thinking him to be a bhikṣu, did not stop him.
Having washed quickly, he came out and sat to dry his body. At that time, a śrāmaṇera came to where he was and called out, "Old man!
You may bathe with me."
He then shook his head, unwilling to wash again, but the novice immediately seized his arm and pulled him along. He spoke these words:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are all impure; they touch my washed body with their unclean hands."
He replied, "I am a śramaṇa; what are you? She answered:
"I am a heretic," he said, and then addressed the people,
"Who brought a heretic into the bathhouse?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When you are bathing, you may guard the gate; if you see a bhikṣu entering, you should ask his name.
They then asked for the names even of those they were acquainted with, and the Buddha said:

"You should not do so. At that time, the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kośala, traveling through the human realm until he reached a village named Icchānaṅgala; there was a grove there where the Buddha stayed.
In another village there was a brahmin named Puṣpa, who possessed vast fiefdoms and enjoyed an abundance of wealth without lack; King Prasenajit constantly provided him with offerings.

The teacher Supuṣpa had a personal disciple named Vṛkṣaprabha, who was widely learned, intelligent, and eloquent in debate without impediment; together with five hundred others, he studied and recited the essential scriptures of the Brahmins under Supuṣpa.

At that time, Sumana heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, the son of the Śākyas, had renounced worldly affairs, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and gone forth into homelessness with right faith. He had already attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; his great fame was known throughout distant and near lands, and he was revered by gods and humans as one whose ten titles were perfectly radiant. Having realized awakening spontaneously without receiving it from a teacher, he knew according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, and there will be no further existence. He proclaimed the sublime Dharma—excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, skillful in its phrasing and meaning, a pure, singular, and complete holy life.
"While wandering among the people of the Kosalans, he has now come here, intending to dwell in the forest of the Plowing Village.

I have previously read in ancient books that if a person’s body is adorned with the thirty-two marks, such a person has only two possible destinies: [either to become a Universal Monarch or a Fully Enlightened Buddha]."

If he had remained at home, he would have become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents, transforming the world through the Dharma and possessing the seven treasures—namely, the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the military commander treasure. He would have been endowed with a thousand sons of upright appearance and majestic bearing, possessed of great power and peerless valor; wherever they went, others would welcome them and submit of their own accord. Throughout the four seas, there would be none who did not receive his transformation, and there would be no enemies, nor any need for weapons or the suffering of strife. Ruling the common people solely by means of the True Dharma, they would all practice the ten wholesome deeds and dwell in peace and happiness.
"If one leaves the household life, as described above, they shall realize great bodhi.
At that time, having heard this matter, Supuṣpa said to his disciple Vṛkṣaja: "Do you know now?"

"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākyas, has renounced the Śākya clan, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and gone forth into homelessness," and so on, as extensively described above.
His fame has spread throughout the world as he travels among the people; now he has arrived at the village of Khānumata in Kośala and is dwelling within the great forest.
I have previously read ancient scriptures which state that if a person’s body is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, such a person has only two possible destinies:
if they remain at home, they shall become a wheel-turning monarch;
if they renounce the household life, they shall attain Buddhahood, their fame spreading far and wide as described above.
"You should now go there and personally observe for yourself: are the marks and signs you have heard of real, or are they false? Druma replied:

"According to the Teacher's instruction," they said, and together with the village elders, brahmins who were intelligent and widely learned, they went to where the World-Honored One was. Having arrived before the Buddha, they stood to one side.

The brahmins greeted the Blessed One with various words of consolation and then sat down before him; the Blessed One immediately taught them the subtle Dharma, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them so that they were filled with joy.
While the Buddha was preaching the Dharma, that young brahmin (māṇava) walked back and forth before the Buddha wearing leather sandals.

He would come for a brief moment to listen, but after speaking with disruptive questions, he would depart; in the presence of the World-Honored One, he harbored extreme arrogance, lacking any sense of fear or reverence, and with a rebellious mind, he considered himself superior.
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"How could you now engage in such a matter as debating the treatises on exegesis?
Great Brahmin, you speak at random."
He asked, “Gautama! What fault is there in me?”
The Buddha said:

"When I was engaged in discussion with learned and eminent men, you were walking back and forth without ceasing while wearing leather sandals; you did not understand the proper sequence and lacked a heart of reverence and obedience, asking confused questions that were contrary and defiant."
He said: "Gautama!
According to our Brahmin dharma, when one engages in conversation with another, whether standing, sitting, or lying down, it is not considered a fault for all to converse together."
"These shaven-headed śramaṇas are bound by afflictions and do not produce sons or daughters; what fault is there in engaging in conversation with them during our discourse?
The Buddha said, "You have come to me for a specific purpose, yet you have not yet received instruction from this venerable person."
Upon hearing these words, he gave rise to anger and an intolerant mind, desiring to engage the Buddha in debate.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "O Gautama!..."
"The Śākyas are like wild elephants; they do not give rise to reverence, offerings, or respect toward the brahmins.
The Buddha said, "Jyotiṣka!"
"What fault do the sons of the Śākyas have that you speak such words? He replied:
"Gautama! In the past, on account of my preceptor and for my own business, I went to the city of Kapilavastu.
From high towers, the Śākya men and women saw me entering the city and walking along the road; they all pointed at me from afar and said to one another:"
"This is the young brahmin Vṛkṣavardhana, a disciple of the brahmin Supuṣpa.
He merely pointed him out from afar, showing no heart of respect or offerings.
The Buddha said, "Māṇava!
It is like the hundred-tongued bird that produces many sounds, dwelling within its nest and speaking as it pleases."
"What fault is there if the Śākyas converse as they please within their own homes? He replied, "O Gautama!"
"In this world there are only four great castes:
namely, the Brahmins, the Kṣatriyas, the Vaiśyas, and the Śūdras.
All these people respect, make offerings to, and revere the Brahmins; yet among this Śākya clan, such is not the case."
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This young brahmin treats the Śākya clan like wild elephants; his insults are far too excessive.
I should now explain to him the origins of his past causes and conditions, as well as the roots of his lineage, so that he may cease his arrogance."
Having formed this thought, he saw that in a past life, the young brahmin had been born from a maidservant of the Śākyas; thus, the Śākyas were his masters.
He addressed the māṇava, saying:
"What is your clan now? He replied:
“Gautama! My clan name is Kātyāyana. The Buddha said:
“Māṇava! I now see that your ancestors of old were born of a Śākya slave woman; today, these Śākyas are your masters.”
Then the other elder brahmins spoke together to the Buddha, saying:
"O Gautama! Do not say that Yajñadatta was born of a slave woman."
Why is this? This tree-born one is learned, intelligent, and eloquent, engaging in debate without impediment; he converses with Gautama, exchanging arguments based on the true Dharma.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"If you say that the tree has produced one of great learning and great wisdom who can engage in debate, then you all should remain silent and let him speak."
"If you are unable, you may remain silent; you yourselves should speak.
The brahmins said, "Jātiśroṇa possesses great wisdom and can engage in debate with Gautama; let us remain silent for now."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Jyotiṣka, saying:
"In ancient times there was a king named Ikṣvāku, who fathered four sons:
the first was named Jvalanmukha, the second was named Kharakarṇa, the third was named Gajaskandha, and the fourth was named Valayapāda."
The four sons were all banished for their transgressions.

At that time, each of the four youths took his own sister and departed together for another region. They arrived at the side of the Snowy Mountains, by the bank of a river, which was the former dwelling place of the seer Kapila; not far from there, they each constructed grass huts to settle in. Subsequently, they abandoned their own biological sisters and took those born of different mothers as wives, and each begot sons and daughters.
At that time, King Ikṣvāku, longing for his sons, asked the ministers, "Where are my sons? They replied:

"Great King! There was once a matter concerning you that led to everyone being banished; I shall recount the details of those events, including how each of them subsequently gave birth to sons and daughters.
The king said to his minister:
"Can my son perform such a deed? He replied, "He can."
The King immediately rose to his full height, extended his right hand, and uttered this sigh:
"My son is capable of such deeds.
Because of that minister’s verbal proclamation, the clan was named Śākya, which here means "Capable" (Neng).
"Maṇava! Have you ever heard of such a matter concerning the Śākya clan? He replied:
“I have heard it. “Māṇava!

In the Ikṣvāku royal house there was an excellent maidservant named Diśāṃprajñapti, who was beautiful in appearance. She became the wife of a certain ṛṣi, and subsequently gave birth to a son. As soon as he was born, he spoke:”
"Do not rub your body yet; wait until I have finished bathing and removing my impurities.
In times past, people all called ghosts by the name "Arrow-path" (Ārava); have you ever heard of this lineage?
When the young brahmin heard this, he remained silent.
Thus, after being questioned three times in full, he remained silent and gave no answer.
Then the deity Vajrapāṇi raised his vajra above the youth’s head, emitting great flames of fire that blazed with brilliant radiance, and declared:
“Māṇava! When the Buddha asked three times and you feigned a mind of evasion by not answering, I would have immediately crushed your head with a mallet into seven pieces.”

Through the Buddha’s majestic power, the young brahmin beheld Vajrapāṇi; he was instantly seized with great terror, his heart filled with anxiety and his hair standing on end, as he addressed the Buddha: “Gautama!
"I have previously heard that such a lineage exists.
Then those elder Brahmins spoke thus: "It is exactly as Gautama has said;
we all believe that this original progenitor of the tree-people was truly the son of a slave woman."
At that time, the young brahmin saw him and said, "You slave!
His heart was filled with distress and shame; he stood there with his head bowed, unable to speak.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the World-Honored One further thought to himself:
"I should now comfort Druma so that he may be freed from his grief and distress.
He immediately spoke for him again of various causes and conditions and various parables, causing him to cease his arrogant mind and abandon his sorrow and suffering. Then, he addressed him, saying:
“Māṇava! Set this matter aside for now.
You may now pursue your original intention.”

At that time, Jyotiṣka examined the Buddha’s body for the thirty-two marks; he saw only thirty, being unable to discern the remaining two—the mark of the private parts and the mark of the tongue—and he spoke this verse:
"I have heard it said of the Great Muni That he possessed the thirty-two marks;
But as I now examine the Buddha’s form, Not one of these marks appears upon his body."
I have not yet beheld the Honored One among Men; perhaps he remains in some hidden place.
This mark of the broad and long, wondrous tongue is unknown to those within this world.
I pray that you will manifest this mark for me, to dispel the doubts in my heart.
The Fully Awakened One of great renown is difficult for people of the world to behold. *Vinayakṣudrakavastu*,
Fascicle 34, *Mūlasarvāstivādavinaya-kṣudrakavastu*.
Fascicle Thirty-Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The Ninth Section of the Eighth Chapter: The Remainder of the Summary Verses; Relating the Matter of the Brahmin Supuṣpa. At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:

"This young brahmin, Citta, has examined my body throughout to observe the thirty-two marks; he has already seen thirty of them, yet he has doubts regarding two. He has not yet been able to see the two marks of the private parts and the tongue."
"I shall now employ a skillful means to manifest the mark of the concealed organ so that he may see it.
He then extended his tongue until it reached the hairline and covered his entire face; having seen this, the man thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is endowed with all the marks and possesses two kinds of activities: [the physical and the verbal]."
"If he remains in the secular world, he will become a Wheel-Turning King;
if he leaves the household life, he will attain Perfect Enlightenment, such that his fame will not fail to reach everywhere.
At that time, the young brahmin was filled with great joy and took his leave of the Buddha.
At that time, the brahmin Supuṣpa was sitting in a garden conversing with various elders, waiting for Jyotiṣka.
Then Jyotiṣka saw Supuṣpa from afar.
He then approached them, paid homage at their feet and those of the other elders, and sat to one side.
Puṣpa addressed him, saying: "Māṇava!..."
"That Gautama possesses a good reputation that pervades the ten directions and is endowed with all the marks and signs—
is this not indeed true? He replied, "Great Master!"
"What everyone praises regarding his deeds is entirely true; have you ever engaged in conversation with him?
He replied, "I have spoken with him."
"Whatever discourse you had there, relate it all to me in its proper sequence.
Then the young brahmin related to the Blessed One his entire conversation with Supuṣpa.
Having heard this, he gave rise to great anger and immediately raised his foot to trample upon the other’s head, saying in a rage:

"What an excellent messenger you are, capable of accomplishing such a task! You have caused even my own self to sink into the evil realms; for all the errors that occurred during your discussion with him, you have now implicated me as well in those transgressions."
"However, as it was already late in the afternoon, I was unable to go at once to pay my respects and inquire after your health; I shall wait until tomorrow and go in person.

That very night, he prepared various kinds of excellent and sublime food and drink. As soon as morning arrived, he transported them by carriage and went to where the World-Honored One was. Upon arrival, filled with joy, he exchanged greetings and sat to one side, addressing the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
“I have prepared pure food for the Gautama and brought it here; I pray that you will compassionately and mercifully accept it.
At that time, Ānanda was fanning the Blessed One from behind to provide cool air. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“You should now inform all the bhikṣus in this village and have them assemble in the regular dining hall.”
Then Ānanda, having gone and delivered the message, gathered them all in the regular dining hall and returned to inform the Buddha:
"Everyone has assembled; may the Buddha know that the time has come."
The World-Honored One went there and sat upon the seat.

When the brahmin saw that the Buddha and the assembly of monks were all seated, he personally took exquisite food and drink to offer to the Buddha and the monks. When the great assembly had finished eating, chewed their tooth-sticks, and washed their hands, they put away the alms bowls; the brahmin then took a small mat and sat before the Buddha to listen to the essential teachings of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the food and drink provided by the brahmin, and after expressing his appreciation, he spoke these verses:
"Fire is the foremost among sacrifices; The first verse is the foremost among treatises;
The king is the foremost among men; The ocean is the foremost among all streams."
Among the stars, the moon is supreme; among lights, the sun is supreme.
Within the worlds of the ten directions, among both the ordinary and the holy, the Buddha is supreme.
Whoever practices giving will certainly obtain its benefit and profit.
"If one gives for the sake of happiness, one will surely obtain peace and joy in the future.
At that time, there was among the assembly a mahallaka bhikṣu who, upon hearing the Buddha recite this verse, continued to chew dry cakes with loud noises even though he was already fully satiated.
Seeing this, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Gautama, do the śrāvaka disciples practice according to the teachings?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
“There are those who rely [on the Dharma] and those who do not rely [on it]. “Gautama!
As I observe this now, there are those who delight in the Dharma and those who are greedy for food.”
"Gautama! Do you have a disciple named Jyotiṣka who has come to the Buddha’s presence to engage in discussion?
The Buddha said:
"He has come and briefly conversed with him.
"Gautama! I would be grateful if you would relate to me in detail all the questions and answers exchanged during their conversation."
The Buddha then explained it to him in successive order.
At that time, the brahmin said to the Buddha: “Gautama!

As for those born of this tree, they are ignorant and of little learning, harboring arrogance in their hearts; they fail to give rise to fear or reverence and thus lightly touch your venerable countenance. We only pray that, out of compassion, you will forgive their transgression.
The Buddha told the brahmin,
“I have already forgiven you.
Then the brahmin spoke again to the Buddha, saying:

“Gautama! When I am riding in a carriage, or when I am holding the horse’s reins, or when I am raising my whip and shouting loudly—at such times, may it be known that I, the Brahmin Puṣpa, prostrate at the feet of the Buddha and inquire whether he is free from illness and affliction, and whether his daily life is light and easy, and his strength and well-being are secure?”
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Gautama! If you see me walking along the road, or taking off my leather sandals, or stepping aside from the path, or extending my arm—on such occasions, as before, you should know that I am offering my respectful greetings.”
He spoke again, saying:

“Gautama! If at any time you see me conversing with someone among my own assembly, and I should move from my seat, or remove my upper garment, or take off my turban—at that moment, as before, let it be known that I am offering my respectful greetings.”
For what reason? O Gautama!
In our Brahmin dharma, we seek only reputation; all our clothing, food, and articles of enjoyment are obtained solely through reputation. Therefore, I well protect the public in this regard.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This brāhmaṇa is extremely arrogant; I should now quench his pride and preach the Dharma for him."

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately proclaimed, instructed, benefited, and gladdened them, just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, habitually teaches the Dharma: namely, he spoke of giving or of observing the precepts; he explained how the five desires have little flavor and many faults and evils, how afflictions defile and cause one to sink into the cycle of birth and death, and how one must seek liberation through the pure state of nirvana. He extensively expounded upon such teachings.

The World-Honored One, knowing that they were joyful and sympathetic, had developed a pure mind and were fit vessels for the Dharma, and were capable of receiving and upholding the sublime teachings, further expounded for them at length the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. It was like a clean cloth easily taking on the color of the dye.
At that moment, while still seated, the brahmin realized the principle of the Truths (satyadarśana), became free from doubt, and attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti).
He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke these words:

“I have now renounced the world; I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and accept the five precepts (pañca-śikṣāpada). May you bear witness that I am an upāsaka endowed with pure mindfulness.”
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he took his leave and departed.
The Buddha thought to himself:
“That brahmin mocked me well; because the elderly bhikṣu did not stop eating while reciting the verses on giving, one should not eat at such a time.”
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"That brahmin was well-suited for his mockery; because the mahallaka recited the verse on giving while eating without restraint, he incurred such ridicule and disgrace."
"If there is a bhikṣu who, while the verse for the offering of alms is being recited, does not cease eating, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

When the Buddha had thus prescribed that one should not eat while the verse is being recited, they did not dare to eat; consequently, those at the end of the row failed to eat as the time passed. The Buddha said:
"If there is a bhikṣu who, while the verse for the offering of alms is being recited, does not hear the sound of it being recited or does not understand its meaning, he may eat without fault."
"If one hears the sound but does not understand the meaning, there is no offense regarding the food.
However, if one hears the sound, understands the meaning, and eats, it is an offense against the Dharma.

Regarding this rule established by the Buddha that one must not eat if one hears the sound and understands the meaning, it happened that at a certain residence many people were seated together. Consequently, those at the end of the row had to move forward to the front; hearing the verses of the offering, they all refrained from eating, and thus the time for their meal passed. The Buddha said:
"If one hears the sound of these [verses] and also understands their meaning, one should not eat; rather, wait until two or three stanzas have been recited, and then eating will be without fault.
At that time, while the Blessed One was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, he put on his robes and took his bowl at the time for the morning meal and entered the city to beg for food.
There was another bhikṣu who was also wandering for alms; he arrived at a garden and stood waiting there, where he saw men and women giving rise to evil thoughts and forming improper desires.
The Buddha, seeing that the bhikṣu was harboring improper thoughts associated with unwholesomeness, approached him and said: "Bhikṣu!
You are sowing seeds of suffering within yourself and emitting foul-smelling excrement; it is impossible that flies and insects would not feed upon this."
Having heard this, he thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One now knows my wicked mind.
He was immediately seized with great terror, the hair on his body stood on end, and he departed from the garden.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"When a bhikṣu remains in an improper place, there are such faults as these.
Having finished his almsround, he returned to his original location; after eating his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and entered his cell to sit in meditative seclusion.
In the late afternoon, he arose from meditative concentration and sat down among the assembly of monks. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Just now, having entered the city for alms, I saw a certain bhikṣu who, while also seeking alms, had gone into a grove where he gave rise to harmful reflections and improper thoughts of sensual desire."
Knowing that the man had conceived such an evil thought, I went up to him and said to him: "O Bhikṣu, Bhik�u!
It is impossible that flies and insects would not eat the foul excrement from which you have sown the seeds of suffering within your own body."
Having heard this, he thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One now knows my wicked mind.
He was immediately seized with great terror, the hair on his body standing on end, and he departed from the garden.
"Therefore, bhikṣus, you should not stand or remain in improper places.
If you do so, you shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One, Great Virtuous One!
Within the Noble Teaching, what is called the seed of suffering and evil?
What is meant by ‘stench and excrement flowing forth, upon which flies and insects all feed’?”
The Buddha said,
“Monks! The seeds of suffering refer to these three kinds of sinful, unwholesome, and wrong modes of deliberation.”
What are the three?
They are the thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, and the thought of cruelty.
As for "foul excrement flowing out," foul excrement refers to the five objects of sensory desire.
These are forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
As for "outflow," it refers to the mind bound by desire, which pursues the six objects through the six sense faculties, flowing and never remaining still.

The "flies" refers to those in the world who, failing to restrain their minds regarding the six bases of contact, give rise to greed, hatred, and so forth, as well as sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, thereby committing evil deeds.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
“Failing to restrain the eyes, ears, and so forth, one is dragged away by desire;
The seeds of suffering are planted within the body, And a foul stench constantly flows forth.”
Whether dwelling in a village or residing in a secluded, quiet place,
if one constantly fails to contemplate the True Dharma throughout the day and night,
then by relying on sinful thoughts, one will give rise to false discursive thinking.
Those who distance themselves from the conditions for dwelling in pleasure shall receive bitter retribution.
But those who cultivate tranquil concentration and exert themselves in supreme wisdom always sleep in peace and security, untroubled by flies or insects.
"Associate with virtuous friends, And follow what the superior ones have taught;
If one can train in this way, One shall not undergo further rebirth.
As the World-Honored One has said:

"A bhikṣu should not stand or remain in an improper place. [The question arises: "What is meant by an 'improper place'? The Buddha said: "There are five kinds of improper places: [1] the king's inner palace; [2] a woman’s private quarters; [3] a place where liquor is being sold; [4] a place where meat is being butchered;
and [5] a place where one is about to be executed."
"The households of public announcers, prostitutes, taverns, royal families, and *caṇḍāla* families—these are called the five places that are not within one’s sphere of activity.
The summary verse for the tenth section of the eighth chapter states:
"Because of snakes, one should inspect bedding; One should not perform a formal greeting with only a single garment on."
When first arriving at a monastery, an elderly person should pay homage to four [elders].
The circumstances were as follows:
at Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who wished to depart on a journey and entrusted his bedding and requisites to a friend, requesting him to guard them.

At that time, the bhikṣu placed his bedding back in its original location but did not use it; subsequently, a venomous snake came seeking a place to stay and coiled itself beneath the mattress to dwell there.
A guest bhikṣu arrived and stayed there; after resting for a short while, he paid homage at the Buddha’s stūpa and other bhikṣus, and as evening fell, they returned to their quarters.
The resident bhikṣu said to him:
“Venerable one!...”
"This is water, soil, lamp oil, and bedding previously laid out; having become weary from traveling, one may wash one's feet and sleep peacefully.

Due to the power of past karma, he did not inspect the bedding and immediately fell asleep. He lay down upon a snake, which emerged from its retreat and bit the bhikṣu. Suffering the pain, the bhikṣu writhed upon the snake, and within a brief moment, both lost their lives.
When dawn broke, the host came to call him; since he was already dead, there was no one left to attend to him. The host thought to himself:
"He must have been utterly exhausted from his journey and has fallen into a deep sleep; once he has slept his fill, he will surely wake up on his own."
When the time for the meal was approaching, he came again and knocked on the door, calling out, "Please rise; it is nearly time for the meal.
As there was no response, he took the key and entered the room. He saw that the monk was dead, and upon turning over the bedding, he further saw that a snake was also dead.
The assembly gathered to look and discovered that he had been bitten by a snake; they reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha thought to himself:
"Failure to inspect one's bedding has led to this total loss.
He then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"One who has received a commission from another should entrust the bedding to the administrator, or may at any time personally sun it and place it on a rack, tying it so that it does not fall."
"If you wish to sleep, you must observe [the surroundings].
At night, he looked about with the light of a lamp.
The Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus; you may examine them in advance during the daytime.
At that time, the bhikṣus turned over all their bedding, both new and old. The Buddha said: "One should examine the old, but do not turn over the new.
When there is a protective cloth (under-linens), it should be shaken out from time to time; otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
The setting was in Śrāvastī.

There were two bhikṣus living in the same room; at that time, one bhikṣu took a young man as his disciple. This disciple slept much and would only wake up after a long time, so the preceptor frequently rebuked him.

Later, as dawn approached, he suddenly started up in alarm and, merely wearing his *saṃkakṣikā*, went to where his teacher was. His teacher was just rising and about to put on his lower garment (*antarvāsaka*).

The disciple drew near, prostrated at the teacher’s feet, and stood up; because he had recently shaved his head, the teacher’s lower garment became caught upon it and remained there like a turban. The disciple’s own upper robe also slipped off, so that both teacher and disciple were completely exposed.
That bhikṣu saw them and replied,
"Venerable sirs!
I now know well that you are all men, fully endowed with male organs."
At that time, the two men each felt ashamed and departed in silence. Their teacher then immediately rebuked his disciples. Other bhikṣus asked him:
"What fault have you committed that you are constantly subject to your teacher's anger?"
He replied, "In the past, there was a cause for my anger; now that there is no fault, the bond between teacher and disciple is severed. I am departing now!
He asked again, "For what reason?"
He then informed him fully, saying:
"Venerable One! You truly have committed a transgression; your reproach was entirely appropriate."
Upon hearing this, he remained silent.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, considering that his teacher’s reprimand was in accordance with the Dharma, addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, you must not pay homage to another while wearing only a single robe, nor must you accept homage while wearing only a single robe. Whoever violates this shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
The setting was in Rājagṛha. As the Blessed One had said:
"One should not fail to show courtesy toward other bhikṣus, nor should one fail to relieve their fatigue.

At that time, a great many bhikṣus came from various regions to pay homage at the caitya; yet not a single person relieved them of their exhaustion. They remained wherever they were, as if they had been expelled—some in front of eaves, some in gate-houses, and some beneath trees.
At that time, some faithful brahmins and householders, having seen him, asked:
"Noble one! For what reason have you been expelled and are now staying here?"
He replied, "O virtuous one!
I have not been expelled; I am a guest who has newly arrived."
The brāhmaṇa said: "If that is so, why do you not stay inside the room? [He replied:
"I have no one to rely upon; who else would accept me?"
"We have come here for a brief moment to pay our respects at the holy traces of the Sage; we shall stay wherever we find ourselves and return before long.
When the people heard this, they all felt resentment and shame, saying:
"We have heard that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are by nature impartial in their hearts. Where, then, is there any practice of impartiality?"
"Seeing fellow practitioners of the holy life arriving as guests, you did not allow them to stay.
When the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
