"From now on, whenever any guest monk enters a monastery, he should first pay homage to four senior monks and stand before them; the host should then, with a kind heart, provide him with lodging according to the Dharma."

Later, at another time, there was a guest bhikṣu traveling through the countryside who, as evening approached, arrived at the city of Rājagṛha. Knowing the Buddha’s precept regarding the etiquette of honoring those of seniority, he asked the bhikṣus:
"Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, where is he now?"
He replied, "In the Bamboo Grove Monastery.
He then went there at once and knocked on the door, calling out. At that time, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya asked:
"Who is it? He replied, "I am a guest monk."
The Venerable One called him in and had him rest.
The visiting monk asked,
"Where is the Venerable Mahākāśyapa now?"
He replied, "Venerable sir!
He is in the Pipphaliguha cave."
Then the visiting monk went there as instructed and made inquiries as before. The Venerable One called him in, comforted him, and had him rest;
he then asked, "Where is the Venerable Cunda now?"
He replied, "He is at Vulture Peak Mountain.
The visiting monk then went there to inquire after him; the Venerable One invited him inside and, as before, instructed him to rest.
A visiting monk asked,
"Where is the Venerable Daśabala Kāśyapa now? He replied:
"He is currently in the Saindhika Cave.
The visiting monk then departed; having seen the Venerable One, he engaged in the same exchange as before, which caused him to cease [his journey].
The visiting monk replied:
"Now that dawn has broken, it is time to go for alms; we must not remain any longer.
He spoke these words: "As the World-Honored One has said:..."

"The instruction that 'a visiting monk must first be made to prostrate before the four senior elders' wherever he arrives" is a skillful means to discipline the visitor and prevent him from remaining at ease.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I did not previously command that visiting bhikṣus pay homage to the venerable elders of the earth; I only sent them to pay their respects to the four elders of this very place.
A summary verse says:
"The World-Honored One, as the Most Exalted, extensively expounded the conduct of his disciples."
Vassakāra questioned the Great Master, who then expounded the seven and six dharmas.
The setting was the city of Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Venerable Mahānāma arose from meditative concentration in the late afternoon, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side. He then addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Disciple, I pray that you will explain for me all the practices regarding how a disciple should serve a teacher.
The Buddha told Bhadrika:
“I shall now explain for you the methods by which a bhikṣu’s disciples and followers should provide service; you should listen attentively.”

As a disciple, one should always maintain a sense of reverence and a mind of awe toward one's preceptor; not for the sake of fame, nor seeking profit and sustenance, one must rise early and personally inquire of the two teachers:
"Are the four elements at ease? Is your daily life light and comfortable?"
Aside from attending to the urinal for the purpose of massaging his body, if the teacher says,
"I am currently ill," one should inquire about the ailment,
then go to a physician and explain the cause of the illness in detail, requesting a prescription for treatment; one should then carry out the cure exactly as the physician instructs.
If the teacher possesses medicinal substances himself, they should be used for compounding; if he does not have them, one may ask his close relatives.
If there are many relatives, one should ask the teacher, saying:
"From which relative should I seek them?"
Having received the teacher’s instruction, one should depart as told.
If there are no relatives, one should go to other households to seek [medicine] according to the instructions, or visit infirmaries and places where medicine is distributed.
If such a person is not present, one should attend to them by relying on their own karma, providing care regarding food and drink.

When the illness permits, one should provide them with a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*). At the place where the teacher intends to chew the tooth-stick, one should first sweep it clean and prepare a maṇḍala, arranging a stool, a water vessel for rinsing, as well as cleansing powder, earth, a tooth-stick, and a tongue-scraper.
Having finished washing and rinsing, one should set aside the necessary items.
If the teacher suffers from eye ailments, one should consult a physician to prepare medicinal ointment for him and apply it with a cloth.
Next, one should present his robes; as for the remaining garments, they should be folded and stacked so as not to be disheveled.
When the teacher performs the ritual prostration at the stupa, he should enter the room and sweep the floor; if there is dust or dirt, he should wipe it away with cow dung or green leaves.

Next, one should personally pay homage to the venerable image and pay homage to the preceptor; or else, inquire after their well-being and report matters to them. One should perform prostrations three times each day, and according to one's own ability, also extend respectful greetings to fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*).
Next, one should diligently apply oneself to seated meditation and recitation; every half-month, one must inspect and sun-dry one's bedding and mats.
When it is time for the meal, one should wash both alms bowls.
If one is a bhikṣu who lives on alms, one should carry the heavy bowl oneself and give the lighter one to the teacher.
If it is during the cold season, one should give the heavy *saṃghāṭī* to the teacher for him to wear, while keeping the lighter one oneself.
If it is during the hot season, one should give the lighter one to the teacher and keep the heavier one oneself.
If traveling against the wind, request that the teacher be in front and you yourself be behind.
If traveling with the wind, you yourself should be in front, allowing the teacher to be behind.
If crossing a river, one should assist and support the teacher until they have safely crossed.
When going on almsround, one should ask the teacher whether they will go together or separately;
if the teacher says they will go together, one may follow along.
If one obtains parched flour, bean cakes, or sour gruel, one should place them in one’s own bowl;
if one obtains rice, milk curds, rock sugar, cooked rice cakes, or granulated sugar, one should place them in the teacher’s bowl.
Having obtained food through alms, he returns to his original location, prepares two small altars, and spreads various leaves upon them. He may then arrange two seats and sit cross-legged to eat.
If he practices separately, he shall take the food he has obtained and present it to his preceptor, saying:
"I have now obtained this food; you should take what you require."
The preceptor should then receive [the food] with due moderation.
If he resides in the monastery, the disciple should first wash the vessels and go to the kitchen to ask the administrator:
"What food and drink will be prepared today for the Saṃgha?"
The administrator, out of respect, informed him; he returned and said to his teacher, "Today the Saṃgha has prepared such food.
Should I invite you to take some?"
Having brought [the items] in accordance with the instructions, the preceptor should receive them after considering the proper measure and the appropriate time.

At the place where the two masters perform their ablutions and rinsing, one should sweep it clean, construct a maṇḍala, arrange a small seat and water vessels, and provide earth and tooth-sticks for cleansing according to the Dharma.

If it is necessary to wash the feet, one should wash them for the teacher; this may be done simply with water, or by applying oil and rubbing it off with a powder, followed by washing again. One should then present him with leather sandals and inquire about his meal.
He asked again:
"Will you practice wholesome deeds here,
or will you go instead to another secluded dwelling?"
If it is said, "You may go to the daytime dwelling," one should take one's seating materials;
that dwelling place should be swept and sprinkled clean, and from time to time smeared with cow dung.

If there is one studying recitation, one should provide them with the scriptures; if there is one studying meditative contemplation, one should instruct them in the cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*).

When returning, one should inspect the bedding and mats. Having washed one's own feet, one should next pay homage to the honored images and fellow practitioners, prostrating according to one’s capacity. One should arrange a seat for the teacher and wash his feet as before.
If it is cold, one should maintain the intention to provide warm water for them.
If it is hot, one should hold a fan to bring them coolness.
The teacher, likewise, should recognize the proper time to have them perform work, ensuring that they do not pass their time in vain.
"When performing tasks such as working on robes or alms bowls, all work should first attend to the master's property,
and only thereafter attend to one's own. The Buddha said, "Ghoṣila!"
You should now know that all the disciples and followers within the community of bhikṣus should regard their two teachers as they would their own parents;
the teachers, in turn, should regard their disciples as their own children, attending to them with mutual care whether they are ill, until they have recovered or even unto death.
I shall now briefly explain this matter for you: it should be performed in this manner.
If one does not rely upon it, one incurs an offense against the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*) in accordance with that action.

If one can act thus, the disciple, with a mind of reverence and compliance, serves as an attendant to the teacher, enabling the succession of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*) to continue without interruption—just as a lotus flower situated in a pond grows and flourishes day and night.
"Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way.
When the Venerable Viśeṣagāmin and the other bhikṣus had heard what the Buddha said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The setting was Rājagṛha, at Vulture Peak Mountain.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, the ruler of Magadha, was at odds with the Vṛji kingdom. In the midst of a great assembly, King Ajātaśatru addressed the people, saying:
"The peaceful, prosperous, and joyful [kingdom] is in opposition to me; I wish to raise an army and go forth to punish them, so as to utterly destroy and disperse them."
The King said to the minister, the Brahmin Varṣākāra:
"Go to the Buddha’s presence, prostrate at his feet, and inquire on my behalf whether he is well, free from ailment, free from distress, and in good health and spirits."
Next, he spoke again, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
King Ajātaśatru has spoken these words before the assembly: [text continues]"
"That kingdom is prosperous and happy, contrary to my own interests; I wish to raise an army and go there to punish them and cause them all to be broken and dispersed.
Will the World-Honored One permit this?
As the World-Honored One has predicted, you should all receive [this message] and return to report it to me."
"Why is this? Because the words of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha are not false.

At that time, Varṣākāra, having received the King's command, mounted a white horse chariot, holding a golden staff with a golden pitcher suspended from it, and departed from Rājagṛha to go to where the Buddha was.

Upon reaching the place where he dismounted, he proceeded on foot up Vulture Peak Mountain. Arriving at the presence of the World-Honored One, he greeted him with a joyful countenance and, sitting to one side, addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

The King Ajātaśatru, Lord of Magadha, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and respectfully inquired after his well-being, asking whether he was free from ailment and affliction, and whether his strength and health were secure.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha said to the brahmin:
"May the King and you both be free from illness and enjoy peace and happiness.
Then the brahmin, conveying the King's words, addressed the Buddha in succession, relating the matter in detail.
“I do not yet know what instructions the World-Honored One has bestowed.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
“Not long ago, while I was in the country of Kṛṣi, I stayed there during the three-month summer retreat. At that time, I proclaimed to the assembly the seven dharmas of non-retrogression.”
"Brahmin! When the people of that country uphold these seven kinds of non-retrogressive dharmas, the population of the realm increases day by day, and wholesome qualities suffer no decline."

The brahmin said: "I am unable to understand the profound and essential meaning set forth by the Venerable One; I only pray that you will, out of compassion, explain it to me in detail so that I may attain understanding."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha, holding a fan to waft a cool breeze. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Have you heard or learned whether the people of the country of the Bulis have gathered in great numbers to discuss the meaning of the Dharma?"
“Venerable Sir! I have heard that many people in that country gather together to discuss and debate the meaning of the Dharma.
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:

“If, in that country, many people gather to discuss and evaluate the meaning of the Dharma, you should know that in that country the wholesome dharmas will daily increase and suffer no decline. Ānanda!”
"Have you ever heard that in the country of the Vṛji, the people are so harmonious that they rise together and sit together to deliberate on the affairs of state?
He replied, "I have heard so."
The detailed explanation was as above. The Buddha also addressed the brahmin with the same full discourse as above, up until the point where it says, "There is no loss of wholesome qualities;
this is the second [point]. "Ānanda!"

Have you ever heard or known that the people of that country do not seek what should not be sought, do not allow what ought to be attained to be interrupted, and always joyfully comply with the state's commands?
He replied, “I have heard it.
The full account was related as above. The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa, also explaining it in detail as above, up until the third point: that wholesome qualities are not diminished.

“Ānanda! Have you ever heard or known that the women and maidens of that country—whether protected by their mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters, paternal aunts, or kinsmen, and guarded by one another, subject to reprimand and punishment for transgressions, or the wives and concubines of others, or even those who have been betrothed with flowers as their future wives—ever engage in unrighteous acts impulsively?”
He replied, “I have heard it.
The details were as explained above. The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa, also explaining in full as above, up until: “...and thus no wholesome qualities are diminished,” which was the fourth [point].
“Ānanda! Have you heard or known that the people of that country show reverence and make offerings to their parents and teachers, and follow their instructions without any resentment or distress?”
He replied, "I have heard it," and so forth, as explained above.
The Buddha told the brahmin, repeating everything as stated above, up until: "...the wholesome dharmas shall suffer no diminution. (5) "Ānanda!
Have you heard or known whether the people of that country constantly perform offerings at the caitya, ensuring that all ancient and venerable rites are not allowed to fall into disuse?"
The full explanation continues until: "Sixth, there is no decline in wholesome qualities. "Ānanda!

Have you not heard that the people of that country possess a profound and respectful heart toward the Arhats, constantly maintaining right mindfulness? They pray that those who have not yet come may all come here, and that those who have already arrived may dwell in peace and security; and they provide them with all necessary requisites—robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—so that nothing is lacking?"
The full explanation continues until the seventh point, that there is no decline in wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*).
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"If all the people in that country practice these seven kinds of non-retrogressive dharmas, you should know that the country will always experience growth; there shall be no loss, and wholesome qualities will flourish."
The brahmin said, "Venerable Sir!
If the people of that country practice even one of these seven dharmas, King Ajātaśatru ought not to levy punishment upon them, much less when they fully observe all seven dharmas."
The brāhmaṇa said: "Venerable Gautama!
I have many affairs and wish to take my leave."
The Buddha said,
"As you wish. At that time,
the brahmin, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
After the brahmin had taken his leave of the Buddha and departed, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"You should go and inform all the bhikṣus residing on Vulture Peak Mountain, commanding them to assemble in the Hall of Service."
Then Ānanda immediately announced this to the entire assembly of bhikṣus, and once they had all gathered in the hall, he returned to the Buddha’s presence, stood to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One! [The assembly has assembled.]”
“Bhikṣus, all have assembled; may the Buddha know that the time has come.
When the Buddha had arrived at the hall and taken his seat, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now teach you the seven dharmas that prevent decline. Listen closely and attend well to my words.”
What are the seven? O bhikṣus!

When you frequently assemble in large numbers to discuss the meaning of the Dharma, you should know that this is the first [benefit]: the bhikṣus' merit increases and their wholesome qualities suffer no loss.

"O Bhikṣus! If you assemble together in harmony, rising together, sitting together, and performing ritual acts together, you should know that merit increases and wholesome dharmas suffer no loss; this is the second point."

"O bhikṣus! You should not strive for that which ought not to be sought, nor should you fail to obtain that which ought to be obtained. Always joyfully practice all that is the true teaching. Know this: in this way, merit increases and wholesome dharmas suffer no decline. This is the third [point]."
"O Bhikṣus! All forms of attachment that arise together with craving, which delight in and aspire toward the continuity of future existences—by means of these, one revolves in saṃsāra.

If these are eliminated, you should know that one will dwell in peace and happiness, causing the merit of the bhikṣus to increase and their wholesome qualities to remain undiminished. This is the fourth [point]."

"O monks! If there is a monk who has long been ordained, who has practiced the pure holy life for twenty full years, who is praised by the elders and masters of great virtue, who is well-known to his fellow practitioners of the holy life, and whom the assembly all reveres, honors, and makes offerings to with deep respect—such that they delight in hearing his spoken instructions—know that in this way his merit increases and his wholesome qualities suffer no decline; this is the fifth."

"O bhikṣus! If there is a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya who, receiving inferior bedding and seating, gives rise to a mind of contentment—know that in this way his merit increases and wholesome dharmas do not diminish. This is the sixth."

"O Bhikṣus! If there is a bhikṣu who applies himself with earnest care toward his fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*), constantly maintaining right mindfulness so that those fellow practitioners who have not yet come may come to this place; and once they have arrived, he causes them to dwell in peace and comfort, never giving rise to weariness [in their minds]; and he provides them with all necessary requisites—new clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other essential supplies—so that they lack nothing; and so on, as extensively explained, until: 'the wholesome dharmas suffer no diminution. This is the seventh."

"O bhikṣus! When you are able to practice these seven kinds of dharmas, you should know that all the wholesome dharmas of the bhikṣus will constantly increase, without any decline, and you shall dwell in peace and happiness."
“O bhikṣus! There are furthermore seven kinds of dharmas that prevent decline; you should listen.
What are these seven?

If the bhikṣus show reverence, make offerings, respect, and praise the Great Teacher, they will dwell in peace and happiness when acting in this way; furthermore, it will cause the community of bhikṣus to increase in wholesome qualities without any decline. Thus ends the first [point].

Thus it should be understood: one should give rise to a mind of earnest devotion, respect, and veneration toward the Dharma, the precepts, matters of instruction, matters of heedfulness, matters of bedding and seating, and matters of the cultivation of meditative concentration. When acting in this way, one attains dwelling in peace and happiness, and causes the assembly of bhikṣus to increase in wholesome qualities without decline. This concludes the seventh [point].
“O bhikṣus! There are furthermore seven kinds of dharmas that prevent decline; you should listen.
What are the seven?

If bhikṣus do not delight in busy work, do not delight in idle talk, do not cling to sleep, do not enjoy socializing or associating with evil friends, do not crave fame or profit by inquiring after others, and constantly cultivate meditative concentration; if they do not give rise to complacency regarding higher realization and maintain a mind free from despondency, continuing without even a moment’s rest until they have realized the true truths—when acting in this way, they dwell in peace and happiness, causing the assembly of bhikṣus to increase in wholesome dharmas without decline. This concludes the seventh [point].
"O bhikṣus! Furthermore, there are seven kinds of dharmas that prevent decline; you should listen.
What are these seven?

If there is a bhikṣu who possesses pure faith, has a sense of shame and dread of blame, is endowed with great diligence, and possesses mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—when acting in this manner, he dwells in peace and happiness, causing the assembly of bhikṣus to increase in wholesome qualities and suffer no decline. This concludes the seventh [chapter].
“O bhikṣus! Furthermore, there are seven kinds of dharmas that prevent decline; you should listen.
What are the seven?

Knowing the Dharma, knowing the meaning, knowing the time, knowing the measure, knowing oneself, knowing one's disciples, and knowing the conduct of others—acting in this way, one dwells in peace and happiness, causing the assembly of bhikṣus to increase in wholesome qualities without decline. This concludes the seventh [section].
“O bhikṣus! There are further seven dharmas. What are the seven?

If there is a bhikṣu who, when practicing the cultivation of the awakening factor of mindfulness, relies on a secluded place, relies on detachment from desire, relies on tranquility, and remains far removed from calamities—and likewise practices diligence, joy, concentration, equanimity;

if, at the time of such cultivation, he relies on a secluded place, relies on detachment from desire, relies on tranquility, and remains far removed from calamities—then by acting in this way, he attains a dwelling in peace and happiness, causing the assembly of bhikṣus to increase in wholesome qualities without decline.

"O bhikṣus! These are the seven dharmas that are irreversible and should be constantly cultivated. You must guard them with single-minded diligence, so that the community of bhikṣus may increase in wholesome qualities and suffer no decline."
“O bhikṣus! There are further six dharmas that cause others to rejoice; you should listen attentively!
I shall explain them for you.”

What are the six? First, one should now practice loving-kindness through physical action (*kāyakarman*). This means that toward the Great Teacher, the noble ones, and fellow practitioners of the holy life, one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and pay homage with the body; one should sweep, scrub, and apply plaster, construct maṇḍalas, arrange various flowers, and burn incense as offerings; or else one should massage their hands and feet, or provide whatever is needed at the appropriate time when seeing them suffering from illness.

When acting in this way, one causes others to rejoice; they come to love, cherish, respect, and honor one another, becoming closely attached, harmonious, and supportive, free from all conflict and dispute, working together with a single mind like water and milk blending.

"Second, I should now practice loving-kindness through verbal action; that is, toward the Great Teacher and my fellow practitioners of the holy life, I shall give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and praise them with words to manifest their true virtues, so that those who have not heard of them may come to know them universally. I shall read and recite the scriptures day and night without ceasing. When acting in this way, I cause others to rejoice, and they will love, cherish, respect, and draw close to me. We shall be harmonious and united, free from all conflict, working together with one mind like water and milk blending."

"Third, I should now practice loving-kindness through mental action; that is, toward my fellow practitioners of the holy life, I shall give rise to a heart of loving-kindness, not conceiving thoughts of envy, malice, or stinginess. Regarding all acts of loving-kindness performed through bodily and verbal actions, I shall maintain focused mindfulness and reflection so as not to let them cease."
Even when facing peril and hardship, one does not pause for a moment; how much less should one deviate from right mindfulness during times of peace?

One should give rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings, refraining from taking their lives or inflicting suffering upon them, and remain far removed from afflictions to reach the state of liberation.

When acting in this manner, one causes others to rejoice; they come to love, cherish, respect, and honor one another, becoming closely attached. They remain harmonious and united without any conflict, working together with a single mind like water and milk blending.

"Fourth, whatever gains and offerings one receives in accordance with the Dharma—even if one obtains only a small amount of food and drink in one's alms bowl—one shall always rejoice and share them with others, never eating in private, and harbor no sense of 'self' or 'other' toward fellow practitioners of the holy life."

When acting in this manner, one causes others to rejoice; they come to love, cherish, respect, and honor one another, becoming intimately attached, harmonious, and supportive, free from all conflict and contention, working together with a single mind like water and milk blending.

"Fifth, regarding the precepts one has received, they are unbroken, unpierced, unmixed, unstained, and undefiled; they are maintained purely from beginning to end and praised by the wise; fellow practitioners of the holy life do not treat them with contempt, and they maintain pure precepts together, sharing equally in both the Dharma and food."
Acting in this way brings joy to others; as it is said at length, "like water and milk blending together.

Sixth, one is able to give rise to right view, free from doubt; this is the noble transcendence that cannot be destroyed, which swiftly brings an end to suffering, and which is shared with fellow practitioners of the holy life.
When acting in this way, one causes others to rejoice; as has been explained at length, it is like water and milk blending together. "O bhikṣus!
These are called the six dharmas of joy, which you should constantly cultivate and diligently guard, so that the community of bhikṣus may increase in wholesome qualities and suffer no decline."
When the assembly had heard what the Buddha had spoken, they were all filled with joy;
they accepted it with faith and practiced accordingly. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Fascicle 35. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*.
Volume Thirty-Six, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The Second Section of the Summary Verses for the Tenth Subsection of the Eighth Chapter. The internal summary verse says:
The assembly gathered and paid homage to the Great Teacher; hearing the Dharma, they gave rise to right faith.
[Venerable Vassakāra] recounted his own advanced age and spoke of the causes and conditions regarding the rain.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"I now wish to go to the town of Pāṭaliputra. Ānanda said, "So be it."
"World-Honored One!

he said, and immediately accompanied the bhikṣus as they followed the World-Honored One, traveling gradually from the kingdom of Magadha until they reached the village of Pāṭaligrāma and stayed at the edge of a caitya.

At that time, when the people of that town heard that the Buddha had arrived, they all gathered together and went to the site of the stūpa; having approached the World-Honored One, they prostrated at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmins, elders, and householders, saying:
"You should know that there are five faults associated with heedlessness. What are these five?
First, when Brahmins and others are negligent, all their wealth and articles of enjoyment are completely lost on account of this cause.
Second, when a negligent person goes to any assembly because of this cause, they feel shame and are filled with fear.
Third, if a person is heedless, by reason of this, an evil reputation will spread throughout the four quarters.
Fourth, if a person is heedless, by reason of this, at the time of death, remorse will arise in their mind.
Fifth, if a person is negligent, by reason of this, after the end of their life they will fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
These are called the five faults of negligence.
"Furthermore, when Brahmins and others practice heedfulness, there are five benefits. What are the five?
First, all their wealth and articles of enjoyment shall not be lost."
Second, wherever he goes among assemblies, his mind is free from shame or embarrassment and devoid of fear or timidity.
Third, his good reputation flows far and wide throughout the four quarters.
Fourth, at the time of death, one will not give rise to regret.
Fifth, after the end of life, one will be reborn in the heavens and experience long-lasting peace and happiness.
These are called the five benefits of practicing heedfulness.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the brahmins and others of the town of Pāṭaliputra, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, he remained silent.
The various brahmins immediately rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, placed their right knees on the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
“We pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will graciously accept us to visit his quiet lodgings during the day.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, the brahmins prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took their leave, and departed.
After the people had departed, the Buddha went to that secluded dwelling; having arrived there, he washed his feet outside the room and entered to sit in meditative repose.

At that time, the minister Vārṣika of the kingdom of Magadha measured out the four boundaries and established extensive frontiers at the town of Pāṭaligrāma, intending to build a city wall and moat to punish the country of the Kṛṣṇas. At that time, powerful and majestic devas within this town each sought a dwelling place.

At that time, while seated in meditation, the World-Honored One used his divine eye, which surpasses that of humans and devas, to observe those celestial deities each seeking a dwelling place. Then, in the late afternoon, he arose from his meditation and went to a cool spot where he sat and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Have you not heard of the measuring out of cities?"
He addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"I have heard that the minister Vardhana intends to establish a city-state to fortify himself before attacking the northern city.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! Excellent! That the minister Vassakāra possesses such great wisdom as to desire to establish a city that resembles the form of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.”
From my dwelling place, I observed with the divine eye that various great deities were each seeking a place to dwell. Ānanda!
Wherever these powerful deities wish to dwell, within this city, persons of great merit also seek to dwell therein.
However, wherever the gods of the middle regions desire to dwell, there the people of the middle regions and other classes likewise reside. Ānanda!
That city where superior persons dwell, where superior persons hold discourse, and where eminent merchants come to trade and travel without hindrance—this is precisely this city of Pāṭaliputra.
"However, there are three calamities that shall destroy this city:
namely, water, fire, and internal rebellion.

At that time, the minister Vassakāra heard that the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, had been traveling gradually from Magadha and had arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputra, staying at the site of a *caitya*, where he was being venerated by the multitude of people.

Having heard this, he immediately went to where the World-Honored One was; after performing his respects and exchanging greetings, he withdrew to sit at one side. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him, after which he remained silent.
At that time, the minister rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, said:
"Gautama! I pray that tomorrow you and the community of bhikṣus will come to my residence to accept a modest offering."
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, the minister rose from his seat and departed.
When the minister Vardhana arrived at his residence, he informed everyone, both great and small, and that very night prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink.

Once the meal was prepared, at dawn on the following day, he arranged the seats and placed clean water basins; having meticulously prepared the bathing powder and tooth-sticks until everything was complete, he immediately sent a messenger to announce:
"The time has come!"
"The food and drink are prepared; may the Blessed One know that it is time.

Thereupon, at the time for the morning meal, the World-Honored One took up his robe and bowl and, accompanied by the assembly of monks, went to the minister's house and sat down upon the seat prepared for the meal.

When the minister Varṣākāra saw that the Buddha and the great assembly were seated in order, he personally served various kinds of exquisite food and drink, providing for the Buddha and the Sangha until they were all fully satisfied. After they had chewed their tooth-sticks and rinsed their mouths, and the bowls had been withdrawn, [the minister performed his duties].
The minister Vassakāra immediately poured water from a golden pitcher before the Buddha and stood there, making this aspiration:

"By the power of all the excellent and wholesome karma resulting from this offering of mine, may I obtain a joyful retribution; by the force of this merit, may the devas who have long resided within this city enjoy superior benefit and happiness throughout the long night. I pray that you shall invoke their names and offer a blessing."
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to express his sympathetic joy for the offerings provided by the great minister, spoke these verses:
“If a person possesses pure faith and reverently makes offerings to the Great Assembly;
If they always rely upon the true words of the Great Teacher, They shall be praised by all the Buddhas.”
If there be a person of intelligence and wisdom who chooses to dwell in this supreme and wondrous place;
if they make offerings to those pure practitioners who uphold the precepts, one should further proclaim for them these verses of aspiration.
If one intends to practice respectful giving, one should cultivate offerings with a sincere heart;
thereby the celestial hosts will give rise to kindness and compassion, just as parents cherish their own infant.
Having been protected by all the devas, one shall always enjoy supreme bliss in peace;
in every birth, one will constantly encounter virtuous people, until finally reaching the state of the unconditioned.
At that time, the World-Honored One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the great minister with a discourse on the sublime Dharma, after which he rose from his seat and departed.
Then, the minister, realizing that all worldly phenomena ultimately end in abandonment, adjusted his robes, followed behind the World-Honored One, and thought to himself:
"Where the World-Honored One Gautama exits the city, I shall construct a great gate-tower there; and where he crosses the Gaṅgā River, I shall establish a ferry for him."

At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, knowing their thoughts, proceeded along the western road within the city toward the outer gate; facing north, he walked toward the river intending to cross it.

At that moment, many people in the river were wishing to cross; some used grass, wood, gourds, or inflated skins as rafts to ford the water, coming and going in an unceasing stream numbering in the hundreds of millions.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Should I now proceed by walking with composed steps upon the middle of the flowing water,
or should I use my supernatural power to vanish from this shore and reappear on the other shore?"
He immediately entered a sublime meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and, according to his intention, vanished from here and reappeared there along with the bhikṣus.
At that moment, a certain bhikṣu spoke this verse:
“Those people seeking to cross over, Come and go in numbers beyond counting;”
With a leather float and reeds, they sought to cross the ford of the Gaṅgā;
yet by the World-Honored One’s supernormal power, together with the assembly of monks,
they reached the opposite shore without further fatigue.
"When the waters of the level plains overflow, what further use is there for digging wells?
When the root of the mind's afflictions is removed, why seek anything else!
At that time, the minister Vassakāra built a gatehouse at the place where the Buddha had exited the city, naming it the Gautama Gate.
The river crossing steps were known as the Gautama Path.
At that time, having reached the northern bank, the Blessed One said to Ānanda:
"I now wish to go to the Upavattana forest north of the village of Kuśinārā."
When the Buddha had arrived there and was seated, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"This is ethical discipline (śīla), this is meditative concentration (samādhi), and this is wisdom (prajñā). Through the power of maintaining ethical discipline, one is able to abide securely for a long time without falling back; through the cultivation of concentration, wisdom is born; and through the power of wisdom, the mind is liberated from attachment, aversion, and delusion."
Thus, those bhikṣus were well-liberated in mind;

having attained right understanding, they knew according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, there is no further existence, and what was to be done has been accomplished."
The Blessed One again addressed Ānanda, saying:
"I now wish to go to the forest outside the village of Veṇugrāmaka. He replied:
“World-Honored One!
We shall depart accordingly.

Having arrived there, at that time the people of that village were afflicted by a pestilence; a certain lay follower (*upāsaka*) of pure faith passed away because of it, and furthermore, other lay followers such as Bhadrika and Yaśas also all passed away.

At that time, during the morning mealtime, the bhikṣus took up their robes and bowls and entered the village to go on almsround in succession, hearing that many people in this village had died from an epidemic.

Having received their food, they each returned to their respective places. When they had finished eating, put away their robes and bowls, and washed their feet, they went together to where the Buddha was. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they sat to one side and said to him:
“World-Honored One!”
"When we entered the village to wander for alms, we heard that many upāsakas had all passed away; we do not yet know where they have been reborn."
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣus!

In this village there are two hundred and fifty upāsakas who have severed the five lower fetters; having passed away from here, they have attained birth by transformation and will attain parinirvāṇa there without ever falling back. Having realized the fruit of non-returning, they shall not come here again."

"O Bhikṣus! Furthermore, more than three hundred upāsakas have passed away from this life; having attenuated passion, hatred, and delusion, they have attained the fruit of once-returning and shall return to this human world but once more before putting an end to suffering."

"O bhikṣus! Among the people in this village, five hundred have already passed away; they had severed the three fetters, attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti), and shall no longer fall back. Having transmigrated seven times among gods and humans, they will reach the end of suffering."
"O bhikṣus! Why trouble yourselves by asking such questions and causing this disturbance?
That those who are born must die is a constant law."

Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the Tathāgata fully knows the phenomena of birth and death; for the sake of all sentient beings, he analyzes and expounds them, revealing the Dharma-gate of the twelvefold dependent origination.

That is to say: because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. Namely: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.

When this does not exist, that does not exist; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease. In this way, this entire vast mass of suffering is utterly extinguished.
I shall now further preach for you the *Dharmādarśa-sūtra*; you should listen attentively and reflect upon it well.
What is the mirror of the Dharma?

It refers to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the noble, pure precepts. You should generate deep respect for these, honoring, making offerings to, prostrating before, and praising them; with right faith and right mindfulness, never allowing them to be interrupted—this is called the mirror of the Dharma, and thus you should uphold it.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, practiced in accordance with his instructions.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"I now wish to go to Vaiśālī; you should inform the great assembly."
Then Ānanda said: “So be it, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha and the assembly of monks gradually arrived at the city and stayed in the Āmra Grove.

At that time, there was a woman in this city—formerly called "Nai-nü," but this is incorrect—who was renowned for her upright and beautiful countenance; her name was Āmrapālī, and she was the mistress of this grove.

Hearing that the World-Honored One had arrived and was staying in her grove, she adorned herself with exquisite garments and necklaces, commanded her female attendants to accompany her, and mounted a precious chariot to go to the World-Honored One’s location. Upon reaching the grove, she immediately alighted from the carriage and proceeded on foot.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma amidst an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus.
Then, seeing the women from afar, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"That group of women wishes to come here; you should all fix your mindfulness and contemplate, do not harbor divergent thoughts, and listen to what I shall say."
"O Bhikṣus! What is called 'contemplation with mindfulness'?

If a bhikṣu should give rise to sinful thoughts or unwholesome states of mind, he should immediately dispel them. He should generate right faith and arouse diligence, gathering the mind so that it abides in right mindfulness without distraction, causing wholesome dharmas to arise and evil thoughts to cease. Through the cultivation of right knowledge, he should bring it to fulfillment and expansion, maintaining continuous right effort without allowing for divergent thoughts."
"Monks, you should thus fix your mindfulness and reflect.
Listen further! Do not harbor divergent thoughts."
"O Bhikṣus, you should know!

Whether going or returning, you should carefully observe your movements; whether bending or stretching, looking down or looking up; whether putting on the saṃghāṭī robe or taking up the robes and bowl; whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, speaking, remaining silent, sleeping, or arising from a state of torpor—you should dwell with right mindfulness, applying the appropriate remedial dharmas."
How does a bhikṣu dwell with right mindfulness?
You should know this now:
it means observing the body internally, exerting right effort, and skillfully subduing [the mind], while recognizing that all worldly things are sorrow and suffering.

Next, one contemplates the external body, the internal and external body; internal feelings, external feelings, and internal and external feelings; the internal mind, the external mind, and the internal and external mind; and internal phenomena, external phenomena, and internal and external phenomena. Regarding these various phenomena, one binds the mindfulness to observe them, gathering the mind to cause it to abide. One should arouse right diligence, being courageous and unceasing, properly subduing the mind; and regarding all worldly things, one should know them to be sorrow and suffering.
"Monks, you should thus maintain focused mindfulness and reflection.
Therefore, you must abide in right mindfulness, for this is my earnest instruction to you regarding the arrival of that assembly of women."
At that time, the assembly of women approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then the World-Honored One preached the sublime Dharma to them, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening them, before remaining silent.
Then Āmrapālī rose from her seat, joined her palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
I pray that out of compassion you and the bhikṣus will accept my humble offering at my home tomorrow."
The World-Honored One remained silent. Knowing that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], they prostrated at his feet, took their leave, and departed.

At that time, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling through the human realm and was staying in the Āmra Grove. Each of them prepared various precious chariots drawn by teams of four horses; they drove blue horses yoked to blue chariots with blue reins and blue whips. They wore blue caps, held blue parasols, carried blue swords, and grasped blue fly-whisks; they donned blue robes, and their necklaces and ointments were all blue in color. All their attendants likewise wore blue clothing.
Furthermore, there were the Licchavis, who formed a separate group with their attendants; their chariots, horses, garments, and necklaces were all yellow.
Another group was entirely red, and another group was entirely white.

Thus, with their respective divisions of troops arranged one after another, they sounded conchs and beat drums as they emerged from Vaiśālī, all desiring to personally behold the Tathāgata and pay him homage with reverence.
Knowing that they wished to come, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Those of you who have not yet seen the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven strolling through their fragrant gardens, you may now observe these Licchavis of Vaiśālī; by virtue of their majesty and their exquisite adornments, they are no different from the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven when they go out to stroll through their fragrant gardens."

When the Licchavis had reached the grove, they alighted from their chariots and proceeded on foot. Approaching the World-Honored One, they prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side desiring to hear the sublime Dharma, and the World-Honored One taught them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them so that each was filled with joy.
At that time, there was a brahmin in the assembly named the youth Pīṅgala; he rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"I now wish to rejoice in and praise [this].
The Buddha said to the māṇava, "Speak as you please."
Having received the Buddha’s permission, he immediately spoke in verse:
“The Great King bears jeweled armor upon his person; As sovereign of the land, he has now attained a noble benefit.
A Buddha has appeared and been born in this place, His fame and renown as lofty as Mount Sumeru.”
Like a white lotus in a pond, blooming at night and scattering its fragrance,
like the flowing radiance of the sun illuminating the realm of space, his light fills the entire world.
One should contemplate the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, Like a great bright torch illuminating the darkness;
He constantly acts as the eye of wisdom for humans and devas, And all who come to see him are brought to subdual.
When the Licchavis heard these words, they praised him with one voice, saying:
"O great Māṇava! Well spoken are these words!"

At that time, there were five hundred Licchavis in the assembly; each removed his upper garment and offered it to the Yellow-haired One. The World-Honored One again taught the Dharma to the great assembly, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, and then remained silent.
Then the Licchavis each rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for us, will accept our humble offering together with the bhikṣus tomorrow within the city."
The Buddha said,
"I have already accepted the invitation of the lady Āmrapālī for the bhikṣus to take a meal tomorrow. He replied:
“Venerable Sir!

I have fallen short compared to that woman; she possesses wisdom, for she invited the World-Honored One first. We were unable to attend upon, revere, and prostrate to him in a timely manner. At a later time, I shall offer my worship.”
The Buddha said, "Excellent!
Having heard the Buddha's praise, his heart was filled with joy; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and departed.
At that time, after seeing those people depart from the Buddha, the Māṇava remained for a short while, then rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."

Upon hearing my praise of the Buddha, those five hundred people rejoiced with one voice; for the sake of these sublime words, each offered me a robe, which I have now brought to present to the Buddha. I pray that you will, out of compassion and pity, graciously accept them.
The Blessed One accepted [the offering] and said:
"Māṇava! When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, five rare and wonderful things also appear in the world."
What are these five? They are as follows:

when a Great Teacher appears in the world—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān—whatever Dharma he teaches is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end; its words and meaning are exquisite, pure, singular, complete, and it possesses the characteristics of the stainless, pristine Brahma-faring.
"You should know that this appearance of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha in the world is the foremost rarity.
Furthermore, if there are those who hear such sublime Dharma and are able to apply their minds skillfully with single-minded scrutiny, withdrawing their sense faculties to reflect and investigate."
"You should know that this is the second rare occurrence in the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha in the world.

Furthermore, when those who hear the Dharma experience joy in their hearts and obtain great, wholesome benefit, giving rise to a mind of weary detachment toward worldly affairs—this is the third rare occurrence in the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha in the world."

"Furthermore, if there are those who hear the Dharma through successive transmission, they all likewise gradually rely upon the teaching to receive and uphold it; this is the fourth rare and marvelous quality of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, appearing in the world."

"Furthermore, those who hear the Dharma apply their mindfulness and contemplate it, thereby being able to penetrate the profound and sublime wisdom; this is the fifth rare and marvelous quality of the appearance of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha in the world."
"Furthermore, Māṇava! One who recognizes kindness and repays it is called a great noble person; they do not forget even a small favor, let alone a great one!
Therefore, you should now apply yourself diligently to practice and study."
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Māṇava rejoiced and accepted it with faith; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and departed.

At that time, the lady Āmrapālī prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink that very night. When the clear dawn arrived, she spread out mats and seats, set out a basin of pure water, tooth-sticks, and tooth-powder, and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
“The meal is ready; may the Buddha know that the time has come.”
At that time, the Blessed One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and together with the assembly of bhikṣus, went to the place where the meal was being served.

Once the Buddha and the great assembly had sat down in order, the lady Āmrapālī, seeing that the Buddha and the great assembly were all seated comfortably, personally served them various kinds of excellent food and drink until everyone was fully satisfied.

When the meal was finished, he next provided him with bathing powder and a tooth-stick; once he had rinsed his mouth and put away his bowl, he took a low seat and sat before the Buddha to listen to the Dharma with a concentrated mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the sake of the girl:
"If a person is not stingy and is able to give, Those who see them will love, respect, and draw near;
Entering into assemblies, they are free from fear, Attaining great benefit and possessing a renowned name."
Therefore, the wise person always practices giving, which causes merit to increase throughout the long night;
gradually eliminating afflictions and destroying stinginess and greed, they enjoy happiness in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Cultivating various wholesome deeds and performing meritorious acts, one will be reborn in heaven after the end of this life;
sporting with hosts of celestial maidens in fragrant gardens, as a disciple of the Buddha, one shall always enjoy peace and happiness.

At that time, the Blessed One further taught the Dharma to the lady Āmrapālī according to her capacity, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening her. Having done so, he rose from his seat and departed.
Returning to his dwelling, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"I now wish to go to the Bamboo Grove; you should inform the great assembly."
Then Ānanda, following the Buddha’s instruction, went with the great assembly to follow the Buddha to the Bamboo Grove, where they stayed in the Veṇuvana forest.
At that time, it was a season of famine and alms were difficult to obtain. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“Now that there is a famine and alms are hard to find, you should seek out like-minded companions and enter the rains retreat as appropriate in various villages and districts throughout Vaiśālī; Ānanda and I shall remain here.”
"If it were not so, it would be difficult to obtain what one seeks through begging.

When the bhikṣus had heard the Buddha’s instruction, each followed their spiritual friends and entered the rains retreat in various places; only Ānanda remained alone to attend upon the Buddha, entering the rains retreat beneath a tree.
During the summer retreat, the Buddha’s body was afflicted by the suffering of illness; enduring various pains and distresses, he nearly reached the point of death.

He thought to himself: "My body is diseased and will not long remain; however, the bhikṣus are scattered in other places. I should not pass into parinirvāṇa apart from the great assembly. I shall instead observe my own body with the signless samādhi so that this suffering may be stilled."
Having formed this thought, he immediately entered a superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*); all the sufferings he experienced were eliminated just as he had intended, and he dwelt in peace.
Then, at the hour of sunset, the Venerable Ānanda arose from his concentration, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and with palms joined, addressed him:
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!"

"Previously, my body and mind were so bewildered and distressed that I could not distinguish between good and evil; I was unable to recite or retain the Dharma I had heard. This was because I saw that the World-Honored One was suffering from various ailments and feared he would soon enter parinirvāṇa. Now that I have heard that the World-Honored One has not yet entered parinirvāṇa, I have regained a measure of clarity."
He further said:
"If the bhikṣus do not all assemble, I shall not enter parinirvāṇa. By reflecting on this, one knows that he will further preach the rare and marvelous Dharma.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you think that I do not enter parinirvāṇa because I am instructing the bhikṣus, such a thing is impossible."
Why is this? How could I now wish to further demonstrate to the bhikṣus a rare and marvelous dharma? Ānanda!

That which I ought to have explained has now been fully explained, so as to bring about complete understanding of all internal and external phenomena—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path.
Ānanda! All Buddhas, Tathāgatas, always expound this Dharma clearly and distinctly, without any heart of secrecy, stinginess, or concealment. Yet, Ānanda!
My body is afflicted with illness and I am about to enter parinirvāṇa; I then had this thought:

"I am now suffering from this disease and my life will surely come to an end. While the bhikṣus are each in different places, it would not be right for me to enter parinirvāṇa apart from this great assembly. It is fitting that I should apply my own mind to observe my body with the samādhi of signlessness (animitta-samādhi), so that these painful afflictions may be stilled."
He then entered into meditative concentration, whereby all the sufferings he had endured were completely healed, and he dwelt in peace and security. Ānanda!

I am now advanced in years, my physical strength is frail, and I am nearly eighty; I subsist by relying on two things, just as a dilapidated cart also relies on two things. For this reason, you should not now be sorrowful or distressed.
However, it is impossible for any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world, which arise from causes and conditions, not to perish and instead attain permanence.

I have previously and constantly taught you this matter: all that is delightful, splendid, cherished, and pleasing in the world will utterly disintegrate; there is no abiding in the separation from those one loves. Therefore, you should know this!

Whether during my present lifetime or after my parinirvāṇa, you yourselves shall be your island and yourselves your refuge; the Dharma shall be your island and the Dharma your refuge, with no other island and no other refuge.
Why is this? Whether during my present lifetime or after my parinirvāṇa, those who rely on the Dharma and delight in upholding the precepts shall be foremost among my śrāvaka disciples.
How is it that a bhikṣu makes himself his island and makes himself his refuge, having no other island and no other refuge?

Ānanda! If bhikṣus are able to skillfully know the characteristics of the internal body, maintaining mindfulness to observe it, gathering the mind to cause it to abide, and exerting vigor to subdue greed, hatred, and all forms of sorrow and affliction.

In this way, one binds the mindfulness to and observes the external body, internal body, and both internal and external bodies; internal sensations, external sensations, and both internal and external sensations; internal mind, external mind, and both internal and external minds; and internal phenomena, external phenomena, and both internal and external phenomena. In these places, one collects the mind to cause it to abide, rouses courageous effort, and subdues greed, hatred, and all forms of sorrow and affliction.
"If a bhikṣu contemplates in this manner, this is called making oneself an island, making oneself a refuge, and dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.
A summary verse states:
"Varuṇā within the Bamboo Grove; repairing the town of Pāṭalī."
Crossing the river, he went to a small village, gradually approaching Nirvāṇa and other [stages].
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"I now wish to go to Vaiśālī."
When Ānanda had heard the Buddha’s instruction, he followed behind the Buddha to the city of Vaiśālī and stayed in the Kūṭāgāraśālā.

At the time for the morning meal, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. Ānanda followed the Buddha as they went, and having completed their alms-round in due order, they returned to their original place. After finishing the meal, putting away the robes and bowl, and completing the ritual rinsing, the Buddha washed his feet and then proceeded to the foot of the Caitya tree called Gṛdhrakūṭa (the Vulture Peak) and sat down.

He addressed Ānanda, saying: "This city of Vaiśālī is magnificent in its produce; fragrant groves and fruit trees flourish everywhere, and its stupas, temples, and clear ponds are most delightful. Within Jambudvīpa, this is the most extraordinary."
Ānanda! If there are those who can cultivate and repeatedly practice the four bases of psychic power, they may remain for an eon or even beyond an eon, all according to their will.
Ānanda! The Tathāgata has extensively cultivated the four bases of psychic power; he possesses complete mastery over remaining for an eon, or even longer than an eon.

At that time, Ānanda remained silent and spoke no word. Thus, although the World-Honored One thrice proclaimed the aforementioned matter, up to the point where he said, "All are entirely at their own disposal," Ānanda likewise remained silent throughout.
The Buddha thought to himself:

"Now Ānanda has been deluded by Māra and his body and mind are confused. Although I have already informed him clearly three times, he remains unable to speak or make a request; from this, I know for certain that he has been deluded by Māra."
He then said to him:
"You should sit in meditative seclusion beneath a tree; you should not dwell in close proximity with you.
Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda immediately went to his place for daytime meditation and sat beneath a tree.
At that time, the evil Māra Pāpīyas approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side. With palms joined in reverence, he addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"The time for parinirvāṇa has arrived; I only pray that the Sugata will enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha said to Māra:
"For what reason do you now say that the time for parinirvāṇa has arrived and request my parinirvāṇa?"
Māra said: "Venerable One!
Once in the past, not long after the Buddha had attained enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree on the banks of the Nairañjanā River, I went to him and said: "
“World-Honored One, you should know that the time for your parinirvāṇa has arrived; we pray only that the Sugata enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha said to me:

“If my noble assembly of śrāvaka disciples have not yet attained wisdom, penetrating understanding, intelligence, and eloquence, such that they can suppress heterodox arguments with the words of the True Dharma and cause the holy teaching to flourish and spread; and if the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās have also not yet been able to firmly cultivate the categories of precepts so as to cause my Brahma-faring to be widely disseminated, benefiting many people and the hosts of devas—then it is not appropriate for me at this time to enter great parinirvāṇa.”
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!

Now the assembly of śrāvakas possesses great wisdom; they are fully endowed with penetrating eloquence that is unimpeded, and by means of the words of the True Dharma, they subdue heterodox doctrines, proclaiming and causing the Noble Teaching to circulate."

Furthermore, since the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās will be able to cause the holy life to spread widely, benefiting many people as well as the hosts of devas, and all matters will reach fulfillment—for these reasons, I now address the World-Honored One:
"The time for parinirvāṇa has arrived; I only pray that the Sugata will enter parinirvāṇa."
The Buddha said to Māra:
"Wait but a moment; before long, after three months have passed, the Tathāgata shall enter the realm of great parinirvāṇa without remainder."
At that time, Māra thought to himself:
“The śramaṇa Gautama speaks without duplicity; he will certainly enter parinirvāṇa.”
Feeling great joy, he suddenly vanished.
The Buddha thought to himself:

"I should now enter such a meditative absorption that, by the power of that concentration, I may retain my vital formations (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) while relinquishing my life-formations (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*)."
Having formed this thought, he immediately entered meditative absorption, retaining the life-force (*jīvita-saṃskāra*) while relinquishing the life-span (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*).
At that moment, the great earth shook in its entirety; the four quarters blazed with fire, stars fell from the sky, and celestial drums resounded spontaneously in the void.
The Buddha emerged from meditative concentration and spoke these verses:
"All that is equal and unequal, the Muni has entirely eliminated;
By attaining internal realization through concentration, He is like a bird that has broken its shell."
Then, at the time of sunset, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his meditative seclusion and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what cause and condition does the great earth tremble?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There are eight causes and conditions for the great earth to tremble."
What are the eight?
This great earth rests upon water; the water rests upon wind; and the wind rests upon space. Ānanda!
At times, when great and violent winds appear in the sky, the water wavers; if the water is shaken, the earth trembles.
Ānanda, this is the first causal condition for the trembling of the great earth.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

A bhikṣu of great majesty and great power, by means of his supernormal powers, perceives this great earth as a small particle and enters into the perception of boundless water, desiring to cause the entire great earth to tremble."
Ānanda, if a bhikṣuṇī or any member of the assembly of devas possessing great majesty and power were to form such a thought, it would likewise cause the entire great earth to tremble. Ānanda!
This is the second cause and condition for the great earth to tremble. Furthermore, Ānanda!

When a Great Bodhisattva descends from Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb, the great earth trembles, and throughout all worlds a brilliant radiance shines forth, far surpassing the light of the heavens. Even those places in the world that are most profound and dark, which the sun and moon—with their great majestic brilliance—cannot illuminate, are all universally bathed in a magnificent and resplendent light at the moment the Bodhisattva manifests birth within his mother’s womb.

Since birth, sentient beings have been unable to see even their own hands; it is only through the illumination of light that they are able to see one another and realize that other sentient beings have also been born here.
Ānanda! This is the third cause and condition for the great earth to tremble.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!"
When a great bodhisattva is first born, the great earth trembles, as described extensively above.
This is the fourth cause and condition for the trembling of the great earth.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
When a bodhisattva attains perfect enlightenment, the great earth trembles, as described at length above.
This is the fifth cause and condition for the trembling of the great earth."

"Furthermore, Ānanda! When the Tathāgata turns the Wheel of Dharma for the third time, the great earth trembles, as described above; this is the sixth cause and condition for the trembling of the great earth."

"Furthermore, Ānanda! When the Tathāgata retains the life-force (*jīvita-saṃskāra*) and relinquishes the vitality-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*), the great earth trembles; blazing light streams forth from the four quarters with brilliant splendor, and celestial drums resound spontaneously in the sky. This is the seventh cause and condition for the trembling of the great earth."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

In three months from now, the Tathāgata will enter the wondrous realm of nirvāṇa without remainder. At that time, the great earth will tremble, and the four quarters, above, and below will be brilliantly illuminated; in the sky, the cries of the devas will sound like the beating of drums."
"Ānanda! This is the eighth cause and condition for the great earth to tremble.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I contemplate the matter spoken of by the Tathāgata—how he sustains the formations of life while relinquishing the formations of longevity—it is for this reason that the great earth trembles throughout.”
The Buddha told Ānanda: "So it is, so it is!
I have retained the force of life (āyu-saṃskāra) while relinquishing the force of longevity (jīvita-saṃskāra)."
Ānanda said: "Venerable Sir!
I have personally heard the Buddha speak thus:"
"If there are those who can cultivate and repeatedly practice the four bases of psychic power, they will attain mastery over remaining for an eon or even beyond an eon."

"Venerable World-Honored One, you have already cultivated and extensively practiced the four bases of psychic power; we only pray that the World-Honored One will remain in the world for one eon, and that the Sugata will remain for more than one eon."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This irrational act is your own fault. Although I have already informed you clearly three times, you were unable to understand my intention because the māra Pāpīyas has deluded and confused your mind."
Ānanda! What do you think? Do the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, ever speak with duality?
He replied, "It is not so. The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent, Ānanda!”
"It is impossible that the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, would utter two different words.
I have already granted permission to Māra; you should not make this request, Ānanda!"
"You should now go to the vicinity of the Bow Stūpa and have all the resident bhikṣus assemble together in the constant dining hall.

At that time, Ānanda went and made the announcement everywhere; once the assembly had gathered, he went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms, and said:
"Virtuous World-Honored One!"
The entire assembly of bhikṣus gathered at the regular dining hall and said, "May the Buddha know that the time has come.
The Buddha rose from his seat, entered the hall, took his place, and addressed the bhikṣus:

"Observe, all of you: all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are subject to change and transformation, and cannot be relied upon. You should deeply cultivate weariness toward them, renounce them, and seek liberation."
"You should all know that there is a sublime Dharma which brings benefit, happiness, and peaceful dwelling in the present life, and likewise brings benefit and happiness in future lives.

You bhikṣus should receive, uphold, read, and recite this Dharma; you should skillfully understand its meaning and reverently practice it, so that the holy life may endure for a long time without perishing."
In this way, such a Dharma attains vast benefit for sentient beings, out of compassion for all, bringing peace and happiness to humans and devas.
What is this supreme Dharma that can attain benefit and happiness in the present life as well as benefit and happiness in future lives?

If bhikṣus uphold, recite, and master its meaning, and practice it with diligence, they will cause the holy life (brahmacarya) to endure long without extinction; such a Dharma will then be widely propagated, benefiting sentient beings, showing compassion for all, and bringing peace and happiness to humans and devas.

That which is called the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path—know that these bring benefit and happiness in the present life as well as in future lives; they should be recited, upheld, and never forgotten.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"I now wish to go to the village of Ghoṣila.
Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda immediately followed behind the Buddha.
When the World-Honored One reached the boundary of the grove to the northwest of Vaiśālī, he turned his entire body to the right like a great elephant king and gazed toward Vaiśālī.
Having personally traveled to this place and paid his respects in person, Ānanda addressed him during the time when the holy teachings were to circulate in the final age:
“World-Honored One!”
“The Tathāgata’s rightward circumambulation and his surveying of the city walls were not without cause;
I pray that you will explain it for me. The Buddha told Ānanda:
“My rightward glance and survey now, as you have said, were not without cause.”

Ānanda! This is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, looking for the very last time toward the city of Vaiśālī. I now wish to go to the Śāla twin trees in the birthplace of the Mallas to enter parinirvāṇa, never to return again; that is why I turn back to look upon this city.
At that time, a bhikṣu, having heard the Buddha’s words, spoke this verse:
“Casting his final glance back at the magnificent city, The Perfectly Awakened One shall not return here again;
Now he intends to go to the site of the Twin Śāla Trees, To the birthplace of the Great Hero, to realize nirvana without remainder.”
When the Blessed One had arrived at the village of Ghoṣila and stayed in the Śālavana forest, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"You should know this! These are morality, concentration, and wisdom. Through the practice of morality, concentration abides for a long time; through the excellent cultivation of concentration, pure wisdom arises; and through the possession of wisdom, one attains liberation from desire, hatred, and delusion. Regarding such a state of liberation of the mind, the noble disciples truly understand it thus:"
"My births are ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.

Thus, he traveled in succession through more than ten villages, preaching the Dharma to sentient beings according to their capacities, until he reached the northern forest outside the city of Suyama, where he stayed.

At that time, the great earth shook in its entirety; smoke and flames blazed fiercely in the four quarters, above, and below; the sun and moon lost their radiance, meteors fell, and celestial drums resounded spontaneously within the realm of space.

Then, at the time of sunset, Ānanda rose from his meditative seclusion and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and with palms joined, addressed him, saying:
“Venerable World-Honored One!
"For what causes and conditions does the great earth tremble?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The great earth trembles for three causes and conditions."
What are these three?
This great earth rests upon water; water rests upon wind; and wind rests upon space. When the wind strikes the water in space, waves arise; and when the water has waves, the earth trembles.
Ānanda! This is the first causal condition for the great earth to tremble. Furthermore, Ānanda!

If a bhikṣu possesses great majesty and great efficacy, he can, by means of his supernormal powers, perceive this great earth as a tiny mote of dust and conceive it as boundless water, thereby causing the entire great earth to tremble.
If a bhikṣuṇī or any deity of great majesty and power causes the great earth to shake, it will tremble throughout.
Ānanda! This is the second cause and condition for the great earth to quake, as explained in detail previously.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
If the Tathāgata were soon to enter parinirvāṇa, the great earth would tremble, as was explained at length previously. Ānanda!"
