"This is the third cause and condition for the great earth to tremble.
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How marvelous!
Great Virtue, you are able to accomplish such inconceivable deeds; before long, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will enter great parinirvāṇa."
"Because of this meaning, the great earth shook, manifesting a rare and marvelous sign.
As previously explained in detail, the Buddha said: "It is so!"
"So it is! It is just as you have said; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, truly is able to accomplish such rare and marvelous qualities. Ānanda!"

In the past, I once caused immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kṣatriyas to behold me; at that time, according to their respective proportions of height and size, I assumed a physical form identical to theirs, and my complexion and voice were likewise similar to theirs.

The meaning they have spoken, I also speak; for those who do not understand it, I shall explain it. Having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them with the supreme Dharma so that they may attain awakening, I then vanish, and they do not know where I am.
He spoke these words:
"Where has he gone? Is he a deva?"
"To be a human being?
That is not within my domain," [said the Buddha]. "Ānanda!"
I am able to accomplish such immeasurable and rare dharmas; it is exactly so among the assemblies of kṣatriyas, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and householders.

From the desire realm and the form realm up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, I have gone to each of those places and manifested myself according to their respective dimensions, lengths, and proportions, as described extensively above.
"Even unto Ānanda! I am able to accomplish such immeasurable and marvelous dharmas.

The remainder of the summary verse for the tenth section of the eighth chapter explains the four black and four white dharmas, the four kinds of śramaṇas, and the departure from Vaiśālī toward the place of nirvāṇa. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should know this: there are both true and false teachings. From this day forward, you must rely upon the sūtras and the teachings, and not rely upon persons."
What is meant by relying on the teaching and not relying on the person?
If a bhikṣu comes and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!..."

"I have heard these words directly from the Tathāgata; having heard them, I have retained them in memory. This discourse on the sūtra and this teaching of the vinaya that I am proclaiming is truly the word of the Buddha.

When a bhikṣu hears such a statement, he should neither praise nor disparage it. He should listen to those words and carefully retain the phrasing, then return to his residence to examine the sūtras and the teachings of the vinaya.
If what they have said contradicts the Sūtras and the Vinaya, one should tell them:
"Venerable friend!
What you have said is not the word of the Buddha; it is your own misinterpretation and does not rely upon the Sūtras and the Vinaya. You must abandon it."
"Furthermore, Ānanda! If a bhikṣu comes and speaks thus:
'Venerable One!'"

"At a certain residence, I saw a great assembly, most of whom were elders well-versed in the Vinaya-piṭaka; there I personally heard these words, and having heard them, I have retained them. They all accord with the Sūtras and the Vinaya and are truly the Buddha’s word."

When this bhikṣu hears what that person says, he should neither praise nor disparage it; he should listen to those words, carefully retain the phrasing, and upon returning to his dwelling, examine the scriptural texts and the Vinaya teachings.
If what they have said contradicts the Sūtras and the Vinaya, one should tell them:
"Venerable sir!
What you have said is not the word of the Buddha; it is your own misinterpretation, as it does not rely upon the Sūtras and the Vinaya. You must abandon it."
"Furthermore, Ānanda! If a bhikṣu comes and speaks thus:
'Venerable one!'"

"At a certain residence, I saw a great many bhikṣus who all upheld the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā. I personally heard these words from them; having heard them, I have retained them in memory. They all conform to the Sūtras and the Vinaya and are truly the Buddha’s word."

When this bhikṣu hears what that person says, he should neither praise nor disparage it; rather, he should listen to their words and carefully retain the phrasing, then return to his dwelling to examine the scriptural texts and the Vinaya teachings.
If what he says contradicts the Sūtras and the Vinaya, one should tell him:
"Venerable sir!
What you have said is not the word of the Buddha; it is your own misinterpretation, as it does not rely upon the Sūtras and the Vinaya. You must abandon it."
"Furthermore, Ānanda! If a bhikṣu comes and speaks thus:
'Venerable one!'"

"At a certain residence, I saw a bhikṣu who was a venerable elder and a wise man; there I personally heard these words, and having heard them, I have retained them. They are all in accordance with the Sūtras and the Vinaya, and are truly the word of the Buddha."

When this bhikṣu hears what that person says, he should neither praise nor disparage it; he should listen to their words and carefully retain the phrasing, then return to his dwelling to consult the sūtras and the Vinaya teachings.
If what they have said contradicts the Sūtras and the Vinaya, one should tell them:
"Venerable sir!
What you have said was not spoken by the Buddha; it is your own mistaken interpretation, as it does not rely upon the Sūtras and the Vinaya, and must therefore be abandoned."
"Furthermore, Ānanda! If a bhikṣu comes and speaks thus:
'Venerable One!'"
"I have heard these words directly from the Tathāgata; having heard them, I have retained them in memory and am now reciting this sūtra and teaching this vinaya.

When a bhikṣu hears such a statement, he should neither praise nor disparage it. He should listen to those words and carefully retain the phrasing, then return to his dwelling place to verify the text against the sūtras and the vinaya teachings.
If what they have said does not contradict the Sūtras and the Vinaya, you should tell them: "Venerable one!
What you have spoken is truly the word of the Buddha; it is well-grasped by you. Relying upon the teachings of the Sūtras and the Vinaya, you should accept and uphold it."
"Furthermore, Ānanda! If a bhikṣu comes and speaks thus:
'Venerable One!'"

"At a certain residence, I saw a great assembly, most of whom were elders well-versed in the Vinaya-piṭaka; there I personally heard these words, and having heard them, I have retained them, knowing they accord with the Sūtras and the Vinaya and are truly the Buddha’s word."

When that bhikṣu hears what has been said, he should neither praise nor disparage it; rather, he should listen to those words and carefully retain their phrasing, then return to his residence to consult the sūtras and the Vinaya teachings.
If what they have said does not contradict the Sūtras and the Vinaya, you should tell them: "Venerable one!
What you have spoken is truly the word of the Buddha; it is well-grasped by you. Relying upon the teachings of the Sūtras and the Vinaya, you should accept and uphold it."
"Furthermore, Ānanda! If a bhikṣu comes and speaks thus:
'Venerable One!'"

"At a certain residence, I saw a great multitude of bhikṣus who all upheld the Sūtras and Vinaya, as well as the Mātṛkā-sūtras; there I personally heard these words, and having heard them, I have retained them in memory—all of which accord with the Sūtras and Vinaya and are truly the word of the Buddha."

When this bhikṣu hears what that person says, he should neither praise nor disparage it; rather, he should listen to their words and carefully retain the phrasing, then return to his dwelling to consult the sūtras and the Vinaya teachings.
If what they have said does not contradict the Sūtras and the Vinaya, you should tell them: "Venerable one!
What you have spoken is truly the word of the Buddha; it is well-grasped by you. Relying upon the teachings of the Sūtras and the Vinaya, you should accept and uphold it."
"Furthermore, Ānanda! If a bhikṣu comes and speaks thus:
'Venerable One!'"

"In a certain residence, I saw a bhikṣu who is a venerable elder and a man of wisdom; there I personally heard these words, and having heard them, I have retained them. They accord with the Sūtras and the Vinaya, and are truly the word of the Buddha."

"When this bhikṣu hears what that person says, he should neither praise nor disparage it; rather, he should listen to their words and carefully retain the phrasing. He should then return to his dwelling and examine the scriptural texts and the Vinaya teachings."
If what they have said does not contradict the Sūtras and the Vinaya, you should tell them: "Venerable one!
What you have spoken is truly the word of the Buddha; it is well-grasped by you. Relying upon the teachings of the Sūtras and the Vinaya, you should accept and uphold it."

"Furthermore, Ānanda! The first four types are called the 'Great Black Teachings. You bhikṣus should reflect upon them well, examine them thoroughly, and recognize deeply that they are evil; these are not the Sūtras, these are not the Vinaya, and these are not the Buddha’s teaching—they must be abandoned."

The latter four types are called the "Great White Exposition. You, bhikṣus, should reflect upon them well, examine them thoroughly, and understand deeply that they are virtuous; these are truly the Sūtras, these are truly the Vinaya, and these are truly the Buddha’s teaching. You should receive and uphold them well.
Ānanda! This is called a bhikṣu relying on the sūtras and teachings rather than on the person; in this manner you should train.
Were it otherwise, it would not be what I have taught.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"I now wish to go to the village of Pāvā—Pāvā here being translated as 'Evil.
He replied: [As instructed.]

"So be it. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to go to the city of Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas, gradually arrived at the village of Pāvā and stayed there, relying on the Ṛṣipatana Forest.

Having heard this, the people deliberated together to travel as one group to the place where the Buddha was; having arrived, they prostrated at his feet and sat to one side. The Buddha then taught them the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them.
At that time, among this assembly was the son of a smith named Cunda, who was also sitting and listening to the Dharma.

When the great multitude had finished hearing the Dharma, they took their leave of the Buddha and departed. Cunda then rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I only pray that the Tathāgata, together with the assembly of noble ones, will come to my residence tomorrow to accept my humble offering.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, he was filled with great joy, took his leave, and departed.

He immediately prepared various kinds of exquisite, fragrant, and delicious food and drink; having arranged the seats and provided pure water, earth powder, and tooth-sticks, he sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Buddha know that it is time."

Then, during the first part of the day, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl, and went with the great assembly to the place where the meal was being served; the Buddha and the community of monks sat down upon their seats.
Once they had taken their seats, Cunda personally took up various offerings and presented them to the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones.
At that time, there was a wicked bhikṣu who secretly stole a copper bowl and hid it under his armpit.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, no one was made to see this; only the Buddha and Cunda saw this improper act.
Once Cunda knew that the Buddha and the Saṅgha were all fully satiated, he immediately served pure water, bean-flour, and tooth-sticks.
Having set aside his bowl and washed his hands and mouth, Cunda then took a small mat and sat before the Buddha, whereupon he addressed the World-Honored One with these verses:
"I have heard that the Muni, the All-Knowing One, Has already transcended the other shore and is free from doubt;
O Supreme Guide, Tamer of Men, I pray you tell me: how many kinds of śramaṇas are there in the world?"
The Blessed One also replied to Cunda with a verse:
"There are four types of śramaṇas, no fifth; I shall now explain them to you in their proper order:
you should know the one who follows the superior path, the one who shows the path, the one who lives by the pure path, and the one who defiles the path."
Cunda again requested, saying:
"World-Honored One, what do you call the supreme path? Who is called a guide to the path?
And what is called a pure livelihood?"
"And those who defile the Path, I pray you, proclaim [them].
The World-Honored One replied:
"Able to remove the arrow of doubt and sever all delusions, one seeks only parinirvāṇa, and no other place."
This one is called the guide for gods and humans; the Buddhas declare this to be the supreme path.
Skillfully understanding the foremost and most excellent meaning, he uses expedient means to reveal the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
The Muni is able to shatter the web of all doubts; he is named the second teacher who shows the way.
If one well proclaims the verses of the Dharma, lives according to the Dharma with few desires,
and is well able to cultivate blameless qualities— this is called the third way of living by the Right Path.
Clad in the robes of liberation of a śramaṇa, yet constantly defiling families without shame;
always speaking words of falsehood and deception—this is called the fourth type of person who defiles the path.
Regarding the true assembly of the great śrāvakas, all householders should examine them well;
it is not the case that none among them are my disciples, and for this reason, one must give rise to deep faith.
How can one who is blameless dwell together with those who are guilty, or a pure person reside in the same place as the impure?
Because of the evil deeds committed by that fool, they cause all noble beings to give rise to doubt.
Do not place your trust in others based on their appearance; do not entrust them with responsibilities simply because you have gathered together for a short time.
For those who are coarse and treacherous often possess deceptive countenances, and they constantly wander through the world deceiving and deluding others.
Just as when a small amount of gold adorns an earring, its substance is still copper and has no value;
with an empty interior and a solid exterior like a false semblance, they gather many disciples and bring disorder to the virtuous.
At that time, having seen the blacksmith’s son provide this offering, the World-Honored One spoke these verses of praise for the merit of sympathetic joy:
“If the merit of giving increases, All enmity and resentment will cease;
Through goodness, one can eliminate evil, And with afflictions exhausted, realize nirvana.”
The Buddha taught the Dharma for them, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening them. Having performed this benefit, he rose from his seat and departed.
The internal summary verse says:
"To the west of Vaiśālī, the Buddha turned back to look at the city."
Having traveled through ten villages, he finally arrived at Pāvā.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"I now wish to go to the city of Kuśinagara."
When Ānanda had heard what the Buddha said, he followed behind the Buddha and gradually proceeded toward the town of Pāvā.
Before reaching the Golden River, they paused for a moment by the side of the road along the way, and the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"I now have a backache; you should fold my uttarāsaṅga into four layers, for I wish to lie down to rest."
When Ānanda had heard the Buddha’s instruction, he immediately folded his robes quickly and said, "It is done;
may the Blessed One know the time.

Thereupon the World-Honored One himself folded his saṃghāṭī and used it as a pillow, lying on his right side with one foot upon the other, maintaining the perception of light. Abiding in right mindfulness with the thought that he would soon arise, having formed this intention, he further addressed Ānanda:
“You should go quickly to the Kakutthā River and take a bowl full of water; I wish to drink it and also sprinkle it upon my body.

Having heard this, Ānanda took his bowl and went to the riverbank. At that time, five hundred wagons had just recently crossed the river, so the water was all turbid. He filled his bowl with this water and returned to the Buddha’s presence, saying:
“Venerable Sir!”

"Five hundred chariots have recently crossed this river, so that the water is all turbid; we pray that the World-Honored One will use it for washing his hands and feet, as it is unfit for drinking. The Golden River is not far away, where clear water may be found."

The Buddha accepted the water and washed his feet and wiped his face; as his body became somewhat more at ease, he rose and sat cross-legged, dwelling with his body upright and mindfulness manifest before him.

At that time, a powerful minister named Pūrṇa passed by that way and saw the World-Honored Buddha sitting beneath a tree, his appearance and deportment upright and handsome, a joy for all to behold. His body and mind were tranquil and exceedingly well-disciplined, like a magnificent golden pillar radiating brilliant light.
Having seen him, he approached and prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, then sat to one side. The Buddha asked him:
"Do you now take delight in the pure Dharma of the śramaṇas?"
"Do you take pleasure in the Dharma of the brahmins?
The minister replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"I delight in the pure Dharma of Kālāma.
The Buddha said to the minister,
"For what further reason do you delight in that pure Dharma?"
He replied: "Venerable Sir!
Once, while Kālāma was traveling along the road and staying beneath a tree, five hundred chariots passed by that spot. After a short time, another person arrived and asked him:”
"Did you see five hundred chariots pass by here? He replied, "I did not."
Again he asked:
"Did you hear the sound? He replied:
"I did not hear it.
He asked again,
"Were you perhaps asleep, O virtuous one?"
He replied, "I was not sleeping.
[The king asked,] "If you were not sleeping, why did you neither see nor hear five hundred chariots pass by here?"
He replied, "I do not sleep;
my mind is constantly awake, yet I neither see nor hear because of the power of meditative concentration.
Upon hearing this, he thought to himself:
"How rare is this superior person! To have such a mind so tranquil and contemplative.

Furthermore, as the carriage moved, it rattled and kicked up clouds of dust that flew about; yet he was neither seen nor heard by them, for they were covered by his body and robes. Therefore, I conceived pure faith in him and took delight in his Dharma.
The Buddha said to the minister, "What do you think?
Between the sound produced by five hundred chariots and the roar of a thunderclap in the midst of space, which is greater?"
He replied, "Venerable Sir!
It is not merely five hundred carriages; even if a hundred thousand million chariots were to make a great clamor, how could it ever surpass the sound of a thunderclap?"
"Great Minister, you should know!

Previously, while staying here in this village within my multi-storied pavilion, I took up my robe and bowl at the time of the morning meal and entered the village to beg for food. Having finished eating, I put away my robe and bowl, washed my feet, and remained seated in meditative composure within the pavilion."

Suddenly, a thunderclap struck with a great crash; at that moment, the four oxen and two plowmen, along with the two elder brothers of the householder, heard this loud sound and, overcome by terror, all lost their lives simultaneously, while the people of the city raised a great cry.

At that time, I rose from my meditative seclusion and went out from the pavilion to walk in meditation. Then, a certain person came out from the city and approached me; he prostrated at my feet and followed me as I walked. I then asked him:
"For what reason is there such a loud outcry and great clamor within the city?"
He replied to me, saying:

"Just now in the city, heaven suddenly thundered and sent down a great lightning bolt; four oxen, two plowmen, and the two elder brothers of the householder were all struck dead at once by this terror."
"Therefore, a great sound arose within the city. He asked me:
"Venerable One!..."
"How could you not have heard this great thunderous sound? I replied,
"I did not hear it."
He spoke again, saying:
“World-Honored One, are you sleeping? He replied:
"I did not sleep; although I was inwardly conscious, I did not hear from without. He then thought:
"How rare it is that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha dwells in such tranquility that he does not hear the sound of this great thunderous roar!"
"He has thus conceived pure faith in me.
Having heard this, Pūrṇa said:
"Venerable Sir!"
"How could there be one who does not give rise to reverent faith toward the Buddha? I now give rise to a profound mind of purity toward the Buddha.
At that time, Pūrṇa said to the messenger:
"You may take this new, fine-threaded, golden-yellow cloth of mine and offer it to cover the World-Honored One."
The messenger brought it, and Pūrṇa said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One!
This is a new, high-quality, fine-threaded, golden-yellow cloth. I only pray that you will compassionately accept it for my sake.”
The Blessed One, wishing to grant him the benefit of his request, accepted it.
Pūrṇa spoke again:
"Venerable Blessed One!"
"I wish to further make offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha; I pray that you will grant me your permission.
The Buddha said, "This is a virtuous deed."
Seeing that the Buddha had accepted it, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and departed.
The Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda:
“I wish to wear this golden-yellow cloth, having cut its threads with a knife.”
When Ānanda had heard the Buddha’s instruction, he immediately used a knife to cut off the frayed threads and offered it to the World-Honored One. The Buddha then put it on;
however, the majestic radiance of the Buddha’s body caused the garment to appear golden, such that it no longer possessed its own luster.
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable World-Honored One!
For more than twenty years following the Blessed One, I have never before beheld such a countenance or such radiant, majestic splendor as this.”
"For what cause and condition does this radiance appear so exceptionally brilliant?
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"There are two causes and conditions for the manifestation of this radiant sign that differs from ordinary days."
What are these two?
First, that on this very night a bodhisattva realizes anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
second, that on this very night a Tathāgata enters the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
On these two occasions, such sublime signs appeared.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
I went to the Golden River.

Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda followed behind the Buddha to the riverbank. The Buddha then took off his robes and placed them on the shore; wearing only his undergarment, he entered the river to bathe.
Upon emerging, he dried his body and said to Ānanda: “Cunda will surely feel remorse; you should comfort him and tell him: ‘Cunda!...’”
"You have now gained great benefit, being able to provide this final offering; for it is extremely rare to encounter a Great Teacher who, having accepted such a gift, enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*."
"You should know, Cunda, that there are two causes by which remorse arises in the mind; you should provide him with consolation by speaking these words: 'Cunda!
I have personally heard these words from the Buddha:'"
“There are two kinds of giving whose resultant fruits are peerless: when one has been a bodhisattva, having received food, one immediately realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and when a Tathāgata receives his final meal, he enters the realm of wondrous nirvāṇa without remainder.”
"Ānanda! These two kinds of giving yield fruits and rewards that are beyond compare.
Ānanda, you should know this!"
“Cunda has performed deeds for long life, deeds for great strength, and all such deeds as those for beautiful appearance, rebirth in heaven, wealth, food, noble status, and a retinue have increased.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The bhikṣu Cchanda is by nature fierce and evil, prone to anger and impulsiveness; he constantly utters disrespectful and harsh words toward the other bhikṣus.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how shall we dwell together with him?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, the monk Chanda, who is of evil disposition, should be disciplined through silent exclusion (*tūṣṇīka-pravāsanīya*).

When he is being so disciplined, if he feels remorse and gives rise to a mind of reverence and admiration, and the community knows he has reformed, they should collectively express joy and speak with him as they did before."
The Blessed One again addressed Ānanda:
"I now wish to go to the city of Kuśinagara. Ānanda said:
“As the Blessed One has instructed,” they replied,
and followed after the Buddha toward the birthplace of the Mallas.
Having crossed the Kimikālā River, they stayed by the roadside not far from the city and addressed Ānanda, saying:
“I now have a backache; you may fold my *uttarāsaṅga* into four layers, for I wish to lie down to rest.
Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda immediately and quickly folded the robe and said, “It is done;
may the Blessed One know the time.”
At that time, the World-Honored One folded his saṃghāṭī robe himself, used it as a pillow, and lay down on his right side, as previously described in detail.
He further addressed Ānanda:
"You should proclaim the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment."
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Venerable World-Honored One, you have personally realized and awakened to these factors of enlightenment here, and have taught them to me yourself: based on seclusion, based on dispassion, and based on cessation, one abandons all worldly concerns and diligently cultivates mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. These factors of enlightenment are what the Venerable World-Honored One has proclaimed from his own realization and awakening.”
“Ānanda! If one relies on seclusion and so forth, and practices these seven factors of enlightenment with great diligence and vigor, they shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.”
When these words had been spoken, the Buddha immediately rose from his seat, sat upright, and remained with his body straight, dwelling in right mindfulness and contemplation.
At that time, a bhikṣu spoke this verse:
“The World-Honored One exhorts himself, Commanding the proclamation of the subtle and wondrous Dharma.”
For the sake of all those who are ill, you should speak of the factors of enlightenment.
Since the Great Teacher’s body is afflicted with disease, for the sake of both him and the sick bhikṣus,
expound upon the Dharma-gate of the factors of awakening so that they may attain realization.
Excellent, Ānanda! Your white dharmas are all perfected;
you are clever and possess great wisdom, skillfully expounding the Dharma of the Muni.
You are established in right mindfulness and the discernment of dharmas, and are diligent in the factors of enlightenment beginning with joy.
Pliancy, concentration, and equanimity— The Unsurpassed Tamer of Men has skillfully explained these.
Delighting in hearing the factors of enlightenment,
Though his body was afflicted by illness and pain, He did not refuse, but rose to listen.
The Buddha is the Honored One, the Lord of the Dharma, and he is the one who can provide guidance;
if he regards the Dharma with such profound reverence, how much more so should others!
Furthermore, there are various noble sages who, regarding the teachings of the One of Ten Powers, [should likewise hold them dear].
Even if they encounter the suffering of illness, they rise to listen without wearying themselves.
Since those who skillfully uphold the sūtras, as well as those who clarify the Vinaya and Abhidharma,
still delight in hearing the True Dharma, why should others not listen?
Having heard the World-Honored One’s teaching on detachment, practice it as taught;
by applying mindfulness to the Dharma with diligence, you shall attain the factor of joy.
Because the mind possesses joy, this body will experience pliancy.
From existence, pleasure arises; from pleasure, concentration arises. Through excellent concentration, equanimity arises;
one realizes that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
Thus, one can leave the three realms of existence behind, and the mind of defiled attachment does not arise.
One can leave behind all suffering of existence, take no pleasure in the realms of humans or devas,
and realize unsurpassed nirvāṇa, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
Such great benefits as these all arise from hearing the Dharma.
"Therefore, I exhort you to listen attentively to the sublime Dharma at this final hour.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"You may now proceed to the city of Kuśinagara."
He replied, "So be it.
He then followed behind the Buddha to the birthplace of the strongman, where they stayed in the Śāla grove.
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Now, for my sake, prepare a couch between the twin śāla trees; there I shall lie down with my head to the north, for today at midnight I will surely enter parinirvāṇa."
Then Ānanda, having performed as instructed, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side with palms joined, and said:
"Everything has been arranged exactly as the Buddha commanded."

At that time, the Tathāgata proceeded to the couch and lay down on his right side, with one foot upon the other, maintaining the perception of light, binding his mind in right mindfulness, and abiding in observation with the perception of nirvāṇa.
At that time, Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha, leaning against the couch; weeping and wailing with a loud voice, he spoke these words:
"Alas! How bitter!"
How painful!
How could we have expected the Tathāgata to enter parinirvāṇa so soon?
How could we have expected the Sugata to enter parinirvāṇa so soon?
How sudden! The Eye of the World has been extinguished.

In former times, bhikṣus from all directions would come to the Buddha’s presence, and the Buddha would preach the Dharma for them—good in the beginning, middle, and end; its words and meaning were exquisite, pure, complete, and perfectly white, the very mark of the Brahma-faring life.
Because I was able to hear this most profound and sublime Dharma, he heard of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa today and will not return; thus, such a supreme and wondrous Dharma shall vanish from the world.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "Where is Ānanda now? They replied:
“World-Honored One!

Now, standing behind the Buddha and leaning against the couch, he is weeping with intense grief and speaking these words, as extensively described before, until [he says]: ‘The supreme and wondrous Dharma shall vanish from the world.’”
The Buddha then addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Do not grieve, weep, or be distressed. Why is this?"

As you attend upon the Tathāgata, by performing acts of loving-kindness with the body you shall obtain great benefit and happiness; not only will your single person attain boundless merit, but by performing acts of loving-kindness with speech and acts of loving-kindness with the mind, it shall likewise result in boundless merit.

Ānanda! All Tathāgatas of the past had attendants who served them in this very way, just as you have attended me with such devotion; likewise, all Buddhas of the future will also have attendants who serve them no differently than you.
Ānanda! The nature of worldly phenomena is such that none endure for long; they all ultimately return to extinction, for nothing exists with permanence.
For this reason, you should not now weep and wail, giving rise to great suffering and distress.

One does not see that the phenomena of the world arising from conditions are permanent or indestructible; I have already explained this essential teaching to you at length: all things that are lovely and pleasing to the mind ultimately return to impermanence and are entirely subject to separation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, permeated by great compassion and in order to inspire joy in Ānanda, addressed the bhikṣus:
"A wheel-turning sage king accomplishes four kinds of rare and marvelous things."
What are the four?
Suppose there is a multitude of kṣatriyas who come to the king’s presence; having seen the king, they feel profound joy, and upon hearing the sublime Dharma, their delight increases all the more.

In this way, there were also assemblies of brahmins, assemblies of householders, and various assemblies of śramaṇas who came to the king’s presence; as previously described, they were even more filled with joy.
"You should know that just as there are four marvelous things concerning a wheel-turning monarch,
so too does this Ānanda have four marvelous things. What are these four?"
That is to say, when a great assembly of bhikṣus from the four directions came to where he was, their hearts were filled with joy; hearing the sublime Dharma, their delight increased all the more.
It was the same for the assemblies of bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who came to Ānanda’s presence; they likewise redoubled their joy.
"O bhikṣus! This Ānanda possesses four further rare and wonderful qualities.
What are these four?"
When Ānanda teaches the Dharma to the assembly of bhikṣus, he is skillfully able to explain it so that there is no doubt or obstruction.
All the bhikṣus think to themselves: "Excellent!"
Excellent! Ānanda, you proclaim the sublime Dharma; do not remain silent, nor decline out of weariness, for the hearts of these listeners are never satiated.
When Ānanda had finished preaching the Dharma, he remained silent; likewise, when he preached the Dharma for bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, it was also in this manner.
When Ānanda heard these words, his heart was filled with joy, and he immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Within this land there are six great cities:
They are Śrāvastī, Saketa, Campā, Vārāṇasī, Vaiśālī, and Rājagṛha.
For what reason has the World-Honored One abandoned such a magnificent and blessed land to enter parinirvāṇa in this desolate, stony, remote, and lowly place?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not speak such words!
The city of Kuśinagara is a remote, lowly, and unpleasant place."
Why is this so? Ānanda!

In the distant past, this city of Kuśinagara was a royal capital named Kuśāvatī, peaceful, prosperous, and teeming with people. It measured twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in width. The city was surrounded by seven successive walls and courtyards, all of which were composed of the four precious substances—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The city gates were likewise constructed from these four precious substances, and at each gate stood great ornamental pillars made of the same jewels, reaching a height of seven men.
The moats and ditches outside the city walls are three and a half men deep; their banks are paved with bricks made of precious jewels.
Within the seven courtyards, there are rows of tala trees, all composed of the four kinds of precious substances.

The *kadamba* trees have branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits made of silver; the silver trees are adorned with gold; the lapis lazuli trees are adorned with crystal; and the crystal trees are adorned with lapis lazuli.

When these various trees are stirred by the wind, they produce subtle sounds that delight the hearts of all. Within these groves of trees there are bathing pools, whose foundations, embankments, and pathways are likewise composed of the four precious substances; the railings on their four sides are also made of the four precious substances.

Within the pools there are many lovely flowers—*utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*—flowers that are exceedingly soft, exceedingly fragrant, and ever-blooming. Such flowers as these have no guardians, and may be enjoyed by anyone at will.
Furthermore, on the banks of the pond there are *campaka* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, and *sumanā* flowers; such flowers as these bloom in accordance with the seasons. Ānanda!
Within the groves of trees there are many beautiful women, adorned with exquisite necklaces, who wander at will and provide all food and drink as required.
Furthermore, all those within this city who are attached to the pleasures of the five desires find their hearts' wishes fulfilled as they roam and observe here.

Furthermore, there are always various kinds of drums and musical instruments, with stringed and wind instruments, songs, and dances producing wondrous sounds, all of which exhort and praise the cultivation of various meritorious deeds, the observance of fasts and precepts, and so forth.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

In this city there was a king named Mahāsudassana, who was endowed with the seven treasures and possessed four wonders. These were the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the military-commander-treasure.

Regarding the four rare occurrences: the King’s lifespan was exceedingly long; first as a prince, then as a crown prince, then ascending the throne as king, and finally practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*). He spent eighty-four thousand years in each of these four stages. This is called the first rare occurrence.
Furthermore, the king’s physical appearance was upright and handsome, peerless in the world; this was the second rare wonder.
Moreover, he suffered little illness or affliction, and the food and drink he consumed were wholesome and taken at the proper time; this was the third rare wonder.

Furthermore, the multitude of people served the king with loyalty and filial piety, regarding him as their father; the king, in turn, cherished them as if they were his own infant children. When the king went out on an excursion, he traveled by carriage and commanded his driver, saying:
"You should now draw the carriage slowly so that the multitude may see me."
“The King constantly gives rise to compassion for the common people;
this is the fourth rare quality. Furthermore, Ānanda!
At that time, there were people of the kingdom who, carrying various treasures such as gold, silver, and mani-jewels, came to the King’s presence and said:”
"Great King! I possess this treasure and respectfully offer it to Your Majesty; I pray that you will compassionately accept it.
At that time, the king said:
"You all should know! I already possess such treasures in abundance; truly, I have no need for them.
Although the people made this request two or three times, the king ultimately would not accept it.
At that time, he thought to himself:
"I brought these items originally hoping to present them to the King; since the King will not accept them, what shall I do?
It is best to place them before the King and return each to its original location."
Having had this thought, he set down the treasures and departed.
The king then thought:
"These precious treasures were obtained in accordance with the Dharma and were not sought through wrongful means; it is now fitting that I use them to construct a Dharma Hall."
At that time, there were eighty-four thousand minor kings of various cities who, hearing that the Great King was about to construct a Dharma Hall, all went to the King’s presence and said:
"We only pray that the Holy King will not trouble his divine mind."
"We, your subjects, hope to construct [a palace] for Your Majesty.
At that time, the Great King said to his ministers:
"I possess sufficient treasures; there is no need for you to trouble yourselves."
Thus the various kings entreated him a second and a third time, yet the king did not grant his permission.
Then the minor kings came forward to support the king’s feet, or grasped the hem of his robe, and with palms joined, they addressed him:
"May Your Majesty remain at ease; we shall build it for you."
When the king saw their earnestness, he silently gave his consent.
Having learned this, the various kings each returned to their own places, each taking with them gold, silver, and other treasures.
Furthermore, each person brought a pillar made entirely of precious gems and came before the king, saying:
“O Sage King! All that is required is already fully prepared; we do not know where you wish to undertake this meritorious work, nor its scale, whether great or small.”
The King said:
"To the east of this city, select a site of superior topography measuring one yojana in length and breadth; there you may construct it.
Having heard this, the kings immediately went to that location and erected a Dharma hall according to the specified dimensions.

Ānanda! The rafters, beams, capitals, and brackets required for that hall, as well as the galleries, railings, porches, and surrounding corridors—all such things were fashioned from precious materials such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Furthermore, the couches, mats, seats, rugs, cushions, pillows, tables, chests, boxes, and garments were all adorned with various jewels.

Ānanda! Beneath the hall’s steps, between each pillar, there shall stand a tree; on the trunk of each tree, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the four jewels are arranged, mutually adorned with jewels, just as previously described.

A gentle breeze stirred them, producing harmonious and elegant sounds like the performance of celestial music. The interior of the hall was entirely covered with golden sand, constantly moistened by the sprinkling of sandalwood-scented water. Paths were demarcated by golden cords, and jeweled nets were suspended on all four sides, with various precious bells hanging from them—all the finest adornments of the world.

At that time, eighty-four thousand kings together constructed a Dharma Hall, completing its adornments. Beside this hall, they constructed many bathing pools, each forty li square. All the steps and terraces were magnificently decorated with the four precious substances. Within these pools were four kinds of flowers, and outside the pools there were various land-growing flowers, all as previously described.

Furthermore, in various rows before the hall, there were *tāla* trees made of the four precious substances; their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were all mutually adorned, and when stirred by the wind, they produced sounds as previously described.
Every place they occupied was strewn with golden sand and sprinkled with scented water; jeweled bells, chiming harmoniously, were suspended everywhere.
At that time, once the kings had finished their elaborate adornments, they all addressed the King together, saying:
"May Your Majesty be informed!..."
"The Dharma hall and all the groves and springs have been constructed with the utmost magnificence; I pray that Your Majesty will deign to visit.
Upon hearing this, the King thought:

"This sublime Dharma hall should not be used by me first. It would be appropriate to invite all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and those of virtuous conduct, and to provide them within this hall with every kind of offering in accordance with the Dharma."
Thereupon, he established a great assembly for almsgiving according to his thoughts and provided for all; having done so, he further thought:
"I should not now be negligent or attached to pleasure in this Dharma hall."

He then took one person to serve as his attendant and personally entered the hall to purely cultivate the Brahma-faring. Thereupon, upon a golden couch with silver railings, he sat cross-legged in right mindfulness and contemplation; distancing himself from all unwholesome dharmas of the desire realm and eliminating directed thought and evaluation, he realized the first dhyāna.

Rising from the golden couch, he next ascended the silver couch, which was adorned with alternating patterns of gold, lapis lazuli, and crystal; upon these, the king was able to successively realize and master deep meditative absorptions, eliminating all hindrances and burdens.
At that time, eighty-four thousand palace ladies and maidservants went to the place where the Lady Jewel was and said to her:

"O Great Lady! We, all of us, having received the King’s gracious favor, have long been deprived of his attendance and our hearts are filled with deep longing; we all wish to pay our respects and hope you will grant us permission."
Then the Chief Queen replied to the Minister of the Armed Forces, saying:
"You should know this now!

We in the inner palace have not seen the King for a long time and our hearts are filled with deep longing and affection. It is fitting that we attend upon him; you should prepare the carriage at once."
The minister addressed him, saying:
"If this is so, I humbly request that Your Majesty command all your attendants to ensure that all their ornaments are of yellow color."
He spoke again, saying:
"Now, let me first command the eighty-four thousand minor kings to muster their troops.
The kings followed his orders and first deployed eighty thousand elephant-mounted units, with the Elephant King Dīrghanakha as their leader.
Next, he prepared the horse-drawn carriages, with the Cloud-Rising Horse King as the lead;
next, he prepared the chariot-drawn carriages, with the Joyfully Resounding Chariot as the lead.

These two classes also numbered eighty thousand, all adorned with jewels of the most exquisite and supreme beauty; the Great Queen of the State rode in a resounding carriage, and the court ladies she led were likewise so adorned.

His entire retinue all rode upon elephants and horses; their majestic appearance was solemn and grave, with banners and drums blinding the sun, startling heaven and shaking the earth as they proceeded together to the Dharma Hall.
At that time, the King asked:
"For what cause and condition [have you come]?"
"The chariots and horses are so numerous and crowded that they produce a great clamor.

The usher replied, "The Great Lady of the kingdom, along with the minor princes and all the court ladies, are all dressed in yellow garments. Their flower garlands, banners, and parasols are entirely adorned in yellow. Their number is so vast that it cannot be fully described; they have come here together to pay their respects."
The King said, "You may prepare a seat within this hall; I shall go to observe it.
Having received the command, the messenger prepared a golden throne and then addressed the King, saying:
"The preparations are complete.
At that time, the King descended slowly from the terrace; halfway down the steps, he saw from afar a yellow ceremonial procession, magnificent and grandly arrayed, and he thought to himself:
"These dignified manners are most delightful; how magnificent is this exquisite and extraordinary splendor!"
Once the King was seated, the Great Queen of the realm paid her respects before him, then withdrew to stand to one side and said:
"Great King! These eighty-four thousand precious women, adorned and beautiful, I respectfully offer to Your Majesty; I pray that you will graciously accept them and not cast them aside."
At that time, the eighty-four thousand subordinate kings, each with a precious military force as their leader, addressed him, saying: "Great King!
Here now are these elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as the eighty-four thousand cities and towns, with the city of Kuśāvatī as the foremost."
Furthermore, there are eighty-four thousand pavilions, all exquisitely adorned and most marvelous; we only pray that Your Majesty will take pity on us, accept them, and grant us your protection.
The king said:
"Sister, you should know!
Previously, I was extremely close to you; who would have thought that today you would act like an enemy, urging me toward what is contrary to the Dharma!"
When the queens heard that the Great King had addressed them as "sisters," they wept and said,
"Now we perceive from the King's intent that he wishes to abandon us.
Wiping their tears with their robes, they spoke again to the King:
"Why is it, Great King, that you were formerly so intimate with us in heart, yet now act like an enemy?
At that time, the king told them:
"You should know this!"

Human life is brief; all who are born must die. Both I and all others alike shall return to destruction. Even if one possesses hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, they are like enemies disguised as friends who will surely bring about one’s own ruin;

though one harbors deep attachment, one must ultimately part from them. Ministers, attendants, chariots, horses, and grand palaces—such wondrous things, immeasurable and boundless, numbering eighty-four thousand each—all end in impermanence and cannot endure for long.
"Therefore, the wise should quickly distance themselves from this; they should diligently cultivate the pure conduct (brahmacarya) and not give rise to defiled attachment.
When the ladies heard these words of the king, they knew that he would not accept their request and that it did not accord with their wishes.

At that time, having exhorted and instructed extensively according to the Dharma, the king returned to the golden pavilion and sat cross-legged upon a silver throne. He gave rise to a mind of great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, pervading the ten directions boundlessly; having cultivated this universally, he remained with a composed mind. Rising from the concentration of loving-kindness, he next gave rise to compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, treating all sentient beings in the same way throughout the ten directions. His pavilion and throne were interlaced with various precious jewels.
At that time, the king cultivated each of the four Brahma-abodes one by one, severing all desires.
As his life was drawing to a close, he was oppressed by death and felt deep distress; after his life ended, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“From the city of Kuśinagara to the twin śāla trees on the bank of the Hiranyavatī River at the Makuṭabandhana Caitya, the birthplace of the Mallas—within this circuit of twelve yojanas, the Tathāgata, when he was formerly a wheel-turning monarch, relinquished his life six times.”
Now, attaining parinirvāṇa here once again constitutes the seventh.
Furthermore, for the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, there shall be no eighth place in the worlds of the ten directions where he relinquishes his body and life.
"Why is this? Because my births have been exhausted, I have severed all afflictions and karma, and shall no longer undergo further existence in other realms.
At that time, the Venerable Upamāna was standing before the Buddha, and the Buddha said to Upamāna:
"You should not now remain standing before me.
At that moment, the bhikṣu immediately withdrew from the Buddha's presence.
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have attended upon the World-Honored One for more than twenty years, yet I have never heard him utter such harsh words of reproach as he did toward the bhikṣu Upamāna.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The long-lived devas of immeasurable hundreds of kalpas have gathered together in mutual censure, speaking these words:”

"In this world, the appearance of the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, is exceedingly rare; he manifests but once in an age, like the udumbara flower. This very day, at midnight, he will certainly enter the realm of wondrous nirvana without remainder."
"Because of this majestic power, the bhikṣu stands before the Buddha, so that we have no leisure to approach the World-Honored One, make offerings to him, or pay him respect.
Ānanda addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"How great is the number of the celestial hosts who have come?"
The Buddha said:

"From the Golden River southward to the Twin Trees at Kuśinagara, extending as far as the Yaṣṭī-caitya, within this entire circuit of twelve yojanas, there are gods of great majesty and power standing shoulder to shoulder; there is not even enough space between them to stand a staff."
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Upamāna, what karma did he perform in the past to possess such great majestic power?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Upamāna himself previously performed this karma and now returns to experience its results. This was explained in detail as in other instances, up to the recitation of the verse.

"O Bhikṣus! In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Kāśyapa, endowed with the ten titles, who dwelt at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near Vārāṇasī. At that time, Upamāna had become a renunciant."
At that time, the bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city to beg for food; it was this man’s turn to guard the monastery.
Suddenly, a black wind and torrential rain arose, and as it was bitterly cold, he thought to himself:
"The fellow practitioners will encounter this bitter cold and hardship; their robes will all be soaked when they arrive. I should now prepare everything properly to wait for them."

Having formed this thought, he entered the bathhouse, lit a fire to warm the water, and prepared the bedding. He then tied ropes beneath the corridor to form a rack and went to the entrance of the monastery to await the bhikṣus.
Once he had arrived, he entered the room, took the damp clothes, washed them thoroughly, and placed them on a rack; he then set aside clean garments for the bhikṣu to wear.

Once their fatigue was dispelled and their bodies and minds were warmed, all suffering from the cold vanished, and they were filled with joy and delight. The bhikṣu guarding the monastery knelt upright with palms joined before the great assembly and made this aspiration:

"By the roots of virtue produced through my having removed the suffering and secured the happiness of these fellow practitioners of the holy life, may I—just as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa bestowed a prophecy upon the young brahmin—that in the future, when the human lifespan is one hundred years, I shall attain perfect enlightenment under the name Śākyamuni."
May I go forth as a monk within that Buddha’s Dharma, sever all afflictions, and realize the fruit of Arhatship;
by virtue of my merit in offering lamps, may my bodily radiance be such that no deva can approach it.
"You should know this!

By the power of that vow, he has gone forth in my Dharma; having severed all afflictions and realized the fruit of Arhatship, he possesses such great majestic virtue that none of these devas can approach him."
Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After the Great Virtuous World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, how shall I reverently make offerings to the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should desist for now!
As for the matters you have asked about, faithful brahmins, householders, and others shall provide for them themselves."
He addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“Regarding all that the elders have prepared, what are their arrangements?
The Buddha said:
"Each one shall follow the funeral rites of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin).
He asked again,
"What are the specific procedures for the rites of a Wheel-Turning King?"
The Buddha said:
“You should now know this!

After a Wheel-Turning Sage King has passed away, his body is wrapped from head to foot with five hundred *kārṣāpaṇas* of the finest fine cotton wool, and adorned with five hundred exquisite garments for both upper and lower parts. A coffin of iron is filled with fragrant oil, and the king is carried and placed within it; thereafter the lid is closed, and the coffin is cremated with various kinds of fragrant wood.”

Next, he sprinkled fragrant milk to extinguish the flames, then collected the King’s bones and placed them in a golden jar. At the crossroads, he erected a great stūpa and offered respectful worship, veneration, and praise with banners, canopies, umbrellas, and various exquisite incenses and flowers, establishing a grand sacrificial feast.
"Ānanda! Just as one honors and makes offerings to a Wheel-Turning Sage King, the offerings made by humans and devas after my parinirvāṇa shall exceed this twofold.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
“You should now go to the city of Kuśinagara and proclaim my words to the five hundred warriors:
‘O people, you should know!

The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, will certainly this very day at midnight enter the wondrous realm of Nirvāṇa without remainder. You should quickly do what ought to be done, lest you later regret it, saying:’”
“Within this territory, the Great Teacher has entered parinirvāṇa;
we were unaware of it and did not perform offerings.

When the Venerable Ānanda had heard the Buddha’s instruction, he took his saṃghāṭī robe and, accompanied by a single attendant, went immediately to the Assembly Hall in the city of Kuśinagara, where five hundred strongmen were gathered there discussing other matters.
Then Ānanda, conveying the command of the World-Honored One, addressed the warriors, saying:

"Since you have all assembled, you should listen well: this very day at midnight, the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, will certainly enter the realm of great parinirvāṇa without remainder. You should do whatever needs to be done; do not later regret it by saying such words as:
'The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, entered parinirvāṇa within our own territory, yet we were unable to offer even a small measure of worship.'"

When the warriors heard these words, each of them, together with their wives, children, kinsmen, friends, and servants, invited one another to go to the Śāla grove. There they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit at one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the sublime Dharma for them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them. Then the warriors rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, bared their right shoulders, joined their palms in reverence, gazed up at the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"O Virtuous World-Honored One!..."
We, [Name] and others, are all noble and powerful warriors of the city of Kuśinagara.
We vow to take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha for as long as we live, and we shall receive and train in the precepts.
At that time, Ānanda thought to himself:

"If those strongmen were to receive the training of a lay follower (upāsaka) individually from the World-Honored One one by one, it would take such a long time that it would hinder and obstruct their attainment of parinirvāṇa."
"I should now invite him so that we may receive the precepts together at one time.
Having formed this thought, he rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!"

These warriors, together with their numerous retinues and followers, each having such distinct names, wish to take refuge in the Triple Gem and seek the five precepts; however, if they were to receive them individually, it would likely cause undue delay.
"I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will receive us all at once.
Then Ānanda, in the presence of the World-Honored One, received their names and administered the precepts for them all at once.
When the warriors heard the Buddha’s teaching and further received the rules of training, they were filled with great joy; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took their leave, and departed.

At that time, when the World-Honored One was still a bodhisattva dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven, he surveyed the world with five kinds of observations; the sons of the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm purified his mother’s womb three times, and he manifested the form of a white elephant and entered her womb.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Gandharva King Sunanda:

"You should now know that the Bodhisattva, while in the Tuṣita Palace, has observed the world through five matters; he has purified the mother’s womb through the three purifications of the sons of the six heavens of desire, and manifested the form of a white elephant to descend into the mother’s womb. We ought to go together to provide protection."
Then the Gandharva King addressed him, saying:
"Great Heaven! You may depart;
I shall meanwhile perform various musical performances here."
At that time, as the Bodhisattva emerged from his mother’s womb, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the King of Music, Sunanda, saying:
"You should know now!
As the Bodhisattva has emerged from his mother’s womb, we ought to go forth and serve as his attendants."
The answer was as before.
While he was playing with the other youths, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the King of Music, saying:
"You should know now that the Bodhisattva is playing with the youths; you ought to go and attend upon him."
The answer was as before.

Having contemplated and understood old age, sickness, and death, the Bodhisattva felt deep distress and retired to the forests and wilds to practice various ascetic disciplines. Later, he consumed sixteen rounds of milk gruel from two cowherd girls; his physical strength was restored, and he partook of various foods and drinks, bathing his body and anointing it with ghee and oil.
At that time, Śakra again commanded the Lord of Music (Gandharva) to provide protection, but his reply was as before.

When the World-Honored One had subdued the host of thirty-six billion celestial Māra armies and attained unsurpassed wisdom, the Brahma King came to invite him to Vārāṇasī; there he turned the Wheel of Dharma in twelve aspects three times and established the various rules of training (śikṣāpada).
"All those who were to be delivered through this connection have now been delivered; he has gone to the city of Kuśinagara and lies down for the final time.

At that moment, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again commanded the Music God (Gandharva), as extensively described before, even to the point of saying, "You may go to listen to the Dharma," to which [the Music God] replied, "I shall first perform various musical pieces."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Music God, saying:
"You should know now!
The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One lies down for the last time; he will surely enter parinirvāṇa, so you should offer worship."
The answer was the same as before.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"The non-Buddhist Subhadra is capable of coming to my presence and receiving my discipline; however, the god Kāma lacks the nature of coming here on his own."
He further reflected:

"Whosoever is liberated by a Śrāvaka is also liberated by the Tathāgata; however, those who must be liberated by a Buddha cannot be liberated by others. Because he awaits this supreme and skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), I should now liberate that Sundarī."
Having formed this thought, he immediately entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*). By the power of that concentration, he manifested a body at his final place of rest.

He further manifested a glass lute (*vīṇā*) with a thousand strings; vanishing from his resting place while holding the lute, he went to the Heaven of the Thirty-three and stood before the gate of the palace of the Gandharva King Sunanda.

At that time, Supriyā, relying on her own pride and arrogance, claimed there was no one who could surpass her in playing the *vīṇā* lute; she took delight in making music and sporting within her own palace, becoming deeply attached to those pleasures.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the gatekeeper:
"You should go and inform King Bandhumat, saying:
'A gandharva has arrived at the gate and wishes to have an audience.'"
Then the gatekeeper entered and reported this in full. The king, being arrogant, replied:
"Is there any other gandharva besides me? He answered:
"There is another; she is currently outside the gate.
Having heard this, Sunda was overcome with unbearable emotion and immediately went out the door herself, saying: "O Noble Sir!
"Are you a gandharva?
The Buddha said,
"I am indeed now the King of the Gandharvas."
"If that is so, please come and perform music for us. He replied,
"Great Seer!..."
"Excellent; I can play together with you.
The Buddha then played the *vīṇā* (lute) alongside him; the Buddha severed one string and he also severed one, yet there was no deficiency in either sound.
When the Buddha cut off two strings, he also cut off two; yet their resonance was identical.
When the Buddha cut off three or four, it was likewise so, even until each had only one string remaining, yet the sound did not differ.

The Buddha then cut off the music entirely, and as he snapped his fingers in mid-air, the elegant melody was twice as superior as usual; the other could not do so, and feeling a sense of wonder, he subdued his pride, realizing that the other’s musical art surpassed his own.
Having observed this, the World-Honored One immediately concealed his gandharva form and restored his original appearance.

At that time, the musical deity beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, with a body of true golden color, adorned all over by the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. His brilliant radiance surpassed a thousand suns; like a king of jewel mountains, those who gazed upon him forgot their weariness. Having seen him, he was filled with joy and gave rise to profound reverence and respect. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to listen to the essentials of the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing their faculties and dispositions, taught them the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths according to their capacities so that they might attain awakening. They were then able to use the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter the twenty-fold mountain of false views regarding the self, and thus realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having realized the Truths, he was deeply moved by his own good fortune and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
What I have now attained could not have been accomplished for me by father, mother, king, devas, my kinsmen or friends, nor by any other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."

Only the World-Honored One, out of his compassionate mindfulness and pity, has caused me today to dry up the ocean of blood, transcend the mountain of bones, close the gates to the evil realms, open the path to nirvana, and establish me upon the paths of humans and devas.

I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha as an upāsaka; from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall refrain from taking life and so forth, up to refraining from drinking intoxicants, and thus receive the three refuges along with the five precepts.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having again taught the Dharma to them, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, immediately entered meditative concentration and vanished from his place in the celestial palace, returning to the twin śāla trees at his final resting place.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu, Scroll Thirty-Seven.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu, Scroll Thirty-Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. Chapter Eight, Sub-section Ten:

A Summary Verse on the Remainder of the Discourse on Nirvāṇa. At that time, in the city of Kuśinagara, there was a renunciant non-Buddhist named Subhadra (Skt. *Subhadra*), one hundred and twenty years of age and physically decrepit. All the warriors of the city of Kuśinagara felt great reverence for Subhadra, honoring and making offerings to him as they would to an Arhat.
Not far from here is a great lotus pond named Mandākinī; on its bank stands an udumbara tree, where the brahmin Bhadraśāla frequently dwells.

In the past, when the Bodhisattva was in the Tuṣita Heaven and entered his mother’s womb in the form of a white elephant, the *udumbara* tree flower first began to emerge. At the time of his birth, it gradually developed color and luster; during his youth, as the flower was about to bloom, he grew weary of old age, sickness, and death and retired to the mountain forests. When the flower became somewhat larger, its shape resembled a crow’s beak; while practicing austerities, it appeared withered and shriveled. After he abandoned those austerities, his breath became free-flowing as he partook of various foods—as extensively described before—until finally, upon attaining perfect enlightenment, the flower fully blossomed.

When the Brahma King came to invite [the Buddha] to turn the Wheel of Dharma in Vārāṇasī, those trees and flowers flourished with brilliant colors and splendor, their exquisite fragrance pervading all directions and realms.

Nevertheless, the Buddha’s great compassion extends universally to all who have a karmic connection with him; having extensively delivered beings throughout the worlds he visited, he proceeded to Kuśinagara for his final reclining. Yet this flower tree has become withered and shriveled in both form and color, causing those who see it to exclaim in astonishment.
At that time, Subhadra, observing these portents, thought to himself:
"There must surely be some calamity in the city of Kuśinagara.
Then, a protective deity of the kingdom raised a great voice and addressed the people, saying:
"Today, at the hour of midnight, the Tathāgata will surely enter the realm of the wondrous Nirvāṇa without remainder.
Upon hearing these words, the brahmin Bhadra thought to himself:
"Alas! How tragic!"
"Alas! That Great Śramaṇa Gautama will surely attain parinirvāṇa this very night.

Yet, I have harbored doubts regarding the Dharma I have attained myself; I constantly reflect: 'When, by what means, shall I be able to see that person and inquire about what I have not yet understood?'"
"What a pity!
The Eye of the Dharma will soon perish.
You should go at once to inquire of him in person."
"If I am granted the favor of your great compassion and pity to resolve this for me, I shall forever attain liberation from all my doubts.
Having formed this thought, he departed from the city of Kuśinagara and proceeded to the site of the Twin Śāla Trees.
At that time, Ānanda, seeing that the sun—the Buddha—was about to set, was walking to and fro on the open ground outside the temple gate with a mind and body full of sorrow.
When Subhadra saw him, he approached and said: "Ānanda! You..."

"I have heard that the Śramaṇa Gautama possesses all-encompassing wisdom and impartially delivers all sentient beings; yet, I have always harbored doubts regarding the Dharma I have attained myself, and though I have frequently wished to hear what I have not yet heard, I have never been able to fulfill this wish."
Now we have heard the celestial voice proclaiming to us all that the Tathāgata will certainly enter nirvāṇa tonight.
Venerable sir, could you perhaps petition him on our behalf, so that we might personally present our doubts before him?
Ānanda said, "Sobhita!
You should not speak such words now to trouble the World-Honored One; for my Great Teacher currently suffers from back pain and cannot find ease."
Thus Subhadra requested this three times, yet Ānanda did not report it at all.
He spoke again, saying: "Ānanda!"

In the past, I heard an ancient seer, a brahmin of venerable age, great virtue, and exemplary conduct, say: "The appearance of Buddhas in the world is like that of the udumbara flower; they appear but once in hundreds of millions of kalpas."

"The Tathāgata will surely enter nirvana today; harboring confusion within my heart, I wish to consult him with questions. I only hope that you, Great Virtue, will speak on my behalf, for it would be most fortunate indeed if I were able to see the Buddha."
Ānanda said: “Sobhita!
At present, our Great Teacher’s body is afflicted and he is very unwell; do not trouble him intentionally.”
Sudatta pleaded earnestly as before, but the Venerable One did not grant his wish.
While Ānanda and Sudatta were conversing together outside the gate of the monastery, [the following occurred].
With his pure divine ear, which transcends that of humans and gods, the Buddha heard every word they spoke and said to Ānanda:
"You should not prevent Subhadra now; let him come to see me and ask whatever questions he wishes."

Why is this? This virtuous man is one for whom I, as my very last act, shall preach the Dharma to an outsider so that he may give rise to right faith, and whom I shall personally summon with the words "Come, bhikṣu! to become my disciple.

At that time, having heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had compassionately granted his permission, Subhadra was filled with joy beyond measure and leaped for delight. He approached the World-Honored One and engaged in various forms of conversation with him, then withdrew to stand to one side and said: “Gautama!
"I wish to inquire; I pray that you will grant me your attention and explain this for me.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Ask whatever you wish."
He then asked: "Gautama!
I have observed all the various classes of outsiders, each establishing their own distinct tenets, as follows:"

Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarī Gośālīputra, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyanīputra, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra—each of these teachers propounded his own distinct doctrine; it was not known which among them was correct.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately summoned Subhadra and spoke these verses for him:
"At the age of twenty-nine, I left the household life to seek the sublime Dharma;
For over fifty years since then, I have devoted myself exclusively to the practice of morality, concentration, and wisdom."
"With a single mind free from distraction, one seeks only the True Principle;
apart from this True Dharma, there is no other true śramaṇa.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he further addressed Bhadra:

"This is the Eightfold Noble Path well-expounded by the Buddhas; it is exceedingly rare and difficult to encounter. Apart from this, if one seeks even one, two, three, or four fruits of the śramaṇa’s path, they can never be obtained."
Therefore, one who seeks the fruits of the śramaṇa within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya and the eight branches of the Noble Path will certainly attain them.
Furthermore, Subhadda!

Apart from these eight noble dharmas, there are various non-Buddhist brahmins and others who each cling to their own views; some claim that the three periods of time are without cause or effect, and that the merit and goodness they cultivate are all empty and of no benefit.
Therefore, amidst the assembly of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, I let out a great lion’s roar and declare:
"All who practice cultivation shall obtain their karmic fruits."

When this Dharma was being taught, the brahmin Subhadra became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; he gained indestructible faith in the Truths, crossed over the river of craving, severed the web of doubt, and spontaneously realized all subtle and wondrous Dharmas. He then rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and addressed Ānanda as follows: “The Great Master is so revered that it is difficult to request instruction of him.

I observe, Venerable Sir, that you have attained great and excellent benefit, having fortunately encountered the Unsurpassed Dharma King, who is the supreme one among all teachers for the conferral of empowerment. By the power of the Master, I too have well realized [the truth]. I now earnestly hope to go forth within the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, seeking full ordination to become a bhikṣu and cultivate the conduct of a śramaṇa.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This Subhadra has now heard the Dharma and attained realization; his heart delights in going forth, as described at length above, until he has attained the status of a bhikṣu. I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on him and deliver him.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the virtuous one:
"Welcome, bhikṣu; you may practice the holy life.

As soon as the Buddha spoke these words, he assumed the usual deportment, received the full ordination, and became a bhikṣu. With single-minded diligence and vigor, he was not negligent, and formed this thought:
“Good son! For what reason have you shaved off your hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and with right faith gone forth from home to cultivate the holy life for the sake of the unsurpassed path,
so as to attain personal realization within this very life?”
“Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.
At that time, Subhadra gave rise to a mind of penetrating realization and immediately and swiftly realized the fruit of Arhatship. Having attained liberation of mind, he further thought:
“I cannot bear to witness the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; it is fitting that I depart first.”
Having formed this thought, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
I wish to enter parinirvāṇa first."
The Buddha asked Subhadra,
"Are you entering nirvana now? He replied:
"So it is," he replied, having been questioned thus a second and a third time. The Buddha said:
"All conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent; you yourself can know the proper time for what must be done. What more need I say?"
As Subhadra was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he thought to himself:
"I must now perform five kinds of empowerments before passing away:
let all who come to behold me see my body with its hair and beard shaven and wearing the saṃghāṭī robe; do not let them see the ritual observances of the non-Buddhists."
Furthermore, when the various non-Buddhists come to carry me away, do not allow my body to be lifted; only those who practice the same holy life (sabrahmacārin) shall be able to carry me off.
Also, when entering the bathing pool to wash my body, ensure that the non-Buddhists cannot reach the bottom; only those who practice the same holy life shall be able to wash my body.
Furthermore, when the various non-Buddhists enter the water, it shall cause fish and turtles to become agitated and distressed, while my fellow practitioners of the holy life remain free from harm.
Moreover, the various non-Buddhists shall be unable to ignite my remains, whereas my fellow practitioners of the holy life shall cause the fire to catch.
Having performed these five kinds of consecrations and reflections, he entered parinirvāṇa.
