When the various non-Buddhists heard that the brahmin Subhadra had entered parinirvāṇa, they took musical instruments, banners, flags, and parasols, went to the city of Kuśinagara, and at the crossroads addressed the people, saying:
"You should all know!..."
That great śramaṇa Gautama constantly says this:

"Only within my Dharma are there the Eightfold Noble Path and the four fruits of the śramaṇa; these do not exist among the outsiders," as explained at length previously, up until his uttering the lion’s roar.
"However, within my Dharma, my fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin), the Great Teacher Subhadra, has also attained nirvāṇa;
how does he differ from them? The bhikṣus replied, "If you claim that we are your disciples, then take us as you please."
However, although many non-Buddhists lifted it together, they could not move it, much less carry it away. The bhikṣus said,
"Since you cannot do it, we shall lift it ourselves."
He replied, "So be it.
The bhikṣus then lifted [the bowl] together and departed, while the non-Buddhist remained silent.
Furthermore, when various non-Buddhists came to the bathing pool, the bhikṣus said, "Now you may bathe your bodies for the sake of your fellow practitioners of the holy life.
When they entered the water, they could not find its bottom and were further harassed by fish and turtles; the bhikṣus, however, were not so.
The bhikṣu replied, "If these are your fellow practitioners of the holy life, you should burn them yourselves.
However, when the non-Buddhists attempted to set them on fire, they were unable to ignite them; yet when the bhikṣu lit the fire, it immediately burst into a blazing flame.
At that time, the multitude of people mocked the non-Buddhists, who each departed with shame, their heads bowed low.

Then, the warriors of the city of Kuśinagara, witnessing this extraordinary marvel at the presence of the World-Honored One, conceived a redoubled sense of reverence and pure faith. Each harboring deep affection and longing, they spoke thus: "The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One lies here for the final time;

though his body manifests illness and his limbs are uneasy, he was still able to preach the Dharma for the sake of Subhadra, causing him to swiftly realize the fruit of Arhatship, and further enabling all the warriors of the city of Kuśinagara to obtain excellent benefit."
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:

"The Tathāgata now manifests illness in his body, with his limbs and joints in discomfort; yet he is still able to cause the brahmin Bhadra to cross the ocean of birth and death, realize arhatship, and reach ultimate nirvāṇa, bringing an end to all suffering."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "You should know this!

It is not yet rare that I have now severed the roots of the three poisons, am liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction, possess all-encompassing wisdom, and have attained great mastery over all realms; thus, it is no difficulty for me to cause that Suvīra to emerge from the ocean of birth and death and attain the ultimate state of dwelling in nirvāṇa."

In the past, while wandering in saṃsāra, I was possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion; I had not yet severed birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction; and I lacked the wisdom to reflect well. Even so, while among the animals, I was still able to sacrifice my own life for the sake of the brahmin Bhadra and the various warriors of the city of Kuśinagara.
I shall speak for you; you should listen attentively!

"In the distant past, in a great mountain marsh, there was a deer king who dwelt with a thousand deer surrounding him in the forest. He possessed great wisdom and could foresee the requirements of the moment."
While he was staying there, a hunter saw him and went to inform the king.
The king then surrounded the area with his troops on all sides. The deer king thought to himself:
"If I cannot rescue these deer, they will surely be slaughtered by this hunter."
At that time, the deer king looked around in all directions and thought to himself:
"By what skillful means can I now enable this herd of deer to escape from this suffering and calamity?"

Then he saw that at the foot of a deep mountain there was a mountain stream flowing swiftly out of the valley; the deer, being weak and frail, were unable to swim or leap across. The Deer King entered the stream and stood across the current, letting out a great cry to announce to the herd:
"Come quickly! Leap from this bank onto my back and cross to the other side; you will surely survive."
"If we do not do so, we shall meet with slaughter.
Thereupon, the herd of deer one after another stepped upon the back of the great deer king, and all crossed the swift river, escaping their peril.

As the hooves of the herd of deer trampled him, the king of deer’s hide was pierced through and his flesh consumed until only his backbone remained; though he suffered extreme agony, his mind never wavered, for he ensured that the entire herd crossed safely, still harboring concern for those who had not yet crossed: "Who remains behind?"

Among the herd of deer, there was one fawn that could not leap across; at that time, although the king of the deer was undergoing extreme suffering, he still harbored a compassionate thought and disregarded his own person, emerging from the water, taking the fawn, and placing it upon his back to carry it to the other shore.
The deer king surveyed them all around and, knowing that they had all crossed over, made this vow at the moment his strength was failing and his life was ending:

"I have rescued these deer and this fawn, delivering them from the peril of death at the cost of my own body and life. May it be that when I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in the future, I shall enable them to cross the net of birth and death and establish them in the state of ultimate, wondrous nirvana."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think? Do not harbor any other thoughts."
The king of deer in those days was none other than myself; the herd of deer were the various warriors of the city of Kuśinagara; and the fawn was none other than Subhadra.
"Furthermore, monks!

Just as when I was among the animals due to my lack of wisdom—breathing uneasily and undergoing various bitter sufferings while my skin, flesh, limbs, and joints were being torn apart—I rescued the virtuous one (Sudatta) and brought him to a state of fearlessness."
Listen well! In the distant past, in Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who ruled the world according to the Dharma, as described at length in the sūtras.
The king possessed an intelligent horse that could foresee future events; consequently, neighboring kingdoms stood in awe and all came to pay tribute.
When the horse passed away, the minor kings sent envoys to announce:
"King Brahmadatta, you must now pay your share of taxes to us; if you do not, you shall not be permitted to leave the city."
"If you see those who oppose us, we shall come together to destroy their kingdom.
The king said to the messenger,
"I will neither send the tax nor leave the city."
Thereupon, he searched throughout the kingdom for a wise horse and eventually found one in another place.

It was the season of spring, when the flowers and trees were in full bloom and the flocks of birds sang in harmony, most delightful to hear; the king mounted the wise horse and, accompanied by his court ladies, went to enjoy himself in a fragrant garden.

At that time, hearing that King Brahmadatta, together with his ministers, aides, and palace ladies, was sporting outside without any fear, the minor kings did not immediately enter the city; instead, they consulted one another and each mobilized the four divisions of their armies, arriving at the city gates.
The minister addressed the king, saying:
"The minor kings have shown no respect for the imperial decree; daring to incite rebellion, they have come to knock at the city gates. We pray that you will prepare for defense.
Having heard this, the king issued an order to seek out a wise horse.
"Quickly prepare the fourfold army; I myself shall go forth to strike them down.

At that time, the king mounted his horse, arrayed his troops, and took an oath before the multitude as they engaged in battle together. Relying on his own prowess, the king stood alone at the vanguard, when he was struck by a spear from the enemy host. His intestines and stomach were all forced out, and he suffered various agonizing torments so unbearable that his life was nearly at its end.

He then thought: "The king has fallen into dire distress; it would be improper for me not to rescue him. I must endure these bitter pains to enable the king to escape this calamity and reach the city gate, arriving at a place of safety."

Having formed this thought, he looked all around but saw no way to enter the city. However, outside the city there was a great bathing pool named Brahmā-vimala, situated near the royal palace; within that pool were four lotuses—blue, yellow, red, and white—all of which completely filled it.
At that time, the Wise Horse, disregarding its own life, leaped into the pond and stepped upon the lotus leaves; carrying the king across the peril, it entered the palace directly.
As soon as the king had dismounted, the horse’s life came to an end.
Then the minor kings vied with one another to enter the groves, searching everywhere but failing to find him; they withdrew their troops, plundered, and each returned to his own abode.
King Brahmadatta, having escaped this peril and preserved his life, addressed the ministers and the people of Vārāṇasī, saying:
"If there should be anyone who can save the life of a consecrated Kṣatriya great king, what reward shall be granted?"
The ministers said to the king,
"You may divide half of the kingdom [with him]. The king said:
"This wise horse was able to save my life; now that the horse has died, how shall I repay its kindness?

The ministers replied, "For the sake of the wise horse, you should hold an untimely White Lotus Assembly at the four gates of the city, extensively practicing acts of charity and vigorously cultivating meritorious deeds to support his journey to the afterlife."
The King said, "Excellent! You should proceed with it immediately."

At that time, the king immediately ordered the crown prince, the ladies of the inner palace, ministers, officials, and the common people to adorn the thoroughfares. Incense, flowers, banners, canopies, and bright lamps were arranged and displayed everywhere until they were filled to overflowing, making it as delightful as the Garden of Joy (Nandana-vana).
The King ordered the drum to be beaten to proclaim far and near:

"Tomorrow, I intend to establish an untimely White Lotus Assembly for the sake of the Wise Horse at the four gates of the city; you should inform one another to gather at the site of the Dharma to receive my offerings."
"When the time came for the assembly to gather, I provided whatever was required so that everyone’s wishes were fully satisfied. Monks, what do you think?

At that time, the wise horse was none other than myself. For the sake of that king, I underwent all manner of suffering and torment; though my body was torn apart, I disregarded my own life and limb, yet I was still able to rescue him and free him from peril."
At that time, the bhikṣus again had doubts and requested of the World-Honored One,
saying: "Venerable Sir,
what karma did the venerable Bhadrika previously perform?"
"Now he is the final disciple of the Great Teacher.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should know this!"
The karma one has created oneself is now returned to oneself to be experienced; this is explained at length elsewhere, even including the recitation of verses. O Bhikṣus!

In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the lifespan of humans was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa, the tenth [of the Buddhas], whose title was "Endowed with All Qualities" (Saṃbuddha). He resided at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī.

At that time, that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha had a grandson named Aśoka, who went forth into homelessness seeking liberation. Believing that the fruit of liberation could be attained naturally, he did not diligently cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path; thus, after a long period had passed, he had still not realized the fruit and was wandering through the human world, spending the summer retreats wherever he happened to be.

At that time, the Tathāgata had delivered all for whom he had a karmic connection; having completed what was to be done, he was like a fire extinguished when its fuel is exhausted, and at the hour of midnight, he was about to enter parinirvāṇa.

At that moment, the bhikṣu was beneath an Aśoka tree, and the deity of that tree, hearing that the Tathāgata Kāśyapa was about to enter parinirvāṇa, wept with such sorrow that her tears fell like rain, drenching the body of the Aśoka tree.
The bhikṣu looked up and asked the deity,
"For what reason are you weeping so bitterly?
The tree deity replied:
"Tonight at midnight, Kāśyapa Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa.
When those bhikṣus heard these words, their hearts were pierced with such piercing agony as if arrows had entered them; they wailed and wept, crying out in loud lamentation.
The tree deity asked,
"For what reason do you weep? He replied:

“Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha was my maternal uncle; though I relied upon him, I did not practice diligently. Since he has passed far away, it is difficult for me to pay him homage. Being an ordinary person, I lack the power to go quickly; for this reason, I weep.”
The tree deity replied, "Indeed, I have the power to cause you to arrive swiftly; however, I do not know whether seeing the Buddha will be of benefit to you.
The bhikṣu replied:
"I am extremely courageous; if I were to see the Buddha, I would surely be able to practice according to his teachings and realize the benefits of the fruit.
At that moment, the tree deity, by means of supernatural power, swiftly led this bhikṣu to the presence of the Buddha.

Having seen the Buddha, they gave rise to a pure mind and made vast vows; at that time, the Tathāgata, according to their individual capacities, taught them the sublime Dharma, and they realized the fruit of Arhatship. Unable to bear seeing the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa, they therefore attained extinction before him.
At that time, having seen that the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus had entered parinirvāṇa, the tree deity felt deep affection and longing, and thought to herself:

"All the supreme benefits now obtained by this venerable one were due to me; by this merit, I pray that in a future age, when the lifespan of humans is one hundred years, I may receive the prophecy from the Buddha Kāśyapa as a young brahmin (maṇava), attain perfect enlightenment under the name Śākyamuni, and at the time of his parinirvāṇa, I shall have already attained the fruit of an arhat and entered nirvāṇa before him."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What do you think? The celestial deity at that time was none other than the present-day Subhadra."
"For this reason, at all times you should distance yourself from evil friends and draw near to virtuous spiritual mentors; you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
In a secluded place, I had this thought:

"A spiritual friend is half of the holy life; it is through the power of a good friend that practitioners are able to accomplish their practice. Because one obtains a good friend, one distances oneself from evil friends. For this reason, one knows that a good friend is half of the holy life."
The Buddha said: "Ānanda, do not speak these words:
'A virtuous friend is half of the holy life.'"

Why is this? Because a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is the entirety of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). By means of them, one is able to distance oneself from evil friends, refrain from committing all manner of evils, and constantly cultivate all forms of goodness, thereby possessing the characteristics of the holy life that are purely singular, stainless, complete, and perfect.

For this reason, if one obtains virtuous companions and dwells together with them, there is nothing regarding the matter of *nirvāṇa* that will not be accomplished; therefore, it is called the "complete holy life" (*brahmacarya*). Why is this so?

Ānanda! It is by virtue of spiritual friends that I enable all sentient beings to attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; were it not for such virtuous friends, this would not be possible.
"Ānanda! You should diligently practice and study that which I have taught.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"For this reason, from this time forward, you should not arbitrarily grant the going forth or the full ordination to non-Buddhists, with the exception of those of the Śākya clan and those non-Buddhists who serve fire and wear topknots."

If someone wearing the robes of an outsider comes seeking to go forth and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), one should question them regarding the obstructing factors (*antarāyika-dharma*) and grant it to this person.
Why? Because this is my own kinsman and possesses the necessary conditions (*pratyaya*).

Those who tend the sacred fire claim that there is karmic efficacy because there are causes, conditions, and the fruits of diligent exertion; therefore, without requiring them to undergo the period of co-residence, they were immediately granted the status of renunciants and received full ordination.

If any other followers of non-Buddhist paths come seeking to receive the going-forth or full ordination, their preceptor-teacher should provide them with robes and have them consume the community's regular food while living together for four months.
If, upon observing a person’s character and conduct, you find them to be gentle and pliant and capable of being delivered, you should grant them the going forth as well as full ordination;
thus should it be known. "Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!

If there are teachings that can produce benefit and happiness in the present and future lives, you should receive, uphold, read, and recite them, and explain them to others so as not to let them fall into oblivion; this is for the sake of ensuring that the holy life (brahmacarya) may long endure in the world, bringing peace and happiness to gods and humans, and providing benefit and welfare to all sentient beings.
What is this Dharma? It consists of:

the discourses (sūtra), the verses (geya), the prophecies (vyākaraṇa), the stanzas (gāthā), the spontaneous utterances (udāna), the causal narratives (nidāna), the past events (itivṛttaka), the birth stories (jātaka), the extensive teachings (vaipulya), the marvelous accounts (adbhutadharma), the parables (avadāna), and the expositions (upadeśa).

If one can receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice according to the teachings of these twelve divisions of the Dharma, one will be able to produce benefit and happiness in both the present and the future, and even bring about compassion for all sentient beings and the long endurance of the Buddha-dharma.
"O bhikṣus! After my parinirvāṇa, you should think thus:
'Today we have no Great Teacher.'"

"You should not give rise to such a view. I have commanded you to recite the Prātimokṣa every half-month; you should know that this is your Great Teacher and your refuge, no different from my remaining in the world."

Furthermore, from this day forward, junior bhikṣus should not address senior elders by their clan name or personal name; they should address them as "Venerable One" (bhadanta) or "Long-lived One" (āyuṣmat). Senior bhikṣus, in turn, should address juniors as "Long-lived One."

However, a senior bhikṣu should maintain a heart of compassion and protection toward a junior one, giving rise to thoughts of loving-kindness; he should provide mutual assistance with robes, alms bowls, bowl-covers, or waist-bands so that no need goes unmet, or further instruct them in recitation and meditative reflection so that they may progress daily. In this way, the Dharma of mine can flourish.
If it were not so, the Dharma would surely perish quickly.

Furthermore, O Bhikṣus, there are four places in this region where faithful sons and daughters of noble family should, for as long as they live, constantly maintain mindfulness and cultivate a heart of reverence.
What are the four? First, the place where the Buddha was born;
second, the place where he attained perfect enlightenment;
Third, the place where the Wheel of Dharma was turned;
fourth, the place where he entered Great Parinirvāṇa.

If one can personally pay homage at these four sites, or reverently offer salutations from afar with sincere devotion, giving rise to pure faith and constantly fixing the mind upon them, one will surely be reborn in the heavens after the end of this life.

"Compared to the West, I have personally visited eight locations where the Tathāgata resided during his lifetime of over fifty years: first, the place of his birth; second, the place of his attainment of enlightenment;

third, the place where he turned the wheel of Dharma; fourth, the place on Vulture Peak Mountain; fifth, the place in Vaiśālī; sixth, the place where he descended from heaven; seventh, the place in the Jeta Grove; and eighth, the place in the Twin Śāla Trees where he entered parinirvāṇa."
The fourth is a fixed location; all others are indefinite.
A summary verse says:
"The Dharma was generated at Vulture Peak, extensively spread beneath the Jeta Grove; with single-minded devotion, one's merit surpasses that of a thousand pieces of gold."
Furthermore, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"If you have any doubts, you should all ask them now. Should there be any questions regarding the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, or concerning the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, I shall answer them for you."
Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As I understand what the Buddha has now taught, he commands all bhikṣus that they should ask whatever doubts they may have."

"Yet, among this assembly, there is not a single person who harbors any doubt regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, or the Truths of Suffering, Accumulation, Cessation, and the Path that requires further questioning.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent!"

"Ānanda! Since you are able to speak such words with such thorough and accurate penetration, and since I observe within this assembly with my wisdom that there is indeed no one who harbors doubt regarding the Jewel of the Truths—this is the final act of the Tathāgata."
At that time, out of great compassion and pity, the Tathāgata removed his upper garment and revealed his physical form, saying to the bhikṣus:
"You should now behold the Buddha’s body; you should now behold the Buddha’s body."
"Why is this? Because a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower.
At that time, all the bhikṣus remained silent. The Buddha said:
"All phenomena are thus: all conditioned things are impermanent; this is my final instruction.

Having spoken these words, he settled his mind in right mindfulness and entered the first dhyāna. Emerging from that, he proceeded in successive order through the second dhyāna, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, remaining in profound and silent composure.
Then Ānanda asked the Venerable Aniruddha:
"Has our Great Teacher now entered parinirvāṇa, or has he not yet entered it? He replied:
"The Buddha has not yet entered parinirvāṇa; he merely abides in the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. Ānanda said:

"I have personally heard these words from the Buddha: 'If the World-Honored Buddha enters the ultimate concentration (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*) and remains motionless, immediately thereafter the Eye of the World will close and he will surely enter parinirvāṇa.'"

At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and entered the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) in reverse order. From the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he emerged and entered the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); next, he entered the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); next, the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); next, the fourth dhyāna; then the third, the second, and the first dhyāna. Emerging from the first dhyāna, he re-entered the second, third, and fourth dhyānas. Remaining tranquil and unmoving, he then entered the realm of nirvāṇa with no remainder (*anupadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu*).

At that time, immediately after the World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa, the great earth shook violently, meteors appeared in the daytime, all directions blazed with fire, and the devas in the sky beat their drums.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was staying at the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place, near Rājagṛha. Seeing the great earth tremble, he immediately composed his mind and observed: "What is the cause of this?"
He then saw the Tathāgata enter Great Parinirvāṇa and thought to himself:
"Now that I no longer have the Great Teacher, I shall abide solely by the Dharma; as for the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), what more can be said?"
He further thought:

"This King Ajātaśatru, son of Bimbisāra, has recently developed the root of faith. If he hears that the Buddha has entered nirvana, he will surely die from vomiting hot blood; I should now prepare a skillful expedient in advance."
Having formed this thought, he immediately summoned the city minister Varṣākāra and said:
"Do you know, sir? The Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa.
King Ajātaśatru has only recently developed the faculty of faith; if he hears that the Buddha has entered nirvāṇa, he will surely vomit hot blood and die."
"I should now prepare a skillful means in advance.
He then explained it to him in due order:
"Virtuous one, you should go quickly to a garden and, within a magnificent hall, depict the Buddha’s past causes and conditions according to the Dharma."

In the past, while the Bodhisattva was in the Tuṣita Heaven palace and was about to descend to be born, he contemplated five matters; the devaputras of the desire realm purified the mother’s body three times, and he entered her womb in the form of a young elephant. After his birth, he left the city to renounce the world, practiced austerities for six years, and sat upon the Vajrāsana beneath the Bodhi tree to attain perfect enlightenment.
Next, he went to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī and, for the sake of the five bhikṣus, turned the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths in its three phases and twelve aspects.
Subsequently, in the city of Śrāvastī, he manifested great supernormal powers for the assembly of humans and devas.

Next, he went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to extensively proclaim the essentials of the Dharma for his mother, Māyā; three jeweled staircases descended to Jambudvīpa, and at the city of Saṅkāśya, humans and devas looked up to him with thirsty longing.

Having manifested his transformative birth in various regions throughout all lands and brought his work for the benefit of beings to completion, he was about to enter parinirvāṇa; thus, he proceeded to the city of Kuśinagara to the twin śāla trees, where he lay with his head to the north and entered great nirvāṇa.

Once all the traces of the Tathāgata’s transformative activities throughout his entire life had been depicted, eight caskets equal in size to a human being were then constructed and placed beside the hall; the first seven caskets were filled to the brim with fresh butter, while the eighth casket contained perfumed water made from ox-head sandalwood.
If he goes out in his carriage, you may say to the King:
"Please deign to turn your divine carriage aside and visit the fragrant garden in person to view the paintings.
When the King has seen them, he will ask Varṣākāra:
"What is this that you are describing?

He then recounted it for the king in successive order, exactly as depicted in the painting, beginning from the descent from Tuṣita into his mother’s womb and ending with his reclining with his head to the north beneath the twin śāla trees.
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately fainted and rolled upon the ground; he was then quickly moved into the first casket.
In this manner, he was placed in the second, third, fourth, and so on up to the seventh, after which he was set in the casket of fragrant water, whereupon the king regained consciousness.

At that time, after the Venerable One had finished instructing him in succession, he departed for the city of Kuśinagara. Once the minister Varṣākāra had carried out all the matters exactly as the Venerable One had instructed, the king happened to go out, and the minister addressed him, saying:
"I pray that Your Majesty would deign to turn your carriage for a moment to tour and observe the garden."

When the king arrived at the garden, he saw that the murals within the hall were novel and extraordinary, depicting [the Buddha’s life] from his initial birth until his reclining beneath the twin śāla trees.
The king asked his ministers, "Could it be that the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa?"
At that time, Varṣākāra remained silent and offered no reply.
Seeing this, the king realized that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa; he immediately broke into wailing, fainted, and rolled upon the ground.
The minister immediately moved the body into a casket of ghee; after doing this seven times, he finally cast it into scented water, whereupon the King gradually regained his composure.
At that time, when the Tathāgata entered nirvāṇa, blossoms from the twin śāla trees fell and scattered, completely covering his golden body.
At that time, a bhikṣu, having witnessed this event, spoke a verse:
"When the World-Honored One was entering nirvāṇa, The most excellent śāla trees bent their branches downward to provide shade, And further scattered upon him famous flowers."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, also spoke in verse:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing.
When arising and ceasing have ceased, nirvāṇa is bliss."
Then the Brahma King also spoke in verse:
"In all worlds, those who are born must return to death;
the power of impermanence is greatest, and all conditioned phenomena utterly perish."
"The Great Master, the Eye of the World, whose Ten Powers are peerless;
having completed his work of transformation, he rests in parinirvāṇa beneath the twin śāla trees.
At that time, the Venerable Āniruddha also spoke in verse:
"The Buddha has no inhalation or exhalation, and his mind is likewise serene;
the Eye of the World is now closed, tranquil, peaceful, and unmoving.
The World-Honored One, endowed with the ten powers, having completed his transformation, has entered the realm of no-remainder."
Seeing and hearing of all sentient beings, their hair stands on end and their hearts are struck with terror.
Let not your mind sink into despair, nor harbor grief and affliction;
the Buddha has realized true liberation (*vimukti*), like the extinguishing of a lamp’s flame.

At that time, when the bhikṣus saw that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had entered parinirvāṇa, they were each filled with grief. Some were bewildered and distressed, rolling upon the ground, beating their breasts and crying out loudly, their hearts overcome by sorrow and misery. Others contemplated the principles of the Dharma and spoke thus:
"We should now exercise self-restraint and patience; for the World-Honored One often said:
'All things that are radiant, lovely, and delightful, though they may be esteemed, ultimately return to impermanence and end in separation.'"
Then Āniruddha said to Ānanda: "Venerable one! You should exhort the great assembly to restrain themselves for now;
do not violate the proper decorum and do not wail with such great lamentation."
Why is this? Because there are currently present here gods with lifespans of hundreds of thousands of kalpas who, all feeling revulsion and shame, speak thus:

"How is it that a bhikṣu, having gone forth in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, cannot properly contemplate the nature of impermanence and instead gives rise to sorrow and suffering?"
Ānanda said: "How many are these hosts of devas? He replied:

"From this city of Kuśinagara, as far as the Golden River and the twin śāla trees, reaching the Caitya of the Mallas' Crown-tying, for twelve yojanas all around these four boundaries, the gods of great majesty and virtue completely fill the space, leaving no gap even large enough to stand a staff."

When these devas saw the Buddha enter nirvana, each was filled with grief and sorrow; they beat their breasts in anguish and fainted upon the ground. Yet, as before, some consoled one another, urging them to restrain themselves, noting that all things ultimately end in impermanence and must all be parted from.
At that time, the Venerable Āniruddha extensively expounded the essential points of the Dharma for Ānanda and the great assembly until daybreak; meanwhile, the bhikṣus listened in silence.
Āniruddha spoke again to Ānanda, saying:

"You should now go to the city of Kuśinagara and inform the Mallas that yesterday at midnight, the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has already entered the realm of the wondrous Nirvāṇa without remainder."
"Virtuous ones, you should now quickly perform what is to be done; do not later regret it.
He spoke again, saying:
"The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has entered parinirvāṇa within your city. Why do you not offer worship to repay the Buddha’s compassionate grace?"
When Ānanda had heard these words, he immediately took his celestial robe and, taking a bhikṣu as his attendant, went to the Hall of the Gathering of Warriors.
There were five hundred people already present in the hall when the Venerable One addressed them, saying:
"O you valiant men and the great assembly, the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has already entered the realm of the wondrous Nirvāṇa without remainder at midnight."
"Virtuous ones, you should now quickly perform what must be done; do not harbor regrets later.
He spoke again, saying:
"The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has entered parinirvāṇa in your city; why do you not offer worship to repay the Buddha’s compassionate kindness?"

When the warriors heard this proclamation, some fainted and rolled upon the ground; others beat their breasts and cried out loudly, their bodies trembling so violently that they could not support themselves. Still others spoke these words in a loud voice:
"In the presence of the Buddha, we have heard it said:
'The world is impermanent; all things must eventually part.'"
Then the warriors said to one another:

"We should each take various flower garlands, unguents, powdered incense, burning incense, as well as all manner of exquisite objects, music, and drums, and go quickly to the Twin Śāla Trees to present our offerings."

Together with the great ministers and counselors, each accompanied by their retinues—men and women, young and old, as well as friends and acquaintances—they departed from the city of Kuśinagara and proceeded to the site of the Twin Śāla Trees.

Having arrived there, they expressed their grief before the lion throne where the Buddha lay; then, each taking whatever exquisite incenses, famous flowers, countless banners, streamers, silken fabrics, food, and rare delicacies, and performing extensive offerings with various musical performances, they addressed Ānanda, saying:
"The Unsurpassed Dharma King has already entered parinirvāṇa; we do not know how the funeral rites should now be conducted."
The Venerable One replied, "However,
I have already received the Buddha’s instruction that all funeral rites shall be conducted according to those of a Wheel-Turning King. He asked:
“What is the procedure for this? He replied:

“First, wrap the body in white cotton wool; next, encircle the entire body with a thousand layers of white cotton cloth. Place it within a golden coffin filled with fragrant oil, cover it with a golden lid, and pile up sandalwood and various coastal incenses. Then, cremate it with fire.”

Afterwards, he poured cow’s milk over the fire to extinguish it; the remaining relics were placed in a golden vase, and a stūpa was erected at a major crossroads. It was surrounded on all sides with suspended silk banners and canopies, and offerings of ointments, powdered incense, and burning incense were made, accompanied by the performance of various musical arts, as he paid reverent homage and established a great assembly for almsgiving.
"This is the method for cremating and burying a Wheel-Turning King; the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, is far superior to this.
When the strongmen heard these words, they said to the Venerable One:
"We understand your meaning, yet this matter cannot be accomplished in one, two, or three days."
"If you remain for seven days, it can then be accomplished as previously described. He replied, "So be it."

At that time, the people immediately prepared everything according to the funeral rites of a Wheel-Turning King as previously described, leaving nothing incomplete. From the city of Kuśinagara for a distance of twelve *yojanas* all the way to the Āmrapālī Grove (Ke-guan-zhidi), immeasurable sentient beings who looked up to him with devotion gathered like clouds. Each carrying incense, flowers, various musical instruments, and articles of offering, the Mallas and their retinues all departed the city and went between the twin trees to the lion bed, where they arranged everything and made offerings with all their hearts.
At that time, among the Mallas there was an elder who addressed the assembly, saying:

"All you present, let the women hold the banners and streamers while the men carry the bier. We shall take various flowers, silks, ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, and musical instruments, enter through the western gate of Kuśinagara, exit through the eastern gate, cross the Hiraṇyavatī River, and proceed to the sublime site of the Mallas' Crown-binding Caitya to enshrine [the body] and cremate it with fire."
At that time, having heard these words, the people each vied with one another to lift the golden coffin; yet although they exerted all their strength together, they could not move it at all.
Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Venerable Aniruddha, saying:
"The strong men of the city of Kuśinagara have exhausted their physical strength, yet they cannot move the Tathāgata’s golden coffin. I do not know what the reason for this may be."
The Venerable One replied:

"This was the intention of the devas, wishing that the strongmen and the people—women holding banners and streamers, men carrying the honored palanquin—should follow the Tathāgata with dignified decorum. We devas together held flowers and silks, burned various wonderful incenses, and performed celestial music to present extensive offerings. Entering through the western gate and exiting through the eastern gate, they were to cross the River of Golden Sand and proceed to the Keśava Caitya; for this reason, because the ceremonial arrangements were not yet complete, he could not move."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Elder, saying, "If it be so, let it be according to the will of the deva.
Then the Mallas, following the deva’s wish, prepared everything as previously arranged; they arrived carrying the palanquin, lifting it up lightly and bearing it along.

At that time, from the sky there fell rain consisting of *utpala* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, *padma* flowers, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, as well as powdered incense of *agaru*, powdered sandalwood, powdered *tagara-tamāla*, and *mandārava* flowers and the like.
Hundreds of thousands of kinds of celestial music played simultaneously in the void, while celestial flower-canopies followed like clouds, and billions of celestial garments were scattered about.
At that time, the various warriors of the city of Kuśinagara said to one another, "The devas have already made their offerings; it is now our turn to do so.

Then the warriors, along with all other men and women of high and low station, prepared incense, flowers, and solemn processions in hundreds of thousands of varieties beyond reckoning. With reverent offerings, they followed the golden coffin through the city, crossing the River of Golden Sand to reach the Keśava Caitya, where the scattered flowers accumulated to the height of the knees.

At that time, there was a non-Buddhist brahmin who, having heard that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa and had gone to the Śāla grove, was carrying several stalks of flowers back toward the village of Pāvā. On the way, he encountered Mahākāśyapa, who was accompanied by five hundred disciples with dignified and solemn deportment, proceeding to the Twin Śāla trees to pay homage at the feet of the Great Teacher. Seeing the non-Buddhist, he asked him:
"Where have you come from?"
"Where do you intend to go?
The non-Buddhist replied,
"I have come from Kuśinagara and am about to proceed to the village of Pāvā."
Kāśyapa, knowing [the answer], asked intentionally:
"Have you come from there? Do you know whether my Great Teacher, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, is well in his four great elements?"
The non-Buddhist replied:
"I have come from there; I personally saw that the Venerable Gautama had already entered parinirvāṇa seven days ago.
Since his passing, all humans and devas have offered various kinds of incense, flowers, and solemn rites to fully honor the relics of his remains. I obtained these flowers from that assembly."

Among the five hundred people led by Mahākāśyapa, there was an elder bhikṣu who was by nature dull-witted and unable to distinguish between good and evil; upon hearing the words of the non-Buddhists, he uttered these coarse words:
"How wonderful! How delightful!"
How joyful! From this day forward, we shall be freed from the constraints of the various precepts that dictate: "This should be done; this should not be done."
"All these matters shall now cease.
From this day forward, whether you can uphold them or not depends entirely upon me; that which may be practiced should be practiced, and that which is unnecessary should be discarded."

When that old man uttered these words, the devas in the sky, hearing his unrighteous speech, immediately used their supernormal powers to suppress the sound so that no one else could hear it; only Kāśyapa understood these words.
At that time, for the sake of instructing them, the Venerable One paused briefly by the side of the road; sitting together with the assembly, he addressed them, saying:
"Venerable ones!..."

All conditioned phenomena in the world are impermanent; their nature is not solid and thus difficult to rely upon. They cannot endure for long and all return to dispersal and extinction; you should give rise to weary detachment and not produce attachment.
"Let us cease this matter; let us go quickly to see the Buddha’s entire body.

Then all the warriors and the fourfold assembly first wrapped the Tathāgata’s body in cotton wool, followed by winding it completely with a thousand pieces of white cotton cloth. They placed him in a coffin filled with fragrant oil and covered it with a golden lid. Each took fragrant wood and burned it according to the ritual, yet the fire would not catch.
Then Āniruddha said to Ānanda:
"Though you wish to kindle a fire, there will ultimately be no way for it to catch. He asked:
"Why is that? He replied, "It is because the devas do not allow the fire to ignite."
He asked again, "By what cause? He replied:

“Mahākāśyapa is coming along the road with five hundred followers, wishing to see the World-Honored One’s golden body and personally witness its cremation; it is for his sake that the heavens have not allowed the fire to burn.”
Then Ānanda immediately announced this matter to the entire assembly, and in a short while, the venerable one’s followers all arrived.

The people of the city of Kuśinagara saw the venerable one’s retinue approaching from afar; each person took up incense, flowers, and various musical instruments, and went before the venerable one to prostrate themselves at his feet.

At that time, there was a great multitude of immeasurable hundreds of thousands who followed the Venerable One to the presence of the World-Honored One. They removed the fragrant wood and opened the great golden coffin; having unfolded the thousand layers of cloth and the cotton padding, they gazed upon the Honored Countenance and prostrated themselves at his feet. At that moment, there were only four senior elder *śrāvakas*: the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Nanda, the Venerable Daśabalakāśyapa, and the Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
However, Mahākāśyapa possessed great merit and received abundant offerings; his robes, bowl, and medicinal requisites were in surplus. The Venerable One thought to himself:
"I shall now personally prepare an offering for the World-Honored One."

He immediately prepared one thousand pieces of white cotton cloth and cotton wool; first wrapping [the body] with the wool and then binding it with the cloth, he placed it within the golden coffin and poured oil until it was full. He covered it with a golden lid, piled up various fragrant woods, and withdrew to stand at one side.
Through the remaining majesty of the Buddha and the power of the devas, fire spontaneously broke out among all the fragrant woods.
Then Ānanda circumambulated the pyre to the right and spoke this verse:
"The Tathāgata’s wondrous body has entered parinirvāṇa; Spontaneous fire has arisen to consume his remaining body."
"Only one pair of outer and inner robes shall remain; all the thousand garments shall be consumed by the fire.

At that time, the warriors of the city of Kuśinagara wished to extinguish the fire by pouring cow's milk upon it. Before they had even poured it, four trees suddenly sprang up from within the mass of flames:

first, a golden milk-tree; second, a crimson milk-tree; third, a bodhi tree; and fourth, an udumbara tree. From these trees, milk flowed forth spontaneously, causing the fires to be entirely extinguished.

At that time, the nobles and commoners of the city of Kuśinagara together collected the śarīra, placed them in a golden jar, and set it upon a carriage adorned with the seven precious gems. They made extensive offerings of various kinds of incense, flowers, sandalwood, liquid incense, powdered incense, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, and streamers, accompanied by the sounds of music and song; they carried it into the city and installed it upon a magnificent hall, where they once again performed offerings as grand as before.

At that time, the warriors of the village of Pāvā heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had entered parinirvāṇa in the city of Kuśinagara seven days prior, and that immeasurable humans and devas were extensively making offerings. They assembled the fourfold army from their village—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—and each equipped themselves with various weapons, intending to go together to the city of Kuśinagara to divide the śarīra.
Having arrived at the city, he addressed the people, saying:

"The Unsurpassed Dharma King, the compassionate father of all sentient beings—our fellow men have for a long night made offerings to and revered him, personally receiving his instruction and upholding the True Dharma."
Now that he has entered parinirvāṇa, we wish to take some of his remaining relics and carry them to the village of Pāvā, where we shall erect a stūpa to enshrine and venerate them.
When the people within the city heard this announcement, they all spoke thus:

"The World-Honored One, our Teacher and Guide, was our compassionate father who personally received and guided us with his instruction. Since he has entered parinirvāṇa within our realm, we shall retain his entire body of relics here for eternal kalpas to offer worship; we will by no means share them with the people of other towns."
Then the people of Pāpā sent a messenger with this reply:
"If you divide [the property], it will be well;
if you do not give it to us, we shall seize it by force."
Upon hearing this, the city-dwellers said to that assembly,
"Engaging in battle in vain will never achieve anything.
At that time, those from the villages of Cālakya, Bhaṭṭika, Ārāmada, and Veṇugrāma, as well as the Śākyas of Kapilavastu and the Licchavis of Vaiśālī, all gathered together.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru of the kingdom of Magadha, having heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had entered parinirvāṇa in the city of Kuśinagara, and that all humans and devas were making extensive offerings, [acted accordingly].
Upon hearing this news, he was overcome with great sorrow and distress, and he said to his minister Varṣākāra:
"Do you know what has happened?

I have heard that the World-Honored One has already entered parinirvāṇa; in the city of Kuśinagara, great offerings are being made, and various regions are vying with one another to come and seize the relics by force. I shall now go there as well to request the remains of his body."
The minister said, “If that is so, we should prepare our troops and proceed to the city of Kuśinagara.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru mounted a great elephant intending to go to where the Buddha was; as soon as he ascended the elephant, he remembered the profound kindness of the Buddha, and his heart fainted, causing him to fall from the elephant and roll upon the ground. After a long while he regained consciousness and mounted a horse, but because he could not restrain himself from remembering the Buddha’s kindness, he fell again to the ground. Once he had fully recovered, he addressed the minister Varṣākāra:

"I am currently unable to go in person to the Buddha's presence. You all should now lead the fourfold army to the city of Kuśinagara and convey my instructions, inquiring whether the Mallas are free from illness and affliction, whether their daily life is light and easy, and whether they are living in peace and happiness."
"While the World-Honored One was alive, he guided and received us with constant diligence throughout the long night; he was our Great Teacher.

Now that he has entered parinirvāṇa within your assembly, we pray that you will grant us a portion of his remaining relics. We wish to erect a stūpa in the city of Rājagṛha and offer our profound respect through various offerings of incense, flowers, music, and other honors."
Vairāṭī replied, "As the King commands.
She immediately prepared the fourfold army and proceeded to the city of Kuśinagara, where she addressed the Mallas, saying:

"May you all listen! King Ajātaśatru of the kingdom of Magadha sends his greetings to you and has related everything as before. The Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, constantly brings us benefit and enables us to attain peace and happiness; he is worthy of honor and reverence."

Now that you have entered parinirvāṇa in the village of Bhaṇḍagāma, we pray that you will grant us a portion of your relics; we shall erect a stūpa in Rājagṛha and extensively perform offerings there.
The warriors said: "The World-Honored One was indeed one who benefited and brought peace and happiness to all living beings; he is worthy of honor and reverence.
Yet, as he has now entered parinirvāṇa within our village, the King wishes to see a portion of his remaining relics. This is truly difficult to obtain."
Then the minister Vassakāra said to the warriors:
"If you gentlemen are able to give [it] up, that would be well; if you do not share it, I shall augment my military forces and seize it by force."
He replied, "As you wish.

At that time, the multitude gathered in great numbers, crowding the city corner. All the men and women who were warriors within the city were skilled in archery; they immediately brought forth their elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, arraying the fourfold army with full discipline, intending to engage in battle against the troops of the seven towns.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu, Fascicle 38.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu, Fascicle 39.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. Chapter Eight, Section Ten:

A Summary Verse on the Remainder of the *Nirvāṇa*, followed by the Account of the Council of Five Hundred. At that time, there was a Brahmin named Tuluṇa who was present within the assembly. Seeing these people wishing to contend for the relics and engage in mutual combat, he feared that injury might occur and that it would bring harm to the Buddha’s teachings. He personally grasped a long banner and, with it, signaled to the great multitude, addressing the warriors of Kuśinagara:
“Gentlemen, please desist! Do not fight!”
I now wish to set forth for you the points of increase and decrease.

Recently, I heard that this Great Śramaṇa Gautama, out of compassion for all sentient beings, exerted himself with fervent diligence throughout incalculable eons, enduring acts of malice and harm. For a long time he disciplined himself and praised the practice of forbearance; by these causes and conditions, he attained unsurpassed enlightenment. His mental conduct is as impartial as space, and he universally delivers all sentient beings; yet when the merit of beings is exhausted, he abandons them and enters nirvāṇa.
It has been only seven days since my transformation ceased, yet for you to raise armies and wage war is truly contrary to this.
I pray that none of you engage in conflict; I shall divide [the kingdom] equally so that all may rejoice.

The bodily relics of the Buddha have been divided into eight portions, each to be used for making offerings and benefiting all sentient beings; I pray that you will likewise grant me a portion of the reliquary jar, so that I may carry it back to my own country to construct a stūpa.
When the warriors of the city of Kuśinagara heard this, they replied: “So be it!

Furthermore, for a long night, the Great Master, the World-Honored One, cultivated patience and did not commit acts of killing, as was extensively explained before. It would be a virtuous thing if you would now follow his teaching and divide [the relics] equally for us.”

Having received this permission, the brahmin divided the śarīra into eight portions: the first portion he gave to the Mallas of Kuśinagara, who made extensive offerings; the second portion to the Mallas of Pāvā; the third portion to the Mallas of Allakappa; the fourth portion to the Mallas of Rāmagrāma; the fifth portion to the Licchavis of Vaiśālī; the sixth portion to the Śākyas of Kapilavastu; the seventh portion to the Vrjis of Vaiśālī; and the eighth portion to the minister Varṣākāra of the kingdom of Magadha.

Once these people had each received their share, they returned to their respective places and erected stūpas, where they paid homage with reverence and offered abundant worship of music, incense, and flowers.
At that time, the Brahmin Tuladhāra took a vessel for measuring the śarīras and erected a stūpa in his own village to make offerings.
There was a young brahmin named Pipphala who was also among the assembly, and he addressed the people, saying:

"The grace of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni is universal; since he attained parinirvāṇa in your village, there is no portion of the World-Honored One’s śarīras that belongs to me. However, I pray that you will grant me the remaining charcoal and embers, so that I may erect a stūpa at the site of Pipphala to make offerings."
At that time, there were eight stupas for the relics of the World-Honored One in Jambudvīpa; the ninth was the stupa for the [gold] vessel, and the tenth was the stupa for the charcoal.

In total, the Tathāgata’s relics amounted to one *shuo* and six *dou*, which were divided into eight portions. Seven portions remained in Jambudvīpa, while the fourth portion, obtained at the site of Āluma, was enshrined and venerated within a dragon palace.
Furthermore, the Buddha has four sets of tooth-relics:
one is in the abode of Śakra Devendra;
one is in the kingdom of Gandhāra.
One was in the kingdom of Kaliṅga;
one was in the palace of the Nāga King Sāgara at the village of Ārāmavatī. Stūpas were erected for each to be venerated.

At that time, King Aśoka of the city of Pāṭaliputra opened the seven stūpas and took their relics, extensively establishing eighty-four thousand sacred stūpas throughout Jambudvīpa to be universally venerated.

Adorned by the majestic power of this stūpa, the world is graced; devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, spirits, and others all pay it homage, revere it, and make offerings to it. It causes the True Dharma to shine forth and not perish, and whatever aspirations one may have will be fulfilled without exception.

The following is the account of the First Council of Five Hundred held at Rājagṛha. At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata was born into the Śākya clan; he attained perfect enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha, turned the sublime Wheel of Dharma in Vārāṇasī, and entered parinirvāṇa in the city of Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas.

The Venerable Śāriputra entered parinirvāṇa together with a great assembly of eighty thousand bhikṣus; the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana also entered parinirvāṇa together with seventy thousand bhikṣus; and the World-Honored One likewise attained parinirvāṇa together with eighteen thousand bhikṣus.

At that time, there were devas of long life who had lived through many kalpas; seeing the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they were filled with sorrow and grief. Furthermore, seeing that all the noble ones had likewise passed into extinction, they gave rise to this censure:
"The Sūtras, Vinaya, and Mātṛkās—the true and authentic treasury of the Dharma—taught by the World-Honored One have not been compiled. Will you not allow the True Teaching to be reduced to ashes?"
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, knowing the intention of those devas, addressed the bhikṣus: "You should know!

The Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, each accompanied by a great multitude of bhikṣus, being unable to bear seeing the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa, have both already passed into parinirvāṇa before him."
Now, the World-Honored One has further entered parinirvāṇa together with eighteen thousand bhikṣus.
Thereupon, the devas of immeasurable kalpas who possess long lifespans all gave rise to lamentation and reproach, saying:
"Why have you not compiled the Three Baskets of the Noble Teachings? Will you allow the Tathāgata’s profound and wondrous Dharma to be reduced to ashes?"
They all replied, “We shall inform one another that we should convene a council; this is a matter of great importance.
The assembly all said, “Excellent!”
"We shall do as you say. Then Kāśyapa addressed the Saṃgha, saying:
"Who among this assembly is the youngest?"
He replied, "The Venerable Pūrṇa. Then Mahākāśyapa said:
“Pūrṇa! Strike the *gandī* and assemble the entire Saṃgha.
Having heard this, Pūrṇa entered the fourth dhyāna in a secluded place and, by the power of his meditative concentration, focused his mindfulness and engaged in contemplation.

Having completed his observation, he arose from meditative concentration and struck the *gandi* bell; then four hundred and ninety-nine great Arhats arrived from various directions, gathered like clouds at this place, and took their seats.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa said:
"Have all the venerable bhikṣu-saṃgha gathered?
Examine carefully who has not yet assembled."
Then all the bhikṣus surveyed everywhere and said to Mahākāśyapa, “The bhikṣus from all directions have all assembled; only the Venerable Gavāmpati has not yet arrived.”
At that time, the bhikṣu Go-pāla was dwelling in seclusion within the Śirīṣa Palace. Mahākāśyapa said to Pūrṇa:
"You should now go to where the venerable Go-pāla resides and speak these words to him:
'The community of bhikṣus, with Mahākāśyapa as their leader, sends word to ask whether the Venerable One is free from illness.'"
“There is business for the Saṃgha; you should come quickly.

Having heard this, Pūrṇa entered a profound meditative absorption. By the power of that concentration, he vanished from the city of Kuśinagara and emerged in the Śirīṣa Palace. He approached the Venerable One, prostrated at his feet, and said to him:
“The community of bhikṣus, with Mahākāśyapa as their leader, sends word: ‘May you be free from illness,’ and they speak thus:”
“There is business for the Saṃgha; you should come quickly.
Although the Venerable One was free from all desires, he still possessed the habitual tendencies of attachment, and so he said to Pūrṇa:
“Welcome, O Āyuṣmat!”
Could it be that the Great Master, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, has departed for another realm due to his karmic conditions?
Or is there some dispute among the Saṃgha?
Or have the various non-Buddhists given rise to slander against the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata?
Furthermore, do non-Buddhists and others gather their followers to create obstacles for my Tathāgata’s śrāvaka disciples?
Or do the various disciples of the Tathāgata not have their afflictions increase and treat one another with contempt?
Are there not śramaṇas or brahmins who go against the Buddha’s teaching?
Are there not foolish people who will cause a schism in the Saṃgha?
Is there no person of evil views who, by means of words resembling the Dharma, will delude and confuse the Tathāgata’s true and authentic Dharma?

Do you not have many fellow practitioners of the holy life who abandon the superior activities of recitation, study, and meditative reflection, instead delighting in worldly talk that is of no benefit?

Furthermore, do you not harbor doubts or hesitation regarding two paths—speaking what is not Dharma as Dharma, or speaking Dharma as not Dharma; speaking what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, or speaking Vinaya as not Vinaya?

Is it not the case that some bhikṣus are disturbed by the defilement of stinginess and greed, turning their backs on the six dharmas of harmonious respect, and failing to show mutual affection when seeing guests arrive or fellow practitioners of the holy life?
Is there no bhikṣu of evil character who would cause faithful laymen and brahmins to turn their backs on the Buddha’s True Dharma and return to external paths?

Is there no bhikṣu who practices wrong livelihoods such as plowing fields or engaging in trade, who serves kings with flattery and crookedness, who divines fortune and misfortune, and who accumulates impure wealth for as long as he lives?
Is there not a bhikṣu who, regarding the practice of *dhūta* austerities and the use of inferior bedding, gives rise to feelings of aversion and contempt?
Is there not one who, though not truly a śramaṇa, claims to be a śramaṇa, and causes disturbance and harassment among those of like religious life?

"Since you, Pūrṇa, have come here from afar, you should say that the Great Virtuous World-Honored One is at ease and free from ailment; yet you address Kāśyapa as the leader—is it not because the Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One has abandoned all sentient beings and entered forever into the realm of great *nirvāṇa* without remainder?"
"Is it not that the world has lost its helmsman and is seized by terror?
Has the One Possessing the Ten Powers and Fearlessness been swallowed by the ghost of impermanence?
Has the one capable of awakening all sentient beings for their benefit fallen into sleep and failed to wake?"
Could it be that the sun of the Buddha’s radiance has set?
Could it be that the full moon of the Tathāgata has been obscured by the enemy asuras, its light hidden from view?

Could it be that the most honored Great Teacher of the trichiliocosm, the supreme wish-fulfilling tree adorned with the flowers of the factors of enlightenment and fragrant with the lovely scent of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, has been broken down by the mad elephant of impermanence?
"Is it not that the Tathāgata’s lamp of wisdom has been blown out by the wind of ignorance?
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa, having heard these words, spoke this verse:
"The assembly of śrāvakas has gathered, Their wisdom is all fierce and sharp;..."
To ensure that the Dharma remains for a long time, we rely solely upon the Venerable One.
The ship of the Buddha’s teachings has already sunk, and the mountain of wisdom has crumbled;
the Master’s most excellent assembly all desire to return to true tranquility.
"I only pray that you will go there quickly to join in the binding of the World-Honored One’s teaching;
this is a great matter, not a trivial one, and it is for this reason that I have been sent to summon you.
At that time, the Venerable Gopiśāla said to Pūrṇa:
"Cease your speech," he said,
and replied with a verse:
"If the Unsurpassed Lamp of Wisdom remains in the world, I vow to go there to pay homage to the Honored One's countenance."
Now that my conditions have ended and I enter nirvana, what wise person could possibly go there?
You should now take my three robes and bowl and offer them to that great assembly of those worthy of offerings;
as for me, I now enter stillness and shall not be born again—only I pray that your holy compassion will grant me full forgiveness.

Having spoken these words, he immediately rose from his seat, ascended into the air, and manifested the eighteen transformations while emitting various rays of light. He transformed himself into fire to cremate his own body and attained parinirvāṇa; thereupon, four streams of water flowed forth from within his body.
The first water spoke this verse:
"Our merit and virtue are exhausted; Now, suddenly, we have encountered abandonment.
The Sun of Wisdom in the world has already hidden its radiance; All the deluded multitudes have no one to save them."
The second water spoke this verse:
"All conditioned phenomena perish in an instant; From birth until their end, they all return to suffering.
This is merely the false conceptualization of ordinary beings; Both an agent and a recipient are entirely non-existent."
The third water spoke this verse:
"The wise person’s mind is always free from negligence, Swiftly cultivating and perfecting all wholesome dharmas;
Yet beauty, youth, and life alike perish, Constantly devoured by impermanence."
The fourth water spoke this verse:
"I now bow my head to the Buddha’s disciple, who has accomplished all that was to be done;
out of reverence for the Great Teacher, he enters parinirvāṇa, like a young calf following the departure of the bull king."

At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa, having made offerings to the bodily relics of the Cowherd, took his robes and bowl and entered a profound meditative absorption. He vanished from the Śrīṣa palace and appeared at the Twin Trees in the city of Kuśinagara. Having approached Mahākāśyapa and the five hundred bhikṣus and paid them due respect as was appropriate, he placed his robes and bowl before the Elder.
He spoke in verse:
"Having heard that the Holy Lord has entered parinirvāṇa, all his meritorious deeds have followed him as well;
here are his robe and bowl which I have brought, and I only pray that the Saṃgha will grant me their forgiveness."
At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"O fellow practitioners of the holy life, listen all of you well.
He then spoke these verses:
"He has followed the noble teaching and his body has perished; The remaining Arhats are mostly in nirvana.
The present Saṃgha is united with one mind; For the sake of humans and devas, you should perform the compilation."
Then Kāśyapa again exhorted the great assembly to remain firm in their resolve and not enter *parinirvāṇa*, speaking these verses:
"O virtuous ones, do not follow the example of that cowherd, Who entered final extinction within the palace of Śrīṣa;
You should not hastily pass into *parinirvāṇa*; You ought instead to perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings."
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, together with five hundred bhikṣus, established a formal agreement, saying:
"All you people, listen to what I say! Since the Sun of the Buddha has set, I fear the Dharma will likewise perish. We now wish to assemble together to compile the treasury of the Dharma."

Those people, having recently lost their Great Teacher, were each filled with grief and distress; if they were to hold the council right here, the monastic communities from the four directions would come and cause a commotion, and since their minds would be unsettled, the task could not be successfully accomplished.

However, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree in the kingdom of Magadha; now that his Dharma-body has passed away, we should proceed there to hold the council.
Some said, "Excellent! Others said:
"We should go to the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Then Mahākāśyapa addressed the assembly, saying:

"The King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī in the kingdom of Magadha, has recently conceived faith; he is able to provide the four requisites for sustaining the body to the Great Assembly so that they lack for nothing. We ought to convene the council with him as our patron."
At that time, the entire great assembly all acclaimed it as excellent.
Furthermore, some said:
"All of us have fully realized the fruit of Arhatship; Ānanda alone remains at the stage of a learner."

Furthermore, this venerable one served as the personal attendant to the Blessed One during his lifetime and was able to receive and uphold the entire treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma; yet, since his fruit has not yet been fully perfected, what is to be done?

Kāśyapa said: "If it is to be done in this way, I fear that other disciples may feel resentment; therefore, as a skillful means, you should appoint Ānanda to be the one who distributes the water, while the others go themselves."
The great assembly replied,
“Excellent! Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, standing before the assembly, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Are you able to serve as the water-distributor for the community? He replied,
"I am able."
Then Kāśyapa performed the formal procedure of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to appoint him:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This venerable Bhikṣu Ānanda has personally attended upon the Buddha and is fully capable of receiving and upholding the entire treasury of the Dharma."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that the monk Ānanda be appointed to provide service for the community of monks as a water-distributor.
The motion is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This venerable bhikṣu Ānanda has long served the Buddha in close attendance and is fully capable of receiving and upholding the entire treasury of the Dharma. The Saṃgha now appoints Ānanda to distribute water for the assembly."
"If the Venerable Ones consent to Ānanda serving water for the assembly, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.
"The Saṃgha has already appointed the Venerable Ānanda to serve water for the assembly. The Saṃgha has given its consent, as indicated by their silence. Thus do I now uphold this."
Then Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda, "You and the great assembly should travel among the people and proceed to that land of Magadha; I shall take the direct route and depart."
At that time, Ānanda traveled together with the assembly toward Rājagṛha.

Kāśyapa arrived there first. King Ajātaśatru had deep faith in the Buddha; whenever he saw the Buddha from afar while riding an elephant, he would throw himself down to the ground, yet by the Buddha’s majestic power, his body remained unhurt.
As the king rode upon his great elephant, he saw Kāśyapa from afar; remembering the Tathāgata, he immediately threw himself down.
At that moment, the Venerable One, through his supernormal power, supported him so that no harm was done, and said:
"Great King, you should know!"
The Tathāgata, the Great Teacher, always dwells in meditative concentration, whereas his śrāvaka disciples are not so.

If they do not maintain mindfulness and observe, they will not know what occurred previously; thus, there may be instances where they observe and instances where they do not. For this reason, I now establish a regulation together with the King.
"If you see a śrāvaka disciple of the Tathāgata, O King, when you are riding an elephant or horse, you should not hastily cast down your body; you ought to preserve and protect yourself.
The King said, "I shall follow the Venerable One's instruction."
"Venerable One, you should know that if the Buddha were still in the world, I would personally make offerings to him; now that he has entered parinirvāṇa, where can I express my reverence?
You, sir, are the World-Honored One whom I revere."
"Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s teachings have all been entrusted to you.
Having said this, he addressed the great minister:
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa, please provide the four types of requisites so that there is no lack.
The Venerable replied,
"Great King, you should know this!"

The Buddha realized Great Enlightenment in this country and attained the perfection of the Dharmakāya; now, having erected the Dharma-banner at the King’s court and compiled the Tripiṭaka, the great assembly of bhikṣus has arrived together on the road.
The king said,
"Excellent! Whatever the noble assembly requires, I shall provide it all."

At that time, before long, the assembly of noble ones was about to arrive at the great city of Rājagṛha. When the king heard they were approaching, he issued a command to his ministers and to all the people, both high and low, from near and far, to adorn the city walls and sweep the streets, and to prepare exquisite flowers, incense, precious banners, flags, and canopies, as well as hundreds of thousands of kinds of musical performances.
The king, along with the queen, the crown prince, the ladies of the inner palace, and the people of the kingdom, all went out of the city to welcome the assembly of noble ones.

Once they had entered the city and the great multitude was seated, the king paid his respects before the presiding elder; joining his palms and kneeling for a long time, he addressed the Venerable Kāśyapa, saying:
"Today the noble assembly has all come here to bring great benefit to all sentient beings; whatever they require, I shall provide."
"I do not know at what location it would be appropriate to arrange the assembly for the Council.
At that time, the Venerable One replied:
"If the Council were held here in the Bamboo Grove of this city, monks from various places would come and create such a commotion that there might be interference and disruption."
“If we go to Vulture Peak Mountain, it will not be peaceful; however, the foot of the Pipphala Cave is suitable for the council, though there are no bedding materials there.
Upon hearing these words, the King was deeply filled with joy and replied to Kāśyapa:
“If the council is indeed held at that place, I shall provide whatever bedding and requisites are required.”
Then Kāśyapa addressed the great assembly, saying:

"Now this Great King, for the sake of the noble assembly, has prepared at the site of the Piṇḍola Cave where the council is to be held; whatever may be required shall be provided so that there is no lack. You, members of the great assembly, should proceed there."

The King said to Kāśyapa, “When the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, he did not inform me. I only pray that the Venerable One will remain long in this world; should you eventually pass into parinirvāṇa, I beseech you to grant me prior notice.”
At that time, Kāśyapa silently gave his consent.
Then the Venerable One thought further:
"During the first half of the summer retreat, I shall have the dwellings and bedding repaired; when the second half of the summer arrives, I shall convene the council."
The Venerable One then examined Ānanda’s mind and said to the Venerable Aniruddha:

"In this great assembly praised by the Blessed One, who among those still in training possesses passion, hatred, and delusion, and being possessed of craving and grasping, has not yet accomplished what was to be done?"

Then Āniruddha entered the fourth dhyāna and surveyed the assembly; he saw that only the Venerable Ānanda remained on the stage of training, still bound by all the afflictions, with his task yet unfinished.
Having observed this, he addressed Kāśyapa, saying:

"Venerable One, you should know that these great śrāvakas are all pure and free from any corruption; they are exclusively steadfast and endowed with great merit, having accomplished what was to be done, and are worthy of receiving the most supreme offerings of devas and humans."
"Only Ānanda alone remains on the stage of training; he is still bound by all afflictions and has not yet accomplished his task.
At that time, Kāśyapa immediately observed:
"Is this Ānanda to be tamed through consolation?"
"Should he be subdued through censure?
Seeing that he could only be subdued by words of censure, [the Buddha] immediately called Ānanda amidst the assembly:
"You should go out!"
"Now this distinguished assembly should not perform the compilation together with such as you.
When Ānanda heard these words, they pierced his heart like an arrow; his entire body trembled with fear, and he said: "Venerable Kāśyapa!"

Let this matter rest; I pray you will grant me your forgiveness. I have not violated the precepts, nor my views, nor my dignified demeanor, nor my right livelihood, nor have I committed any transgression against the Saṃgha. Why, then, am I suddenly being expelled?
The Venerable replied:
"You have served the Buddha as his personal attendant; how can it be considered a marvel that you have violated your views, precepts, dignified conduct, and right livelihood?
As for your claim that you have committed no offense against the Saṅgha, rise and take up a tally; I shall expose your transgressions so that you may know them for yourself."
Then Ānanda rose from his seat; as he arose, the trichiliocosm shook in three ways:
namely, a slight tremor, a moderate tremor, and a great tremor;
a slight quaking, a moderate quaking, and a great quaking.
With slight, moderate, and great trembling, all the devas in the void opened their eyes, raised their voices, and spoke these words: "Alas!..."
The Great Kāśyapa was able to obtain such true words of mantra; yet this Ānanda, though remaining close to the World-Honored One, immediately uttered such bitter words of reproach to reprimand him.
Then Kāśyapa said to Ānanda: "You say, 'I have committed no offense against the Saṃgha';
how then can you claim to be free from fault regarding the Saṃgha?"
"You know that the World-Honored One does not permit women to leave the household life, as they are by nature prone to arrogance and deceit.
As the Buddha has said: 'Ānanda!'"
Do not request for women to go forth or receive full ordination. Why is this?
