If women were allowed to go forth within my Dharma, the Dharma would not endure for long; it would be like a fine rice field damaged by frost and hail, resulting in no grain at all.
"Thus it is, Ānanda!
If women were permitted to go forth, the Dharma would surely decline and could not endure for long.
Since you requested that the Buddha ordain them, is this not a transgression?"
Ānanda said, "Venerable Sir, please desist! You should grant me your forgiveness;

it was not out of any other motive that I requested the ordination of women. However, Mahāprajāpatī is the Buddha’s maternal aunt, and Queen Māyā passed away seven days after giving birth to the Buddha."
The Lord of the World personally nourished me with his milk; since there is such profound kindness, how could I not repay it?
Furthermore, I have heard that all Buddhas of the past had the fourfold assembly, and I hope that the Buddha will be the same as them.
"First, to repay his profound kindness; second, out of concern for our clan. For these reasons, I requested the Buddha to ordain these women.
I pray that you will forgive this transgression. Kāśyapa replied, "Ānanda!"

This is not an act of gratitude, but rather the destruction of the very body of the True Dharma; it is like bringing down a great frost and hail upon the field of the Buddha, whereby you have caused only a small remnant to remain of the True Dharma that was destined to abide in the world for a full thousand years.
Furthermore, as for the claim that one should contemplate one’s lineage, this too is irrational; those who have left the household life have forever renounced kinship and affection.

Moreover, regarding the claim, "I have heard that all Buddhas of the past had the fourfold assembly, and I hope to be like them," in times of yore people were all possessed of few desires, and their attachment, aversion, delusion, and other afflictions were entirely slight; thus they were fit to leave the household life, but now it is not so.
"The World-Honored One did not grant permission; yet you pressed him with such persistence that you caused the Buddha to grant it.
This is your first fault. Cast down one tally.
"Furthermore, Ānanda, there is another fault: [you have]..."

Furthermore, suppose there were someone who, having extensively cultivated the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), desired to remain in the world for an eon or more than an eon; yet you did not, on behalf of sentient beings, entreat the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to remain in the world for an eon.
He replied, "Venerable One!
I had no other thought; at that moment, I was obscured by Māra."

He replied: "This is a great transgression; how could it be possible? The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has long since exhausted all habitual tendencies, yet he is being obstructed by Māra Pāpīyas—this is the second transgression; cast down one tally."
“You have another fault: while the World-Honored One was alive, he spoke a parable, yet you explained the matter differently in his very presence. This is the third fault; cast down a tally.”
"You have another fault: the World-Honored One once gave you a robe of golden-yellow hue to wash, yet you stepped on it and wrung it out; is this not a fault?"
Ānanda said, "There was no one else present; therefore, my treading upon it was not out of arrogance.
The Venerable One said:
"If there is no one there, why not throw it upward?
The devas in the void will surely assist you.
This is the fourth fault; you may place another tally down."
"You have another fault: when the World-Honored One was about to proceed to the twin trees for his parinirvāṇa and required water for thirst, you offered him turbid water; is this not a fault?"
Ānanda said, "When I was fetching water, it happened that five hundred wagons were crossing the Kakutthā River; there was no clear water to be found, so this was not my fault."
He replied: "This was your fault.

At that time, why did you not turn your bowl upward toward the sky? Then the devas would have spontaneously poured the water of eight virtues into your bowl. This is your fifth fault; you may set down another tally."
“Furthermore, you have committed another fault. As the World-Honored One has said:

‘I shall cause the bhikṣus to recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half-month; regarding all the minor and lesser precepts therein, I wish to set them aside so that the Saṃgha of bhikṣus may dwell in peace and happiness.’”
Since you did not ask,
"I do not yet know what among these is called a minor-minor precept," there is now no opportunity for inquiry; how should this be understood?

For now, let us speak of the four *pārājika* dharmas, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas, the two *aniyata* dharmas, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas, the ninety *pāyattika* dharmas, the four *prātideśanīya* dharmas, and the numerous *śaikṣa* dharmas; apart from these, they are called the minor and lesser precepts (*kṣudrānukṣudra-śikṣāpada*).
Some say: "From the four *pārājika* offenses down to the four *pratisaṃyukta-dharma*, the remainder are called the minor and very minor precepts (*khuddānukhuddaka-sikkhāpada*). Others say:
"From the four *pārājika* offenses down to the ninety *pāyantika* offenses, the remainder are called minor and very minor.
Some say: "From the first [offense] down to the thirtieth, the remainder are called minor and very minor."
Some say: "From the first [offense] up to the two indeterminate offenses, the remainder are called minor and very minor. Others say:
"Only four are defeats; the rest are called minor and very minor.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know at all which were the minor and very minor [offenses].
During this interval, the non-Buddhists heard of this and, seizing the opportunity, spoke as follows:

"The śramaṇa Gautama has established very strict boundaries; while he was alive, his teachings were practiced in their entirety by his śrāvaka disciples, but upon his passing and after his body was consumed by fire, the teachings will perish accordingly. As for all the prohibitions and precepts, those who like them will retain them, while those who do not like them will abandon them, and most will fail to practice them."
"Why did you not inquire of the World-Honored One on behalf of future sentient beings?
For this reason, you shall incur the offense of subsequent regret. Ānanda replied:
"Venerable Sir!
It was not that I lacked the intention to ask; rather, at that time, being separated from the Tathāgata caused me such great sorrow and suffering. He replied:

"This too is a fault. You have personally attended upon the Buddha; how could you not know that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, yet give rise to grief and distress? This constitutes a great error. This is the sixth fault; you may set down another tally."
“You have another transgression: in the midst of the lay assembly, before the women, you manifested the Buddha’s mark of the concealed male organ.
He replied, “Venerable Sir!”

I have no other thought; for all women, the feverish affliction of intense lustful passion binds us, but if we were to see the Blessed One’s mark of the concealed organ, that lustful passion would immediately cease.
The Venerable One said:

"Since you lack the supernormal knowledge of others' minds and the eye of wisdom, how could you know that when women see the Buddha’s hidden organ, their lustful defilements are immediately extinguished?
This is the seventh fault; you may set down another tally."

“Furthermore, you have committed a transgression: you arbitrarily revealed the Buddha’s golden-hued body to the women. Upon seeing the Buddha’s body, they immediately shed tears that defiled the venerable form; this is your fault.”
Ānanda said: "It is not that I am shameless; rather, I thought this:
'If there are sentient beings who behold the World-Honored One’s wondrously colored body, they will all exclaim:'"
“May my own body become exactly like that of the Buddha.
Kāśyapa said: “Since you lack the wisdom-eye of knowing others' minds, how could you know that sentient beings have made such a vow?”
This is your eighth fault; you may cast another tally.
Furthermore, it is improper for you, who have not yet abandoned desire, to remain within this assembly of those who have abandoned desire.
"You should rise and depart; you are not fit to participate in the compilation of the scriptures with this most excellent assembly of noble ones.

When the Venerable Ānanda had been thus interrogated by the Venerable Mahākāśyapa regarding the eight matters of his minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*), he looked around in all four directions and, filled with sorrow and lamentation, spoke these words:
"Alas, how bitter! Alas, what suffering!"
"How have I come to this? Having newly been separated from the Tathāgata, without refuge or protector, and having lost the Great Radiance, whom shall I address?
While the Venerable Kāśyapa was interrogating that offender, the devas in the sky uttered cries of lamentation and said to one another:
"Great Seer, you should know!"

"The hosts of devas increase while the asuras diminish; the True Dharma of the World-Honored One will surely abide for a long time. This Great Śrāvaka is close to the Buddha on the path; he interrogated that Venerable One with eight matters. As this Great Śrāvaka’s virtue is second only to the Buddha, I therefore know that the Buddha-Dharma shall not perish."
Then Ānanda again addressed the Venerable One, saying:
"Venerable Sir, please desist!
I pray you grant me joy; I shall speak of my transgression according to the Dharma and dare not commit it again."
However, when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was on the verge of entering parinirvāṇa, he spoke these words: "Ānanda!
After my parinirvāṇa, do not be distressed, sorrowful, or wail and weep; I now entrust you to Mahākāśyapa."
"How could it be that the Venerable One, seeing my slight transgression, would not tolerate it? I pray you grant me joy so that I may uphold the Great Master’s teaching.
Kāśyapa said, "Do not weep!
"Since the wholesome dharmas have increased through you and not diminished, we must compile the entire holy teaching of the Tathāgata.
You should now depart from this assembly of noble ones; you ought not to participate in the compilation together with us."
Then the Venerable Aniruddha said to the Venerable Kāśyapa,
“Without Ānanda, how shall we perform the compilation?”

He replied: “Although this Ānanda is endowed with manifold virtues, he has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire, hatred, and delusion; being still a learner (śaikṣa) with further work to do, he cannot participate in the compilation together with us.”
Then Kāśyapa again addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should depart at once!
You must exert yourself in that which you ought to do; having attained the fruit of Arhatship, the assembly may join with you in the compilation."

At that time, Ānanda, feeling deep sorrow and longing at his separation from the Great Master, was further distressed by the reproaches and expulsion he had received; departing from there, he went to the village of Uruvilvā to observe the summer retreat, taking a young boy from the village as his attendant.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda applied himself with extreme diligence and constantly preached the sublime Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
Then the youth thought to himself:
"Has my upādhyāya attained freedom from desire while still on the stage of training?"
"Has he attained freedom from desire as one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
I should now enter into a meditative absorption (samāpatti) to examine his mind.

He immediately entered concentration and saw that the Venerable One’s mind was that of one still in training (śaikṣa) who had attained freedom from desire. Having seen this, he emerged from concentration, went to where the Venerable One was, stood to one side, and spoke these verses:
"Relying on a secluded spot beneath a tree, you should single-mindedly contemplate the palace of Nirvana;
now, Master, be diligent and apply yourself to practice with care, and before long you shall surely return to the path of perfect quiescence."

At that time, having heard the essential meaning spoken by the youth, the Venerable One spent the day either sitting or walking, refining his mind through the practice of the dharmas that counteract the hindrances; during the first watch of the night, whether walking or sitting, he likewise resolutely and purely eliminated those obstructing dharmas.

Then, during the middle watch of the night, he washed his feet and entered his room. He lay down on his right side with one foot upon the other, maintaining the perception of light and the mental application of mindfulness.

While still attending to this intention, before his head had even reached the pillow, he exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), his mind attained liberation, and he realized the fruit of Arhatship, experiencing the bliss of liberation.
He immediately proceeded to Rājagṛha and went to where the great assembly was; when the assembly learned that he had attained the fruit [of Arhatship], they all praised him as a mahāpuruṣa.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, together with five hundred arhats, went to the Pipphalī Cave; once they had assembled, he addressed the great assembly, saying:
"You should know this!"

In future ages, there will be bhikṣus who are dull-witted and distracted; if there were no summary verses (uddāna), they would be unable to recite, chant, or master the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
"Therefore, we should first collect the verses (gāthās) that are relevant to our affairs before the meal, and after the meal, we may collect the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they said to the Venerable One:
"We shall first collect the gāthās now."
Having arrived after the meal, he said:
"Which one should we assemble first?
The Venerable One replied:
"It would be well to first collect the scriptures.
Then, five hundred arhats together requested the Venerable Mahākāśyapa to ascend the lion throne. Once the Venerable had taken his seat, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Venerable friend!..."
"Are you able to discern and compile the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata?
He replied, "I am able."
The Venerable One then made the formal motion:
"May the noble Saṃgha listen!
This venerable Ānanda is capable of discerning and compiling the discourses and Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission that the venerable Ānanda be appointed by the Saṃgha to select and compile the discourses spoken by the Tathāgata.
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This Venerable Ānanda is capable of discerning and compiling the discourses and teachings spoken by the Tathāgata.
The Saṃgha now appoints the Venerable Ānanda for the purpose of discerning and compiling the discourses and teachings spoken by the Tathāgata.
If the Venerable Ones consent to Ānanda’s selection and compilation of the discourses spoken by the Tathāgata, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.

“The Saṅgha has already completed the selection and compilation of the discourses spoken by the Tathāgata for the venerable Ānanda; the Saṅgha has granted its consent, as indicated by its silence. Thus do I now uphold this.”
At that time, as the Venerable Ānanda was about to preach the Dharma, five hundred arhats each spread their saṃghāṭī robes upon their seats.

At that time, Ānanda looked around in all four directions; he gave rise to thoughts of compassion for all sentient beings, felt profound reverence for the True Dharma, and conceived a heart of veneration toward those living the holy life (*brahmacarya*). He circumambulated the high seat to the right, bowed his head in respect, and before the elders, paid homage according to the Dharma while contemplating impermanence. Pressing his hand against the seat, he sat upright with body straight.

Next, he observed the assembly of noble ones, who were like a deep, tranquil, and vast ocean, and then thought to himself: "I have personally heard this sutra from the Buddha’s own lips; whether it was spoken in oral tradition, in the Dragon Palace, or in the heavens, I have received and upheld it all without forgetting. I should now speak it."
At that time, the assembly of devas said to one another:
"Virtuous ones, you should know!
The noble Ānanda is about to proclaim the sūtras and teachings spoken by the Tathāgata; you should listen with a single-minded focus."
At that time, a son of heaven spoke a verse, saying:
“If one can establish the sublime Dharma, Bringing benefit to the trichiliocosm;
The Noble One’s Dharma is fearless, Like the roar of a lion.”
"You, O virtuous ones, should with utmost sincerity listen to the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
those who desire peace and happiness should understand this true meaning.
At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa addressed Ānanda in verse:
"Venerable One, you should now proclaim the Buddha’s words, which are the most supreme among all phenomena;
whatever Dharma the Great Teacher has taught is entirely capable of benefiting sentient beings."

At that time, Ānanda, upon hearing the name of the Great Master, felt a deep sense of longing and devotion; he then turned his head toward the place of parinirvāṇa, joined his palms with utmost sincerity, and spoke these words in a resonant voice:
"Thus have I heard: at one time the Bhagavān was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five bhikṣus, saying:
"This is the noble truth of suffering; by applying correct attention to the Dharma as it has been heard, one can give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening."
"In this regard, the detailed exposition is as in the *Sūtra on the Three Turnings of the Wheel of Dharma* mentioned above.
Then, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya said to Mahākāśyapa: "This subtle and wondrous Dharma was heard directly from the Buddha;

the World-Honored One, out of his great compassion, proclaimed it for my sake. By the power of this sūtra, he has enabled us to dry up the boundless ocean of blood and tears, to transcend the mountain of bones, to close the gates to the evil realms and the Avīci hell, and to well open the path to the celestial palaces and liberation. This was when he spoke this subtle, profound, and wondrous sūtra."
"Having heard this, I have attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, free from all dust and defilements; eighty thousand devas have likewise received benefit.

When these words were spoken, all the devas in the sky and those bhikṣus who had not yet abandoned desire felt such agony as if their hearts were being pierced by a thousand arrows; they wailed and cried out, saying:
"Alas! What suffering!"
"Alas! How bitter!
And he spoke in verse, saying:
"How tragic is this world!"
Impermanence makes no distinction;
it destroys this treasury of jewels and dries up the ocean of merit.
Having personally heard this Dharma of liberation from the Buddha’s presence, I [realize this].
"Now, in another place, they proclaim the words of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, when the great assembly heard this discourse on the sūtra, they all spoke these words:
"Alas! What a calamity!"
"The power of impermanence is great and makes no distinction; it can destroy such an eye of the world.

At that time, Kauṇḍinya immediately rose from his seat and remained crouching. When the other arhats saw this, they all conceived a heart of reverence and likewise rose from their seats, remaining crouching, and spoke these words:
"Alas! What a calamity!"
"The power of impermanence is great! How could we have personally heard the Dharma from the World-Honored One?
Now it is merely a report.
Then he spoke in verse:
“The Honored One among devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits has passed away; for what reason should we not return to tranquility?
With the absence of All-Knowing One, the world is empty; who would consider this life to be superior?”
At that time, all the Arhats entered the fourth dhyāna and, by the power of their vows, surveyed the world. Each arose from meditative concentration and addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Have you come for the sake of the Dharma?"
He replied, "Venerable sir, I have come for the sake of the Dharma."
"Have you venerable ones also come for the sake of the Dharma? They replied, "It is so."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa thought to himself:

"I have already compiled the sūtras first spoken by the Blessed One; they meet with no opposition nor any reproach among my fellow practitioners of the holy life. Therefore, it should be known that these sūtras are the true teaching of the Buddha."
Again, he addressed Ānanda:
"In what other place did the World-Honored One preach the second sutra?
At that time, Ānanda replied with a clear and resonant voice:
“The Blessed One was also in Vārāṇasī. “To whom did he speak? “To the five bhikṣus.”
"What was said? He replied: "It was said as follows:"
“O bhikṣus, you should know that there are four noble truths. What are the four?
They are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin [of suffering], the noble truth of the cessation [of suffering], and the noble truth of the path.”
What is the noble truth of suffering?

It is the suffering of birth, the suffering of illness, the suffering of old age, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
To speak briefly, the suffering of the aggregates within the five destinies is called "suffering.
What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
It is craving that accompanies delight and pleasure, finding delight everywhere; this is called the "origin."
What is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

It refers to the complete cessation, relinquishing, and vomiting out of this craving accompanied by delight, which finds gratification in various places and leads to renewed existence; when such craving and attachment are entirely exhausted, one realizes sublime *nirvāṇa*. This is called the cessation of suffering.
What is the noble truth of the path leading to cessation?
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; this is called the noble truth of the path leading to cessation.

When this Dharma was taught, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya attained liberation of the mind from all afflictions, while the other four bhikṣus were freed from dust and defilement and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Then the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya said to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:

"I personally heard such teachings as these from the Buddha; having heard the Dharma, my mind was liberated from all afflictions, and the other four bhikṣus were freed from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye."

“I have already compiled the second discourse taught by the Blessed One; it is without contradiction among those of the same holy life, nor is it subject to reproach or rejection. Therefore, you should know that this sutra is the true teaching of the Buddha.”
He further addressed Ānanda:
"In what place did the World-Honored One preach the third sutra?
At that time, Ānanda replied with a clear and resonant voice:
“The World-Honored One was also at Vārāṇasī.
“To whom did he speak? “To the five bhikṣus.”
"What was said? He replied, "It was spoken thus: 'Thus have I heard.'"
"At one time the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park of the Benefactor of Sages. He addressed the five bhikṣus, saying:
'You bhikṣus, you should know this!
Form is not the self.'"
If form were the self, then form should not become ill or experience suffering and affliction.
One might wish, "May my form be thus," or "May my form not be thus"; yet since it does not follow one's wishes, one should know that form is not the self.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
The detailed account is as previously stated.
The Buddha addressed the five bhikṣus, saying: "What do you think?"
"Is form permanent or is it impermanent? He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"Form is impermanent.

The Buddha said, "Since form is impermanent, it is suffering—whether it be the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, or the suffering of conditioned formations. Yet, do my many-hearing disciples cling to the existence of a self?"
"Is form itself the self? Do I possess forms? Do forms belong to me? Or do I dwell within forms?
"No, World-Honored One."

“In this way, you should know that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise both permanent and impermanent. Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; superior or inferior; far or near—all of it is entirely without self.”

"O bhikṣus, you should skillfully observe with right wisdom; all such feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—whether past, future, or present—should all be observed with right wisdom as previously described."

If my noble disciples, the śrāvakas, contemplate these five aggregates of clinging and know that there is no self nor anything belonging to a self, having contemplated thus, they then know the world as being without a grasper or a grasped, and neither subject to transformation.
"By means of self-awakening alone, I have realized nirvana; my births are ended, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.
When he spoke this Dharma, the minds of the five bhikṣus and the others were liberated from all afflictions.
At that time, all the Arhats had this thought: "We have already compiled the third Sūtra spoken by the World-Honored One;

it is without contradiction among our fellow practitioners of the holy life, nor is there any cause for reproach or aversion. Therefore, you should know that this Sūtra is the true teaching of the Buddha."
He further spoke these words:
"As for the other sūtras and teachings that the World-Honored One may have preached in royal palaces, villages, or cities, Ānanda now recites them all; the Arhats together perform the compilation."
However, those associated with the five aggregates are established by means of the "Chapter on Aggregates.
Those associated with the six sense bases and the eighteen elements are established by means of the "Chapter on Bases and Elements."
If it corresponds to the Noble Truth of Dependent Origination, it is established as being dependent origination itself.
If it is spoken by a Śrāvaka, it is established within the section on the Śrāvakas.
If it is spoken by the Buddha, it is established within the Chapter on the Buddha.

If it is associated with the applications of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, or the path, it is established within the Chapter on the Factors of the Noble Path.
If a sutra is associated with verses (gāthā), it is called the *Saṃyukta Āgama*—the older term "Za" (Miscellaneous) captures its meaning.
If a sutra is taught in extended detail, it is called the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
If the sūtras are taught according to their middling length, these are called the *Madhyama Āgama*.
If the sūtras teach matters consisting of one sentence, two sentences, and so on up to ten sentences, these are called the *Ekottara Āgama*.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda, "There are only as many Āgama sūtras as these; there are no others."
Having spoken thus, he descended from his high seat.
At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa addressed the great assembly, saying:
"You should know this!"
"The Sūtras spoken by the Blessed One have already been compiled together; it is now time to compile the Vinaya.
Having heard these words, they all said, "Excellent!"

At that time, among the assembly, there was only the Venerable Upāli, who was extremely well-versed in the origins of the Vinaya. Kāśyapa then ascended the high seat and addressed the great assembly, saying:
"You should all know this!"
The Venerable Upāli was thoroughly proficient in the Vinaya;
the Blessed One declared him to be "the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya."
"Therefore, I request that you convene a council to compile the Vinaya.
The Great Assembly replied:
"Excellent."
At that time, Kāśyapa said to Upāli,
"Venerable one!
Are you capable of discerning and compiling the Vinaya spoken by the Tathāgata?"
He replied, “I can.
The Venerable One then made the formal motion (jñapti):
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This venerable Upāli is capable of discerning and compiling the Vinaya spoken by the Tathāgata.
If the Saṃgha deems the time right and grants its consent, the Saṃgha should authorize the appointment of the venerable Upāli to discern and compile the Vinaya spoken by the Tathāgata.”
"The motion is thus announced.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) was performed according to the preceding announcement.
At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa, having completed the *karmavācanā*, descended from his seat, and Upāli immediately ascended the lion throne.

Chapter Eight, Section Ten: The Sixth Verse Summary of the Remaining Five Hundred and the Events of the Seven Hundred Councils. At that time, Kāśyapa said to Upāli:
"In what place did the World-Honored One establish the first rule of training?"
Upāli replied with a clear voice:
"The Blessed One was at Vārāṇasī. [The King asked:
"To whom was this spoken?"
“It was the five bhikṣus. “What was the matter? “It was this:
one should train oneself to wear the lower robe (nivāsana) neatly, neither too high nor too low.”
Having spoken these words, all the Arhats together entered the *prāntakoṭika-samādhi*; by the power of their vows, they surveyed the world and then arose from that concentration.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa had this thought:

"I have compiled the first training rule (*śikṣāpada*) spoken by the Blessed One; it is without contradiction among those who practice the holy life, nor is it subject to reproach or rejection. Therefore, you should know that this Vinaya was spoken by the Buddha."
Again he addressed Upāli:
"In what place did the Blessed One proclaim the second training rule?
Then Upāli replied with a clear and resonant voice:
"In Vārāṇasī. "To whom was this spoken? "To the five bhikṣus."
"What is that matter? "It means one should train oneself to wear the three robes in a neat and orderly manner.

Having said these words, all the Arhats entered the meditative concentration of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*); by the power of their vows, they surveyed the world and then arose from that concentration.
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"I have already compiled the second training rule of the Blessed One," as described in detail above.
Again he addressed Upāli:
“In what place did the Blessed One proclaim the third training rule?
Upāli replied with a clear and resonant voice:
"In the village of Kalandaka. "To whom was this spoken?
"It was to the bhikṣu Sūtra, the son of Kalandaka."

"What is that matter? It means that if a bhikṣu who has received the prohibitive precepts engages in sexual intercourse with another bhikṣu, or even with an animal, he incurs a pārājika offense and may not dwell together [with the Saṃgha]."
Having spoken these words, all the Arhats entered the *prāntakoṭika-samādhi*; by the power of their vows, they surveyed the world and then arose from that concentration.
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"I have completed the compilation, as previously described in detail."
Regarding the remaining rules of training (*śikṣāpada*), which the Blessed One had extensively prescribed for the bhikṣus in royal palaces and villages, Upāli recounted them all in full.

Once the Arhats had completed the compilation, they established: "This is called the Pārājika rule; this is called the Saṃghāvaśeṣa rule; these are the two Aniyata rules; the thirty Naiḥsargika-pāyattika rules; the ninety Pāyattika rules; the four Pratideśanīya rules; the numerous Śaikṣa rules; and the seven Adhikaraṇa-śamatha rules. This is the original enactment; this is the subsequent enactment; this is the fixed rule; and this is the subsequent permission."

Thus is the going forth; thus is the full ordination (*upasampadā*); thus are the formal acts consisting of a single motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), and a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*); thus is one fit for ordination and thus is one unfit for ordination; thus is the *poṣadha* ceremony performed; thus is the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) observed; thus are the invitation at the end of the retreat (*pravāraṇā*) and all other matters, even down to miscellaneous affairs—these are the *nidānas*, *muktakas*, and so forth.
Once the Vinaya had been compiled, the Venerable Upāli descended from his high seat.
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"People of future generations will have little wisdom and dull faculties; they will understand by relying on the literal text and fail to penetrate its profound meaning."
"I should now recite a mātṛkā myself, so that the meaning of the Sūtras and Vinaya shall not be lost.
Having formed this thought, he performed the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* and informed the assembly so that they would know.
Once the assembly had granted their permission, he ascended the high seat and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I shall now personally expound the *Mātṛkā*, making all that is of definitive meaning clearly manifest."
That is to say:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;

the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, the four dharma-phrases, the absence of contention, the knowledge of aspiration, and the meditative absorptions of the limit, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, as well as the various mixed cultivations of concentration, the correct entry into clear realization, conventional knowledge, śamatha, vipaśyanā, the collection of dharmas, and the aggregates of dharmas—all these together are termed *mātṛkā*.

Having spoken these words, all the Arhats together entered the meditative absorption of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*); having observed in succession, they arose from that concentration, as described in detail previously.
Therefore, you should know:
"This is the Sūtra; this is the Vinaya; this is the Abhidharma"—this is the true teaching of the Buddha.
Having thus compiled them, [he said:]...
At that time, the yakṣas upon the earth all raised their voices and spoke thus:
"Virtuous ones, you should know!
With the noble Mahākāśyapa as the leader, five hundred arhats have gathered together to compile the Noble Teachings of the Tathāgata’s Tripiṭaka."
"By this cause and condition, the hosts of devas will increase and the asuras will diminish.

When the yakṣas dwelling in the air heard these words, they too raised a great cry that reached the Cāturmahārājika, Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahma, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Śuddhāvāsa, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, and Sudarśana heavens; in an instant, the sound ascended to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
All these devas raised their voices and declared:
"The devas flourish and the asuras diminish.
When the five hundred arhats had completed the council, this was known as the Council of Five Hundred.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa spoke in verse:
“O virtuous ones, you have compiled the teachings of the Dharma King, Out of compassion for all living beings.
All his words are immeasurable in extent; Now they have been gathered together without omission.”
"The world is deluded and unable to comprehend this;
I shall act as a bright lamp to remove the cataracts from their eyes. Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa thought again:

“I have already compiled the Noble Teachings of the Tripiṭaka. Now, through the power of meditative concentration, I observe that the Dharma taught by the Blessed One will endure long in the world; whatever was to be done in accordance with the Tathāgata’s instructions has been fully accomplished.”
The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, has shown me the right path; by practicing according to his instructions, I have repaid a small portion of the Buddha’s compassionate grace.
Who could ever fully repay the Tathāgata’s kindness and virtue?

I have compiled all the final instructions left by the World-Honored One, the Great Teacher, for the benefit of sentient beings. Having been parted from the Great Teacher for a long time, I no longer have anyone to rely upon; this foul body of the five aggregates is weary from its burdens, and as the time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived, it is not fitting for me to remain much longer.
Having formed this thought, he spoke in verse:
“I have compiled the teachings of the Muni, so that the True Dharma may increase;
May it long abide for the benefit of the world, Bringing welfare to sentient beings and freeing them from all delusions.”
Those devoid of shame have been subdued; those possessing a sense of shame and remorse are all gathered under my care.
Having completed all beneficial deeds, it is now fitting for me to enter parinirvāṇa.
Then Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda: "Do you know this?
The World-Honored One entrusted his teachings to me before entering parinirvāṇa; now I, in turn, wish to enter parinirvāṇa and entrust these teachings to you. You must preserve and uphold them well."
He spoke again, saying:

"After my parinirvāṇa, there shall be the wife of a merchant chief in the city of Rājagṛha who will give birth to a son. At the time of his birth, he shall emerge wrapped in a śāṇaka garment; for this reason, he shall be named Śāṇaka. This is a type of hemp not previously known in this land, which people of high status and others can weave into cloth."

The former name "Śāṇakavāsin" is an error. Later, having entered the sea to seek various precious goods and returned safely, he established the Five-Year Great Assembly (pañcavārṣika) within the Buddhist community; he was then permitted to go forth as a monk, and all the teachings of the Buddha were entrusted to him.
Having spoken these words, Kāśyapa again thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One, who practiced all manner of ascetic austerities out of great compassion, is my true and virtuous friend. Adorned with immeasurable merits, wherever his physical relics remain, I shall now respectfully make offerings to them all before entering nirvana."

Having formed this thought, he used his supernormal powers to go to the four great caityas—namely, the place of birth, the place of attaining enlightenment, the place of turning the wheel of Dharma, and the place of parinirvāṇa—as well as other sites containing śarīra relics, where he made offerings with the utmost sincerity.
Having entered the dragon palace and made offerings to the Buddha’s tooth relic, he ascended into the air and proceeded to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, desiring to pay homage to the Buddha’s tooth relic.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the other devas, seeing Kāśyapa bowing in respectful prostration, asked him:
"For what reason have you come here?"
The Venerable replied,
"I wish to make my final offering to the stupa containing the tooth-relics of the World-Honored One.
When the devas heard these final words, they were filled with grief and remained silent.

At that time, Śakra took the Buddha’s tooth and gave it to Kāśyapa. The Venerable One received the tooth, placed it in the palm of his hand, gazed at it without blinking, and then set it upon the crown of his head.

Furthermore, he scattered mandārava flowers, various lotuses, and powdered gośīrṣa sandalwood upon the elephant’s tusks as an offering; having briefly expounded the Dharma for Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the other devas, he vanished from the summit of Mount Sumeru and reappeared in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa again thought to himself:
"I have already previously promised King Ajātaśatru that I would inform him when the time for my parinirvāṇa arrives.
Having had this thought, he went to the royal palace and said to the gatekeeper:
"Announce to the King for me, saying:
'Kāśyapa is now at the gate and wishes to see the Great King.
When the gatekeeper heard these words, he entered the palace; having reached the presence of the King, he found that the King was asleep. He immediately returned and reported to Kāśyapa, saying:
"Noble one! The Great King is currently asleep.
The Venerable replied:
"You should go once more and awaken the King for me.
The gatekeeper replied, "The King's nature is violent and cruel; he is difficult to approach."
"I do not dare now, for I fear the King will reprimand me in anger or execute me.
Kāśyapa told him, "If that is the case,
wait until after the King has awakened and inform me of it."
“Mahākāśyapa, desiring to enter parinirvāṇa, has come to the king’s gate to take his leave of the king.
Having spoken these words, he proceeded to Mount Kukkuṭapāda, where he spread grass within the three peaks and sat down, thinking thus:
“I should now use the rag-robe bestowed upon me by the World-Honored One to cover my body, so that it remains until Maitreya descends to be born.”
"That Bhagavān, by means of this body of mine, has shown it to all his disciples and the great assembly to inspire in them a sense of weary detachment.
He then entered meditative absorption, covering his body with three peaks so that he remained as if in a sealed chamber, unbroken.
He further thought:
"If King Ajātaśatru comes here, the mountain shall open for him.
If the king does not see my body, he will vomit hot blood and die."
Having reflected thus, he entered meditative absorption and relinquished his life-force (*āyur-saṃskāra*).
At that moment, the great earth shook in six ways; meteors fell, all directions blazed with flames, and the gods in the sky beat their drums.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa leaped into the air and manifested various supernatural transformations: he emitted clear water or released flames of fire, and caused dense clouds to rise everywhere, pouring down heavy rain.

Having performed these deeds, he entered the stone chamber and lay down on his right side with one foot叠疊 (repeatedly stacked) upon the other, entering the realm of the wondrous *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
At that time, Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas all had this thought:
"By what cause and condition does the great earth tremble?"

They then observed together and saw that Kāśyapa had entered *nirvāṇa*. Immediately, accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of devas, each holding *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *pāṇḍarīka* lotuses, as well as powdered *gośīrṣa-candana* and aloeswood incense, they all went to the place where the Venerable One’s body lay. With various celestial flowers and exquisite powdered incense, they scattered them over his body as an offering. Having completed the offerings, the three mountains immediately closed together, covering him entirely from above.
At that time, those devas, having been separated from the Venerable One, were overcome with great sorrow and distress, and spoke these words:
"Our grief has not yet subsided since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; why must we now again fall into such lamentation?"
The former residents of the Piṇḍola Cave are now merely empty names, and all their superior dharmas have likewise departed.
The kingdom of Magadha no longer possesses its former splendor; for impoverished sentient beings, the field of merit has been severed, and all wholesome dharmas have utterly perished.

Just as when a second Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, at this very moment the mountain of Dharma will suddenly collapse, the ship of Dharma will capsize and sink, and the tree of Dharma will crumble. The ocean of Dharma will dry up, and the hosts of Māra will rejoice; all the true Dharma that teaches and transforms sentient beings, as well as all beneficial deeds, shall completely vanish.
When those devas had finished uttering such words of lamentation, they prostrated at the Venerable One’s feet and suddenly vanished.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, while asleep, had a dream in which he saw the rafters and beams of his palace collapse; he was suddenly startled awake.

When the gatekeeper saw that the king had awakened from his sleep, he reported in full to the king the words entrusted to him by Kāśyapa; upon hearing these words, the king fainted and fell to the ground.

At that time, his attendants sprinkled clear, cold water on his face, whereupon he regained consciousness. He went to the Bamboo Grove Monastery to see Ānanda, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and wailed and wept while speaking these words:
"I have heard that the Venerable Mahākāśyapa has entered parinirvāṇa."
Then Ānanda went with the king to Mount Kukkuṭapāda—formerly called "Chicken Foot," but later termed "Venerable Foot" because the Venerable One resided there.

Furthermore, there is a footprint of the Buddha on the ridge; however, "Kukkutapāda" (Chicken Foot) and "Gurupāda" (Venerable Foot) are interchangeable in Sanskrit phonology, both indicating the place where the Venerable One resided.

Once he had reached the mountain, the great yakṣas opened the three peaks. Having seen this, the King further beheld the places where the devas were making offerings with *māndārava* flowers, various lotuses, sandalwood, aloeswood, and all kinds of floral perfumes.

At that moment, the king immediately raised his hands and wailed in grief; overcome by despair, he collapsed to the ground like a great tree cut at its roots. After a long while, he finally rose and sought to gather firewood.
Then, having seen this, Ānanda said to him: "Great King,
why are you gathering firewood?"
He replied, “I wish to burn it.
The Venerable One said:
"Do not speak such words.

This Venerable One’s body is sustained by meditative concentration; until the future descent of Maitreya Bodhisattva, he will remain here accompanied by ninety-six koṭis of śrāvakas, and upon his arrival, he will take up the Venerable One’s remains to show them to all the śrāvakas."
He said:
"This Kāśyapa is the foremost disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha; among those who practice the dhūta austerities with few desires and contentment, he is the most preeminent."
"The teachings spoken by Śākyamuni can serve to establish the Eye of Dharma through compilation.
At that time, the śrāvakas will think:
"In past ages, the human body was lowly and small, while the Buddha's body was vast and great."
Then that World-Honored One took up the saṃghāṭī robe of Kāśyapa and showed it to the assembly of śrāvakas, saying:
"This is the saṃghāṭī robe worn by Śākyamuni, the Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha."

At that time, ninety-six koṭis of śrāvakas, having heard these words, immediately realized the fruit of arhatship; they all diligently practiced the conduct of fewness of desires, contentment, and the destruction of taints.
"Therefore, Venerable Sir, this remains of your body are sustained by the power of meditative concentration;
they cannot be consumed by fire, and a stūpa may be constructed over them.
After the king had departed, the three mountains closed back together to cover his body, and a stūpa was built upon them.
The King prostrated at Ānanda’s feet and said,
“Venerable Sir!
I did not witness the Buddha entering parinirvāṇa, nor did I behold the passing away of the Venerable Kāśyapa.”
"If the Noble One enters parinirvāṇa, I shall wish to see him.
The Venerable One granted his consent.
Then, having returned safely from the great ocean and set aside his goods, Śaṇḍaka went to the Bamboo Grove Monastery.
At that time, Ānanda was performing walking meditation (caṅkrama) at the entrance of the Gandhakuṭī. Having seen him, [the merchant] prostrated at his feet and said:
"I have returned safely from the great ocean; this is due to the power of the Triple Gem. I now wish to establish a five-year Dharma assembly to make offerings to the Buddha and the Saṃgha."
"Where is the World-Honored One now? He replied, "My son!"
"The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa.
When Śaṅkhaka heard this, he fainted and fell to the ground; after water was sprinkled on him and he regained consciousness, he asked again:
"Where are the Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and Mahākāśyapa?"
He replied, "They have both already entered parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing this, he was overcome with profound grief and immediately organized a grand five-year festival. Then the Venerable One said:

“Son! Within the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) of the Buddha-dharma, you have already practiced the attraction through material gifts (*āmiṣasaṃgraha*); now you should further perform the practice of attraction through the Dharma (*dharmasaṃgraha*). He replied:
"Venerable One! What are you doing now?
The Venerable replied:
"Son! You may go forth from home to practice within the Buddha's teaching. He replied:
"It shall be done accordingly.
The Venerable One then granted him the going forth and conferred full ordination (*upasampadā*). Once the *karmavācanā* ritual was completed, he made this vow:
"From this day forward until the end of my life, I shall always wear the *śāṇaka* robe."

This bhikṣu was intelligent and possessed the faculty of retention; he grasped it upon hearing it just once. Ānanda had personally received and upheld eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma from the Buddha, and Śaṇavāsa received them all in their entirety, becoming fully endowed with the three types of higher knowledge and thoroughly proficient in the Tripitaka.
At that time, Ānanda and the bhikṣus were at the Bamboo Grove Monastery. There, one bhikṣu spoke this verse:
"If a person lives for a hundred years And does not see a white water-heron, It is not as good as being born for a single day And obtaining the sight of a white water-heron."
When Ānanda heard this, he said to that bhikṣu:
"What you have recited was not spoken by the Great Teacher.
Rather, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke thus:"
"If a person lives for a hundred years, Without understanding arising and ceasing;
It is not as good as living for a single day, And attaining the understanding of arising and ceasing."
"You should now know that there are two kinds of people in the world who constantly slander the holy teaching:
those who lack faith and are prone to anger, and those who, though they have faith, misunderstand it;
they falsely cling to the meaning of the sūtras like an elephant sinking into deep mud."
They shall surely suffer loss for themselves, because they lack wisdom;
listening with false understanding is as useless as poison—this should be known.
Therefore, those who are wise, having listened, are able to practice correctly.
"As the afflictions gradually fade away, you shall attain the fruit of liberation.
Having heard this instruction, he informed his teacher, who said:
"Ānanda is old and dim-sighted; he lacks the strength to remember and uphold [the teachings]."
"What you say is frequently forgotten and lost; it cannot necessarily be relied upon or trusted.
You should simply continue to recite and uphold it as before.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda came back again to listen and examine, and seeing that [the recitation] was based on erroneous speech, he reported this.
"Son! I have already told you that the Blessed One does not speak in such a manner.
Then those bhikṣus reported the words of their teacher in full to the Venerable One.
Having heard this, the Venerable One thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu was personally instructed by me, yet he does not heed my words; what can be done?
Even if it were the Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, or Mahākāśyapa, the situation would be the same."

"Those great virtuous ones have all already entered nirvana; yet by the power of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness and compassion, he is able to cause the Eye of the Dharma to remain in the world for a thousand years.
Thereupon, he lamented: "The venerable elders have already passed away, and those who are new do not practice in unison."
In silent contemplation, I consider my own body to be like a bird within its shell.
All past kinsmen have dispersed, and even my acquaintances have likewise passed away;
among all such acquaintances, none surpasses mindfulness within meditative concentration.
All the lamps of the world, which shine brightly to dispel the manifold darkness and are able to shatter ignorance and delusion— even these are all non-existent.
Those to be converted are boundless, yet the one who can guide them is but a single being.
"Like a solitary *caitya* in the wilderness, or the lone tree remaining in a ruined forest.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the bhikṣu Sanakavāsin:
"The Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having entrusted the teaching of the Blessed One to me, has entered parinirvāṇa."

I now entrust this to you and shall enter parinirvāṇa; you should protect it. In the country of Mardava, there is Mount Mūlasthāna where you should build a residence. In that country, there is the son of an elder whom the World-Honored One has already prophesied will become the master of the monastery.
Furthermore, within this kingdom there is a perfume seller named Gupta who shall have a son named Upagupta; you should ordain him as a monk.
The World-Honored One has prophesied that he shall be known as the Buddha Without Marks.
"However, after my parinirvāṇa, one hundred years hence, I shall perform great Buddha-work.
Having heard these words, Śaṇavāsa said:
"I shall do as the Upādhyāya instructs."
The Venerable One replied, “You should remain well-established; I shall enter parinirvāṇa, and I shall inform the King of this.
At that time, Ānanda again thought to himself:
"If I were to attain parinirvāṇa here, King Ajātaśatru and the city of Vaiśālī have long been at odds; they would certainly not share my bodily relics."
"If I were to attain parinirvāṇa within the city of Vaiśālī, King Ajātaśatru would not receive a share [of my relics].
It would be best for me now to attain final extinction within the waters of the Gaṅgā River."
Having formed this thought, he was about to depart.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru saw in a dream during sleep that the pole of his own parasol had broken; having seen this dream, the king suddenly woke up in alarm.
When the gatekeeper saw that the king had awakened from his sleep, he reported in full to the king the words entrusted to him by Ānanda.
Upon hearing these words, the king fainted on the ground; only after water was sprinkled upon him did he revive, saying these words:
"In what place has the Venerable Ānanda entered parinirvāṇa?"
Then Śaṅkhaka replied to the king in verse:
“This Venerable One is born from the Buddha; Following the Buddha, he guards the treasury of the Dharma.
Seeking to realize nirvāṇa and sever birth-and-death, For this reason, he has already set out for Vaiśālī.”
At that time, having heard these words, King Ajātaśatru prepared his fourfold army and proceeded to the banks of the Gaṅgā River.
Then, the devas who had long resided in the city of Vaiśālī spoke from the midst of the sky to the people, saying:
“The Venerable Ānanda, the Lamp of the World, Out of compassion for immeasurable multitudes of sentient beings;”
"Filled with a heart of sorrowful feeling, he is about to enter parinirvāṇa; he has now arrived at the city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī arrayed their fourfold army and proceeded to the riverbank.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, joined his palms, and said:
"The World-Honored One, whose eyes are like blue lotuses, has reached the end of conditioned existence and realized true extinction;
now you, O Benevolent One, likewise wish to seek parinirvāṇa—only pray, remain here and leave behind your physical body."
At that time, all the people of Vaiśālī also prostrated from afar and requested him to leave behind a physical relic.
Having seen this, the Venerable One thought thus and spoke these verses:
"I now wish to do so for Ajātaśatru, But the Licchavis harbor resentment in their hearts."
If the śarīra remains in Vaiśālī, the people of Rājagṛha will again be stricken with grief.
It would be fitting to give half to Rājagṛha and keep half for the city of Vaiśālī;
thus both places may reach a peaceful settlement without conflict, and each may offer worship according to their own wishes.
At that time, as the Venerable One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, this great earth shook in six ways.
Then, there was a rishi who, leading five hundred disciples, traveled through the air to the Venerable One’s location and, joining his palms, addressed him, saying: "O Mahābhāga!..."
"I now wish to go forth in this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination, and to become a bhikṣu.
At that time, the Venerable One thought to himself:
"How has my disciple come to this place?"
Thereupon, by means of his supernormal powers, he instantly cut off all paths for human passage within the water; as soon as the thought arose, five hundred disciples arrived simultaneously.
The Venerable One then transformed the water into dry land—an island where no human tracks remained—and granted the five hundred men the going-forth and full ordination.

While the formal proclamation (*jñapti*) was being made, those five hundred people attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*); at the third proclamation (*karmavācanā*), they severed all afflictions and realized arhatship.

Because this Great Sage (Mahākāśyapa) received full ordination (*upasampadā*) at midday while standing in the water, the people of that time called him "Midday" (*Madhyāhnika*) or "Water-Abider. [The original term is *Madhyandinna*: *madhya* means "middle" and *indina* means "day"; thus he was named after that, and called "Midday."
Some say it is Maudgalyāyana; "Maud" means "middle" and "galyāyana" means "water.
Because he went forth from home while in the water, he was given the name "Water-born" (Maudgalyāyana).
Regarding the one formerly known as Madhyantika, his name alone was mentioned previously without any detailed account of the reasons; therefore, I have provided this commentary to clarify them.
At that time, having completed his tasks, the Venerable One prostrated at Ānanda’s feet and spoke these words:
“The World-Honored One’s last convert, that Subhadra, has already attained parinirvāṇa. I too shall enter nirvāṇa before him; I do not wish to witness the passing of my upādhyāya.”
The Venerable One replied:

"Son! The World-Honored One entrusted the Teaching to Kāśyapa before entering parinirvāṇa; Mahākāśyapa then transmitted it to me, and I now transmit it to you. You must skillfully protect and uphold all the teachings."
The World-Honored One declared:
"In the kingdom of Kaśmīra, the requisites for bedding and seating are easily obtained; it is the foremost place for being in accord with meditative concentration."
The Buddha further prophesied of you:
"One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Madhyāntika who shall cause my teachings to spread throughout this country."
"Therefore, you should now propagate the holy transformation there. He replied, "I shall do so."

The Venerable Ānanda immediately manifested a supernormal transformation, entering parinirvāṇa like water extinguishing fire; he then divided his body in half, giving one half to Ajātaśatru and the other half to the assembly of Vaiśālī.
The verse says:
"With the vajra of sharp wisdom, he dissolved his own body and caused it to shatter;
half he gave to the King of the City-Lords, and half he gave to the people of Vaiśālī."
At that time, having obtained half of the body, the city of Vaiśālī constructed a stūpa and offered worship; King Ajātaśatru likewise constructed a stūpa at Pāṭaliputra and offered worship.
At that time, the Venerable Madhyāntika had this thought:
"My preceptor entrusted me with these words:
'The Buddha's teaching shall be propagated in the land of Kaśmīra.'"
The World-Honored One also prophesied:
"In a future age, there shall be a bhikṣu named Madhyāntika who, in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, will subdue a venomous dragon named Huṇḍa and cause my teaching to flourish."
"I should now fulfill the Great Master’s intention.

He immediately went to that kingdom and sat cross-legged. Since this kingdom was protected by a nāga, the nāga could not be subdued unless it was provoked; he therefore entered meditative concentration and caused the earth of this kingdom to quake in six ways.
Upon seeing the earth tremble, the dragon struck with thunder and lightning and sent down a torrential rain to terrify the Venerable One.

At that time, the Venerable One immediately entered the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*); though the dragon’s power was formidable, he could not even move a corner of the Bhikṣu’s robe.
The dragon immediately sent down hail upon the Venerable One, which transformed into celestial flowers falling in profusion.
The dragon, becoming even more enraged, further hurled axes, hatchets, and various other weapons, all of which were transformed into *kubjaka* flowers that scattered over his body.
A verse in the sky proclaims:
"When thunder and hail descend from the sky, they transform into exquisite lotus flowers;
even if swords and staves should approach, they all become various necklaces."
"The dragon manifested great wrathful power, and the mountain peaks all fell down;
yet the Venerable One, King of the Snowy Mountains, remained pure in radiance and unmoved.

Because of the power of his concentration on loving-kindness, neither fire, sword, nor poison could harm him. When the dragon witnessed this, he was struck with great wonder and approached the Venerable One, saying these words:
"Noble one! What do you require now? He replied:
"You may allow me a place where I can settle," the dragon said.
"This matter is difficult to accomplish."
The Venerable One said:
"The World-Honored One has commanded me to dwell here, and further stated:
'In the kingdom of Kaśmīra, requisites such as lodgings and bedding are easily obtained; it is the foremost place for being in accord with meditative concentration.'"
Question: "Is this a prediction (vyākaraṇa) made by the Buddha?
Answer: [As follows:]
"It is indeed so," the dragon said.
"How many grounds are required?"
He replied, "The place where he sat in the full lotus posture.
The dragon said:
"This is given as an offering.
The Venerable One sat cross-legged, pressing down the mouth of the Nine Valleys;
the dragon asked, "How many disciples does the Venerable One have?"
The Venerable One entered meditative concentration and perceived:
"Five hundred Arhats are coming to stay here.
The Dragon said:
“Do as you wish; if even one person is missing, I shall take back the land.
The Venerable One said, “So be it.”
"Wherever there is one who receives, there is a donor; I now wish to have all people come together to dwell in this place.
The nāga said, "As you please."
At that time, people arrived from the four directions; the Venerable One then personally led them to demarcate the boundaries of the cities, towns, and villages.
Once they had been settled, the people came together and said to the Venerable One, "We inhabitants have now received security and peace, but how shall we provide for our livelihood and sustenance?"
The Venerable One, by means of his supernormal powers, led the multitude to Mount Gandhamādana and addressed them, saying:
"All of you, pull up the roots of saffron."

At that time, there were great nāgas on Mount Gandhamādana who, seeing the incense being uprooted, all became enraged and intended to send down thunder and hail. The Venerable One then subdued them and informed them fully of what had occurred.
Nāga said: "Venerable One!
For how long shall the Tathāgata’s teaching remain?"
The Venerable One replied,
"He will remain in the world for a thousand years. The nāga said:
“We establish this covenant together that it shall be used as you wish for as long as the Tathāgata’s teaching remains in the world.
The Venerable One said,
“Excellent.”

He then took fragrant roots with each of those people and returned to Kaśmīra, where they planted and expanded them; thus, until the disappearance of the Buddha’s teaching, they have never allowed them to decline.

At that time, having ensured that all people from the four quarters were well settled, the Venerable One manifested various supernatural feats, causing all the donors and fellow practitioners of the holy life to rejoice, and then passed into *nirvāṇa* without remainder, like an extinguished fire.
Then those people each used ox-head sandalwood to cremate the remaining remains and immediately erected a stūpa at that site.
At that time, the Venerable Śaṇaka ordained Upagupta—translated here as "Little Protector"—and caused the Buddha’s teaching to spread widely. He then said to Upagupta:
"You should now know this!"
The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, entrusted his teachings to Mahākāśyapa and then entered nirvāṇa.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa likewise entrusted the teachings to my upādhyāya and entered nirvāṇa.
My preceptor, having entrusted me with the Dharma, has also entered parinirvāṇa; I now entrust you with the Dharma and shall likewise enter parinirvāṇa.
You should now properly protect and uphold the Noble Teaching, ensuring that it does not decline or perish.
"Whatever has been prescribed by the Buddha should all be respectfully practiced.

Having given these instructions, Śaṇaka, together with the donors and his fellow practitioners of the holy life, skillfully taught the Dharma until they were filled with joy; he then manifested various miraculous feats—flames shooting upward from his body and clear streams flowing downward—and entered the realm of the wondrous Nirvāṇa without remainder.

At that time, Upagupta entrusted the Dharma to the Venerable Kṣemadatta (translated into Chinese as Yougui, "Possessing Shame"). Once he had propagated and disseminated the teachings of the True Dharma, he in turn entrusted them to the Venerable Kṛṣṇa (in Sanskrit, Kṛṣṇa; translated into Chinese as Heise, "Black"), and subsequently entrusted them to the Venerable Sudarśana (in Sanskrit, Sudarśana).

All such great dragon-elephants have already passed away; the Great Master has entered parinirvāṇa, and the sun of the Buddha having set, the world is left without refuge. Thus, in due course, one hundred and ten years later—

At that time, the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī performed ten kinds of impure acts, which contravened the teachings established by the World-Honored One; they did not conform to the Sūtras nor rely upon the Vinaya, deviating from correct principle. Yet these bhikṣus regarded them as pure and practiced them all together, even though such matters were not to be found within the Sūtras or the Vinaya.

What are the ten? First, when the bhikṣus at that time perform an illegal and discordant *karmavācanā*, an illegal and concordant *karmavācanā*, or a legal and discordant *karmavācanā*, and the great assembly, upon hearing this proposal, grants their assent with loud voices—this is called the "purification through loud-voiced assent."
This is to contravene the Buddha’s teachings and deviate from correct principle; it does not accord with the Sūtras nor rely upon the Vinaya.

At that time, the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī, performing what is impure while regarding it as pure, saw this unrighteousness—how could they neglect it without inquiry, yet instead praise, proclaim, and collectively follow it?
Second, at times the bhikṣus perform illegal and discordant *karmavācanā*, illegal and concordant *karmavācanā*, or legal and discordant *karmavācanā*.
When others see this, they all rejoice in it; this is what is called "rejoicing in the pure dharma."

This is to contravene the Buddha’s teachings and deviate from correct principle; it does not accord with the Sūtras nor rely upon the Vinaya. Yet, at that time, the bhikṣus regarded it as pure, praising and proclaiming it, and all followed it together.

Third, if the bhikṣus dig the earth with their own hands or instruct others to do so, this is called the "purification by prior action" (*pūrvakṛta-śuddhi*); the detailed explanation is as above, and so on, until all practice it together.

Fourth, the bhikṣus store salt in tubes, handle it with their own hands, maintain possession of it, and use it as they please to mix with *kālika* (time-limited) medicines for consumption; this is called the "purification method regarding salt," which all together followed and practiced.

Fifth, when the bhikṣus have not yet traveled even one or half a *yojana*, they take separate meals; this is called the "Purity of Traveling on the Road" (*adhvāna-viśuddhi-dharma*), which all shall together observe and practice.

Sixth, when the bhikṣus do not perform the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food), they eat with two fingers; this is called the "two-finger pure rite" (*dvyaṅgulaviśuddhi*), which all followed accordingly.
Seventh, the bhikṣus shall drink alcohol mixed with water; this is called the "purification rite for treating illness," and they shall all practice it together.

Eighth, the bhikṣus shall take one *śoṇa* of milk and curd, mix them with water and stir them; they may drink this at improper times; this is called the "purification rite for curd-milk beverage" (*dadhimanda*), and they shall all practice it together.

Ninth, when the bhikṣus make a new sitting mat, they do not personally use it unless they have attached to it a patch from an old one the size of a single Buddha-span. This is called the purification rite for sitting mats, which all should collectively observe and practice.
Tenth, the bhikṣus themselves took fine alms bowls, wiped them clean with incense and flowers, and had a śrāmaṇera carry them from door to door, announcing to all people as follows:

"To all persons currently residing in the city of Vaiśālī, as well as to the merchants and travelers arriving from the four distant quarters: if you have any offerings—be they gold, silver, or cowries—to place within these bowls, you shall obtain great benefit and inexhaustible wealth and happiness."
Having obtained great profit, they divided all the gold and treasures among themselves; this was termed the "purification rite for gold and treasures.

This was a violation of the Buddha’s teachings and a departure from correct principle; it did not accord with the Sūtras nor rely upon the Vinaya. At that time, the bhikṣus performed impure acts while regarding them as pure, praising and proclaiming them so that all followed suit.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was in Vaiśālī. He had a disciple named Saṃgharakṣita (in Sanskrit: Sarvakāma), who was an Arhat dwelling in the eight liberations, possessing few desires, being content, and living with a restrained sense of occasion.

This person had a disciple in the village of Vāsava named Yaśas (in Sanskrit, Yaśas), who was also an Arhat dwelling in the eight liberations; he traveled through the human world with five hundred disciples and arrived at the city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, when the bhikṣus wished to distribute the communal goods, the official in charge came and addressed the Venerable Yaśas, saying:
"The Saṃgha has acquired some goods which we now wish to divide; you may come and receive your share."
He replied, "Venerable sir! From where was this profit obtained?"
"By whom was this bestowed?
He then related the matter in detail, exactly as he had obtained the object.
Having heard this, the Venerable One thought to himself:
"Is it only in this matter that an evil sore has arisen, or are there other matters as well?
He then entered meditative concentration to investigate and saw that, being lax regarding the precepts, he had committed various evil deeds and engaged in ten kinds of unrighteous acts.
Having seen this and desiring that the Dharma endure for a long time, he immediately went to where the Venerable Rādhagupta was, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Venerable One!..."

Is it appropriate for bhikṣus to perform such a formal act of collective consent (*sāmīcī*) with loud voices? In truth, this is contrary to the Dharma; yet when they see it being performed, does the great assembly consider this loud, collective consent to be in accordance with the Dharma?
The Venerable One asked:
"What is meant by 'dharmas agreed upon'? He replied:

"In this city of Vaiśālī, the bhikṣus perform illegal and discordant *karmavācanā*, illegal and concordant *karmavācanā*, and legal and discordant *karmavācanā*; yet the great assembly loudly consents to these matters. This is what is called the 'pure dharma of loud communal consent'."
"Is this matter appropriate?
The Venerable One replied, "It should not be so."
Question: "Where did the Tathāgata establish the prohibition against doing so? Answer:
"In the city of Campā. He asked again: "For whom?"
He replied, "For the group of six. He asked:
"What offense is incurred?
He replied, "The offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)."
"Venerable sir, this is the first matter; it contradicts the Buddha's teachings, deviates from correct principle, does not accord with the Sūtras, and does not rely upon the Vinaya."
Yet these bhikṣus perform impure acts while regarding them as pure, praising and proclaiming them, and all together following them.
Venerable sir, you ought not to neglect or overlook such evil matters.
Upon hearing these words, he remained silent and said,
"This matter is already known.
He was asked again:
“Venerable sir!
Is it appropriate to perform such an act of sympathetic joy?
The Venerable asked:
"What is meant by 'concurring with the Dharma'? He replied:

"When these bhikṣus perform an illegal and discordant *karmavācanā*, or perform an illegal but concordant *karmavācanā*, or perform a legal but discordant *karmavācanā*, and the assembly concurs with them—this is what is called 'concurring with the pure Dharma.'"
"Is this matter appropriate?
The Venerable One replied, "It should not be so."
Question: "Where did the Tathāgata establish the prohibition against doing so? Answer:
"In the city of Campā. He asked again, "For whom?"
He replied, "For the group of six. He asked:
"What offense does one incur?
He replied, "One incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing)."
“Venerable Sir! This is the second matter;
it is a transgression of the Buddha’s teachings, as explained at length above, and so forth, up to: Venerable Sir, you ought not to tolerate or neglect such an evil matter.”
He remained silent, having understood this matter.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir, is it proper to perform such an old practice as the *pārivāsika-śuddhi*?"
The Venerable One asked:
"What is meant by the 'purification through prior affairs'? He replied:
"These bhikṣus dig the earth with their own hands or instruct others to do so, yet the assembly considers this to be the 'purification through ancient practice.
Is this appropriate?"
The Venerable One said, "It should not be so. He asked:
"Where did the Tathāgata establish the prohibition against doing so? He replied, "In Śrāvastī."
He asked again, "For whom? He replied:
“[It was] for the group of six. Question:
“What offense was committed?”
He replied, "One incurs an offense of falling (pāyattika). "Venerable Sir!"
This is the third matter.
This indeed contravenes the Buddha’s teaching, as explained at length previously; even the Venerable One should not neglect or abandon such an evil deed.
He remained silent, for this matter was already known.
Again he asked:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Is the procedure for purifying through the salt-transaction like this?
The Venerable asked: "What is meant by the procedure for purifying through the salt-transaction?"

He replied: "These bhikṣus keep salt in tubes for their own use; they mix it with food that is to be consumed at the proper time and eat according to their desire, regarding this as 'salt-purification' (lavaṇa-śuddhi)."
"Is this appropriate? The Venerable One replied, "It should not be so."
Question: "Where did the Tathāgata establish the prohibition against doing so? Answer:
"In Rājagṛha. He asked again, "For whom?"
He replied, “For the Venerable Śāriputra. He asked:
"What offense does one incur? He replied,
"One incurs a pāyattika offense."
“Venerable Sir! This is the fourth matter; it is a transgression of the Buddha’s teaching. As explained at length above, the Venerable Sir should not neglect or overlook such an evil matter.”
He remained silent, for this matter was already known.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Is the practice of the path thus purified through cooperation?
The Venerable asked: "What is called the purification of the practice of the path?"
He replied, "These bhikṣus travel for one or even half a yojana and then take separate meals, considering this to be 'purity through traveling.
Is this appropriate?"
The Venerable One said, "It should not be so. He asked:
"Where did the Tathāgata establish the prohibition against doing so? He replied, "In Rājagṛha."
He asked again, "For whom? He replied:
"It was for Devadatta. He asked:
"What offense did he commit?"
He replied, "One incurs a pāyattika offense. "Venerable sir!"

This is the fifth matter; it constitutes a transgression of the Buddha’s teachings, as explained at length previously, up to the point that the Venerable One should not neglect or tolerate such evil conduct.
He remained silent, for this matter was already known.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Is the purification by two fingers performed in this manner?
The Venerable One asked,
"What is meant by 'purification by two fingers'?"
He replied: "These bhikṣus do not perform the ritual for leftover food (vighasa-kalpa), yet they eat with two fingers, considering this to be the 'two-finger purification' (dvyaṅguli-śuddhi).
Is this appropriate?"
The Venerable One said, "It should not be so. He asked:
"Where did the Tathāgata establish the prohibition against doing so? He replied, "In Śrāvastī."
He asked again, "For whom? He replied:
"Welcome," he said. He then asked: "What offense have you committed?"

The Venerable One asked,

He replied: "These bhikṣus have taken one *śoṇa* of milk and curd, mixed them with water, and stirred them together to drink at an improper time, regarding it as the 'purification by curd-milk juice' (*dadhimanda-śuddhi*)."
"Is this appropriate? The Venerable One replied, "It should not be so."
Question: "Where did the Tathāgata establish the prohibition against doing so? Answer:
“In Śrāvastī. He asked again, “For whom?”
He replied, "For seventeen groups of bhikṣus. He asked:
